Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Allah created knowledge (al-'ilm) from a green light, then made it speak twenty-eight letters of the origin of speech, and prepared them with the sound that is heard and uttered. So knowledge uttered them, and the first of all that was [.....] [an illegible word]. So it looked at some of them, and they became humble and lowly before their Lord, Exalted, and swayed in awe of Him, and prostrated, and so they became a hamzah. When Allah, Exalted, saw their humility, He extended it, lengthened it, and favoured it, and so it became an alif. Then He made the pen speak letter by letter, up to twenty-eight letters, and made them the basis of speech, the books, the sounds, the languages, and all the acts of worship until the Day of Resurrection. All of them are in Abjad."

And He made the alif, because of its humility, the key to His first name, and placed it before all the letters. As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, the scholars differed in its interpretation.

'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, he said: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing (A'lam)."

Abu Rawq narrated from al-Dahhak concerning His saying ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing."

Mujahid and Qatadah said: "Alif-Lam-Mim is a name of the names of the Qur'an."

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "(Alif) is the key to the name of Allah, (Lam) is the key to His name al-Latif, and (Mim) is the key to His name al-Majid."

Khalid narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Alif-Lam-Mim is an oath."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "(Alif) is the blessings (ala') of Allah, (Lam) is His kindness (lutf), and (Mim) is His dominion (mulk)."

In some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas: "(Alif) is Allah, (Lam) is Jibril, and Allah swore by them that this Book is ﴿without doubt in it﴾." It is possible that its meaning according to this interpretation is: Allah sent down this Book upon the tongue of Jibril to Muhammad (ﷺ).

The people of allusion (ahl al-ishara) said: "(Alif) is 'ana' (I), (Lam) is 'li' (for me), (Mim) is 'minni' (from me)."

It is related from 'Ali ibn Musa al-Rida, from Ja'far al-Sadiq, when he was asked about His saying ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, that he said: "In the Alif there are six attributes of the attributes of Allah: the beginning (ibtida'), because Allah began all creation; and (Alif) is the beginning of the letters; and equilibrium (istiwa'): He is just, not unjust; and (Alif) is even (mustawi) in its essence; and singleness (infirad): Allah is One (fard) and the Alif is one (fard); and the connection of creation to Allah, while Allah is not connected to creation: they need Him, and He is free of need of them. Likewise the Alif is not joined to a letter, the letters are joined, and it is detached from others; and Allah is distinct from all His creation in all His attributes; and its meaning is from affinity (ulfah). Just as Allah is the cause of the affinity of creation, so the Alif is the one upon which the letters have become affine, and it is the cause of their affinity."

The wise said: "The intellects of creation are unable at the beginning of His address, and that is the locus of understanding, so that they may know that there is no path for anyone to know the realities of His address except through their knowledge. So inability to know Allah is the reality of His address."

As for the grammatical position (mahall) of ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ in i'rab (grammatical inflection), it is in the nominative (raf') as the subject of the beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is what follows it. It was said: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ is a beginning, and ﴿Dhalika﴾ is another beginning, and ﴿al-Kitab﴾ is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first beginning.

**Dhalika:** The common readers (al-'Ammah) read ﴿dhalika﴾ with a fatha on the dhal, and likewise ﴿hadhihi﴾ and ﴿hatan﴾. Abu 'Amr permitted imalah (vowel-inclination) in these. The dhal is for the noun, the lam is a support ('imad), and the kaf is address (khitab), and it points to the absent (one).

**Al-Kitab:** in the sense of "the written" (al-maktub), like al-hisab (the reckoning) and al-'imad (the support). A poet said:

"I gave good news to my dependants when I saw a page
that came to you from the proofs, its book being recited."

[[Jami' al-Bayan li al-Tabari: 3/341.]]

Or its written (form), so the verbal noun is placed in the position of the noun, as one says of the created: "khalq" (creation), and of the formed: "tasvir" (formation), and as He said: "dirham min darb al-amir" (dirhams struck by the amir), meaning they are struck. Its root is from kutb, which is joining letters to one another, derived from the saying of the people: "kataba al-kharaz" (he bound the beads), when he strung them into two parts. The string of beads is called "kutbah," and its plural is "kutub."

Dhu al-Murrah said:

"And a lank (fara') hide, its cords tied with thongs,
loosened and its wrappings were fastened, so the kutub..."

[[al-Sihah: 1/208.]]

It is said: "katabtu al-baghl," when I tied its saddlebag and it was forbidden from its travel by its nature, and from this the soldiers are called "katibah" (battalion), and its plural is "kata'ib."

A poet said:

"And a battalion came, trailing
in iron, for them is a treasure."

They differed regarding this ﴿al-Kitab﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: "It is the Qur'an." On this view, ﴿dhalika﴾ means ﴿hadha﴾ (this), like His saying, Exalted: ﴿And that is Our argument which We gave to Ibrahim﴾ [6:83], meaning: this.

Khafaf ibn Nadbah al-Sulami said:

"If my horses have been struck in their midst,
then rely on an eye, and aim at Malik.
I say to him, while the spear bends its back:
'Look carefully, Khafaf, that I am that one (dhalik)!'"

He means [this].

Abu al-Duha narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Its meaning is: that is the Book which I informed you that I would direct to you."

'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib said: "That is the Book which I promised you on the Day of the Covenant."

Yaman ibn Ri'ab said: "That is the Book which I mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "It is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz)."

'Ikrimah said: "It is the Torah, the Gospel, and the earlier books."

al-Farra' said: "Allah, Exalted, promised His Prophet that He would send down to him a Book which water would not erase and which would not wear out through much repetition. When He sent down the Qur'an, He said: 'This is the Book which I promised you.'"

Ibn Kaysan said: "Its interpretation is that Allah, Exalted, sent down before al-Baqarah some dozen surahs, all of which the polytheists denied. Then He sent down Surat al-Baqarah after them, and said: ﴿That is the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an that preceded al-Baqarah."

It was said: "That is the Book which Malik ibn al-Sayf the Jew denied."

**La rayba fihi:** there is no doubt in it, that it is from Allah.

He said: ﴿Guidance﴾, meaning: it is guidance. The sentence ends at His saying ﴿fihi﴾ (in it). It was said: "Huwa" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: guiding; its estimated meaning being: there is no doubt in its guidance for the God-fearing.

The People of Meanings said: "Its outward form is a negation, and its inward meaning is a prohibition, meaning: do not doubt it," like His saying, Exalted: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no disputing during the pilgrimage﴾ [2:197], meaning: do not commit obscenity, do not commit wickedness, and do not dispute about the guidance, the clarification, and what a person is guided by and made clear by.

**Chapter on taqwa (God-consciousness)**

﴿Guidance for those who are God-conscious (al-muttaqin)﴾: know that taqwa (God-consciousness) is originally from *waqa*, from *waqaytu* (I protected), so the waw was changed to ta', like *al-tukalan* (reliance), whose origin is *wukalan* from *wakaltu* (I entrusted); and *al-takhamah* (indigestion), whose origin is *wukhamah*, from *wakhama mi'datuhu* (his stomach was upset) when he could not digest.

The scholars differed concerning the meaning of taqwa and the reality of the muttaqi (the God-conscious person).

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The summary of taqwa is in the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct...﴾ [16:90], the verse."

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 1/82.]] [62]

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The muttaqi is the one who guards against shirk (polytheism), the major sins, and the indecencies."

Ibn 'Umar said: "Taqwa is that one does not see himself as better than anyone."

al-Hasan said: "The muttaqi is the one who says to everyone he sees: 'This one is better than me.'"

'Umar ibn al-Khattab said to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "Tell me about taqwa." He said: "Have you taken a path full of thorns?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And what did you do in it?" He said: "I was cautious and I gathered up my garments." Ka'b said: "That is taqwa."

Ibn al-Mu'tazz versified it:

"Leave off sins, small and great,
that is taqwa.
Placing your foot carefully upon the ground of thorns,
guarding against what you see.
Do not belittle a small sin,
for mountains are made of pebbles."

[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/162.]]

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "Taqwa is not standing in prayer by night and fasting by day with mixing in between. Rather, taqwa is leaving what Allah has forbidden and performing what Allah has made obligatory. Whatever is provided after that is good upon good."

It was said to Talq ibn Habib: "Describe taqwa for us." He said: "Taqwa is an act which Allah seeks, upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah. And taqwa is leaving disobedience to Allah, upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah."

Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah said: "A man is not God-conscious until he guards against greed and guards against anger."

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "The one who is God-conscious is one who does not violate what is sacred (li muharram la tuharram), meaning within the sanctuary (al-haram)."

Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "The muttaqi is the one who leaves what he is not sure is permissible, out of caution regarding what may be harmful."

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The God-conscious were named only because they leave what is not harmful, out of caution against falling into what is harmful."

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 1/83.]] [63]

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 2, verses 1–7 (part 2 of 3)**

Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Fudayl said: Piety (taqwa, God-consciousness) is that a person loves for others what he loves for himself.

Al-Junayd ibn Muhammad said: The pious person is not one who loves for people what he loves for himself. Rather, the pious person is one who loves for people more than he loves for himself. Do you know what happened to my teacher Sari ibn al-Mughallis? One day a friend of his greeted him, and he returned the greeting while frowning and not welcoming him. I asked him about this, and he said: "It has reached me that when a Muslim greets his brother and his brother returns the greeting, a hundred mercies are divided between them: ninety for the two of them, and ten for the other. So I wished that the ninety should be for him."

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: The pious person is one who has no adversary.

Sari ibn al-Mughallis said: The pious person is one who hates himself.

Al-Shibli said: The pious person is one who seeks nothing other than God.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: The truest word the Arabs ever spoke is the verse of Labid:
"Surely everything other than God is vain." [Lisan al-Arab: 5/351]

Al-Thawri said: The pious person is one who has shunned the world and kept little of it.

Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Maqri said: It is keeping away from everything that distances you from God.

Al-Qasim ibn al-Qasim said: It is safeguarding the etiquettes of the Shari'ah (sacred law).

Abu Zayd said: It is abstaining from all doubtful matters (shubuhat).

He also said: The pious person is one who, when he speaks, speaks for God; when he is silent, is silent for God; and when he mentions something, mentions it for God, exalted is He.

Al-Fudayl said: A servant does not become one of the pious until his enemy feels safe from him just as his friend does.

Sahl said: The pious person is one who has disowned his own power and strength.

He also said: Piety is that God does not see you where He has forbidden you, and does not miss you where He has commanded you.

It was also said: Piety is following the example of the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was said: Piety is that you guard your heart against heedlessness, your self against desires, your throat against pleasures, and your limbs against sins. Then it is hoped for you to attain what has dominion over the earth and the heavens.

Abu al-Qasim (Hakim) said: Piety is good character.

Some of them said: A man's piety may be known by three things: good trust in God regarding what has not been attained, good contentment regarding what has been attained, and good patience regarding what has been lost.

It was said: The pious person is one who guards himself against following his desire.

Malik said: Wahb ibn Kaysan related to us that some jurists of Madinah wrote to Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that the people of piety have signs by which they are recognized: patience in trials, contentment with the decree, gratitude for blessings, and humility before the rulings of the Qur'an.

Maymun ibn Mihran said: A man does not become pious until he is more strict in calling himself to account than a miserly partner and an oppressive ruler.

Abu Turab said: Before piety there are obstacles, and whoever does not pass them does not attain it: choosing hardship over ease, choosing speech that is necessary over excess, choosing humility over honor, choosing exertion over comfort, and choosing death over life.

Some of the wise said: A man does not reach the summit (sanam) of piety unless he is such that, if what is in his heart were placed on a tray and carried around the market, he would not be ashamed of anything in it.

It was said: Piety is that you adorn your inner self for the Truth just as you adorn your outward self for the people.

Abu al-Darda' said:
"A man wishes to be given his desire,
but God refuses except what He wills.
The man says: 'My gain and my treasure'—
and the fear of God is the best of what is gained."
[Al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/25]

**Section on Faith (iman)**

"Those who believe in the unseen" (alladhina yu'minuna bil-ghayb).

Know that the reality of faith (iman) is affirmation (tasdiq) by the heart, because the address directed to them with the word "believe" (amanu) is in the language of the Arabs, and the Arabs knew faith only as affirmation. Its meaning in the language was not transferred to another meaning, for had there been a transfer from the lexical meaning, it would have been transmitted, as it was transmitted regarding prayer (salat), whose original meaning is supplication.

Since this is the case, we are obliged to take the command according to what their language requires. Such is the saying of God, exalted, in the story of Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, and his sons: ﴿You will not be believed by us even if we are truthful﴾ [Surah Yusuf 12:17], meaning: you will not be taken as one who affirms us.

Another indication from this verse is that when He mentioned faith, He linked it to the unseen, so that it would be known that it is affirmation of the report concerning what is unseen. Then He singled it out from the rest of the obligatory acts of worship of the body and of wealth, saying: ﴿and who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them﴾.

Another proof is that wherever God mentions faith, He attributes it to the heart, saying: ﴿Among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths, but their hearts have not believed﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah 5:41], and He said: ﴿while his heart is at peace with faith﴾, and He said: ﴿Those—He has written faith into their hearts﴾ [Surah al-Mujadilah 58:22]. Similar examples are many.

As for the position of Islam (islam) relative to faith, it is like the position of the sun relative to light: every sun is light, but not every light is a sun; and every musk is fragrant, but not every fragrance is musk. Likewise, every faith is Islam, but not every Islam is faith, when it is not affirmation. This is because Islam is submission and humility. This is indicated by God's saying: ﴿The bedouins say, "We have believed." Say: "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [Surah al-Hujurat 49:14], out of fear of the sword.

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Faith is secret," and he pointed to his chest, "and Islam is public" [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 1/86] [63]. And his (ﷺ) saying: "O assembly of those who have submitted with their tongues, while faith has not entered their hearts!" [Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/585, no. 8021] [65].

Likewise, his answer to Jibril differed regarding Islam and faith: he answered regarding faith with affirmation, and regarding Islam with the obligations of the religion. This is what was related by Abu Burayda, whose name is Yahya ibn Ma'mar, who said: The first to speak about qadar (divine decree) in Basra was Sa'id al-Juhani. I and Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Himyari set out, either for hajj or for 'umrah, and we said: "If we meet one of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), we will ask him about what this man says regarding qadar." We happened upon Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab entering the mosque, so I and my companion flanked him, one of us on his right and the other on his left. I thought my companion would leave the speaking to me, so I said: "Abu Abd al-Rahman, there have appeared before us people who recite the Qur'an and seek knowledge," and he mentioned from their speech that "they claim there is no qadar, and that the matter is newly begun." He said: "When you meet them, tell them that I am innocent of them and they are innocent of me. By Him by whom Abd Allah ibn Umar swears, if one of them had gold equal to Mount Uhud and spent it, God would not accept it from him until he believes in qadar."

Then he said: My father, Umar ibn al-Khattab, related to us: "While we were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) one day, there came upon us a man with exceedingly white garments and exceedingly black hair, showing no trace of travel, and none of us knew him. He sat down beside the Prophet (ﷺ), leaned his knees against his knees, placed his palms on his thighs, and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about Islam.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Islam is that you testify that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, establish prayer, give zakat, fast the month of Ramadan, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to do so.' He said: 'You have spoken the truth.' He said: We were astonished at him, asking and then affirming! He said: 'Tell me about faith.' He said: 'That you believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in qadar, its good and its evil.' He said: 'Tell me about ihsan (excellence).' He said: 'That you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you.' He said: 'Tell me about the Hour.' He said: 'The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking.' He said: 'Tell me about its signs.' He said: 'That the slave-girl gives birth to her mistress, and that you see the barefoot, naked, destitute herdsmen of sheep competing in building tall buildings.'" He said: Then he went off, and we remained for a while, and then he said: "O Umar, who was the questioner?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "That was Jibril, peace be upon him, who came to you to teach you your religion" [Sahih Muslim: 1/28–29, in full] [Note: the text as given].

Then the affirmation of the tongue and the actions of the body is called faith (iman) by way of some relation and some kind of closeness, because they are among its laws, its extensions, its signs, and its indications, just as we say: "I saw joy in the face of so-and-so," and "I saw the knowledge of Zayd in his book," while joy and knowledge are in the heart.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Faith has seventy-some branches, the lowest of which is removing harm from the road, and the highest of which is the testimony that there is no god but God" [66] [Musnad Ahmad: 2/445; Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/36].

And from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Faith has seventy-some branches, and modesty (haya') is a branch of faith" [67] [Sahih Muslim: 1/46].

Al-Hasan ibn Ali said: Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honor his face, related to me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Faith is knowledge with the heart, affirmation with the tongue, and action with the limbs" [68] [al-Mu'jam al-Awsat: 6/226].

And from Ali ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-Abidin, who said: My father related to us, the master of the youth of the people of Paradise, who said: My father related to us, the master of the successors (awsiya'), who said: Muhammad, the master of the prophets, related to us, who said: "Faith is a spoken word, an acted deed, recognition by the intellects, and following the Messenger" [72] [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 1/86].

As for the unseen (al-ghayb), it is what is hidden from the eyes and fixed in the hearts. It is a verbal noun (masdar) placed in the position of a noun, so the absent one is called ghayb, just as the fasting person is called sawm, the visitor is called zawr, and the one who is just is called 'adl.

Al-Rabi' ibn Abi al-'Aliyah, on ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾, said: They believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, its Paradise, its Fire, and its meeting, and they believe in life after death and in resurrection. All of this is unseen.

Amr ibn al-Aswad, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, on ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾, said: [it means] in God. Whoever believes in God has believed in the unseen [Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/43].

Sufyan, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, on His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾, said: The unseen is the Qur'an. Al-Kalbi said: [it means] what has been revealed of the Qur'an and what has not yet come.

Al-Dahhak said: The unseen is "there is no god but God" and what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Waqid said: It means revelation (wahy). Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ [Surah al-Najm 53:35], and His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen; He does not reveal His unseen to anyone﴾ [Surah al-Jinn 72:26], and His saying: ﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾ [Surah al-Takwir 81:24].

Al-Hasan said: It means the Hereafter. Abd Allah ibn Hani said: It is what was hidden from them of the sciences of the Qur'an.

Zayd ibn Aslam related from his father, from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), that he said: "I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Do you know which of the people of faith (ahl al-iman) is the most excellent?' They said: 'O Messenger of God, the angels.' He said: 'They are so, and they deserve that, and what prevents them, since God has placed them in the rank in which He placed them? Rather, others too [are like that].'" We said: "O Messenger of God, the prophets?" He said: "They are so, and they deserve that, and what prevents them? Rather, others too." We said: "O Messenger of God, then who are they?" He said: "People who will come after me, who are in the loins of men, who will believe in me though they have not seen me, who will find the leaf hung up and act upon what is in it. These are the most excellent of the people of faith in faith" [73] [Musnad Abi Ya'la: 1/147].

Al-Hasan related, from al-Harith ibn Qays, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "Before God is what you have preceded us in, O companions of Muhammad, of seeing the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "We, before God, count your faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) though you did not see him. Then Abd Allah said: 'The matter of Muhammad was clear to whoever saw him. By Him besides whom there is no god, no believer has believed more excellently than the faith of the unseen.' Then he recited: ﴿those who believe in the unseen and establish prayer﴾." That is, they perpetuate it, perform it continually, and guard it at its times, with its bowings, prostrations, rights, and limits. Everyone who persists in something and performs it is called its establisher (muqim); it is said: "So-and-so established the hajj among the people," and "the people established their market," and they did not suspend it. A poet said:
"So do not hurry your affair, but make it lasting;
for your staff has not prayed (salla) like one who keeps it up."
[Taj al-'Arus: 8/295]
That is, he meant by prayer here the five prayers, and mentioned it in the singular, as in His saying: ﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah 2:213], meaning the books. The original meaning of prayer (salah) in the language is supplication (du'a'). Then a worship was added to it, and its whole was called prayer, because the predominant feature of this worship is supplication.

Abu Hatim al-Kharazmi said: Its derivation is from al-Sala, which is fire. Its origin is gentleness and good treatment of a thing. That is because when a crooked piece of wood is to be straightened, they heat it over fire and straighten it between two pieces of wood. Therefore the one who prays should be deliberate in his prayer, guard its limits outwardly and inwardly, and not hasten or be careless in it. A poet said:
"So do not hurry your affair, but make it lasting;
for your staff has not prayed like one who keeps it up."
That is, your affair is not straightened like a building.

﴿And from what We have provided for them﴾: We gave them. Provision (rizq), according to the People of the Sunnah, is that from which benefit has been validly obtained. If it is food, it is to be eaten; if it is clothing, it is to be worn and protected; if it is a dwelling, its benefit is in residing in it. The one who benefits may benefit from what has been made available for benefit in two ways: lawfully and unlawfully. Therefore we say that God provides both the lawful and the unlawful. [The original meaning of] provision in the language is portion and fortune.

﴿spend﴾: give in charity. The original meaning of spending (infaq) is removal from the hand or from ownership. It is said: "The goods sold were spent (nafaqa) when many buyers came and they left quickly," and "the animal was spent (nafaqat) when its spirit left it." The nafiqa' of the jerboa (yarbu') comes from this, because when it is approached from the direction of the qasi'a (its outer burrow), it strikes the nafiqa' with its head, and so it exits (infaqa wa anfaqa) from it. And the nafaq is a tunnel in the earth that has an outlet to another place from which one emerges.

﴿And those who believe﴾: that is, affirm (yusaddiqun) ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾: O Muhammad, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and what was sent down before you﴾: meaning the earlier books, such as the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa, the Psalms (Zabur), the Gospel (Injil), and others.

﴿and the Hereafter﴾: that is, the Abode of the Hereafter. It is called the Hereafter (akhirah) because it comes after this world, and because it was delayed until the world perishes and then it comes into being.

﴿they are certain﴾: they know and are certain that it will come. The pronoun ﴿hum﴾ has entered as emphasis; the Kufans call it 'imad (support), and the Basrans call it fasl (separator).

﴿Those﴾: the people of this description. Ula'ika (those) is a noun built on kasra, and has no singular from its own form. The kaf is an address marker. The position of ﴿ula'ika﴾ in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is nominative (raf') as subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in His saying ﴿upon guidance﴾: right direction, clarity, and correctness; ﴿from their Lord﴾. ﴿Ula'ika﴾ is a subject, and ﴿hum﴾ is a support (ʿimad). ﴿The successful ones﴾ is the predicate of the subject: they are the saved, the victorious; they succeeded in Paradise and were saved from the Fire. It was also said: they are the ones who remain in reward and everlasting bliss.

The original meaning of success (falah) in the language is survival (baqa'). Labid said:
"We alight in lands all of which were alighted in before us,
and we hope for survival after 'Ad and Himyar."
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/182]
Another said:
"If a living man could attain survival,
the fighters of the spears would have attained it,
Abu Bara'—the mud of the slanderer (al-misyah)." [Taj al-'Arus: 2/146; Lisan al-Arab: 2/454, where it reads "Abu Bara' mudrat al-sayyah," and al-misyah is one who goes about spreading slander and evil in the land.]

Mujahid said: Four verses at the beginning of this surah were revealed concerning the believers, two verses after them were revealed concerning the disbelievers, and thirteen verses after them were revealed concerning the hypocrites.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾: meaning the polytheists of the Arabs. Al-Dahhak said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and five of his household. Al-Kalbi said: It means the Jews. It was also said: the hypocrites.

Disbelief (kufr) is denial and rejection. Its origin is from kufr, which is covering and concealing. From this comes the saying for the plowman: kafir, because he covers the seed. God, exalted, said: ﴿it pleases the farmers (kuffar) with its growth﴾ [Surah al-Hadid 57:20], meaning the sowers. The sea is also called kafir, and the night is called kafir. Labid said:
"Until when it cast a hand into the kafir,
and the darkness of the gaps (thughur) concealed its gloom,
on a night whose clouds concealed the stars."
[Lisan al-Arab: 5/147; Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 1/162]
From this comes al-mutakaffir bil-silah (one who covers himself with weapons), who is the armored man whose weapon covers his entire body.

The disbeliever is called kafir because he conceals the truth, and the Oneness of God and His blessings, and the prophethood of His prophets.

﴿It is all the same for them﴾: that is, it is one and equal for them. It is a noun derived from equality (tasawi).

Al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan), commentary on surah 2, verses 1–7 (part 3 of 3):

ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ: I warned them and cautioned them.

The scholars of meaning (ahl al-ma'ani) said: indhar (warning) and i'lam (informing) together with tahdhir (cautioning). It is said: "anzartuhum fa-nadharu," meaning "I informed them so they knew." In the proverb: "wa-qad a'dhara man andhar" (he who warns has indeed given an excuse). Regarding His words ﴿أَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ﴾ and its sisters, there are four readings:

Making both hamzas clear (tahqiq al-hamzatayn), which is the dialect of Tamim and the reading of the people of Kufa, because the interrogative alif entered upon the alif of qat' (the cutting hamza), the hamza that was joined to the verb's initial fa' was dropped, and its madd was substituted for it, out of dislike of combining two hamzas. This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

Inserting an alif between the two hamzas, which is the reading of the people of Syria in the narration of Hisham and one of the two narrations from Abu 'Amr.

The poet said:
"Tattalat fa-istashrafat qarabatuhu... fa-qalna lahu: a-anta Zayd, la bal qamar"
[Thus it is in the manuscript, and we have not found it.]

And the khabar (declarative form) is used, relying on the answer to the interrogative; this is the reading of al-Zuhri.

ـأَمْ: a conjunction coordinating with the interrogative.

لَمْ: a particle of jazm (apocopation) that does not come before anything except a verb, because jazm is specific to verbs.

﴿لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ... ﴿لَمْ تُنذِرْهُمْ﴾: ﴿تُنذِرْهُمْ﴾ means "you warn them"; ﴿لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ means "they will not believe." This verse is specific to those upon whom the word of punishment has been decreed in God's prior knowledge. Its outward form is an inshā' (a performative/imperative-type statement), but its meaning is an ikhbar (a report). Then he mentioned the cause of their refusal to believe, saying:

﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ﴾: that is, He sealed upon their hearts. Khatm (sealing) and tab' (stamping) have one meaning, and both are covering a thing [and securing it] [The manuscript is illegible; what we have written is from al-Qurtubi's tafsir: 1/186.] so that nothing else can enter it.

So the meaning of the verse: God stamped and locked and bolted their hearts, so they neither comprehend a report nor understand it. This is supported by His words: ﴿أَمْ عَلَى قُلُوبٍ أَقْفَالُهَا﴾ [Muhammad: 24].

Some of them said: the meaning of tab' and khatm is that God judged them to be disbelievers and wretched, as one says to a man: "I have sealed upon you that you will never prosper."

﴿وَعَلَى سَمْعِهِمْ﴾: so they do not hear the truth and do not benefit from it. He used the singular "sam'" because it is a maṣdar (verbal noun), and maṣdars are neither dualized nor pluralized. It was also said that he meant the hearing of each one of them, as one says: "Bring me the head of two rams," meaning the head of each of them. The poet said:
"Kulu fi nisfi batnikum ta'ishu... fa-inna zamanakum zaman khamis"

Sibawayh said: the singular of "sam'" indicates the plural, since there is no singularization of two plurals, as in His words: ﴿يُخْرِجُهُم مِّنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ﴾, meaning "the lights."

The poet al-Ra'i said:
"Bihā judhaf al-ḥasrā fa-ammā 'iẓāmuhā... fa-bīḍun wa-ammā jilduhā fa-ṣalīb"
[Its speaker is 'Alqama ibn 'Abda; see his Diwan: 27 and Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/324.]

Ibn 'Ablah read: ﴿وَعَلَى أَسْمَارِهِمْ﴾ [and upon their hearings], and the sentence is complete at His words ﴿وَعَلَى سَمْعِهِمْ﴾.

Then He said: ﴿وَعَلَى أَبْصَارِهِمْ غِشَاوَةٌ﴾: that is, a covering and a veil, so they do not see the truth. From it comes ghashiyat al-sarj (the saddle's covering). Al-Mufaddal ibn Muhammad al-Dabbi read ﴿غِشَاوَةً﴾ in the accusative, as if he implied a verb or a clause governing the sealing: that is, "and He placed upon their sights a covering." This is supported by His words: ﴿وَجَعَلَ عَلَى بَصَرِهِ غِشَاوَةً﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 23].

Al-Hasan read ﴿غُشَاوَةٌ﴾ with a damma on the ghayn; al-Khudri read ﴿غَشَاوَةٌ﴾ with a fatha on the ghayn; and the companions of 'Abd Allah read ﴿غَشْوَةٌ﴾ with a fatha on the ghayn and without an alif.

﴿وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾: killing and captivity in this world, and the painful punishment in the Hereafter. 'Adhab (punishment) is everything that burdens a person and is hard upon him; from it comes: "'adhhabahu al-siwat" (the whip tormented him), in terms of the presence of pain in it. Al-Khalil said: 'adhab is what prevents a person from his desire; from it comes "al-ma' al-'adhb" (sweet water), because it prevents thirst.

Then it was revealed concerning the hypocrites: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul al-Khazraji, Mu'attib ibn Bishr, Jadd ibn Qays, and their companions, when they said: "Come, let us make a pact by which we may be safe from Muhammad and his companions, and at the same time remain holding to our religion." So they agreed to profess the word of faith with their tongues while believing the opposite, and most of them were from the Jews. Then God said:

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 2, verses 1–7 (part 1 of 3)**

Madani (revealed in Medina). It has two hundred and eighty-six verses according to the Kufan count (al-'Adad al-Kufi). It is the "sanad" (support) of the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali (peace be upon him). It contains twenty-five thousand and five hundred letters, and six thousand one hundred and twenty-one words.

'Abd Allah ibn Hamid informed us, by my reading to him: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yusuf informed us: Ya'qub ibn Sufyan al-Saghir narrated to us: Ya'qub ibn Sufyan al-Kabir narrated to us: Hisham ibn 'Ammar narrated to us: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us: Shu'ayb ibn Zurayn narrated to us, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from 'Ikrimah, who said: "The first surah revealed in Medina was Surat al-Baqarah."

**Its virtues:**

Abu al-Hasan 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Tabarani informed us of it: Di'lij ibn Ahmad al-Shajari informed us in Baghdad: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Harun narrated to us: Khandaf narrated to us, from 'Ali: Hassan ibn Ibrahim narrated to us: Khalid ibn Shu'ayb al-Muzani narrated to us, from Abu Hazim, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, everything has a summit, and the summit of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqarah. Whoever recites it in his house at night, a devil will not enter his house for three nights, and whoever recites it in his house by day, a devil will not enter his house for three days."

[[Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/565, no. 2549.]] [59]

And Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn Ahmad al-Murattib informed us, by my reading to him: Abu 'Amr ibn Mutarrif narrated to us: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn al-Musayyab narrated to us: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Husayn narrated to us: Yusuf ibn al-Asbat narrated to us: Hassan ibn al-Muhajir narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Learn al-Baqarah, for taking it is a blessing, leaving it is a regret, and the people of falsehood (al-batalah) cannot master it."

[[Musnad Ahmad: 5/352.]] [60]

Abu al-Husayn 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Muqri informed us: Abu Ahmad 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ali al-Hafiz narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Mandah informed us: Abu Mus'ab narrated to us: 'Imran ibn Talhah al-Laythi narrated to us, from Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) sent out a detachment, then followed them, examining them on their recitation. A man from among them came, and he said: "What do you have of the Qur'an?" until he reached the last of them, who was the youngest of them in age. He said: "What do you have of the Qur'an?" He said: "Such and such, and Surat al-Baqarah." He said: "Go out, and this one is trustworthy over you." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, he is the youngest of us in age." He said: "He has Surat al-Baqarah."

[[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 4/234, with variation.]] [61]

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾. The scholars differed concerning the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-mu'jamah) with which surahs begin. Many of them held that they are among the ambiguous (mutashabihat) matters whose knowledge Allah has reserved for Himself. So we believe in their revelation and we entrust their interpretation (ta'wil) to Allah.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Every book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur'an is the openings of the surahs."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) said: "Every book has an essence, and the essence of this Book is the letters of spelling (huruf al-tahajji)."

Others explained them. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "They are the names of Allah, broken up. If people were to arrange them well, they would know the Greatest Name of Allah. Do you not see that you say: ﴿Alif-Lam-Ra﴾ and you say: ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ and you say: ﴿Nun﴾, and it becomes ﴿al-Rahman﴾? So it is in this manner with the rest of them, except that we cannot pronounce them joined together or combine them."

Qatadah said: "They are the names of the Qur'an."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "They are names for the surahs that begin with them."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are oaths which Allah swore by," and it is related that "they are a praise which Allah praised Himself with."

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "There is no letter among them except that it is the key to a name of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and there is no letter among them except that it is in the (time of) affliction and trial (bala'), and there is no letter among them except that it is in the term of one people and the appointed times of others."

'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya said: "The meaning of these letters is that Allah mentioned them, saying: 'Hear them broken up, so that when they come to you joined together, you will have known them before that.' Likewise, children are first taught them broken up. Allah made them hear them broken up and separate, so that they would recognize them when they came to them, and then He made them hear them joined together."

Abu Rawq said: "They are written for the disbelievers. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite aloud in all the prayers, and the polytheists would say: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, so that you may overcome﴾ [41:26]. So they would sometimes clap, sometimes whistle, and sometimes utter (nonsense) in order to confuse the Prophet (ﷺ). When the Messenger of Allah saw that, he recited quietly in the noon and afternoon prayers and recited aloud in the others, and they would harass him and hurt him. So Allah, Exalted, revealed these disjointed letters. When they heard them, they remained bewildered and pondering, and they occupied themselves with that instead of harming and confusing him. Thus this was a cause of their listening and a path to their benefit."

Al-Akhfash said: "Allah swore only by the letters of spelling because of their nobility and excellence, and because they are the building blocks of His revealed Books in the different tongues, and the building blocks of His Beautiful Names and Sublime Attributes, and the foundations of the speech of the nations by which they communicate and by which they mention Allah and make Him one. It is as if He swore by these letters that the Qur'an is His Book and His speech, ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾."

Al-Naqib said: "They are an alert (nabhah) and a resumption (istinaf), so that it is known that the first speech has ended, like your saying: 'La, inna Zaydan dhahaba (No, Zayd has indeed gone).'"

The best and most solid of the sayings concerning it is that they are a demonstration of the miraculousness of the Qur'an and of the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), because each of these twenty-eight letters...

The Arabs express the part by the whole, as in His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them: bow down, they do not bow down﴾ [77:48], meaning: pray, they do not pray. And His saying: ﴿Prostrate and draw near﴾ [96:19]; so He expressed prayer by bowing and prostration, since they are among its pillars. And He said: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [3:182], meaning all your bodies. And He said: ﴿We will brand him upon the snout﴾ [68:16], meaning the nose; so He expressed the body by the hand, and the face by the nose.

A poet said about his wife:

"When I saw her matter in my line (khatti)...
and she was deceitful in lie and tricks,
I took from her by the horns of a grey-haired...
so my striking her with them and my cutting continued."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/132; Lisan al-'Arab: 10/480.]]

So he expressed by the word "khatti" the whole of the letters of Abjad.

A speaker says: "(Ab-Ta-Tha)," and he does not mean these four letters only, to the exclusion of others, but he means all of them. And I recited ﴿al-Hamdu lillah﴾, and he means the whole surah. Examples of this are many. And likewise Allah expressed by these letters the whole of the letters of spelling. The indication in this is that Allah, Exalted, alerted the Arabs and challenged them, saying: "I have sent down this Book from among the twenty-eight (letters) which are your language and your tongue, and upon which the building blocks of your speech rest. So if Muhammad is the Prophet who says it from his own self, then bring something like it, or ten surahs like it, or a surah like it." When they were unable to do that after exertion, it was established that it is a miracle.

This is the saying of al-Mubarrad and a group of the People of Meanings (Ahl al-Ma'ani). If it is said: "Can one letter be a return (reference) to the meaning? And do you find in the speech of the Arabs that one says: 'Alif-Lam-Mim, Zayd is standing'? and 'Ha-Mim, 'Amr has gone'?" We say: Yes, this is the habit of the Arabs: they point with a single word to all the letters and express by it about them.

The rajaz poet said:

"I said to her: 'Stop (qifi)!' so she said: 'Qaf (Q)!'
Do not think that we have forgotten the galloping (al-ijaf)."

[[Sharh Shafiyat Ibn al-Hajib: 4/264; the first line is found in Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/155.]]

That is, "Stop, you (qif anta)."

Sibawayh recited for Ghaylan:

"They called to them: 'Alla, join (them)!' 'Alla, ta!'
They all said together: 'Alla, fa!'"

[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/156.]]

That is: "Do you not ride?" so they said: "Alla, fa-rkabu (Then ride!)."

Qutrub recited about a girl:

"Umm 'Amr promised me that she would ta
anoint my head and delouse me, ta."

He meant: that she would come and wipe (my head).

al-Zajjaj recited:

"With good, goodness, and if evil, fa
and I do not desire evil except that you ta."

He meant by his saying "fa": and if (it is) evil, then evil is for him; and by his saying "ta": except that you will (it).

al-Akhfash said: "These letters are unvowelled (sakinah), because the letters of the alphabet are not inflected (la tu'rab). Rather, one pauses on each letter with the intention of pausing (niyyat al-sakt), and one must separate them by counting in the saying: wahid, ithnan, thalathah, arba'ah (one, two, three, four)."

Abu al-Najm said:

"I came from the presence of Ziyad like one bent with age,
my two legs drawing lines in a varied line,
writing in the road the letter Lam of the Alif."

When one introduces one of the conjunctive letters, one moves it.

Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

"When they gather upon an alif, and a waw,
and a ya', there arises a dispute among them."

These letters are masculine when pronounced, and feminine by considering the word (kalimah).

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "Allah created knowledge (al-'ilm) from a green light, then made it speak twenty-eight letters of the origin of speech, and prepared them with the sound that is heard and uttered. So knowledge uttered them, and the first of all that was [.....] [an illegible word]. So it looked at some of them, and they became humble and lowly before their Lord, Exalted, and swayed in awe of Him, and prostrated, and so they became a hamzah. When Allah, Exalted, saw their humility, He extended it, lengthened it, and favoured it, and so it became an alif. Then He made the pen speak letter by letter, up to twenty-eight letters, and made them the basis of speech, the books, the sounds, the languages, and all the acts of worship until the Day of Resurrection. All of them are in Abjad."

And He made the alif, because of its humility, the key to His first name, and placed it before all the letters. As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, the scholars differed in its interpretation.

'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, he said: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing (A'lam)."

Abu Rawq narrated from al-Dahhak concerning His saying ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing."

Mujahid and Qatadah said: "Alif-Lam-Mim is a name of the names of the Qur'an."

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "(Alif) is the key to the name of Allah, (Lam) is the key to His name al-Latif, and (Mim) is the key to His name al-Majid."

Khalid narrated from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Alif-Lam-Mim is an oath."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "(Alif) is the blessings (ala') of Allah, (Lam) is His kindness (lutf), and (Mim) is His dominion (mulk)."

In some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas: "(Alif) is Allah, (Lam) is Jibril, and Allah swore by them that this Book is ﴿without doubt in it﴾." It is possible that its meaning according to this interpretation is: Allah sent down this Book upon the tongue of Jibril to Muhammad (ﷺ).

The people of allusion (ahl al-ishara) said: "(Alif) is 'ana' (I), (Lam) is 'li' (for me), (Mim) is 'minni' (from me)."

It is related from 'Ali ibn Musa al-Rida, from Ja'far al-Sadiq, when he was asked about His saying ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾, that he said: "In the Alif there are six attributes of the attributes of Allah: the beginning (ibtida'), because Allah began all creation; and (Alif) is the beginning of the letters; and equilibrium (istiwa'): He is just, not unjust; and (Alif) is even (mustawi) in its essence; and singleness (infirad): Allah is One (fard) and the Alif is one (fard); and the connection of creation to Allah, while Allah is not connected to creation: they need Him, and He is free of need of them. Likewise the Alif is not joined to a letter, the letters are joined, and it is detached from others; and Allah is distinct from all His creation in all His attributes; and its meaning is from affinity (ulfah). Just as Allah is the cause of the affinity of creation, so the Alif is the one upon which the letters have become affine, and it is the cause of their affinity."

The wise said: "The intellects of creation are unable at the beginning of His address, and that is the locus of understanding, so that they may know that there is no path for anyone to know the realities of His address except through their knowledge. So inability to know Allah is the reality of His address."

As for the grammatical position (mahall) of ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ in i'rab (grammatical inflection), it is in the nominative (raf') as the subject of the beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is what follows it. It was said: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ is a beginning, and ﴿Dhalika﴾ is another beginning, and ﴿al-Kitab﴾ is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first beginning.

**Dhalika:** The common readers (al-'Ammah) read ﴿dhalika﴾ with a fatha on the dhal, and likewise ﴿hadhihi﴾ and ﴿hatan﴾. Abu 'Amr permitted imalah (vowel-inclination) in these. The dhal is for the noun, the lam is a support ('imad), and the kaf is address (khitab), and it points to the absent (one).

**Al-Kitab:** in the sense of "the written" (al-maktub), like al-hisab (the reckoning) and al-'imad (the support). A poet said:

"I gave good news to my dependants when I saw a page
that came to you from the proofs, its book being recited."

[[Jami' al-Bayan li al-Tabari: 3/341.]]

Or its written (form), so the verbal noun is placed in the position of the noun, as one says of the created: "khalq" (creation), and of the formed: "tasvir" (formation), and as He said: "dirham min darb al-amir" (dirhams struck by the amir), meaning they are struck. Its root is from kutb, which is joining letters to one another, derived from the saying of the people: "kataba al-kharaz" (he bound the beads), when he strung them into two parts. The string of beads is called "kutbah," and its plural is "kutub."

Dhu al-Murrah said:

"And a lank (fara') hide, its cords tied with thongs,
loosened and its wrappings were fastened, so the kutub..."

[[al-Sihah: 1/208.]]

It is said: "katabtu al-baghl," when I tied its saddlebag and it was forbidden from its travel by its nature, and from this the soldiers are called "katibah" (battalion), and its plural is "kata'ib."

A poet said:

"And a battalion came, trailing
in iron, for them is a treasure."

They differed regarding this ﴿al-Kitab﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: "It is the Qur'an." On this view, ﴿dhalika﴾ means ﴿hadha﴾ (this), like His saying, Exalted: ﴿And that is Our argument which We gave to Ibrahim﴾ [6:83], meaning: this.

Khafaf ibn Nadbah al-Sulami said:

"If my horses have been struck in their midst,
then rely on an eye, and aim at Malik.
I say to him, while the spear bends its back:
'Look carefully, Khafaf, that I am that one (dhalik)!'"

He means [this].

Abu al-Duha narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Its meaning is: that is the Book which I informed you that I would direct to you."

'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib said: "That is the Book which I promised you on the Day of the Covenant."

Yaman ibn Ri'ab said: "That is the Book which I mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "It is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz)."

'Ikrimah said: "It is the Torah, the Gospel, and the earlier books."

al-Farra' said: "Allah, Exalted, promised His Prophet that He would send down to him a Book which water would not erase and which would not wear out through much repetition. When He sent down the Qur'an, He said: 'This is the Book which I promised you.'"

Ibn Kaysan said: "Its interpretation is that Allah, Exalted, sent down before al-Baqarah some dozen surahs, all of which the polytheists denied. Then He sent down Surat al-Baqarah after them, and said: ﴿That is the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an that preceded al-Baqarah."

It was said: "That is the Book which Malik ibn al-Sayf the Jew denied."

**La rayba fihi:** there is no doubt in it, that it is from Allah.

He said: ﴿Guidance﴾, meaning: it is guidance. The sentence ends at His saying ﴿fihi﴾ (in it). It was said: "Huwa" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: guiding; its estimated meaning being: there is no doubt in its guidance for the God-fearing.

The People of Meanings said: "Its outward form is a negation, and its inward meaning is a prohibition, meaning: do not doubt it," like His saying, Exalted: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no disputing during the pilgrimage﴾ [2:197], meaning: do not commit obscenity, do not commit wickedness, and do not dispute about the guidance, the clarification, and what a person is guided by and made clear by.

**Chapter on taqwa (God-consciousness)**

﴿Guidance for those who are God-conscious (al-muttaqin)﴾: know that taqwa (God-consciousness) is originally from *waqa*, from *waqaytu* (I protected), so the waw was changed to ta', like *al-tukalan* (reliance), whose origin is *wukalan* from *wakaltu* (I entrusted); and *al-takhamah* (indigestion), whose origin is *wukhamah*, from *wakhama mi'datuhu* (his stomach was upset) when he could not digest.

The scholars differed concerning the meaning of taqwa and the reality of the muttaqi (the God-conscious person).

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The summary of taqwa is in the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct...﴾ [16:90], the verse."

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 1/82.]] [62]

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The muttaqi is the one who guards against shirk (polytheism), the major sins, and the indecencies."

Ibn 'Umar said: "Taqwa is that one does not see himself as better than anyone."

al-Hasan said: "The muttaqi is the one who says to everyone he sees: 'This one is better than me.'"

'Umar ibn al-Khattab said to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "Tell me about taqwa." He said: "Have you taken a path full of thorns?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And what did you do in it?" He said: "I was cautious and I gathered up my garments." Ka'b said: "That is taqwa."

Ibn al-Mu'tazz versified it:

"Leave off sins, small and great,
that is taqwa.
Placing your foot carefully upon the ground of thorns,
guarding against what you see.
Do not belittle a small sin,
for mountains are made of pebbles."

[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/162.]]

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "Taqwa is not standing in prayer by night and fasting by day with mixing in between. Rather, taqwa is leaving what Allah has forbidden and performing what Allah has made obligatory. Whatever is provided after that is good upon good."

It was said to Talq ibn Habib: "Describe taqwa for us." He said: "Taqwa is an act which Allah seeks, upon a light from Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah. And taqwa is leaving disobedience to Allah, upon a light from Allah, fearing the punishment of Allah."

Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah said: "A man is not God-conscious until he guards against greed and guards against anger."

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "The one who is God-conscious is one who does not violate what is sacred (li muharram la tuharram), meaning within the sanctuary (al-haram)."

Shahr ibn Hawshab said: "The muttaqi is the one who leaves what he is not sure is permissible, out of caution regarding what may be harmful."

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The God-conscious were named only because they leave what is not harmful, out of caution against falling into what is harmful."

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 1/83.]] [63]

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 2, verses 1–7 (part 2 of 3)**

Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Fudayl said: Piety (taqwa, God-consciousness) is that a person loves for others what he loves for himself.

Al-Junayd ibn Muhammad said: The pious person is not one who loves for people what he loves for himself. Rather, the pious person is one who loves for people more than he loves for himself. Do you know what happened to my teacher Sari ibn al-Mughallis? One day a friend of his greeted him, and he returned the greeting while frowning and not welcoming him. I asked him about this, and he said: "It has reached me that when a Muslim greets his brother and his brother returns the greeting, a hundred mercies are divided between them: ninety for the two of them, and ten for the other. So I wished that the ninety should be for him."

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: The pious person is one who has no adversary.

Sari ibn al-Mughallis said: The pious person is one who hates himself.

Al-Shibli said: The pious person is one who seeks nothing other than God.

Ja'far al-Sadiq said: The truest word the Arabs ever spoke is the verse of Labid:
"Surely everything other than God is vain." [Lisan al-Arab: 5/351]

Al-Thawri said: The pious person is one who has shunned the world and kept little of it.

Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Maqri said: It is keeping away from everything that distances you from God.

Al-Qasim ibn al-Qasim said: It is safeguarding the etiquettes of the Shari'ah (sacred law).

Abu Zayd said: It is abstaining from all doubtful matters (shubuhat).

He also said: The pious person is one who, when he speaks, speaks for God; when he is silent, is silent for God; and when he mentions something, mentions it for God, exalted is He.

Al-Fudayl said: A servant does not become one of the pious until his enemy feels safe from him just as his friend does.

Sahl said: The pious person is one who has disowned his own power and strength.

He also said: Piety is that God does not see you where He has forbidden you, and does not miss you where He has commanded you.

It was also said: Piety is following the example of the Prophet (ﷺ).

It was said: Piety is that you guard your heart against heedlessness, your self against desires, your throat against pleasures, and your limbs against sins. Then it is hoped for you to attain what has dominion over the earth and the heavens.

Abu al-Qasim (Hakim) said: Piety is good character.

Some of them said: A man's piety may be known by three things: good trust in God regarding what has not been attained, good contentment regarding what has been attained, and good patience regarding what has been lost.

It was said: The pious person is one who guards himself against following his desire.

Malik said: Wahb ibn Kaysan related to us that some jurists of Madinah wrote to Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that the people of piety have signs by which they are recognized: patience in trials, contentment with the decree, gratitude for blessings, and humility before the rulings of the Qur'an.

Maymun ibn Mihran said: A man does not become pious until he is more strict in calling himself to account than a miserly partner and an oppressive ruler.

Abu Turab said: Before piety there are obstacles, and whoever does not pass them does not attain it: choosing hardship over ease, choosing speech that is necessary over excess, choosing humility over honor, choosing exertion over comfort, and choosing death over life.

Some of the wise said: A man does not reach the summit (sanam) of piety unless he is such that, if what is in his heart were placed on a tray and carried around the market, he would not be ashamed of anything in it.

It was said: Piety is that you adorn your inner self for the Truth just as you adorn your outward self for the people.

Abu al-Darda' said:
"A man wishes to be given his desire,
but God refuses except what He wills.
The man says: 'My gain and my treasure'—
and the fear of God is the best of what is gained."
[Al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/25]

**Section on Faith (iman)**

"Those who believe in the unseen" (alladhina yu'minuna bil-ghayb).

Know that the reality of faith (iman) is affirmation (tasdiq) by the heart, because the address directed to them with the word "believe" (amanu) is in the language of the Arabs, and the Arabs knew faith only as affirmation. Its meaning in the language was not transferred to another meaning, for had there been a transfer from the lexical meaning, it would have been transmitted, as it was transmitted regarding prayer (salat), whose original meaning is supplication.

Since this is the case, we are obliged to take the command according to what their language requires. Such is the saying of God, exalted, in the story of Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him, and his sons: ﴿You will not be believed by us even if we are truthful﴾ [Surah Yusuf 12:17], meaning: you will not be taken as one who affirms us.

Another indication from this verse is that when He mentioned faith, He linked it to the unseen, so that it would be known that it is affirmation of the report concerning what is unseen. Then He singled it out from the rest of the obligatory acts of worship of the body and of wealth, saying: ﴿and who establish prayer and spend from what We have provided for them﴾.

Another proof is that wherever God mentions faith, He attributes it to the heart, saying: ﴿Among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths, but their hearts have not believed﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah 5:41], and He said: ﴿while his heart is at peace with faith﴾, and He said: ﴿Those—He has written faith into their hearts﴾ [Surah al-Mujadilah 58:22]. Similar examples are many.

As for the position of Islam (islam) relative to faith, it is like the position of the sun relative to light: every sun is light, but not every light is a sun; and every musk is fragrant, but not every fragrance is musk. Likewise, every faith is Islam, but not every Islam is faith, when it is not affirmation. This is because Islam is submission and humility. This is indicated by God's saying: ﴿The bedouins say, "We have believed." Say: "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [Surah al-Hujurat 49:14], out of fear of the sword.

And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Faith is secret," and he pointed to his chest, "and Islam is public" [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 1/86] [63]. And his (ﷺ) saying: "O assembly of those who have submitted with their tongues, while faith has not entered their hearts!" [Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/585, no. 8021] [65].

Likewise, his answer to Jibril differed regarding Islam and faith: he answered regarding faith with affirmation, and regarding Islam with the obligations of the religion. This is what was related by Abu Burayda, whose name is Yahya ibn Ma'mar, who said: The first to speak about qadar (divine decree) in Basra was Sa'id al-Juhani. I and Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Himyari set out, either for hajj or for 'umrah, and we said: "If we meet one of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), we will ask him about what this man says regarding qadar." We happened upon Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab entering the mosque, so I and my companion flanked him, one of us on his right and the other on his left. I thought my companion would leave the speaking to me, so I said: "Abu Abd al-Rahman, there have appeared before us people who recite the Qur'an and seek knowledge," and he mentioned from their speech that "they claim there is no qadar, and that the matter is newly begun." He said: "When you meet them, tell them that I am innocent of them and they are innocent of me. By Him by whom Abd Allah ibn Umar swears, if one of them had gold equal to Mount Uhud and spent it, God would not accept it from him until he believes in qadar."

Then he said: My father, Umar ibn al-Khattab, related to us: "While we were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) one day, there came upon us a man with exceedingly white garments and exceedingly black hair, showing no trace of travel, and none of us knew him. He sat down beside the Prophet (ﷺ), leaned his knees against his knees, placed his palms on his thighs, and said: 'O Muhammad, tell me about Islam.' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Islam is that you testify that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, establish prayer, give zakat, fast the month of Ramadan, and make pilgrimage to the House if you are able to do so.' He said: 'You have spoken the truth.' He said: We were astonished at him, asking and then affirming! He said: 'Tell me about faith.' He said: 'That you believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, and that you believe in qadar, its good and its evil.' He said: 'Tell me about ihsan (excellence).' He said: 'That you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you.' He said: 'Tell me about the Hour.' He said: 'The one asked about it knows no more than the one asking.' He said: 'Tell me about its signs.' He said: 'That the slave-girl gives birth to her mistress, and that you see the barefoot, naked, destitute herdsmen of sheep competing in building tall buildings.'" He said: Then he went off, and we remained for a while, and then he said: "O Umar, who was the questioner?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "That was Jibril, peace be upon him, who came to you to teach you your religion" [Sahih Muslim: 1/28–29, in full] [Note: the text as given].

Then the affirmation of the tongue and the actions of the body is called faith (iman) by way of some relation and some kind of closeness, because they are among its laws, its extensions, its signs, and its indications, just as we say: "I saw joy in the face of so-and-so," and "I saw the knowledge of Zayd in his book," while joy and knowledge are in the heart.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Faith has seventy-some branches, the lowest of which is removing harm from the road, and the highest of which is the testimony that there is no god but God" [66] [Musnad Ahmad: 2/445; Kanz al-'Ummal: 1/36].

And from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Faith has seventy-some branches, and modesty (haya') is a branch of faith" [67] [Sahih Muslim: 1/46].

Al-Hasan ibn Ali said: Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honor his face, related to me that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Faith is knowledge with the heart, affirmation with the tongue, and action with the limbs" [68] [al-Mu'jam al-Awsat: 6/226].

And from Ali ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-Abidin, who said: My father related to us, the master of the youth of the people of Paradise, who said: My father related to us, the master of the successors (awsiya'), who said: Muhammad, the master of the prophets, related to us, who said: "Faith is a spoken word, an acted deed, recognition by the intellects, and following the Messenger" [72] [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 1/86].

As for the unseen (al-ghayb), it is what is hidden from the eyes and fixed in the hearts. It is a verbal noun (masdar) placed in the position of a noun, so the absent one is called ghayb, just as the fasting person is called sawm, the visitor is called zawr, and the one who is just is called 'adl.

Al-Rabi' ibn Abi al-'Aliyah, on ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾, said: They believe in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, its Paradise, its Fire, and its meeting, and they believe in life after death and in resurrection. All of this is unseen.

Amr ibn al-Aswad, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, on ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾, said: [it means] in God. Whoever believes in God has believed in the unseen [Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/43].

Sufyan, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, on His saying ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾, said: The unseen is the Qur'an. Al-Kalbi said: [it means] what has been revealed of the Qur'an and what has not yet come.

Al-Dahhak said: The unseen is "there is no god but God" and what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Waqid said: It means revelation (wahy). Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ [Surah al-Najm 53:35], and His saying: ﴿Knower of the unseen; He does not reveal His unseen to anyone﴾ [Surah al-Jinn 72:26], and His saying: ﴿And he is not stingy with the unseen﴾ [Surah al-Takwir 81:24].

Al-Hasan said: It means the Hereafter. Abd Allah ibn Hani said: It is what was hidden from them of the sciences of the Qur'an.

Zayd ibn Aslam related from his father, from Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), that he said: "I was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Do you know which of the people of faith (ahl al-iman) is the most excellent?' They said: 'O Messenger of God, the angels.' He said: 'They are so, and they deserve that, and what prevents them, since God has placed them in the rank in which He placed them? Rather, others too [are like that].'" We said: "O Messenger of God, the prophets?" He said: "They are so, and they deserve that, and what prevents them? Rather, others too." We said: "O Messenger of God, then who are they?" He said: "People who will come after me, who are in the loins of men, who will believe in me though they have not seen me, who will find the leaf hung up and act upon what is in it. These are the most excellent of the people of faith in faith" [73] [Musnad Abi Ya'la: 1/147].

Al-Hasan related, from al-Harith ibn Qays, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "Before God is what you have preceded us in, O companions of Muhammad, of seeing the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "We, before God, count your faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) though you did not see him. Then Abd Allah said: 'The matter of Muhammad was clear to whoever saw him. By Him besides whom there is no god, no believer has believed more excellently than the faith of the unseen.' Then he recited: ﴿those who believe in the unseen and establish prayer﴾." That is, they perpetuate it, perform it continually, and guard it at its times, with its bowings, prostrations, rights, and limits. Everyone who persists in something and performs it is called its establisher (muqim); it is said: "So-and-so established the hajj among the people," and "the people established their market," and they did not suspend it. A poet said:
"So do not hurry your affair, but make it lasting;
for your staff has not prayed (salla) like one who keeps it up."
[Taj al-'Arus: 8/295]
That is, he meant by prayer here the five prayers, and mentioned it in the singular, as in His saying: ﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah 2:213], meaning the books. The original meaning of prayer (salah) in the language is supplication (du'a'). Then a worship was added to it, and its whole was called prayer, because the predominant feature of this worship is supplication.

Abu Hatim al-Kharazmi said: Its derivation is from al-Sala, which is fire. Its origin is gentleness and good treatment of a thing. That is because when a crooked piece of wood is to be straightened, they heat it over fire and straighten it between two pieces of wood. Therefore the one who prays should be deliberate in his prayer, guard its limits outwardly and inwardly, and not hasten or be careless in it. A poet said:
"So do not hurry your affair, but make it lasting;
for your staff has not prayed like one who keeps it up."
That is, your affair is not straightened like a building.

﴿And from what We have provided for them﴾: We gave them. Provision (rizq), according to the People of the Sunnah, is that from which benefit has been validly obtained. If it is food, it is to be eaten; if it is clothing, it is to be worn and protected; if it is a dwelling, its benefit is in residing in it. The one who benefits may benefit from what has been made available for benefit in two ways: lawfully and unlawfully. Therefore we say that God provides both the lawful and the unlawful. [The original meaning of] provision in the language is portion and fortune.

﴿spend﴾: give in charity. The original meaning of spending (infaq) is removal from the hand or from ownership. It is said: "The goods sold were spent (nafaqa) when many buyers came and they left quickly," and "the animal was spent (nafaqat) when its spirit left it." The nafiqa' of the jerboa (yarbu') comes from this, because when it is approached from the direction of the qasi'a (its outer burrow), it strikes the nafiqa' with its head, and so it exits (infaqa wa anfaqa) from it. And the nafaq is a tunnel in the earth that has an outlet to another place from which one emerges.

﴿And those who believe﴾: that is, affirm (yusaddiqun) ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾: O Muhammad, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and what was sent down before you﴾: meaning the earlier books, such as the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa, the Psalms (Zabur), the Gospel (Injil), and others.

﴿and the Hereafter﴾: that is, the Abode of the Hereafter. It is called the Hereafter (akhirah) because it comes after this world, and because it was delayed until the world perishes and then it comes into being.

﴿they are certain﴾: they know and are certain that it will come. The pronoun ﴿hum﴾ has entered as emphasis; the Kufans call it 'imad (support), and the Basrans call it fasl (separator).

﴿Those﴾: the people of this description. Ula'ika (those) is a noun built on kasra, and has no singular from its own form. The kaf is an address marker. The position of ﴿ula'ika﴾ in i'rab (grammatical analysis) is nominative (raf') as subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in His saying ﴿upon guidance﴾: right direction, clarity, and correctness; ﴿from their Lord﴾. ﴿Ula'ika﴾ is a subject, and ﴿hum﴾ is a support (ʿimad). ﴿The successful ones﴾ is the predicate of the subject: they are the saved, the victorious; they succeeded in Paradise and were saved from the Fire. It was also said: they are the ones who remain in reward and everlasting bliss.

The original meaning of success (falah) in the language is survival (baqa'). Labid said:
"We alight in lands all of which were alighted in before us,
and we hope for survival after 'Ad and Himyar."
[Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/182]
Another said:
"If a living man could attain survival,
the fighters of the spears would have attained it,
Abu Bara'—the mud of the slanderer (al-misyah)." [Taj al-'Arus: 2/146; Lisan al-Arab: 2/454, where it reads "Abu Bara' mudrat al-sayyah," and al-misyah is one who goes about spreading slander and evil in the land.]

Mujahid said: Four verses at the beginning of this surah were revealed concerning the believers, two verses after them were revealed concerning the disbelievers, and thirteen verses after them were revealed concerning the hypocrites.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾: meaning the polytheists of the Arabs. Al-Dahhak said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and five of his household. Al-Kalbi said: It means the Jews. It was also said: the hypocrites.

Disbelief (kufr) is denial and rejection. Its origin is from kufr, which is covering and concealing. From this comes the saying for the plowman: kafir, because he covers the seed. God, exalted, said: ﴿it pleases the farmers (kuffar) with its growth﴾ [Surah al-Hadid 57:20], meaning the sowers. The sea is also called kafir, and the night is called kafir. Labid said:
"Until when it cast a hand into the kafir,
and the darkness of the gaps (thughur) concealed its gloom,
on a night whose clouds concealed the stars."
[Lisan al-Arab: 5/147; Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 1/162]
From this comes al-mutakaffir bil-silah (one who covers himself with weapons), who is the armored man whose weapon covers his entire body.

The disbeliever is called kafir because he conceals the truth, and the Oneness of God and His blessings, and the prophethood of His prophets.

﴿It is all the same for them﴾: that is, it is one and equal for them. It is a noun derived from equality (tasawi).

Al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan), commentary on surah 2, verses 1–7 (part 3 of 3):

ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ: I warned them and cautioned them.

The scholars of meaning (ahl al-ma'ani) said: indhar (warning) and i'lam (informing) together with tahdhir (cautioning). It is said: "anzartuhum fa-nadharu," meaning "I informed them so they knew." In the proverb: "wa-qad a'dhara man andhar" (he who warns has indeed given an excuse). Regarding His words ﴿أَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ﴾ and its sisters, there are four readings:

Making both hamzas clear (tahqiq al-hamzatayn), which is the dialect of Tamim and the reading of the people of Kufa, because the interrogative alif entered upon the alif of qat' (the cutting hamza), the hamza that was joined to the verb's initial fa' was dropped, and its madd was substituted for it, out of dislike of combining two hamzas. This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.

Inserting an alif between the two hamzas, which is the reading of the people of Syria in the narration of Hisham and one of the two narrations from Abu 'Amr.

The poet said:
"Tattalat fa-istashrafat qarabatuhu... fa-qalna lahu: a-anta Zayd, la bal qamar"
[Thus it is in the manuscript, and we have not found it.]

And the khabar (declarative form) is used, relying on the answer to the interrogative; this is the reading of al-Zuhri.

ـأَمْ: a conjunction coordinating with the interrogative.

لَمْ: a particle of jazm (apocopation) that does not come before anything except a verb, because jazm is specific to verbs.

﴿لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ... ﴿لَمْ تُنذِرْهُمْ﴾: ﴿تُنذِرْهُمْ﴾ means "you warn them"; ﴿لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ means "they will not believe." This verse is specific to those upon whom the word of punishment has been decreed in God's prior knowledge. Its outward form is an inshā' (a performative/imperative-type statement), but its meaning is an ikhbar (a report). Then he mentioned the cause of their refusal to believe, saying:

﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ﴾: that is, He sealed upon their hearts. Khatm (sealing) and tab' (stamping) have one meaning, and both are covering a thing [and securing it] [The manuscript is illegible; what we have written is from al-Qurtubi's tafsir: 1/186.] so that nothing else can enter it.

So the meaning of the verse: God stamped and locked and bolted their hearts, so they neither comprehend a report nor understand it. This is supported by His words: ﴿أَمْ عَلَى قُلُوبٍ أَقْفَالُهَا﴾ [Muhammad: 24].

Some of them said: the meaning of tab' and khatm is that God judged them to be disbelievers and wretched, as one says to a man: "I have sealed upon you that you will never prosper."

﴿وَعَلَى سَمْعِهِمْ﴾: so they do not hear the truth and do not benefit from it. He used the singular "sam'" because it is a maṣdar (verbal noun), and maṣdars are neither dualized nor pluralized. It was also said that he meant the hearing of each one of them, as one says: "Bring me the head of two rams," meaning the head of each of them. The poet said:
"Kulu fi nisfi batnikum ta'ishu... fa-inna zamanakum zaman khamis"

Sibawayh said: the singular of "sam'" indicates the plural, since there is no singularization of two plurals, as in His words: ﴿يُخْرِجُهُم مِّنَ الظُّلُمَاتِ إِلَى النُّورِ﴾, meaning "the lights."

The poet al-Ra'i said:
"Bihā judhaf al-ḥasrā fa-ammā 'iẓāmuhā... fa-bīḍun wa-ammā jilduhā fa-ṣalīb"
[Its speaker is 'Alqama ibn 'Abda; see his Diwan: 27 and Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/324.]

Ibn 'Ablah read: ﴿وَعَلَى أَسْمَارِهِمْ﴾ [and upon their hearings], and the sentence is complete at His words ﴿وَعَلَى سَمْعِهِمْ﴾.

Then He said: ﴿وَعَلَى أَبْصَارِهِمْ غِشَاوَةٌ﴾: that is, a covering and a veil, so they do not see the truth. From it comes ghashiyat al-sarj (the saddle's covering).
