He went and took the hand of Abu Bakr and said: "Welcome, O Sincere One (al-Siddiq), lord of the clan of Taym, shaykh of Islam, the second of the Messenger of God ﷺ in the cave, and the one who gave his soul and wealth to him." Then he took the hand of ‘Umar and said: "Welcome, lord of the clan of ‘Adi ibn Ka‘b, al-Faruq, the strong one in the religion of God, who gave his soul and wealth to the Messenger of God." Then he took the hand of ‘Ali and said: "Welcome, cousin of the Messenger of God and his son-in-law, lord of the clan of Hashim, other than the Messenger of God ﷺ." ‘Ali said: "Hold back, for God's sake, and fear God, and do not be a hypocrite, for the hypocrites are the worst creatures of God." ‘Abd Allah said: "Gently, Abu al-Hasan, is this what you say to me? By God, our faith is like your faith and our affirmation like your affirmation." Then they separated. ‘Abd Allah said to his companions: "How did you see me act? When you meet them, do as I have done." They praised him and said: "We will remain with you as long as you live." The Muslims returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of that, so God revealed: ﴿وَإِذا لَقُوا﴾, that is, met, meaning the hypocrites ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

(The original form of "laqu" was "laqiyu"; the ḍamma was felt heavy on the yā’, so it was moved onto the qāf, and the wāw and yā’ both being silent, they were dropped because they came together.)

Muhammad ibn al-Sumay‘ read: wa-idha lāqū, and both have the same meaning.

﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: meaning Abu Bakr and his companions. ﴿قالُوا آمَنَّا كأيمانكم﴾. ﴿وَإِذا خَلَوْا﴾: they returned. It may also be from seclusion (khalwa): one says khalawtu bihi, khalawtu ilayhi, khalawtu ma‘ahu, all with the same meaning.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "ila" here has the meaning of "ma‘a" (with), like His saying: ﴿أُحِلَّ لَكُمْ لَيْلَةَ الصِّيامِ الرَّفَثُ إِلى نِسائِكُمْ﴾ ("It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to go in unto your wives") [Surah al-Baqara: 187], meaning: with your wives; and His saying: ﴿لا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوالَهُمْ إِلى أَمْوالِكُمْ﴾ ("do not consume their wealth along with your wealth") [Surah al-Nisa’: 2]; and His saying: ﴿مَنْ أَنْصارِي إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾ ("who are my helpers to God?") [Al ‘Imran: 52]. Al-Nabigha said:
"Do not leave me to threats as if I were, among people, a mangy camel smeared with tar."
[Lisan al-Arab: 15/435.]
That is, among the people.

Another said:
"And he stretched his two arms into a pool, along with a fleshy-chested one with a loose shoulder."
[Lisan al-Arab: 3/156.]
That is, along with the fleshy-chested one.

﴿إِلى شَياطِينِهِمْ﴾: that is, their chiefs, their great ones, their leaders and their soothsayers.

Ibn ‘Abbas said: they are five men from the Jews; there is no soothsayer except that with him is a devil who follows him: Ka‘b ibn al-Ashraf in Medina, Abu Burda among the Banu Aslam, ‘Abd Allah among Juhayna, ‘Awf ibn ‘Amir among the Banu Asad, and ‘Abd Allah ibn al-Sawda’ in Syria.

The shaytan is the rebellious, disobedient one among the jinn and mankind, and among every thing; from it the viper (al-nadnad) is called shaytan. God Most High said: ﴿طَلْعُها كَأَنَّهُ رُؤُسُ الشَّياطِينِ﴾ ("its shoots are like the heads of devils") [Surah al-Saffat: 65], meaning the snakes. The Arabs say: "Beware of that creature, for it is a shaytan."

In a hadith: "If a man passes in front of one of you while he is praying, let him prevent him; if he refuses, let him fight him, for he is a shaytan."

It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he saw a man following a pigeon, and he said: "A shaytan following a shaytan" [In some sources: "his shaytan"].
[74] [Musnad Ahmad: 2/345; Kanz al-‘Ummal: 15/218.]

He meant the wicked shepherd, the caller.

It is reported of one of them that in the midst of his speech he said: "All that is because a shaytan mounted me." It was said to him: "Which of the shayatin mounted you?" He said: "Anger."

Abu al-Najm said:
"I and every poet among the human race have a shaytan: mine is male and his is female."
[Sharh Nahj al-Balagha by Ibn Abi al-Hadid: 19/425.]

﴿قالُوا إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾: that is, on your religion and as your helpers.

﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾: at Muhammad and his Companions.

﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾: that is, He repays them for their mockery. The repayment is named by the name of the initial act, since it is similar to it in form, like His saying: ﴿جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُها﴾ ("the requital of an evil deed is an evil deed like it") [Surah al-Shura: 40], where the repayment of an evil deed is named an evil deed.

‘Amr ibn Kulthum said:
"Let no one act ignorantly against us, lest we act ignorantly beyond the ignorance of the ignorant."
[Lisan al-Arab: 3/177 and 8/64.]

Another said:
"We repay them the measure of the cup for what they did, and whoever treats his paternal cousin with injustice is himself unjustly treated."
Thus the repayment is named injustice.

It was also said: the meaning is: God rebukes them, exposes them, and condemns their action, because mockery and derision among the Arabs mean blame and ignorance-ascription, as one says: "So-and-so is mocked today," meaning he is blamed. God said: ﴿وَإِذا سَمِعْتُمْ آياتِ اللَّهِ يُكْفَرُ بِها وَيُسْتَهْزَأُ بِها﴾ ("when you hear the signs of God being disbelieved in and mocked") [Surah al-Nisa’: 140], meaning: blamed. And He related, speaking of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿إِنْ تَسْخَرُوا مِنَّا فَإِنَّا نَسْخَرُ مِنْكُمْ كَما تَسْخَرُونَ﴾ ("if you mock us, then we mock you as you mock") [Surah Hud: 38].

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is: God exposes the believers' hypocrisy [to the believers].

Ibn ‘Abbas said: it is that God will, on the Day of Resurrection, let the believers, who are in Paradise, look down upon the hypocrites, who are in the Fire. They will say to them: "Would you like to enter Paradise?" They will say: "Yes." Then a door of Paradise is opened for them, and it is said to them: "Enter." They hasten toward it, and they turn about in the Fire; when they reach the door, it is shut upon them and they are returned to the Fire, and the believers laugh at them. That is His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ أَجْرَمُوا كانُوا مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَضْحَكُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed") up to His saying: ﴿فَالْيَوْمَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنَ الْكُفَّارِ يَضْحَكُونَ﴾ ("So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers") [Surah al-Mutaffifin: 34].

Al-A‘mash narrated from Khaythama from ‘Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Some people will be ordered to Paradise until, when they draw near it and smell its fragrance and look at what God has prepared in it for its people of honour, they will be called: 'Turn them away from it.' He said: 'They will return in grief and remorse, such as no creation has returned with.' They will say: 'O our Lord, if You had caused us to enter the Fire before You showed us what You have shown us, it would have been easier for us.' Then God, majestic is His majesty, will say: 'This is what I intended for you: you feared people and did not fear Me, you honoured people and did not honour Me, and you used to show off to people with your deeds, contrary to what you used to see in Me in your hearts. So today I will make you taste My punishment, along with what I have withheld from you of My reward.'"
[Kanz al-‘Ummal: 3/484, with variation.]

It was also said: it is His forsaking them and depriving them of success and guidance.

This is His saying afterward: ﴿وَيَمُدُّهُمْ﴾: He leaves them, gives them respite, and prolongs for them. Its root is increase; it is said: "the river extended" (madda al-nahr), and madda: another period of time.

Ibn Muhaysin and Shibl read: ﴿وَيُمِدُّهُمْ﴾ with a ḍamma on the yā’ and a kasra on the mīm; the two are dialects with the same meaning, because madd (extension) mostly comes in evil and imdad (supplying) in good. God, Mighty and Majestic, said of madd: ﴿وَنَمُدُّ لَهُ مِنَ الْعَذابِ مَدًّا﴾ ("We will extend for him of the punishment an extension") [Surah Maryam: 79]; and about imdad He said: ﴿وَأَمْدَدْناكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("and We supplied you with wealth and children") [Surah al-Isra’: 6]; and He said: ﴿أَيَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّما نُمِدُّهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ مالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("Do they think that what We supply them with of wealth and children") [Surah al-Mu’minun: 55]; and He said: ﴿وَيُمْدِدْكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("and He will supply you with wealth and children") [Surah Nuh: 12].

﴿فِي طُغْيانِهِمْ﴾: their disbelief, their misguidance and their ignorance. The root of ṭughyān is exceeding the measure: one says "a scale in which there is ṭughyān," meaning it exceeds the measure in its evenness. God Most High said: ﴿إِنَّا لَمَّا طَغَى الْماءُ﴾ ("When the water overflowed") [Surah al-Haqqa: 11], meaning it exceeded the limit ordained for it; and He said to Pharaoh: ﴿إِنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("indeed he has transgressed") [Surah Ta-Ha: 24], meaning he went to excess in his claim when he said: ﴿أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلى﴾ ("I am your most exalted lord") [Surah al-Nazi‘at: 24].

﴿يَعْمَهُونَ﴾: they pass on, wandering in error, bewildered.
One says: ‘amiha ya‘mahu ‘amhan and ‘umuwwan, and ‘amiha fahuwa ‘amih, and ‘amih: when he is deviating from the truth. Ru’ba said:
"And a desert whose edges are in desert, blind to guidance, with the ignorant wandering."
[Lisan al-Arab: 13/519.]

﴿أُولئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ بِالْهُدى﴾:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They took error and left guidance." Its meaning is that they exchanged disbelief for faith. He expressed it with the wording of purchase (shirāʾ) and trade (tijārah) figuratively, because purchase and trade both come back to exchange (istibdāl) and choice (ikhtiyār), since each of the two parties in a sale chooses what is in the other's hand over what is in his own. The poet said:

I took by the forelock a bald-headed man,
and by the shining front teeth the one with the gap,
and by the tall, long-lived one, a stout-bodied man,
just as the Muslim bought Christianity when he became a Christian. [[al-Tibyan, al-Tusi: 1/83.]]

That is, he chose Christianity over Islam.

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read اشْتَرَوِا الضَّلالَةَ (ishtarawi al-ḍalālah) with a kasrah on the waw, because the dammah of the plural-related waw is moved to the kasrah, the ʿadwa (the original movement) being moved to the lighter vowel, the kasrah, for ease of pronunciation.

فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ (fa-mā ribiḥat tijāratuhum): that is, they did not profit in their trade.

The Arabs say: "ribiḥa bayʿuka" (your sale profited) and "khasirat ṣafqatuka" (your bargain lost), and "nāma layluka" (your night slept). That is, you profited and lost in your sale, and you slept through your night. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿فَإِذا عَزَمَ الْأَمْرُ﴾ [[Surat Muhammad: 21.]] ("but when the matter is resolved"), and He says: ﴿بَلْ مَكْرُ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهارِ﴾ [[Surat Saba': 33.]] ("rather, the plotting of the night and the day").

The poet said:

One-eyed as he is from Nayhan: his day is blind,
but his night is clear-sighted.

Another said:

Ḥārith, you have relieved my worry,
so my night slept and my grief was lifted.

Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAblah read (fa-mā ribiḥat tijāratuhum) in the plural (tijārātuhum).

وَما كانُوا مُهْتَدِينَ (wa-mā kānū muhtadīn): from error. He said: they were not correct in their trade.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Every one of you is a merchant, so let each man look at what his trade is." Allah says: ﴿فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ﴾, and He says: ﴿هَلْ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلى تِجارَةٍ تُنْجِيكُمْ مِنْ عَذابٍ أَلِيمٍ﴾ [[Surat al-Saff: 10.]] ("Shall I direct you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?").

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 8–16 (part 1 of 2):

�´وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَقُولُ آمَنَّا﴾: i.e., we affirm (saddaqna) by God and by the Last Day (al-yawm al-akhir): that is, the Day of Resurrection. [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 10/243, and Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 174.]

God Most High said: ﴿وَمَا هُمْ بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and they are not believers").

Al-nas (the people): they are a group of animals distinguished by the human form, and it is the plural of insan (human being). Insan originally was insiyan with a yā’, and they dropped the yā’ and transferred its vowel to the sīn, so it became insan. Do you not see that when you diminish it (form the diminutive), you restore the yā’ to it and say unaysiyan?

The scholars differed about the reason for this name. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was named insan because a covenant was made with it and it forgot (nasiya). God Most High said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَهِدْنا إِلى آدَمَ مِنْ قَبْلُ فَنَسِيَ﴾ ("We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot") [Surah Ta-Ha: 115]. And a poet said:
"And you were named insan because you are forgetful."
[Came in prose-like form rather than verse in Lisan al-Arab: 6/11.]

Some of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: it was named insan for its visibility (zuhur) and for the perceiving of it (qadas al-basir iyyahu), from your saying: ānastu kadha, meaning: I perceived such-and-such. God Most High said: ﴿آنَسَ مِنْ جانِبِ الطُّورِ ناراً﴾ ("he perceived a fire from the side of the mount") [Surah al-Qasas: 29]. It was also said: because it takes comfort (yasta’nisu) in it, and it was said: when God created Adam, He made him comfortable with his wife, so he was named insan.

﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾: i.e., they oppose God and deny Him. The root of khada' (deception) in the language is concealment, and from it is said [for the room in which goods are kept] makhda‘ (a storeroom). The one who deceives (al-mukhadi‘) shows the opposite of what he conceals. Some said: the root of khida‘ in the language is corruption, and a poet said:
"White of colour, delicious of taste, good of saliva, when saliva is corrupted (khada‘)."
[Lisan al-Arab: 8/65.]
That is, it corrupted (fasada).

So its meaning would be: they corrupt by what they conceal within themselves and what they hide in their hearts. It was also said that its meaning is: they deceive God according to their own claim and in their own supposition, meaning that they dared against God until they supposed that they could deceive Him. This is like His saying: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلى إِلهِكَ الَّذِي ظَلْتَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفاً﴾ ("look at your god to which you were devoted") [Surah Ta-Ha: 97], meaning according to your supposition and by your claim.

It was also said: the meaning is that they act in God's religion in a way that is deception among themselves. And it was said: the meaning is that they deceive His Messenger, like His saying: ﴿فَلَمَّا آسَفُونا انْتَقَمْنا مِنْهُمْ﴾ ("when they angered Us, We took vengeance on them") [Surah al-Zukhruf: 55], meaning: they angered Us. And His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يُؤْذُونَ اللَّهَ﴾ ("those who injure God") [Surah al-Ahzab: 57], meaning: the friends of God, because God, glorified is He, is not harmed or deceived. So God Most High made clear that whoever harms a prophet of His prophets or a friend of His friends deserves punishment, just as if he harmed His Messenger and deceived him. Evidence for this is the reported report: God Most High says: "Whoever harms a friend of Mine has declared war against Me" [Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/137].

It was also said: the mention of God, glorified is He, in His saying ﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾ is an embellishment and adornment for the hearer of the speech, and the intended object of the deception is the believers, like His saying: ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّما غَنِمْتُمْ مِنْ شَيْءٍ فَأَنَّ لِلَّهِ خُمُسَهُ وَلِلرَّسُولِ﴾ ("know that whatever you gain of spoils, a fifth of it is for God and for the Messenger") [Surah al-Anfal: 41]. Then, deception (mukhada‘a) is in proportion to the action, and the intensive form (al-mufa‘ala) mostly comes in an action shared between two, like fighting (muqatala), trading (mudaraba) and mutual abuse (mushatama). It may also come from one party, as when you say: ṭāraqtu al-na‘l (I repaired the sandal), ‘āqabtu al-liṣṣ (I punished the thief), and ‘āfāka Allāh (God granted you well-being). God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَقاسَمَهُما إِنِّي لَكُما لَمِنَ النَّاصِحِينَ﴾ ("and he swore to them, 'I am surely a sincere adviser to you both'") [Surah al-A‘raf: 21], and He said: ﴿قاتَلَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("God fight them") [Surah al-Tawba: 30]. The deception here is an expression for an action that belongs to one party, whereas God does not engage in deception.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: i.e., and they deceive the believers by their saying, when they see them: "We believe," while they are not believers. Some said: among their deception of the believers was that they would sit with the believers and mix with them until the believers became comfortable with them and counted them among themselves, so they would disclose to them their secrets, which they would then convey to their enemies. God Most High said:
﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ إِلَّا أَنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ ("and they deceive none but themselves"), because the harm of their deception returns to them; it is as if in reality they deceive themselves. That is because God Most High informs His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ of their secrets and hypocrisy, so they are disgraced in this world and deserve severe punishment in the Hereafter.

The people of allusion (ahl al-ishara) said: only one who does not know the inner realities deceives; as for one who knows the inner realities, whoever deceives him is only deceiving himself.

The readers differed on His saying: ﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ﴾. Shayba, Nafi‘, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ala’ read ﴿يُخادِعُونَ﴾ with an alif, treating it as the form of mufa‘ala that belongs to one party, and we have mentioned its report; and its confirmation is the first letter. As for His saying ﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾, they did not differ about it except what was narrated from Abu Hamza al-Shami, who read: (yakhda‘una Allah), while the rest read ﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ﴾ according to the more famous and more precise of the two dialects, and Abu 'Ubayd chose it.

﴿وَما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [Surah al-Baqara: 9]: and they do not perceive, meaning: they do not know that it is so.

﴿فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ﴾: doubt and hypocrisy. From it is said: so-and-so sickens in promise when he does not fulfil it. The root of marad (sickness) is weakness and lassitude. So doubt in religion and hypocrisy were named [sickness by which] weakens the body, diminishes its strength, and because it leads to destruction through punishment, just as sickness in the body leads to destruction and death.

﴿فَزادَهُمُ اللَّهُ مَرَضاً﴾: God increased them in sickness: doubt, hypocrisy and destruction.

﴿وَلَهُمْ عَذابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾: a painful, grievous punishment whose pain reaches their hearts; it is in the sense of mu’lim (painful), like the saying of ‘Amr ibn Ma‘di Karib:
"From the fragrant herb of the caller, the one who hears, it keeps me awake while my companions sleep."
[Lisan al-Arab: 8/164.]
That is, al-musma‘ (the one heard), meaning its phantom.

﴿بِما كانُوا يَكْذِبُونَ﴾: (ma) is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), meaning: by their lying against God and His Messenger in secret.

The people of Kufa read: with a fatha on the yā’ and a light dhāl, meaning: by their lying, when they said "We believe" while they were not believers.

﴿وَإِذا﴾: a particle of time meaning "at that time," and it indicates the occurrence of an awaited action and contains the meaning of a conditional. ﴿قِيلَ﴾: a past passive verb. It was originally qawl, like qīl; the kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so its kasra was moved to the first radical of the verb, and the wāw became a yā’ because of the kasra before it. This is the high dialect, on which the common readers rely, and it is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd.

Al-Kisa’i and Ya‘qub read: qīla, ghīḍa, ḥīla, sīqa, jī’a, shī’a and shītu, with ishmam (partial rounding) of the ḍamma in them, so that it indicates the altered wāw and serves as a separator between the initial and the verbal-noun.

﴿لَهُمْ﴾: meaning the hypocrites; it was also said: the Jews. The believers said to them: ﴿لا تُفْسِدُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ ("do not corrupt on the earth") by disbelief, disobedience, and dividing people away from faith in Muhammad and the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: by altering the religion, changing the sunna and distorting the Book of God.

﴿قالُوا إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ﴾: ﴿أَلا﴾ is a word of alerting; ﴿إِنَّهُمْ﴾: ﴿هُمُ﴾ is an emphatic support; ﴿الْمُفْسِدُونَ﴾ ("they are the corrupters"); ﴿وَلكِنْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾: what punishment has been prepared for them.

﴿وَإِذا قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾: meaning [he said] [the zayd is added to complete the meaning]: the believers said to the Jews: ﴿آمِنُوا كَما آمَنَ النَّاسُ﴾ ("believe as the people have believed"), and they are ‘Abd Allah ibn Salam and others among the believers from the People of the Book.

﴿قالُوا أَنُؤْمِنُ كَما آمَنَ السُّفَهاءُ﴾: the foolish, the ignorant. God said: ﴿أَلا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ السُّفَهاءُ وَلكِنْ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("they are indeed the foolish, but they do not know" that they are so). It was also said: they do not render knowledge its due. The historian said: the safīh (foolish) is the liar who deliberately contradicts what he knows.

Qutrub said: the safīh is the hasty, unjust one who acts contrary to the truth.

The readers differed on His saying ﴿السُّفَهاءُ أَلا﴾. Some made both hamzas clear, which is the school of the people of Kufa and the dialect of Tamim.

As for Abu 'Amr and the people of the Hijaz, they hamzated the first and softened the second, seeking lightness. Al-Farra’ preferred omitting the first and hamzating the second, arguing that what is resumed (yustaʾnaf, i.e., with the hamza) is what one pauses upon.

﴿وَإِذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾.

Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul al-Khazraji was the greatest of the hypocrites, from the clan of Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubada. Whenever he met Sa‘d he would say: "How excellent is the religion of Muhammad." But when he returned to the chiefs of his people, they would say: "Shall we disbelieve?" He would say: "Hold your hands by the religion of your fathers." Then God revealed this verse.

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, as a proof against him. That was because they went out one day and a group of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ met them. ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said to his companions: "Watch how I will ward these foolish ones away from you." He went and took the hand of Abu Bakr and said: "Welcome, O Sincere One (al-Siddiq), lord of the clan of Taym, shaykh of Islam, the second of the Messenger of God ﷺ in the cave, and the one who gave his soul and wealth to him." Then he took the hand of ‘Umar and said: "Welcome, lord of the clan of ‘Adi ibn Ka‘b, al-Faruq, the strong one in the religion of God, who gave his soul and wealth to the Messenger of God." Then he took the hand of ‘Ali and said: "Welcome, cousin of the Messenger of God and his son-in-law, lord of the clan of Hashim, other than the Messenger of God ﷺ." ‘Ali said: "Hold back, for God's sake, and fear God, and do not be a hypocrite, for the hypocrites are the worst creatures of God." ‘Abd Allah said: "Gently, Abu al-Hasan, is this what you say to me? By God, our faith is like your faith and our affirmation like your affirmation." Then they separated. ‘Abd Allah said to his companions: "How did you see me act? When you meet them, do as I have done." They praised him and said: "We will remain with you as long as you live." The Muslims returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of that, so God revealed: ﴿وَإِذا لَقُوا﴾, that is, met, meaning the hypocrites ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

(The original form of "laqu" was "laqiyu"; the ḍamma was felt heavy on the yā’, so it was moved onto the qāf, and the wāw and yā’ both being silent, they were dropped because they came together.)

Muhammad ibn al-Sumay‘ read: wa-idha lāqū, and both have the same meaning.

﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: meaning Abu Bakr and his companions. ﴿قالُوا آمَنَّا كأيمانكم﴾. ﴿وَإِذا خَلَوْا﴾: they returned. It may also be from seclusion (khalwa): one says khalawtu bihi, khalawtu ilayhi, khalawtu ma‘ahu, all with the same meaning.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "ila" here has the meaning of "ma‘a" (with), like His saying: ﴿أُحِلَّ لَكُمْ لَيْلَةَ الصِّيامِ الرَّفَثُ إِلى نِسائِكُمْ﴾ ("It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to go in unto your wives") [Surah al-Baqara: 187], meaning: with your wives; and His saying: ﴿لا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوالَهُمْ إِلى أَمْوالِكُمْ﴾ ("do not consume their wealth along with your wealth") [Surah al-Nisa’: 2]; and His saying: ﴿مَنْ أَنْصارِي إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾ ("who are my helpers to God?") [Al ‘Imran: 52]. Al-Nabigha said:
"Do not leave me to threats as if I were, among people, a mangy camel smeared with tar."
[Lisan al-Arab: 15/435.]
That is, among the people.

Another said:
"And he stretched his two arms into a pool, along with a fleshy-chested one with a loose shoulder."
[Lisan al-Arab: 3/156.]
That is, along with the fleshy-chested one.

﴿إِلى شَياطِينِهِمْ﴾: that is, their chiefs, their great ones, their leaders and their soothsayers.

Ibn ‘Abbas said: they are five men from the Jews; there is no soothsayer except that with him is a devil who follows him: Ka‘b ibn al-Ashraf in Medina, Abu Burda among the Banu Aslam, ‘Abd Allah among Juhayna, ‘Awf ibn ‘Amir among the Banu Asad, and ‘Abd Allah ibn al-Sawda’ in Syria.

The shaytan is the rebellious, disobedient one among the jinn and mankind, and among every thing; from it the viper (al-nadnad) is called shaytan. God Most High said: ﴿طَلْعُها كَأَنَّهُ رُؤُسُ الشَّياطِينِ﴾ ("its shoots are like the heads of devils") [Surah al-Saffat: 65], meaning the snakes. The Arabs say: "Beware of that creature, for it is a shaytan."

In a hadith: "If a man passes in front of one of you while he is praying, let him prevent him; if he refuses, let him fight him, for he is a shaytan."

It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he saw a man following a pigeon, and he said: "A shaytan following a shaytan" [In some sources: "his shaytan"].
[74] [Musnad Ahmad: 2/345; Kanz al-‘Ummal: 15/218.]

He meant the wicked shepherd, the caller.

It is reported of one of them that in the midst of his speech he said: "All that is because a shaytan mounted me." It was said to him: "Which of the shayatin mounted you?" He said: "Anger."

Abu al-Najm said:
"I and every poet among the human race have a shaytan: mine is male and his is female."
[Sharh Nahj al-Balagha by Ibn Abi al-Hadid: 19/425.]

﴿قالُوا إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾: that is, on your religion and as your helpers.

﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾: at Muhammad and his Companions.

﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾: that is, He repays them for their mockery. The repayment is named by the name of the initial act, since it is similar to it in form, like His saying: ﴿جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُها﴾ ("the requital of an evil deed is an evil deed like it") [Surah al-Shura: 40], where the repayment of an evil deed is named an evil deed.

‘Amr ibn Kulthum said:
"Let no one act ignorantly against us, lest we act ignorantly beyond the ignorance of the ignorant."
[Lisan al-Arab: 3/177 and 8/64.]

Another said:
"We repay them the measure of the cup for what they did, and whoever treats his paternal cousin with injustice is himself unjustly treated."
Thus the repayment is named injustice.

It was also said: the meaning is: God rebukes them, exposes them, and condemns their action, because mockery and derision among the Arabs mean blame and ignorance-ascription, as one says: "So-and-so is mocked today," meaning he is blamed. God said: ﴿وَإِذا سَمِعْتُمْ آياتِ اللَّهِ يُكْفَرُ بِها وَيُسْتَهْزَأُ بِها﴾ ("when you hear the signs of God being disbelieved in and mocked") [Surah al-Nisa’: 140], meaning: blamed. And He related, speaking of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿إِنْ تَسْخَرُوا مِنَّا فَإِنَّا نَسْخَرُ مِنْكُمْ كَما تَسْخَرُونَ﴾ ("if you mock us, then we mock you as you mock") [Surah Hud: 38].

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is: God exposes the believers' hypocrisy [to the believers].

Ibn ‘Abbas said: it is that God will, on the Day of Resurrection, let the believers, who are in Paradise, look down upon the hypocrites, who are in the Fire. They will say to them: "Would you like to enter Paradise?" They will say: "Yes." Then a door of Paradise is opened for them, and it is said to them: "Enter." They hasten toward it, and they turn about in the Fire; when they reach the door, it is shut upon them and they are returned to the Fire, and the believers laugh at them. That is His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ أَجْرَمُوا كانُوا مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَضْحَكُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed") up to His saying: ﴿فَالْيَوْمَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنَ الْكُفَّارِ يَضْحَكُونَ﴾ ("So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers") [Surah al-Mutaffifin: 34].

Al-A‘mash narrated from Khaythama from ‘Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Some people will be ordered to Paradise until, when they draw near it and smell its fragrance and look at what God has prepared in it for its people of honour, they will be called: 'Turn them away from it.' He said: 'They will return in grief and remorse, such as no creation has returned with.' They will say: 'O our Lord, if You had caused us to enter the Fire before You showed us what You have shown us, it would have been easier for us.' Then God, majestic is His majesty, will say: 'This is what I intended for you: you feared people and did not fear Me, you honoured people and did not honour Me, and you used to show off to people with your deeds, contrary to what you used to see in Me in your hearts. So today I will make you taste My punishment, along with what I have withheld from you of My reward.'"
[Kanz al-‘Ummal: 3/484, with variation.]

It was also said: it is His forsaking them and depriving them of success and guidance.

This is His saying afterward: ﴿وَيَمُدُّهُمْ﴾: He leaves them, gives them respite, and prolongs for them. Its root is increase; it is said: "the river extended" (madda al-nahr), and madda: another period of time.

Ibn Muhaysin and Shibl read: ﴿وَيُمِدُّهُمْ﴾ with a ḍamma on the yā’ and a kasra on the mīm; the two are dialects with the same meaning, because madd (extension) mostly comes in evil and imdad (supplying) in good. God, Mighty and Majestic, said of madd: ﴿وَنَمُدُّ لَهُ مِنَ الْعَذابِ مَدًّا﴾ ("We will extend for him of the punishment an extension") [Surah Maryam: 79]; and about imdad He said: ﴿وَأَمْدَدْناكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("and We supplied you with wealth and children") [Surah al-Isra’: 6]; and He said: ﴿أَيَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّما نُمِدُّهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ مالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("Do they think that what We supply them with of wealth and children") [Surah al-Mu’minun: 55]; and He said: ﴿وَيُمْدِدْكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("and He will supply you with wealth and children") [Surah Nuh: 12].

﴿فِي طُغْيانِهِمْ﴾: their disbelief, their misguidance and their ignorance. The root of ṭughyān is exceeding the measure: one says "a scale in which there is ṭughyān," meaning it exceeds the measure in its evenness. God Most High said: ﴿إِنَّا لَمَّا طَغَى الْماءُ﴾ ("When the water overflowed") [Surah al-Haqqa: 11], meaning it exceeded the limit ordained for it; and He said to Pharaoh: ﴿إِنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("indeed he has transgressed") [Surah Ta-Ha: 24], meaning he went to excess in his claim when he said: ﴿أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلى﴾ ("I am your most exalted lord") [Surah al-Nazi‘at: 24].

﴿يَعْمَهُونَ﴾: they pass on, wandering in error, bewildered.
One says: ‘amiha ya‘mahu ‘amhan and ‘umuwwan, and ‘amiha fahuwa ‘amih, and ‘amih: when he is deviating from the truth. Ru’ba said:
"And a desert whose edges are in desert, blind to guidance, with the ignorant wandering."
[Lisan al-Arab: 13/519.]

﴿أُولئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ بِالْهُدى﴾:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They took error and left guidance." Its meaning is that they exchanged disbelief for faith. He expressed it with the wording of purchase (shirāʾ) and trade (tijārah) figuratively, because purchase and trade both come back to exchange (istibdāl) and choice (ikhtiyār), since each of the two parties in a sale chooses what is in the other's hand over what is in his own. The poet said:

I took by the forelock a bald-headed man,
and by the shining front teeth the one with the gap,
and by the tall, long-lived one, a stout-bodied man,
just as the Muslim bought Christianity when he became a Christian. [[al-Tibyan, al-Tusi: 1/83.]]

That is, he chose Christianity over Islam.

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read اشْتَرَوِا الضَّلالَةَ (ishtarawi al-ḍalālah) with a kasrah on the waw, because the dammah of the plural-related waw is moved to the kasrah, the ʿadwa (the original movement) being moved to the lighter vowel, the kasrah, for ease of pronunciation.

فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ (fa-mā ribiḥat tijāratuhum): that is, they did not profit in their trade.

The Arabs say: "ribiḥa bayʿuka" (your sale profited) and "khasirat ṣafqatuka" (your bargain lost), and "nāma layluka" (your night slept). That is, you profited and lost in your sale, and you slept through your night. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿فَإِذا عَزَمَ الْأَمْرُ﴾ [[Surat Muhammad: 21.]] ("but when the matter is resolved"), and He says: ﴿بَلْ مَكْرُ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهارِ﴾ [[Surat Saba': 33.]] ("rather, the plotting of the night and the day").

The poet said:

One-eyed as he is from Nayhan: his day is blind,
but his night is clear-sighted.

Another said:

Ḥārith, you have relieved my worry,
so my night slept and my grief was lifted.

Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAblah read (fa-mā ribiḥat tijāratuhum) in the plural (tijārātuhum).

وَما كانُوا مُهْتَدِينَ (wa-mā kānū muhtadīn): from error. He said: they were not correct in their trade.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Every one of you is a merchant, so let each man look at what his trade is." Allah says: ﴿فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ﴾, and He says: ﴿هَلْ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلى تِجارَةٍ تُنْجِيكُمْ مِنْ عَذابٍ أَلِيمٍ﴾ [[Surat al-Saff: 10.]] ("Shall I direct you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?").

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 8–16 (part 1 of 2):

�´وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَقُولُ آمَنَّا﴾: i.e., we affirm (saddaqna) by God and by the Last Day (al-yawm al-akhir): that is, the Day of Resurrection. [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 10/243, and Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 174.]

God Most High said: ﴿وَمَا هُمْ بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and they are not believers").

Al-nas (the people): they are a group of animals distinguished by the human form, and it is the plural of insan (human being). Insan originally was insiyan with a yā’, and they dropped the yā’ and transferred its vowel to the sīn, so it became insan. Do you not see that when you diminish it (form the diminutive), you restore the yā’ to it and say unaysiyan?

The scholars differed about the reason for this name. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was named insan because a covenant was made with it and it forgot (nasiya). God Most High said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَهِدْنا إِلى آدَمَ مِنْ قَبْلُ فَنَسِيَ﴾ ("We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot") [Surah Ta-Ha: 115]. And a poet said:
"And you were named insan because you are forgetful."
[Came in prose-like form rather than verse in Lisan al-Arab: 6/11.]

Some of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: it was named insan for its visibility (zuhur) and for the perceiving of it (qadas al-basir iyyahu), from your saying: ānastu kadha, meaning: I perceived such-and-such. God Most High said: ﴿آنَسَ مِنْ جانِبِ الطُّورِ ناراً﴾ ("he perceived a fire from the side of the mount") [Surah al-Qasas: 29]. It was also said: because it takes comfort (yasta’nisu) in it, and it was said: when God created Adam, He made him comfortable with his wife, so he was named insan.

﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾: i.e., they oppose God and deny Him. The root of khada' (deception) in the language is concealment, and from it is said [for the room in which goods are kept] makhda‘ (a storeroom). The one who deceives (al-mukhadi‘) shows the opposite of what he conceals. Some said: the root of khida‘ in the language is corruption, and a poet said:
"White of colour, delicious of taste, good of saliva, when saliva is corrupted (khada‘)."
[Lisan al-Arab: 8/65.]
That is, it corrupted (fasada).

So its meaning would be: they corrupt by what they conceal within themselves and what they hide in their hearts. It was also said that its meaning is: they deceive God according to their own claim and in their own supposition, meaning that they dared against God until they supposed that they could deceive Him. This is like His saying: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلى إِلهِكَ الَّذِي ظَلْتَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفاً﴾ ("look at your god to which you were devoted") [Surah Ta-Ha: 97], meaning according to your supposition and by your claim.

It was also said: the meaning is that they act in God's religion in a way that is deception among themselves. And it was said: the meaning is that they deceive His Messenger, like His saying: ﴿فَلَمَّا آسَفُونا انْتَقَمْنا مِنْهُمْ﴾ ("when they angered Us, We took vengeance on them") [Surah al-Zukhruf: 55], meaning: they angered Us. And His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يُؤْذُونَ اللَّهَ﴾ ("those who injure God") [Surah al-Ahzab: 57], meaning: the friends of God, because God, glorified is He, is not harmed or deceived. So God Most High made clear that whoever harms a prophet of His prophets or a friend of His friends deserves punishment, just as if he harmed His Messenger and deceived him. Evidence for this is the reported report: God Most High says: "Whoever harms a friend of Mine has declared war against Me" [Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/137].

It was also said: the mention of God, glorified is He, in His saying ﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾ is an embellishment and adornment for the hearer of the speech, and the intended object of the deception is the believers, like His saying: ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّما غَنِمْتُمْ مِنْ شَيْءٍ فَأَنَّ لِلَّهِ خُمُسَهُ وَلِلرَّسُولِ﴾ ("know that whatever you gain of spoils, a fifth of it is for God and for the Messenger") [Surah al-Anfal: 41]. Then, deception (mukhada‘a) is in proportion to the action, and the intensive form (al-mufa‘ala) mostly comes in an action shared between two, like fighting (muqatala), trading (mudaraba) and mutual abuse (mushatama). It may also come from one party, as when you say: ṭāraqtu al-na‘l (I repaired the sandal), ‘āqabtu al-liṣṣ (I punished the thief), and ‘āfāka Allāh (God granted you well-being). God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَقاسَمَهُما إِنِّي لَكُما لَمِنَ النَّاصِحِينَ﴾ ("and he swore to them, 'I am surely a sincere adviser to you both'") [Surah al-A‘raf: 21], and He said: ﴿قاتَلَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("God fight them") [Surah al-Tawba: 30]. The deception here is an expression for an action that belongs to one party, whereas God does not engage in deception.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: i.e., and they deceive the believers by their saying, when they see them: "We believe," while they are not believers. Some said: among their deception of the believers was that they would sit with the believers and mix with them until the believers became comfortable with them and counted them among themselves, so they would disclose to them their secrets, which they would then convey to their enemies. God Most High said:
﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ إِلَّا أَنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ ("and they deceive none but themselves"), because the harm of their deception returns to them; it is as if in reality they deceive themselves. That is because God Most High informs His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ of their secrets and hypocrisy, so they are disgraced in this world and deserve severe punishment in the Hereafter.

The people of allusion (ahl al-ishara) said: only one who does not know the inner realities deceives; as for one who knows the inner realities, whoever deceives him is only deceiving himself.

The readers differed on His saying: ﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ﴾. Shayba, Nafi‘, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ala’ read ﴿يُخادِعُونَ﴾ with an alif, treating it as the form of mufa‘ala that belongs to one party, and we have mentioned its report; and its confirmation is the first letter. As for His saying ﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾, they did not differ about it except what was narrated from Abu Hamza al-Shami, who read: (yakhda‘una Allah), while the rest read ﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ﴾ according to the more famous and more precise of the two dialects, and Abu 'Ubayd chose it.

﴿وَما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [Surah al-Baqara: 9]: and they do not perceive, meaning: they do not know that it is so.

﴿فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ﴾: doubt and hypocrisy. From it is said: so-and-so sickens in promise when he does not fulfil it. The root of marad (sickness) is weakness and lassitude. So doubt in religion and hypocrisy were named [sickness by which] weakens the body, diminishes its strength, and because it leads to destruction through punishment, just as sickness in the body leads to destruction and death.

﴿فَزادَهُمُ اللَّهُ مَرَضاً﴾: God increased them in sickness: doubt, hypocrisy and destruction.

﴿وَلَهُمْ عَذابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾: a painful, grievous punishment whose pain reaches their hearts; it is in the sense of mu’lim (painful), like the saying of ‘Amr ibn Ma‘di Karib:
"From the fragrant herb of the caller, the one who hears, it keeps me awake while my companions sleep."
[Lisan al-Arab: 8/164.]
That is, al-musma‘ (the one heard), meaning its phantom.

﴿بِما كانُوا يَكْذِبُونَ﴾: (ma) is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), meaning: by their lying against God and His Messenger in secret.

The people of Kufa read: with a fatha on the yā’ and a light dhāl, meaning: by their lying, when they said "We believe" while they were not believers.

﴿وَإِذا﴾: a particle of time meaning "at that time," and it indicates the occurrence of an awaited action and contains the meaning of a conditional. ﴿قِيلَ﴾: a past passive verb. It was originally qawl, like qīl; the kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so its kasra was moved to the first radical of the verb, and the wāw became a yā’ because of the kasra before it. This is the high dialect, on which the common readers rely, and it is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd.

Al-Kisa’i and Ya‘qub read: qīla, ghīḍa, ḥīla, sīqa, jī’a, shī’a and shītu, with ishmam (partial rounding) of the ḍamma in them, so that it indicates the altered wāw and serves as a separator between the initial and the verbal-noun.

﴿لَهُمْ﴾: meaning the hypocrites; it was also said: the Jews. The believers said to them: ﴿لا تُفْسِدُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ ("do not corrupt on the earth") by disbelief, disobedience, and dividing people away from faith in Muhammad and the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: by altering the religion, changing the sunna and distorting the Book of God.

﴿قالُوا إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ﴾: ﴿أَلا﴾ is a word of alerting; ﴿إِنَّهُمْ﴾: ﴿هُمُ﴾ is an emphatic support; ﴿الْمُفْسِدُونَ﴾ ("they are the corrupters"); ﴿وَلكِنْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾: what punishment has been prepared for them.

﴿وَإِذا قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾: meaning [he said] [the zayd is added to complete the meaning]: the believers said to the Jews: ﴿آمِنُوا كَما آمَنَ النَّاسُ﴾ ("believe as the people have believed"), and they are ‘Abd Allah ibn Salam and others among the believers from the People of the Book.

﴿قالُوا أَنُؤْمِنُ كَما آمَنَ السُّفَهاءُ﴾: the foolish, the ignorant. God said: ﴿أَلا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ السُّفَهاءُ وَلكِنْ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("they are indeed the foolish, but they do not know" that they are so). It was also said: they do not render knowledge its due. The historian said: the safīh (foolish) is the liar who deliberately contradicts what he knows.

Qutrub said: the safīh is the hasty, unjust one who acts contrary to the truth.

The readers differed on His saying ﴿السُّفَهاءُ أَلا﴾. Some made both hamzas clear, which is the school of the people of Kufa and the dialect of Tamim.

As for Abu 'Amr and the people of the Hijaz, they hamzated the first and softened the second, seeking lightness. Al-Farra’ preferred omitting the first and hamzating the second, arguing that what is resumed (yustaʾnaf, i.e., with the hamza) is what one pauses upon.

﴿وَإِذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾.

Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul al-Khazraji was the greatest of the hypocrites, from the clan of Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubada. Whenever he met Sa‘d he would say: "How excellent is the religion of Muhammad." But when he returned to the chiefs of his people, they would say: "Shall we disbelieve?" He would say: "Hold your hands by the religion of your fathers." Then God revealed this verse.

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, as a proof against him. That was because they went out one day and a group of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ met them. ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said to his companions: "Watch how I will ward these foolish ones away from you." He went and took the hand of Abu Bakr and said: "Welcome, O Sincere One (al-Siddiq), lord of the clan of Taym, shaykh of Islam, the second of the Messenger of God ﷺ in the cave, and the one who gave his soul and wealth to him." Then he took the hand of ‘Umar and said: "Welcome, lord of the clan of ‘Adi ibn Ka‘b, al-Faruq, the strong one in the religion of God, who gave his soul and wealth to the Messenger of God." Then he took the hand of ‘Ali and said: "Welcome, cousin of the Messenger of God and his son-in-law, lord of the clan of Hashim, other than the Messenger of God ﷺ." ‘Ali said: "Hold back, for God's sake, and fear God, and do not be a hypocrite, for the hypocrites are the worst creatures of God." ‘Abd Allah said: "Gently, Abu al-Hasan, is this what you say to me? By God, our faith is like your faith and our affirmation like your affirmation." Then they separated. ‘Abd Allah said to his companions: "How did you see me act? When you meet them, do as I have done." They praised him and said: "We will remain with you as long as you live." The Muslims returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of that, so God revealed: ﴿وَإِذا لَقُوا﴾, that is, met, meaning the hypocrites ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

(The original form of "laqu" was "laqiyu"; the ḍamma was felt heavy on the yā’, so it was moved onto the qāf, and the wāw and yā’ both being silent, they were dropped because they came together.)

Muhammad ibn al-Sumay‘ read: wa-idha lāqū, and both have the same meaning.

﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: meaning Abu Bakr and his companions. ﴿قالُوا آمَنَّا كأيمانكم﴾. ﴿وَإِذا خَلَوْا﴾: they returned. It may also be from seclusion (khalwa): one says khalawtu bihi, khalawtu ilayhi, khalawtu ma‘ahu, all with the same meaning.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "ila" here has the meaning of "ma‘a" (with), like His saying: ﴿أُحِلَّ لَكُمْ لَيْلَةَ الصِّيامِ الرَّفَثُ إِلى نِسائِكُمْ﴾ ("It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to go in unto your wives") [Surah al-Baqara: 187], meaning: with your wives; and His saying: ﴿لا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوالَهُمْ إِلى أَمْوالِكُمْ﴾ ("do not consume their wealth along with your wealth") [Surah al-Nisa’: 2]; and His saying: ﴿مَنْ أَنْصارِي إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾ ("who are my helpers to God?") [Al ‘Imran: 52]. Al-Nabigha said:
"Do not leave me to threats as if I were, among people, a mangy camel smeared with tar."
[Lisan al-Arab: 15/435.]
That is, among the people.

Another said:
"And he stretched his two arms into a pool, along with a fleshy-chested one with a loose shoulder."
[Lisan al-Arab: 3/156.]
That is, along with the fleshy-chested one.

﴿إِلى شَياطِينِهِمْ﴾: that is, their chiefs, their great ones, their leaders and their soothsayers.

Ibn ‘Abbas said: they are five men from the Jews; there is no soothsayer except that with him is a devil who follows him: Ka‘b ibn al-Ashraf in Medina, Abu Burda among the Banu Aslam, ‘Abd Allah among Juhayna, ‘Awf ibn ‘Amir among the Banu Asad, and ‘Abd Allah ibn al-Sawda’ in Syria.

The shaytan is the rebellious, disobedient one among the jinn and mankind, and among every thing; from it the viper (al-nadnad) is called shaytan. God Most High said: ﴿طَلْعُها كَأَنَّهُ رُؤُسُ الشَّياطِينِ﴾ ("its shoots are like the heads of devils") [Surah al-Saffat: 65], meaning the snakes. The Arabs say: "Beware of that creature, for it is a shaytan."

In a hadith: "If a man passes in front of one of you while he is praying, let him prevent him; if he refuses, let him fight him, for he is a shaytan."

It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he saw a man following a pigeon, and he said: "A shaytan following a shaytan" [In some sources: "his shaytan"].
[74] [Musnad Ahmad: 2/345; Kanz al-‘Ummal: 15/218.]

He meant the wicked shepherd, the caller.

It is reported of one of them that in the midst of his speech he said: "All that is because a shaytan mounted me." It was said to him: "Which of the shayatin mounted you?" He said: "Anger."

Abu al-Najm said:
"I and every poet among the human race have a shaytan: mine is male and his is female."
[Sharh Nahj al-Balagha by Ibn Abi al-Hadid: 19/425.]

﴿قالُوا إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾: that is, on your religion and as your helpers.

﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾: at Muhammad and his Companions.

﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾: that is, He repays them for their mockery. The repayment is named by the name of the initial act, since it is similar to it in form, like His saying: ﴿جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُها﴾ ("the requital of an evil deed is an evil deed like it") [Surah al-Shura: 40], where the repayment of an evil deed is named an evil deed.

‘Amr ibn Kulthum said:
"Let no one act ignorantly against us, lest we act ignorantly beyond the ignorance of the ignorant."
[Lisan al-Arab: 3/177 and 8/64.]

Another said:
"We repay them the measure of the cup for what they did, and whoever treats his paternal cousin with injustice is himself unjustly treated."
Thus the repayment is named injustice.

It was also said: the meaning is: God rebukes them, exposes them, and condemns their action, because mockery and derision among the Arabs mean blame and ignorance-ascription, as one says: "So-and-so is mocked today," meaning he is blamed. God said: ﴿وَإِذا سَمِعْتُمْ آياتِ اللَّهِ يُكْفَرُ بِها وَيُسْتَهْزَأُ بِها﴾ ("when you hear the signs of God being disbelieved in and mocked") [Surah al-Nisa’: 140], meaning: blamed. And He related, speaking of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿إِنْ تَسْخَرُوا مِنَّا فَإِنَّا نَسْخَرُ مِنْكُمْ كَما تَسْخَرُونَ﴾ ("if you mock us, then we mock you as you mock") [Surah Hud: 38].

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is: God exposes the believers' hypocrisy [to the believers].

Ibn ‘Abbas said: it is that God will, on the Day of Resurrection, let the believers, who are in Paradise, look down upon the hypocrites, who are in the Fire. They will say to them: "Would you like to enter Paradise?" They will say: "Yes." Then a door of Paradise is opened for them, and it is said to them: "Enter." They hasten toward it, and they turn about in the Fire; when they reach the door, it is shut upon them and they are returned to the Fire, and the believers laugh at them. That is His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ أَجْرَمُوا كانُوا مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَضْحَكُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed") up to His saying: ﴿فَالْيَوْمَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنَ الْكُفَّارِ يَضْحَكُونَ﴾ ("So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers") [Surah al-Mutaffifin: 34].

Al-A‘mash narrated from Khaythama from ‘Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Some people will be ordered to Paradise until, when they draw near it and smell its fragrance and look at what God has prepared in it for its people of honour, they will be called: 'Turn them away from it.' He said: 'They will return in grief and remorse, such as no creation has returned with.' They will say: 'O our Lord, if You had caused us to enter the Fire before You showed us what You have shown us, it would have been easier for us.' Then God, majestic is His majesty, will say: 'This is what I intended for you: you feared people and did not fear Me, you honoured people and did not honour Me, and you used to show off to people with your deeds, contrary to what you used to see in Me in your hearts. So today I will make you taste My punishment, along with what I have withheld from you of My reward.'"
[Kanz al-‘Ummal: 3/484, with variation.]

It was also said: it is His forsaking them and depriving them of success and guidance.

This is His saying afterward: ﴿وَيَمُدُّهُمْ﴾: He leaves them, gives them respite, and prolongs for them. Its root is increase; it is said: "the river extended" (madda al-nahr), and madda: another period of time.

Ibn Muhaysin and Shibl read: ﴿وَيُمِدُّهُمْ﴾ with a ḍamma on the yā’ and a kasra on the mīm; the two are dialects with the same meaning, because madd (extension) mostly comes in evil and imdad (supplying) in good. God, Mighty and Majestic, said of madd: ﴿وَنَمُدُّ لَهُ مِنَ الْعَذابِ مَدًّا﴾ ("We will extend for him of the punishment an extension") [Surah Maryam: 79]; and about imdad He said: ﴿وَأَمْدَدْناكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("and We supplied you with wealth and children") [Surah al-Isra’: 6]; and He said: ﴿أَيَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّما نُمِدُّهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ مالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("Do they think that what We supply them with of wealth and children") [Surah al-Mu’minun: 55]; and He said: ﴿وَيُمْدِدْكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("and He will supply you with wealth and children") [Surah Nuh: 12].

﴿فِي طُغْيانِهِمْ﴾: their disbelief, their misguidance and their ignorance. The root of ṭughyān is exceeding the measure: one says "a scale in which there is ṭughyān," meaning it exceeds the measure in its evenness. God Most High said: ﴿إِنَّا لَمَّا طَغَى الْماءُ﴾ ("When the water overflowed") [Surah al-Haqqa: 11], meaning it exceeded the limit ordained for it; and He said to Pharaoh: ﴿إِنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("indeed he has transgressed") [Surah Ta-Ha: 24], meaning he went to excess in his claim when he said: ﴿أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلى﴾ ("I am your most exalted lord") [Surah al-Nazi‘at: 24].

﴿يَعْمَهُونَ﴾: they pass on, wandering in error, bewildered.
One says: ‘amiha ya‘mahu ‘amhan and ‘umuwwan, and ‘amiha fahuwa ‘amih, and ‘amih: when he is deviating from the truth. Ru’ba said:
"And a desert whose edges are in desert, blind to guidance, with the ignorant wandering."
[Lisan al-Arab: 13/519.]

﴿أُولئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ بِالْهُدى﴾:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They took error and left guidance." Its meaning is that they exchanged disbelief for faith. He expressed it with the wording of purchase (shirāʾ) and trade (tijārah) figuratively, because purchase and trade both come back to exchange (istibdāl) and choice (ikhtiyār), since each of the two parties in a sale chooses what is in the other's hand over what is in his own. The poet said:

I took by the forelock a bald-headed man,
and by the shining front teeth the one with the gap,
and by the tall, long-lived one, a stout-bodied man,
just as the Muslim bought Christianity when he became a Christian. [[al-Tibyan, al-Tusi: 1/83.]]

That is, he chose Christianity over Islam.

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read اشْتَرَوِا الضَّلالَةَ (ishtarawi al-ḍalālah) with a kasrah on the waw, because the dammah of the plural-related waw is moved to the kasrah, the ʿadwa (the original movement) being moved to the lighter vowel, the kasrah, for ease of pronunciation.

فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ (fa-mā ribiḥat tijāratuhum): that is, they did not profit in their trade.

The Arabs say: "ribiḥa bayʿuka" (your sale profited) and "khasirat ṣafqatuka" (your bargain lost), and "nāma layluka" (your night slept). That is, you profited and lost in your sale, and you slept through your night. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿فَإِذا عَزَمَ الْأَمْرُ﴾ [[Surat Muhammad: 21.]] ("but when the matter is resolved"), and He says: ﴿بَلْ مَكْرُ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهارِ﴾ [[Surat Saba': 33.]] ("rather, the plotting of the night and the day").

The poet said:

One-eyed as he is from Nayhan: his day is blind,
but his night is clear-sighted.

Another said:

Ḥārith, you have relieved my worry,
so my night slept and my grief was lifted.

Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAblah read (fa-mā ribiḥat tijāratuhum) in the plural (tijārātuhum).

وَما كانُوا مُهْتَدِينَ (wa-mā kānū muhtadīn): from error. He said: they were not correct in their trade.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Every one of you is a merchant, so let each man look at what his trade is." Allah says: ﴿فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ﴾, and He says: ﴿هَلْ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلى تِجارَةٍ تُنْجِيكُمْ مِنْ عَذابٍ أَلِيمٍ﴾ [[Surat al-Saff: 10.]] ("Shall I direct you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?").

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 8–16 (part 1 of 2):

�´وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَقُولُ آمَنَّا﴾: i.e., we affirm (saddaqna) by God and by the Last Day (al-yawm al-akhir): that is, the Day of Resurrection. [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 10/243, and Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 174.]

God Most High said: ﴿وَمَا هُمْ بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and they are not believers").

Al-nas (the people): they are a group of animals distinguished by the human form, and it is the plural of insan (human being). Insan originally was insiyan with a yā’, and they dropped the yā’ and transferred its vowel to the sīn, so it became insan. Do you not see that when you diminish it (form the diminutive), you restore the yā’ to it and say unaysiyan?

The scholars differed about the reason for this name. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was named insan because a covenant was made with it and it forgot (nasiya). God Most High said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ عَهِدْنا إِلى آدَمَ مِنْ قَبْلُ فَنَسِيَ﴾ ("We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot") [Surah Ta-Ha: 115]. And a poet said:
"And you were named insan because you are forgetful."
[Came in prose-like form rather than verse in Lisan al-Arab: 6/11.]

Some of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: it was named insan for its visibility (zuhur) and for the perceiving of it (qadas al-basir iyyahu), from your saying: ānastu kadha, meaning: I perceived such-and-such. God Most High said: ﴿آنَسَ مِنْ جانِبِ الطُّورِ ناراً﴾ ("he perceived a fire from the side of the mount") [Surah al-Qasas: 29]. It was also said: because it takes comfort (yasta’nisu) in it, and it was said: when God created Adam, He made him comfortable with his wife, so he was named insan.

﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾: i.e., they oppose God and deny Him. The root of khada' (deception) in the language is concealment, and from it is said [for the room in which goods are kept] makhda‘ (a storeroom). The one who deceives (al-mukhadi‘) shows the opposite of what he conceals. Some said: the root of khida‘ in the language is corruption, and a poet said:
"White of colour, delicious of taste, good of saliva, when saliva is corrupted (khada‘)."
[Lisan al-Arab: 8/65.]
That is, it corrupted (fasada).

So its meaning would be: they corrupt by what they conceal within themselves and what they hide in their hearts. It was also said that its meaning is: they deceive God according to their own claim and in their own supposition, meaning that they dared against God until they supposed that they could deceive Him. This is like His saying: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلى إِلهِكَ الَّذِي ظَلْتَ عَلَيْهِ عاكِفاً﴾ ("look at your god to which you were devoted") [Surah Ta-Ha: 97], meaning according to your supposition and by your claim.

It was also said: the meaning is that they act in God's religion in a way that is deception among themselves. And it was said: the meaning is that they deceive His Messenger, like His saying: ﴿فَلَمَّا آسَفُونا انْتَقَمْنا مِنْهُمْ﴾ ("when they angered Us, We took vengeance on them") [Surah al-Zukhruf: 55], meaning: they angered Us. And His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يُؤْذُونَ اللَّهَ﴾ ("those who injure God") [Surah al-Ahzab: 57], meaning: the friends of God, because God, glorified is He, is not harmed or deceived. So God Most High made clear that whoever harms a prophet of His prophets or a friend of His friends deserves punishment, just as if he harmed His Messenger and deceived him. Evidence for this is the reported report: God Most High says: "Whoever harms a friend of Mine has declared war against Me" [Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/137].

It was also said: the mention of God, glorified is He, in His saying ﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾ is an embellishment and adornment for the hearer of the speech, and the intended object of the deception is the believers, like His saying: ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّما غَنِمْتُمْ مِنْ شَيْءٍ فَأَنَّ لِلَّهِ خُمُسَهُ وَلِلرَّسُولِ﴾ ("know that whatever you gain of spoils, a fifth of it is for God and for the Messenger") [Surah al-Anfal: 41]. Then, deception (mukhada‘a) is in proportion to the action, and the intensive form (al-mufa‘ala) mostly comes in an action shared between two, like fighting (muqatala), trading (mudaraba) and mutual abuse (mushatama). It may also come from one party, as when you say: ṭāraqtu al-na‘l (I repaired the sandal), ‘āqabtu al-liṣṣ (I punished the thief), and ‘āfāka Allāh (God granted you well-being). God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَقاسَمَهُما إِنِّي لَكُما لَمِنَ النَّاصِحِينَ﴾ ("and he swore to them, 'I am surely a sincere adviser to you both'") [Surah al-A‘raf: 21], and He said: ﴿قاتَلَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("God fight them") [Surah al-Tawba: 30]. The deception here is an expression for an action that belongs to one party, whereas God does not engage in deception.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: i.e., and they deceive the believers by their saying, when they see them: "We believe," while they are not believers. Some said: among their deception of the believers was that they would sit with the believers and mix with them until the believers became comfortable with them and counted them among themselves, so they would disclose to them their secrets, which they would then convey to their enemies. God Most High said:
﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ إِلَّا أَنْفُسَهُمْ﴾ ("and they deceive none but themselves"), because the harm of their deception returns to them; it is as if in reality they deceive themselves. That is because God Most High informs His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ of their secrets and hypocrisy, so they are disgraced in this world and deserve severe punishment in the Hereafter.

The people of allusion (ahl al-ishara) said: only one who does not know the inner realities deceives; as for one who knows the inner realities, whoever deceives him is only deceiving himself.

The readers differed on His saying: ﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ﴾. Shayba, Nafi‘, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu ‘Amr ibn al-‘Ala’ read ﴿يُخادِعُونَ﴾ with an alif, treating it as the form of mufa‘ala that belongs to one party, and we have mentioned its report; and its confirmation is the first letter. As for His saying ﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللَّهَ﴾, they did not differ about it except what was narrated from Abu Hamza al-Shami, who read: (yakhda‘una Allah), while the rest read ﴿وَما يَخْدَعُونَ﴾ according to the more famous and more precise of the two dialects, and Abu 'Ubayd chose it.

﴿وَما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [Surah al-Baqara: 9]: and they do not perceive, meaning: they do not know that it is so.

﴿فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ مَرَضٌ﴾: doubt and hypocrisy. From it is said: so-and-so sickens in promise when he does not fulfil it. The root of marad (sickness) is weakness and lassitude. So doubt in religion and hypocrisy were named [sickness by which] weakens the body, diminishes its strength, and because it leads to destruction through punishment, just as sickness in the body leads to destruction and death.

﴿فَزادَهُمُ اللَّهُ مَرَضاً﴾: God increased them in sickness: doubt, hypocrisy and destruction.

﴿وَلَهُمْ عَذابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾: a painful, grievous punishment whose pain reaches their hearts; it is in the sense of mu’lim (painful), like the saying of ‘Amr ibn Ma‘di Karib:
"From the fragrant herb of the caller, the one who hears, it keeps me awake while my companions sleep."
[Lisan al-Arab: 8/164.]
That is, al-musma‘ (the one heard), meaning its phantom.

﴿بِما كانُوا يَكْذِبُونَ﴾: (ma) is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), meaning: by their lying against God and His Messenger in secret.

The people of Kufa read: with a fatha on the yā’ and a light dhāl, meaning: by their lying, when they said "We believe" while they were not believers.

﴿وَإِذا﴾: a particle of time meaning "at that time," and it indicates the occurrence of an awaited action and contains the meaning of a conditional. ﴿قِيلَ﴾: a past passive verb. It was originally qawl, like qīl; the kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so its kasra was moved to the first radical of the verb, and the wāw became a yā’ because of the kasra before it. This is the high dialect, on which the common readers rely, and it is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd.

Al-Kisa’i and Ya‘qub read: qīla, ghīḍa, ḥīla, sīqa, jī’a, shī’a and shītu, with ishmam (partial rounding) of the ḍamma in them, so that it indicates the altered wāw and serves as a separator between the initial and the verbal-noun.

﴿لَهُمْ﴾: meaning the hypocrites; it was also said: the Jews. The believers said to them: ﴿لا تُفْسِدُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ ("do not corrupt on the earth") by disbelief, disobedience, and dividing people away from faith in Muhammad and the Qur'an. Al-Dahhak said: by altering the religion, changing the sunna and distorting the Book of God.

﴿قالُوا إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ﴾: ﴿أَلا﴾ is a word of alerting; ﴿إِنَّهُمْ﴾: ﴿هُمُ﴾ is an emphatic support; ﴿الْمُفْسِدُونَ﴾ ("they are the corrupters"); ﴿وَلكِنْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾: what punishment has been prepared for them.

﴿وَإِذا قِيلَ لَهُمْ﴾: meaning [he said] [the zayd is added to complete the meaning]: the believers said to the Jews: ﴿آمِنُوا كَما آمَنَ النَّاسُ﴾ ("believe as the people have believed"), and they are ‘Abd Allah ibn Salam and others among the believers from the People of the Book.

﴿قالُوا أَنُؤْمِنُ كَما آمَنَ السُّفَهاءُ﴾: the foolish, the ignorant. God said: ﴿أَلا إِنَّهُمْ هُمُ السُّفَهاءُ وَلكِنْ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("they are indeed the foolish, but they do not know" that they are so). It was also said: they do not render knowledge its due. The historian said: the safīh (foolish) is the liar who deliberately contradicts what he knows.

Qutrub said: the safīh is the hasty, unjust one who acts contrary to the truth.

The readers differed on His saying ﴿السُّفَهاءُ أَلا﴾. Some made both hamzas clear, which is the school of the people of Kufa and the dialect of Tamim.

As for Abu 'Amr and the people of the Hijaz, they hamzated the first and softened the second, seeking lightness. Al-Farra’ preferred omitting the first and hamzating the second, arguing that what is resumed (yustaʾnaf, i.e., with the hamza) is what one pauses upon.

﴿وَإِذا لَقُوا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾.

Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak from Ibn ‘Abbas, who said: ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul al-Khazraji was the greatest of the hypocrites, from the clan of Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubada. Whenever he met Sa‘d he would say: "How excellent is the religion of Muhammad." But when he returned to the chiefs of his people, they would say: "Shall we disbelieve?" He would say: "Hold your hands by the religion of your fathers." Then God revealed this verse.

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas: this verse was revealed concerning ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, as a proof against him. That was because they went out one day and a group of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ met them. ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy said to his companions: "Watch how I will ward these foolish ones away from you." He went and took the hand of Abu Bakr and said: "Welcome, O Sincere One (al-Siddiq), lord of the clan of Taym, shaykh of Islam, the second of the Messenger of God ﷺ in the cave, and the one who gave his soul and wealth to him." Then he took the hand of ‘Umar and said: "Welcome, lord of the clan of ‘Adi ibn Ka‘b, al-Faruq, the strong one in the religion of God, who gave his soul and wealth to the Messenger of God." Then he took the hand of ‘Ali and said: "Welcome, cousin of the Messenger of God and his son-in-law, lord of the clan of Hashim, other than the Messenger of God ﷺ." ‘Ali said: "Hold back, for God's sake, and fear God, and do not be a hypocrite, for the hypocrites are the worst creatures of God." ‘Abd Allah said: "Gently, Abu al-Hasan, is this what you say to me? By God, our faith is like your faith and our affirmation like your affirmation." Then they separated. ‘Abd Allah said to his companions: "How did you see me act? When you meet them, do as I have done." They praised him and said: "We will remain with you as long as you live." The Muslims returned to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of that, so God revealed: ﴿وَإِذا لَقُوا﴾, that is, met, meaning the hypocrites ‘Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

(The original form of "laqu" was "laqiyu"; the ḍamma was felt heavy on the yā’, so it was moved onto the qāf, and the wāw and yā’ both being silent, they were dropped because they came together.)

Muhammad ibn al-Sumay‘ read: wa-idha lāqū, and both have the same meaning.

﴿الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾: meaning Abu Bakr and his companions. ﴿قالُوا آمَنَّا كأيمانكم﴾. ﴿وَإِذا خَلَوْا﴾: they returned. It may also be from seclusion (khalwa): one says khalawtu bihi, khalawtu ilayhi, khalawtu ma‘ahu, all with the same meaning.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "ila" here has the meaning of "ma‘a" (with), like His saying: ﴿أُحِلَّ لَكُمْ لَيْلَةَ الصِّيامِ الرَّفَثُ إِلى نِسائِكُمْ﴾ ("It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to go in unto your wives") [Surah al-Baqara: 187], meaning: with your wives; and His saying: ﴿لا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوالَهُمْ إِلى أَمْوالِكُمْ﴾ ("do not consume their wealth along with your wealth") [Surah al-Nisa’: 2]; and His saying: ﴿مَنْ أَنْصارِي إِلَى اللَّهِ﴾ ("who are my helpers to God?") [Al ‘Imran: 52]. Al-Nabigha said:
"Do not leave me to threats as if I were, among people, a mangy camel smeared with tar."
[Lisan al-Arab: 15/435.]
That is, among the people.

Another said:
"And he stretched his two arms into a pool, along with a fleshy-chested one with a loose shoulder."
[Lisan al-Arab: 3/156.]
That is, along with the fleshy-chested one.

﴿إِلى شَياطِينِهِمْ﴾: that is, their chiefs, their great ones, their leaders and their soothsayers.

Ibn ‘Abbas said: they are five men from the Jews; there is no soothsayer except that with him is a devil who follows him: Ka‘b ibn al-Ashraf in Medina, Abu Burda among the Banu Aslam, ‘Abd Allah among Juhayna, ‘Awf ibn ‘Amir among the Banu Asad, and ‘Abd Allah ibn al-Sawda’ in Syria.

The shaytan is the rebellious, disobedient one among the jinn and mankind, and among every thing; from it the viper (al-nadnad) is called shaytan. God Most High said: ﴿طَلْعُها كَأَنَّهُ رُؤُسُ الشَّياطِينِ﴾ ("its shoots are like the heads of devils") [Surah al-Saffat: 65], meaning the snakes. The Arabs say: "Beware of that creature, for it is a shaytan."

In a hadith: "If a man passes in front of one of you while he is praying, let him prevent him; if he refuses, let him fight him, for he is a shaytan."

It is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he saw a man following a pigeon, and he said: "A shaytan following a shaytan" [In some sources: "his shaytan"].
[74] [Musnad Ahmad: 2/345; Kanz al-‘Ummal: 15/218.]

He meant the wicked shepherd, the caller.

It is reported of one of them that in the midst of his speech he said: "All that is because a shaytan mounted me." It was said to him: "Which of the shayatin mounted you?" He said: "Anger."

Abu al-Najm said:
"I and every poet among the human race have a shaytan: mine is male and his is female."
[Sharh Nahj al-Balagha by Ibn Abi al-Hadid: 19/425.]

﴿قالُوا إِنَّا مَعَكُمْ﴾: that is, on your religion and as your helpers.

﴿إِنَّما نَحْنُ مُسْتَهْزِؤُنَ﴾: at Muhammad and his Companions.

﴿اللَّهُ يَسْتَهْزِئُ بِهِمْ﴾: that is, He repays them for their mockery. The repayment is named by the name of the initial act, since it is similar to it in form, like His saying: ﴿جَزاءُ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِثْلُها﴾ ("the requital of an evil deed is an evil deed like it") [Surah al-Shura: 40], where the repayment of an evil deed is named an evil deed.

‘Amr ibn Kulthum said:
"Let no one act ignorantly against us, lest we act ignorantly beyond the ignorance of the ignorant."
[Lisan al-Arab: 3/177 and 8/64.]

Another said:
"We repay them the measure of the cup for what they did, and whoever treats his paternal cousin with injustice is himself unjustly treated."
Thus the repayment is named injustice.

It was also said: the meaning is: God rebukes them, exposes them, and condemns their action, because mockery and derision among the Arabs mean blame and ignorance-ascription, as one says: "So-and-so is mocked today," meaning he is blamed. God said: ﴿وَإِذا سَمِعْتُمْ آياتِ اللَّهِ يُكْفَرُ بِها وَيُسْتَهْزَأُ بِها﴾ ("when you hear the signs of God being disbelieved in and mocked") [Surah al-Nisa’: 140], meaning: blamed. And He related, speaking of Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿إِنْ تَسْخَرُوا مِنَّا فَإِنَّا نَسْخَرُ مِنْكُمْ كَما تَسْخَرُونَ﴾ ("if you mock us, then we mock you as you mock") [Surah Hud: 38].

Al-Hasan said: the meaning is: God exposes the believers' hypocrisy [to the believers].

Ibn ‘Abbas said: it is that God will, on the Day of Resurrection, let the believers, who are in Paradise, look down upon the hypocrites, who are in the Fire. They will say to them: "Would you like to enter Paradise?" They will say: "Yes." Then a door of Paradise is opened for them, and it is said to them: "Enter." They hasten toward it, and they turn about in the Fire; when they reach the door, it is shut upon them and they are returned to the Fire, and the believers laugh at them. That is His saying: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ أَجْرَمُوا كانُوا مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا يَضْحَكُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed") up to His saying: ﴿فَالْيَوْمَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنَ الْكُفَّارِ يَضْحَكُونَ﴾ ("So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers") [Surah al-Mutaffifin: 34].

Al-A‘mash narrated from Khaythama from ‘Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Some people will be ordered to Paradise until, when they draw near it and smell its fragrance and look at what God has prepared in it for its people of honour, they will be called: 'Turn them away from it.' He said: 'They will return in grief and remorse, such as no creation has returned with.' They will say: 'O our Lord, if You had caused us to enter the Fire before You showed us what You have shown us, it would have been easier for us.' Then God, majestic is His majesty, will say: 'This is what I intended for you: you feared people and did not fear Me, you honoured people and did not honour Me, and you used to show off to people with your deeds, contrary to what you used to see in Me in your hearts. So today I will make you taste My punishment, along with what I have withheld from you of My reward.'"
[Kanz al-‘Ummal: 3/484, with variation.]

It was also said: it is His forsaking them and depriving them of success and guidance.

This is His saying afterward: ﴿وَيَمُدُّهُمْ﴾: He leaves them, gives them respite, and prolongs for them. Its root is increase; it is said: "the river extended" (madda al-nahr), and madda: another period of time.

Ibn Muhaysin and Shibl read: ﴿وَيُمِدُّهُمْ﴾ with a ḍamma on the yā’ and a kasra on the mīm; the two are dialects with the same meaning, because madd (extension) mostly comes in evil and imdad (supplying) in good. God, Mighty and Majestic, said of madd: ﴿وَنَمُدُّ لَهُ مِنَ الْعَذابِ مَدًّا﴾ ("We will extend for him of the punishment an extension") [Surah Maryam: 79]; and about imdad He said: ﴿وَأَمْدَدْناكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("and We supplied you with wealth and children") [Surah al-Isra’: 6]; and He said: ﴿أَيَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّما نُمِدُّهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ مالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("Do they think that what We supply them with of wealth and children") [Surah al-Mu’minun: 55]; and He said: ﴿وَيُمْدِدْكُمْ بِأَمْوالٍ وَبَنِينَ﴾ ("and He will supply you with wealth and children") [Surah Nuh: 12].

﴿فِي طُغْيانِهِمْ﴾: their disbelief, their misguidance and their ignorance. The root of ṭughyān is exceeding the measure: one says "a scale in which there is ṭughyān," meaning it exceeds the measure in its evenness. God Most High said: ﴿إِنَّا لَمَّا طَغَى الْماءُ﴾ ("When the water overflowed") [Surah al-Haqqa: 11], meaning it exceeded the limit ordained for it; and He said to Pharaoh: ﴿إِنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("indeed he has transgressed") [Surah Ta-Ha: 24], meaning he went to excess in his claim when he said: ﴿أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلى﴾ ("I am your most exalted lord") [Surah al-Nazi‘at: 24].

﴿يَعْمَهُونَ﴾: they pass on, wandering in error, bewildered.
One says: ‘amiha ya‘mahu ‘amhan and ‘umuwwan, and ‘amiha fahuwa ‘amih, and ‘amih: when he is deviating from the truth. Ru’ba said:
"And a desert whose edges are in desert, blind to guidance, with the ignorant wandering."
[Lisan al-Arab: 13/519.]

﴿أُولئِكَ الَّذِينَ اشْتَرَوُا الضَّلالَةَ بِالْهُدى﴾:

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They took error and left guidance." Its meaning is that they exchanged disbelief for faith. He expressed it with the wording of purchase (shirāʾ) and trade (tijārah) figuratively, because purchase and trade both come back to exchange (istibdāl) and choice (ikhtiyār), since each of the two parties in a sale chooses what is in the other's hand over what is in his own. The poet said:

I took by the forelock a bald-headed man,
and by the shining front teeth the one with the gap,
and by the tall, long-lived one, a stout-bodied man,
just as the Muslim bought Christianity when he became a Christian. [[al-Tibyan, al-Tusi: 1/83.]]

That is, he chose Christianity over Islam.

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read اشْتَرَوِا الضَّلالَةَ (ishtarawi al-ḍalālah) with a kasrah on the waw, because the dammah of the plural-related waw is moved to the kasrah, the ʿadwa (the original movement) being moved to the lighter vowel, the kasrah, for ease of pronunciation.

فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ (fa-mā ribiḥat tijāratuhum): that is, they did not profit in their trade.

The Arabs say: "ribiḥa bayʿuka" (your sale profited) and "khasirat ṣafqatuka" (your bargain lost), and "nāma layluka" (your night slept). That is, you profited and lost in your sale, and you slept through your night. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿فَإِذا عَزَمَ الْأَمْرُ﴾ [[Surat Muhammad: 21.]] ("but when the matter is resolved"), and He says: ﴿بَلْ مَكْرُ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهارِ﴾ [[Surat Saba': 33.]] ("rather, the plotting of the night and the day").

The poet said:

One-eyed as he is from Nayhan: his day is blind,
but his night is clear-sighted.

Another said:

Ḥārith, you have relieved my worry,
so my night slept and my grief was lifted.

Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAblah read (fa-mā ribiḥat tijāratuhum) in the plural (tijārātuhum).

وَما كانُوا مُهْتَدِينَ (wa-mā kānū muhtadīn): from error. He said: they were not correct in their trade.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: "Every one of you is a merchant, so let each man look at what his trade is." Allah says: ﴿فَما رَبِحَتْ تِجارَتُهُمْ﴾, and He says: ﴿هَلْ أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلى تِجارَةٍ تُنْجِيكُمْ مِنْ عَذابٍ أَلِيمٍ﴾ [[Surat al-Saff: 10.]] ("Shall I direct you to a trade that will save you from a painful punishment?").

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 8–16 (part 1 of 2):

�´وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَقُولُ آمَنَّا﴾: i.e., we affirm (saddaqna) by God and by the Last Day (al-yawm al-akhir): that is, the Day of Resurrection. [See Tafsir al-Tabari: 10/243, and Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 174.]

God Most High said: ﴿وَمَا هُمْ بِمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and they are not believers").

Al-nas (the people): they are a group of animals distinguished by the human form, and it is the plural of insan (human being).
