The scholars differed about these names. Al-Rabi' and Ibn Anas said: they are the names of the angels. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the names of his offspring.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: Allah taught him the name of every thing, even the dish and the small dish.

Muqatil said: Allah created everything — animals, inanimate objects and others — then taught Adam their names, all of them. He said to him: "O Adam, this is a horse, this is a mule, this is a donkey," until he had gone through all of them. Then He presented those things as He presented the existing things to the angels. Thus He said: ﴿then He presented them﴾ and did not say "presented it," and He returned it to the persons and named things, because accidents cannot be presented.

It is also said: Allah taught Adam, peace be upon him, the craft of every thing.

Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, said: Allah taught Adam the names of creatures, towns, cities, mountains, predators, the names of birds and trees, the names of what was and what will be, and every soul that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will bring into being until the Day of Resurrection; and He presented those names to the angels.

He said: "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful." Indeed the khalifa I place on the earth will cause corruption therein and shed blood. Allah the Exalted meant by this: "How do you claim knowledge of what has not yet occurred, when you do not know what you see and witness?"

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ — that I will not create a creature except that you will be more knowledgeable and better than it. The angels said, acknowledging their inability and apologising.

They said: Glory be to You — declaring You free of objection, because of Your knowledge in Your judgment and management. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun; meaning, "We glorify a glorification," according to al-Khalil's view.

al-Kisa'i said: it is outside the description. It is also said: it is in the vocative construction, meaning: "O Your glory."

We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed You are the All-Knowing about Your creation, the All-Wise in Your command.

For al-ḥakīm (the Wise) there are two meanings. One: the one who makes the act firm, as in His saying: ﴿a painful punishment﴾, and "a painful wound." The poet said:

"Does the echo of the calling companion of Rayhanah, the one who hears, keep me awake, while my companions sleep?"

meaning: the painful and aching one, and "the one who makes to hear." In this interpretation it is an adjective of act.

The other meaning is "the judge, the knower," and in that case it is an adjective of essence. The root of wisdom in Arabic speech is prevention. One says: "I prevented the orphan from corruption and restrained him," meaning I prevented him. Jarir said:

"Sons of Hanifah, restrain your foolish ones; indeed I fear that I will become angry at you."

The bit that is placed across a horse's mouth is called ḥikma, because it prevents the horse from turning aside, and wisdom prevents from falsehood; and what is not beautiful is not permitted in the judicious matter, by preventing it from disorder. In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne, since Allah commanded the angels to report what they did not know, while He knew their inability to do so.

When their inability became evident, Allah the Exalted said: "O Adam, inform them of their names." So he named every thing by its name, and joined every thing to its kind.

When he informed them of their names — told them. He said: "Did I not tell you, O My angels? Indeed I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth — what is hidden in them and what will be. And I know what you reveal of humility and obedience to Adam, and what you conceal" — what you hide within yourselves of enmity toward him. It is also said: "what you reveal" is their acknowledgment of inability and apology, and "what you conceal" is their dislike of Adam's appointment as khalifa.

Ibn Abbas said: Iblis passed by the body of Adam, which lay between Makkah and al-Ta'if without a spirit in it, and said: "For what matter was this created?" Then he entered through its mouth and came out through its back, and said: "It will not hold together except by the hollow." Then he said to the angels with him: "Do you see that if this is preferred over you and you are commanded to obey it, what would you do?" They said: "We will obey the command of our Lord." Iblis said within himself: "By Allah, if I am empowered over it I will destroy it, and if it is empowered over me I will disobey it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And I know what you reveal﴾ — meaning the angels' obedience — ﴿and what you conceal﴾ — meaning Iblis's disobedience.

al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "what you reveal" means their saying: ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein...﴾; "what you conceal" means their saying that He would not create a creature better, more knowledgeable, or more honoured by Him than them.

On the definition of the noun and its divisions

Our companions said: The noun (ism) is every utterance that indicates a meaning and a thing, and it is derived from the sima, which is the mark by which a thing is known. Its divisions are eight: a proper noun, like Zayd, 'Amr, Fatimah, 'A'ishah, dar (house), and faras (horse).

Another is the permanent noun, like your saying: rajul (man), imra'ah (woman), shams (sun), qamar (moon), hajar (stone), madar (clay), and similar. It is called permanent because it does not change or separate: one does not call the sun "moon" nor the moon "stone."

Another is the separable noun, like: saghir (small), kabir (large), tifl (child), kahl (elderly), qalil (few), kathir (many). It is called separable because it was not the name it bears, and the meaning it names may depart from it.

Another is the derived noun, like: katib (writer), khayyat (tailor), sa'igh (goldsmith), sabbagh (dyer). The noun is derived from its verb.

Another is the annexed noun, like: ghulam Ja'far (Ja'far's servant), rukub 'Amr ('Amr's riding), dar Zayd (Zayd's house).

Another is the noun of resemblance, like your saying: so-and-so is a lion, a donkey, a spark of fire.

Another is the relational noun, which establishes itself and establishes another, like your saying: father (ab), mother (umm), brother (akh), sister (ukht), son (ibn), daughter (bint), husband (zawj), wife (zawjah). When you say "father," you have established it and established a child for it; when you say "brother," you have established it and established a sister for it.

Another is the generic noun: a single word that indicates many things, like your saying: animal (hayawan), people (nas), and similar.

And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam — a prostration of honour and greeting, not a prostration of prayer and worship. Its parallel is His saying in the story of Joseph: ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾. That was the greeting of people, one honouring another, and placing the face on the ground was not done; rather it was bowing, glorifying and kissing. When Islam came, that was abolished by the greeting of peace.

In a hadith: Mu'adh ibn Jabal returned from Yemen and prostrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The face of the Messenger of Allah changed, and he said: "What is this?" He said: "I saw the Jews prostrating to their rabbis and the Christians prostrating to their priests." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Stop, O Mu'adh. The Jews and Christians lied; prostration is only to Allah, Exalted."

Some said: it was a real prostration, with Adam made a qibla for them, and the prostration was to Allah, just as the Ka'bah was made a qibla for the prayer of believers, and the prayer is to Allah, Exalted.

Ibn Mas'ud said: Allah commanded them to bring Adam, and the angels prostrated, while Adam was [turned] to the Lord of the worlds.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: its meaning is: "Acknowledge to Adam that he is better and more honoured by Me than you, and so acknowledge it." According to the view of Abdullah and Ubayy, prostration means submission, obedience and humbling, as the poet said:

"You see the hills prostrating to the hooves of the horses in it."

Adam is on the pattern of af'al, and therefore it is not declined.

Al-Suddi, from one who narrated to him from Ibn Abbas, said: Adam was named so because he was created from the surface of the earth (adim al-ard). Some said he was named so because he was created from dust, and dust in the Hebrew tongue is adam. Others said he was named so for the ruddiness of his complexion, since he was brown-skinned; his kunya was Abu Muhammad and Abu al-Bashar.

Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, said: There is no one in Paradise called by a kunya except Adam, who is called Abu Muhammad.

The common readers read lil-malā'ikati with a kasra on the ta'. Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the ta', likening the ta' of feminine marking to the alif of the hamzat al-wasl in His saying: isjudu, because the alif of hamzat al-wasl drops in connected speech, and because it is an added, non-original letter, just as the feminine ta' is an added, non-original letter; and no stable element answers the alif of isjudu.

It is also said: he disliked the damma on the jim after the kasra on the ta', because the Arabs dislike a damma after a kasra for its heaviness. This is a very weak reading, and the grammarians agreed in declaring it an error.

So they prostrated — meaning the angels, except Iblis. His name was 'Azazil; when he disobeyed, his form was changed and his name was changed, and he was called Iblis because he was despaired (ublisa) of Allah's mercy, as one says: "O wicked one," and "O sinner." It is in the accusative as an exception, and it is not declined because of the combination of foreignness and definiteness.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 30–39 (part 2 of 2)**

*Abā* means he refused and did not prostrate. *Wastakbara* means he was arrogant and exalted himself against prostrating. *Wa kāna* means he became one of the disbelievers. ﴿And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned﴾ [Hud 11:43].

Most exegetes said: its meaning is that in His prior knowledge he was among the disbelievers, for whom wretchedness was decreed.

Al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws from him weeping and says: 'Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so he will have Paradise. I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so I will have the Fire.'" [82] [Musnad Ahmad 2/443.]

Ziyad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: When Noah boarded the ship, he found Iblis at its *kawthal* [the *kawthal* is the stern of the ship]. He said to him: "Woe to you! People have been split apart because of you." He said: "So what do you command me?" He said: "Repent." He said: "Ask your Lord whether there is any repentance for me." It was said to him that his repentance was to prostrate to the grave of Adam. He said: "I left him alive; I will prostrate to him dead."

﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. This is because Adam, peace be upon him, was in the Garden lonely, and had no one to sit with him and keep him company. He slept a sleep, and Allah the Exalted created his wife from his *qasīrā* [the lower rib], from his left side, without Adam sensing it or feeling any pain. Had there been any pain in that, a man would not feel tender toward a woman. When Adam woke from his sleep, he found Hawwa' sitting by his head, in the most beautiful form Allah had created. He said to her: "Who are you?" She said: "I am your wife, whom Allah created for you so that you may find rest in me and I may find rest in you." Then the angels, to test Adam's knowledge, said: "O Adam, what is this?" He said: "A woman." They said: "What is her name?" He said: "Hawwa'." They said: "Why were you named Hawwa'?" He said: "Because she was created from a living thing (*ḥayy*)." They said: "Do you love her, O Adam?" He said: "Yes." They said to Hawwa': "Do you love him?" She said: "No," while in her heart there was many times the love he had for her. They said: "If a woman were truthful in her love for her husband, Hawwa' would be truthful."

**(Issue:)** The Qadariyyah said: the Garden in which Allah settled Adam and Hawwa' was not the Garden of Eternity, but a garden from the gardens of this world. They argued that the Garden is not a place of trial and obligation.

**(Response:)** We have agreed (*ajma'nā*) that the people of Paradise are commanded in it to know (Allah) and are obligated to that.

Another response: Allah the Exalted is able to combine opposites. So He showed Adam a trial in the Garden, and showed Abraham a blessing in the Fire, so that the servant would neither feel secure from his Lord nor despair of His mercy, and so that he would know that He may do whatever He wills.

They also argued that whoever enters the Garden cannot leave it, since Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they will not be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr 15:48].

The response to this: whoever enters it as a reward will never leave it. Adam did not enter it as a reward. Do you not see that Ridwan, the keeper of the Garden, enters it and then leaves it? Iblis, too, was inside the Garden and was expelled from it.

﴿And eat from it freely﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]: *raghadan* means abundantly and in large quantity. *Ḥaythu shi'tumā* means how you wish, when you wish, and where you wish.

﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. Some scholars said: the prohibition fell upon a kind of tree. Others said: it fell upon a particular tree, and they differed about it.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah ennoble his face) said: it is the tree of camphor.

Qatadah said: it is the tree of knowledge, and in it is everything.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: it is the wheat-ear (*sunbulah*).

It was also said: it is the *ḥabalah*, which is the root-stem of the vine.

Abu Ruq, from al-Dahhak: it is the fig tree.

﴿So you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35], meaning wrongdoers against yourselves through disobedience. The root meaning of *ẓulm* (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

﴿So he caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning he lured (*istamāla*) Adam and Hawwa', and removed them and drove them away.

Hamzah recited: ﴿Then the Satan caused them to slip﴾, and he is Iblis. *Shaytān* is on the pattern *fay'āl* from *shaṭana*, meaning he became distant. 

It was said: it is from *shāṭa*, and the *nūn* in it is not original. The Satan was so named because of his rebellion and his distance from good and from the mercy of Allah the Exalted.

﴿From it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning from the Garden. It was said: from obedience.

﴿And He brought them out from what they were in﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning from the bliss. This is because Iblis wanted to enter the Garden and whisper to Adam and Hawwa'. The guardians prevented him. So he came to the serpent, which was among the most beautiful of animals, with four legs like the legs of a camel. It was among the guardians of the Garden and was a friend to Iblis. He asked it to let him enter into its mouth, and it let him enter into its mouth, and passed by the guardians while they did not know, and so he entered the Garden. When Adam entered the Garden and saw what was in it of bliss and honor, he said: "If only there were eternity..." So Satan seized that moment from him and came to him from the direction of eternity. When he entered the Garden, he stood before Adam and Hawwa', and they did not know that he was Iblis. He wailed over them a wailing that saddened them, and he wept, and he was the first to wail. They said: "Why do you weep?" He said: "I weep for you, for you will die and be separated from what you are in of bliss and honor." This entered their hearts and they were grieved. He went away, then came to them again and said: ﴿O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:120]. He refused to accept from him. So he swore to them by Allah that he was truly among the sincere advisers (﴿lamina al-nāṣiḥīn﴾) [al-A'raf 7:21]. They were deceived, and they did not think that anyone would swear by Allah falsely. Hawwa' hastened to eat from the tree, then gave it to Adam until he ate it.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Yazid ibn Abdullah ibn Qusayt, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib swear by Allah without exception: Adam did not eat from the tree while he was in his senses. Rather, Hawwa' gave him wine to drink until he became intoxicated, then she led him to it, and he ate. When they both ate, their garments fell away from them and their private parts became visible, and they were expelled from the Garden. This is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We said﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning to Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent: ﴿Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]. So Adam descended in Sarandib of the land of India, onto a mountain called Nawdhah. It was said: Washm. Hawwa' descended in Jeddah, Iblis in al-Ubullah, and it was said in Maysan, and the serpent in Isfahan.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]: *balāgh* (sufficiency) and *mustamta'* (enjoyment).

﴿For a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning until the appointed time of your lifespans and the end of your lives.

From Ibrahim ibn al-Ash'ath, who said: I heard Ibrahim ibn Adham say: that single eating brought us a long grief.

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37]: *fa-talaqqā* means he was taught. *Ādam* was preserved (*ḥuffiẓa*) when he was taught, and understood when he was inspired.

The common readers recited *Ādamu* with a *ḍammah* on the *mīm*, and *kalimātin* with a *kasrah* on the *tā'*.

Ibn Kathir recited with a *fatḥah* on the *mīm*, meaning the words came to Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿From his Lord, words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37] were the cause of the acceptance of his repentance. The exegetes differed about those words. Ibn Abbas said: they are that Adam said: "O Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did Your mercy not precede Your wrath toward me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then why did You expel me from it?" He said: "Because of the evil of your disobedience." He said: "O Lord, do You see that if I repent and reform, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is the words."

Ubayd ibn Umayr said: it is that Adam said: "O Lord, do You see what I did? Was it something I invented against myself, or something You decreed upon me before You created me?" He said: "Rather, something I decreed upon you before I created you." He said: "O Lord, as You decreed it upon me, forgive me." [Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur 1/59.]

Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam and Moses disputed. Moses said to him: 'You are Adam who misled people and expelled them from the Garden to the earth?' Adam said to him: 'You are Moses whom Allah gave the knowledge of everything and chose over the people with His message?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you blame me for a matter that was written against me to do before I was created?' So Adam overcame Moses in the argument." [83] [al-Musannaf (Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani) 11/113.]

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are his saying: ﴿There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done wrong to myself, so forgive me, indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. And he said: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the Forgiving, the Merciful. There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. O Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy on me, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."

Ikrimah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37]: they said: it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. Likewise al-Hasan and Mujahid said.

Some of them said: Adam, peace be upon him, looked at the Throne and saw written on its leg: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar al-Faruq." He said: "O Lord, I ask You by the right of Muhammad that You forgive me," and He forgave him.

It was also said: this interpretation is what Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was taken up to the heavens, and I saw written on the leg of the Throne: 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar al-Faruq.'" [Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned it in al-Mawdu'at 1/328.] [Al-Muttaqi al-Hindi narrated from Ali the saying of Adam: "O Allah, I ask You by the right of Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, glory be to You, there is no god but You, I have done evil and wronged myself, so accept my repentance, for You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful." Kanz al-Ummal 2/359, no. 4237, the verse's entry; al-Durr al-Manthur 1/60, the commentary on the verse. And al-Suyuti narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the words, and he said: "He asked by the right of Muhammad, Ali, Fatimah, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, that You accept his repentance." Al-Durr al-Manthur 1/60.]

It was also said: they are three things: fear, hope, and weeping.

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: It reached me that when Adam was sent down to the earth, he remained three hundred years without raising his head, out of shame before Allah the Exalted.

Ibn Abbas said: the weeping of Adam and Hawwa' over what they had lost of the bliss of the Garden lasted two hundred years. They did not eat or drink for forty days, and Adam did not approach Hawwa' for a hundred years.

﴿So He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37], meaning He pardoned him. ﴿Indeed He is the Accepting of repentance﴾, who accepts the repentance of His servants; ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His creation.

﴿We said: Go down from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], meaning Adam and Hawwa'. It was said: Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent. ﴿Then if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], O children of Adam, a book and a messenger. ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], regarding what lies ahead of them, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], over what they left behind.

﴿But those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], meaning rejected, ﴿and denied Our signs﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], meaning the Qur'an, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], neither leaving it nor dying in it.

When your Lord said — meaning, "and [when] He said." Some say the sense is: "Remember when your Lord said." Every such occurrence in the Qur'an follows this pattern.

"Idh" (when, for past time) and "idha" (when, for future time) are both particles of time, except that "idh" refers to the past and "idha" to the future, though one may be placed in the position of the other.

Al-Mubarrad said: When "idh" is used with a future verb, its meaning is past, as in His saying: ﴿And [remember] when they plotted against you﴾ and ﴿when he said﴾, meaning, "when they plotted" and "when he said." And when "idha" is used with a past verb, its meaning is future, as in His saying: ﴿So when the Great Calamity comes﴾ and ﴿So when the Deafening Blast comes﴾ and ﴿When the help of Allah comes﴾, meaning "comes." The poet said:

"Then may Allah reward him on our behalf when He rewards [him] — gardens of Eden and the heights to the heights."

meaning, "He rewards him."

to the angels — those who were on the earth. The angels (al-malā'ika) are the messengers; the singular is malak. Its origin is malak, plural malā'ika, and it derives from al-malaka, al-mālika and al-alūk, meaning "message." One says: alikni ila fulan, meaning "be my messenger to him," and the form was transposed, becoming mala'ik. The poet said:

"I am not for mankind, but for a messenger descending from the atmosphere of heaven, pouring down."

Then the hamza was dropped for lightness, and because of its frequent use it became malak.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said regarding malak: the Arabs do not derive its verb nor conjugate it, and it is among what its knowledge has escaped.

Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa — meaning a substitute for you, and one raised up to Me. It was called khalifa because it succeeds the one who departs and comes after him. Thus the khalifa is one who carries out a command on behalf of the one who commands. Zayd ibn Ali read it as khaliqa (with the qāf).

The exegetes said: That is because Allah the Exalted created the heavens and the earth, and created the angels and the jinn. He settled the angels in the heavens and settled the jinn on the earth, and they worshipped for a long time on the earth. Then envy and insolence appeared among them, so they fought and caused corruption. Allah sent to them a host of angels called the Jinn — their chief was the enemy of Allah, Iblis — and they were the guardians of the Gardens, named after the Garden (jannah). They descended to the earth and expelled the jinn from its surface, so they joined them in the mountain ranges and the islands of the sea. The angels settled the earth, and Allah lightened their worship, so they loved to remain on earth for that reason. Allah gave Iblis rule over the earth, rule over the lowest heaven, and the treasury of the Gardens, so he worshipped Allah sometimes on the earth, sometimes in the heaven, and sometimes in the Garden.

When he saw that, pride and self-admiration entered him, and he said to himself: "Allah has given me this kingdom only because I am the most honoured of the angels in His sight and the greatest in rank with Him." When pride appeared, dismissal came. So Allah said to him and to his host:

Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa. When He said that to them, they disliked it, because they were less in worship among the angels, and because dismissal is severe.

They said: Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein through sins, and shed blood — pour out blood — without right?

If it is asked: How did they know that, when it is unseen?

The answer is what al-Suddi said: When Allah said that to them, they said, "And what will come from that khalifa?" He said: "He will have offspring who will cause corruption on the earth [and envy one another] — thus in the manuscript — and some of them will kill others." At that they said: Will You place in it — and the meaning is "so they said." The fa' of sequence is omitted, as in the poet's words:

"When I saw Nabat, helpers, I hitched up my garment above my knees; I was a neighbour to them among the Christians."

meaning, "so I was."

Most of the exegetes said: They meant: as the sons of the jinn did, they measured the absent by the present. Some scholars of meaning said there is ellipsis and abbreviation in it, meaning: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood? Or will You place in it one who does not cause corruption and does not shed blood?" — based on His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾, meaning "like one who is not devoutly obedient." This is the choice of al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl.

And we glorify You with Your praise.

al-Hasan said: They say, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," and this is the prayer of creation and their glorification, and by it they are provided for.

Evidence for this is the hadith transmitted from Abu Dharr, who said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which speech is most excellent?" He said: "What Allah has chosen for His angels: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him."

It is also said the meaning is: "We pray to You by Your command." Tasbih can mean declaring Allah free of imperfection and can mean prayer; hence the prayer is called subha. It is also said the meaning is: "We pray and recite in it the Opening of the Book."

And we sanctify You — and we declare You free of imperfection. The lām is supplementary. It is also said it is the lām of purpose, meaning: "And we purify our hearts for Your sake from associating others with You, and our bodies from disobeying You."

Some scholars said: In the verse there is inversion and transposition; its meaning is: "We glorify and sanctify You, and to You belongs praise," because if the verse is taken according to the first interpretation, it contradicts the angels' claim to purity through self-reliance on works. If it is taken according to this interpretation, it resembles their speech of recounting Allah's blessing and attributing it to Allah, as if they said: "That we glorified You, sanctified You, and obeyed You, and worshipped You — all of that is by Your praise, not by ourselves." Allah said:

Indeed I know what you do not know — concerning My appointing of a khalifa on the earth and the wisdom in it. So do not object to Me in My judgment and My management. It is also said: He meant, "I know that among those whom I will appoint on the earth are prophets, saints, scholars, and righteous people." It is also said: "I know that they will sin, and I will forgive them."

Some wise men said: Allah the Exalted brought Adam out of the Garden before He made him enter it. This is according to His saying: ﴿Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa﴾. Then his leaving the Garden because of his sin shows that it was by the decree and predestination of Allah.

Ibn Nujayh, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed I know what you do not know﴾, said: He knew from Iblis the disobedience and that He had created him for it.

Ibn Shihab, from Humayd, from Abu Hurayrah, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Adam and Musa argued. Musa said to him: 'You are Adam, whom your sin expelled from the Garden.' Adam said to him: 'You are Musa, whom Allah chose for His message and His speech, yet you blame me for a matter decreed before I was created.' So Adam won the argument against Musa."

Section on the meaning of khalifa

It is said: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked Talhah, al-Zubayr, Ka'b and Salman: "What is the khalifa in relation to the king?"

Talhah and al-Zubayr said: "We do not know." Salman said: "The khalifa is one who is just among the subjects, distributes among them equally, shows compassion to them as a man shows compassion to his family, and judges by the Book of Allah." Ka'b said: "I did not think there was anyone in the assembly who knew the difference between khalifa and king except me, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has filled Salman with wisdom, knowledge and justice."

Zadhan transmitted from Salman that Umar said to him: "Am I a king or a khalifa?" Salman said: "If you collect from the land of the Muslims a dirham, or less or more, and place it in other than its right place, then you are a king." He said: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wept.

From Yunus: Mu'awiyah used to say when he sat on the pulpit: "O people, the caliphate is not for gathering wealth nor for scattering it, but the caliphate is by truth, judgment by justice, and holding people to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

And He taught Adam the names, all of them. That is because when Allah said to the angels, "Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa," they said among themselves: "Let our Lord create whatever He wills; He will not create a creature better or more honoured by Him than us. And if it is better than us, we are more knowledgeable than it, for we were created before it and have seen what it has not seen." When they were impressed with their knowledge and worship, Allah the Exalted favoured Adam, peace be upon him, over them with knowledge, and taught him all the names. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The scholars differed about these names. Al-Rabi' and Ibn Anas said: they are the names of the angels. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the names of his offspring.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: Allah taught him the name of every thing, even the dish and the small dish.

Muqatil said: Allah created everything — animals, inanimate objects and others — then taught Adam their names, all of them. He said to him: "O Adam, this is a horse, this is a mule, this is a donkey," until he had gone through all of them. Then He presented those things as He presented the existing things to the angels. Thus He said: ﴿then He presented them﴾ and did not say "presented it," and He returned it to the persons and named things, because accidents cannot be presented.

It is also said: Allah taught Adam, peace be upon him, the craft of every thing.

Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, said: Allah taught Adam the names of creatures, towns, cities, mountains, predators, the names of birds and trees, the names of what was and what will be, and every soul that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will bring into being until the Day of Resurrection; and He presented those names to the angels.

He said: "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful." Indeed the khalifa I place on the earth will cause corruption therein and shed blood. Allah the Exalted meant by this: "How do you claim knowledge of what has not yet occurred, when you do not know what you see and witness?"

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ — that I will not create a creature except that you will be more knowledgeable and better than it. The angels said, acknowledging their inability and apologising.

They said: Glory be to You — declaring You free of objection, because of Your knowledge in Your judgment and management. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun; meaning, "We glorify a glorification," according to al-Khalil's view.

al-Kisa'i said: it is outside the description. It is also said: it is in the vocative construction, meaning: "O Your glory."

We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed You are the All-Knowing about Your creation, the All-Wise in Your command.

For al-ḥakīm (the Wise) there are two meanings. One: the one who makes the act firm, as in His saying: ﴿a painful punishment﴾, and "a painful wound." The poet said:

"Does the echo of the calling companion of Rayhanah, the one who hears, keep me awake, while my companions sleep?"

meaning: the painful and aching one, and "the one who makes to hear." In this interpretation it is an adjective of act.

The other meaning is "the judge, the knower," and in that case it is an adjective of essence. The root of wisdom in Arabic speech is prevention. One says: "I prevented the orphan from corruption and restrained him," meaning I prevented him. Jarir said:

"Sons of Hanifah, restrain your foolish ones; indeed I fear that I will become angry at you."

The bit that is placed across a horse's mouth is called ḥikma, because it prevents the horse from turning aside, and wisdom prevents from falsehood; and what is not beautiful is not permitted in the judicious matter, by preventing it from disorder. In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne, since Allah commanded the angels to report what they did not know, while He knew their inability to do so.

When their inability became evident, Allah the Exalted said: "O Adam, inform them of their names." So he named every thing by its name, and joined every thing to its kind.

When he informed them of their names — told them. He said: "Did I not tell you, O My angels? Indeed I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth — what is hidden in them and what will be. And I know what you reveal of humility and obedience to Adam, and what you conceal" — what you hide within yourselves of enmity toward him. It is also said: "what you reveal" is their acknowledgment of inability and apology, and "what you conceal" is their dislike of Adam's appointment as khalifa.

Ibn Abbas said: Iblis passed by the body of Adam, which lay between Makkah and al-Ta'if without a spirit in it, and said: "For what matter was this created?" Then he entered through its mouth and came out through its back, and said: "It will not hold together except by the hollow." Then he said to the angels with him: "Do you see that if this is preferred over you and you are commanded to obey it, what would you do?" They said: "We will obey the command of our Lord." Iblis said within himself: "By Allah, if I am empowered over it I will destroy it, and if it is empowered over me I will disobey it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And I know what you reveal﴾ — meaning the angels' obedience — ﴿and what you conceal﴾ — meaning Iblis's disobedience.

al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "what you reveal" means their saying: ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein...﴾; "what you conceal" means their saying that He would not create a creature better, more knowledgeable, or more honoured by Him than them.

On the definition of the noun and its divisions

Our companions said: The noun (ism) is every utterance that indicates a meaning and a thing, and it is derived from the sima, which is the mark by which a thing is known. Its divisions are eight: a proper noun, like Zayd, 'Amr, Fatimah, 'A'ishah, dar (house), and faras (horse).

Another is the permanent noun, like your saying: rajul (man), imra'ah (woman), shams (sun), qamar (moon), hajar (stone), madar (clay), and similar. It is called permanent because it does not change or separate: one does not call the sun "moon" nor the moon "stone."

Another is the separable noun, like: saghir (small), kabir (large), tifl (child), kahl (elderly), qalil (few), kathir (many). It is called separable because it was not the name it bears, and the meaning it names may depart from it.

Another is the derived noun, like: katib (writer), khayyat (tailor), sa'igh (goldsmith), sabbagh (dyer). The noun is derived from its verb.

Another is the annexed noun, like: ghulam Ja'far (Ja'far's servant), rukub 'Amr ('Amr's riding), dar Zayd (Zayd's house).

Another is the noun of resemblance, like your saying: so-and-so is a lion, a donkey, a spark of fire.

Another is the relational noun, which establishes itself and establishes another, like your saying: father (ab), mother (umm), brother (akh), sister (ukht), son (ibn), daughter (bint), husband (zawj), wife (zawjah). When you say "father," you have established it and established a child for it; when you say "brother," you have established it and established a sister for it.

Another is the generic noun: a single word that indicates many things, like your saying: animal (hayawan), people (nas), and similar.

And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam — a prostration of honour and greeting, not a prostration of prayer and worship. Its parallel is His saying in the story of Joseph: ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾. That was the greeting of people, one honouring another, and placing the face on the ground was not done; rather it was bowing, glorifying and kissing. When Islam came, that was abolished by the greeting of peace.

In a hadith: Mu'adh ibn Jabal returned from Yemen and prostrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The face of the Messenger of Allah changed, and he said: "What is this?" He said: "I saw the Jews prostrating to their rabbis and the Christians prostrating to their priests." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Stop, O Mu'adh. The Jews and Christians lied; prostration is only to Allah, Exalted."

Some said: it was a real prostration, with Adam made a qibla for them, and the prostration was to Allah, just as the Ka'bah was made a qibla for the prayer of believers, and the prayer is to Allah, Exalted.

Ibn Mas'ud said: Allah commanded them to bring Adam, and the angels prostrated, while Adam was [turned] to the Lord of the worlds.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: its meaning is: "Acknowledge to Adam that he is better and more honoured by Me than you, and so acknowledge it." According to the view of Abdullah and Ubayy, prostration means submission, obedience and humbling, as the poet said:

"You see the hills prostrating to the hooves of the horses in it."

Adam is on the pattern of af'al, and therefore it is not declined.

Al-Suddi, from one who narrated to him from Ibn Abbas, said: Adam was named so because he was created from the surface of the earth (adim al-ard). Some said he was named so because he was created from dust, and dust in the Hebrew tongue is adam. Others said he was named so for the ruddiness of his complexion, since he was brown-skinned; his kunya was Abu Muhammad and Abu al-Bashar.

Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, said: There is no one in Paradise called by a kunya except Adam, who is called Abu Muhammad.

The common readers read lil-malā'ikati with a kasra on the ta'. Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the ta', likening the ta' of feminine marking to the alif of the hamzat al-wasl in His saying: isjudu, because the alif of hamzat al-wasl drops in connected speech, and because it is an added, non-original letter, just as the feminine ta' is an added, non-original letter; and no stable element answers the alif of isjudu.

It is also said: he disliked the damma on the jim after the kasra on the ta', because the Arabs dislike a damma after a kasra for its heaviness. This is a very weak reading, and the grammarians agreed in declaring it an error.

So they prostrated — meaning the angels, except Iblis. His name was 'Azazil; when he disobeyed, his form was changed and his name was changed, and he was called Iblis because he was despaired (ublisa) of Allah's mercy, as one says: "O wicked one," and "O sinner." It is in the accusative as an exception, and it is not declined because of the combination of foreignness and definiteness.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 30–39 (part 2 of 2)**

*Abā* means he refused and did not prostrate. *Wastakbara* means he was arrogant and exalted himself against prostrating. *Wa kāna* means he became one of the disbelievers. ﴿And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned﴾ [Hud 11:43].

Most exegetes said: its meaning is that in His prior knowledge he was among the disbelievers, for whom wretchedness was decreed.

Al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws from him weeping and says: 'Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so he will have Paradise. I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so I will have the Fire.'" [82] [Musnad Ahmad 2/443.]

Ziyad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: When Noah boarded the ship, he found Iblis at its *kawthal* [the *kawthal* is the stern of the ship]. He said to him: "Woe to you! People have been split apart because of you." He said: "So what do you command me?" He said: "Repent." He said: "Ask your Lord whether there is any repentance for me." It was said to him that his repentance was to prostrate to the grave of Adam. He said: "I left him alive; I will prostrate to him dead."

﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. This is because Adam, peace be upon him, was in the Garden lonely, and had no one to sit with him and keep him company. He slept a sleep, and Allah the Exalted created his wife from his *qasīrā* [the lower rib], from his left side, without Adam sensing it or feeling any pain. Had there been any pain in that, a man would not feel tender toward a woman. When Adam woke from his sleep, he found Hawwa' sitting by his head, in the most beautiful form Allah had created. He said to her: "Who are you?" She said: "I am your wife, whom Allah created for you so that you may find rest in me and I may find rest in you." Then the angels, to test Adam's knowledge, said: "O Adam, what is this?" He said: "A woman." They said: "What is her name?" He said: "Hawwa'." They said: "Why were you named Hawwa'?" He said: "Because she was created from a living thing (*ḥayy*)." They said: "Do you love her, O Adam?" He said: "Yes." They said to Hawwa': "Do you love him?" She said: "No," while in her heart there was many times the love he had for her. They said: "If a woman were truthful in her love for her husband, Hawwa' would be truthful."

**(Issue:)** The Qadariyyah said: the Garden in which Allah settled Adam and Hawwa' was not the Garden of Eternity, but a garden from the gardens of this world. They argued that the Garden is not a place of trial and obligation.

**(Response:)** We have agreed (*ajma'nā*) that the people of Paradise are commanded in it to know (Allah) and are obligated to that.

Another response: Allah the Exalted is able to combine opposites. So He showed Adam a trial in the Garden, and showed Abraham a blessing in the Fire, so that the servant would neither feel secure from his Lord nor despair of His mercy, and so that he would know that He may do whatever He wills.

They also argued that whoever enters the Garden cannot leave it, since Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they will not be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr 15:48].

The response to this: whoever enters it as a reward will never leave it. Adam did not enter it as a reward. Do you not see that Ridwan, the keeper of the Garden, enters it and then leaves it? Iblis, too, was inside the Garden and was expelled from it.

﴿And eat from it freely﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]: *raghadan* means abundantly and in large quantity. *Ḥaythu shi'tumā* means how you wish, when you wish, and where you wish.

﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. Some scholars said: the prohibition fell upon a kind of tree. Others said: it fell upon a particular tree, and they differed about it.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah ennoble his face) said: it is the tree of camphor.

Qatadah said: it is the tree of knowledge, and in it is everything.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: it is the wheat-ear (*sunbulah*).

It was also said: it is the *ḥabalah*, which is the root-stem of the vine.

Abu Ruq, from al-Dahhak: it is the fig tree.

﴿So you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35], meaning wrongdoers against yourselves through disobedience. The root meaning of *ẓulm* (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

﴿So he caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning he lured (*istamāla*) Adam and Hawwa', and removed them and drove them away.

Hamzah recited: ﴿Then the Satan caused them to slip﴾, and he is Iblis. *Shaytān* is on the pattern *fay'āl* from *shaṭana*, meaning he became distant. 

It was said: it is from *shāṭa*, and the *nūn* in it is not original. The Satan was so named because of his rebellion and his distance from good and from the mercy of Allah the Exalted.

﴿From it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning from the Garden. It was said: from obedience.

﴿And He brought them out from what they were in﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning from the bliss. This is because Iblis wanted to enter the Garden and whisper to Adam and Hawwa'. The guardians prevented him. So he came to the serpent, which was among the most beautiful of animals, with four legs like the legs of a camel. It was among the guardians of the Garden and was a friend to Iblis. He asked it to let him enter into its mouth, and it let him enter into its mouth, and passed by the guardians while they did not know, and so he entered the Garden. When Adam entered the Garden and saw what was in it of bliss and honor, he said: "If only there were eternity..." So Satan seized that moment from him and came to him from the direction of eternity. When he entered the Garden, he stood before Adam and Hawwa', and they did not know that he was Iblis. He wailed over them a wailing that saddened them, and he wept, and he was the first to wail. They said: "Why do you weep?" He said: "I weep for you, for you will die and be separated from what you are in of bliss and honor." This entered their hearts and they were grieved. He went away, then came to them again and said: ﴿O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:120]. He refused to accept from him. So he swore to them by Allah that he was truly among the sincere advisers (﴿lamina al-nāṣiḥīn﴾) [al-A'raf 7:21]. They were deceived, and they did not think that anyone would swear by Allah falsely. Hawwa' hastened to eat from the tree, then gave it to Adam until he ate it.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Yazid ibn Abdullah ibn Qusayt, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib swear by Allah without exception: Adam did not eat from the tree while he was in his senses. Rather, Hawwa' gave him wine to drink until he became intoxicated, then she led him to it, and he ate. When they both ate, their garments fell away from them and their private parts became visible, and they were expelled from the Garden. This is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We said﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning to Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent: ﴿Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]. So Adam descended in Sarandib of the land of India, onto a mountain called Nawdhah. It was said: Washm. Hawwa' descended in Jeddah, Iblis in al-Ubullah, and it was said in Maysan, and the serpent in Isfahan.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]: *balāgh* (sufficiency) and *mustamta'* (enjoyment).

﴿For a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning until the appointed time of your lifespans and the end of your lives.

From Ibrahim ibn al-Ash'ath, who said: I heard Ibrahim ibn Adham say: that single eating brought us a long grief.

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37]: *fa-talaqqā* means he was taught. *Ādam* was preserved (*ḥuffiẓa*) when he was taught, and understood when he was inspired.

The common readers recited *Ādamu* with a *ḍammah* on the *mīm*, and *kalimātin* with a *kasrah* on the *tā'*.

Ibn Kathir recited with a *fatḥah* on the *mīm*, meaning the words came to Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿From his Lord, words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37] were the cause of the acceptance of his repentance. The exegetes differed about those words. Ibn Abbas said: they are that Adam said: "O Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did Your mercy not precede Your wrath toward me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then why did You expel me from it?" He said: "Because of the evil of your disobedience." He said: "O Lord, do You see that if I repent and reform, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is the words."

Ubayd ibn Umayr said: it is that Adam said: "O Lord, do You see what I did? Was it something I invented against myself, or something You decreed upon me before You created me?" He said: "Rather, something I decreed upon you before I created you." He said: "O Lord, as You decreed it upon me, forgive me." [Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur 1/59.]

Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam and Moses disputed. Moses said to him: 'You are Adam who misled people and expelled them from the Garden to the earth?' Adam said to him: 'You are Moses whom Allah gave the knowledge of everything and chose over the people with His message?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you blame me for a matter that was written against me to do before I was created?' So Adam overcame Moses in the argument." [83] [al-Musannaf (Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani) 11/113.]

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are his saying: ﴿There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done wrong to myself, so forgive me, indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. And he said: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the Forgiving, the Merciful. There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. O Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy on me, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."

Ikrimah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37]: they said: it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. Likewise al-Hasan and Mujahid said.

Some of them said: Adam, peace be upon him, looked at the Throne and saw written on its leg: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar al-Faruq." He said: "O Lord, I ask You by the right of Muhammad that You forgive me," and He forgave him.

It was also said: this interpretation is what Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was taken up to the heavens, and I saw written on the leg of the Throne: 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar al-Faruq.'" [Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned it in al-Mawdu'at 1/328.] [Al-Muttaqi al-Hindi narrated from Ali the saying of Adam: "O Allah, I ask You by the right of Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, glory be to You, there is no god but You, I have done evil and wronged myself, so accept my repentance, for You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful." Kanz al-Ummal 2/359, no. 4237, the verse's entry; al-Durr al-Manthur 1/60, the commentary on the verse. And al-Suyuti narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the words, and he said: "He asked by the right of Muhammad, Ali, Fatimah, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, that You accept his repentance." Al-Durr al-Manthur 1/60.]

It was also said: they are three things: fear, hope, and weeping.

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: It reached me that when Adam was sent down to the earth, he remained three hundred years without raising his head, out of shame before Allah the Exalted.

Ibn Abbas said: the weeping of Adam and Hawwa' over what they had lost of the bliss of the Garden lasted two hundred years. They did not eat or drink for forty days, and Adam did not approach Hawwa' for a hundred years.

﴿So He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37], meaning He pardoned him. ﴿Indeed He is the Accepting of repentance﴾, who accepts the repentance of His servants; ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His creation.

﴿We said: Go down from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], meaning Adam and Hawwa'. It was said: Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent. ﴿Then if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], O children of Adam, a book and a messenger. ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], regarding what lies ahead of them, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], over what they left behind.

﴿But those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], meaning rejected, ﴿and denied Our signs﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], meaning the Qur'an, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], neither leaving it nor dying in it.

When your Lord said — meaning, "and [when] He said." Some say the sense is: "Remember when your Lord said." Every such occurrence in the Qur'an follows this pattern.

"Idh" (when, for past time) and "idha" (when, for future time) are both particles of time, except that "idh" refers to the past and "idha" to the future, though one may be placed in the position of the other.

Al-Mubarrad said: When "idh" is used with a future verb, its meaning is past, as in His saying: ﴿And [remember] when they plotted against you﴾ and ﴿when he said﴾, meaning, "when they plotted" and "when he said." And when "idha" is used with a past verb, its meaning is future, as in His saying: ﴿So when the Great Calamity comes﴾ and ﴿So when the Deafening Blast comes﴾ and ﴿When the help of Allah comes﴾, meaning "comes." The poet said:

"Then may Allah reward him on our behalf when He rewards [him] — gardens of Eden and the heights to the heights."

meaning, "He rewards him."

to the angels — those who were on the earth. The angels (al-malā'ika) are the messengers; the singular is malak. Its origin is malak, plural malā'ika, and it derives from al-malaka, al-mālika and al-alūk, meaning "message." One says: alikni ila fulan, meaning "be my messenger to him," and the form was transposed, becoming mala'ik. The poet said:

"I am not for mankind, but for a messenger descending from the atmosphere of heaven, pouring down."

Then the hamza was dropped for lightness, and because of its frequent use it became malak.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said regarding malak: the Arabs do not derive its verb nor conjugate it, and it is among what its knowledge has escaped.

Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa — meaning a substitute for you, and one raised up to Me. It was called khalifa because it succeeds the one who departs and comes after him. Thus the khalifa is one who carries out a command on behalf of the one who commands. Zayd ibn Ali read it as khaliqa (with the qāf).

The exegetes said: That is because Allah the Exalted created the heavens and the earth, and created the angels and the jinn. He settled the angels in the heavens and settled the jinn on the earth, and they worshipped for a long time on the earth. Then envy and insolence appeared among them, so they fought and caused corruption. Allah sent to them a host of angels called the Jinn — their chief was the enemy of Allah, Iblis — and they were the guardians of the Gardens, named after the Garden (jannah). They descended to the earth and expelled the jinn from its surface, so they joined them in the mountain ranges and the islands of the sea. The angels settled the earth, and Allah lightened their worship, so they loved to remain on earth for that reason. Allah gave Iblis rule over the earth, rule over the lowest heaven, and the treasury of the Gardens, so he worshipped Allah sometimes on the earth, sometimes in the heaven, and sometimes in the Garden.

When he saw that, pride and self-admiration entered him, and he said to himself: "Allah has given me this kingdom only because I am the most honoured of the angels in His sight and the greatest in rank with Him." When pride appeared, dismissal came. So Allah said to him and to his host:

Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa. When He said that to them, they disliked it, because they were less in worship among the angels, and because dismissal is severe.

They said: Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein through sins, and shed blood — pour out blood — without right?

If it is asked: How did they know that, when it is unseen?

The answer is what al-Suddi said: When Allah said that to them, they said, "And what will come from that khalifa?" He said: "He will have offspring who will cause corruption on the earth [and envy one another] — thus in the manuscript — and some of them will kill others." At that they said: Will You place in it — and the meaning is "so they said." The fa' of sequence is omitted, as in the poet's words:

"When I saw Nabat, helpers, I hitched up my garment above my knees; I was a neighbour to them among the Christians."

meaning, "so I was."

Most of the exegetes said: They meant: as the sons of the jinn did, they measured the absent by the present. Some scholars of meaning said there is ellipsis and abbreviation in it, meaning: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood? Or will You place in it one who does not cause corruption and does not shed blood?" — based on His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾, meaning "like one who is not devoutly obedient." This is the choice of al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl.

And we glorify You with Your praise.

al-Hasan said: They say, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," and this is the prayer of creation and their glorification, and by it they are provided for.

Evidence for this is the hadith transmitted from Abu Dharr, who said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which speech is most excellent?" He said: "What Allah has chosen for His angels: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him."

It is also said the meaning is: "We pray to You by Your command." Tasbih can mean declaring Allah free of imperfection and can mean prayer; hence the prayer is called subha. It is also said the meaning is: "We pray and recite in it the Opening of the Book."

And we sanctify You — and we declare You free of imperfection. The lām is supplementary. It is also said it is the lām of purpose, meaning: "And we purify our hearts for Your sake from associating others with You, and our bodies from disobeying You."

Some scholars said: In the verse there is inversion and transposition; its meaning is: "We glorify and sanctify You, and to You belongs praise," because if the verse is taken according to the first interpretation, it contradicts the angels' claim to purity through self-reliance on works. If it is taken according to this interpretation, it resembles their speech of recounting Allah's blessing and attributing it to Allah, as if they said: "That we glorified You, sanctified You, and obeyed You, and worshipped You — all of that is by Your praise, not by ourselves." Allah said:

Indeed I know what you do not know — concerning My appointing of a khalifa on the earth and the wisdom in it. So do not object to Me in My judgment and My management. It is also said: He meant, "I know that among those whom I will appoint on the earth are prophets, saints, scholars, and righteous people." It is also said: "I know that they will sin, and I will forgive them."

Some wise men said: Allah the Exalted brought Adam out of the Garden before He made him enter it. This is according to His saying: ﴿Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa﴾. Then his leaving the Garden because of his sin shows that it was by the decree and predestination of Allah.

Ibn Nujayh, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed I know what you do not know﴾, said: He knew from Iblis the disobedience and that He had created him for it.

Ibn Shihab, from Humayd, from Abu Hurayrah, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Adam and Musa argued. Musa said to him: 'You are Adam, whom your sin expelled from the Garden.' Adam said to him: 'You are Musa, whom Allah chose for His message and His speech, yet you blame me for a matter decreed before I was created.' So Adam won the argument against Musa."

Section on the meaning of khalifa

It is said: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked Talhah, al-Zubayr, Ka'b and Salman: "What is the khalifa in relation to the king?"

Talhah and al-Zubayr said: "We do not know." Salman said: "The khalifa is one who is just among the subjects, distributes among them equally, shows compassion to them as a man shows compassion to his family, and judges by the Book of Allah." Ka'b said: "I did not think there was anyone in the assembly who knew the difference between khalifa and king except me, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has filled Salman with wisdom, knowledge and justice."

Zadhan transmitted from Salman that Umar said to him: "Am I a king or a khalifa?" Salman said: "If you collect from the land of the Muslims a dirham, or less or more, and place it in other than its right place, then you are a king." He said: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wept.

From Yunus: Mu'awiyah used to say when he sat on the pulpit: "O people, the caliphate is not for gathering wealth nor for scattering it, but the caliphate is by truth, judgment by justice, and holding people to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

And He taught Adam the names, all of them. That is because when Allah said to the angels, "Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa," they said among themselves: "Let our Lord create whatever He wills; He will not create a creature better or more honoured by Him than us. And if it is better than us, we are more knowledgeable than it, for we were created before it and have seen what it has not seen." When they were impressed with their knowledge and worship, Allah the Exalted favoured Adam, peace be upon him, over them with knowledge, and taught him all the names. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The scholars differed about these names. Al-Rabi' and Ibn Anas said: they are the names of the angels. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the names of his offspring.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: Allah taught him the name of every thing, even the dish and the small dish.

Muqatil said: Allah created everything — animals, inanimate objects and others — then taught Adam their names, all of them. He said to him: "O Adam, this is a horse, this is a mule, this is a donkey," until he had gone through all of them. Then He presented those things as He presented the existing things to the angels. Thus He said: ﴿then He presented them﴾ and did not say "presented it," and He returned it to the persons and named things, because accidents cannot be presented.

It is also said: Allah taught Adam, peace be upon him, the craft of every thing.

Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, said: Allah taught Adam the names of creatures, towns, cities, mountains, predators, the names of birds and trees, the names of what was and what will be, and every soul that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will bring into being until the Day of Resurrection; and He presented those names to the angels.

He said: "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful." Indeed the khalifa I place on the earth will cause corruption therein and shed blood. Allah the Exalted meant by this: "How do you claim knowledge of what has not yet occurred, when you do not know what you see and witness?"

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ — that I will not create a creature except that you will be more knowledgeable and better than it. The angels said, acknowledging their inability and apologising.

They said: Glory be to You — declaring You free of objection, because of Your knowledge in Your judgment and management. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun; meaning, "We glorify a glorification," according to al-Khalil's view.

al-Kisa'i said: it is outside the description. It is also said: it is in the vocative construction, meaning: "O Your glory."

We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed You are the All-Knowing about Your creation, the All-Wise in Your command.

For al-ḥakīm (the Wise) there are two meanings. One: the one who makes the act firm, as in His saying: ﴿a painful punishment﴾, and "a painful wound." The poet said:

"Does the echo of the calling companion of Rayhanah, the one who hears, keep me awake, while my companions sleep?"

meaning: the painful and aching one, and "the one who makes to hear." In this interpretation it is an adjective of act.

The other meaning is "the judge, the knower," and in that case it is an adjective of essence. The root of wisdom in Arabic speech is prevention. One says: "I prevented the orphan from corruption and restrained him," meaning I prevented him. Jarir said:

"Sons of Hanifah, restrain your foolish ones; indeed I fear that I will become angry at you."

The bit that is placed across a horse's mouth is called ḥikma, because it prevents the horse from turning aside, and wisdom prevents from falsehood; and what is not beautiful is not permitted in the judicious matter, by preventing it from disorder. In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne, since Allah commanded the angels to report what they did not know, while He knew their inability to do so.

When their inability became evident, Allah the Exalted said: "O Adam, inform them of their names." So he named every thing by its name, and joined every thing to its kind.

When he informed them of their names — told them. He said: "Did I not tell you, O My angels? Indeed I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth — what is hidden in them and what will be. And I know what you reveal of humility and obedience to Adam, and what you conceal" — what you hide within yourselves of enmity toward him. It is also said: "what you reveal" is their acknowledgment of inability and apology, and "what you conceal" is their dislike of Adam's appointment as khalifa.

Ibn Abbas said: Iblis passed by the body of Adam, which lay between Makkah and al-Ta'if without a spirit in it, and said: "For what matter was this created?" Then he entered through its mouth and came out through its back, and said: "It will not hold together except by the hollow." Then he said to the angels with him: "Do you see that if this is preferred over you and you are commanded to obey it, what would you do?" They said: "We will obey the command of our Lord." Iblis said within himself: "By Allah, if I am empowered over it I will destroy it, and if it is empowered over me I will disobey it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And I know what you reveal﴾ — meaning the angels' obedience — ﴿and what you conceal﴾ — meaning Iblis's disobedience.

al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "what you reveal" means their saying: ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein...﴾; "what you conceal" means their saying that He would not create a creature better, more knowledgeable, or more honoured by Him than them.

On the definition of the noun and its divisions

Our companions said: The noun (ism) is every utterance that indicates a meaning and a thing, and it is derived from the sima, which is the mark by which a thing is known. Its divisions are eight: a proper noun, like Zayd, 'Amr, Fatimah, 'A'ishah, dar (house), and faras (horse).

Another is the permanent noun, like your saying: rajul (man), imra'ah (woman), shams (sun), qamar (moon), hajar (stone), madar (clay), and similar. It is called permanent because it does not change or separate: one does not call the sun "moon" nor the moon "stone."

Another is the separable noun, like: saghir (small), kabir (large), tifl (child), kahl (elderly), qalil (few), kathir (many). It is called separable because it was not the name it bears, and the meaning it names may depart from it.

Another is the derived noun, like: katib (writer), khayyat (tailor), sa'igh (goldsmith), sabbagh (dyer). The noun is derived from its verb.

Another is the annexed noun, like: ghulam Ja'far (Ja'far's servant), rukub 'Amr ('Amr's riding), dar Zayd (Zayd's house).

Another is the noun of resemblance, like your saying: so-and-so is a lion, a donkey, a spark of fire.

Another is the relational noun, which establishes itself and establishes another, like your saying: father (ab), mother (umm), brother (akh), sister (ukht), son (ibn), daughter (bint), husband (zawj), wife (zawjah). When you say "father," you have established it and established a child for it; when you say "brother," you have established it and established a sister for it.

Another is the generic noun: a single word that indicates many things, like your saying: animal (hayawan), people (nas), and similar.

And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam — a prostration of honour and greeting, not a prostration of prayer and worship. Its parallel is His saying in the story of Joseph: ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾. That was the greeting of people, one honouring another, and placing the face on the ground was not done; rather it was bowing, glorifying and kissing. When Islam came, that was abolished by the greeting of peace.

In a hadith: Mu'adh ibn Jabal returned from Yemen and prostrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The face of the Messenger of Allah changed, and he said: "What is this?" He said: "I saw the Jews prostrating to their rabbis and the Christians prostrating to their priests." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Stop, O Mu'adh. The Jews and Christians lied; prostration is only to Allah, Exalted."

Some said: it was a real prostration, with Adam made a qibla for them, and the prostration was to Allah, just as the Ka'bah was made a qibla for the prayer of believers, and the prayer is to Allah, Exalted.

Ibn Mas'ud said: Allah commanded them to bring Adam, and the angels prostrated, while Adam was [turned] to the Lord of the worlds.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: its meaning is: "Acknowledge to Adam that he is better and more honoured by Me than you, and so acknowledge it." According to the view of Abdullah and Ubayy, prostration means submission, obedience and humbling, as the poet said:

"You see the hills prostrating to the hooves of the horses in it."

Adam is on the pattern of af'al, and therefore it is not declined.

Al-Suddi, from one who narrated to him from Ibn Abbas, said: Adam was named so because he was created from the surface of the earth (adim al-ard). Some said he was named so because he was created from dust, and dust in the Hebrew tongue is adam. Others said he was named so for the ruddiness of his complexion, since he was brown-skinned; his kunya was Abu Muhammad and Abu al-Bashar.

Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, said: There is no one in Paradise called by a kunya except Adam, who is called Abu Muhammad.

The common readers read lil-malā'ikati with a kasra on the ta'. Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the ta', likening the ta' of feminine marking to the alif of the hamzat al-wasl in His saying: isjudu, because the alif of hamzat al-wasl drops in connected speech, and because it is an added, non-original letter, just as the feminine ta' is an added, non-original letter; and no stable element answers the alif of isjudu.

It is also said: he disliked the damma on the jim after the kasra on the ta', because the Arabs dislike a damma after a kasra for its heaviness. This is a very weak reading, and the grammarians agreed in declaring it an error.

So they prostrated — meaning the angels, except Iblis. His name was 'Azazil; when he disobeyed, his form was changed and his name was changed, and he was called Iblis because he was despaired (ublisa) of Allah's mercy, as one says: "O wicked one," and "O sinner." It is in the accusative as an exception, and it is not declined because of the combination of foreignness and definiteness.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 30–39 (part 2 of 2)**

*Abā* means he refused and did not prostrate. *Wastakbara* means he was arrogant and exalted himself against prostrating. *Wa kāna* means he became one of the disbelievers. ﴿And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned﴾ [Hud 11:43].

Most exegetes said: its meaning is that in His prior knowledge he was among the disbelievers, for whom wretchedness was decreed.

Al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws from him weeping and says: 'Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so he will have Paradise. I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so I will have the Fire.'" [82] [Musnad Ahmad 2/443.]

Ziyad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: When Noah boarded the ship, he found Iblis at its *kawthal* [the *kawthal* is the stern of the ship]. He said to him: "Woe to you! People have been split apart because of you." He said: "So what do you command me?" He said: "Repent." He said: "Ask your Lord whether there is any repentance for me." It was said to him that his repentance was to prostrate to the grave of Adam. He said: "I left him alive; I will prostrate to him dead."

﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. This is because Adam, peace be upon him, was in the Garden lonely, and had no one to sit with him and keep him company. He slept a sleep, and Allah the Exalted created his wife from his *qasīrā* [the lower rib], from his left side, without Adam sensing it or feeling any pain. Had there been any pain in that, a man would not feel tender toward a woman. When Adam woke from his sleep, he found Hawwa' sitting by his head, in the most beautiful form Allah had created. He said to her: "Who are you?" She said: "I am your wife, whom Allah created for you so that you may find rest in me and I may find rest in you." Then the angels, to test Adam's knowledge, said: "O Adam, what is this?" He said: "A woman." They said: "What is her name?" He said: "Hawwa'." They said: "Why were you named Hawwa'?" He said: "Because she was created from a living thing (*ḥayy*)." They said: "Do you love her, O Adam?" He said: "Yes." They said to Hawwa': "Do you love him?" She said: "No," while in her heart there was many times the love he had for her. They said: "If a woman were truthful in her love for her husband, Hawwa' would be truthful."

**(Issue:)** The Qadariyyah said: the Garden in which Allah settled Adam and Hawwa' was not the Garden of Eternity, but a garden from the gardens of this world. They argued that the Garden is not a place of trial and obligation.

**(Response:)** We have agreed (*ajma'nā*) that the people of Paradise are commanded in it to know (Allah) and are obligated to that.

Another response: Allah the Exalted is able to combine opposites. So He showed Adam a trial in the Garden, and showed Abraham a blessing in the Fire, so that the servant would neither feel secure from his Lord nor despair of His mercy, and so that he would know that He may do whatever He wills.

They also argued that whoever enters the Garden cannot leave it, since Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they will not be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr 15:48].

The response to this: whoever enters it as a reward will never leave it. Adam did not enter it as a reward. Do you not see that Ridwan, the keeper of the Garden, enters it and then leaves it? Iblis, too, was inside the Garden and was expelled from it.

﴿And eat from it freely﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]: *raghadan* means abundantly and in large quantity. *Ḥaythu shi'tumā* means how you wish, when you wish, and where you wish.

﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. Some scholars said: the prohibition fell upon a kind of tree. Others said: it fell upon a particular tree, and they differed about it.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah ennoble his face) said: it is the tree of camphor.

Qatadah said: it is the tree of knowledge, and in it is everything.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: it is the wheat-ear (*sunbulah*).

It was also said: it is the *ḥabalah*, which is the root-stem of the vine.

Abu Ruq, from al-Dahhak: it is the fig tree.

﴿So you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35], meaning wrongdoers against yourselves through disobedience. The root meaning of *ẓulm* (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

﴿So he caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning he lured (*istamāla*) Adam and Hawwa', and removed them and drove them away.

Hamzah recited: ﴿Then the Satan caused them to slip﴾, and he is Iblis. *Shaytān* is on the pattern *fay'āl* from *shaṭana*, meaning he became distant. 

It was said: it is from *shāṭa*, and the *nūn* in it is not original. The Satan was so named because of his rebellion and his distance from good and from the mercy of Allah the Exalted.
