﴿From it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning from the Garden. It was said: from obedience.

﴿And He brought them out from what they were in﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning from the bliss. This is because Iblis wanted to enter the Garden and whisper to Adam and Hawwa'. The guardians prevented him. So he came to the serpent, which was among the most beautiful of animals, with four legs like the legs of a camel. It was among the guardians of the Garden and was a friend to Iblis. He asked it to let him enter into its mouth, and it let him enter into its mouth, and passed by the guardians while they did not know, and so he entered the Garden. When Adam entered the Garden and saw what was in it of bliss and honor, he said: "If only there were eternity..." So Satan seized that moment from him and came to him from the direction of eternity. When he entered the Garden, he stood before Adam and Hawwa', and they did not know that he was Iblis. He wailed over them a wailing that saddened them, and he wept, and he was the first to wail. They said: "Why do you weep?" He said: "I weep for you, for you will die and be separated from what you are in of bliss and honor." This entered their hearts and they were grieved. He went away, then came to them again and said: ﴿O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:120]. He refused to accept from him. So he swore to them by Allah that he was truly among the sincere advisers (﴿lamina al-nāṣiḥīn﴾) [al-A'raf 7:21]. They were deceived, and they did not think that anyone would swear by Allah falsely. Hawwa' hastened to eat from the tree, then gave it to Adam until he ate it.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Yazid ibn Abdullah ibn Qusayt, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib swear by Allah without exception: Adam did not eat from the tree while he was in his senses. Rather, Hawwa' gave him wine to drink until he became intoxicated, then she led him to it, and he ate. When they both ate, their garments fell away from them and their private parts became visible, and they were expelled from the Garden. This is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We said﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning to Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent: ﴿Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]. So Adam descended in Sarandib of the land of India, onto a mountain called Nawdhah. It was said: Washm. Hawwa' descended in Jeddah, Iblis in al-Ubullah, and it was said in Maysan, and the serpent in Isfahan.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]: *balāgh* (sufficiency) and *mustamta'* (enjoyment).

﴿For a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning until the appointed time of your lifespans and the end of your lives.

From Ibrahim ibn al-Ash'ath, who said: I heard Ibrahim ibn Adham say: that single eating brought us a long grief.

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37]: *fa-talaqqā* means he was taught. *Ādam* was preserved (*ḥuffiẓa*) when he was taught, and understood when he was inspired.

The common readers recited *Ādamu* with a *ḍammah* on the *mīm*, and *kalimātin* with a *kasrah* on the *tā'*.

Ibn Kathir recited with a *fatḥah* on the *mīm*, meaning the words came to Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿From his Lord, words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37] were the cause of the acceptance of his repentance. The exegetes differed about those words. Ibn Abbas said: they are that Adam said: "O Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did Your mercy not precede Your wrath toward me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then why did You expel me from it?" He said: "Because of the evil of your disobedience." He said: "O Lord, do You see that if I repent and reform, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is the words."

Ubayd ibn Umayr said: it is that Adam said: "O Lord, do You see what I did? Was it something I invented against myself, or something You decreed upon me before You created me?" He said: "Rather, something I decreed upon you before I created you." He said: "O Lord, as You decreed it upon me, forgive me." [Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur 1/59.]

Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam and Moses disputed. Moses said to him: 'You are Adam who misled people and expelled them from the Garden to the earth?' Adam said to him: 'You are Moses whom Allah gave the knowledge of everything and chose over the people with His message?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you blame me for a matter that was written against me to do before I was created?' So Adam overcame Moses in the argument." [83] [al-Musannaf (Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani) 11/113.]

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are his saying: ﴿There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done wrong to myself, so forgive me, indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. And he said: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the Forgiving, the Merciful. There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. O Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy on me, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."

Ikrimah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37]: they said: it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. Likewise al-Hasan and Mujahid said.

Some of them said: Adam, peace be upon him, looked at the Throne and saw written on its leg: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar al-Faruq." He said: "O Lord, I ask You by the right of Muhammad that You forgive me," and He forgave him.

It was also said: this interpretation is what Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was taken up to the heavens, and I saw written on the leg of the Throne: 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar al-Faruq.'" [Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned it in al-Mawdu'at 1/328.] [Al-Muttaqi al-Hindi narrated from Ali the saying of Adam: "O Allah, I ask You by the right of Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, glory be to You, there is no god but You, I have done evil and wronged myself, so accept my repentance, for You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful." Kanz al-Ummal 2/359, no. 4237, the verse's entry; al-Durr al-Manthur 1/60, the commentary on the verse. And al-Suyuti narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the words, and he said: "He asked by the right of Muhammad, Ali, Fatimah, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, that You accept his repentance." Al-Durr al-Manthur 1/60.]

It was also said: they are three things: fear, hope, and weeping.

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: It reached me that when Adam was sent down to the earth, he remained three hundred years without raising his head, out of shame before Allah the Exalted.

Ibn Abbas said: the weeping of Adam and Hawwa' over what they had lost of the bliss of the Garden lasted two hundred years. They did not eat or drink for forty days, and Adam did not approach Hawwa' for a hundred years.

﴿So He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37], meaning He pardoned him. ﴿Indeed He is the Accepting of repentance﴾, who accepts the repentance of His servants; ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His creation.

﴿We said: Go down from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], meaning Adam and Hawwa'. It was said: Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent. ﴿Then if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], O children of Adam, a book and a messenger. ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], regarding what lies ahead of them, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], over what they left behind.

﴿But those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], meaning rejected, ﴿and denied Our signs﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], meaning the Qur'an, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], neither leaving it nor dying in it.

When your Lord said — meaning, "and [when] He said." Some say the sense is: "Remember when your Lord said." Every such occurrence in the Qur'an follows this pattern.

"Idh" (when, for past time) and "idha" (when, for future time) are both particles of time, except that "idh" refers to the past and "idha" to the future, though one may be placed in the position of the other.

Al-Mubarrad said: When "idh" is used with a future verb, its meaning is past, as in His saying: ﴿And [remember] when they plotted against you﴾ and ﴿when he said﴾, meaning, "when they plotted" and "when he said." And when "idha" is used with a past verb, its meaning is future, as in His saying: ﴿So when the Great Calamity comes﴾ and ﴿So when the Deafening Blast comes﴾ and ﴿When the help of Allah comes﴾, meaning "comes." The poet said:

"Then may Allah reward him on our behalf when He rewards [him] — gardens of Eden and the heights to the heights."

meaning, "He rewards him."

to the angels — those who were on the earth. The angels (al-malā'ika) are the messengers; the singular is malak. Its origin is malak, plural malā'ika, and it derives from al-malaka, al-mālika and al-alūk, meaning "message." One says: alikni ila fulan, meaning "be my messenger to him," and the form was transposed, becoming mala'ik. The poet said:

"I am not for mankind, but for a messenger descending from the atmosphere of heaven, pouring down."

Then the hamza was dropped for lightness, and because of its frequent use it became malak.

Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said regarding malak: the Arabs do not derive its verb nor conjugate it, and it is among what its knowledge has escaped.

Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa — meaning a substitute for you, and one raised up to Me. It was called khalifa because it succeeds the one who departs and comes after him. Thus the khalifa is one who carries out a command on behalf of the one who commands. Zayd ibn Ali read it as khaliqa (with the qāf).

The exegetes said: That is because Allah the Exalted created the heavens and the earth, and created the angels and the jinn. He settled the angels in the heavens and settled the jinn on the earth, and they worshipped for a long time on the earth. Then envy and insolence appeared among them, so they fought and caused corruption. Allah sent to them a host of angels called the Jinn — their chief was the enemy of Allah, Iblis — and they were the guardians of the Gardens, named after the Garden (jannah). They descended to the earth and expelled the jinn from its surface, so they joined them in the mountain ranges and the islands of the sea. The angels settled the earth, and Allah lightened their worship, so they loved to remain on earth for that reason. Allah gave Iblis rule over the earth, rule over the lowest heaven, and the treasury of the Gardens, so he worshipped Allah sometimes on the earth, sometimes in the heaven, and sometimes in the Garden.

When he saw that, pride and self-admiration entered him, and he said to himself: "Allah has given me this kingdom only because I am the most honoured of the angels in His sight and the greatest in rank with Him." When pride appeared, dismissal came. So Allah said to him and to his host:

Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa. When He said that to them, they disliked it, because they were less in worship among the angels, and because dismissal is severe.

They said: Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein through sins, and shed blood — pour out blood — without right?

If it is asked: How did they know that, when it is unseen?

The answer is what al-Suddi said: When Allah said that to them, they said, "And what will come from that khalifa?" He said: "He will have offspring who will cause corruption on the earth [and envy one another] — thus in the manuscript — and some of them will kill others." At that they said: Will You place in it — and the meaning is "so they said." The fa' of sequence is omitted, as in the poet's words:

"When I saw Nabat, helpers, I hitched up my garment above my knees; I was a neighbour to them among the Christians."

meaning, "so I was."

Most of the exegetes said: They meant: as the sons of the jinn did, they measured the absent by the present. Some scholars of meaning said there is ellipsis and abbreviation in it, meaning: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood? Or will You place in it one who does not cause corruption and does not shed blood?" — based on His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾, meaning "like one who is not devoutly obedient." This is the choice of al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl.

And we glorify You with Your praise.

al-Hasan said: They say, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," and this is the prayer of creation and their glorification, and by it they are provided for.

Evidence for this is the hadith transmitted from Abu Dharr, who said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Which speech is most excellent?" He said: "What Allah has chosen for His angels: Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him."

It is also said the meaning is: "We pray to You by Your command." Tasbih can mean declaring Allah free of imperfection and can mean prayer; hence the prayer is called subha. It is also said the meaning is: "We pray and recite in it the Opening of the Book."

And we sanctify You — and we declare You free of imperfection. The lām is supplementary. It is also said it is the lām of purpose, meaning: "And we purify our hearts for Your sake from associating others with You, and our bodies from disobeying You."

Some scholars said: In the verse there is inversion and transposition; its meaning is: "We glorify and sanctify You, and to You belongs praise," because if the verse is taken according to the first interpretation, it contradicts the angels' claim to purity through self-reliance on works. If it is taken according to this interpretation, it resembles their speech of recounting Allah's blessing and attributing it to Allah, as if they said: "That we glorified You, sanctified You, and obeyed You, and worshipped You — all of that is by Your praise, not by ourselves." Allah said:

Indeed I know what you do not know — concerning My appointing of a khalifa on the earth and the wisdom in it. So do not object to Me in My judgment and My management. It is also said: He meant, "I know that among those whom I will appoint on the earth are prophets, saints, scholars, and righteous people." It is also said: "I know that they will sin, and I will forgive them."

Some wise men said: Allah the Exalted brought Adam out of the Garden before He made him enter it. This is according to His saying: ﴿Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa﴾. Then his leaving the Garden because of his sin shows that it was by the decree and predestination of Allah.

Ibn Nujayh, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed I know what you do not know﴾, said: He knew from Iblis the disobedience and that He had created him for it.

Ibn Shihab, from Humayd, from Abu Hurayrah, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Adam and Musa argued. Musa said to him: 'You are Adam, whom your sin expelled from the Garden.' Adam said to him: 'You are Musa, whom Allah chose for His message and His speech, yet you blame me for a matter decreed before I was created.' So Adam won the argument against Musa."

Section on the meaning of khalifa

It is said: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked Talhah, al-Zubayr, Ka'b and Salman: "What is the khalifa in relation to the king?"

Talhah and al-Zubayr said: "We do not know." Salman said: "The khalifa is one who is just among the subjects, distributes among them equally, shows compassion to them as a man shows compassion to his family, and judges by the Book of Allah." Ka'b said: "I did not think there was anyone in the assembly who knew the difference between khalifa and king except me, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has filled Salman with wisdom, knowledge and justice."

Zadhan transmitted from Salman that Umar said to him: "Am I a king or a khalifa?" Salman said: "If you collect from the land of the Muslims a dirham, or less or more, and place it in other than its right place, then you are a king." He said: Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, wept.

From Yunus: Mu'awiyah used to say when he sat on the pulpit: "O people, the caliphate is not for gathering wealth nor for scattering it, but the caliphate is by truth, judgment by justice, and holding people to the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

And He taught Adam the names, all of them. That is because when Allah said to the angels, "Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifa," they said among themselves: "Let our Lord create whatever He wills; He will not create a creature better or more honoured by Him than us. And if it is better than us, we are more knowledgeable than it, for we were created before it and have seen what it has not seen." When they were impressed with their knowledge and worship, Allah the Exalted favoured Adam, peace be upon him, over them with knowledge, and taught him all the names. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The scholars differed about these names. Al-Rabi' and Ibn Anas said: they are the names of the angels. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the names of his offspring.

Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: Allah taught him the name of every thing, even the dish and the small dish.

Muqatil said: Allah created everything — animals, inanimate objects and others — then taught Adam their names, all of them. He said to him: "O Adam, this is a horse, this is a mule, this is a donkey," until he had gone through all of them. Then He presented those things as He presented the existing things to the angels. Thus He said: ﴿then He presented them﴾ and did not say "presented it," and He returned it to the persons and named things, because accidents cannot be presented.

It is also said: Allah taught Adam, peace be upon him, the craft of every thing.

Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, said: Allah taught Adam the names of creatures, towns, cities, mountains, predators, the names of birds and trees, the names of what was and what will be, and every soul that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will bring into being until the Day of Resurrection; and He presented those names to the angels.

He said: "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful." Indeed the khalifa I place on the earth will cause corruption therein and shed blood. Allah the Exalted meant by this: "How do you claim knowledge of what has not yet occurred, when you do not know what you see and witness?"

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ — that I will not create a creature except that you will be more knowledgeable and better than it. The angels said, acknowledging their inability and apologising.

They said: Glory be to You — declaring You free of objection, because of Your knowledge in Your judgment and management. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun; meaning, "We glorify a glorification," according to al-Khalil's view.

al-Kisa'i said: it is outside the description. It is also said: it is in the vocative construction, meaning: "O Your glory."

We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed You are the All-Knowing about Your creation, the All-Wise in Your command.

For al-ḥakīm (the Wise) there are two meanings. One: the one who makes the act firm, as in His saying: ﴿a painful punishment﴾, and "a painful wound." The poet said:

"Does the echo of the calling companion of Rayhanah, the one who hears, keep me awake, while my companions sleep?"

meaning: the painful and aching one, and "the one who makes to hear." In this interpretation it is an adjective of act.

The other meaning is "the judge, the knower," and in that case it is an adjective of essence. The root of wisdom in Arabic speech is prevention. One says: "I prevented the orphan from corruption and restrained him," meaning I prevented him. Jarir said:

"Sons of Hanifah, restrain your foolish ones; indeed I fear that I will become angry at you."

The bit that is placed across a horse's mouth is called ḥikma, because it prevents the horse from turning aside, and wisdom prevents from falsehood; and what is not beautiful is not permitted in the judicious matter, by preventing it from disorder. In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne, since Allah commanded the angels to report what they did not know, while He knew their inability to do so.

When their inability became evident, Allah the Exalted said: "O Adam, inform them of their names." So he named every thing by its name, and joined every thing to its kind.

When he informed them of their names — told them. He said: "Did I not tell you, O My angels? Indeed I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth — what is hidden in them and what will be. And I know what you reveal of humility and obedience to Adam, and what you conceal" — what you hide within yourselves of enmity toward him. It is also said: "what you reveal" is their acknowledgment of inability and apology, and "what you conceal" is their dislike of Adam's appointment as khalifa.

Ibn Abbas said: Iblis passed by the body of Adam, which lay between Makkah and al-Ta'if without a spirit in it, and said: "For what matter was this created?" Then he entered through its mouth and came out through its back, and said: "It will not hold together except by the hollow." Then he said to the angels with him: "Do you see that if this is preferred over you and you are commanded to obey it, what would you do?" They said: "We will obey the command of our Lord." Iblis said within himself: "By Allah, if I am empowered over it I will destroy it, and if it is empowered over me I will disobey it."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And I know what you reveal﴾ — meaning the angels' obedience — ﴿and what you conceal﴾ — meaning Iblis's disobedience.

al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "what you reveal" means their saying: ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein...﴾; "what you conceal" means their saying that He would not create a creature better, more knowledgeable, or more honoured by Him than them.

On the definition of the noun and its divisions

Our companions said: The noun (ism) is every utterance that indicates a meaning and a thing, and it is derived from the sima, which is the mark by which a thing is known. Its divisions are eight: a proper noun, like Zayd, 'Amr, Fatimah, 'A'ishah, dar (house), and faras (horse).

Another is the permanent noun, like your saying: rajul (man), imra'ah (woman), shams (sun), qamar (moon), hajar (stone), madar (clay), and similar. It is called permanent because it does not change or separate: one does not call the sun "moon" nor the moon "stone."

Another is the separable noun, like: saghir (small), kabir (large), tifl (child), kahl (elderly), qalil (few), kathir (many). It is called separable because it was not the name it bears, and the meaning it names may depart from it.

Another is the derived noun, like: katib (writer), khayyat (tailor), sa'igh (goldsmith), sabbagh (dyer). The noun is derived from its verb.

Another is the annexed noun, like: ghulam Ja'far (Ja'far's servant), rukub 'Amr ('Amr's riding), dar Zayd (Zayd's house).

Another is the noun of resemblance, like your saying: so-and-so is a lion, a donkey, a spark of fire.

Another is the relational noun, which establishes itself and establishes another, like your saying: father (ab), mother (umm), brother (akh), sister (ukht), son (ibn), daughter (bint), husband (zawj), wife (zawjah). When you say "father," you have established it and established a child for it; when you say "brother," you have established it and established a sister for it.

Another is the generic noun: a single word that indicates many things, like your saying: animal (hayawan), people (nas), and similar.

And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam — a prostration of honour and greeting, not a prostration of prayer and worship. Its parallel is His saying in the story of Joseph: ﴿and they fell down before him in prostration﴾. That was the greeting of people, one honouring another, and placing the face on the ground was not done; rather it was bowing, glorifying and kissing. When Islam came, that was abolished by the greeting of peace.

In a hadith: Mu'adh ibn Jabal returned from Yemen and prostrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The face of the Messenger of Allah changed, and he said: "What is this?" He said: "I saw the Jews prostrating to their rabbis and the Christians prostrating to their priests." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Stop, O Mu'adh. The Jews and Christians lied; prostration is only to Allah, Exalted."

Some said: it was a real prostration, with Adam made a qibla for them, and the prostration was to Allah, just as the Ka'bah was made a qibla for the prayer of believers, and the prayer is to Allah, Exalted.

Ibn Mas'ud said: Allah commanded them to bring Adam, and the angels prostrated, while Adam was [turned] to the Lord of the worlds.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: its meaning is: "Acknowledge to Adam that he is better and more honoured by Me than you, and so acknowledge it." According to the view of Abdullah and Ubayy, prostration means submission, obedience and humbling, as the poet said:

"You see the hills prostrating to the hooves of the horses in it."

Adam is on the pattern of af'al, and therefore it is not declined.

Al-Suddi, from one who narrated to him from Ibn Abbas, said: Adam was named so because he was created from the surface of the earth (adim al-ard). Some said he was named so because he was created from dust, and dust in the Hebrew tongue is adam. Others said he was named so for the ruddiness of his complexion, since he was brown-skinned; his kunya was Abu Muhammad and Abu al-Bashar.

Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, said: There is no one in Paradise called by a kunya except Adam, who is called Abu Muhammad.

The common readers read lil-malā'ikati with a kasra on the ta'. Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the ta', likening the ta' of feminine marking to the alif of the hamzat al-wasl in His saying: isjudu, because the alif of hamzat al-wasl drops in connected speech, and because it is an added, non-original letter, just as the feminine ta' is an added, non-original letter; and no stable element answers the alif of isjudu.

It is also said: he disliked the damma on the jim after the kasra on the ta', because the Arabs dislike a damma after a kasra for its heaviness. This is a very weak reading, and the grammarians agreed in declaring it an error.

So they prostrated — meaning the angels, except Iblis. His name was 'Azazil; when he disobeyed, his form was changed and his name was changed, and he was called Iblis because he was despaired (ublisa) of Allah's mercy, as one says: "O wicked one," and "O sinner." It is in the accusative as an exception, and it is not declined because of the combination of foreignness and definiteness.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 30–39 (part 2 of 2)**

*Abā* means he refused and did not prostrate. *Wastakbara* means he was arrogant and exalted himself against prostrating. *Wa kāna* means he became one of the disbelievers. ﴿And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned﴾ [Hud 11:43].

Most exegetes said: its meaning is that in His prior knowledge he was among the disbelievers, for whom wretchedness was decreed.

Al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration verse and prostrates, Satan withdraws from him weeping and says: 'Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so he will have Paradise. I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so I will have the Fire.'" [82] [Musnad Ahmad 2/443.]

Ziyad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: When Noah boarded the ship, he found Iblis at its *kawthal* [the *kawthal* is the stern of the ship]. He said to him: "Woe to you! People have been split apart because of you." He said: "So what do you command me?" He said: "Repent." He said: "Ask your Lord whether there is any repentance for me." It was said to him that his repentance was to prostrate to the grave of Adam. He said: "I left him alive; I will prostrate to him dead."

﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. This is because Adam, peace be upon him, was in the Garden lonely, and had no one to sit with him and keep him company. He slept a sleep, and Allah the Exalted created his wife from his *qasīrā* [the lower rib], from his left side, without Adam sensing it or feeling any pain. Had there been any pain in that, a man would not feel tender toward a woman. When Adam woke from his sleep, he found Hawwa' sitting by his head, in the most beautiful form Allah had created. He said to her: "Who are you?" She said: "I am your wife, whom Allah created for you so that you may find rest in me and I may find rest in you." Then the angels, to test Adam's knowledge, said: "O Adam, what is this?" He said: "A woman." They said: "What is her name?" He said: "Hawwa'." They said: "Why were you named Hawwa'?" He said: "Because she was created from a living thing (*ḥayy*)." They said: "Do you love her, O Adam?" He said: "Yes." They said to Hawwa': "Do you love him?" She said: "No," while in her heart there was many times the love he had for her. They said: "If a woman were truthful in her love for her husband, Hawwa' would be truthful."

**(Issue:)** The Qadariyyah said: the Garden in which Allah settled Adam and Hawwa' was not the Garden of Eternity, but a garden from the gardens of this world. They argued that the Garden is not a place of trial and obligation.

**(Response:)** We have agreed (*ajma'nā*) that the people of Paradise are commanded in it to know (Allah) and are obligated to that.

Another response: Allah the Exalted is able to combine opposites. So He showed Adam a trial in the Garden, and showed Abraham a blessing in the Fire, so that the servant would neither feel secure from his Lord nor despair of His mercy, and so that he would know that He may do whatever He wills.

They also argued that whoever enters the Garden cannot leave it, since Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they will not be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr 15:48].

The response to this: whoever enters it as a reward will never leave it. Adam did not enter it as a reward. Do you not see that Ridwan, the keeper of the Garden, enters it and then leaves it? Iblis, too, was inside the Garden and was expelled from it.

﴿And eat from it freely﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]: *raghadan* means abundantly and in large quantity. *Ḥaythu shi'tumā* means how you wish, when you wish, and where you wish.

﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. Some scholars said: the prohibition fell upon a kind of tree. Others said: it fell upon a particular tree, and they differed about it.

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah ennoble his face) said: it is the tree of camphor.

Qatadah said: it is the tree of knowledge, and in it is everything.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Muqatil said: it is the wheat-ear (*sunbulah*).

It was also said: it is the *ḥabalah*, which is the root-stem of the vine.

Abu Ruq, from al-Dahhak: it is the fig tree.

﴿So you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35], meaning wrongdoers against yourselves through disobedience. The root meaning of *ẓulm* (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

﴿So he caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning he lured (*istamāla*) Adam and Hawwa', and removed them and drove them away.

Hamzah recited: ﴿Then the Satan caused them to slip﴾, and he is Iblis. *Shaytān* is on the pattern *fay'āl* from *shaṭana*, meaning he became distant. 

It was said: it is from *shāṭa*, and the *nūn* in it is not original. The Satan was so named because of his rebellion and his distance from good and from the mercy of Allah the Exalted.

﴿From it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning from the Garden. It was said: from obedience.

﴿And He brought them out from what they were in﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning from the bliss. This is because Iblis wanted to enter the Garden and whisper to Adam and Hawwa'. The guardians prevented him. So he came to the serpent, which was among the most beautiful of animals, with four legs like the legs of a camel. It was among the guardians of the Garden and was a friend to Iblis. He asked it to let him enter into its mouth, and it let him enter into its mouth, and passed by the guardians while they did not know, and so he entered the Garden. When Adam entered the Garden and saw what was in it of bliss and honor, he said: "If only there were eternity..." So Satan seized that moment from him and came to him from the direction of eternity. When he entered the Garden, he stood before Adam and Hawwa', and they did not know that he was Iblis. He wailed over them a wailing that saddened them, and he wept, and he was the first to wail. They said: "Why do you weep?" He said: "I weep for you, for you will die and be separated from what you are in of bliss and honor." This entered their hearts and they were grieved. He went away, then came to them again and said: ﴿O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:120]. He refused to accept from him. So he swore to them by Allah that he was truly among the sincere advisers (﴿lamina al-nāṣiḥīn﴾) [al-A'raf 7:21]. They were deceived, and they did not think that anyone would swear by Allah falsely. Hawwa' hastened to eat from the tree, then gave it to Adam until he ate it.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Yazid ibn Abdullah ibn Qusayt, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib swear by Allah without exception: Adam did not eat from the tree while he was in his senses. Rather, Hawwa' gave him wine to drink until he became intoxicated, then she led him to it, and he ate. When they both ate, their garments fell away from them and their private parts became visible, and they were expelled from the Garden. This is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We said﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning to Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent: ﴿Go down, some of you being enemies to others﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]. So Adam descended in Sarandib of the land of India, onto a mountain called Nawdhah. It was said: Washm. Hawwa' descended in Jeddah, Iblis in al-Ubullah, and it was said in Maysan, and the serpent in Isfahan.

﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36]: *balāgh* (sufficiency) and *mustamta'* (enjoyment).

﴿For a time﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], meaning until the appointed time of your lifespans and the end of your lives.

From Ibrahim ibn al-Ash'ath, who said: I heard Ibrahim ibn Adham say: that single eating brought us a long grief.

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37]: *fa-talaqqā* means he was taught. *Ādam* was preserved (*ḥuffiẓa*) when he was taught, and understood when he was inspired.

The common readers recited *Ādamu* with a *ḍammah* on the *mīm*, and *kalimātin* with a *kasrah* on the *tā'*.

Ibn Kathir recited with a *fatḥah* on the *mīm*, meaning the words came to Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿From his Lord, words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37] were the cause of the acceptance of his repentance. The exegetes differed about those words. Ibn Abbas said: they are that Adam said: "O Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did Your mercy not precede Your wrath toward me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then why did You expel me from it?" He said: "Because of the evil of your disobedience." He said: "O Lord, do You see that if I repent and reform, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is the words."

Ubayd ibn Umayr said: it is that Adam said: "O Lord, do You see what I did? Was it something I invented against myself, or something You decreed upon me before You created me?" He said: "Rather, something I decreed upon you before I created you." He said: "O Lord, as You decreed it upon me, forgive me." [Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur 1/59.]

Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Adam and Moses disputed. Moses said to him: 'You are Adam who misled people and expelled them from the Garden to the earth?' Adam said to him: 'You are Moses whom Allah gave the knowledge of everything and chose over the people with His message?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Do you blame me for a matter that was written against me to do before I was created?' So Adam overcame Moses in the argument." [83] [al-Musannaf (Abd al-Razzaq al-San'ani) 11/113.]

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they are his saying: ﴿There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done wrong to myself, so forgive me, indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. And he said: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the Forgiving, the Merciful. There is no god but You, glory be to You, and praise be to You. O Lord, I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy on me, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."

Ikrimah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37]: they said: it is His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf 7:23]. Likewise al-Hasan and Mujahid said.

Some of them said: Adam, peace be upon him, looked at the Throne and saw written on its leg: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar al-Faruq." He said: "O Lord, I ask You by the right of Muhammad that You forgive me," and He forgave him.

It was also said: this interpretation is what Ibn Jurayj narrated from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was taken up to the heavens, and I saw written on the leg of the Throne: 'There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar al-Faruq.'" [Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned it in al-Mawdu'at 1/328.] [Al-Muttaqi al-Hindi narrated from Ali the saying of Adam: "O Allah, I ask You by the right of Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, glory be to You, there is no god but You, I have done evil and wronged myself, so accept my repentance, for You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful." Kanz al-Ummal 2/359, no. 4237, the verse's entry; al-Durr al-Manthur 1/60, the commentary on the verse. And al-Suyuti narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the words, and he said: "He asked by the right of Muhammad, Ali, Fatimah, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, that You accept his repentance." Al-Durr al-Manthur 1/60.]

It was also said: they are three things: fear, hope, and weeping.

Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: It reached me that when Adam was sent down to the earth, he remained three hundred years without raising his head, out of shame before Allah the Exalted.

Ibn Abbas said: the weeping of Adam and Hawwa' over what they had lost of the bliss of the Garden lasted two hundred years. They did not eat or drink for forty days, and Adam did not approach Hawwa' for a hundred years.

﴿So He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:37], meaning He pardoned him. ﴿Indeed He is the Accepting of repentance﴾, who accepts the repentance of His servants; ﴿the Merciful﴾ toward His creation.

﴿We said: Go down from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], meaning Adam and Hawwa'. It was said: Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent. ﴿Then if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], O children of Adam, a book and a messenger. ﴿Whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], regarding what lies ahead of them, ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:38], over what they left behind.

﴿But those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], meaning rejected, ﴿and denied Our signs﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], meaning the Qur'an, ﴿those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:39], neither leaving it nor dying in it.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 40–48:

O Children of Israel (Banī Isrā'īl), the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob). The meaning of Isrā'īl is "the elect of Allah" (ṣafwat Allāh), and Īl is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is also said that its meaning is "servant of Allah" (ʿabd Allāh).

It is also said that he was named thus because Ya'qub and ʿĪṣ were twins who fought in their mother's womb. Ya'qub wanted to come out first, but ʿĪṣ prevented him and said: "By Allah, if you come out before me, I will break through in my mother's womb and kill her." So Ya'qub held back, ʿĪṣ came out, and Ya'qub seized ʿĪṣ's heel, so ʿĪṣ came out before Ya'qub.

ʿĪṣ was named so because he disobeyed (ʿaṣā) and came out before Ya'qub. ʿĪṣ was the more beloved of the two to their father, and Ya'qub was the more beloved to their mother. ʿĪṣ and Ya'qub were the sons of Isḥāq (Isaac), and my uncle [said]: Isḥāq said to ʿĪṣ: "My son, bring me game meat and come close to me, and I will invoke for you the supplication my father invoked for me." ʿĪṣ was a hairy man, and Ya'qub was a smooth-skinned man. ʿĪṣ went out to hunt, and his mother said to Ya'qub: "My son, go to the flock, slaughter a sheep from it, roast it, wrap yourself in its skin, and bring it to your father, and say to him: 'I am ʿĪṣ.'" Ya'qub did so. When he came, [Isḥāq] said: "My son, eat." He said: "Who are you?" He said: "Your son ʿĪṣ." [He said: "Come near me," and he came near, and he touched him and said: "The touch is the touch of ʿĪṣ, but the scent is the scent of Ya'qub."] His mother said: "He is your son, so invoke for him." He said: "Bring your food," and he brought it, and he ate from it. Then he said: "Come close to me," and he came close, and he invoked for him that Allah place among his descendants prophets and kings. Ya'qub then rose and left, and ʿĪṣ came and said: "I have brought you the game you commanded me to bring." He said: "My son, your brother Ya'qub has preceded you." ʿĪṣ became angry and said: "By Allah, I will kill him." He said: "My son, there remains for you a supplication, so come and I will invoke it for you." He invoked for him, saying: "Your descendants will be a great number like the dust, and no one other than them will rule over them..." [[The manuscript has a blank; we completed the story from Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/244–225.]].

"Remember..."

Al-Sha'bi narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever does not thank for little does not thank for much, whoever does not thank people does not thank Allah, speaking of the blessing of Allah is gratitude, and abandoning it is disbelief, and community is mercy while division is punishment." [84] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/278; al-Shukr lillah of Ibn Abi al-Dunya: 7.]]

"My blessing" (niʿmatī): he meant "my blessings" (niʿamī), and it is singular [in form but with the meaning of plural], as in His saying, Exalted is He: "And if you should count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it" [[Surah Ibrahim: 34.]], and a number cannot apply to a singular.

"Which I bestowed upon you": that is, upon your forefathers. Allah split the sea for them, saved them from Pharaoh, destroyed their enemy, and gave them their homes and wealth as an inheritance; He shaded them with clouds ("and We shaded you with the clouds") in the wilderness from the heat of the sun; He made for them a pillar of light that illuminated for them at night when there was no moonlight; He sent down to them the manna and the quails; He caused twelve springs to gush forth for them; [and He sent down] [[A blank in the manuscript; what we have written is the apparent reading.]] to them the Torah, in which is an explanation of everything they need — blessings from Allah that cannot be counted.

"Fulfill My covenant, and I will fulfill your covenant": the covenant I made with you; I will fulfill your covenant by admitting you to Paradise and accomplishing for you what I promised you.

Al-Zuhri read "Awuffa" with the doubled letter for emphasis; it is said that wafā and awfā both mean the same thing, and their root meaning is completion.

Al-Kalbi said: He made a covenant with the Children of Israel through the tongue of Musa: "I will raise from the descendants of Isma'il a prophet who is unlettered. Whoever follows him [and believes in him], I will pardon his sin, admit him to Paradise, and give him a double reward." This is His saying: "And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: you must make it clear to the people and not conceal it" [[Surah Al ʿImran: 187.]], meaning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Qatada said: It is the covenant that Allah took from them in His saying: "And We took the covenant of the Children of Israel" [[Surah al-Ma'idah: 70.]] and His saying, Exalted is He: "a goodly loan" [[Surah al-Baqarah: 245.]]. This is His saying "Fulfill My covenant," then He said: "I will remove from you your misdeeds" [[Surah al-Ma'idah: 12.]] — the verse. This is His saying "I will fulfill your covenant."

[Another view is] His saying: "And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: you shall not worship except Allah" [[Surah al-Baqarah: 83.]] — the verse.

Al-Hasan said: It is His saying: "And when We took your covenant and raised above you the mountain" [[Surah al-Baqarah: 63.]] — the verse.

Isma'il ibn Ziyad said: "And do not flee from the battlefield": I will admit you to Paradise; its evidence is His saying: "And they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs" [[Surah al-Ahzab: 15.]].

It is also said: "Fulfill [your side] on the condition of servanthood, and I will fulfill [My side] on the condition of lordship."

The people of allusion said: "Fulfill [your covenant] in the house of My trial on the carpet of My service; I will fulfill your covenant in the house of My blessing on the carpet of My honor, through My nearness and My vision."

"And fear Me alone" (wa-iyyāya farhabūn): fear Me regarding breaking the covenant. [The letter yā' after the nūn was dropped in these verses and throughout the Qur'an according to the original form, and the rest omitted it following the script of the Mushaf.]

"And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you": that is, the Torah, in its affirmation of monotheism, prophethood, and reports, and some of the laws. It was revealed concerning Ka'b and his companions among the scholars and chiefs of the Jews.

"And do not be the first to disbelieve in it": that is, the first to disbelieve in the Qur'an. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/360.]] The Jews had pledged allegiance to them on this, so "you will bear your sins and their sins."

"And do not trade My verses": that is, the clarification of Muhammad's description and attributes. "For a small price": something insignificant. This is because the chiefs of the Jews had incomes they took from their lower classes and common people, taking from them a fixed amount every year from their crops. [They feared that if they made clear] the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and pledged allegiance to him, those meals and leadership would be lost to them, so they chose this world over the Hereafter.

"And fear Me alone": fear Me regarding the matter of Muhammad, not regarding what you might lose of leadership and food.

"And do not mix truth with falsehood": do not mix and do not confuse. It is said: [labastu ʿalayhim al-amr albisuhu labsan, meaning I mixed it up for them] [[Addition from Tafsir al-Tabari 1/362.]], i.e., I mixed up and made the truth that was sent down to you, concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), resemble falsehood.

"With falsehood": which you conceal, namely what you find in your books of his description and attributes.

Muqatil said: The Jews acknowledged some of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealed some of it, and they differed about that. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "And do not mix the truth" that you affirm and make clear "with falsehood", meaning with what you conceal. The truth is their clarification, and the falsehood is their concealment.

It is also said: its meaning is "do not mix the truth [... with falsehood]" as an attribute or a state.

"And conceal the truth": meaning do not conceal the truth, as in His saying: "Do not betray Allah and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts" [[Surah al-Anfal: 27.]].

"While you know": that he is a prophet sent.

"And establish the prayer": meaning preserve the five prayers at their appointed times, [and their pillars] and their bowing and prostration.

"And give zakat": meaning pay the obligatory zakat of your wealth. The origin of zakat is purity, growth, and increase.

"And bow with those who bow": meaning pray with those who pray, Muhammad and his companions. He addresses the Jews and expresses prayer by bowing because it is one of its pillars, just as He expressed giving by the hand, as in His saying: "That is for what your hands have sent forward" [[Surah Al ʿImran: 181.]] and "for what your hands have earned" [[Surah al-Shura: 30.]], and by the neck for the whole body, in His saying: "We have fastened his bird to his neck" [[Surah al-Isra': 13.]], and the nose for [.............] [[A lacuna in the manuscript.]].

[Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people — obedience and righteous deeds — and forget yourselves — you abandon them — while you recite the Scripture? A severe rebuke. Will you not then reason — i.e., will you not restrain yourselves from falling into this ruinous state?] [[A blank in the manuscript; the explanation of the verses is from al-Qurtubi's tafsir: 1/365.]].

"And seek help through patience and prayer..."

"And indeed it is difficult [upon them both, but he referred to the more prevalent, which is prayer], as in His saying: 'And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah' and His saying: 'When they see a trade or amusement, they scatter toward it.' He returned the pronoun to silver because it is the more prevalent and general, and to trade because it is the more excellent and important... 'And indeed it' is one of the two; he meant that each of these qualities is indeed difficult." It is also said: the pronoun returns to each of them, as He, Exalted, said: "And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign" [[Surah al-Mu'minun: 50.]] and did not say "two signs," meaning: We made each of them a sign.

A good person whose knowledge is adorned by forbearance... and whoever attains it has succeeded in relief.

That is, whoever attains each of them.

Another said:

"For every worry of the worries there is room, but evening and morning have no success with it."

[[Sharh al-Radi ʿala al-Kafiyah: 4/494, where it reads: "no endurance with it."]]

It is also said: the pronoun returns to prayer, because patience is included within prayer, as in His saying: "And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him" [[Surah al-Tawbah: 62.]], and He did not say "please them both," because the Messenger's pleasure is included within Allah's pleasure, so the pronoun returned to Allah.

The poet, who was Hassan, said:

"Indeed the bloom of youth and black hair, as long as they are not disobeyed, are madness."

He did not say "disobey them," returning it to youth, because black hair is included within it. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said:

[The pronoun returns to seeking help.] Its meaning: that seeking help through patience and prayer is indeed heavy and difficult, "except for the humble" — meaning the believers. Ibn ʿAbbas said: meaning those who pray. Al-Warraq: the worshippers who obey. Muqatil ibn Hayyan: the humble. Al-Hasan: the fearful. Al-Zajjaj said: the khashi' is one who shows the marks of humiliation and submission upon himself, like a house that has fallen into ruin after being inhabited; this is the origin of the word. [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/374.]]

Al-Nabigha said:

"Ash like kohl for the eye, whose traces you cannot distinguish, and a ditch like the stump of a pool, broken and humbled."

"Who think" (alladhīna yazunnūn): meaning they know and are certain, as in His saying: "Indeed I thought that I would meet my account" [[Surah al-Haqqah: 21.]], meaning I was certain of it.

Duraid ibn al-Simmah said:

"I said to them: 'Be certain of two thousand armored men, their chiefs in the Persian coats of mail.'"

Meaning: be certain.

The word ẓann is among the words with opposite meanings: it can mean doubt and certainty, as rajāʾ can mean hope and fear.

"That they will meet their Lord": meaning they will witness their Lord in the Hereafter, "and that to Him they will return": so He will recompense them for their deeds.

"O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds" — meaning the worlds of your time.

"And fear a Day": that is, beware of a day and fear the day.

"No soul will avail" (lā tajzī): that is, will not suffice, will not satisfy, will not benefit.

From this is the hadith of Abu Burda ibn Dayyan concerning the sacrifice: "It will not suffice for anyone after you."

Abu al-Sammak al-ʿAdawi read: lā tuǧzi' with a dammed tā' and hamzated yā', from ajza'a yujzi'u, meaning it suffices.

The poet said:

"And I have sufficed the affair of the worlds, and it was not for him to suffice except the complete and the son of the complete."

[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 1/378.]]

Al-Zajjaj said: there is an implied element in the verse, meaning: "no soul will avail for another soul anything" of the hardships and adversities.

The poet recited:

"And a day we witnessed, Sulaym and ʿĀmir..."

meaning: we witnessed in it.

It is also said: the meaning is: no believing soul and no disbelieving soul will suffice for a disbelieving soul.

"Nor will intercession be accepted from it" — if it was disbelieving.

The people of Makkah and Basra read with the tā' for the feminine form of "intercession". The rest read with the yā' because the verb precedes.

Qatada read: "wa-lā yaqbalu minhā shafāʿatan," with an open yā' and an accusative "shafāʿah," meaning "Allah does not accept."

"Nor will any ransom (ʿadl) be taken from it" — the ransom they used to give in this world. The ransom is called ʿadl because it equals the one ransomed and is like him, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "or its equivalent in fasting" [[Surah al-Ma'idah: 95.]].

"Nor will they be helped" — that is, they will not be prevented from the punishment of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: The Jews used to claim that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so Allah made them despair of that.

The people of Makkah and Basra read with the tā' for the feminine form of "intercession". The rest read with the yā' because the verb precedes.

Qatada read: "wa-lā yaqbalu minhā shafāʿatan," with an open yā' and an accusative "shafāʿah," meaning "Allah does not accept."

"Nor will any ransom (ʿadl) be taken from it" — the ransom they used to give in this world. The ransom is called ʿadl because it equals the one ransomed and is like him, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "or its equivalent in fasting" [[Surah al-Ma'idah: 95.]].

"Nor will they be helped" — that is, they will not be prevented from the punishment of Allah.

Al-Zajjaj said: The Jews used to claim that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so Allah made them despair of that.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 49–54 (part 1 of 2):

And when We saved you: that is, your forefathers and ancestors. He counted it a favour upon them because they were saved by their salvation, and the virtues of fathers are the glories of sons.

As for His saying, ﴿And We saved you﴾ [2:50]: its root is "we cast you upon al-najah," and al-najah is the high and wide part of the land. This is the original meaning. Then every one who attains success was called "najin" (one who is saved), as if he had come out of narrowness and hardship into ease and comfort.

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i recited: "wa-idh najjākum" (with the single letter of the root doubled and the verb in the singular).

﴿From the people of Pharaoh﴾: that is, his partisans, followers, household, his kin, and the people of his religion. Its origin is from "al-awwal," which means return, as if it returns to you (uwwal). In origin there were two hamzas, and one of them was replaced by a long vowel (madd) and lightening.

Pharaoh: he is al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan, and he was from the Amalekites.

﴿They inflict upon you the worst torment﴾: that is, they impose upon you and make you taste the most severe and worst torment. This is because Pharaoh made the Children of Israel servants and slaves, and divided them according to their work. One group built, another group ploughed and planted, another group served, and whoever was not in any of these occupations had to pay the poll-tax (jizya).

﴿They slaughter your sons and let your women live﴾.

Ibn Muhaysin recited with lightening: the yā' and the bā' vowelled with fatḥa in "yudhabbihūna" (in the sense of slaughter), and the doubling (tashdid) is for intensity. This is because Pharaoh saw in his dream as if a fire came from Bayt al-Maqdis until it enveloped the houses of Egypt, burned them, burned the Copts, and left the Children of Israel. This frightened him, so he summoned the magicians and soothsayers and asked them about his dream. They said: "A boy will be born among the Children of Israel who will be the cause of your destruction, the end of your kingdom, and the change of your religion." So Pharaoh ordered the killing of every boy born among the Children of Israel, and he gathered the midwives from among the people of his kingdom and said to them: "Let no boy of the Children of Israel fall into your hands except that he is killed, and let no girl be but that she is spared." He appointed people to watch them and carry this out. Death spread among the elders of the Children of Israel, so the chiefs of the Copts entered upon Pharaoh and said to him: "Death has befallen the Children of Israel, and you are slaughtering their young, while their elders die, and soon the work will fall upon us." So Pharaoh ordered that they slaughter for one year and leave for one year. Harun was born in the year in which they did not slaughter, so he was spared, and Musa was born in the year in which they did slaughter.

﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾: in your being saved from them there was a great blessing. And the word "bala' (trial)" is used in two senses:

the blessings and the calamities [...]

[Blank in the manuscript.]

﴿And when We divided the sea for you ...﴾ [Unreadable text.]

the sea: This is because when the destruction of Pharaoh drew near, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded Musa to journey by night with the Children of Israel, and commanded them to keep lamps lit in their houses until morning. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought out to them every illegitimate child among the Copts who were among the Children of Israel, and He brought out [from the Children of Israel every illegitimate child among them] [Supplement from al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/84; the manuscript has a blank] to the Copts, until each one of them returned to his father. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent death upon the Copts, and every firstborn died, so they were occupied with burying them [away from pursuing them until] [Supplement from Tafsir al-Tabari: 1/396] the sun rose. Musa, peace be upon him, went out with six hundred thousand and twenty thousand fighting men, none of them younger than twenty or older than sixty, apart from the offspring. When they wanted to set out, the wandering (al-tih) was imposed upon them, so they did not know where to go. Musa, peace be upon him, summoned the elders of the Children of Israel and asked them about that.

They said: "When Yusuf, peace be upon him, was approaching death, he took a covenant from his brothers that they would not leave Egypt until they took him out with them. That is why the road was closed to us." So he asked them about the location of his grave, and they did not know.

Musa stood calling out: "I beseech Allah, whoever knows where the grave of Yusuf is, to inform me of it. And whoever does not know, let his ears be deaf to my words." He kept passing between two men calling out, and they did not hear his voice, until an old woman of theirs heard him and said: "Do you see, if I guide you to his grave, will you give me whatever I ask of you?" He refused her and said: "Until I ask my Lord." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded him to grant her request. She said: "I am an old, great woman who cannot walk, so carry me and take me out of Egypt; this is for the world. As for the Hereafter, I ask you that I not descend into a chamber of Paradise except that I descend with you." He said: "Yes." She said: "He is in the depths of the water, in the Nile, so pray to Allah that He hold back the water from him." He prayed to Allah and He held back the water from him, and he prayed that the rising of dawn be delayed until he finished the matter of Yusuf. Musa dug at that place and extracted him in a coffer of marble, and he carried him until he buried him in al-Sham. Then the road opened for them.

They set out, with Musa at their rear and Harun at their front. Pharaoh learned of them, so he gathered his people and commanded them not to go out in pursuit of the Children of Israel until the rooster crowed. By Allah, no rooster crowed that night.

Pharaoh went out in pursuit of the Children of Israel, and at his vanguard was Haman, with one million and seven hundred thousand, and among them were seventy thousand of the dark-coloured horses, apart from the rest of the mixed breeds. The Children of Israel proceeded until they reached the sea, and the water was at its highest rise.

They looked, and behold, there was Pharaoh, and that was when the sun rose. They remained perplexed and said: "O Musa, what shall we do? What is the way out? Pharaoh is behind us and the sea is before us." Musa said: ﴿By no means! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [26:62]. Then He revealed to him: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff﴾ [26:63]. He struck it but it did not obey him. Allah revealed to him: "Be gentle with it," so Musa struck it with his staff and said: "Split, Abu Khalid, by the permission of Allah." ﴿So it split, and each part was like a huge mountain﴾ [26:63]. And there appeared in it twelve paths, one path for each tribe. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent the wind and the sun upon the bed of the sea until it became dry.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Mu'awiya sent to Ibn 'Abbas and asked him about a place where the sun had risen only once. He wrote back to him: "It is the place from which the sea split for the Children of Israel." [al-Bidaya wa'l-Nihaya: 8/334, which mentions the remainder of the story.]

The Children of Israel plunged into the sea, each tribe in its own path, and on either side of them the water was like a huge mountain, and they could not see one another. They were frightened, and each tribe said: "Our brothers have all drowned." So Allah revealed to the state of the water: "Become interlaced," and the water became like latticed windows so that they could see one another and hear one another's speech, until they crossed the sea safely. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾, that is, We said, and We separated the water to the right and to the left.

﴿And We saved you﴾ from the people of Pharaoh and from drowning.

﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾. This is because Pharaoh, when he reached the sea and saw it split, said to his people: "Look at the sea, it has split out of awe of me, so that I may overtake my enemies and my slaves who ran away, and kill them. Enter the sea!" His people were afraid to enter it, and there was no female horse among Pharaoh's horses; they were all males. So Jibril, peace be upon him, came on a female horse in heat and went ahead of them and plunged into the sea. When the horses smelled her scent, they rushed into the sea after her until they all plunged into the sea. Mikail came on a horse behind the people, urging them on and saying to them: "Catch up with your companions!" When Jibril came out of the sea and the first of them was about to come out, Allah, Exalted, commanded the sea to seize them, and it closed over them, and He drowned them all, and that was in full view of the Children of Israel. This is His saying: ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾.

﴿And you were looking on﴾ at their fate.

﴿And when We appointed for Musa forty nights﴾. This is because when the Children of Israel felt safe from their enemy and entered Egypt, they had no book or law to which they could refer, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, promised Musa that He would send down the Torah to them. Musa said to his people: "I am going to the appointed time of my Lord, and I will bring you a book containing the explanation of what you should do and what you should avoid." So he appointed them forty nights, thirty of Dhu al-Qa'da and ten of Dhu al-Hijja, and he appointed his brother Harun as his successor over them.

When the promised time came, Jibril came on a horse called the horse of life, which does not touch anything without it coming to life, to take Musa to his Lord. When al-Samiri saw him, and he was a goldsmith from the people of Bajaro, whose name was Mikha (and Ibn 'Abbas said: his name was Musa ibn Zafar; he was a hypocrite who had outwardly embraced Islam, and he was from a people who worshipped cows, so the love of cows had entered his heart), when he saw Jibril on that horse, he said: "This has a matter." He took a handful of the dust from the hoof-print of Jibril's horse. The Children of Israel had borrowed a great deal of ornaments from the people of Pharaoh when they wanted to leave Egypt, for a festival of theirs, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, destroyed the people of Pharaoh, so those ornaments remained in the hands of the Children of Israel. When Musa arrived, al-Samiri said: "The goods and ornaments you borrowed from the people of Pharaoh are spoils of war, and they are not lawful for you. Dig a pit and bury them in it until Musa returns, and he will see his opinion regarding them." They did that.

When the ornaments were gathered, al-Samiri fashioned them, then he threw into them the handful he had taken from the dust of Jibril's horse, and there came out a calf of gold, set with jewels, as beautiful as could be, and it lowed a lowing. Al-Suddi said: It used to low and walk, [and say:] ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot﴾ [20:88], that is, he left it here and went out to seek him.

The Children of Israel had broken the promise, so they counted a day and a night as two days. When twenty days had passed and Musa, peace be upon him, had not returned, and they saw the calf and heard the words of al-Samiri, eight thousand men among them were seduced by the calf, and they clung to it, worshipping it besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And when We appointed for Musa﴾: Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited "wa'adnā" without an alif throughout the Qur'an, and the rest recited "wā'adnā" with an alif, and this is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud. Whoever recited without an alif said: because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the sole one who makes the promise, and the Qur'an speaks of it thus, as in His saying: ﴿Allah has promised﴾ [4:95], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you a true promise﴾ [14:22]. Whoever recited with an alif said: "The form of mufā'ala (mutual action) may come from one party, as in their saying: 'I punished the thief,' 'May Allah grant you well-being,' and 'I struck the sandal.'"

Al-Zajjaj said: "wā'adnā" is good, because acceptance and obedience stand in the position of mutual promising; so the promise is from Allah and the acceptance is from Musa.

Musa: he is Musa ibn 'Imran ibn Yasahar ibn Qahat ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub.

﴿Forty nights﴾. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited "arbi'īn" with a kasra on the bā', and this is a dialect form, and "laylatan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) and explanation. Time was linked to the night rather than the day because the months of the Arabs were set by the course of the moon, and the crescent appears at night. It was also said that darkness is older than light, and night was created before day. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [36:37], and so on.

﴿Then you took the calf﴾. Abu al-'Aliya said: It was named "the calf" because they hastened (ta'ajjalū) to it before the return of Musa, peace be upon him.

﴿After him﴾: after Musa's departure to the mountain for the appointed meeting.

﴿And you were wrongdoers﴾: harming yourselves by disobedience, and placing worship in other than its proper place.

﴿Then We pardoned you﴾: that is, We left you and did not uproot you,
from his saying, peace be upon him: "Trim the moustaches and leave the beards." It was also said: We erased your sins, from the saying of the Arabs: "The wind effaced the dwellings, so they were effaced."

﴿After that﴾: that is, after your worship of the calf.

﴿So that you might be grateful﴾: in order that you might thank My pardon of you and My kindness to you.

The scholars differed concerning the reality of gratitude (shukr). Ibn 'Abbas said: it is obedience with all the limbs to the Lord of creation, openly and secretly.

Al-Hasan said: the thanks for a blessing is to mention it. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [93:11].

Al-Fadl said: the thanks for every blessing is that Allah is not disobeyed after that blessing.

Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Warraq: The reality of gratitude is knowing the Benefactor, and that you do not regard any share for yourself in the blessing, but see it as from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [16:53]. This is indicated by what Sayf ibn Maymun narrated from al-Husayn: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Musa, peace be upon him, said: 'O Lord, how was Adam able to render thanks for what You bestowed upon him of Your blessings? You created him with Your hand, made Your angels prostrate to him, and settled him in Your Paradise.' So Allah revealed to him: 'Adam knew that all of that is from Me and from My side, and that is his gratitude.'" [85] [Rawdat al-Wa'izin (al-Fattal al-Nisaburi): p. 473; al-Shukr li-llah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya: p. 70.]

And from Ishaq ibn Najih al-Malati, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "My God, how can I thank You when I cannot reach Your thanks except by Your blessing?" Allah, Exalted, revealed to him: "Do you not know that the blessings you have are from Me?" He said: "Yes, my Lord." He said: "Then be content with that as your gratitude."

Wahb said: Likewise Musa said: "O Lord, You have bestowed upon me abundant blessings and commanded me to thank You for them, and my thanks for every blessing from You upon me is itself a further blessing." Allah said: "O Musa, you have learned the knowledge that no knowledge escapes. It is enough from My servant that he knows that whatever blessing he has is from Me and from My side."

Al-Junayd said: The reality of gratitude is the inability to give thanks.

It is narrated of Dawud, peace be upon him, that he said: "Glory be to Him who made the servant's acknowledgment of his inability to thank Him a form of thanks, just as He made his acknowledgment of his inability to know Him a form of knowing."

Some of them said: Gratitude is that one does not see the blessing at all, but sees the Benefactor.

Abu 'Uthman al-Khayri: The truth of gratitude is that you do not praise with your tongue anyone other than the Benefactor.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, from Abu Bakr al-Razi, from al-Shibli: Gratitude is humility under the vision of the favour.

It was said: Gratitude consists of five things: keeping away from evil deeds, guarding good deeds, opposing desires, offering acts of obedience, and watching over the Lord of the heavens.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi say: Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Qannad was asked in the mosque, in the presence of Abu Bakr ibn 'Adus, while I was present: "Who are the most grateful of the grateful?" He said: "The one who is pure from sins, who counts himself among the sinners; the one who strives in supererogatory acts beyond the obligatory ones, and counts himself among the negligent; and the one who is content with little of this world, and counts himself among the destitute. These are the most grateful of the grateful."

Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Dhu al-Nur: Gratitude to one above you is through obedience, to your equal through reciprocation, and to one below you through kindness and bounty.

﴿And when We gave Musa the Book and the Criterion﴾. Mujahid and al-Farra' said: they are one thing, and the Arabs repeat a thing when its wording differs, out of a suspicion of difference. Al-Farra' recited:

"I offered the hide to his two forearms,
and he found her words false and deceitful."

Antara said:

"I greeted a campsite whose traces had become old,
it was effaced and emptied after Umm al-Haytham."

Al-Zajjaj said: This is the correct view, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the Criterion for Musa in another place, saying: ﴿And We gave Musa and Harun the Criterion﴾ [21:48].

Al-Kisa'i said: "al-Furqan" is an epithet for "al-Kitab," meaning: ﴿And when We gave Musa the Book and the Criterion﴾, which distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful, between disbelief and faith, and between promise and threat. The waw was added to it as it is added to epithets, as in the saying: "So-and-so is good and tall." He recited:

"To the king, the resolute and the son of the leader,
and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."

The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿Then We gave Musa the Book, completed upon the one who did good, and a detailed explanation of everything﴾ [6:154].

Qutrub said: He meant by it the Criterion, and there is an implicit element in the verse, its meaning being: ﴿And when We gave Musa the Book and Muhammad the Criterion﴾.

﴿So that you might be guided﴾ by these two books. So one of the two names was dropped, as in the poet's saying:

"You see him as if Allah were slitting his nose,
and his eyes, if his master spends the night with him, are narrowed."

Ibn 'Abbas said: By the Criterion he meant victory over the enemies, the victory that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave Musa, and the destruction of Pharaoh and his people. This is indicated by His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We sent not down upon Our servant on the day of the Criterion, the day the two hosts met﴾ [8:41], which is the day of Badr.

Yaman ibn Rabab said: "al-Furqan" means the splitting of the sea, which is among the great signs, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We parted the sea for you and saved you﴾.

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by your taking of the calf [as a god]. So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

Ibn Rabab's remark continues: "Wronged yourselves" means you harmed yourselves by taking the calf as a god. They said: "What shall we do, and what is the remedy?" He said: "So turn in repentance, return" ﴿to your Creator﴾, meaning your Originator. Abu 'Amr would reduce the hamza, dropping the vowel to a jussive-like sukun, in His saying ﴿bari'kum﴾ and ﴿yamurukum﴾ and ﴿yansurkum﴾, seeking lightness. [That is, by eliding the vowel; it is also reported from him as sukun, while the others recited without elision.] Like the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

*So today I drink, not bearing sin from God, nor as one who drinks uninvited.* [Lisan al-'Arab: 10/426.]

And he recited:

*When they go crooked, I say "companion, straighten them," across the desert like swimming ships.* [Sharh Shafiyat Ibn al-Hajib: 4/225, and Lisan al-'Arab: 12/432.]

He said: ﴿So kill yourselves﴾, so that the innocent would kill the guilty. ﴿That killing is best for you in the sight of your Creator.﴾ Ibn Jarir said: God, Mighty and Majestic, refused to accept the repentance of the Children of Israel except in the state they disliked, that they fight one another when they worshipped the calf.

Qatadah said: the punishment of the calf-worshippers was killing, because they had apostatized, and disbelief makes blood lawful.

Qatadah recited: ﴿fa-aqīlū anfusakum﴾, from iqalah (seeking revocation), meaning seek to have your stumble removed through repentance. When Moses intended the killing, they said: "We submit to the command of God, Exalted is He," so they sat in the courtyards hidden, and the people unsheathed daggers against them. A man would see his son, his father, his paternal uncle, his people, his friend and his neighbor, yet they could not proceed in obedience to God's command. They said: "O Moses, how shall we act?" So God sent a mist and a black cloud, so that no one could see another. It was said to them: whoever loosens his turban, or lifts his gaze to his killer, or shields himself with a hand or foot, is struck, and his repentance is rejected. So they kept killing one another until evening. When the killing increased among them, Aaron and Moses called out, wept, grieved, humbled themselves, and said: "O Lord, the Children of Israel are being destroyed, the remnant, the remnant!" Then God, Mighty and Majestic, lifted the cloud and commanded them to lay down their weapons and cease killing.

The dead were uncovered, thousands of them, and this weighed heavily on Moses. God revealed to him: "Would it not satisfy you that I admit both the killer and the killed into Paradise? Whoever among them was killed is a martyr, and whoever remains, I will expiate his sins." This is His saying ﴿Then He accepted your repentance﴾, meaning: since you did as He commanded, He accepted your repentance and pardoned you.

﴿Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾
