And when Moses prayed for water for his people, [the sīn in "istasqā" is the sīn of request (sīn al-mas'alah), like in "istaʿlama" and "istakhbara," meaning he asked for water for his people. This was because they became thirsty in the wilderness (al-tīh), and they said: "O Moses, where are we to get drink?" So Moses asked for water for them, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him:] So We said, "Strike the rock with your staff," and it was of the wood of Paradise (āS al-jannah), ten cubits long, the length of Moses, with two branches that shone with light in the darkness, and its name was Ghalīq. Ādam, peace be upon him, had brought it with him from Paradise to earth, and the younger ones inherited it from the elders until it reached Shuʿayb, who gave it to Moses.

[The rock:] They differed about it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Moses (ﷺ) would strike for them the nearest rock from among the rocks, and from it a spring gushed forth for each of the twelve tribes, and a stream flowed from each spring to the tribe that was appointed to drink from it. Then they said: "If Moses loses his staff…" So Allah, Exalted, revealed to Moses: "Do not strike the rocks, but speak to them, and they will obey you, so that perhaps they will take heed."

They said: "What will we do if we reach sand and a land with no rocks?" So Moses carried a rock with him, and wherever they alighted, he set it down.

Others said: it was a specific rock, known by a particular identity, and the evidence for this is the words of Allah, Exalted: "the rock" (al-ḥajar), where the alif and lām make it definite, like your saying "I saw the man" (ra'aytu al-rajul). Then they differed about what kind of rock it was.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was a light, square rock, like a man's head, which he was commanded to carry; he would place it in his saddlebag, and when they needed water, he would set it down and strike it with his staff.

In some books it is said that it was marble.

Abū Rawq said: the rock was of kadān (soft stone), and in it were twelve holes, from each hole a spring of sweet, pure water would gush forth, and they would take it. When they were finished and Moses wished to carry it, he struck it with his staff and the water would vanish. He used to ask for water six hundred thousand times each day.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: it is the rock upon which Moses placed his garment when he wanted to bathe, when they accused him of having a swelling in his testicles (al-udrah) [al-udrah: swelling of the two testicles]. The rock fled with his garment and passed by an assembly of the Children of Israel, until it became evident that he was not afflicted with that. When the rock stopped, Jibrīl came to Moses and said: "Allah says: lift this rock, for in it there is power, and in it you have a miracle." Allah, Exalted, mentioned this in His words: "O you who believe, do not be like those who harmed Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah" [Sūrat al-Aḥzāb: 69]. So Moses lifted it and placed it in his saddlebag, and whenever he needed water he struck it with the staff.

This is what was narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Children of Israel used to bathe naked, each looking at the private parts of the others, and Moses used to bathe alone. They said: 'By Allah, nothing prevents Moses from bathing with us except that he has a swelling.' He said: Once he went to bathe, and Moses placed his garment upon a rock, and the rock fled with his garment. He said: So Moses pursued it, saying, 'My garment, O rock! My garment, O rock!' until the Children of Israel saw the private parts of Moses, and they said, 'By Allah, there is no defect in Moses.' He said: The rock stopped after they had looked at it, and he took his garment, and he began striking the rock." [88] [Musnad Aḥmad: 2/315.]

Abū Hurayrah said: "We have seen in the rock six or seven marks made by Moses' strikes."

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā al-Kinānī said: Moses' strikes were twelve, and upon the place of each strike appeared something like a woman's breast; then it burst forth into flowing rivers, and this is His words: "so it gushed forth" (fa-nfajarat).

In the verse there is an implicit omission and abbreviation; its estimated sense is: "Strike, and it gushed forth," i.e., flowed. The root of infijār is: splitting and spreading, and from it comes "the dawn broke" (fajr al-nahār).

"From it twelve springs" (mink ithnatā ʿashrata ʿaynan): the common readers read the shīn with sukūn (ithnatā ʿashrata), for lightening; al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl al-Anṣārī read it with fatḥah (ʿashrata) according to the original form; and Abū [.....] [a word unreadable in the manuscript] read it with kasrah.

"Each people knew their drinking place" (qad ʿalima kullu unāsin mashrabahum): the place of their drinking; it may also be used as a verbal noun, like "al-mudkhal" and "al-mukhraj."

"Eat and drink" (kulū wa-ishrabū): that is, We said to them: eat of the manna and drink of the water, for all this is from the provision of Allah, which comes without hardship, cost, or consequence.

"And do not commit abuse in the land, causing corruption" (wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍi mufsidīn): it is said: ʿathā yaʿthī ʿathyan, and ʿathā yaʿthū ʿathwan, and ʿāha yaʿīthu ʿaythan and ʿuyūthan (in three dialects), and it means severe corruption.

Ibn al-Raqqāʿ said:
"Were it not for shame, and that my head has been whitened by grey hair (ʿathā)…
I would have visited Umm al-Qāsim."

"And when you said, 'O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food'…" The verse was revealed because they became bored of the manna and quail and grew weary of them. Al-Ḥasan said: they were people of onions, garlic, and lentils, and their dispositions returned to their old habits, and they longed for what their customs had accustomed them to, so they said: "We will not endure one kind of food," and they abandoned the manna and quail. They said "one" (wāḥid) though they were two, because the Arabs express the dual with the singular, and the singular with the dual, as in His words: "from both of them come forth pearls and coral" [Sūrat al-Raḥmān: 22], though they come forth only from the salt water, not the sweet.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: they used to knead the manna and quail together so that it became one dish, and they would eat it.

"So call upon your Lord" (fa-ud/ʿu rabbaka): ask; "for us" (lanā): for our sake. "Let Him bring forth for us of what the earth grows of its herbs (baqlihā) and its cucumbers (qiththāʾihā)": the common reading is with a kasrah on the qāf. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif, and al-Ashyab al-ʿUqaylī read wa-quththāʾihā with a ḍammah on the qāf, which is the dialect of Tamīm.

"And its garlic (fūmihā)": Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-fūm is bread; the Arabs say: "fawwimū lanā," i.e., bake bread for us. ʿAṭāʾ and Abū Mālik said: it is wheat, and this is an ancient dialect. The poet said:
"I used to think myself like the richest of men
who settled in Medina without cultivating wheat (fawm)."

[ ... ] [a word unreadable in the manuscript]: it is all kinds of grain.

Al-Kalbī, al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Muʿarraj said: it is garlic, and al-Muʿarraj recited for Ḥassān:
"And you are a people of base origins;
your food is garlic (fūm) and onion (ḥawqal)."

He means garlic and onion, for the Arabs interchange fāʾ and thāʾ, saying for gum-tree sap ʿurfuṭ: maghāthīr and maghāfīr, and for grave: jadf and jadth. The proof of this interpretation is that in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh it reads "wa-thawmihā" (and its garlic).

"And its lentils and its onions" (wa-ʿadasihā wa-baṣalihā).

It is narrated on the authority of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, from his father ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhumā), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Upon you is lentils, for it is blessed and sanctified, and it softens the heart and increases tears, and seventy prophets have blessed it, the last of them being ʿĪsā (peace be upon him)." [89]

Then Moses said to them at that time: "Will you exchange…" (a-tastabdilūna); in the codex of Ubayy it is "a-tubdilūna."

"That which is lower" (alladhī huwa adnā): more base and worse.

Al-Farrāʾ related from Zuhayr al-ʿUrqī that he read "adnāʾ" with a hamzah; the common readers omit the hamzah. Some grammarians said: it is adwan; the nūn was moved forward and the wāw changed to yāʾ, as in their saying "awlā" from "al-waylu."

"For that which is better" (bi-alladhī huwa khayr): more noble and superior. Its meaning: will you leave what is better and desire what is worse? It is also permissible that this good and bad refer to the kinds and types of food, and it is also permissible that they refer to Allah's choice for them and their choice for themselves.

"Go down to a city" (ihbiṭū miṣran): meaning, if you refuse other than this, then go down to a city of the cities; had he intended a specific Egypt, he would have said "Miṣr" without tanwīn, as in His words: "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills" [Sūrat Yūsuf: 99]. This is the meaning of Qatādah's statement.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is the Egypt of Moses and Pharaoh.

Al-Aʿmash said: it is the Egypt of which Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī was governor. The evidence for this view is the recitation of al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥah: "Miṣr" without tanwīn, making it definite, and likewise it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy without alif. It is only declined in this view because of its lightness and few letters, like Duʿd, Hind, and Ḥamal and the like. The poet said:
"And the maker of the sun a Miṣr, no doubt about it,
between the day and the night, separated."

"For you shall have what you asked" (fa-inna lakum mā saʾaltum): of the plants of the earth.

"And they were struck" (wa-ḍuribat): were made. "Upon them" (ʿalayhim): and they were obliged. "Abasement" (al-dhillah): humiliation and disgrace. They said: [it is] the jizyah, the evidence for which is His words: "until they give the jizyah with willing submission, and they are humbled" [Sūrat al-Tawbah: 29]. [.....] [a word unreadable in the manuscript] said: it is the kustībanj, the belt of Jewish identity.

"And wretchedness" (al-maskanah): meaning, the possessor of poverty; they appear as if they were poor though they were wealthy. It was also said: humiliation and poverty of heart, so that among the people of the faiths none is more abased or more greedy for wealth than the Jews. Maskanah is a form from "sakūn" (stillness), and from it the poor is called miskīn because of his stillness and few movements. It is said: "There is no one among the Banū Fulān more still than Fulān," i.e., more poor.

"And they returned with anger from Allah" (wa-bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin mina Allāh): i.e., they returned, according to al-Kisāʾī and others. Abū Rawq said: they deserved it, and the bāʾ is redundant. Abū ʿUbaydah said: they bore it and acknowledged it; from it is the transmitted supplication: "I acknowledge Your blessing upon me and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." The anger of Allah upon them is His condemnation of them and His threat to them in this world, and the sending of punishment upon them in the hereafter; likewise His hatred and wrath.

"That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah" (dhālika bi-annahum kānū yakfurūna bi-āyāti Allāh): with respect to the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that he is the Merciful in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Furqān.

"And they used to kill" (wa-yaqtulūna): the common reading is with lightening, from qatl; al-Sulamī read it with doubling, from taqtīl.

"The prophets" (al-nabiyyīn): the well-known reading is with doubling (tashdīd) without hamzah (al-nabiyyīn), from "non-hamzated," and Nāfiʿ alone read it with hamzah (al-nabiʾīn). Whoever reads it with hamzah means "the one who informs," from the Arab saying: "anba'a al-nabī inbāʾan," and "nabbaʾa yunabbiʾu tanbiʾatan" have the same meaning; Allah, Exalted, said: "When he informed her of it, she said: 'Who informed you of this?'" [Sūrat al-Taḥrīm: 3]. Whoever omits the hamzah has two possibilities: first, he intended the hamzah and dropped it for lightness, because of its frequent use; the second, that it means "elevated," derived from "nubuwwah," which is an elevated place; it is said: "nubiʾa al-shayʾu ʿan al-makān," i.e., it rose above the place.

The poet said:
"Indeed my side is raised from the bed,
like the rising of the couch above the hills."

There is another possibility: al-Kisāʾī said: "nabī" without hamzah means "the road," and the messenger was called a prophet because he is a road to guidance; and from this is the poet's saying:
"I would have become a pebble-strewn path
in place of the prophet, from the Kāthib (a hill)."

The meaning of the verse: "and they kill the prophets" (wa-yaqtulūna al-nabiyyīn).

"Without right" (bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq): like Isaiah, Zechariah, John, and the rest of the prophets whom the Jews killed.

In a report: the Jews killed seventy [in the source: forty-three] prophets in one hour early in the day; then a hundred men and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up, commanded those who killed them with what is right, and forbade them from what is wrong, and they were all killed by the end of that day.

"That is because they disobeyed and transgressed" (dhālika bi-mā ʿaṣaw wa-kānū yaʿtadūn): they transgress My command and commit My prohibitions.

"Indeed those who believed, and those who were Jews" (inna alladhīna āmanū wa-alladhīna hādū): meaning the Jews. Scholars differed about the reason for their being named so. Some said: they were called that because they "hādū," i.e., repented from worshipping the calf, as in His words, reporting about them: "Indeed we have turned back to You" [Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: 156].

Abū ʿUbaydah recited:
"Indeed I am a man who, in praising him, is a hāʾid,"
i.e., a repentant one.

Others said: because they "hādū," i.e., deviated from Islam and from the religion of Moses. It is said: "hāda yahūdu hūdan" when he deviated. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
"Salmā and her neighbors know
that I am among people, inclined toward her, a hāʾid,"
i.e., leaning toward her.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: because they "yatahawwadūn," i.e., they moved when reciting the Torah, and they say: "the heavens and the earth moved when Allah brought Moses the Torah."

Abū al-Simmāk al-ʿAdawī, whose name was Qaʿnab, read "hādaw" with fatḥah on the dāl, from "al-mahādāh," meaning some of them inclined to others in their religion.

"And the Christians" (wa-al-naṣārā): they differed about the reason for this name. al-Zuhrī said: they were called Naṣārā because the disciples said: "We are the helpers of Allah" (naḥnu anṣār Allāh).

Muqātil said: because they followed a village called Nāṣirah, and they were ascribed to it.

Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad said: al-Naṣārā is the plural of Naṣrān, as in saying nadmān and nadāmā.

He recited:
"You see him, when the evening falls, bent over,
and in the morning he is to his Lord a Naṣrān, sunbathing."

The relative yāʾ was attached to it, as they say to one with a beard "liḥyānī," and to one with a neck "raqqābī."

Al-Zajjāj said: it is permissible that it be the plural of Naṣrī, as they say "baʿīr ḥabarī" and "ibil ḥabārā"; they were called Naṣārā for their affiliation with Naṣrah, which is a village where ʿĪsā and his mother used to live.

"And the Sabians" (wa-al-ṣābiʾīn): the people of Medina read without hamzah, al-ṣābīn and al-ṣābūn throughout the Qur'an; the rest read with hamzah, which is the original form. It is said: "ṣabā yaṣbū ṣabwan," when he inclined and went out from one religion to another.

Al-Farrāʾ said: it is said of everyone who innovates a religion: "qad ṣabaʾa and aṣbaʾa," with one meaning; its root is inclination. He recited:
"When the horses' flanks turned away from us,
I thought the chest of the camel was the rising dawn."

They differed about who the Sabians are:
ʿUmar said: they are a group of the People of the Book whose slaughtered animals are the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book; this was also said by al-Suddī.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: their slaughtered animals are not lawful, nor is marriage to their women.

Mujāhid said: they are a tribe toward Syria between the Jews and the Magians, having no religion.

al-Suddī said: they are a group of the People of the Book, and this is the opinion of Abū Ḥanīfah.

Qatādah and Muqātil said: they are a people who affirm Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and worship the angels, recite the Psalms, and pray toward the Kaʿbah; they took a little from every religion.

al-Kalbī said: they are a people between the Jews and the Christians, who shave the middles of their heads and love their remembrancers.

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā said: they passed away and became extinct, so there is neither a trace nor a remnant.

"Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day" (man āmana bi-Allāh wa-al-yawm al-ākhir): the scholars differed about the ruling and meaning of the verse, and they have two approaches to it:

The first: He meant by His words "Indeed those who believed" (inna alladhīna āmanū) true belief and the binding of faith. Then they differed about who these believers are: some said: they are those who believed in ʿĪsā and did not become Jews, nor Christians, nor Sabians, and awaited the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Others said: they are seekers of religion, among them: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, Qays ibn Sāʿidah, Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, al-Barrāʾ al-Sindī, Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, Salmān al-Fārisī, Yaḥyā the monk, and the delegation of the Negus. They believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) before his mission; some of them reached him and followed him, and some did not reach him.

It was also said: they are the believers of past nations.

It was also said: the believers of this Ummah.

"And those who were Jews" (wa-alladhīna hādū): meaning those who were upon the religion of Moses (peace be upon him) and did not alter or change it.

"And the Christians" (wa-al-naṣārā): those who were upon the religion of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) and did not alter it, and died upon that.

They said: these two names stuck to them from the time of Moses and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them both), when they were upon the truth; the name remained upon them just as Islam remained upon the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). And the Sabians, during their uprightness: whoever among them believed, i.e., died while believing, because the reality of faith is brotherhood.

He said: it is permissible that the waw in it be an implied one, i.e., "and whoever believes after you, O Muhammad, until the Day of Resurrection."

The second approach: that those mentioned in the beginning of the verse as believers are so only in a figurative sense and by naming, not in ruling and reality. Then they differed about it:

Some of them said: those who believed in the earlier prophets and the former scriptures, and did not believe in you or in your book.

Others said: it refers to the hypocrites. The meaning is: "Indeed, those who believe" with their tongues but have not believed in their hearts. A parallel to this verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾.

"And those who were Jews" (alladhina hadu): i.e., those who held Judaism, the religion that was altered after Musa (peace be upon him). "And the Christians" (al-nasara): those who held Christianity, the religion altered after Isa (peace be upon him). "And the Sabians" (al-sabi'in): meaning the categories of disbelievers. "Whoever believes in Allah" is among the categories mentioned in the verse.

There is an ellipsis and an implied element in it, its estimated form being: "whoever among them believes in Allah and the Last Day," because the word (man, "whoever") is suitable for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine and the feminine.

Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [[Surat al-An'am: 25.]] ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ [[Surat Yunus: 43.]] ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [[Surat Yunus: 42.]]. He says: ﴿And whoever of you devotes herself to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [[Surat al-Ahzab: 31.]], and al-Farazdaq said, in the comparison:

"Come, for if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, you will be like the one whom I called, the two who keep company."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 13/419.]]

﴿And no fear shall come upon them concerning what they have put forward,﴾

﴿nor shall they grieve over what they have left behind.﴾ It was also said: "no fear shall come upon them" means of abiding in the Fire, and "nor shall they grieve" means at being cut off from the Almighty King. Also, "no fear shall come upon them" from the major sins, and I forgive them; "nor shall they grieve" over the minor sins, for I expiate them.

It was also said: "no fear shall come upon them" concerning what they undertook of crimes, and "nor shall they grieve over what they committed of sins," because of what Islam had already erased of their sins for them.

And when Moses prayed for water for his people, [the sīn in "istasqā" is the sīn of request (sīn al-mas'alah), like in "istaʿlama" and "istakhbara," meaning he asked for water for his people. This was because they became thirsty in the wilderness (al-tīh), and they said: "O Moses, where are we to get drink?" So Moses asked for water for them, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him:] So We said, "Strike the rock with your staff," and it was of the wood of Paradise (āS al-jannah), ten cubits long, the length of Moses, with two branches that shone with light in the darkness, and its name was Ghalīq. Ādam, peace be upon him, had brought it with him from Paradise to earth, and the younger ones inherited it from the elders until it reached Shuʿayb, who gave it to Moses.

[The rock:] They differed about it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Moses (ﷺ) would strike for them the nearest rock from among the rocks, and from it a spring gushed forth for each of the twelve tribes, and a stream flowed from each spring to the tribe that was appointed to drink from it. Then they said: "If Moses loses his staff…" So Allah, Exalted, revealed to Moses: "Do not strike the rocks, but speak to them, and they will obey you, so that perhaps they will take heed."

They said: "What will we do if we reach sand and a land with no rocks?" So Moses carried a rock with him, and wherever they alighted, he set it down.

Others said: it was a specific rock, known by a particular identity, and the evidence for this is the words of Allah, Exalted: "the rock" (al-ḥajar), where the alif and lām make it definite, like your saying "I saw the man" (ra'aytu al-rajul). Then they differed about what kind of rock it was.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was a light, square rock, like a man's head, which he was commanded to carry; he would place it in his saddlebag, and when they needed water, he would set it down and strike it with his staff.

In some books it is said that it was marble.

Abū Rawq said: the rock was of kadān (soft stone), and in it were twelve holes, from each hole a spring of sweet, pure water would gush forth, and they would take it. When they were finished and Moses wished to carry it, he struck it with his staff and the water would vanish. He used to ask for water six hundred thousand times each day.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: it is the rock upon which Moses placed his garment when he wanted to bathe, when they accused him of having a swelling in his testicles (al-udrah) [al-udrah: swelling of the two testicles]. The rock fled with his garment and passed by an assembly of the Children of Israel, until it became evident that he was not afflicted with that. When the rock stopped, Jibrīl came to Moses and said: "Allah says: lift this rock, for in it there is power, and in it you have a miracle." Allah, Exalted, mentioned this in His words: "O you who believe, do not be like those who harmed Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah" [Sūrat al-Aḥzāb: 69]. So Moses lifted it and placed it in his saddlebag, and whenever he needed water he struck it with the staff.

This is what was narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Children of Israel used to bathe naked, each looking at the private parts of the others, and Moses used to bathe alone. They said: 'By Allah, nothing prevents Moses from bathing with us except that he has a swelling.' He said: Once he went to bathe, and Moses placed his garment upon a rock, and the rock fled with his garment. He said: So Moses pursued it, saying, 'My garment, O rock! My garment, O rock!' until the Children of Israel saw the private parts of Moses, and they said, 'By Allah, there is no defect in Moses.' He said: The rock stopped after they had looked at it, and he took his garment, and he began striking the rock." [88] [Musnad Aḥmad: 2/315.]

Abū Hurayrah said: "We have seen in the rock six or seven marks made by Moses' strikes."

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā al-Kinānī said: Moses' strikes were twelve, and upon the place of each strike appeared something like a woman's breast; then it burst forth into flowing rivers, and this is His words: "so it gushed forth" (fa-nfajarat).

In the verse there is an implicit omission and abbreviation; its estimated sense is: "Strike, and it gushed forth," i.e., flowed. The root of infijār is: splitting and spreading, and from it comes "the dawn broke" (fajr al-nahār).

"From it twelve springs" (mink ithnatā ʿashrata ʿaynan): the common readers read the shīn with sukūn (ithnatā ʿashrata), for lightening; al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl al-Anṣārī read it with fatḥah (ʿashrata) according to the original form; and Abū [.....] [a word unreadable in the manuscript] read it with kasrah.

"Each people knew their drinking place" (qad ʿalima kullu unāsin mashrabahum): the place of their drinking; it may also be used as a verbal noun, like "al-mudkhal" and "al-mukhraj."

"Eat and drink" (kulū wa-ishrabū): that is, We said to them: eat of the manna and drink of the water, for all this is from the provision of Allah, which comes without hardship, cost, or consequence.

"And do not commit abuse in the land, causing corruption" (wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍi mufsidīn): it is said: ʿathā yaʿthī ʿathyan, and ʿathā yaʿthū ʿathwan, and ʿāha yaʿīthu ʿaythan and ʿuyūthan (in three dialects), and it means severe corruption.

Ibn al-Raqqāʿ said:
"Were it not for shame, and that my head has been whitened by grey hair (ʿathā)…
I would have visited Umm al-Qāsim."

"And when you said, 'O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food'…" The verse was revealed because they became bored of the manna and quail and grew weary of them. Al-Ḥasan said: they were people of onions, garlic, and lentils, and their dispositions returned to their old habits, and they longed for what their customs had accustomed them to, so they said: "We will not endure one kind of food," and they abandoned the manna and quail. They said "one" (wāḥid) though they were two, because the Arabs express the dual with the singular, and the singular with the dual, as in His words: "from both of them come forth pearls and coral" [Sūrat al-Raḥmān: 22], though they come forth only from the salt water, not the sweet.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: they used to knead the manna and quail together so that it became one dish, and they would eat it.

"So call upon your Lord" (fa-ud/ʿu rabbaka): ask; "for us" (lanā): for our sake. "Let Him bring forth for us of what the earth grows of its herbs (baqlihā) and its cucumbers (qiththāʾihā)": the common reading is with a kasrah on the qāf. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif, and al-Ashyab al-ʿUqaylī read wa-quththāʾihā with a ḍammah on the qāf, which is the dialect of Tamīm.

"And its garlic (fūmihā)": Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-fūm is bread; the Arabs say: "fawwimū lanā," i.e., bake bread for us. ʿAṭāʾ and Abū Mālik said: it is wheat, and this is an ancient dialect. The poet said:
"I used to think myself like the richest of men
who settled in Medina without cultivating wheat (fawm)."

[ ... ] [a word unreadable in the manuscript]: it is all kinds of grain.

Al-Kalbī, al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Muʿarraj said: it is garlic, and al-Muʿarraj recited for Ḥassān:
"And you are a people of base origins;
your food is garlic (fūm) and onion (ḥawqal)."

He means garlic and onion, for the Arabs interchange fāʾ and thāʾ, saying for gum-tree sap ʿurfuṭ: maghāthīr and maghāfīr, and for grave: jadf and jadth. The proof of this interpretation is that in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh it reads "wa-thawmihā" (and its garlic).

"And its lentils and its onions" (wa-ʿadasihā wa-baṣalihā).

It is narrated on the authority of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, from his father ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhumā), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Upon you is lentils, for it is blessed and sanctified, and it softens the heart and increases tears, and seventy prophets have blessed it, the last of them being ʿĪsā (peace be upon him)." [89]

Then Moses said to them at that time: "Will you exchange…" (a-tastabdilūna); in the codex of Ubayy it is "a-tubdilūna."

"That which is lower" (alladhī huwa adnā): more base and worse.

Al-Farrāʾ related from Zuhayr al-ʿUrqī that he read "adnāʾ" with a hamzah; the common readers omit the hamzah. Some grammarians said: it is adwan; the nūn was moved forward and the wāw changed to yāʾ, as in their saying "awlā" from "al-waylu."

"For that which is better" (bi-alladhī huwa khayr): more noble and superior. Its meaning: will you leave what is better and desire what is worse? It is also permissible that this good and bad refer to the kinds and types of food, and it is also permissible that they refer to Allah's choice for them and their choice for themselves.

"Go down to a city" (ihbiṭū miṣran): meaning, if you refuse other than this, then go down to a city of the cities; had he intended a specific Egypt, he would have said "Miṣr" without tanwīn, as in His words: "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills" [Sūrat Yūsuf: 99]. This is the meaning of Qatādah's statement.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is the Egypt of Moses and Pharaoh.

Al-Aʿmash said: it is the Egypt of which Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī was governor. The evidence for this view is the recitation of al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥah: "Miṣr" without tanwīn, making it definite, and likewise it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy without alif. It is only declined in this view because of its lightness and few letters, like Duʿd, Hind, and Ḥamal and the like. The poet said:
"And the maker of the sun a Miṣr, no doubt about it,
between the day and the night, separated."

"For you shall have what you asked" (fa-inna lakum mā saʾaltum): of the plants of the earth.

"And they were struck" (wa-ḍuribat): were made. "Upon them" (ʿalayhim): and they were obliged. "Abasement" (al-dhillah): humiliation and disgrace. They said: [it is] the jizyah, the evidence for which is His words: "until they give the jizyah with willing submission, and they are humbled" [Sūrat al-Tawbah: 29]. [.....] [a word unreadable in the manuscript] said: it is the kustībanj, the belt of Jewish identity.

"And wretchedness" (al-maskanah): meaning, the possessor of poverty; they appear as if they were poor though they were wealthy. It was also said: humiliation and poverty of heart, so that among the people of the faiths none is more abased or more greedy for wealth than the Jews. Maskanah is a form from "sakūn" (stillness), and from it the poor is called miskīn because of his stillness and few movements. It is said: "There is no one among the Banū Fulān more still than Fulān," i.e., more poor.

"And they returned with anger from Allah" (wa-bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin mina Allāh): i.e., they returned, according to al-Kisāʾī and others. Abū Rawq said: they deserved it, and the bāʾ is redundant. Abū ʿUbaydah said: they bore it and acknowledged it; from it is the transmitted supplication: "I acknowledge Your blessing upon me and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." The anger of Allah upon them is His condemnation of them and His threat to them in this world, and the sending of punishment upon them in the hereafter; likewise His hatred and wrath.

"That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah" (dhālika bi-annahum kānū yakfurūna bi-āyāti Allāh): with respect to the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that he is the Merciful in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Furqān.

"And they used to kill" (wa-yaqtulūna): the common reading is with lightening, from qatl; al-Sulamī read it with doubling, from taqtīl.

"The prophets" (al-nabiyyīn): the well-known reading is with doubling (tashdīd) without hamzah (al-nabiyyīn), from "non-hamzated," and Nāfiʿ alone read it with hamzah (al-nabiʾīn). Whoever reads it with hamzah means "the one who informs," from the Arab saying: "anba'a al-nabī inbāʾan," and "nabbaʾa yunabbiʾu tanbiʾatan" have the same meaning; Allah, Exalted, said: "When he informed her of it, she said: 'Who informed you of this?'" [Sūrat al-Taḥrīm: 3]. Whoever omits the hamzah has two possibilities: first, he intended the hamzah and dropped it for lightness, because of its frequent use; the second, that it means "elevated," derived from "nubuwwah," which is an elevated place; it is said: "nubiʾa al-shayʾu ʿan al-makān," i.e., it rose above the place.

The poet said:
"Indeed my side is raised from the bed,
like the rising of the couch above the hills."

There is another possibility: al-Kisāʾī said: "nabī" without hamzah means "the road," and the messenger was called a prophet because he is a road to guidance; and from this is the poet's saying:
"I would have become a pebble-strewn path
in place of the prophet, from the Kāthib (a hill)."

The meaning of the verse: "and they kill the prophets" (wa-yaqtulūna al-nabiyyīn).

"Without right" (bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq): like Isaiah, Zechariah, John, and the rest of the prophets whom the Jews killed.

In a report: the Jews killed seventy [in the source: forty-three] prophets in one hour early in the day; then a hundred men and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up, commanded those who killed them with what is right, and forbade them from what is wrong, and they were all killed by the end of that day.

"That is because they disobeyed and transgressed" (dhālika bi-mā ʿaṣaw wa-kānū yaʿtadūn): they transgress My command and commit My prohibitions.

"Indeed those who believed, and those who were Jews" (inna alladhīna āmanū wa-alladhīna hādū): meaning the Jews. Scholars differed about the reason for their being named so. Some said: they were called that because they "hādū," i.e., repented from worshipping the calf, as in His words, reporting about them: "Indeed we have turned back to You" [Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: 156].

Abū ʿUbaydah recited:
"Indeed I am a man who, in praising him, is a hāʾid,"
i.e., a repentant one.

Others said: because they "hādū," i.e., deviated from Islam and from the religion of Moses. It is said: "hāda yahūdu hūdan" when he deviated. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
"Salmā and her neighbors know
that I am among people, inclined toward her, a hāʾid,"
i.e., leaning toward her.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: because they "yatahawwadūn," i.e., they moved when reciting the Torah, and they say: "the heavens and the earth moved when Allah brought Moses the Torah."

Abū al-Simmāk al-ʿAdawī, whose name was Qaʿnab, read "hādaw" with fatḥah on the dāl, from "al-mahādāh," meaning some of them inclined to others in their religion.

"And the Christians" (wa-al-naṣārā): they differed about the reason for this name. al-Zuhrī said: they were called Naṣārā because the disciples said: "We are the helpers of Allah" (naḥnu anṣār Allāh).

Muqātil said: because they followed a village called Nāṣirah, and they were ascribed to it.

Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad said: al-Naṣārā is the plural of Naṣrān, as in saying nadmān and nadāmā.

He recited:
"You see him, when the evening falls, bent over,
and in the morning he is to his Lord a Naṣrān, sunbathing."

The relative yāʾ was attached to it, as they say to one with a beard "liḥyānī," and to one with a neck "raqqābī."

Al-Zajjāj said: it is permissible that it be the plural of Naṣrī, as they say "baʿīr ḥabarī" and "ibil ḥabārā"; they were called Naṣārā for their affiliation with Naṣrah, which is a village where ʿĪsā and his mother used to live.

"And the Sabians" (wa-al-ṣābiʾīn): the people of Medina read without hamzah, al-ṣābīn and al-ṣābūn throughout the Qur'an; the rest read with hamzah, which is the original form. It is said: "ṣabā yaṣbū ṣabwan," when he inclined and went out from one religion to another.

Al-Farrāʾ said: it is said of everyone who innovates a religion: "qad ṣabaʾa and aṣbaʾa," with one meaning; its root is inclination. He recited:
"When the horses' flanks turned away from us,
I thought the chest of the camel was the rising dawn."

They differed about who the Sabians are:
ʿUmar said: they are a group of the People of the Book whose slaughtered animals are the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book; this was also said by al-Suddī.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: their slaughtered animals are not lawful, nor is marriage to their women.

Mujāhid said: they are a tribe toward Syria between the Jews and the Magians, having no religion.

al-Suddī said: they are a group of the People of the Book, and this is the opinion of Abū Ḥanīfah.

Qatādah and Muqātil said: they are a people who affirm Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and worship the angels, recite the Psalms, and pray toward the Kaʿbah; they took a little from every religion.

al-Kalbī said: they are a people between the Jews and the Christians, who shave the middles of their heads and love their remembrancers.

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā said: they passed away and became extinct, so there is neither a trace nor a remnant.

"Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day" (man āmana bi-Allāh wa-al-yawm al-ākhir): the scholars differed about the ruling and meaning of the verse, and they have two approaches to it:

The first: He meant by His words "Indeed those who believed" (inna alladhīna āmanū) true belief and the binding of faith. Then they differed about who these believers are: some said: they are those who believed in ʿĪsā and did not become Jews, nor Christians, nor Sabians, and awaited the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Others said: they are seekers of religion, among them: Ḥabīb al-Najjār, Qays ibn Sāʿidah, Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, al-Barrāʾ al-Sindī, Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, Salmān al-Fārisī, Yaḥyā the monk, and the delegation of the Negus. They believed in the Prophet (ﷺ) before his mission; some of them reached him and followed him, and some did not reach him.

It was also said: they are the believers of past nations.

It was also said: the believers of this Ummah.

"And those who were Jews" (wa-alladhīna hādū): meaning those who were upon the religion of Moses (peace be upon him) and did not alter or change it.

"And the Christians" (wa-al-naṣārā): those who were upon the religion of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) and did not alter it, and died upon that.

They said: these two names stuck to them from the time of Moses and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them both), when they were upon the truth; the name remained upon them just as Islam remained upon the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). And the Sabians, during their uprightness: whoever among them believed, i.e., died while believing, because the reality of faith is brotherhood.

He said: it is permissible that the waw in it be an implied one, i.e., "and whoever believes after you, O Muhammad, until the Day of Resurrection."

The second approach: that those mentioned in the beginning of the verse as believers are so only in a figurative sense and by naming, not in ruling and reality. Then they differed about it:

Some of them said: those who believed in the earlier prophets and the former scriptures, and did not believe in you or in your book.

Others said: it refers to the hypocrites. The meaning is: "Indeed, those who believe" with their tongues but have not believed in their hearts. A parallel to this verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾.

"And those who were Jews" (alladhina hadu): i.e., those who held Judaism, the religion that was altered after Musa (peace be upon him). "And the Christians" (al-nasara): those who held Christianity, the religion altered after Isa (peace be upon him). "And the Sabians" (al-sabi'in): meaning the categories of disbelievers. "Whoever believes in Allah" is among the categories mentioned in the verse.

There is an ellipsis and an implied element in it, its estimated form being: "whoever among them believes in Allah and the Last Day," because the word (man, "whoever") is suitable for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine and the feminine.

Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [[Surat al-An'am: 25.]] ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ [[Surat Yunus: 43.]] ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [[Surat Yunus: 42.]]. He says: ﴿And whoever of you devotes herself to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [[Surat al-Ahzab: 31.]], and al-Farazdaq said, in the comparison:

"Come, for if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, you will be like the one whom I called, the two who keep company."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 13/419.]]

﴿And no fear shall come upon them concerning what they have put forward,﴾

﴿nor shall they grieve over what they have left behind.﴾ It was also said: "no fear shall come upon them" means of abiding in the Fire, and "nor shall they grieve" means at being cut off from the Almighty King. Also, "no fear shall come upon them" from the major sins, and I forgive them; "nor shall they grieve" over the minor sins, for I expiate them.

It was also said: "no fear shall come upon them" concerning what they undertook of crimes, and "nor shall they grieve over what they committed of sins," because of what Islam had already erased of their sins for them.

And when Moses prayed for water for his people, [the sīn in "istasqā" is the sīn of request (sīn al-mas'alah), like in "istaʿlama" and "istakhbara," meaning he asked for water for his people. This was because they became thirsty in the wilderness (al-tīh), and they said: "O Moses, where are we to get drink?" So Moses asked for water for them, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to him:] So We said, "Strike the rock with your staff," and it was of the wood of Paradise (āS al-jannah), ten cubits long, the length of Moses, with two branches that shone with light in the darkness, and its name was Ghalīq. Ādam, peace be upon him, had brought it with him from Paradise to earth, and the younger ones inherited it from the elders until it reached Shuʿayb, who gave it to Moses.

[The rock:] They differed about it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Moses (ﷺ) would strike for them the nearest rock from among the rocks, and from it a spring gushed forth for each of the twelve tribes, and a stream flowed from each spring to the tribe that was appointed to drink from it. Then they said: "If Moses loses his staff…" So Allah, Exalted, revealed to Moses: "Do not strike the rocks, but speak to them, and they will obey you, so that perhaps they will take heed."

They said: "What will we do if we reach sand and a land with no rocks?" So Moses carried a rock with him, and wherever they alighted, he set it down.

Others said: it was a specific rock, known by a particular identity, and the evidence for this is the words of Allah, Exalted: "the rock" (al-ḥajar), where the alif and lām make it definite, like your saying "I saw the man" (ra'aytu al-rajul). Then they differed about what kind of rock it was.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was a light, square rock, like a man's head, which he was commanded to carry; he would place it in his saddlebag, and when they needed water, he would set it down and strike it with his staff.

In some books it is said that it was marble.

Abū Rawq said: the rock was of kadān (soft stone), and in it were twelve holes, from each hole a spring of sweet, pure water would gush forth, and they would take it. When they were finished and Moses wished to carry it, he struck it with his staff and the water would vanish. He used to ask for water six hundred thousand times each day.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: it is the rock upon which Moses placed his garment when he wanted to bathe, when they accused him of having a swelling in his testicles (al-udrah) [al-udrah: swelling of the two testicles]. The rock fled with his garment and passed by an assembly of the Children of Israel, until it became evident that he was not afflicted with that. When the rock stopped, Jibrīl came to Moses and said: "Allah says: lift this rock, for in it there is power, and in it you have a miracle." Allah, Exalted, mentioned this in His words: "O you who believe, do not be like those who harmed Moses, but Allah cleared him of what they said, and he was honored in the sight of Allah" [Sūrat al-Aḥzāb: 69]. So Moses lifted it and placed it in his saddlebag, and whenever he needed water he struck it with the staff.

This is what was narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Children of Israel used to bathe naked, each looking at the private parts of the others, and Moses used to bathe alone. They said: 'By Allah, nothing prevents Moses from bathing with us except that he has a swelling.' He said: Once he went to bathe, and Moses placed his garment upon a rock, and the rock fled with his garment. He said: So Moses pursued it, saying, 'My garment, O rock! My garment, O rock!' until the Children of Israel saw the private parts of Moses, and they said, 'By Allah, there is no defect in Moses.' He said: The rock stopped after they had looked at it, and he took his garment, and he began striking the rock." [88] [Musnad Aḥmad: 2/315.]

Abū Hurayrah said: "We have seen in the rock six or seven marks made by Moses' strikes."

ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā al-Kinānī said: Moses' strikes were twelve, and upon the place of each strike appeared something like a woman's breast; then it burst forth into flowing rivers, and this is His words: "so it gushed forth" (fa-nfajarat).

In the verse there is an implicit omission and abbreviation; its estimated sense is: "Strike, and it gushed forth," i.e., flowed. The root of infijār is: splitting and spreading, and from it comes "the dawn broke" (fajr al-nahār).

"From it twelve springs" (mink ithnatā ʿashrata ʿaynan): the common readers read the shīn with sukūn (ithnatā ʿashrata), for lightening; al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl al-Anṣārī read it with fatḥah (ʿashrata) according to the original form; and Abū [.....] [a word unreadable in the manuscript] read it with kasrah.

"Each people knew their drinking place" (qad ʿalima kullu unāsin mashrabahum): the place of their drinking; it may also be used as a verbal noun, like "al-mudkhal" and "al-mukhraj."

"Eat and drink" (kulū wa-ishrabū): that is, We said to them: eat of the manna and drink of the water, for all this is from the provision of Allah, which comes without hardship, cost, or consequence.

"And do not commit abuse in the land, causing corruption" (wa-lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍi mufsidīn): it is said: ʿathā yaʿthī ʿathyan, and ʿathā yaʿthū ʿathwan, and ʿāha yaʿīthu ʿaythan and ʿuyūthan (in three dialects), and it means severe corruption.

Ibn al-Raqqāʿ said:
"Were it not for shame, and that my head has been whitened by grey hair (ʿathā)…
I would have visited Umm al-Qāsim."

"And when you said, 'O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food'…" The verse was revealed because they became bored of the manna and quail and grew weary of them. Al-Ḥasan said: they were people of onions, garlic, and lentils, and their dispositions returned to their old habits, and they longed for what their customs had accustomed them to, so they said: "We will not endure one kind of food," and they abandoned the manna and quail. They said "one" (wāḥid) though they were two, because the Arabs express the dual with the singular, and the singular with the dual, as in His words: "from both of them come forth pearls and coral" [Sūrat al-Raḥmān: 22], though they come forth only from the salt water, not the sweet.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: they used to knead the manna and quail together so that it became one dish, and they would eat it.

"So call upon your Lord" (fa-ud/ʿu rabbaka): ask; "for us" (lanā): for our sake. "Let Him bring forth for us of what the earth grows of its herbs (baqlihā) and its cucumbers (qiththāʾihā)": the common reading is with a kasrah on the qāf. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif, and al-Ashyab al-ʿUqaylī read wa-quththāʾihā with a ḍammah on the qāf, which is the dialect of Tamīm.

"And its garlic (fūmihā)": Ibn ʿAbbās said: al-fūm is bread; the Arabs say: "fawwimū lanā," i.e., bake bread for us. ʿAṭāʾ and Abū Mālik said: it is wheat, and this is an ancient dialect. The poet said:
"I used to think myself like the richest of men
who settled in Medina without cultivating wheat (fawm)."

[ ... ] [a word unreadable in the manuscript]: it is all kinds of grain.

Al-Kalbī, al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Muʿarraj said: it is garlic, and al-Muʿarraj recited for Ḥassān:
"And you are a people of base origins;
your food is garlic (fūm) and onion (ḥawqal)."

He means garlic and onion, for the Arabs interchange fāʾ and thāʾ, saying for gum-tree sap ʿurfuṭ: maghāthīr and maghāfīr, and for grave: jadf and jadth. The proof of this interpretation is that in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh it reads "wa-thawmihā" (and its garlic).

"And its lentils and its onions" (wa-ʿadasihā wa-baṣalihā).

It is narrated on the authority of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, from his father ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhumā), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Upon you is lentils, for it is blessed and sanctified, and it softens the heart and increases tears, and seventy prophets have blessed it, the last of them being ʿĪsā (peace be upon him)." [89]

Then Moses said to them at that time: "Will you exchange…" (a-tastabdilūna); in the codex of Ubayy it is "a-tubdilūna."

"That which is lower" (alladhī huwa adnā): more base and worse.

Al-Farrāʾ related from Zuhayr al-ʿUrqī that he read "adnāʾ" with a hamzah; the common readers omit the hamzah. Some grammarians said: it is adwan; the nūn was moved forward and the wāw changed to yāʾ, as in their saying "awlā" from "al-waylu."

"For that which is better" (bi-alladhī huwa khayr): more noble and superior. Its meaning: will you leave what is better and desire what is worse? It is also permissible that this good and bad refer to the kinds and types of food, and it is also permissible that they refer to Allah's choice for them and their choice for themselves.

"Go down to a city" (ihbiṭū miṣran): meaning, if you refuse other than this, then go down to a city of the cities; had he intended a specific Egypt, he would have said "Miṣr" without tanwīn, as in His words: "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills" [Sūrat Yūsuf: 99]. This is the meaning of Qatādah's statement.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is the Egypt of Moses and Pharaoh.

Al-Aʿmash said: it is the Egypt of which Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī was governor. The evidence for this view is the recitation of al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥah: "Miṣr" without tanwīn, making it definite, and likewise it is in the codex of ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy without alif. It is only declined in this view because of its lightness and few letters, like Duʿd, Hind, and Ḥamal and the like. The poet said:
"And the maker of the sun a Miṣr, no doubt about it,
between the day and the night, separated."

"For you shall have what you asked" (fa-inna lakum mā saʾaltum): of the plants of the earth.

"And they were struck" (wa-ḍuribat): were made. "Upon them" (ʿalayhim): and they were obliged. "Abasement" (al-dhillah): humiliation and disgrace. They said: [it is] the jizyah, the evidence for which is His words: "until they give the jizyah with willing submission, and they are humbled" [Sūrat al-Tawbah: 29]. [.....] [a word unreadable in the manuscript] said: it is the kustībanj, the belt of Jewish identity.

"And wretchedness" (al-maskanah): meaning, the possessor of poverty; they appear as if they were poor though they were wealthy. It was also said: humiliation and poverty of heart, so that among the people of the faiths none is more abased or more greedy for wealth than the Jews. Maskanah is a form from "sakūn" (stillness), and from it the poor is called miskīn because of his stillness and few movements. It is said: "There is no one among the Banū Fulān more still than Fulān," i.e., more poor.

"And they returned with anger from Allah" (wa-bāʾū bi-ghaḍabin mina Allāh): i.e., they returned, according to al-Kisāʾī and others. Abū Rawq said: they deserved it, and the bāʾ is redundant. Abū ʿUbaydah said: they bore it and acknowledged it; from it is the transmitted supplication: "I acknowledge Your blessing upon me and I acknowledge my sin, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." The anger of Allah upon them is His condemnation of them and His threat to them in this world, and the sending of punishment upon them in the hereafter; likewise His hatred and wrath.

"That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah" (dhālika bi-annahum kānū yakfurūna bi-āyāti Allāh): with respect to the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that he is the Merciful in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Furqān.

"And they used to kill" (wa-yaqtulūna): the common reading is with lightening, from qatl; al-Sulamī read it with doubling, from taqtīl.

"The prophets" (al-nabiyyīn): the well-known reading is with doubling (tashdīd) without hamzah (al-nabiyyīn), from "non-hamzated," and Nāfiʿ alone read it with hamzah (al-nabiʾīn). Whoever reads it with hamzah means "the one who informs," from the Arab saying: "anba'a al-nabī inbāʾan," and "nabbaʾa yunabbiʾu tanbiʾatan" have the same meaning; Allah, Exalted, said: "When he informed her of it, she said: 'Who informed you of this?'" [Sūrat al-Taḥrīm: 3]. Whoever omits the hamzah has two possibilities: first, he intended the hamzah and dropped it for lightness, because of its frequent use; the second, that it means "elevated," derived from "nubuwwah," which is an elevated place; it is said: "nubiʾa al-shayʾu ʿan al-makān," i.e., it rose above the place.

The poet said:
"Indeed my side is raised from the bed,
like the rising of the couch above the hills."

There is another possibility: al-Kisāʾī said: "nabī" without hamzah means "the road," and the messenger was called a prophet because he is a road to guidance; and from this is the poet's saying:
"I would have become a pebble-strewn path
in place of the prophet, from the Kāthib (a hill)."

The meaning of the verse: "and they kill the prophets" (wa-yaqtulūna al-nabiyyīn).

"Without right" (bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq): like Isaiah, Zechariah, John, and the rest of the prophets whom the Jews killed.

In a report: the Jews killed seventy [in the source: forty-three] prophets in one hour early in the day; then a hundred men and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up, commanded those who killed them with what is right, and forbade them from what is wrong, and they were all killed by the end of that day.

"That is because they disobeyed and transgressed" (dhālika bi-mā ʿaṣaw wa-kānū yaʿtadūn): they transgress My command and commit My prohibitions.

"Indeed those who believed, and those who were Jews" (inna alladhīna āmanū wa-alladhīna hādū): meaning the Jews. Scholars differed about the reason for their being named so. Some said: they were called that because they "hādū," i.e., repented from worshipping the calf, as in His words, reporting about them: "Indeed we have turned back to You" [Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: 156].

Abū ʿUbaydah recited:
"Indeed I am a man who, in praising him, is a hāʾid,"
i.e., a repentant one.

Others said: because they "hādū," i.e., deviated from Islam and from the religion of Moses. It is said: "hāda yahūdu hūdan" when he deviated. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
"Salmā and her neighbors know
that I am among people, inclined toward her, a hāʾid,"
i.e., leaning toward her.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: because they "yatahawwadūn," i.e., they moved when reciting the Torah, and they say: "the heavens and the earth moved when Allah brought Moses the Torah."

Abū al-Simmāk al-ʿAdawī, whose name was Qaʿnab, read "hādaw" with fatḥah on the dāl, from "al-mahādāh," meaning some of them inclined to others in their religion.

Muqātil said: because they followed a village called Nāṣirah, and they were ascribed to it.

Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad said: al-Naṣārā is the plural of Naṣrān, as in saying nadmān and nadāmā.

He recited:
"You see him, when the evening falls, bent over,
and in the morning he is to his Lord a Naṣrān, sunbathing."

"When the horses' flanks turned away from us,
I thought the chest of the camel was the rising dawn."

Ibn ʿAbbās said: their slaughtered animals are not lawful, nor is marriage to their women.

Mujāhid said: they are a tribe toward Syria between the Jews and the Magians, having no religion.

al-Suddī said: they are a group of the People of the Book, and this is the opinion of Abū Ḥanīfah.

Qatādah and Muqātil said: they are a people who affirm Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and worship the angels, recite the Psalms, and pray toward the Kaʿbah; they took a little from every religion.

The second approach: that those mentioned in the beginning of the verse as believers are so only in a figurative sense and by naming, not in ruling and reality. Then they differed about it:

Some of them said: those who believed in the earlier prophets and the former scriptures, and did not believe in you or in your book.

Others said: it refers to the hypocrites. The meaning is: "Indeed, those who believe" with their tongues but have not believed in their hearts. A parallel to this verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾.

"And those who were Jews" (alladhina hadu): i.e., those who held Judaism, the religion that was altered after Musa (peace be upon him). "And the Christians" (al-nasara): those who held Christianity, the religion altered after Isa (peace be upon him). "And the Sabians" (al-sabi'in): meaning the categories of disbelievers. "Whoever believes in Allah" is among the categories mentioned in the verse.

There is an ellipsis and an implied element in it, its estimated form being: "whoever among them believes in Allah and the Last Day," because the word (man, "whoever") is suitable for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine and the feminine.

Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [[Surat al-An'am: 25.]] ﴿And among them are those who look at you﴾ [[Surat Yunus: 43.]] ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [[Surat Yunus: 42.]]. He says: ﴿And whoever of you devotes herself to Allah and His Messenger﴾ [[Surat al-Ahzab: 31.]], and al-Farazdaq said, in the comparison:

"Come, for if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, you will be like the one whom I called, the two who keep company."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 13/419.]]

﴿And no fear shall come upon them concerning what they have put forward,﴾

﴿nor shall they grieve over what they have left behind.﴾ It was also said: "no fear shall come upon them" means of abiding in the Fire, and "nor shall they grieve" means at being cut off from the Almighty King. Also, "no fear shall come upon them" from the major sins, and I forgive them; "nor shall they grieve" over the minor sins, for I expiate them.

It was also said: "no fear shall come upon them" concerning what they undertook of crimes, and "nor shall they grieve over what they committed of sins," because of what Islam had already erased of their sins for them.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 63–73 (part 1 of 2):

Remember when We took your covenant, O assembly of the Jews. And We raised above you the Mount (al-Tur), which in Syriac (al-Suryaniyya) is, according to some, the word for mountain. Some have said: there is no language in the world except that it is found in the Qur'an.

Abu 'Ubayda and the scholars of precision (al-hudhdhaq) said: it is not permissible that there be in the Qur'an a language other than the language of the Arabs, because God, exalted is He, says: ﴿An Arabic Qur'an﴾ and He says: ﴿in clear Arabic tongue﴾. Such words and their like are only a point of agreement between the two languages.

We have found "al-Tur" in the speech of the Arabs, and Jarir said:
"If Solomon sees the jinn, they will be made familiar with it,
and if Solomon sees the beloved (of the mountain), he will descend."

The exegetes said: the reason is that God, exalted is He, sent down the Torah to Moses and commanded his people to act by its rulings, but they refused to accept it and to act by what is in it, because of the burdens and heavy obligations it contained. His law was heavy, so God, exalted is He, commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him) to lift a mountain the size of their camp, which was a farsakh by a farsakh, and to raise it above their heads to the height of a man's stature.

Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas: God commanded a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, and it was uprooted from its base until it stood over their heads like a canopy.

'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas: God raised the Tur above their heads, sent a fire from before their faces, the salt sea came to them from behind, and it was said to them: ﴿Take what We have given you﴾, that is, what We have given you.

﴿with strength﴾: with earnestness and persistence. In it there is an implied element, meaning: and We said to them: take.

﴿and remember what is in it﴾: that is, memorize it, know it and act by it. The "dhal" in the reading of Abu... (fa-dhakkaru) is with a shadda and a kasra on the shadda'd alif, and "fi" is a particle... and "tadhakkaru ma fihi," and both meanings are: take admonition from it. ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾: so that you may be saved from destruction in this world and from punishment in the Hereafter. If you accept it and do what you were commanded, well and good; otherwise I will crush you with this mountain, drown you in the sea, and burn you with this fire. When they saw there was no escape for them, they accepted, and they prostrated out of fear, while they kept glancing at the mountain as they prostrated. Thus it became a custom among the Jews that they prostrate only on the halves of their faces. When the mountain was removed, they said: O Moses, we have heard and obeyed, and had it not been for the mountain we would not have obeyed you.

﴿Then you turned away﴾: you turned away and disobeyed.

﴿after that﴾: that is, after the taking of the covenant and the raising of the mountain.

﴿Had it not been for the grace of God upon you and His mercy﴾: by delaying punishment from you.

﴿you would have been among the losers﴾: you would have become among the vanquished through punishment and the loss of both this world and the Hereafter.

﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath﴾: That is because they were of the people of David (peace be upon him), in a land called Ayla. God forbade them the hunting of fish on the Sabbath day. When the Sabbath came, no fish would remain in the sea without gathering there, so that they would thrust their snouts out of the water in safety. When the Sabbath passed, they would disperse and return to the sea. This is the meaning of God's words: ﴿When their fish come to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they do not keep Sabbath, they do not come to them﴾. Some men dug pools around the sea and channeled rivers from it to them. On Friday evening they opened those rivers, and the waves brought the fish to the pools, but they could not get out because of the depth of the pools and the scarcity of water. On Sunday they took them. It was also said: they would set nets and hooks on Friday and take them out on Sunday. They did this for a time, their wealth increased, and no punishment came down upon them. Their hearts hardened, they persisted in sin, and they said: "We see that the Sabbath has only been made lawful for us." When they did this, the people of the town, who were seventy thousand, became three groups: one group refrained and forbade, another refrained but did not forbid, and a third violated the sanctity. Those who forbade were twelve thousand. When the wrongdoers refused to accept their advice, those who forbade said: "By God, we will not dwell with you in one town." They divided the town with a wall, and they remained like this for two years. David cursed them, and God, mighty and majestic, became angry with them because of their persistence in disobedience. One day those who forbade went out through their gate, while the wrongdoers had not opened their gates and none of them came out. When the others delayed, they climbed over the wall and found them all to be apes. They remained three days and then perished, and no transformed creature survives beyond three days, and they did not reproduce. This is the saying of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿So We said to them: Be apes, despised﴾, a command of transformation.

﴿khasi'in﴾: expelled, humiliated, in the dialect of Kinana, said by Mujahid, Qatada and al-Rabi'.

Abu Rawq said: it means mute, not speaking, evidenced by God's saying: ﴿He said: Be driven away therein, and do not speak to Me﴾.

It is also said: distanced from every good.

﴿So We made it﴾: that is, the apes; it is also said: the town; and it is also said: the punishment.

﴿a deterrent﴾: a punishment, a lesson, and a public disgrace. Its root is from "nakl," which is a shackle, its plural being "ankal." A bridle is also called "nakl."

﴿for what was before it and what was after it﴾: Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' said: its meaning is a punishment for their past sins and a lesson for those after them.

Qatada: We made that punishment a recompense for their earlier sins before their prohibition from hunting, and ﴿what was after it﴾ refers to their disobedience in taking fish after the prohibition.

It is also said: ﴿for what was before it﴾ refers to the punishment of the Hereafter, and ﴿what was after it﴾ refers to their admonition in this world, so that they are remembered by it until the Day of Resurrection.

It is also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, and its sense is: "So We made it and what followed it, of the punishment prepared for them in the Hereafter, a deterrent and a recompense for what was before it," that is, for their earlier sins in transgressing on the Sabbath day.

﴿and an admonition﴾: an exhortation and a lesson. ﴿for the God-fearing﴾: for the believers of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), so that they do not do the like of what they did.

﴿And when Moses said to his people: Indeed God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ The verse: The reason is that a slain man was found among the Children of Israel named 'Amil, and they did not know his killer, and they differed over his killer and the cause of his killing. 'Ata' and al-Suddi said:

There was among the Children of Israel a man of great wealth, and he had a poor cousin with no heir other than him. When his death was prolonged, he killed him to inherit from him.

Some said: 'Amil had a female cousin under him, who had no equal among the Children of Israel in beauty and grace, and her cousin killed him so that he could marry her.

Ibn al-Kalbi said: his nephew killed him in order to marry his daughter. When he killed him, he carried him from his town to another town and left him there.

It was also said: he left him between two towns.

'Ikrima: The Children of Israel had a mosque with twelve doors, one for each tribe. A slain man was found at the door of one tribe.

It was said: he was dragged to the door of another tribe, and the two tribes disputed over him.

Ibn Sirin said: the killer slew him, then carried him and placed him at the door of a man among them, then in the morning sought vengeance for his blood and claimed it against him. He said: the relatives of the slain came to Moses, brought people, claimed against them the killing, and asked for retaliation. Moses asked them about it, and they denied it. The matter of the slain became unclear to Moses, and dispute arose among them.

Al-Kalbi said: that was before the law of the oath (qasama) was revealed in the Torah. So they asked Moses to call upon God to clarify it for them, and Moses asked his Lord, and He commanded them to slaughter a cow. Moses said to them: ﴿Indeed God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾.

﴿They said: Do you take us in mockery, O Moses?﴾ That is, do you mock us when we ask you about the slain and you command us to slaughter a cow? They said this because the two matters seemed far apart outwardly, and they did not know the wisdom in it.

Ibn Muhaysin read: ﴿Ayattakhidhuna﴾ with a ya', he said: they meant God. This is not surprising from their ignorance, for they are the ones who said: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾.

In this there are three readings of "huzuwan": "huzu'an" with lightening and hamza, and similarly "kufu'an," which is the reading of al-A'mash, Hamza, Khalaf and Isma'il. "Huzu'an" and "kufu'an" with emphasis and hamza is the reading of Abu 'Amr and the people of Hijaz and Syria, and the choice of al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. "Huzuwan" and "kufuwan" with emphasis without hamza, and in the narration of Hafs ibn Sulayman al-Bazzaz from 'Asim. All of them are valid dialects with the meaning of mockery. Moses (peace be upon him) said: ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾, that is, among those who mock the believers. When the people knew that slaughtering the cow was a resolve from God, mighty and majestic, they asked Him for its description.

﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is﴾. Had they chosen any ordinary cow and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them, but they made it hard upon themselves, so God made it hard upon them. Their strictness was by God's measure and wisdom. The reason for this, as al-Suddi and others mentioned, is as follows:

A man among the Children of Israel was so dutiful to his father that a man came to him with a pearl. He bought it for fifty thousand, and there was a surplus. He said to the seller: "My father is asleep, and the key of the chest is under his head. Wait for me until he wakes and I will give you the price." The seller said: "Wake your father and give me the money." He said: "I will not do that, but I will increase it for you by ten thousand; wait for me until my father wakes." The man said: "I will give you ten thousand more if you wake your father and pay quickly." He said: "And I will increase it for you by twenty thousand if you wait for my father to wake." He did so, and the man did not wake his father. His dutifulness to his father resulted in God making that cow his, and He commanded the Children of Israel to slaughter that very cow.

Ibn 'Abbas, Wahb and others said: There was a righteous man among the Children of Israel who had a young son, and he had a calf. He took the calf to a thicket and said: "O God, I entrust this calf to You for my son until he grows up." The man died, and the calf was left in the thicket and became a wild cow that fled from anyone who tried to catch it. When the son grew up, he was dutiful to his mother. He divided his night into three parts: he prayed one third, slept one third, and sat at his mother's head one third. In the morning he went out, gathered firewood on his back, and brought it to the market to sell as God willed. Then he gave a third in charity, ate a third, and gave a third to his mother. One day his mother said to him: "Your father left you a calf and went with it to a certain thicket and entrusted it to God, mighty and majestic. Go to it and call upon Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac that it be returned to you. Among its signs is that when you look at it, it will seem to you as if the rays of the sun come out of its skin." It was called "al-Mudhahhaba" for its beauty, yellowness and purity of color. The youth went to the thicket and saw it grazing, and he said: "I adjure you by the family of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac and Jacob." It came running until it stood before him. He seized its neck and led it, and the cow spoke by God's permission and said: "O youth, dutiful to his mother, mount me, for that is easier for you." The youth said: "My mother did not command me to that; she only said: take it by its neck." The cow said: "By the God of the Children of Israel, if you had mounted me you would never have been able to hold me. Go on, for if you commanded the mountain to be uprooted from its base and go with you, it would do so because of your dutifulness to your mother." The youth set out, and the enemy of God, Iblis, met him in the form of a shepherd and said: "O youth, I am a man of cattle herders who longed for his family. I took a bull from my herd and loaded it with my provisions and goods, but when I reached halfway, I went to relieve myself on the high middle of the mountain and could not manage it, and I fear for my life. If you would carry me on your cow and save me from death, I will give you its price, two cows like yours." The youth refused and said: "Go and put your trust in God; if God knew of your certainty He would deliver you without provisions or mount." Iblis said: "If you wish, sell it to me at your own judgment, or if you wish, carry me on it and I will give you ten like it." The youth said: "My mother did not command me to this." While the youth was thus, a bird flew up before the cow, and the cow fled into the wilderness and the herder vanished. The youth called it by the name of the family of Abraham, and the cow returned to him and said: "O youth, dutiful to his mother, did you not see the bird that flew? It was Iblis, the enemy of God, who snatched me away. Had he mounted me, you would never have been able to hold me. When you invoked the family of Abraham, a angel came, snatched me from Iblis's hand and returned me to you, because of your dutifulness to your mother and your obedience to her."

The youth brought her to his mother, and she said to him: "You are poor and have no wealth, and gathering firewood by day and standing in prayer by night is hard for you. Go and sell this cow and take its price." He said: "For how much shall I sell it?" She said: "For three dinars, and do not sell it without my consent and counsel." That was the price of a cow at that time. The youth took her to the market, and God sent an angel in human form, created by His power, to inform the youth how dutiful he was to his mother, and God is Aware of His servants. The angel said to him: "For how much do you sell this cow?" He said: "For three dinars, but I stipulate your consent with my mother." The angel said: "Six dinars, and do not consult your mother." The youth said: "Even if you gave me its weight in gold, I would not take it except with my mother's consent." He returned to his mother and told her the price. She said: "Go back and sell it for six, with my consent." The youth took the cow to the market, and came to the angel, who said: "Did you consult your mother?" The youth said: "She commanded me not to sell it for less than six, provided I consult her." The angel said: "Then I will give you twelve on condition that you do not consult her." The youth came back to his mother and told her. She said: "That man who comes to you and gives you is an angel who comes to you in the form of a human to test you. When he comes to you, say: Do you command us to sell this cow or not?" He did so, and the angel said to him: "Go to your mother and say to her: For how much is this cow? For Moses son of 'Imran is buying it from you for a slain man among the Children of Israel. Do not sell it except for its hide full of dinars." They kept the cow, and God decreed for the Children of Israel the slaughter of that very cow, and commanded them to do so. They said: "Describe it to us," and He described it to them, until He described that very cow, as a reward to him for his dutifulness to his mother, as a grace from Him.

As a grace from Him and a mercy. This is the saying of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾, that is, ask. Thus it is in the codex of 'Abd Allah: "Ask your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is and what its age is." Moses said: ﴿Indeed He says it is a cow neither old nor virgin﴾, meaning: God says: "It is a cow neither old nor young." "Old" and "virgin" are in the nominative by supposing "it is": "it is neither aged nor virgin."

Mujahid, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash: "fariḍ" is the aged one that no longer bears, one says of her: "faradat, yafradu, furudan." The poet said:
"A dark bay, black-colored, not aged,
nor a mature one with spotted color."

And the reciter said:
"O Lord, a man of grudge against me, aged,
with periods like the periods of a menstruating woman,"
meaning: an ancient hatred.

"Bikr" is the young female who has never borne.

Al-Suddi said: "bikr" is the one who has borne only one calf, and the letter "ha'" was dropped from it for specification.

"'Awan" is between two ages. Al-Akhfash said: "'awan" is one who has given birth several times; its plural is "'un," and from it one says: "'awwanat, ta'wiyan."

﴿So do what you are commanded﴾: slaughter the cow, and do not repeat the question.

﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is﴾: the place of "ma" is nominative as subject, and "lawnuha" is the predicate. Al-Dahhak read "lawnuha" in the accusative, as if it were governed by two causes, and made "ma" superfluous.

﴿He said: Indeed He says it is a cow, yellow, its color intensely bright﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: intensely yellow. 'Adi ibn Zayd said:
"Indeed I give the drink, intensely yellow,
as if the musk of its scent perfumes it."

Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi': "pure."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr: yellow in color and hooves.

al-Hasan: black, for the Arabs call black "yellow." al-A'sha said:
"Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts,
their colts are yellow like raisins."

Al-Qutaybi said: it is an error to say that "yellow" here means black, because this is an error regarding the descriptions of cows. It is rather about the descriptions of camels, for black camels have drunk their blackness until it became yellow. Moreover, if he had meant black, he would not have emphasized it with "intensely bright," for "faqi'" is one intensely yellow. As one says: "white, intensely white," "black, deep black," "red, bright red," "green, verdant green."

﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾: pleasing and delighting them with its beauty and purity of color, because the eye is pleased and delights in looking at a thing.

Al-Hasan said: Whoever wears yellow sandals, his worry diminishes [[Attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas in Tadhkirat al-Mawdu'at: 158.]], because God says: ﴿Yellow, its color bright, pleasing to the beholders﴾ [and] ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is; surely cattle are alike to us."﴾ Are they grazing or working?

Inna al-baqar (indeed the cattle): this is the reading of the common people. Muhammad Dhu al-Shama al-Umawi read inna al-baqir, which is a collective noun for cattle, like al-jamal for a group of camels. The poet said:

*Why do I see you, after your absence, desolate, a ruin like the ruined basin of the cattle?*

Qutrub said: the plural of baqara is baqar, baqir, baqir, buqur and baqur.

If it is asked: since He said "tashabaha" (it became confused) and "al-baqar" is a collective noun, why did He not say "tashabahat"? It is answered with three opinions:
