Inna al-baqar (indeed the cattle): this is the reading of the common people. Muhammad Dhu al-Shama al-Umawi read inna al-baqir, which is a collective noun for cattle, like al-jamal for a group of camels. The poet said:

*Why do I see you, after your absence, desolate, a ruin like the ruined basin of the cattle?*

Qutrub said: the plural of baqara is baqar, baqir, baqir, buqur and baqur.

If it is asked: since He said "tashabaha" (it became confused) and "al-baqar" is a collective noun, why did He not say "tashabahat"? It is answered with three opinions:

First: it is masculine because it is a collective noun in form (al-baqar), as in His saying ﴿As if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar: 20].

Al-Mubarrad said: Sibawayh was asked about this verse [and] he said: every plural whose letters are fewer than those of its singular is treated as masculine by the Arabs. He cited the verse of al-A'sha:

*Bid farewell to Hurayra, for the caravan is departing,*

where he did not say "murtahilun" (departing, masculine plural). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that the species of cattle has become confused for us.

﴿Tashabaha ʿalayna﴾ (it has become confused for us). There are seven readings of tashabaha:

Tashabaha, with a fatha on the ta' and the ha' and a light shadda-less shin: this is the reading of the common people, and it is a past-tense verb with a masculine singular form.

Al-Hasan read tashabahu, with an open ta' and a damma on the ha' and a light shin, meaning tashabaha.

Al-A'raj read tashsabahu, with a fatha on the ta', a shadda on the shin and a damma on the ha', meaning yatashabahu.

Mujahid read tashabbaha, like the reading of al-A'raj except without the alif, as in "tahammala" and "tahammala" (similar forms).

In the codex of Ubayy: tashabahat, on the pattern of tafaʿalat, with the ta' for the feminization of "baqar".

Ibn Abi Ishaq read tashsabahat with a shadda on the shin. Abu Hatim said: this is an error, because the ta' is not assimilated in this pattern except in the imperfect.

al-A'mash read muta­shabih ʿalayna, making it a noun.

The meaning of the verse: its matter has been confused and become ambiguous for us, so we are not guided to it.

﴿Wa inna in shaʾa Allah la-muhtadun﴾ (and we, God willing, shall be guided) to its description.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By God, if they had only made clear [what was required], it would have been made clear for them until the end of time."

He said: "Indeed He says it is a cow neither broken-in (dhalul) — made docile by work. It is said: a man is dhalil (humbled), clearly humbled; and an animal is dhalula, clearly tame."

﴿Tuthir al-ardh﴾ (it plows the earth), that is, it is like it for tillage.

﴿Wa la tasqi al-harth﴾ (nor irrigates the field), ﴿musallamatun﴾ (sound), free of defects. Al-Hasan said: sound in its limbs, showing no trace of work.

﴿La shiyata fiha﴾ (there is no blemish in it). ʿAtaʾ said: no defect in it.

Qatada said: no white at all in it.

Mujahid said: no white and no black in it.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: no color in it that contrasts with the majority of its color.

﴿Fa-lamma qala hadha qalu al-ana jiʾta bi-l-haqq﴾ (When he said this, they said: "Now you have brought the truth"), that is, with the complete and clear description.

It is said: the cow with which the slain man was brought back to life belonged to his heir who had killed him. He was the first to begin asking about it, hoping they would not find it. They searched for it and found none with its full description except with the dutiful youth. So they bought it from him for the weight of its hide in gold.

Al-Suddi said: they bought it for ten times its weight in gold.

﴿Fa-dhabahuha wa ma kadu yafʿalun﴾ (So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done so) because of the high price.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: and they had almost not found it, given the gathering of its descriptions.

﴿Wa-idh qatalatum nafsan﴾ (And when you killed a soul), meaning ʿAmil; and this verse is the beginning of the story.

﴿Fa-ddaraʾtum fiha﴾ (and you disputed about it), that is, differed about it, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, and from it is the saying of the poet about the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

*He used to purify, and was the best partner, neither evading nor disputing.*

al-Dahhak said: you contended with one another.

ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Yahya: you doubted.

al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas: you pushed back against one another. The root of al-diraʾ is pushing: one throws it on this one and that on that one, and each defends himself, as in His saying ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾ [al-Raʿd: 22; al-Qasas: 54], and His saying ﴿and it averts from her the punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 8]. The root of His saying [..........] [a word not legible], and the bāʾ is an extra particle.

Abu ʿUbayda: they bore it and acknowledged it, and from it the transmitted supplication [...........] [a word not legible]. The original is: fa-dāraʾtum, then tadāraʾtum, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the dāl and an alif was introduced so that the first letter's sukun could be pronounced, like His saying ﴿ithaqqaltum﴾ [al-Tawba: 39].

﴿Wa Allahu mukhrijun ma kuntum taktumun﴾ (And God will bring forth what you were concealing), that is, what you were hiding.

﴿Fa-qulna idribuhu﴾ (So We said: strike him), meaning the slain man.

﴿Bi-baʿdiha﴾ (with a part of it), that is, with part of the cow. They differed about which part it was. Ibn ʿAbbas said: strike him with the bone that lies beside the thighs, which is the vital spot.

al-Dahhak: with its tongue. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this is the most preferable opinion, because what was intended was that the revival of the slain man should be by speech, and the tongue is its instrument.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr: it was struck with its tail. Yaman said: and this is the most correct interpretation, because the coccyx is the foundation of the body upon which creation is built, and it is the first thing created and the last to decay.

Mujahid: with its tail.

ʿIkrima and al-Kalbi: with its right thigh.

al-Suddi: with the piece between its shoulders; and it was said: with its ear.

So they did that, and the slain man rose alive by God's permission, and its veins were gushing blood, and he said: "So-and-so killed me." Then he fell and died on the spot. There is an abbreviation in the verse, and its full sense is: We said, strike him with part of it, and he struck, and he was revived, like His saying ﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], meaning: and he broke his fast, then the number [of days]; and His saying ﴿So whoever among you is sick or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom﴾ [al-Baqara: 196], meaning: and he shaved, then a ransom.

﴿Kadhalika yuhyi Allahu al-mawta﴾ (Thus God gives life to the dead), just as He revived ʿAmil after his death, thus God gives life to the dead.

﴿Wa yurikum ayatihi﴾ (and shows you His signs), His evident signs. ﴿La-ʿallakum taʿqilun﴾ (that perhaps you may reason).

Al-Waqidi said: everything in the Qur'an is in the sense of "li-kay" (in order that) except the one in al-Shuʿara: ﴿wa tattakhidhuna masanic la-ʿallakum takhludun﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 129], where it means "as if you will abide," so that you do not die.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 63–73 (part 1 of 2):

Remember when We took your covenant, O assembly of the Jews. And We raised above you the Mount (al-Tur), which in Syriac (al-Suryaniyya) is, according to some, the word for mountain. Some have said: there is no language in the world except that it is found in the Qur'an.

Abu 'Ubayda and the scholars of precision (al-hudhdhaq) said: it is not permissible that there be in the Qur'an a language other than the language of the Arabs, because God, exalted is He, says: ﴿An Arabic Qur'an﴾ and He says: ﴿in clear Arabic tongue﴾. Such words and their like are only a point of agreement between the two languages.

We have found "al-Tur" in the speech of the Arabs, and Jarir said:
"If Solomon sees the jinn, they will be made familiar with it,
and if Solomon sees the beloved (of the mountain), he will descend."

The exegetes said: the reason is that God, exalted is He, sent down the Torah to Moses and commanded his people to act by its rulings, but they refused to accept it and to act by what is in it, because of the burdens and heavy obligations it contained. His law was heavy, so God, exalted is He, commanded Gabriel (peace be upon him) to lift a mountain the size of their camp, which was a farsakh by a farsakh, and to raise it above their heads to the height of a man's stature.

Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas: God commanded a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, and it was uprooted from its base until it stood over their heads like a canopy.

'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas: God raised the Tur above their heads, sent a fire from before their faces, the salt sea came to them from behind, and it was said to them: ﴿Take what We have given you﴾, that is, what We have given you.

﴿with strength﴾: with earnestness and persistence. In it there is an implied element, meaning: and We said to them: take.

﴿and remember what is in it﴾: that is, memorize it, know it and act by it. The "dhal" in the reading of Abu... (fa-dhakkaru) is with a shadda and a kasra on the shadda'd alif, and "fi" is a particle... and "tadhakkaru ma fihi," and both meanings are: take admonition from it. ﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾: so that you may be saved from destruction in this world and from punishment in the Hereafter. If you accept it and do what you were commanded, well and good; otherwise I will crush you with this mountain, drown you in the sea, and burn you with this fire. When they saw there was no escape for them, they accepted, and they prostrated out of fear, while they kept glancing at the mountain as they prostrated. Thus it became a custom among the Jews that they prostrate only on the halves of their faces. When the mountain was removed, they said: O Moses, we have heard and obeyed, and had it not been for the mountain we would not have obeyed you.

﴿Then you turned away﴾: you turned away and disobeyed.

﴿after that﴾: that is, after the taking of the covenant and the raising of the mountain.

﴿Had it not been for the grace of God upon you and His mercy﴾: by delaying punishment from you.

﴿you would have been among the losers﴾: you would have become among the vanquished through punishment and the loss of both this world and the Hereafter.

﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath﴾: That is because they were of the people of David (peace be upon him), in a land called Ayla. God forbade them the hunting of fish on the Sabbath day. When the Sabbath came, no fish would remain in the sea without gathering there, so that they would thrust their snouts out of the water in safety. When the Sabbath passed, they would disperse and return to the sea. This is the meaning of God's words: ﴿When their fish come to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they do not keep Sabbath, they do not come to them﴾. Some men dug pools around the sea and channeled rivers from it to them. On Friday evening they opened those rivers, and the waves brought the fish to the pools, but they could not get out because of the depth of the pools and the scarcity of water. On Sunday they took them. It was also said: they would set nets and hooks on Friday and take them out on Sunday. They did this for a time, their wealth increased, and no punishment came down upon them. Their hearts hardened, they persisted in sin, and they said: "We see that the Sabbath has only been made lawful for us." When they did this, the people of the town, who were seventy thousand, became three groups: one group refrained and forbade, another refrained but did not forbid, and a third violated the sanctity. Those who forbade were twelve thousand. When the wrongdoers refused to accept their advice, those who forbade said: "By God, we will not dwell with you in one town." They divided the town with a wall, and they remained like this for two years. David cursed them, and God, mighty and majestic, became angry with them because of their persistence in disobedience. One day those who forbade went out through their gate, while the wrongdoers had not opened their gates and none of them came out. When the others delayed, they climbed over the wall and found them all to be apes. They remained three days and then perished, and no transformed creature survives beyond three days, and they did not reproduce. This is the saying of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿So We said to them: Be apes, despised﴾, a command of transformation.

﴿khasi'in﴾: expelled, humiliated, in the dialect of Kinana, said by Mujahid, Qatada and al-Rabi'.

Abu Rawq said: it means mute, not speaking, evidenced by God's saying: ﴿He said: Be driven away therein, and do not speak to Me﴾.

It is also said: distanced from every good.

﴿So We made it﴾: that is, the apes; it is also said: the town; and it is also said: the punishment.

﴿a deterrent﴾: a punishment, a lesson, and a public disgrace. Its root is from "nakl," which is a shackle, its plural being "ankal." A bridle is also called "nakl."

﴿for what was before it and what was after it﴾: Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi' said: its meaning is a punishment for their past sins and a lesson for those after them.

Qatada: We made that punishment a recompense for their earlier sins before their prohibition from hunting, and ﴿what was after it﴾ refers to their disobedience in taking fish after the prohibition.

It is also said: ﴿for what was before it﴾ refers to the punishment of the Hereafter, and ﴿what was after it﴾ refers to their admonition in this world, so that they are remembered by it until the Day of Resurrection.

It is also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the verse, and its sense is: "So We made it and what followed it, of the punishment prepared for them in the Hereafter, a deterrent and a recompense for what was before it," that is, for their earlier sins in transgressing on the Sabbath day.

﴿and an admonition﴾: an exhortation and a lesson. ﴿for the God-fearing﴾: for the believers of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), so that they do not do the like of what they did.

﴿And when Moses said to his people: Indeed God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ The verse: The reason is that a slain man was found among the Children of Israel named 'Amil, and they did not know his killer, and they differed over his killer and the cause of his killing. 'Ata' and al-Suddi said:

There was among the Children of Israel a man of great wealth, and he had a poor cousin with no heir other than him. When his death was prolonged, he killed him to inherit from him.

Some said: 'Amil had a female cousin under him, who had no equal among the Children of Israel in beauty and grace, and her cousin killed him so that he could marry her.

Ibn al-Kalbi said: his nephew killed him in order to marry his daughter. When he killed him, he carried him from his town to another town and left him there.

It was also said: he left him between two towns.

'Ikrima: The Children of Israel had a mosque with twelve doors, one for each tribe. A slain man was found at the door of one tribe.

It was said: he was dragged to the door of another tribe, and the two tribes disputed over him.

Ibn Sirin said: the killer slew him, then carried him and placed him at the door of a man among them, then in the morning sought vengeance for his blood and claimed it against him. He said: the relatives of the slain came to Moses, brought people, claimed against them the killing, and asked for retaliation. Moses asked them about it, and they denied it. The matter of the slain became unclear to Moses, and dispute arose among them.

Al-Kalbi said: that was before the law of the oath (qasama) was revealed in the Torah. So they asked Moses to call upon God to clarify it for them, and Moses asked his Lord, and He commanded them to slaughter a cow. Moses said to them: ﴿Indeed God commands you to slaughter a cow﴾.

﴿They said: Do you take us in mockery, O Moses?﴾ That is, do you mock us when we ask you about the slain and you command us to slaughter a cow? They said this because the two matters seemed far apart outwardly, and they did not know the wisdom in it.

Ibn Muhaysin read: ﴿Ayattakhidhuna﴾ with a ya', he said: they meant God. This is not surprising from their ignorance, for they are the ones who said: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾.

In this there are three readings of "huzuwan": "huzu'an" with lightening and hamza, and similarly "kufu'an," which is the reading of al-A'mash, Hamza, Khalaf and Isma'il. "Huzu'an" and "kufu'an" with emphasis and hamza is the reading of Abu 'Amr and the people of Hijaz and Syria, and the choice of al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. "Huzuwan" and "kufuwan" with emphasis without hamza, and in the narration of Hafs ibn Sulayman al-Bazzaz from 'Asim. All of them are valid dialects with the meaning of mockery. Moses (peace be upon him) said: ﴿He said: I seek refuge in God from being among the ignorant﴾, that is, among those who mock the believers. When the people knew that slaughtering the cow was a resolve from God, mighty and majestic, they asked Him for its description.

﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is﴾. Had they chosen any ordinary cow and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them, but they made it hard upon themselves, so God made it hard upon them. Their strictness was by God's measure and wisdom. The reason for this, as al-Suddi and others mentioned, is as follows:

A man among the Children of Israel was so dutiful to his father that a man came to him with a pearl. He bought it for fifty thousand, and there was a surplus. He said to the seller: "My father is asleep, and the key of the chest is under his head. Wait for me until he wakes and I will give you the price." The seller said: "Wake your father and give me the money." He said: "I will not do that, but I will increase it for you by ten thousand; wait for me until my father wakes." The man said: "I will give you ten thousand more if you wake your father and pay quickly." He said: "And I will increase it for you by twenty thousand if you wait for my father to wake." He did so, and the man did not wake his father. His dutifulness to his father resulted in God making that cow his, and He commanded the Children of Israel to slaughter that very cow.

Ibn 'Abbas, Wahb and others said: There was a righteous man among the Children of Israel who had a young son, and he had a calf. He took the calf to a thicket and said: "O God, I entrust this calf to You for my son until he grows up." The man died, and the calf was left in the thicket and became a wild cow that fled from anyone who tried to catch it. When the son grew up, he was dutiful to his mother. He divided his night into three parts: he prayed one third, slept one third, and sat at his mother's head one third. In the morning he went out, gathered firewood on his back, and brought it to the market to sell as God willed. Then he gave a third in charity, ate a third, and gave a third to his mother. One day his mother said to him: "Your father left you a calf and went with it to a certain thicket and entrusted it to God, mighty and majestic. Go to it and call upon Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac that it be returned to you. Among its signs is that when you look at it, it will seem to you as if the rays of the sun come out of its skin." It was called "al-Mudhahhaba" for its beauty, yellowness and purity of color. The youth went to the thicket and saw it grazing, and he said: "I adjure you by the family of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac and Jacob." It came running until it stood before him. He seized its neck and led it, and the cow spoke by God's permission and said: "O youth, dutiful to his mother, mount me, for that is easier for you." The youth said: "My mother did not command me to that; she only said: take it by its neck." The cow said: "By the God of the Children of Israel, if you had mounted me you would never have been able to hold me. Go on, for if you commanded the mountain to be uprooted from its base and go with you, it would do so because of your dutifulness to your mother." The youth set out, and the enemy of God, Iblis, met him in the form of a shepherd and said: "O youth, I am a man of cattle herders who longed for his family. I took a bull from my herd and loaded it with my provisions and goods, but when I reached halfway, I went to relieve myself on the high middle of the mountain and could not manage it, and I fear for my life. If you would carry me on your cow and save me from death, I will give you its price, two cows like yours." The youth refused and said: "Go and put your trust in God; if God knew of your certainty He would deliver you without provisions or mount." Iblis said: "If you wish, sell it to me at your own judgment, or if you wish, carry me on it and I will give you ten like it." The youth said: "My mother did not command me to this." While the youth was thus, a bird flew up before the cow, and the cow fled into the wilderness and the herder vanished. The youth called it by the name of the family of Abraham, and the cow returned to him and said: "O youth, dutiful to his mother, did you not see the bird that flew? It was Iblis, the enemy of God, who snatched me away. Had he mounted me, you would never have been able to hold me. When you invoked the family of Abraham, a angel came, snatched me from Iblis's hand and returned me to you, because of your dutifulness to your mother and your obedience to her."

The youth brought her to his mother, and she said to him: "You are poor and have no wealth, and gathering firewood by day and standing in prayer by night is hard for you. Go and sell this cow and take its price." He said: "For how much shall I sell it?" She said: "For three dinars, and do not sell it without my consent and counsel." That was the price of a cow at that time. The youth took her to the market, and God sent an angel in human form, created by His power, to inform the youth how dutiful he was to his mother, and God is Aware of His servants. The angel said to him: "For how much do you sell this cow?" He said: "For three dinars, but I stipulate your consent with my mother." The angel said: "Six dinars, and do not consult your mother." The youth said: "Even if you gave me its weight in gold, I would not take it except with my mother's consent." He returned to his mother and told her the price. She said: "Go back and sell it for six, with my consent." The youth took the cow to the market, and came to the angel, who said: "Did you consult your mother?" The youth said: "She commanded me not to sell it for less than six, provided I consult her." The angel said: "Then I will give you twelve on condition that you do not consult her." The youth came back to his mother and told her. She said: "That man who comes to you and gives you is an angel who comes to you in the form of a human to test you. When he comes to you, say: Do you command us to sell this cow or not?" He did so, and the angel said to him: "Go to your mother and say to her: For how much is this cow? For Moses son of 'Imran is buying it from you for a slain man among the Children of Israel. Do not sell it except for its hide full of dinars." They kept the cow, and God decreed for the Children of Israel the slaughter of that very cow, and commanded them to do so. They said: "Describe it to us," and He described it to them, until He described that very cow, as a reward to him for his dutifulness to his mother, as a grace from Him.

As a grace from Him and a mercy. This is the saying of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us﴾, that is, ask. Thus it is in the codex of 'Abd Allah: "Ask your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is and what its age is." Moses said: ﴿Indeed He says it is a cow neither old nor virgin﴾, meaning: God says: "It is a cow neither old nor young." "Old" and "virgin" are in the nominative by supposing "it is": "it is neither aged nor virgin."

Mujahid, Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash: "fariḍ" is the aged one that no longer bears, one says of her: "faradat, yafradu, furudan." The poet said:
"A dark bay, black-colored, not aged,
nor a mature one with spotted color."

And the reciter said:
"O Lord, a man of grudge against me, aged,
with periods like the periods of a menstruating woman,"
meaning: an ancient hatred.

"Bikr" is the young female who has never borne.

Al-Suddi said: "bikr" is the one who has borne only one calf, and the letter "ha'" was dropped from it for specification.

"'Awan" is between two ages. Al-Akhfash said: "'awan" is one who has given birth several times; its plural is "'un," and from it one says: "'awwanat, ta'wiyan."

﴿So do what you are commanded﴾: slaughter the cow, and do not repeat the question.

﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is﴾: the place of "ma" is nominative as subject, and "lawnuha" is the predicate. Al-Dahhak read "lawnuha" in the accusative, as if it were governed by two causes, and made "ma" superfluous.

﴿He said: Indeed He says it is a cow, yellow, its color intensely bright﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: intensely yellow. 'Adi ibn Zayd said:
"Indeed I give the drink, intensely yellow,
as if the musk of its scent perfumes it."

Qatada, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Rabi': "pure."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr: yellow in color and hooves.

al-Hasan: black, for the Arabs call black "yellow." al-A'sha said:
"Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts,
their colts are yellow like raisins."

Al-Qutaybi said: it is an error to say that "yellow" here means black, because this is an error regarding the descriptions of cows. It is rather about the descriptions of camels, for black camels have drunk their blackness until it became yellow. Moreover, if he had meant black, he would not have emphasized it with "intensely bright," for "faqi'" is one intensely yellow. As one says: "white, intensely white," "black, deep black," "red, bright red," "green, verdant green."

﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾: pleasing and delighting them with its beauty and purity of color, because the eye is pleased and delights in looking at a thing.

Al-Hasan said: Whoever wears yellow sandals, his worry diminishes [[Attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas in Tadhkirat al-Mawdu'at: 158.]], because God says: ﴿Yellow, its color bright, pleasing to the beholders﴾ [and] ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is; surely cattle are alike to us."﴾ Are they grazing or working?

Inna al-baqar (indeed the cattle): this is the reading of the common people. Muhammad Dhu al-Shama al-Umawi read inna al-baqir, which is a collective noun for cattle, like al-jamal for a group of camels. The poet said:

*Why do I see you, after your absence, desolate, a ruin like the ruined basin of the cattle?*

Qutrub said: the plural of baqara is baqar, baqir, baqir, buqur and baqur.

If it is asked: since He said "tashabaha" (it became confused) and "al-baqar" is a collective noun, why did He not say "tashabahat"? It is answered with three opinions:

First: it is masculine because it is a collective noun in form (al-baqar), as in His saying ﴿As if they were trunks of uprooted palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar: 20].

Al-Mubarrad said: Sibawayh was asked about this verse [and] he said: every plural whose letters are fewer than those of its singular is treated as masculine by the Arabs. He cited the verse of al-A'sha:

*Bid farewell to Hurayra, for the caravan is departing,*

where he did not say "murtahilun" (departing, masculine plural). Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that the species of cattle has become confused for us.

﴿Tashabaha ʿalayna﴾ (it has become confused for us). There are seven readings of tashabaha:

Tashabaha, with a fatha on the ta' and the ha' and a light shadda-less shin: this is the reading of the common people, and it is a past-tense verb with a masculine singular form.

Al-Hasan read tashabahu, with an open ta' and a damma on the ha' and a light shin, meaning tashabaha.

Al-A'raj read tashsabahu, with a fatha on the ta', a shadda on the shin and a damma on the ha', meaning yatashabahu.

Mujahid read tashabbaha, like the reading of al-A'raj except without the alif, as in "tahammala" and "tahammala" (similar forms).

In the codex of Ubayy: tashabahat, on the pattern of tafaʿalat, with the ta' for the feminization of "baqar".

Ibn Abi Ishaq read tashsabahat with a shadda on the shin. Abu Hatim said: this is an error, because the ta' is not assimilated in this pattern except in the imperfect.

al-A'mash read muta­shabih ʿalayna, making it a noun.

The meaning of the verse: its matter has been confused and become ambiguous for us, so we are not guided to it.

﴿Wa inna in shaʾa Allah la-muhtadun﴾ (and we, God willing, shall be guided) to its description.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "By God, if they had only made clear [what was required], it would have been made clear for them until the end of time."

He said: "Indeed He says it is a cow neither broken-in (dhalul) — made docile by work. It is said: a man is dhalil (humbled), clearly humbled; and an animal is dhalula, clearly tame."

﴿Tuthir al-ardh﴾ (it plows the earth), that is, it is like it for tillage.

﴿Wa la tasqi al-harth﴾ (nor irrigates the field), ﴿musallamatun﴾ (sound), free of defects. Al-Hasan said: sound in its limbs, showing no trace of work.

﴿La shiyata fiha﴾ (there is no blemish in it). ʿAtaʾ said: no defect in it.

Qatada said: no white at all in it.

Mujahid said: no white and no black in it.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: no color in it that contrasts with the majority of its color.

﴿Fa-lamma qala hadha qalu al-ana jiʾta bi-l-haqq﴾ (When he said this, they said: "Now you have brought the truth"), that is, with the complete and clear description.

It is said: the cow with which the slain man was brought back to life belonged to his heir who had killed him. He was the first to begin asking about it, hoping they would not find it. They searched for it and found none with its full description except with the dutiful youth. So they bought it from him for the weight of its hide in gold.

Al-Suddi said: they bought it for ten times its weight in gold.

﴿Fa-dhabahuha wa ma kadu yafʿalun﴾ (So they slaughtered it, though they had almost not done so) because of the high price.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: and they had almost not found it, given the gathering of its descriptions.

﴿Wa-idh qatalatum nafsan﴾ (And when you killed a soul), meaning ʿAmil; and this verse is the beginning of the story.

﴿Fa-ddaraʾtum fiha﴾ (and you disputed about it), that is, differed about it, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, and from it is the saying of the poet about the Messenger of God (ﷺ):

*He used to purify, and was the best partner, neither evading nor disputing.*

al-Dahhak said: you contended with one another.

ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Yahya: you doubted.

al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas: you pushed back against one another. The root of al-diraʾ is pushing: one throws it on this one and that on that one, and each defends himself, as in His saying ﴿and they repel evil with good﴾ [al-Raʿd: 22; al-Qasas: 54], and His saying ﴿and it averts from her the punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 8]. The root of His saying [..........] [a word not legible], and the bāʾ is an extra particle.

Abu ʿUbayda: they bore it and acknowledged it, and from it the transmitted supplication [...........] [a word not legible]. The original is: fa-dāraʾtum, then tadāraʾtum, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the dāl and an alif was introduced so that the first letter's sukun could be pronounced, like His saying ﴿ithaqqaltum﴾ [al-Tawba: 39].

﴿Wa Allahu mukhrijun ma kuntum taktumun﴾ (And God will bring forth what you were concealing), that is, what you were hiding.

﴿Fa-qulna idribuhu﴾ (So We said: strike him), meaning the slain man.

﴿Bi-baʿdiha﴾ (with a part of it), that is, with part of the cow. They differed about which part it was. Ibn ʿAbbas said: strike him with the bone that lies beside the thighs, which is the vital spot.

al-Dahhak: with its tongue. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: this is the most preferable opinion, because what was intended was that the revival of the slain man should be by speech, and the tongue is its instrument.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr: it was struck with its tail. Yaman said: and this is the most correct interpretation, because the coccyx is the foundation of the body upon which creation is built, and it is the first thing created and the last to decay.

Mujahid: with its tail.

ʿIkrima and al-Kalbi: with its right thigh.

al-Suddi: with the piece between its shoulders; and it was said: with its ear.

So they did that, and the slain man rose alive by God's permission, and its veins were gushing blood, and he said: "So-and-so killed me." Then he fell and died on the spot. There is an abbreviation in the verse, and its full sense is: We said, strike him with part of it, and he struck, and he was revived, like His saying ﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], meaning: and he broke his fast, then the number [of days]; and His saying ﴿So whoever among you is sick or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom﴾ [al-Baqara: 196], meaning: and he shaved, then a ransom.

﴿Kadhalika yuhyi Allahu al-mawta﴾ (Thus God gives life to the dead), just as He revived ʿAmil after his death, thus God gives life to the dead.

﴿Wa yurikum ayatihi﴾ (and shows you His signs), His evident signs. ﴿La-ʿallakum taʿqilun﴾ (that perhaps you may reason).

Al-Waqidi said: everything in the Qur'an is in the sense of "li-kay" (in order that) except the one in al-Shuʿara: ﴿wa tattakhidhuna masanic la-ʿallakum takhludun﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 129], where it means "as if you will abide," so that you do not die.

Then your hearts became hard after that. Al-Kalbi said: After that they said, "We did not kill him," and they lied. Never were they more blind of heart or more intense in denying their prophet than they were at that time. Then God said: ﴿Then your hearts became hard﴾. Al-Kalbi and Abu Rawq said: they dried up and became rigid. Sa'id al-Barbari said:

"I see no trace of the remembrance on my body,
while the rope on the hard mountain leaves a mark."

Abu 'Ubayda: they dried up.

Al-Waqidi: they dried up from severity, so they did not soften.

Al-Mu'arrikh: they became coarse. It was also said: they turned black.

Al-Zajjaj said: the interpretation of qaswa (hardness) is the loss of softness, [and Sibawayh said] and humility and submissiveness are absent.

﴿After that﴾: that is, after the proofs had become manifest.

﴿Then they were﴾: their harshness and rigidity.

﴿Like stones, or even harder in hardness﴾: that is, rather even harder in hardness, like the words of the poet:

"[She appeared] like the horn of the sun in the brightness of forenoon,
and her form, or you are sweeter in the eye."[[Majma' al-Bayan: 1/281.]]

That is, "rather"; and it was also said that it carries the meaning of "and," with the alif being extra, meaning "and even harder in hardness," like God's words ﴿sinful or ungrateful﴾[[Surah al-Insan: 24.]], meaning "and ungrateful."

Abu Hayat read: ﴿or even harder in hardening (qasawa)﴾. Al-Kisa'i said: qaswa and qasawa are the same, like shiqwa and shaqawa.

Then He excused the stones and preferred them over the hard heart, saying: ﴿And indeed among stones there are those from which rivers gush forth﴾. Malik ibn Dinar read yanfajiru with the nun, like His words ﴿so there gushed forth﴾[[Surah al-Baqarah: 60.]]. In the codex of Ubayy it reads: "minha al-anhar" – returning the pronoun to the stones.

﴿And indeed among them are those that split open﴾: that is, they crack. This is how al-A'mash read it.

﴿So water comes out from them. And indeed among them are those that fall down﴾: they descend from the top of the mountain to its base.

﴿From fear of God, the Mighty and Majestic.﴾ And your hearts, O assembly of Jews, do not soften, do not humble themselves, and do not bring forth good.

﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾: a warning and threat, that is, He will not abandon the punishment for what you do, but will recompense you for it.

﴿Do you then hope﴾: that is, do you expect, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions,

﴿that they will believe you﴾: that the Jews will confirm you.

﴿And there was a group of them﴾: a faction among them,

﴿who heard the words of God﴾: meaning the Torah,

﴿then distorted it﴾: that is, altered it, meaning its rulings,

﴿after they had understood it﴾: known it and comprehended it, just as they altered the verse of stoning, which Muhammad (ﷺ) described.

﴿while they knew﴾ that they were lying. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah, Wahb and al-Suddi.

Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: this verse was revealed concerning the seventy chosen men, because when they went with Moses to the appointed time and heard God's speech and what He commanded and forbade, they returned to their people. The truthful ones reported exactly what they had heard, but a group among them said: "We heard God at the end of His speech saying: If you are able to do these things, then do them, and if you wish, do not do them, and there is no harm."

﴿And when they meet﴾: Ibn al-Sumay'a read laqu; meaning the hypocritical Jews,

﴿those who believe﴾ with their tongues but not with their hearts, meaning Abu Bakr and his companions among the believers.

﴿They say: "We believe," like your belief, and "We testify that Muhammad is truthful, whom we find in our book by his description and attributes."

﴿And when they are alone, some of them return to others﴾: that is, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad, Wahb ibn Yahuda and others of the Jewish leaders, and they rebuked them for this, saying:

﴿Do you tell them what God has opened to you?﴾ Al-Kalbi said: what God has decreed upon you in your book, that Muhammad is true and that his saying is truth. Al-Qadi al-Fattah al-Kisa'i said: what He has made clear to you in your book [of knowledge of the sending of Muhammad and the glad tidings of him].

Al-Waqidi: what God has sent down to you in this world and the Hereafter, similar to ﴿We would have opened upon them blessings from heaven and earth﴾[[Surah al-A'raf: 96.]], meaning "We sent down."

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash: what God has bestowed upon you and given you.

﴿So that they may argue with you﴾: that is, dispute with you and argue against you with your words [meaning the companions of Muhammad],

﴿with it before your Lord﴾. Some said: it is that a man among the Muslims, whenever he meets his kinsman, ally and friend among the Jews, asks him about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they say, "It is indeed true," [they say: you have acknowledged in your book that he is a true prophet, then you follow him], and he is a prophet. Then they return to their leaders, who rebuke them for it.

Al-Suddi said: some Jews had believed and then became hypocrites, and they would tell the believers about what punishments they had suffered. Their leaders said to them: ﴿Do you tell them what God has opened to you?﴾, that is, the punishment He sent down, so that they might reproach you with it and say:

"We are more honored by God than you."

[Ibn Jarir on] al-Qasim ibn Abi Barra: this is the saying of the Jews of Qurayza to one another when the Prophet (ﷺ) reviled them. He said: "O brothers of apes and swine and worshippers of false gods!" They said: "Who informed Muhammad of this? This came from none but you."

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾: Do you not have the mind of humanity?

God said: ﴿Do they not know that God knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾ – what they hide and what they show, meaning the Jews. Ibn Muhaysin read "ma" (what) in the second person address (taku nun...). And among them

﴿are the unlettered (ummiyyun)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: meaning those who do not know the meanings of the Book. They memorize it and recite it without understanding, and do not know what is in it.

Al-Kalbi said: they cannot read the Book nor write it. The evidence for this interpretation is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are an unlettered nation; we do not write and we do not reckon the month, it is thus, thus, and thus."[91]

The people of meanings said: "ummi" is related to umma (nation), and what the common people hold as the meaning of ummi is the commoner who has no discernment; or it is the plural of ummi, related to umm (mother), as if he remains in his original state, the feminine ending having been removed because it is extra, and the nisba ya' being extra too, and it was transferred to distinguish it from the ya' of possession.

﴿They know not the Book except as wishful fancies (amani)﴾. The majority read it with a doubled ya'.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-A'raj read amani with a single ya' throughout the Qur'an, dropping one of the two yas for lightness, being the ya' of the plural, like mafatih and mafatih (keys).

Abu Hatim said: every plural of this kind that is a singular with doubling, you have in it both the doubled and the undoubled forms, like fakhati, amani, aghani, and others. They differed on the meaning of amani. Al-Kalbi said: it means they know only what their scholars tell them of them.

Abu Rawq and Abu 'Ubayda: recitation and reading by heart, and they do not read it in books. The evidence for this is God's words: ﴿except when he wishes, Satan casts into his wish﴾[[Surah al-Hajj: 52.]], and its recitation.

The poet said:

"He wished for the Book of God at the first night,
and at its end he met the fate of the doves of destiny."

Mujahid and Qatadah: lies and falsehood.

[Ibn Jarir on] al-Qasim ibn Abi Barra: this is the saying of the Jews of Qurayza to one another when the Prophet (ﷺ) reviled them. He said: "O brothers of apes and swine and worshippers of false gods!" They said: "Who informed Muhammad of this? This came from none but you."

﴿Will you not then reason?﴾: Do you not have the mind of humanity?

God said: ﴿Do they not know that God knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾ – what they hide and what they show, meaning the Jews. Ibn Muhaysin read "ma" (what) in the second person address (taku nun...). And among them

﴿are the unlettered (ummiyyun)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: meaning those who do not know the meanings of the Book. They memorize it and recite it without understanding, and do not know what is in it.

Al-Kalbi said: they cannot read the Book nor write it. The evidence for this interpretation is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are an unlettered nation; we do not write and we do not reckon the month, it is thus, thus, and thus."[91]

The people of meanings said: "ummi" is related to umma (nation), and what the common people hold as the meaning of ummi is the commoner who has no discernment; or it is the plural of ummi, related to umm (mother), as if he remains in his original state, the feminine ending having been removed because it is extra, and the nisba ya' being extra too, and it was transferred to distinguish it from the ya' of possession.

﴿They know not the Book except as wishful fancies (amani)﴾. The majority read it with a doubled ya'.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and al-A'raj read amani with a single ya' throughout the Qur'an, dropping one of the two yas for lightness, being the ya' of the plural, like mafatih and mafatih (keys).

Abu Hatim said: every plural of this kind that is a singular with doubling, you have in it both the doubled and the undoubled forms, like fakhati, amani, aghani, and others. They differed on the meaning of amani. Al-Kalbi said: it means they know only what their scholars tell them of them.

Abu Rawq and Abu 'Ubayda: recitation and reading by heart, and they do not read it in books. The evidence for this is God's words: ﴿except when he wishes, Satan casts into his wish﴾[[Surah al-Hajj: 52.]], and its recitation.

The poet said:

"He wished for the Book of God at the first night,
and at its end he met the fate of the doves of destiny."

Mujahid and Qatadah: lies and falsehood.

Al-Farra': the amani are fabricated tales.

Some Arabs said to Ibn [Dalb]: "Is this something you narrated or something you wished?"

By the wishes of the prophets they meant what their scholars wrote from their own selves, then attributed to God Most High, by changing the description of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya: meaning they wish upon God falsehood and lies, like their saying ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days﴾[[Surah al-Baqarah: 80.]], and their saying ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews﴾[[Surah al-Baqarah: 111.]], and their saying ﴿We are the children of God and His beloved﴾[[Surah al-Ma'idah: 18.]].

﴿And they do not but assume (yazunnun) a mere assumption and delusion﴾, not reality and certainty. Said by Qatadah and al-Rabi'.

Mujahid said: [... they lie].

﴿So woe﴾

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Woe (al-wayl) is a valley in Hell into which the disbeliever plunges for forty autumns before reaching its bottom."[92]

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: a valley in Hell, which if the mountains of this world were moved through it, they would melt from its intense heat.

Ibn Buraydah: a mountain of pus and blood.

Ibn 'Abbas: intensity of punishment.

Ibn Kaysan: a word that every distressed person utters.

Al-Zajjaj: a word used by everyone who falls into ruin, and its origin is punishment and destruction.

It was also said: it is the supplication of the disbelievers against themselves, with woe and perdition.

﴿For those who write the Book with their own hands, then say, "This is from God," to purchase with it a small price.﴾ This is because the rabbis of the Jews feared the loss of their kingdom and the end of their leadership when the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Medina, and they schemed to hinder the Jews from believing in him. They set about altering his description in the Torah. His description in it was: good-looking, with fine hair, with kohl-dark eyes, of medium build. They changed it and wrote in its place: tall, blue-eyed, with straight hair. So when their common folk asked them about Muhammad (ﷺ), they read to them what they had written, and they found it contrary to the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and so they denied him. God Most High said:

﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾: from altering the description of Muhammad.

﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾: from the food they consume. The word "hands" is for emphasis, like the saying "I walked on my feet" and "I saw with my eye." God Most High said: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾[[Surah al-An'am: 38.]].

The poet said:

"You looked, but did not look with your eye at a sight."

Abu Malik said: this verse was revealed concerning the scribe who wrote for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He had read al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would dictate "ghafuran rahiman" and he would write "alimun hakimun"; the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Write as you wish." He would dictate "alimun hakimun" and he would write "sami'an basiran"; the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Write as you wish." He said: that man then apostatized from Islam and joined the polytheists.

He said: "Does Muhammad not know you? I used to write whatever I wished." That man died, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the earth will not accept him."[93]

He said: Abu Talha told me that he went to the place where he had spent the night and found him cast out. Abu Talha said: "What is the matter with this?" They said: "We buried him several times, but the earth would not accept him."

And they said (i.e., the Jews):

"The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days" — a determined measure, after which the punishment will be lifted from us and cease. The scholars differed over what these days are.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina, the Jews were saying: The duration of this world is seven thousand years, and we are punished for one day for every thousand years, and then the punishment will end after seven days. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Qatadah and 'Ata' said: They meant forty days, the period during which their fathers worshipped the calf, which was the length of Musa's (peace be upon him) absence from them.

Al-Hasan and Abu al-Aliyah said: The Jews said: "Indeed our Lord was displeased with us regarding our affair, and He swore to punish us for forty nights, after which He will admit us into Paradise." So the Fire will not touch us except for forty days, the fulfilment of the oath (tahillat al-qasam). Allah the Exalted said, refuting them: "Say, O Muhammad: ﴿Have you taken ...﴾" — the alif of interrogation (alif al-istifham) has entered upon the alif of connection (alif al-wasl), [the reading being] qul a-ttakhadhtum.

﴿with Allah a covenant?﴾ — a firm pledge that He will not punish you except for this period.

﴿Then Allah will not break His covenant﴾ — His promise. Ibn Mas'ud said: [the covenant is] by means of a threat. This is indicated by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿except for one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ [Surah Maryam 19:87], meaning, he says: "There is no god but Allah," sincerely.

﴿Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾

He said: ﴿Yes (bala)﴾. "Bal" and "bala" are two particles of correction, and each has two meanings: to negate a past statement and to affirm a future statement. Al-Kisa'i said: The difference between bala and na'am is that bala is an affirmation after denial, while na'am is an answer to a question without negation. So if someone says, "Did you not do such-and-such?" you say "Bala"; if he says, "Did you do such-and-such?" you say "Na'am."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Did there not come to you a warner?﴾ They said, "Bala" [Surah al-Mulk 67:8]. He said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said, "Bala" [Surah al-A'raf 7:172]. And in a non-denial context He said: ﴿Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?﴾ They said, "Na'am" [Surah al-A'raf 7:44]. And they said: ﴿Will we indeed be resurrected, and our first fathers?﴾ [Surah al-Saffat 37:17]. Say: ﴿Na'am﴾. Here He said bala because of the denial that preceded it, namely their words: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days.﴾

﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾ — meaning, shirk.

﴿and his sin has encompassed him﴾ — the people of Medina read khatiyatuhu in the plural (khatiyatuhu), while the rest read khati'atuhu in the singular, which is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. Al-ihatah (encompassing) means surrounding a thing from all its sides. The scholars differed over its meaning here.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd said: It is shirk, such that a man dies upon it. Thus they made the sin (khati'ah) to be shirk.

Some of them said: It is the many sins that make their people deserve the Fire.

Abu Zurayn, from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym, regarding His words ﴿and his sin has encompassed him﴾, said: It is one who dies upon his sin before repenting. The same was said by 'Ikrimah. Muqatil said: He persisted in it.

Mujahid said: It is sins that surround the heart; whenever he commits a sin, it rises until it covers the heart, and this is the rayn (rust).

It is related from Salam ibn Miskin that a man asked al-Hasan about this verse. The questioner said: "Glory be to Allah! I see you have a beard, yet you do not know what the encompassing of sin is! Look in the mushaf: every verse in which Allah the Mighty and Majestic forbade something and informed you that whoever does it will enter the Fire — that is the encompassing sin."

Al-Kalbi said: His sins have destroyed him. The evidence is His words ﴿unless you are surrounded (yuhata bikum)﴾ [Surah Yusuf 12:66], meaning, you are all destroyed.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: His sins have surrounded him, with respect to what good deeds he has, and so they have nullified them.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [This is a general statement specified by exceptions, among them "except one who repents," after it has been taken in its apparent sense.] (From the margin of the manuscript.)

﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds — those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾

And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel in the Torah. Ibn 'Abbas said: The covenant (mithaq) is the firm pledge.

﴿Not to worship except Allah﴾ — read with the ya' (la ya'budun) by Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Humayd. The rest read it with the ta' (la ta'budun), which is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim.

Abu 'Amr said: Do you not see that He says ﴿and speak to people kindly﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah 2:83]? That address is in the ta'.

Al-Kisa'i said: The verb la ya'budun takes the nominative because its meaning is: "We took the covenant of the Children of Israel that they should not worship except Allah." When the particle "an" was dropped, the verb was put in the nominative. Similar is His words: ﴿la tasfikun﴾ and the parallel of His words: ﴿Do you command me to worship (a'budu) other than Allah?﴾ [Surah al-Zumar 39:64]; he means "an a'bud." When the "an" was removed, the verb returned to the imperfect form.

Tarafah said:

"Ala ayyuha al-zajiri ahdar al-wagha, wa an ashhada al-ladhdhati hal anta mukhalladi"

He means "an ahdar," and when "an" was removed he put it in the nominative.

And Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: la ta'budu in the jussive, as a prohibition — meaning, "and We said to them: Do not worship except Allah."

﴿And to parents, kindness﴾ — and We enjoined upon them kindness to parents, being dutiful and tender towards them.

He said "bi-l-walidayn" although one of them is a mother, because when the masculine and feminine are paired, the masculine prevails, for its lightness and strength.

﴿And to the near of kin﴾ — meaning, and to the kinsfolk. "Al-qurba" is a verbal noun on the pattern fu'la, like "al-husna" and "al-shu'ra."

Tarafah said:

"Wa qarrabat bi-l-qurba wa jaddaka lahu yani... fa-tahayyuka amrun lil-nakithati ashhadu."

﴿And the orphans﴾ — plural of yatim, like nadama and nadim; he is the child who has no father.

﴿And the needy﴾ — meaning, the poor.

﴿And speak to people kindly﴾ — the reading differs over it. Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu al-Aliyah, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read husnan with a dammah on the ha' and a sukun on the sin, which is the choice of Abu Hatim; the evidence is His words ﴿bi-walidayhi husnan﴾ [Surah al-'Ankabut 29:8] and His words ﴿thumma baddala husnan﴾ [Surah al-Naml 27:11].

Ibn Mas'ud and Khalaf read hasanan with a fatha on the ha' and the sin, which is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd; he said: "We chose it because it is an adjective meaning qawlan hasanan (a good word)."

Ibn 'Umar read husunan with a dammah on the ha' and the sin and tanwin, like "al-ru'b," "al-nasb," "al-suht," "al-suhq," and similar.

'Asim and al-Jahdari read ihsanan with an alif.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Talhah ibn Musarrif read husna, joined with al-qurba in the feminine, unrestricted.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard al-Qasim ibn Habib say: I heard Abu Bakr ibn 'Abdus say: Its figurative sense is "kalimah husna," and its meaning is: "Speak to people truthfully and rightly concerning Muhammad (ﷺ). Whoever asks you about him, tell him the truth, explain to him his description, do not conceal his matter, and do not alter his description." This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Juraij and Muqatil. The evidence is His words ﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise (wa'dan hasanan)?﴾ [Surah Ta-Ha 20:86], meaning, a true promise.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: This verse includes both the righteous and the wicked.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: Enjoin them to what is right and forbid them from what is wrong.

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ — ﴿then you turned away﴾, meaning, you turned away from the covenant and the pledge, ﴿except a few of you﴾ — accusative as an exception.

﴿And you are withdrawers﴾ — and that was because a group among them believed.

﴿And when We took your covenant: ﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾ — not spill your blood. Talhah ibn Musarrif read tusfikun with a dammah on the fa', and both are dialects, like ya'rishun and ya'kifun.

Abu Mijlaz read tusaffikun with shaddah, for intensification.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: It means that some of you should not shed the blood of others without right. He said "dima'akum" (your blood) for two reasons: first, that every people who gather upon one religion are like a single soul; and second, that when a man kills another, it is as if he killed himself, because he will be subjected to retaliation and retribution.

﴿Nor expel yourselves from your homes﴾ — meaning, that some of you should not expel others from their homes. [And do not revile those who are your neighbours, lest you drive them to leave through the evil of your neighbourliness.] (From the margin of the manuscript.)

﴿Then you acknowledged this covenant, and you were witnesses to it.﴾ — that it is true, and ﴿and you are witnesses﴾ today to that, O assembly of Jews.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard al-Qasim ibn Habib say: I heard Abu Bakr ibn 'Abdus say: Its figurative sense is "kalimah husna," and its meaning is: "Speak to people truthfully and rightly concerning Muhammad (ﷺ). Whoever asks you about him, tell him the truth, explain to him his description, do not conceal his matter, and do not alter his description." This is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Juraij and Muqatil. The evidence is His words ﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise (wa'dan hasanan)?﴾ [Surah Ta-Ha 20:86], meaning, a true promise.

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: This verse includes both the righteous and the wicked.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: Enjoin them to what is right and forbid them from what is wrong.

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ — ﴿then you turned away﴾, meaning, you turned away from the covenant and the pledge, ﴿except a few of you﴾ — accusative as an exception.

﴿And you are withdrawers﴾ — and that was because a group among them believed.

﴿And when We took your covenant: ﴿You shall not shed your blood﴾ — not spill your blood. Talhah ibn Musarrif read tusfikun with a dammah on the fa', and both are dialects, like ya'rishun and ya'kifun.

Abu Mijlaz read tusaffikun with shaddah, for intensification.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: It means that some of you should not shed the blood of others without right. He said "dima'akum" (your blood) for two reasons: first, that every people who gather upon one religion are like a single soul; and second, that when a man kills another, it is as if he killed himself, because he will be subjected to retaliation and retribution.

﴿Nor expel yourselves from your homes﴾ — meaning, that some of you should not expel others from their homes. [And do not revile those who are your neighbours, lest you drive them to leave through the evil of your neighbourliness.] (From the margin of the manuscript.)

﴿Then you acknowledged this covenant, and you were witnesses to it.﴾ — that it is true, and ﴿and you are witnesses﴾ today to that, O assembly of Jews.

Then you, these are the ones who kill yourselves (the vocative "yā" is omitted here, meaning "O you, these," the address being dropped because the context makes it clear, as in His words: ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried﴾). So "hā'ulā'" is used for calling attention, and it is built on kasra, like "antum" in ﴿you kill yourselves﴾. The reading of the common people is ﴿taqtulūna anfusakum﴾, with light stress, from "qatl" (killing).

Al-Hasan read ﴿tuqattilūna﴾ with emphatic stress, from "taqtīl" (repeated killing).

﴿wa-tukhrijūna fariqan minkum min diyārihim tažāharūna ʿalayhim﴾ is the reading of the common people, namely the people of the Hijaz and al-Sham, Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub, who read ﴿tažžāharūna﴾ with the ẓāʾ doubled. Abu Ḥātim preferred this, and its meaning is "tatažāharūna," with the tāʾ assimilated into the ẓāʾ, like ﴿iththāqaltum﴾ and ﴿iddāraku﴾.

ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah, Ṭalḥah, al-Ḥasan, Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Abu Rajāʾ and al-Kisāʾi read ﴿taẓāharūna﴾ with the ẓāʾ light. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this. The justification for this reading is that they dropped the tāʾ of the agent and kept the tāʾ of address, as in His words ﴿wa-lā taʿāwanū﴾ and His words ﴿mā lakum lā tanāṣarūn﴾.

The poet said:

"You sneeze together around your house,
so all of you, O sons of Ḥammān, have colds."

Ubayy and Mujāhid read ﴿tažahharūna﴾ with shadda and without an alif, meaning "tatažahharūna," [.....] [an unreadable word in the manuscript] together, "ta'āwanūn" (you help one another). The ẓahr is help, so named because one leans his back against the back of his companion.

The poet said:

"Multiply your brothers as much as you can,
[.....] [an unreadable word in the manuscript]
when you call on them for aid, they are a support.

Not much is an alif (one friend and companion),
and indeed one enemy is a great many."

﴿bi-l-ithmi wa-l-ʿudwān﴾: with sin and injustice.

﴿wa-in yātūkum usārā tufādūhum﴾: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, Mujāhid, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ḥumayd, Shibl, al-Juḥdarī, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿usārā tafdūhum﴾ without an alif. al-Ḥasan read ﴿usrā﴾ without an alif, with ﴿tufādūhum﴾ with an alif. al-Nakhaʿī, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā ibn Ri'āb, Ḥamzah, ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Abī Isḥāq read ﴿usrā tafdūhum﴾, both without an alif, and this is the choice of Abu ʿUbayda.

Abu Rajāʾ, Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Qatādah, al-Kisāʾi and Yaʿqub read ﴿usārā tufādūhum﴾, both with an alif, and Abu Ḥātim chose this.

So "al-asrā" is the plural of "asīr," like "jarīḥ" and "jarḥā," "marīḍ" and "marḍā," "ṣarīʿ" and "ṣarʿā." "Al-asārā" is also the plural of "asīr," like "kasālā" and "sukārā." It may also be the plural of "usrā," as in your saying "imra'ah sakrā" and "nisā' sukārā." No one among the trustworthy scholars distinguished between them except Abu ʿAmr.

Abu Hishām narrated from Jubayr al-Juʿfī, from Abu ʿAmr, who said: "What is taken captive is ʿasārā, and what is not captured is usrā." It was also narrated from him by another route that he said: "What has come into their hands are ʿasārā, and what comes surrendering is usrā."

From Abu Bakr al-Naqqāsh, who said: I heard Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā Thaʿlab, when this statement from Abu ʿAmr was reported to him, say: "This is the talk of madmen." He meant there is no difference between them.

It is related from Abu Saʿīd al-Ḍarīr that he said: "The asārā are those who are bound and shackled, and the usrā are those who are taken captive but not bound." As for their saying "tufādūhum," meaning you ransom them with wealth, or you rescue them with a ransom or something else, and ﴿tufādūhum﴾ means you exchange them, he intended the ransoming of a captive by a captive. And ﴿usārā﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

As for the meaning of the verse: al-Suddī said: Allah, mighty and majestic, took a covenant from the Children of Israel in the Torah that none of them should kill another, nor expel one another from their homes. Whenever you find a male or female slave from the Children of Israel, buy them with the price that they are worth and free them. Qurayẓah were allies of the Aws, and al-Naḍīr were allies of the Khazraj, and they used to fight one another in the war of Numayr. Banu Qurayẓah would fight alongside their allies, and Banu al-Naḍīr alongside theirs, and when they prevailed they would destroy their homes and expel them from them. When a man from either of the two parties was taken captive, they would gather to ransom him, even if the captive was from their enemy. The Arabs would reproach them for this and say: "How do they fight them and then ransom them?" And they would say: "We have been commanded to ransom them, and fighting them has been forbidden to us." They said: "Then why do you fight them?" They said: "We are ashamed that our allies be humiliated." That is when Allah, exalted, reproached them, saying: ﴿Then you are these who kill yourselves and expel a party of you from their homes﴾ to the end of the verse. In the verse there is a rearrangement of its order: ﴿and expel a party of you from their homes, support against them in sin and injustice ... and it is forbidden to you to expel them ... and that they come to you as captives, you ransom them.﴾

Allah had taken four covenants from them: to abandon killing, to abandon expulsion, to abandon supporting their enemies against them, and to ransom their captives. They turned away from everything they were commanded except the ransoming. So Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ Their belief was in the ransoming, and their disbelief was in the killing, expulsion and support. Mujāhid said: it means, if you find him in someone else's hand you ransom him, while you kill him with your own hand. It was also said: it means they practise part and abandon part; you ransom the captives of your own tribe, and you abandon the captives of the people of your religion and do not ransom them.

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿So what is the recompense of those among you who do that, O assembly of Jews, but disgrace﴾, meaning humiliation and torment,

﴿in the life of this world﴾. So the disgrace of Qurayẓah was killing and captivity, and the disgrace of Banu al-Naḍīr was exile and banishment from their dwellings and gardens to Adhruʿāt and Rīḥā in al-Sham.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe torment﴾, which is the torment of the Fire. Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, Abu Rajāʾ and al-Ḥasan read ﴿turaddūn﴾ with the tāʾ, because of His words ﴿afa-tu'minūn﴾.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is read with the tāʾ by Madani, Abu Bakr and Yaʿqub; the rest read it with the yāʾ.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought﴾, meaning exchanged,

﴿the life of this world for the Hereafter. So the torment will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning made easier and eased,

﴿nor will they be helped﴾, meaning prevented from the torment of Allah.

And We certainly gave Moses the Book (the Tawrah) all at once. [Gave: a‘tayna.] Book: al-Kitab, the Tawrah, revealed in one piece.

We sent after him one messenger after another. [Wa qaffayna: we followed up, we sent in succession.] Qaffa, to follow someone's track, comes from qafa al-insan (the back of a person). God says: "Do not pursue (taqf) that of which you have no knowledge" [Surah al-Isra 17:36]. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"She said to a sister of hers, 'Look at her from the side...' / 'How can she follow when there is neither plain nor path?'"

And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear signs, the evident proofs and manifest evidences, which God, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned in Surah Al 'Imran and al-Ma'idah.

And We strengthened him (ayyadnahu): We aided and supported him, from al-ad and al-ayd (strength). [See Tafsir al-Tabari 1/568.] Mujahid read ayyadnahu with a long vowel (aydnahu); both are dialectal forms, like karrama and akrama.

With the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus). Ibn Kathir lightened al-qudus wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, while others pronounced it heavily (al-quddus); both are forms like al-ra'b and al-sahat. They differed about "the Holy Spirit." Al-Rabi' and 'Ikrimah said: it is the Spirit which was breathed into him, attributed to Himself in honour and distinction, like the House of God, the She-camel of God, and the servant of God. Al-Quds is God, Mighty and Majestic, indicated by His words: "and a spirit from Him" [Surah al-Nisa 4:171] and His words "So We breathed into it of Our Spirit." Others meant by al-quds purity, that is, the pure Spirit; his spirit was called holy because it was not contained in the loins of stallions nor enclosed in the wombs of females; it was only a command from God, Exalted.

As-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and Ka'b said: the Holy Spirit is Gabriel. Al-Hasan said: al-Quds is God, and His spirit is Gabriel.

As-Suddi said: al-Quds is blessing, and God magnified the blessing of Gabriel when He sent down His revelation to His prophets through his tongue. The support of Jesus, peace be upon him, by Gabriel means two things: he was his companion, going with him wherever he went; and the other is that he ascended with him to heaven. The evidence for this interpretation is His words: "Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth" [Surah al-Nahl 16:102].

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: it is the Greatest Name of God, and by it he would revive the dead and show people those wonders.

Ibn Zayd said: it is the Gospel; God made it a spirit just as He made the Qur'an a spirit for Muhammad ﷺ, as indicated by His words: "And thus We revealed to you a spirit of Our command" [Surah al-Shura 42:52].

When the Jews heard the mention of Jesus, peace be upon him, they said: "O Muhammad, [you are] not like Jesus, as you claim, nor like what is related to us of the prophets (peace be upon them)." They said: "Then bring us what Jesus brought, if you are truthful."

So God, Mighty and Majestic, sent down: "Is it, whenever a messenger comes to you, O company of Jews, with what you do not desire..." — i.e., what you do not love and do not accept.

"...you have become arrogant?" — i.e., you grew proud and haughty, refusing to believe in him.

"A group" — a company, so named because they were a band who broke away from the battle.

"You denied" — Jesus and Muhammad.

"A group you killed" — that is, you killed Zechariah, John, and the rest of the prophets whom they killed.

"And they said" — meaning the Jews: "Our hearts are uncovered (ghulf)." Ibn Muhaysin read it with a damma on the lam; the rest read it with a sukun.

Whoever lightened it, it is the plural of aghlaf, like asfar and safr, ahmar and hamr: one that has a covering and a wrapping, equal to the uncircumcised (aghlaf ghayr al-mukhtatin). Thus aghlaf and a'lam are the same, and the meaning is: upon them is a veil, so they neither understand nor comprehend what you say, O Muhammad.

Said by Mujahid and Qatadah. Its parallel is God's words: "And they say, 'Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to.'" [Surah Fussilat 41:5]

Whoever heavied it, it is the plural of ghilaf, like hijab and hujub, kitab and kutub, and the meaning is: our hearts are receptacles for every knowledge, so we have no need of your knowledge and your book. Said by 'Ata' and Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Kalbi said: they mean receptacles for every knowledge; it hears no speech without retaining it, except your speech, which it does not understand nor retain; had there been any good in it, it would have understood and retained it.

God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "Nay, God has cursed them for their disbelief." The root of la'n is expulsion and distancing. The Arabs say: [nama'] wa la'in, meaning far away. Al-Shammakh said:

"The sandgrouse were startled by him, and I drove away from him the place of the wolf, like the cursed man."

So the meaning of His words "God has cursed them" is that He expelled them and distanced them from every good. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: al-mal'un is the disgraced, the destroyed.

"Few of them believe" — meaning: none of them believes except a few, because more of the polytheists believed than of the Jews; said by Qatadah. On this view, ma is redundant, and the meaning is "few they believe," with qalilan in the accusative as a circumstantial clause.

Ma'mar said: the meaning is that they believe only a little, in what is in their hands, and disbelieve in most of it. On this view qalilan is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and ma is redundant, so it means "with little they believe."

Al-Waqidi and others said: the meaning is that they believe neither little nor much. This is like a man saying to another, "How little you do of such-and-such," meaning "Do not do it at all."

Al-Farra' related from al-Kisa'i: "We passed through a land where little grows of the leek and onion," meaning nothing grows there at all.

"And when there came to them a Book from God" — meaning the Qur'an.

"Confirming what is with them" — agreeing with it. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah read musaddiqan in the accusative as a circumstantial clause.

"And they had been, before, [the ones] who sought victory" — the Jews, before the sending of Muhammad ﷺ, "istaftahuna": seeking victory. God says: "If you seek victory, the victory has certainly come to you" [Surah al-Anfal 8:19], i.e., if you seek help, victory has come to you.

In a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, he used to seek the start of battle through the poor emigrants.

"Against those who disbelieved" — the polytheists of the Arabs. This was because when a matter became grave for them and an enemy overwhelmed them, they would say: "O God, give us victory over them through the Prophet who is sent at the end of time, whose description and attributes we find in the Torah." [Tafsir al-Jalalayn: 19.] They would say to their polytheist enemies: the time of a prophet who will come confirming what we say has drawn near, and we will kill you with him, before 'Ad and Iram.

"And when there came to them what they recognised" — meaning Muhammad ﷺ, who was not of the Children of Israel; they recognised his description and attributes.

"They disbelieved in him" — out of insolence and envy.

"So the curse of God is upon the disbelievers. Wretched is that for which they sold themselves" — bi's and ni'ma are two verbs of past tense, established for praise and blame, which do not inflect like ordinary verbs. The meaning of the verse: wretched is what they chose for themselves when they exchanged falsehood for truth and disbelief for faith. It was said: the meaning is: wretched is what they sold their share of themselves for.

"That they disbelieve in what God sent down" — meaning the Qur'an.

"Out of insolence" — bagy, and the root of baghy is corruption; one says: baghā al-jurḥ when it festers and swells.

"That God should send down of His bounty" — prophethood and the Book.

"upon whomever of His servants He wills" — Muhammad ﷺ.

"So they incurred wrath upon wrath" — i.e., in addition to wrath.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the first wrath was for their neglect of the Torah, and the second wrath for their disbelief in this prophet whom God chose.

Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah said: the first wrath was for their disbelief in Jesus, peace be upon him, and the Gospel; the second was their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an.

As-Suddi said: the first wrath was for their worship of the calf, and the second for their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ and their alteration of his description.

"And for the disbelievers" — and for those who deny the religion of Muhammad ﷺ among all people.

"is a humiliating punishment" — they will be disgraced and not honoured.

"You denied" — Jesus and Muhammad.

"A group you killed" — that is, you killed Zechariah, John, and the rest of the prophets whom they killed.

Al-Kalbi said: they mean receptacles for every knowledge; it hears no speech without retaining it, except your speech, which it does not understand nor retain; had there been any good in it, it would have understood and retained it.

"They disbelieved in him" — out of insolence and envy.

"So the curse of God is upon the disbelievers. Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 91–93:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down,"﴾ meaning the Qur'an.

﴿They say, "We believe in what was sent down to us,"﴾ meaning the Torah.

﴿And they reject what is after it,﴾ i.e., what is other than it and beyond it.

﴿And it is the truth,﴾ meaning the Qur'an.

﴿Confirming what is with them.﴾ Accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). ﴿Say, "Then why did you kill the prophets of Allah before?"﴾ Say to them, O Muḥammad. The original form of lima is lam, with the alif (of ma) dropped in order to distinguish the interrogative from the declarative, like their saying fīma, bima, lima, mimma, ʿalāma, and ḥatāma. This is a reply to their saying, "We believe in what was sent down to us."

So Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Why did you kill the prophets of Allah before?﴾

﴿If you are believers﴾ in the Torah, while you have betrayed it by killing the prophets. ﴿And Moses did come to you with clear proofs,﴾ with manifest evidences and plain signs.

﴿Then you took the calf [as a god] after him,﴾ i.e., after his departure to the mountain, ﴿while you were wrongdoers.﴾

﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you, [saying], "Take what We have given you with determination, and listen,"﴾ i.e., respond and obey. Obedience is called "hearing" metaphorically, because it is the cause of obedience and response. From this is the saying "Allah hears whoever praises Him," meaning He responds to him. A poet said:

*I called upon Allah until I feared that Allah would not hear what I say,*

i.e., would not respond.

﴿They said, "We hear your word, and we disobey your command."﴾ [Or: "We hear with our ears and disobey with our hearts."] [Note from the margin of the manuscript.]

The scholars of meaning (ahl al-maʿānī) said: they did not say this with their tongues, but when they heard the command and received it with disobedience, that was attributed to them as speech, by way of extension, as the poet said:

*And a watering place, a fly in its pool, [the women] say to the scout, "You have grown lean, so descend."*

﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts,﴾ i.e., the love of the calf, as in Allah's saying, ﴿and ask the town﴾ (Yusuf 82). Al-Nabigha said:

*How then can one who has become a close friend of [her] pass the night? As if I were a welcomed guest.*
