﴿And Abraham enjoined it﴾ – In the codex of ʿAbd Allah it reads "fawassa" (with doubled sad). The people of Medina and Syria read "wa-awsa" with an alif, and so it is in their codices. Abu ʿUbayd said: So I saw it in the codex of ʿUthman. The rest read "wa-wassa" with shadda, and both are dialects; one says "awsaytuhu" and "wassaytuhu" when one commands him to do something, like "anzala" and "nazzala." The Most High said: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers, grant them a little respite﴾ [al-Tariq 86:17]. Confirmation of the form "īṣāʾ" is the Most High's words: ﴿Allah instructs you regarding your children﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:11], and His words: ﴿they [women] shall bequeath﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:12]; and the evidence for the sense of commanding is His words: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut 29:8], and His words: ﴿They will not be able to make a bequest﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:50].

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil: "It means the word of unity: there is no god but Allah." Abu ʿUbayda said: If you wish, you may return the pronoun to the religion (millah), since the religion of Abraham was mentioned; and if you wish, you may return it to the enjoining.

Al-Mufaddal said: "bi-ha" (by it) is a pronoun referring to something unmentioned, like the Most High's words: ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad 38:32]. Ṭarafa said:

*"Upon the like of it, the wide-eyed one, when my companion says: 'Would that I might ransom you from it, and be ransomed!'"*

meaning: from the wasteland.

﴿Abraham enjoined it upon his sons﴾ – the sons: Ishmael and his mother Hagar the Copt; Isaac and his mother Sarah; Midian, [...] (an illegible word in the manuscript), Nafshan, Atun, Yashbaq, Shuwakh; and their mother all together was Qatura bint Yaqtan the Canaanite, whom Abraham married after the death of Sarah.

As for the Most High's words, ﴿and Jacob﴾: he was so named because he and ʿAys were twins; ʿAys came out first from their mother's womb, and Jacob came out following his track, grasping his heel (ʿaqaba). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, and the story has already passed.

It was also said: Jacob was named for the abundance of his offspring (ʿaqib).

On the authority of Safwan ibn Sulaym, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was sent after eight thousand prophets, four thousand of them from the Children of Israel" [Kanz al-ʿUmmal: 11/483, no. 32280; al-Bidaya wa-l-Nihaya: 2/183].

The meaning of the verse: "And he enjoined it also, and Jacob [enjoined] his twelve sons: Rubeel, the eldest of his sons; Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph, and Benjamin, and Ibn Yafin" [in Tafsir al-Tabari (1/790): Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Issachar, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph, Jacob, Simeon, Dan, Benjamin].

﴿O my sons﴾ means "that O my sons," and so it is in the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud. Al-Farra' said: He said this because enjoining is a speech, and its estimate was "and he said: O my sons," like the Most High's words: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:9], meaning: and He said to them, because what matters is the speech. And His words: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children, for the male is like the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:11], meaning: and He says "for the male."

The poet said:

*"I will reveal to you, among what I reveal, a branch of the branches of Najd and a branch of mine in the lands of India."*

meaning: "and I say," because revealing in meaning is like speaking with the tongue.

Ibn Mujahid related from some of them that "wa-Yaʿqub" is also in coordination with "banīhi," since he was among those enjoining.

﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this religion﴾ – He selected Islam for you.

﴿So do not die except as Muslims﴾ – believers. It was said: sincere. It was said: those who entrust themselves. It is related from al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad concerning His words, ﴿So do not die except as Muslims﴾, that it means: "those who think well of their Lord."

﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ – present.

﴿When death came to Jacob﴾ – the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, when they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do you not know that Jacob, on the day he died, enjoined his sons to be Jews?" [see Zad al-Masir: 1/133]. According to this saying [...] (an illegible word) ibn al-Khattab to the Jews.

Al-Kalbi said: When Jacob entered Egypt, he saw them worshipping idols and fires, so he gathered his sons and feared for them that.

﴿When he said to his sons: "What will you worship after me?"﴾ ʿAtaʾ said: Allah does not take a prophet until He gives him the choice between death and life. When Jacob was given the choice, he said: "Give me respite until I ask my sons and enjoin them." Allah did so for him. He gathered his sons and his sons' sons and said to them: "My appointed time has come; what will you worship after me?" – that is, after my death.

﴿They said: "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac, one God; and to Him we are submitting."﴾ Ubayy read: "your God and the God of Abraham and Ismail."

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar al-Jahdari read "wa-ilaha abika" in the singular. They said: because Ishmael was Jacob's paternal uncle, not his father.

The common reading is "ābāʾika" in the plural, and they said: "A man's paternal uncle is the twin of his father."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is the remnant of my fathers" [115],

and he also said: "Return my father to me, for I fear that Quraysh will do to him what Thaqif did to ʿUrwa ibn Masʿud" [116]. He meant al-ʿAbbas.

The Arabs call the paternal uncle "father" and call the maternal aunt "mother." Allah the Most High said: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾ [Yusuf 12:100], meaning Jacob and his maternal aunt, who was Joseph's aunt.

﴿One God﴾ – that is, we know Him and worship Him as one God.

﴿And we are to Him submitting.﴾ ﴿That is a nation﴾ – a community ﴿that has passed away; for it is what it earned﴾ – of religion and deeds.

﴿And for you is what you have earned.﴾

﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾ – rather, you will be asked about what you yourselves do.

﴿Abraham enjoined it upon his sons﴾ – the sons: Ishmael and his mother Hagar the Copt; Isaac and his mother Sarah; Midian, [...] (an illegible word in the manuscript), Nafshan, Atun, Yashbaq, Shuwakh; and their mother all together was Qatura bint Yaqtan the Canaanite, whom Abraham married after the death of Sarah.

As for the Most High's words, ﴿and Jacob﴾: he was so named because he and ʿAys were twins; ʿAys came out first from their mother's womb, and Jacob came out following his track, grasping his heel (ʿaqaba). This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, and the story has already passed.

It was also said: Jacob was named for the abundance of his offspring (ʿaqib).

On the authority of Safwan ibn Sulaym, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I was sent after eight thousand prophets, four thousand of them from the Children of Israel" [Kanz al-ʿUmmal: 11/483, no. 32280; al-Bidaya wa-l-Nihaya: 2/183].

The meaning of the verse: "And he enjoined it also, and Jacob [enjoined] his twelve sons: Rubeel, the eldest of his sons; Simeon, Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph, and Benjamin, and Ibn Yafin" [in Tafsir al-Tabari (1/790): Levi, Judah, Zebulun, Issachar, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph, Jacob, Simeon, Dan, Benjamin].

﴿O my sons﴾ means "that O my sons," and so it is in the reading of Ubayy and Ibn Masʿud. Al-Farra' said: He said this because enjoining is a speech, and its estimate was "and he said: O my sons," like the Most High's words: ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:9], meaning: and He said to them, because what matters is the speech. And His words: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children, for the male is like the share of two females﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:11], meaning: and He says "for the male."

The poet said:

*"I will reveal to you, among what I reveal, a branch of the branches of Najd and a branch of mine in the lands of India."*

meaning: "and I say," because revealing in meaning is like speaking with the tongue.

Ibn Mujahid related from some of them that "wa-Yaʿqub" is also in coordination with "banīhi," since he was among those enjoining.

﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this religion﴾ – He selected Islam for you.

﴿So do not die except as Muslims﴾ – believers. It was said: sincere. It was said: those who entrust themselves. It is related from al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad concerning His words, ﴿So do not die except as Muslims﴾, that it means: "those who think well of their Lord."

﴿Or were you witnesses﴾ – present.

﴿When death came to Jacob﴾ – the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, when they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do you not know that Jacob, on the day he died, enjoined his sons to be Jews?" [see Zad al-Masir: 1/133]. According to this saying [...] (an illegible word) ibn al-Khattab to the Jews.

Al-Kalbi said: When Jacob entered Egypt, he saw them worshipping idols and fires, so he gathered his sons and feared for them that.

﴿When he said to his sons: "What will you worship after me?"﴾ ʿAtaʾ said: Allah does not take a prophet until He gives him the choice between death and life. When Jacob was given the choice, he said: "Give me respite until I ask my sons and enjoin them." Allah did so for him. He gathered his sons and his sons' sons and said to them: "My appointed time has come; what will you worship after me?" – that is, after my death.

﴿They said: "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac, one God; and to Him we are submitting."﴾ Ubayy read: "your God and the God of Abraham and Ismail."

Yahya ibn Yaʿmar al-Jahdari read "wa-ilaha abika" in the singular. They said: because Ishmael was Jacob's paternal uncle, not his father.

The common reading is "ābāʾika" in the plural, and they said: "A man's paternal uncle is the twin of his father."

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This is the remnant of my fathers" [115],

and he also said: "Return my father to me, for I fear that Quraysh will do to him what Thaqif did to ʿUrwa ibn Masʿud" [116]. He meant al-ʿAbbas.

The Arabs call the paternal uncle "father" and call the maternal aunt "mother." Allah the Most High said: ﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾ [Yusuf 12:100], meaning Jacob and his maternal aunt, who was Joseph's aunt.

﴿One God﴾ – that is, we know Him and worship Him as one God.

﴿And we are to Him submitting.﴾ ﴿That is a nation﴾ – a community ﴿that has passed away; for it is what it earned﴾ – of religion and deeds.

﴿And for you is what you have earned.﴾

﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾ – rather, you will be asked about what you yourselves do.

Al-Tha'alabi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan)

Commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 135–137:

﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning the leading Jews of Madinah, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Wahb ibn Yahuda and Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, and concerning the Christians of Najran: al-Sayyid and al-Aqib and their companions. That is because each group disputed with the Muslims about the religion, each claiming that it had the greater right to the religion of God than the others. The Jews said: "Our religion is the best of religions, our prophet Musa is the best of the prophets, and our book, the Torah, is the best of books," and they disbelieved in 'Isa, the Injil, Muhammad and the Qur'an.

The Christians said: "Our prophet 'Isa is the best of the prophets, our book the Injil is the best of books, and our religion is the best of religions," and they disbelieved in Muhammad and the Qur'an. Each of the two groups said to the believers: "Follow our religion, for there is no religion but this." [God said:] "Call them to their religion." But except for the Hanifiyyah. Then God Almighty said: ﴿Say, O Muhammad: Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim﴾, i.e., rather, we follow the religion (millah) of Ibrahim. al-A'raj read (bal millatu) in the nominative, as a predicate.

(Hanifan) is in the accusative as a circumstantial/qualifying form (qata'). The intended meaning is "rather, the religion of Ibrahim, the hanif." When the alif and lam were dropped, the indefinite did not follow the definite, so it became detached and was put in the accusative; this is the view of the grammarians of Kufa. The grammarians of Basra said it is in the accusative as a state (hal). Ibn 'Abbas said: al-hanif is one who inclines away from all religions toward the religion of Islam. Its root is from al-hanf, which means an inclination and curvature in the foot, and from it Ahnaf ibn Qays was named.

Mujahid: sincere (mukhlisan).

Kathir ibn Ziyad said: I asked al-Hasan about the Hanifiyyah, and he said: It is the pilgrimage to this House.

al-Dahhak: If the hanif is with a Muslim, then he is the pilgrim; and if not, then he is a Muslim.

Qatadah: Among the Hanifiyyah is circumcision and abandoning marriage to two sisters.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists.﴾ This teaches the Muslims the path of tawhid and the way of faith. So He said: ﴿Say: We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿and what was sent down to Ibrahim﴾, which was ten scrolls,

﴿and Isma'il, and Ishaq, and Ya'qub, and the Tribes (al-Asbat)﴾, meaning the sons of Ya'qub, whose singular is sibt. They were so named because each of them had a multitude of people descended from him; the sibt of a man is his grandson, and from this it is said that al-Hasan and al-Husayn (peace be upon them) were the two grandsons (sibtan) of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The asbat among the Children of Israel were like the tribes among the Arabs and the peoples among non-Arabs.

It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Darir: The original meaning of sibt in the language is an intertwined tree with many branches, so the asbat were named after it because of their multitude. Just as the branches come from one tree, so the asbat were from Ya'qub. Among the asbat there were prophets, and so He said: ﴿and what was sent down to them﴾. It is also said: they were the sons of Ya'qub from his loins, all of whom became prophets.

﴿and what was given to Musa﴾, meaning the Torah,

﴿and 'Isa﴾, the Injil. ﴿And what was given (utiya)﴾ means was granted.

﴿to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them﴾, so that we believe in some and disbelieve in others, as the Jews and Christians did.

﴿And to Him we are Muslims.﴾

When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God ﷺ recited it to the Jews and Christians and said: "Indeed God has commanded me with this." When the Jews heard the mention of 'Isa, they denied and disbelieved in him, and the Christians disbelieved as well, saying that 'Isa was not in the rank of other prophets but was the son of God. Then God Almighty revealed: ﴿And if they believe﴾, meaning the Jews and Christians,

﴿in the same way as you believe in it﴾, i.e., in all that you believe, as your belief. It is also said: "like" here is redundant, meaning "in what you believe in." Ibn 'Abbas used to recite it this way and say: "Read: (fa-in amanu bima amantum bihi)." There is no "like" (mithl) for God, and its parallel is His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, i.e., nothing like Him. The poet said:

O my blamer, leave me from your blame...
One like me does not accept from one like you.

i.e., I do not accept from you.

﴿then they are guided; but if they turn away, they are only in opposition (shiqaq)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and al-Akhfash said: in opposition, in disagreement. It is said: shaqqa yashuqqu mushaqqatan when one opposes, as if each has taken a side other than his companion's side. Its proof is His saying: ﴿Let not my opposition (shiqaqi) lead you to sin﴾, i.e., my opposition. The poet recited:

So he went to her, and the one who hunted her young, in opposition, and some of them were struck and abandoned.

Ibn Salamah and al-Suddi said: in enmity, each taking a side against the other, i.e., striving against him and what burdens him, from His saying: ﴿except with great difficulty to the souls﴾. Its proof is His saying: ﴿That is because they opposed (shaqqu) God and His Messenger﴾, i.e., they were hostile to God and His Messenger.

Bishr ibn Abi Hazim said:

Otherwise know that we and you
are rebels, as long as we live, in opposition.

i.e., in enmity.

Muqatil and Abu 'Ubaydah: in error and disagreement. Its explanation is His saying: ﴿And if you fear a breach (shiqaq) between them﴾, i.e., disagreement between them.

The poet said:

How long shall we kill the scholars by force,
and be struck by division and hypocrisy?

i.e., by error and disagreement.

al-Kisa'i: it is the removal of obedience. Its explanation is His saying: ﴿And whoever opposes (yushaqiq) the Messenger﴾.

al-Hasan: in distance and separation until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿So God will suffice you against them, O Muhammad﴾, meaning the Jews and Christians.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of their words,

﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of their states. God the Almighty sufficed them regarding their affairs: by killing and captivity against the Banu Qurayzah, and expulsion and exile against the Banu al-Nadir, and the jizyah and humiliation against the Christians of Najran.

Completion of Surah al-Baqarah

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 138–141:

﴿صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ Abu al-'Aliyah said: the religion of God.

Mujahid said: Islam.

Ibn 'Abbas said: It is that the Christians, when a child was born to one of them and seven days had passed over him, would dip him in water they had, called al-Ma'udi, and dye him with it to purify him in place of circumcision. When they had done this to him, they would say: "Now he has truly become a Christian." So God, exalted is He, informed that His religion is Islam, not what the Christians do.

Ibn Kaysan said: ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ means the direction of God, that is, the qiblah. He said: It is also said: the proof of God, with which He argued against His servants.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Zajjaj said: the creation of God, from "I dyed the garment" when I changed its color and gave it its form. The meaning then is: God began the creation upon Islam. Its evidence is the words of Muqatil on this verse, ﴿فِطْرَتَ اللَّهِ الَّتِي فَطَرَ النَّاسَ عَلَيْهَا﴾ [Surah al-Rum 30:30], that is, the religion of God.

It is clarified by what Hammam ibn Munabbih related from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Every child is born upon this fitrah. ﴿أَمْ تَقُولُونَ﴾ Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Hafs recited with the ta' (you say), and Abu 'Ubayd chose this. The rest read with the ya' (they say), and Abu Hatim chose this. Whoever reads with the ta' does so because of the address before it, ﴿قُلْ أَتُحَاجُّونَنَا فِي اللَّهِ﴾, and the one after it, ﴿قُلْ أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ أَمِ اللَّهُ﴾. Whoever reads with the ya' it is a report about the Jews and Christians.

﴿إِنَّ إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَالْأَسْبَاطَ كَانُوا هُوداً أَوْ نَصَارَى﴾ God said:

﴿قُلْ﴾ O Muhammad. ﴿أَأَنْتُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِدِينِهِمْ﴾

﴿أَمِ اللَّهُ﴾ And God has informed me that he was not a Jew nor a Christian, but was a ḥanīf, a Muslim...

﴿وَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنْ كَتَمَ﴾ hid.

﴿شَهَادَةً عِنْدَهُ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ that is, their knowledge that Abraham and his sons were Muslims, and that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the truth and a messenger.

﴿وَمَا اللَّهُ بِغَافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ ﴿تِلْكَ أُمَّةٌ قَدْ خَلَتْ لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ﴾ the verse.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 142–143:

﴿سَيَقُولُ السُّفَهاءُ الجهال﴾.

﴿مِنَ النَّاسِ ما وَلَّاهُمْ﴾ صرفهم وحوّلهم.

﴿عَنْ قِبْلَتِهِمُ الَّتِي كانُوا عَلَيْها﴾ من بيت المقدس. نزلت في اليهود ومشركي العرب بمكّة ومنافقي المدينة، فطعنوا في تحويل القبلة، وقال مشركو مكّة: قد تردّد على محمّد أمره، واشتاق إلى مولده ومولد آبائه، قد توجّه نحو قبلتكم، وهو راجع إلى دينكم عاجلا.

قال الله: ﴿قُلْ لِلَّهِ الْمَشْرِقُ وَالْمَغْرِبُ﴾ ملكا، والخلق عبيده، يحولهم كيف شاء.

﴿يَهْدِي مَنْ يَشاءُ إِلى صِراطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ﴾. ﴿وَكَذلِكَ جَعَلْناكُمْ أُمَّةً وَسَطاً﴾ عدلا خيارا. تقول العرب: انزل وسط الوادي، أي تخيّر موضعا فيه، ويقال لرسول الله ﷺ: هو وسط قريش نسبا، أي خيرهم. قال الله تعالى: ﴿قالَ أَوْسَطُهُمْ﴾ (سورة القلم: 28)، أي أخيرهم وأعدلهم، وأصله أنّ خير الأشياء أوسطها. قال زهير:

هم وسط ترضى الأنام لحكمهم ... إذا نزلت احدى الليالي بمعظم

وقال الكلبي: يعني متوسطة أهل دين وسط بين الغلو والتقصير، لأنّهما مذمومان في الدّين.

قال ثعلب: يقال: جلس وسط القوم ووسط الدّار، وكذلك فيما يحتمل البينونة [واحتمل وسطا له] (كلام غير مقروء وما أثبتناه هو الظاهر) بالفتح، وكذلك فيما لا يحتمل البينونة.

نزلت هذه الآية في مرحب وربيع وأصحابهما من رؤساء اليهود، قالوا لمعاذ بن جبل: ما ترك محمّد قبلتنا إلّا حسدا، وإنّ قبلتنا قبلة الأنبياء، ولقد علم محمّد أنّا عدل بين النّاس. فقال معاذ: إنّا على حق وعدل. فأنزل الله ﴿وَكَذلِكَ﴾ أي وهكذا، وقيل: الكاف فيه للتشبيه، تقديره: وكما اخترنا إبراهيم وذريته واصطفيناهم ﴿كَذلِكَ جَعَلْناكُمْ أُمَّةً وَسَطاً﴾. مردودة على قوله: ﴿وَلَقَدِ اصْطَفَيْناهُ فِي الدُّنْيا﴾ (سورة البقرة: 130) الآية.

﴿لِتَكُونُوا شُهَداءَ عَلَى النَّاسِ﴾ يوم القيامة، أنّ الرّسل قد أبلغتهم.

﴿وَيَكُونَ الرَّسُولُ﴾ محمّد ﷺ. ﴿عَلَيْكُمْ شَهِيداً﴾ معدلا مزكّيا لكم. وذلك أنّ الله تعالى يجمع الأولين والآخرين في صعيد واحد، يسمعهم الدّاعي، وينفذهم البصر، ثمّ يقول كفّار الأمم:

﴿أَلَمْ يَأْتِكُمْ نَذِيرٌ﴾ فتشكرون، ويقولون: ما جاءنا من نذير.

فيسأل الأنبياء عن ذلك، فيقولون: قد كذّبوا، قد بلغناهم وأعذرنا إليهم، فيسألهم البيّنة، وهو أعلم بإقامة الحجة. فيؤتى بأمّة محمّد ﷺ فيشهدون لهم أنّهم قد بلغوا. فتقول الأمم الماضية: من أين علموا بذلك وبيننا وبينهم مدة مريدة؟ فيقولون: علمنا ذلك بإخبار الله إيانا في كتابه الناطق على لسان رسوله الصادق. فيؤتى محمّد ﷺ فيسأل عن حال أمّته، فيزكّيهم ويشهد لصدقهم.

﴿وَما جَعَلْنَا الْقِبْلَةَ الَّتِي كُنْتَ عَلَيْها﴾ يعني التحويل عن القبلة الّتي كنت عليها، وهي بيت المقدس.

وقيل: معناه القبلة الّتي أنت عليها، أي الكعبة، كقوله: ﴿كُنْتُمْ خَيْرَ أُمَّةٍ﴾ (سورة آل عمران: 110)، أي أنتم.

﴿إِلَّا لِنَعْلَمَ﴾ لنرى ونميّز ﴿مَنْ يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ في القبلة ﴾ ﴿مِمَّنْ يَنْقَلِبُ عَلى عَقِبَيْهِ﴾ فيرتد ويرجع إلى قبلته الأولى. هذا قول المفسرين. وقال أهل المعاني: معناه إلّا لعلمنا ﴿مَنْ يَتَّبِعُ الرَّسُولَ مِمَّنْ يَنْقَلِبُ عَلى عَقِبَيْهِ﴾، كأنّه سبق ذلك في علمه أنّ تحويل القبلة سبب هداية قوم وضلالة آخرين. وقد تضع العرب لفظ الاستقبال موضع المضي، كقوله: ﴿فَلِمَ تَقْتُلُونَ أَنْبِياءَ اللَّهِ مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ (سورة البقرة: 91)، أي قتلتم.

وقال بعض أهل اللّغة: للعلم منزلتين: علم بالشيء قبل وجوده، وعلم به بعد وجوده، والحكم للعلم الموجود، لأنّه يوجب الثواب والعقاب. فمعنى قوله ﴿لِنَعْلَمَ﴾ أي لنعلم العلم الّذي يستحقّ به العامل الثّواب والعقاب. وهذا على معنى التقدير، كرجل قال لصاحبه: النّار تحرق الحطب، وقال الآخر: لا، فردّ عليه: هات النّار والحطب، ليعلم إنّها تحرقه، أي ليتقرر علم ذلك عندك.

وقوله: ﴿لنعلم﴾ تقديره: ليتقرّر علمنا عندكم. وقيل معناه: ليعلم محمّد ﷺ، فأضاف علمه عليه السّلام إلى نفسه سبحانه تخصيصا وتفصيلا، كقوله: ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يُؤْذُونَ اللَّهَ﴾ (سورة الأحزاب: 57)، وقوله: ﴿فَلَمَّا آسَفُونا انْتَقَمْنا﴾ (سورة الزخرف: 55) ونحوهما.

﴿وَإِنْ كانَتْ﴾ وقد كانت توليه القبلة وتحويلها، فأنّث الفعل لتأنيث الاسم، كقولهم: ذهبت بعض أصابعه. وقيل: هذه الكناية راجعة إلى القبلة بعينها، أراد: وإن كانت الكعبة.

﴿لَكَبِيرَةً﴾ ثقيلة شديدة. ﴿إِلَّا عَلَى الَّذِينَ هَدَى اللَّهُ﴾ أي هداهم الله. وقال سيبويه: (وانّ) تأكيد منه باليمين، ولذلك دخلت اللّام في جوابها.

﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمانَكُمْ﴾ وذلك أنّ يحيى بن أخطب وأصحابه من اليهود قالوا للمسلمين: أخبرونا عن صلاتكم نحو بيت المقدس، أكانت هدى أم ضلالة؟ فإن كانت هدى فقد تحولتم عنها، وإن كانت ضلالة لقد دنتم الله بها، فإن من مات منكم عليها لقد مات على الضلالة.

قال المسلمون: إنّما الهدى ما أمر الله تعالى به، والضلالة ما نهى الله عنه.

قالوا: فما شهادتكم على من مات منكم على قبلتنا، وكان مات قبل أن تحوّل القبلة؟

أسعد بن زرارة من بني النجّار، والبراء بن معرور من بني سلمة، وكانا من النقباء، ومات رجال آخرون. فانطلقت عشائرهم إلى النبيّ ﷺ فقالوا: يا رسول الله، قد صرفك الله إلى قبلة إبراهيم، فكيف إخواننا الّذين ماتوا وهم يصلّون إلى بيت المقدس؟ فأنزل الله تعالى: ﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمانَكُمْ﴾ (سورة البقرة: 143)، أي صلاتكم إلى بيت المقدس.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ بِالنَّاسِ لَرَؤُفٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾

وفي ﴿رؤوف﴾ ثلاث قراءات: مهموز مثقّل، وهي قراءة نافع وابن عامر وحفص، واختيار أبي حاتم، قال: لأنّ أكثر أسماء الله على فعول وفعيل. قال الشاعر:

نطيع رسولنا ونطيع ربّا ... هو الرّحمن كان بنا رؤوفا

وروف غير مهموز مثقّل: قراءة أبي جعفر.

ورؤف مهموز مخفف، وهي قراءة الباقين، واختيار أبي عبيد.

قال جرير:

ترى للمسلمين عليك حقّا ... كفعل الوالد الرءوف الرّحيم

فالرأفة أشدّ الرحمة.

﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمانَكُمْ﴾ وذلك أنّ يحيى بن أخطب وأصحابه من اليهود قالوا للمسلمين: أخبرونا عن صلاتكم نحو بيت المقدس، أكانت هدى أم ضلالة؟ فإن كانت هدى فقد تحولتم عنها، وإن كانت ضلالة لقد دنتم الله بها، فإن من مات منكم عليها لقد مات على الضلالة.

قال المسلمون: إنّما الهدى ما أمر الله تعالى به، والضلالة ما نهى الله عنه.

قالوا: فما شهادتكم على من مات منكم على قبلتنا، وكان مات قبل أن تحوّل القبلة؟

أسعد بن زرارة من بني النجّار، والبراء بن معرور من بني سلمة، وكانا من النقباء، ومات رجال آخرون. فانطلقت عشائرهم إلى النبيّ ﷺ فقالوا: يا رسول الله، قد صرفك الله إلى قبلة إبراهيم، فكيف إخواننا الّذين ماتوا وهم يصلّون إلى بيت المقدس؟ فأنزل الله تعالى: ﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِيعَ إِيمانَكُمْ﴾ (سورة البقرة: 143)، أي صلاتكم إلى بيت المقدس.

﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ بِالنَّاسِ لَرَؤُفٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾

وفي ﴿رؤوف﴾ ثلاث قراءات: مهموز مثقّل، وهي قراءة نافع وابن عامر وحفص، واختيار أبي حاتم، قال: لأنّ أكثر أسماء الله على فعول وفعيل. قال الشاعر:

نطيع رسولنا ونطيع ربّا ... هو الرّحمن كان بنا رؤوفا

وروف غير مهموز مثقّل: قراءة أبي جعفر.

ورؤف مهموز مخفف، وهي قراءة الباقين، واختيار أبي عبيد.

قال جرير:

ترى للمسلمين عليك حقّا ... كفعل الوالد الرءوف الرّحيم

فالرأفة أشدّ الرحمة.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 144–147:**

﴿We see you turning your face about in the sky.﴾ The first thing abrogated (naskh, abrogation) in the matters of the sharia (divine law) was the matter of the qiblah (direction of prayer). That was because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions used to pray in Makkah toward the Ka'bah. When the Prophet (ﷺ) emigrated to Madinah and arrived there, after two nights had passed in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, God commanded him to pray toward the Rock in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), so that it would be closer to the Jews' acceptance of him when he prayed toward their qiblah, along with what they found of his description in the Torah.

This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun).

Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: God said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "These Jews face a house among the houses of God. If [we] faced it..." So he faced it. [They] all said: The Prophet and his companions prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for seventeen months, and the Ansar had prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for two years before the Prophet's arrival.

The Ka'bah was the more beloved of the two qiblahs to the Prophet (ﷺ).

They differed about the reason why he (ﷺ) disliked the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis and preferred the qiblah of the Ka'bah.

Ibn Abbas said: Because it was the qiblah of Abraham, peace be upon him.

Mujahid said: Because the Jews said, "Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our qiblah."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis, the Jews said: "Muhammad claims that he is a prophet, yet no one sees him except in our religion. Does he not pray toward our qiblah and follow our practice? If this is prophethood, then we are more ancient and have a greater share." This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it grieved him, and it increased his longing for the Ka'bah.

Ibn Zayd said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) faced Bayt al-Maqdis, it reached him that the Jews were saying: "By God, we do not know where Muhammad and his companions' qiblah is, until we guided them."

They all said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then said to Jibril: "I wish that God would turn me away from the qiblah of the Jews to another, for I hate them and I hate their agreeing with them." Jibril said: "I am only a servant like you; the matter is not in my hands. So ask your Lord" [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 26; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/142.]].

Then Jibril ascended, and the Messenger of God kept gazing continually at the sky, hoping that Jibril would descend to him with what would come concerning the matter of the qiblah.

﴿We see you turning your face about in the sky﴾: turning and changing your face, O Muhammad, in the sky.

﴿So We shall surely turn you﴾: so We shall certainly turn you, and redirect you.

﴿to a qiblah that pleases you﴾: that you love and are pleased with.

﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾: i.e., toward it and aiming for it.

The poet said:

"And strike the people toward the kings, until the spear-shaft quivers."

I.e., toward them. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place.

"Al-Masjid al-Haram" (the Sacred Mosque): the sacred one, like "al-kitab" in the sense of "al-maktub" (the written) and "al-hisab" in the sense of "al-mahsub" (the reckoned).

﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾: in land or sea, plain or mountain, east or west, ﴿turn your faces toward it﴾. The qiblah was changed in Rajab, after the sun had passed its zenith, two months before the battle of Badr.

Mujahid and others said: This verse was revealed while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in the mosque of Banu Salamah, and he had prayed two rak'ahs of the noon prayer with his companions. He turned during the prayer and faced the water-spout (al-mizab). The men were moved to the place of the women, and the women to the place of the men. That mosque was therefore named "the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs."

Ibn Abbas said: The whole House is a qiblah, the qiblah of the House is its door, the House is the qiblah of the people of the mosque, the mosque is the qiblah of the people of the Haram, and the Haram is the qiblah of all the people of the earth. When the qiblah was changed to the Ka'bah, the Jews said: "O Muhammad, you were not commanded with this" — meaning the qiblah — "and it is nothing but something you have invented from your own self."

Qatadah said: He prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and at times he prayed toward the Ka'bah. "If you had held to our qiblah, we would have hoped that you are our companion whom we await. And we saw you circling the Ka'bah, which is built stones." So God revealed:

﴿Indeed, those who were given the Book know that it is the truth﴾: i.e., the matter of the Ka'bah is the truth. ﴿from their Lord﴾: and that it is the qiblah of Abraham. Then He threatened them, saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what they do﴾ [Abu Ja'far, Ibn ... and al-Kisa'i read it with the ta' (you), and Barid said: "Indeed you, O assembly of ..., seek my union, and ... concerning your reward and your answer." The rest read it with the ya' (they), meaning: God is not unaware of what the Jews do, so He will requite them in this world and the Hereafter] [[From the margin of the manuscript.]].

﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book﴾: i.e., the Jews of Madinah and the Christians of Najran. They said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Bring us a sign just as the prophets before you brought." So God revealed: ﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book﴾.

﴿every sign, they would not follow your qiblah﴾: i.e., the Ka'bah. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said: Why is "la-in" (if indeed) answered with "ma" (not)? Because it has the meaning of "law" (if). It was also said that it is answered with "ma" because of the meaning of an oath, as if he had said: "By God, if you bring to those who were given the Book every sign..." up to ﴿and you are not a follower of their qiblah﴾, because the Jews face Bayt al-Maqdis, and the Christians face the east.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾: i.e., their wishes regarding the matter of the qiblah.

﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾: that it is the truth, and that it is the qiblah of Abraham.

﴿Indeed, you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾: the deniers, who harm themselves.

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾: i.e., the believers among the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

﴿They recognize him﴾: i.e., Muhammad, ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾: among the Christians.

Al-Kalbi on al-Rabi' on Ibn Abbas said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, Umar said to Abdullah ibn Salam: "God has revealed to His Prophet: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons﴾. So how, O Abdullah, is this recognition?"

Abdullah ibn Salam said: "O Umar, I recognized him among you when I saw him, as I recognize my son when I see him playing with the children. And I am more knowing of Muhammad than I am of my son." Umar said: "And how is that?"

He said: "I testify that he is a true messenger from God, and God has described him in our Book. But I do not know what the women do." Umar said to him: "May God grant you success, O son of Salam. You have spoken the truth and been correct."

﴿And indeed, a party of them conceal the truth﴾: i.e., the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the matter of the Ka'bah.

﴿while they know it.﴾ Then He said: ﴿The truth﴾ [147]: i.e., this is the truth, a predicate of a suppressed subject (mubtada').

It was also said: it is in the nominative by the supposition of a verb, i.e., "the truth has come to you," as He said: ﴿And the truth has come to you in this﴾ [[Surah Hud: 120.]].

Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honour his face, read ﴿al-haqqa min Rabbika﴾ in the accusative, as an exhortation (al-ighra').

﴿So never be among the doubters﴾: the disputers, derived from "al-mirya" (doubt). The address in this verse and in what precedes it is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is others. Whatever similar address comes to you, this is its path.

It was also said that it is answered with "ma" because of the meaning of an oath, as if he had said: "By God, if you bring to those who were given the Book every sign..." up to ﴿and you are not a follower of their qiblah﴾, because the Jews face Bayt al-Maqdis, and the Christians face the east.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾: i.e., their wishes regarding the matter of the qiblah.

﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾: that it is the truth, and that it is the qiblah of Abraham.

﴿Indeed, you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾: the deniers, who harm themselves.

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾: i.e., the believers among the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

﴿They recognize him﴾: i.e., Muhammad, ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾: among the Christians.

Al-Kalbi on al-Rabi' on Ibn Abbas said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, Umar said to Abdullah ibn Salam: "God has revealed to His Prophet: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons﴾. So how, O Abdullah, is this recognition?"

Abdullah ibn Salam said: "O Umar, I recognized him among you when I saw him, as I recognize my son when I see him playing with the children. And I am more knowing of Muhammad than I am of my son." Umar said: "And how is that?"

He said: "I testify that he is a true messenger from God, and God has described him in our Book. But I do not know what the women do." Umar said to him: "May God grant you success, O son of Salam. You have spoken the truth and been correct."

﴿And indeed, a party of them conceal the truth﴾: i.e., the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the matter of the Ka'bah.

﴿while they know it.﴾ Then He said: ﴿The truth﴾ [147]: i.e., this is the truth, a predicate of a suppressed subject (mubtada').

It was also said: it is in the nominative by the supposition of a verb, i.e., "the truth has come to you," as He said: ﴿And the truth has come to you in this﴾ [[Surah Hud: 120.]].

Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honour his face, read ﴿al-haqqa min Rabbika﴾ in the accusative, as an exhortation (al-ighra').

﴿So never be among the doubters﴾: the disputers, derived from "al-mirya" (doubt). The address in this verse and in what precedes it is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but what is meant is others. Whatever similar address comes to you, this is its path.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 144–147:**

﴿We see you turning your face about in the sky.﴾ The first thing abrogated (naskh, abrogation) in the matters of the sharia (divine law) was the matter of the qiblah (direction of prayer). That was because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions used to pray in Makkah toward the Ka'bah. When the Prophet (ﷺ) emigrated to Madinah and arrived there, after two nights had passed in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, God commanded him to pray toward the Rock in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), so that it would be closer to the Jews' acceptance of him when he prayed toward their qiblah, along with what they found of his description in the Torah.

This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun).

Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: God said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "These Jews face a house among the houses of God. If [we] faced it..." So he faced it. [They] all said: The Prophet and his companions prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for seventeen months, and the Ansar had prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for two years before the Prophet's arrival.

The Ka'bah was the more beloved of the two qiblahs to the Prophet (ﷺ).

They differed about the reason why he (ﷺ) disliked the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis and preferred the qiblah of the Ka'bah.

Ibn Abbas said: Because it was the qiblah of Abraham, peace be upon him.

Mujahid said: Because the Jews said, "Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our qiblah."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis, the Jews said: "Muhammad claims that he is a prophet, yet no one sees him except in our religion. Does he not pray toward our qiblah and follow our practice? If this is prophethood, then we are more ancient and have a greater share." This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and it grieved him, and it increased his longing for the Ka'bah.

Ibn Zayd said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) faced Bayt al-Maqdis, it reached him that the Jews were saying: "By God, we do not know where Muhammad and his companions' qiblah is, until we guided them."

They all said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then said to Jibril: "I wish that God would turn me away from the qiblah of the Jews to another, for I hate them and I hate their agreeing with them." Jibril said: "I am only a servant like you; the matter is not in my hands. So ask your Lord" [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 26; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/142.]].

Then Jibril ascended, and the Messenger of God kept gazing continually at the sky, hoping that Jibril would descend to him with what would come concerning the matter of the qiblah.

﴿We see you turning your face about in the sky﴾: turning and changing your face, O Muhammad, in the sky.

﴿So We shall surely turn you﴾: so We shall certainly turn you, and redirect you.

﴿to a qiblah that pleases you﴾: that you love and are pleased with.

﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾: i.e., toward it and aiming for it.

The poet said:

"And strike the people toward the kings, until the spear-shaft quivers."

I.e., toward them. It is in the accusative as an adverb of place.

"Al-Masjid al-Haram" (the Sacred Mosque): the sacred one, like "al-kitab" in the sense of "al-maktub" (the written) and "al-hisab" in the sense of "al-mahsub" (the reckoned).

﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾: in land or sea, plain or mountain, east or west, ﴿turn your faces toward it﴾. The qiblah was changed in Rajab, after the sun had passed its zenith, two months before the battle of Badr.

Mujahid and others said: This verse was revealed while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in the mosque of Banu Salamah, and he had prayed two rak'ahs of the noon prayer with his companions. He turned during the prayer and faced the water-spout (al-mizab). The men were moved to the place of the women, and the women to the place of the men. That mosque was therefore named "the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs."

Ibn Abbas said: The whole House is a qiblah, the qiblah of the House is its door, the House is the qiblah of the people of the mosque, the mosque is the qiblah of the people of the Haram, and the Haram is the qiblah of all the people of the earth. When the qiblah was changed to the Ka'bah, the Jews said: "O Muhammad, you were not commanded with this" — meaning the qiblah — "and it is nothing but something you have invented from your own self."

Qatadah said: He prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and at times he prayed toward the Ka'bah. "If you had held to our qiblah, we would have hoped that you are our companion whom we await. And we saw you circling the Ka'bah, which is built stones." So God revealed:

﴿Indeed, those who were given the Book know that it is the truth﴾: i.e., the matter of the Ka'bah is the truth. ﴿from their Lord﴾: and that it is the qiblah of Abraham. Then He threatened them, saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what they do﴾ [Abu Ja'far, Ibn ... and al-Kisa'i read it with the ta' (you), and Barid said: "Indeed you, O assembly of ..., seek my union, and ... concerning your reward and your answer." The rest read it with the ya' (they), meaning: God is not unaware of what the Jews do, so He will requite them in this world and the Hereafter] [[From the margin of the manuscript.]].

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 2, verses 148–152 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿For every nation there is a direction﴾. That is, for every community of a religion there is a qibla.

﴿to which it turns﴾: facing it and turning towards it. One says *wallaytuhu* and *wallaytu ilayhi* ("I turned it" and "I turned towards it"). When you come towards something you say *wallaytu ilayhi*, and when you turn away from it you say *wallaytu 'anhu*.

The root meaning of *tawliyah* is turning away. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Raja' and Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik recited it as *huwa muwalliha* (﴿He is the one who turns it﴾), meaning: turned towards it.

In the codex of Ubayy it reads: *wa-lika qiblatun huwa muwalliha*, and in the codex of 'Abdullah: *wa-li-kull ja'alna qiblatan huwa muwalliha*.

﴿So race to good works﴾: hasten to do good deeds. Its figurative sense is *fa-staqu ila al-khayrat*, i.e., let each of you outstrip the others. The particle of the verb is omitted, as in the saying of the poet:

*wa-huwa al-da'i [......] 'alaykum bi-al-harb... wa-man yamil siwakum fa-innI minhu ghayru mail*

He meant: "whoever inclines towards others than you."

﴿wherever you may be﴾: this refers to the People of the Book.

﴿Allah will bring you all together﴾: on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾.

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾: *haythu* is a particle indicating place. It has three dialectal forms: with *ya'* and *tha'* (*ḥaythu*), which is the dialect of Quraysh and the reading of the majority; scholars differed over the case of its final vowel. Some said it is indeclinable on a *damma*, like *mundhu* and *qattu*. Others said it is in the accusative of termination, as in His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾.

*Ḥaythu* with *ya'* and a fatha on the *tha'* is the reading of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. Al-Kisa'i said: it is pronounced with a fatha because the *ya'* is quiescent, and when two quiescent letters come together in one word they move the second to a fatha, since fatha is the lightest vowel, as in *layta* and *kayfa*.

*Ḥawthu* with *waw* and *damma* is the dialect of Ibn 'Umar. It is reported that he was asked where the worshipper should place his hands during prayer, and he said: "Throw them wherever they fall."

﴿So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, up to: ﴿And wherever you are, O believers, turn your faces towards it﴾.

﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾: here the *lam* is the lam of purpose (*lam kay*), which entered upon *an*, so the preceding *kasra* was written with it. Some omitted the hamza of *an* for ease. *Ḥujjah* is of the pattern *fu'lah*, from *ḥajj*, meaning "clarification," from which comes *maḥajjah*, the clear and well-travelled path, because it is intended. One says *muḥajjah* for disputation, because each of the two opponents seeks to establish his proof and to refute what is in the hand of his adversary.

Scholars differed about the interpretation of this verse and the meaning of the exception (*illa*) in it. Some of the interpreters said: the meaning of the verse is that the qibla was changed to the Ka'bah, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, for if you pray towards it, they would argue against you saying: "Why did you abandon facing the Ka'bah and turn to something else? Unless you have no qibla!" ﴿except those who wronged﴾: they are the Quraysh and the Jews. As for the Quraysh, they would say: "He only returned to the Ka'bah because he knew it was the qibla of his fathers and that it is the truth; and so he will return to our religion, knowing that it is the truth." As for the Jews, they would say: "He did not turn away from Bayt al-Maqdis while knowing it is the truth, unless he does things by his own opinion and claims that he was commanded to do so." This is the view chosen by al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah al-Dabbi, and it is a sound and accepted view.

Others said: the meaning of the verse is ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the People of the Book will have no argument against you. Their argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions in their prayer towards Bayt al-Maqdis was that they would say: "Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qibla is until we guided them!" and "Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our qibla." These are the arguments with which they would argue against the believers, in a spirit of hostility and deception, to mislead the ignorant polytheists. Then He said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾, and they are the polytheists of Mecca. Their argument was that when the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah they said: "Muhammad has become confused in his religion, so he turned towards our qibla, and he knows that we are more rightly guided than him, that he cannot do without us, and that he will soon return to our religion just as he returned to our qibla." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi, and it is the view preferred by Muhammad ibn Jarir.

On these two views, the exception with *illa* is a valid exception in the manner of your saying: "No one among the people travelled except your brother," which affirms travel for the brother, while it is negated for everyone else among the people. Likewise His saying, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those who wronged﴾: it negates that anyone has an argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions because of their turning to the Ka'bah, ﴿except those who wronged﴾ of the Quraysh, for they have an argument against them for the reason we mentioned.

The meaning of *ḥujjah* in these two views is disputation, argument, and false claim, as in His saying: ﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾, i.e., there is no dispute. And His saying: ﴿Do you argue with us about Allah?﴾ and ﴿that they may argue with you﴾ and ﴿and you argue﴾ and ﴿you disputed﴾: all of these mean argumentation and contention, not evidence and proof. The word *alladhina* is in the genitive position, as if He had said "except to those who wronged." When the preposition *lam* was dropped, *alladhina* took its place. So said al-Kisa'i.

Al-Farra' said: its position is accusative by the exception, and [......] from them was returned to the wording *al-nas* because it is general, even though each one of them differs from the other. Allah knows best.

Some said: it is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*) from the first sentence, and its meaning is: "unless there will be an argument against you from all the people, except for those who wronged, for they will argue against you in falsehood and dispute with you by injustice." This is like saying to a man: "All the people are your companions except the wrongdoer to you," meaning [......] that he does not praise you because of his enmity towards you. And like saying to a man: "You have no right with me except if you wrong," and "You have no argument except falsehood, and falsehood is not an argument." This is an exception that is not from the speech of al-Hasan.

Like the saying of one who says: "There is no one in the house except the wild animals," as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

*wa-ma bi-al-rab'i min ahad illa wa-ara li-aya ma... amamha wa-nawi ka-al-hawd bi-al-mazlumah al-jald*

And this is the view of al-Farra' and al-Mu'arrikh.

Abu Rawq said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the Jews, will have no argument against you. This is because they had known that the Ka'bah is the qibla of Ibrahim, and they had found in the Torah that Muhammad would be turned towards it. So Allah turned him towards it, so that they would have no argument, so that they could not argue that: "This Prophet whom we find in our Book will be turned towards it, but you were not turned!" When the Prophet (ﷺ) was turned, their argument disappeared. Then He said: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, meaning: except that they wrong you and conceal what they knew.

Al-Akhfash said: its meaning is "it is sufficient for those who wronged" (*li-kafa al-ladhina zalamu*): ﴿they have no knowledge of it, they follow only assumption﴾, meaning: rather, they follow assumption. And His saying: ﴿and for no one has he any favour to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord﴾, meaning: but rather seeking the countenance of your Lord. So it is an independent sentence apart from the first.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, as transmitted by Abu 'Ubayd: "The place of *illa* here is not an exception, because a wrongdoer does not have an argument. Rather, its place is that of the conjunction *waw*, as if He had said: 'Nor those who wronged,' meaning: 'and those who wronged do not have an argument either.'"

Al-Mufaddal recited:

*ma bi-al-madinah dar ghayr wahidah... dar al-khalifah illa dar Marwan*

And he also recited:

*wa-kull akh mufariqah akhuhu... la-'amr abika illa al-farqadan*

Meaning: "the two Farqadan (stars) are also separated." Al-Akhfash recited:

*wa-ara laha dara bi-aghdarah al-Sayyidan... lam yadrus laha rasm*

*illa ramadan hamidan dafa'at 'anhu al-riyah khawalid suham*

That is: "I see for it a dwelling and ashes."

This view is supported by what Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid transmitted from some of them that some recited ﴿to those who wronged﴾ with a lightened *lam*, meaning ﴿with those who wronged﴾.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿so that people will have no argument﴾, meaning the Jews, ﴿against you﴾ concerning the matter of the Ka'bah, since they would not face it, though it is the qibla of Ibrahim. They would say: "You claim you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, yet you do not face his qibla!" ﴿nor those who wronged﴾, meaning the polytheists of Mecca, because they said: "The Ka'bah is the qibla of our grandfather Ibrahim. Why has Muhammad turned away from it, so that he does not pray towards it, but prays towards the qibla of the Jews?"

Qatrub said: the meaning is "except upon those who wronged," so that its reference returns to the *kaf* and *mim* (of *'alaykum*), i.e., "except upon those who wronged, for upon them is the argument." So the preposition was omitted. This is the choice of Abu Mansur al-Azhari.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi relating it from him, and Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some of them that he said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾ here refers to some people among the Arabs who were Jews and Christians, and who used to argue against the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the rest of the Arabs, they had no argument. And the argument of whoever argued was also refuted and false, because you say to one whose argument you want to break: "You have an argument against me, but it is broken; you argue without an argument, and your argument is weak." So the meaning of the verse: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, from the People of the Book, for they have against you a flimsy argument.

﴿So do not fear them﴾ regarding your turning towards the Ka'bah, and their backing one another against you in argument and reply. ﴿Rather, fear Me﴾: I am your protector, and I will make you prevail over them with proof and victory.

﴿and fear Me﴾ in abandoning it and opposing it.

﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾: this is coordinated (*'atf*) on His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, but rather: and I complete My favour by guiding you to the qibla of Ibrahim, so that the upright religion (*al-milla al-hanifiyyah*) is completed for you.

'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said: "The completion of the favour is dying upon Islam."

It is also reported from him that he said: "The blessings are six: Islam, the Qur'an, Muhammad, concealment (of faults), well-being, and wealth of what is in the hands of people."

﴿and that you may be guided﴾: *la'alla* has six dialects: *'alla*, *la'alla*, *la'anna*, *'anna*, and *la'a*.

It has six meanings, some of which are obligatory from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and others from people:

It may mean interrogation, as when someone says: "Perhaps you did that?" asking a question.

It may mean supposition, as when someone says: "So-and-so has arrived," and the reply is: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "I suppose and think that."

It may mean affirmation, in the position of *ma akhlaqah* ("how fitting it is"), as in His saying: "The prayer has become obligatory," and the reply: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "how fitting it is." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alla al-manaya marratan sata'ud... wa-akhir 'ahd al-za'irin jadid*

It may mean hope and wish, as when you say: "Perhaps Allah will grant me wealth," and "Perhaps I will perform Hajj." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alli fi huda afi wujudi... wa-taqti'i al-tanwaqah wa-ikhtiyali*

*sa-yushik an yatih ila karim... yunalaka bi-al-dhura qabla al-su'al*

It may mean *'asa* ("perhaps"), in which the desired thing may or may not occur, as in His saying: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾, i.e., "perhaps I may reach." Abu Dawud said:

*fa-ablawni baliyatakum la'alli... usalihukum wa-astadriju nawiyya*

Meaning: "my companion." And it may mean *kay* ("in order that") for the consequence, as in His saying: ﴿See how We diversify the verses, that they may understand﴾, i.e., "in order that they may understand," and there are many similar examples. And His saying: ﴿and that you may be guided﴾, i.e., in order that you may be guided from error.

Al-Rabi' said: A Jew disputed with Abu al-'Aliyah and said: "Moses used to pray towards the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "He prayed beside the rock towards the Sacred House." The Jew said: "Between me and you is a righteous mosque, for he carved it from the mountain." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "I have prayed in it, and its qibla is the Sacred House."

He said: Abu al-'Aliyah reported that he passed by the mosque of Dhu al-Qarnayn, whose qibla is the Ka'bah. [See the Tafsir of al-Tabari: 2/48.]

﴿as We sent﴾: the *kaf* here is for comparison, and it requires something to which it refers. The scholars differed about it. Some said: it refers to what precedes it, and the *kaf* of what precedes it is "as," its meaning being: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me, and that I may complete My favour upon you, as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾. So the sending of the Messenger becomes a condition for fear, and an addition to the completion of the favour.

It was also said: its meaning is ﴿and that you may be guided, as We sent﴾.

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: Ibrahim made two supplications, saying: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾. That is the first supplication. The second is his saying: ﴿Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves﴾. Allah sent the Messenger, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), and in this verse He promised to answer the second supplication, and to make from his descendants a Muslim nation to Him. So the meaning of the verse: ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾, by clarifying the laws of your upright religion, and I guide you to the religion of My intimate friend Ibrahim.

﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾: meaning, just as He answered his supplication by sending the Messenger, so He answered his supplication by guiding you to his religion and making you Muslims. This is according to the view of those who connect it to what precedes it, as a response to the first verse, and it is the choice of al-Farra'.

Others said: it is connected to what follows it, which is His saying: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾. Its estimate: ﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves ... so remember Me, I will remember you﴾. So it becomes a part of it with two responses, a preceding and a following one, as you say: "If so-and-so comes to you, then go to him, he will satisfy you." So His saying "then go to him" and "he will satisfy you" are two responses to "if he comes to you." And like your saying: "If you come to me, I will be good to you, I will honour you." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan, and it is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

This verse is addressed to the Arabs and the people of Mecca, meaning: ﴿as We sent among you﴾, O assembly of Arabs, ﴿a messenger from yourselves﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿who recites to you Our verses﴾: meaning the Qur'an.

﴿and purifies you﴾: meaning, they teach you the rulings and the laws of Islam.

﴿So remember Me; I will remember you.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My help." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us﴾, etc.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My forgiveness." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger that you may receive mercy﴾.

Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My reward." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one whose work is good. Those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Whoever obeys Allah has remembered Allah, even if his prayer and fasting and recitation of the Qur'an are few."

[6] [Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/258; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/149.]

It was also said: "Remember Me with monotheism and faith; I will remember you with the gardens and the degrees." Its clarification is: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe ... of gardens﴾.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Monotheism suffices as worship, and Paradise suffices as reward."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Remember Me with gratitude; I will remember you with increase." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me upon the surface of the earth; I will remember you in its belly."

Al-Asfa said: "I saw a Bedouin standing on the day of 'Arafah at the place of standing, saying: 'Voices have cried out to You in all kinds of tongues, asking You for their needs. My need from You is that You remember me when I am decayed, if the people of this world forget me.'"

It was also said: "Remember Me with acts of obedience; I will remember you with well-being." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me in solitude and in company; I will remember you in the open and in the assembly." Its clarification is what is related in some books that Allah said: "I am as My servant thinks of Me, so let him think of Me what he will, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; if he remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it. If he draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running; and if he comes to Me with earth-filling sins, I come to him with an earth-filling forgiveness, provided he does not associate anything with Me."

And it has been said: "Remember Me in ease and prosperity, and I will remember you in hardship and affliction." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify [Allah], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾

Salman al-Farisi said: Indeed, when a servant has a supplication in secret, and then calamity befalls him, the angels say: "Your servant has been struck by calamity," and they intercede for him, and Allah rescues him. But if he has no supplication, they say: "Now [there is no one]; so you do not intercede for him." Its evidence is the word of Pharaoh: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with submission and reliance, and I will remember you with the best choice." Its evidence is: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with longing and love, and I will remember you with union and nearness."

And it has been said: "Remember Me with praise and commendation, and I will remember you with reward." And it has been said: "Remember Me with return [to Me in repentance], and I will remember you with the forgiveness of sin." And it has been said: "Remember Me with supplication, and I will remember you with giving." "Remember Me with request, and I will remember you with bestowal." "Remember Me without heedlessness, and I will remember you without delay." "Remember Me with regret, and I will remember you with generosity." "Remember Me with apology, and I will remember you with forgiveness." "Remember Me with desire, and I will remember you with benefit." "Remember Me with disavowal [of your sins], and I will remember you with bounty." "Remember Me with sincerity, and I will remember you with deliverance." "Remember Me with hearts, and I will remember you with the removal of distress." "Remember Me without forgetfulness, and I will remember you with security." "Remember Me with neediness, and I will remember you with power." "Remember Me with humility and seeking forgiveness, and I will remember you with mercy and pardon." "Remember Me with faith, and I will remember you with Paradise." "Remember Me with Islam, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with the heart, and I will remember you with the lifting of anguish." "Remember Me with a remembrance that passes, and I will remember you with a remembrance that remains." "Remember Me with entreaty, and I will remember you with abundance." "Remember Me with the shade [of humility], and I will remember you with pardon for error." "Remember Me with acknowledgment, and I will remember you with the erasure of transgression." "Remember Me with purity of secret, and I will remember you with pure righteousness." "Remember Me with truthfulness, and I will remember you with gentleness." "Remember Me with clarity, and I will remember you with pardon." "Remember Me with glorification, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with magnification [takbir], and I will remember you with purification." "Remember Me with exaltation, and I will remember you with increase." "Remember Me with intimate conversation, and I will remember you with salvation." "Remember Me by abandoning disdain, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me by abandoning error, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me with striving in creation, and I will remember you with the completion of blessing." "Remember Me from where you are, and I will remember you from where I am." ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater.﴾

Al-Rabi' said regarding this verse: Indeed, Allah remembers whoever remembers Him, increases whoever thanks Him, and punishes whoever disbelieves in Him.

Al-Suddi said regarding it: There is no servant who mentions Allah except that Allah mentions him. No believer mentions Him except that He mentions him with mercy, and no disbeliever mentions Him except that He mentions him with punishment.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: It has reached us that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "I have given My servants what, if I had given it to Jibril and Mika'il, I would have been generous to them. I said: 'Remember Me, and I will remember you.' And I said to Musa: 'Tell the wrongdoers not to mention Me, for I remember whoever mentions Me, and My remembrance of them is that I curse them.'"

Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: Indeed I know when my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, remembers me. It was said: "How is that?" He said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾, and when you remember Allah, the Exalted, He remembers you.

﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ [[Marginal note in the manuscript: by giving; whoever obeys Allah has given thanks, and whoever disobeys Him has disbelieved.]] for My favor,

﴿and do not deny Me.﴾

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 2, verses 148–152 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿For every nation there is a direction﴾. That is, for every community of a religion there is a qibla.

﴿to which it turns﴾: facing it and turning towards it. One says *wallaytuhu* and *wallaytu ilayhi* ("I turned it" and "I turned towards it"). When you come towards something you say *wallaytu ilayhi*, and when you turn away from it you say *wallaytu 'anhu*.

The root meaning of *tawliyah* is turning away. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Raja' and Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik recited it as *huwa muwalliha* (﴿He is the one who turns it﴾), meaning: turned towards it.

In the codex of Ubayy it reads: *wa-lika qiblatun huwa muwalliha*, and in the codex of 'Abdullah: *wa-li-kull ja'alna qiblatan huwa muwalliha*.

﴿So race to good works﴾: hasten to do good deeds. Its figurative sense is *fa-staqu ila al-khayrat*, i.e., let each of you outstrip the others. The particle of the verb is omitted, as in the saying of the poet:

*wa-huwa al-da'i [......] 'alaykum bi-al-harb... wa-man yamil siwakum fa-innI minhu ghayru mail*

He meant: "whoever inclines towards others than you."

﴿wherever you may be﴾: this refers to the People of the Book.

﴿Allah will bring you all together﴾: on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾.

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾: *haythu* is a particle indicating place. It has three dialectal forms: with *ya'* and *tha'* (*ḥaythu*), which is the dialect of Quraysh and the reading of the majority; scholars differed over the case of its final vowel. Some said it is indeclinable on a *damma*, like *mundhu* and *qattu*. Others said it is in the accusative of termination, as in His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾.

*Ḥaythu* with *ya'* and a fatha on the *tha'* is the reading of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. Al-Kisa'i said: it is pronounced with a fatha because the *ya'* is quiescent, and when two quiescent letters come together in one word they move the second to a fatha, since fatha is the lightest vowel, as in *layta* and *kayfa*.

*Ḥawthu* with *waw* and *damma* is the dialect of Ibn 'Umar. It is reported that he was asked where the worshipper should place his hands during prayer, and he said: "Throw them wherever they fall."

﴿So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, up to: ﴿And wherever you are, O believers, turn your faces towards it﴾.

﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾: here the *lam* is the lam of purpose (*lam kay*), which entered upon *an*, so the preceding *kasra* was written with it. Some omitted the hamza of *an* for ease. *Ḥujjah* is of the pattern *fu'lah*, from *ḥajj*, meaning "clarification," from which comes *maḥajjah*, the clear and well-travelled path, because it is intended. One says *muḥajjah* for disputation, because each of the two opponents seeks to establish his proof and to refute what is in the hand of his adversary.

Scholars differed about the interpretation of this verse and the meaning of the exception (*illa*) in it. Some of the interpreters said: the meaning of the verse is that the qibla was changed to the Ka'bah, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, for if you pray towards it, they would argue against you saying: "Why did you abandon facing the Ka'bah and turn to something else? Unless you have no qibla!" ﴿except those who wronged﴾: they are the Quraysh and the Jews. As for the Quraysh, they would say: "He only returned to the Ka'bah because he knew it was the qibla of his fathers and that it is the truth; and so he will return to our religion, knowing that it is the truth." As for the Jews, they would say: "He did not turn away from Bayt al-Maqdis while knowing it is the truth, unless he does things by his own opinion and claims that he was commanded to do so." This is the view chosen by al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah al-Dabbi, and it is a sound and accepted view.

Others said: the meaning of the verse is ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the People of the Book will have no argument against you. Their argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions in their prayer towards Bayt al-Maqdis was that they would say: "Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qibla is until we guided them!" and "Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our qibla." These are the arguments with which they would argue against the believers, in a spirit of hostility and deception, to mislead the ignorant polytheists. Then He said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾, and they are the polytheists of Mecca. Their argument was that when the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah they said: "Muhammad has become confused in his religion, so he turned towards our qibla, and he knows that we are more rightly guided than him, that he cannot do without us, and that he will soon return to our religion just as he returned to our qibla." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi, and it is the view preferred by Muhammad ibn Jarir.

On these two views, the exception with *illa* is a valid exception in the manner of your saying: "No one among the people travelled except your brother," which affirms travel for the brother, while it is negated for everyone else among the people. Likewise His saying, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those who wronged﴾: it negates that anyone has an argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions because of their turning to the Ka'bah, ﴿except those who wronged﴾ of the Quraysh, for they have an argument against them for the reason we mentioned.

The meaning of *ḥujjah* in these two views is disputation, argument, and false claim, as in His saying: ﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾, i.e., there is no dispute. And His saying: ﴿Do you argue with us about Allah?﴾ and ﴿that they may argue with you﴾ and ﴿and you argue﴾ and ﴿you disputed﴾: all of these mean argumentation and contention, not evidence and proof. The word *alladhina* is in the genitive position, as if He had said "except to those who wronged." When the preposition *lam* was dropped, *alladhina* took its place. So said al-Kisa'i.

Al-Farra' said: its position is accusative by the exception, and [......] from them was returned to the wording *al-nas* because it is general, even though each one of them differs from the other. Allah knows best.

Some said: it is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*) from the first sentence, and its meaning is: "unless there will be an argument against you from all the people, except for those who wronged, for they will argue against you in falsehood and dispute with you by injustice." This is like saying to a man: "All the people are your companions except the wrongdoer to you," meaning [......] that he does not praise you because of his enmity towards you. And like saying to a man: "You have no right with me except if you wrong," and "You have no argument except falsehood, and falsehood is not an argument." This is an exception that is not from the speech of al-Hasan.

Like the saying of one who says: "There is no one in the house except the wild animals," as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

*wa-ma bi-al-rab'i min ahad illa wa-ara li-aya ma... amamha wa-nawi ka-al-hawd bi-al-mazlumah al-jald*

And this is the view of al-Farra' and al-Mu'arrikh.

Abu Rawq said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the Jews, will have no argument against you. This is because they had known that the Ka'bah is the qibla of Ibrahim, and they had found in the Torah that Muhammad would be turned towards it. So Allah turned him towards it, so that they would have no argument, so that they could not argue that: "This Prophet whom we find in our Book will be turned towards it, but you were not turned!" When the Prophet (ﷺ) was turned, their argument disappeared. Then He said: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, meaning: except that they wrong you and conceal what they knew.

Al-Akhfash said: its meaning is "it is sufficient for those who wronged" (*li-kafa al-ladhina zalamu*): ﴿they have no knowledge of it, they follow only assumption﴾, meaning: rather, they follow assumption. And His saying: ﴿and for no one has he any favour to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord﴾, meaning: but rather seeking the countenance of your Lord. So it is an independent sentence apart from the first.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, as transmitted by Abu 'Ubayd: "The place of *illa* here is not an exception, because a wrongdoer does not have an argument. Rather, its place is that of the conjunction *waw*, as if He had said: 'Nor those who wronged,' meaning: 'and those who wronged do not have an argument either.'"

Al-Mufaddal recited:

*ma bi-al-madinah dar ghayr wahidah... dar al-khalifah illa dar Marwan*

And he also recited:

*wa-kull akh mufariqah akhuhu... la-'amr abika illa al-farqadan*

Meaning: "the two Farqadan (stars) are also separated." Al-Akhfash recited:

*wa-ara laha dara bi-aghdarah al-Sayyidan... lam yadrus laha rasm*

*illa ramadan hamidan dafa'at 'anhu al-riyah khawalid suham*

That is: "I see for it a dwelling and ashes."

This view is supported by what Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid transmitted from some of them that some recited ﴿to those who wronged﴾ with a lightened *lam*, meaning ﴿with those who wronged﴾.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿so that people will have no argument﴾, meaning the Jews, ﴿against you﴾ concerning the matter of the Ka'bah, since they would not face it, though it is the qibla of Ibrahim. They would say: "You claim you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, yet you do not face his qibla!" ﴿nor those who wronged﴾, meaning the polytheists of Mecca, because they said: "The Ka'bah is the qibla of our grandfather Ibrahim. Why has Muhammad turned away from it, so that he does not pray towards it, but prays towards the qibla of the Jews?"

Qatrub said: the meaning is "except upon those who wronged," so that its reference returns to the *kaf* and *mim* (of *'alaykum*), i.e., "except upon those who wronged, for upon them is the argument." So the preposition was omitted. This is the choice of Abu Mansur al-Azhari.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi relating it from him, and Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some of them that he said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾ here refers to some people among the Arabs who were Jews and Christians, and who used to argue against the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the rest of the Arabs, they had no argument. And the argument of whoever argued was also refuted and false, because you say to one whose argument you want to break: "You have an argument against me, but it is broken; you argue without an argument, and your argument is weak." So the meaning of the verse: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, from the People of the Book, for they have against you a flimsy argument.

﴿So do not fear them﴾ regarding your turning towards the Ka'bah, and their backing one another against you in argument and reply. ﴿Rather, fear Me﴾: I am your protector, and I will make you prevail over them with proof and victory.

﴿and fear Me﴾ in abandoning it and opposing it.

﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾: this is coordinated (*'atf*) on His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, but rather: and I complete My favour by guiding you to the qibla of Ibrahim, so that the upright religion (*al-milla al-hanifiyyah*) is completed for you.

'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said: "The completion of the favour is dying upon Islam."

It is also reported from him that he said: "The blessings are six: Islam, the Qur'an, Muhammad, concealment (of faults), well-being, and wealth of what is in the hands of people."

﴿and that you may be guided﴾: *la'alla* has six dialects: *'alla*, *la'alla*, *la'anna*, *'anna*, and *la'a*.

It has six meanings, some of which are obligatory from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and others from people:

It may mean interrogation, as when someone says: "Perhaps you did that?" asking a question.

It may mean supposition, as when someone says: "So-and-so has arrived," and the reply is: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "I suppose and think that."

It may mean affirmation, in the position of *ma akhlaqah* ("how fitting it is"), as in His saying: "The prayer has become obligatory," and the reply: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "how fitting it is." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alla al-manaya marratan sata'ud... wa-akhir 'ahd al-za'irin jadid*

It may mean hope and wish, as when you say: "Perhaps Allah will grant me wealth," and "Perhaps I will perform Hajj." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alli fi huda afi wujudi... wa-taqti'i al-tanwaqah wa-ikhtiyali*

*sa-yushik an yatih ila karim... yunalaka bi-al-dhura qabla al-su'al*

It may mean *'asa* ("perhaps"), in which the desired thing may or may not occur, as in His saying: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾, i.e., "perhaps I may reach." Abu Dawud said:

*fa-ablawni baliyatakum la'alli... usalihukum wa-astadriju nawiyya*

Meaning: "my companion." And it may mean *kay* ("in order that") for the consequence, as in His saying: ﴿See how We diversify the verses, that they may understand﴾, i.e., "in order that they may understand," and there are many similar examples. And His saying: ﴿and that you may be guided﴾, i.e., in order that you may be guided from error.

Al-Rabi' said: A Jew disputed with Abu al-'Aliyah and said: "Moses used to pray towards the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "He prayed beside the rock towards the Sacred House." The Jew said: "Between me and you is a righteous mosque, for he carved it from the mountain." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "I have prayed in it, and its qibla is the Sacred House."

He said: Abu al-'Aliyah reported that he passed by the mosque of Dhu al-Qarnayn, whose qibla is the Ka'bah. [See the Tafsir of al-Tabari: 2/48.]
