﴿as We sent﴾: the *kaf* here is for comparison, and it requires something to which it refers. The scholars differed about it. Some said: it refers to what precedes it, and the *kaf* of what precedes it is "as," its meaning being: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me, and that I may complete My favour upon you, as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾. So the sending of the Messenger becomes a condition for fear, and an addition to the completion of the favour.

It was also said: its meaning is ﴿and that you may be guided, as We sent﴾.

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: Ibrahim made two supplications, saying: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾. That is the first supplication. The second is his saying: ﴿Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves﴾. Allah sent the Messenger, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), and in this verse He promised to answer the second supplication, and to make from his descendants a Muslim nation to Him. So the meaning of the verse: ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾, by clarifying the laws of your upright religion, and I guide you to the religion of My intimate friend Ibrahim.

﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾: meaning, just as He answered his supplication by sending the Messenger, so He answered his supplication by guiding you to his religion and making you Muslims. This is according to the view of those who connect it to what precedes it, as a response to the first verse, and it is the choice of al-Farra'.

Others said: it is connected to what follows it, which is His saying: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾. Its estimate: ﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves ... so remember Me, I will remember you﴾. So it becomes a part of it with two responses, a preceding and a following one, as you say: "If so-and-so comes to you, then go to him, he will satisfy you." So His saying "then go to him" and "he will satisfy you" are two responses to "if he comes to you." And like your saying: "If you come to me, I will be good to you, I will honour you." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan, and it is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

This verse is addressed to the Arabs and the people of Mecca, meaning: ﴿as We sent among you﴾, O assembly of Arabs, ﴿a messenger from yourselves﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿who recites to you Our verses﴾: meaning the Qur'an.

﴿and purifies you﴾: meaning, they teach you the rulings and the laws of Islam.

﴿So remember Me; I will remember you.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My help." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us﴾, etc.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My forgiveness." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger that you may receive mercy﴾.

Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My reward." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one whose work is good. Those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Whoever obeys Allah has remembered Allah, even if his prayer and fasting and recitation of the Qur'an are few."

[6] [Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/258; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/149.]

It was also said: "Remember Me with monotheism and faith; I will remember you with the gardens and the degrees." Its clarification is: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe ... of gardens﴾.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Monotheism suffices as worship, and Paradise suffices as reward."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Remember Me with gratitude; I will remember you with increase." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me upon the surface of the earth; I will remember you in its belly."

Al-Asfa said: "I saw a Bedouin standing on the day of 'Arafah at the place of standing, saying: 'Voices have cried out to You in all kinds of tongues, asking You for their needs. My need from You is that You remember me when I am decayed, if the people of this world forget me.'"

It was also said: "Remember Me with acts of obedience; I will remember you with well-being." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me in solitude and in company; I will remember you in the open and in the assembly." Its clarification is what is related in some books that Allah said: "I am as My servant thinks of Me, so let him think of Me what he will, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; if he remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it. If he draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running; and if he comes to Me with earth-filling sins, I come to him with an earth-filling forgiveness, provided he does not associate anything with Me."

And it has been said: "Remember Me in ease and prosperity, and I will remember you in hardship and affliction." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify [Allah], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾

Salman al-Farisi said: Indeed, when a servant has a supplication in secret, and then calamity befalls him, the angels say: "Your servant has been struck by calamity," and they intercede for him, and Allah rescues him. But if he has no supplication, they say: "Now [there is no one]; so you do not intercede for him." Its evidence is the word of Pharaoh: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with submission and reliance, and I will remember you with the best choice." Its evidence is: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with longing and love, and I will remember you with union and nearness."

And it has been said: "Remember Me with praise and commendation, and I will remember you with reward." And it has been said: "Remember Me with return [to Me in repentance], and I will remember you with the forgiveness of sin." And it has been said: "Remember Me with supplication, and I will remember you with giving." "Remember Me with request, and I will remember you with bestowal." "Remember Me without heedlessness, and I will remember you without delay." "Remember Me with regret, and I will remember you with generosity." "Remember Me with apology, and I will remember you with forgiveness." "Remember Me with desire, and I will remember you with benefit." "Remember Me with disavowal [of your sins], and I will remember you with bounty." "Remember Me with sincerity, and I will remember you with deliverance." "Remember Me with hearts, and I will remember you with the removal of distress." "Remember Me without forgetfulness, and I will remember you with security." "Remember Me with neediness, and I will remember you with power." "Remember Me with humility and seeking forgiveness, and I will remember you with mercy and pardon." "Remember Me with faith, and I will remember you with Paradise." "Remember Me with Islam, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with the heart, and I will remember you with the lifting of anguish." "Remember Me with a remembrance that passes, and I will remember you with a remembrance that remains." "Remember Me with entreaty, and I will remember you with abundance." "Remember Me with the shade [of humility], and I will remember you with pardon for error." "Remember Me with acknowledgment, and I will remember you with the erasure of transgression." "Remember Me with purity of secret, and I will remember you with pure righteousness." "Remember Me with truthfulness, and I will remember you with gentleness." "Remember Me with clarity, and I will remember you with pardon." "Remember Me with glorification, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with magnification [takbir], and I will remember you with purification." "Remember Me with exaltation, and I will remember you with increase." "Remember Me with intimate conversation, and I will remember you with salvation." "Remember Me by abandoning disdain, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me by abandoning error, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me with striving in creation, and I will remember you with the completion of blessing." "Remember Me from where you are, and I will remember you from where I am." ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater.﴾

Al-Rabi' said regarding this verse: Indeed, Allah remembers whoever remembers Him, increases whoever thanks Him, and punishes whoever disbelieves in Him.

Al-Suddi said regarding it: There is no servant who mentions Allah except that Allah mentions him. No believer mentions Him except that He mentions him with mercy, and no disbeliever mentions Him except that He mentions him with punishment.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: It has reached us that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "I have given My servants what, if I had given it to Jibril and Mika'il, I would have been generous to them. I said: 'Remember Me, and I will remember you.' And I said to Musa: 'Tell the wrongdoers not to mention Me, for I remember whoever mentions Me, and My remembrance of them is that I curse them.'"

Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: Indeed I know when my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, remembers me. It was said: "How is that?" He said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾, and when you remember Allah, the Exalted, He remembers you.

﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ [[Marginal note in the manuscript: by giving; whoever obeys Allah has given thanks, and whoever disobeys Him has disbelieved.]] for My favor,

﴿and do not deny Me.﴾

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 2, verses 148–152 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿For every nation there is a direction﴾. That is, for every community of a religion there is a qibla.

﴿to which it turns﴾: facing it and turning towards it. One says *wallaytuhu* and *wallaytu ilayhi* ("I turned it" and "I turned towards it"). When you come towards something you say *wallaytu ilayhi*, and when you turn away from it you say *wallaytu 'anhu*.

The root meaning of *tawliyah* is turning away. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Raja' and Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik recited it as *huwa muwalliha* (﴿He is the one who turns it﴾), meaning: turned towards it.

In the codex of Ubayy it reads: *wa-lika qiblatun huwa muwalliha*, and in the codex of 'Abdullah: *wa-li-kull ja'alna qiblatan huwa muwalliha*.

﴿So race to good works﴾: hasten to do good deeds. Its figurative sense is *fa-staqu ila al-khayrat*, i.e., let each of you outstrip the others. The particle of the verb is omitted, as in the saying of the poet:

*wa-huwa al-da'i [......] 'alaykum bi-al-harb... wa-man yamil siwakum fa-innI minhu ghayru mail*

He meant: "whoever inclines towards others than you."

﴿wherever you may be﴾: this refers to the People of the Book.

﴿Allah will bring you all together﴾: on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾.

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾: *haythu* is a particle indicating place. It has three dialectal forms: with *ya'* and *tha'* (*ḥaythu*), which is the dialect of Quraysh and the reading of the majority; scholars differed over the case of its final vowel. Some said it is indeclinable on a *damma*, like *mundhu* and *qattu*. Others said it is in the accusative of termination, as in His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾.

*Ḥaythu* with *ya'* and a fatha on the *tha'* is the reading of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. Al-Kisa'i said: it is pronounced with a fatha because the *ya'* is quiescent, and when two quiescent letters come together in one word they move the second to a fatha, since fatha is the lightest vowel, as in *layta* and *kayfa*.

*Ḥawthu* with *waw* and *damma* is the dialect of Ibn 'Umar. It is reported that he was asked where the worshipper should place his hands during prayer, and he said: "Throw them wherever they fall."

﴿So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, up to: ﴿And wherever you are, O believers, turn your faces towards it﴾.

﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾: here the *lam* is the lam of purpose (*lam kay*), which entered upon *an*, so the preceding *kasra* was written with it. Some omitted the hamza of *an* for ease. *Ḥujjah* is of the pattern *fu'lah*, from *ḥajj*, meaning "clarification," from which comes *maḥajjah*, the clear and well-travelled path, because it is intended. One says *muḥajjah* for disputation, because each of the two opponents seeks to establish his proof and to refute what is in the hand of his adversary.

Scholars differed about the interpretation of this verse and the meaning of the exception (*illa*) in it. Some of the interpreters said: the meaning of the verse is that the qibla was changed to the Ka'bah, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, for if you pray towards it, they would argue against you saying: "Why did you abandon facing the Ka'bah and turn to something else? Unless you have no qibla!" ﴿except those who wronged﴾: they are the Quraysh and the Jews. As for the Quraysh, they would say: "He only returned to the Ka'bah because he knew it was the qibla of his fathers and that it is the truth; and so he will return to our religion, knowing that it is the truth." As for the Jews, they would say: "He did not turn away from Bayt al-Maqdis while knowing it is the truth, unless he does things by his own opinion and claims that he was commanded to do so." This is the view chosen by al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah al-Dabbi, and it is a sound and accepted view.

Others said: the meaning of the verse is ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the People of the Book will have no argument against you. Their argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions in their prayer towards Bayt al-Maqdis was that they would say: "Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qibla is until we guided them!" and "Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our qibla." These are the arguments with which they would argue against the believers, in a spirit of hostility and deception, to mislead the ignorant polytheists. Then He said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾, and they are the polytheists of Mecca. Their argument was that when the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah they said: "Muhammad has become confused in his religion, so he turned towards our qibla, and he knows that we are more rightly guided than him, that he cannot do without us, and that he will soon return to our religion just as he returned to our qibla." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi, and it is the view preferred by Muhammad ibn Jarir.

On these two views, the exception with *illa* is a valid exception in the manner of your saying: "No one among the people travelled except your brother," which affirms travel for the brother, while it is negated for everyone else among the people. Likewise His saying, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those who wronged﴾: it negates that anyone has an argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions because of their turning to the Ka'bah, ﴿except those who wronged﴾ of the Quraysh, for they have an argument against them for the reason we mentioned.

The meaning of *ḥujjah* in these two views is disputation, argument, and false claim, as in His saying: ﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾, i.e., there is no dispute. And His saying: ﴿Do you argue with us about Allah?﴾ and ﴿that they may argue with you﴾ and ﴿and you argue﴾ and ﴿you disputed﴾: all of these mean argumentation and contention, not evidence and proof. The word *alladhina* is in the genitive position, as if He had said "except to those who wronged." When the preposition *lam* was dropped, *alladhina* took its place. So said al-Kisa'i.

Al-Farra' said: its position is accusative by the exception, and [......] from them was returned to the wording *al-nas* because it is general, even though each one of them differs from the other. Allah knows best.

Some said: it is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*) from the first sentence, and its meaning is: "unless there will be an argument against you from all the people, except for those who wronged, for they will argue against you in falsehood and dispute with you by injustice." This is like saying to a man: "All the people are your companions except the wrongdoer to you," meaning [......] that he does not praise you because of his enmity towards you. And like saying to a man: "You have no right with me except if you wrong," and "You have no argument except falsehood, and falsehood is not an argument." This is an exception that is not from the speech of al-Hasan.

Like the saying of one who says: "There is no one in the house except the wild animals," as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

*wa-ma bi-al-rab'i min ahad illa wa-ara li-aya ma... amamha wa-nawi ka-al-hawd bi-al-mazlumah al-jald*

And this is the view of al-Farra' and al-Mu'arrikh.

Abu Rawq said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the Jews, will have no argument against you. This is because they had known that the Ka'bah is the qibla of Ibrahim, and they had found in the Torah that Muhammad would be turned towards it. So Allah turned him towards it, so that they would have no argument, so that they could not argue that: "This Prophet whom we find in our Book will be turned towards it, but you were not turned!" When the Prophet (ﷺ) was turned, their argument disappeared. Then He said: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, meaning: except that they wrong you and conceal what they knew.

Al-Akhfash said: its meaning is "it is sufficient for those who wronged" (*li-kafa al-ladhina zalamu*): ﴿they have no knowledge of it, they follow only assumption﴾, meaning: rather, they follow assumption. And His saying: ﴿and for no one has he any favour to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord﴾, meaning: but rather seeking the countenance of your Lord. So it is an independent sentence apart from the first.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, as transmitted by Abu 'Ubayd: "The place of *illa* here is not an exception, because a wrongdoer does not have an argument. Rather, its place is that of the conjunction *waw*, as if He had said: 'Nor those who wronged,' meaning: 'and those who wronged do not have an argument either.'"

Al-Mufaddal recited:

*ma bi-al-madinah dar ghayr wahidah... dar al-khalifah illa dar Marwan*

And he also recited:

*wa-kull akh mufariqah akhuhu... la-'amr abika illa al-farqadan*

Meaning: "the two Farqadan (stars) are also separated." Al-Akhfash recited:

*wa-ara laha dara bi-aghdarah al-Sayyidan... lam yadrus laha rasm*

*illa ramadan hamidan dafa'at 'anhu al-riyah khawalid suham*

That is: "I see for it a dwelling and ashes."

This view is supported by what Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid transmitted from some of them that some recited ﴿to those who wronged﴾ with a lightened *lam*, meaning ﴿with those who wronged﴾.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿so that people will have no argument﴾, meaning the Jews, ﴿against you﴾ concerning the matter of the Ka'bah, since they would not face it, though it is the qibla of Ibrahim. They would say: "You claim you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, yet you do not face his qibla!" ﴿nor those who wronged﴾, meaning the polytheists of Mecca, because they said: "The Ka'bah is the qibla of our grandfather Ibrahim. Why has Muhammad turned away from it, so that he does not pray towards it, but prays towards the qibla of the Jews?"

Qatrub said: the meaning is "except upon those who wronged," so that its reference returns to the *kaf* and *mim* (of *'alaykum*), i.e., "except upon those who wronged, for upon them is the argument." So the preposition was omitted. This is the choice of Abu Mansur al-Azhari.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi relating it from him, and Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some of them that he said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾ here refers to some people among the Arabs who were Jews and Christians, and who used to argue against the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the rest of the Arabs, they had no argument. And the argument of whoever argued was also refuted and false, because you say to one whose argument you want to break: "You have an argument against me, but it is broken; you argue without an argument, and your argument is weak." So the meaning of the verse: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, from the People of the Book, for they have against you a flimsy argument.

﴿So do not fear them﴾ regarding your turning towards the Ka'bah, and their backing one another against you in argument and reply. ﴿Rather, fear Me﴾: I am your protector, and I will make you prevail over them with proof and victory.

﴿and fear Me﴾ in abandoning it and opposing it.

﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾: this is coordinated (*'atf*) on His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, but rather: and I complete My favour by guiding you to the qibla of Ibrahim, so that the upright religion (*al-milla al-hanifiyyah*) is completed for you.

'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said: "The completion of the favour is dying upon Islam."

It is also reported from him that he said: "The blessings are six: Islam, the Qur'an, Muhammad, concealment (of faults), well-being, and wealth of what is in the hands of people."

﴿and that you may be guided﴾: *la'alla* has six dialects: *'alla*, *la'alla*, *la'anna*, *'anna*, and *la'a*.

It has six meanings, some of which are obligatory from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and others from people:

It may mean interrogation, as when someone says: "Perhaps you did that?" asking a question.

It may mean supposition, as when someone says: "So-and-so has arrived," and the reply is: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "I suppose and think that."

It may mean affirmation, in the position of *ma akhlaqah* ("how fitting it is"), as in His saying: "The prayer has become obligatory," and the reply: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "how fitting it is." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alla al-manaya marratan sata'ud... wa-akhir 'ahd al-za'irin jadid*

It may mean hope and wish, as when you say: "Perhaps Allah will grant me wealth," and "Perhaps I will perform Hajj." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alli fi huda afi wujudi... wa-taqti'i al-tanwaqah wa-ikhtiyali*

*sa-yushik an yatih ila karim... yunalaka bi-al-dhura qabla al-su'al*

It may mean *'asa* ("perhaps"), in which the desired thing may or may not occur, as in His saying: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾, i.e., "perhaps I may reach." Abu Dawud said:

*fa-ablawni baliyatakum la'alli... usalihukum wa-astadriju nawiyya*

Meaning: "my companion." And it may mean *kay* ("in order that") for the consequence, as in His saying: ﴿See how We diversify the verses, that they may understand﴾, i.e., "in order that they may understand," and there are many similar examples. And His saying: ﴿and that you may be guided﴾, i.e., in order that you may be guided from error.

Al-Rabi' said: A Jew disputed with Abu al-'Aliyah and said: "Moses used to pray towards the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "He prayed beside the rock towards the Sacred House." The Jew said: "Between me and you is a righteous mosque, for he carved it from the mountain." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "I have prayed in it, and its qibla is the Sacred House."

He said: Abu al-'Aliyah reported that he passed by the mosque of Dhu al-Qarnayn, whose qibla is the Ka'bah. [See the Tafsir of al-Tabari: 2/48.]

﴿as We sent﴾: the *kaf* here is for comparison, and it requires something to which it refers. The scholars differed about it. Some said: it refers to what precedes it, and the *kaf* of what precedes it is "as," its meaning being: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me, and that I may complete My favour upon you, as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾. So the sending of the Messenger becomes a condition for fear, and an addition to the completion of the favour.

It was also said: its meaning is ﴿and that you may be guided, as We sent﴾.

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: Ibrahim made two supplications, saying: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾. That is the first supplication. The second is his saying: ﴿Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves﴾. Allah sent the Messenger, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), and in this verse He promised to answer the second supplication, and to make from his descendants a Muslim nation to Him. So the meaning of the verse: ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾, by clarifying the laws of your upright religion, and I guide you to the religion of My intimate friend Ibrahim.

﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾: meaning, just as He answered his supplication by sending the Messenger, so He answered his supplication by guiding you to his religion and making you Muslims. This is according to the view of those who connect it to what precedes it, as a response to the first verse, and it is the choice of al-Farra'.

Others said: it is connected to what follows it, which is His saying: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾. Its estimate: ﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves ... so remember Me, I will remember you﴾. So it becomes a part of it with two responses, a preceding and a following one, as you say: "If so-and-so comes to you, then go to him, he will satisfy you." So His saying "then go to him" and "he will satisfy you" are two responses to "if he comes to you." And like your saying: "If you come to me, I will be good to you, I will honour you." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan, and it is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

This verse is addressed to the Arabs and the people of Mecca, meaning: ﴿as We sent among you﴾, O assembly of Arabs, ﴿a messenger from yourselves﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿who recites to you Our verses﴾: meaning the Qur'an.

﴿and purifies you﴾: meaning, they teach you the rulings and the laws of Islam.

﴿So remember Me; I will remember you.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My help." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us﴾, etc.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My forgiveness." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger that you may receive mercy﴾.

Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My reward." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one whose work is good. Those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Whoever obeys Allah has remembered Allah, even if his prayer and fasting and recitation of the Qur'an are few."

[6] [Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/258; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/149.]

It was also said: "Remember Me with monotheism and faith; I will remember you with the gardens and the degrees." Its clarification is: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe ... of gardens﴾.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Monotheism suffices as worship, and Paradise suffices as reward."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Remember Me with gratitude; I will remember you with increase." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me upon the surface of the earth; I will remember you in its belly."

Al-Asfa said: "I saw a Bedouin standing on the day of 'Arafah at the place of standing, saying: 'Voices have cried out to You in all kinds of tongues, asking You for their needs. My need from You is that You remember me when I am decayed, if the people of this world forget me.'"

It was also said: "Remember Me with acts of obedience; I will remember you with well-being." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me in solitude and in company; I will remember you in the open and in the assembly." Its clarification is what is related in some books that Allah said: "I am as My servant thinks of Me, so let him think of Me what he will, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; if he remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it. If he draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running; and if he comes to Me with earth-filling sins, I come to him with an earth-filling forgiveness, provided he does not associate anything with Me."

And it has been said: "Remember Me in ease and prosperity, and I will remember you in hardship and affliction." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify [Allah], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾

Salman al-Farisi said: Indeed, when a servant has a supplication in secret, and then calamity befalls him, the angels say: "Your servant has been struck by calamity," and they intercede for him, and Allah rescues him. But if he has no supplication, they say: "Now [there is no one]; so you do not intercede for him." Its evidence is the word of Pharaoh: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with submission and reliance, and I will remember you with the best choice." Its evidence is: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with longing and love, and I will remember you with union and nearness."

And it has been said: "Remember Me with praise and commendation, and I will remember you with reward." And it has been said: "Remember Me with return [to Me in repentance], and I will remember you with the forgiveness of sin." And it has been said: "Remember Me with supplication, and I will remember you with giving." "Remember Me with request, and I will remember you with bestowal." "Remember Me without heedlessness, and I will remember you without delay." "Remember Me with regret, and I will remember you with generosity." "Remember Me with apology, and I will remember you with forgiveness." "Remember Me with desire, and I will remember you with benefit." "Remember Me with disavowal [of your sins], and I will remember you with bounty." "Remember Me with sincerity, and I will remember you with deliverance." "Remember Me with hearts, and I will remember you with the removal of distress." "Remember Me without forgetfulness, and I will remember you with security." "Remember Me with neediness, and I will remember you with power." "Remember Me with humility and seeking forgiveness, and I will remember you with mercy and pardon." "Remember Me with faith, and I will remember you with Paradise." "Remember Me with Islam, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with the heart, and I will remember you with the lifting of anguish." "Remember Me with a remembrance that passes, and I will remember you with a remembrance that remains." "Remember Me with entreaty, and I will remember you with abundance." "Remember Me with the shade [of humility], and I will remember you with pardon for error." "Remember Me with acknowledgment, and I will remember you with the erasure of transgression." "Remember Me with purity of secret, and I will remember you with pure righteousness." "Remember Me with truthfulness, and I will remember you with gentleness." "Remember Me with clarity, and I will remember you with pardon." "Remember Me with glorification, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with magnification [takbir], and I will remember you with purification." "Remember Me with exaltation, and I will remember you with increase." "Remember Me with intimate conversation, and I will remember you with salvation." "Remember Me by abandoning disdain, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me by abandoning error, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me with striving in creation, and I will remember you with the completion of blessing." "Remember Me from where you are, and I will remember you from where I am." ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater.﴾

Al-Rabi' said regarding this verse: Indeed, Allah remembers whoever remembers Him, increases whoever thanks Him, and punishes whoever disbelieves in Him.

Al-Suddi said regarding it: There is no servant who mentions Allah except that Allah mentions him. No believer mentions Him except that He mentions him with mercy, and no disbeliever mentions Him except that He mentions him with punishment.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: It has reached us that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "I have given My servants what, if I had given it to Jibril and Mika'il, I would have been generous to them. I said: 'Remember Me, and I will remember you.' And I said to Musa: 'Tell the wrongdoers not to mention Me, for I remember whoever mentions Me, and My remembrance of them is that I curse them.'"

Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: Indeed I know when my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, remembers me. It was said: "How is that?" He said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾, and when you remember Allah, the Exalted, He remembers you.

﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ [[Marginal note in the manuscript: by giving; whoever obeys Allah has given thanks, and whoever disobeys Him has disbelieved.]] for My favor,

﴿and do not deny Me.﴾

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 2, verses 148–152 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿For every nation there is a direction﴾. That is, for every community of a religion there is a qibla.

﴿to which it turns﴾: facing it and turning towards it. One says *wallaytuhu* and *wallaytu ilayhi* ("I turned it" and "I turned towards it"). When you come towards something you say *wallaytu ilayhi*, and when you turn away from it you say *wallaytu 'anhu*.

The root meaning of *tawliyah* is turning away. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Raja' and Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik recited it as *huwa muwalliha* (﴿He is the one who turns it﴾), meaning: turned towards it.

In the codex of Ubayy it reads: *wa-lika qiblatun huwa muwalliha*, and in the codex of 'Abdullah: *wa-li-kull ja'alna qiblatan huwa muwalliha*.

﴿So race to good works﴾: hasten to do good deeds. Its figurative sense is *fa-staqu ila al-khayrat*, i.e., let each of you outstrip the others. The particle of the verb is omitted, as in the saying of the poet:

*wa-huwa al-da'i [......] 'alaykum bi-al-harb... wa-man yamil siwakum fa-innI minhu ghayru mail*

He meant: "whoever inclines towards others than you."

﴿wherever you may be﴾: this refers to the People of the Book.

﴿Allah will bring you all together﴾: on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾.

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾: *haythu* is a particle indicating place. It has three dialectal forms: with *ya'* and *tha'* (*ḥaythu*), which is the dialect of Quraysh and the reading of the majority; scholars differed over the case of its final vowel. Some said it is indeclinable on a *damma*, like *mundhu* and *qattu*. Others said it is in the accusative of termination, as in His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾.

*Ḥaythu* with *ya'* and a fatha on the *tha'* is the reading of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. Al-Kisa'i said: it is pronounced with a fatha because the *ya'* is quiescent, and when two quiescent letters come together in one word they move the second to a fatha, since fatha is the lightest vowel, as in *layta* and *kayfa*.

*Ḥawthu* with *waw* and *damma* is the dialect of Ibn 'Umar. It is reported that he was asked where the worshipper should place his hands during prayer, and he said: "Throw them wherever they fall."

﴿So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, up to: ﴿And wherever you are, O believers, turn your faces towards it﴾.

﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾: here the *lam* is the lam of purpose (*lam kay*), which entered upon *an*, so the preceding *kasra* was written with it. Some omitted the hamza of *an* for ease. *Ḥujjah* is of the pattern *fu'lah*, from *ḥajj*, meaning "clarification," from which comes *maḥajjah*, the clear and well-travelled path, because it is intended. One says *muḥajjah* for disputation, because each of the two opponents seeks to establish his proof and to refute what is in the hand of his adversary.

Scholars differed about the interpretation of this verse and the meaning of the exception (*illa*) in it. Some of the interpreters said: the meaning of the verse is that the qibla was changed to the Ka'bah, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, for if you pray towards it, they would argue against you saying: "Why did you abandon facing the Ka'bah and turn to something else? Unless you have no qibla!" ﴿except those who wronged﴾: they are the Quraysh and the Jews. As for the Quraysh, they would say: "He only returned to the Ka'bah because he knew it was the qibla of his fathers and that it is the truth; and so he will return to our religion, knowing that it is the truth." As for the Jews, they would say: "He did not turn away from Bayt al-Maqdis while knowing it is the truth, unless he does things by his own opinion and claims that he was commanded to do so." This is the view chosen by al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah al-Dabbi, and it is a sound and accepted view.

Others said: the meaning of the verse is ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the People of the Book will have no argument against you. Their argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions in their prayer towards Bayt al-Maqdis was that they would say: "Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qibla is until we guided them!" and "Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our qibla." These are the arguments with which they would argue against the believers, in a spirit of hostility and deception, to mislead the ignorant polytheists. Then He said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾, and they are the polytheists of Mecca. Their argument was that when the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah they said: "Muhammad has become confused in his religion, so he turned towards our qibla, and he knows that we are more rightly guided than him, that he cannot do without us, and that he will soon return to our religion just as he returned to our qibla." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi, and it is the view preferred by Muhammad ibn Jarir.

On these two views, the exception with *illa* is a valid exception in the manner of your saying: "No one among the people travelled except your brother," which affirms travel for the brother, while it is negated for everyone else among the people. Likewise His saying, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those who wronged﴾: it negates that anyone has an argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions because of their turning to the Ka'bah, ﴿except those who wronged﴾ of the Quraysh, for they have an argument against them for the reason we mentioned.

The meaning of *ḥujjah* in these two views is disputation, argument, and false claim, as in His saying: ﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾, i.e., there is no dispute. And His saying: ﴿Do you argue with us about Allah?﴾ and ﴿that they may argue with you﴾ and ﴿and you argue﴾ and ﴿you disputed﴾: all of these mean argumentation and contention, not evidence and proof. The word *alladhina* is in the genitive position, as if He had said "except to those who wronged." When the preposition *lam* was dropped, *alladhina* took its place. So said al-Kisa'i.

Al-Farra' said: its position is accusative by the exception, and [......] from them was returned to the wording *al-nas* because it is general, even though each one of them differs from the other. Allah knows best.

Some said: it is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*) from the first sentence, and its meaning is: "unless there will be an argument against you from all the people, except for those who wronged, for they will argue against you in falsehood and dispute with you by injustice." This is like saying to a man: "All the people are your companions except the wrongdoer to you," meaning [......] that he does not praise you because of his enmity towards you. And like saying to a man: "You have no right with me except if you wrong," and "You have no argument except falsehood, and falsehood is not an argument." This is an exception that is not from the speech of al-Hasan.

Like the saying of one who says: "There is no one in the house except the wild animals," as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

*wa-ma bi-al-rab'i min ahad illa wa-ara li-aya ma... amamha wa-nawi ka-al-hawd bi-al-mazlumah al-jald*

And this is the view of al-Farra' and al-Mu'arrikh.

Abu Rawq said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the Jews, will have no argument against you. This is because they had known that the Ka'bah is the qibla of Ibrahim, and they had found in the Torah that Muhammad would be turned towards it. So Allah turned him towards it, so that they would have no argument, so that they could not argue that: "This Prophet whom we find in our Book will be turned towards it, but you were not turned!" When the Prophet (ﷺ) was turned, their argument disappeared. Then He said: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, meaning: except that they wrong you and conceal what they knew.

Al-Akhfash said: its meaning is "it is sufficient for those who wronged" (*li-kafa al-ladhina zalamu*): ﴿they have no knowledge of it, they follow only assumption﴾, meaning: rather, they follow assumption. And His saying: ﴿and for no one has he any favour to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord﴾, meaning: but rather seeking the countenance of your Lord. So it is an independent sentence apart from the first.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, as transmitted by Abu 'Ubayd: "The place of *illa* here is not an exception, because a wrongdoer does not have an argument. Rather, its place is that of the conjunction *waw*, as if He had said: 'Nor those who wronged,' meaning: 'and those who wronged do not have an argument either.'"

Al-Mufaddal recited:

*ma bi-al-madinah dar ghayr wahidah... dar al-khalifah illa dar Marwan*

And he also recited:

*wa-kull akh mufariqah akhuhu... la-'amr abika illa al-farqadan*

Meaning: "the two Farqadan (stars) are also separated." Al-Akhfash recited:

*wa-ara laha dara bi-aghdarah al-Sayyidan... lam yadrus laha rasm*

*illa ramadan hamidan dafa'at 'anhu al-riyah khawalid suham*

That is: "I see for it a dwelling and ashes."

This view is supported by what Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid transmitted from some of them that some recited ﴿to those who wronged﴾ with a lightened *lam*, meaning ﴿with those who wronged﴾.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿so that people will have no argument﴾, meaning the Jews, ﴿against you﴾ concerning the matter of the Ka'bah, since they would not face it, though it is the qibla of Ibrahim. They would say: "You claim you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, yet you do not face his qibla!" ﴿nor those who wronged﴾, meaning the polytheists of Mecca, because they said: "The Ka'bah is the qibla of our grandfather Ibrahim. Why has Muhammad turned away from it, so that he does not pray towards it, but prays towards the qibla of the Jews?"

Qatrub said: the meaning is "except upon those who wronged," so that its reference returns to the *kaf* and *mim* (of *'alaykum*), i.e., "except upon those who wronged, for upon them is the argument." So the preposition was omitted. This is the choice of Abu Mansur al-Azhari.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi relating it from him, and Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some of them that he said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾ here refers to some people among the Arabs who were Jews and Christians, and who used to argue against the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the rest of the Arabs, they had no argument. And the argument of whoever argued was also refuted and false, because you say to one whose argument you want to break: "You have an argument against me, but it is broken; you argue without an argument, and your argument is weak." So the meaning of the verse: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, from the People of the Book, for they have against you a flimsy argument.

﴿So do not fear them﴾ regarding your turning towards the Ka'bah, and their backing one another against you in argument and reply. ﴿Rather, fear Me﴾: I am your protector, and I will make you prevail over them with proof and victory.

﴿and fear Me﴾ in abandoning it and opposing it.

﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾: this is coordinated (*'atf*) on His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, but rather: and I complete My favour by guiding you to the qibla of Ibrahim, so that the upright religion (*al-milla al-hanifiyyah*) is completed for you.

'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said: "The completion of the favour is dying upon Islam."

It is also reported from him that he said: "The blessings are six: Islam, the Qur'an, Muhammad, concealment (of faults), well-being, and wealth of what is in the hands of people."

﴿and that you may be guided﴾: *la'alla* has six dialects: *'alla*, *la'alla*, *la'anna*, *'anna*, and *la'a*.

It has six meanings, some of which are obligatory from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and others from people:

It may mean interrogation, as when someone says: "Perhaps you did that?" asking a question.

It may mean supposition, as when someone says: "So-and-so has arrived," and the reply is: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "I suppose and think that."

It may mean affirmation, in the position of *ma akhlaqah* ("how fitting it is"), as in His saying: "The prayer has become obligatory," and the reply: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "how fitting it is." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alla al-manaya marratan sata'ud... wa-akhir 'ahd al-za'irin jadid*

It may mean hope and wish, as when you say: "Perhaps Allah will grant me wealth," and "Perhaps I will perform Hajj." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alli fi huda afi wujudi... wa-taqti'i al-tanwaqah wa-ikhtiyali*

*sa-yushik an yatih ila karim... yunalaka bi-al-dhura qabla al-su'al*

It may mean *'asa* ("perhaps"), in which the desired thing may or may not occur, as in His saying: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾, i.e., "perhaps I may reach." Abu Dawud said:

*fa-ablawni baliyatakum la'alli... usalihukum wa-astadriju nawiyya*

Meaning: "my companion." And it may mean *kay* ("in order that") for the consequence, as in His saying: ﴿See how We diversify the verses, that they may understand﴾, i.e., "in order that they may understand," and there are many similar examples. And His saying: ﴿and that you may be guided﴾, i.e., in order that you may be guided from error.

Al-Rabi' said: A Jew disputed with Abu al-'Aliyah and said: "Moses used to pray towards the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "He prayed beside the rock towards the Sacred House." The Jew said: "Between me and you is a righteous mosque, for he carved it from the mountain." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "I have prayed in it, and its qibla is the Sacred House."

He said: Abu al-'Aliyah reported that he passed by the mosque of Dhu al-Qarnayn, whose qibla is the Ka'bah. [See the Tafsir of al-Tabari: 2/48.]

﴿as We sent﴾: the *kaf* here is for comparison, and it requires something to which it refers. The scholars differed about it. Some said: it refers to what precedes it, and the *kaf* of what precedes it is "as," its meaning being: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me, and that I may complete My favour upon you, as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾. So the sending of the Messenger becomes a condition for fear, and an addition to the completion of the favour.

It was also said: its meaning is ﴿and that you may be guided, as We sent﴾.

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: Ibrahim made two supplications, saying: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾. That is the first supplication. The second is his saying: ﴿Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves﴾. Allah sent the Messenger, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), and in this verse He promised to answer the second supplication, and to make from his descendants a Muslim nation to Him. So the meaning of the verse: ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾, by clarifying the laws of your upright religion, and I guide you to the religion of My intimate friend Ibrahim.

﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾: meaning, just as He answered his supplication by sending the Messenger, so He answered his supplication by guiding you to his religion and making you Muslims. This is according to the view of those who connect it to what precedes it, as a response to the first verse, and it is the choice of al-Farra'.

Others said: it is connected to what follows it, which is His saying: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾. Its estimate: ﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves ... so remember Me, I will remember you﴾. So it becomes a part of it with two responses, a preceding and a following one, as you say: "If so-and-so comes to you, then go to him, he will satisfy you." So His saying "then go to him" and "he will satisfy you" are two responses to "if he comes to you." And like your saying: "If you come to me, I will be good to you, I will honour you." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan, and it is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

This verse is addressed to the Arabs and the people of Mecca, meaning: ﴿as We sent among you﴾, O assembly of Arabs, ﴿a messenger from yourselves﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿who recites to you Our verses﴾: meaning the Qur'an.

﴿and purifies you﴾: meaning, they teach you the rulings and the laws of Islam.

﴿So remember Me; I will remember you.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My help." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us﴾, etc.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My forgiveness." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger that you may receive mercy﴾.

Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My reward." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one whose work is good. Those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Whoever obeys Allah has remembered Allah, even if his prayer and fasting and recitation of the Qur'an are few."

[6] [Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/258; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/149.]

It was also said: "Remember Me with monotheism and faith; I will remember you with the gardens and the degrees." Its clarification is: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe ... of gardens﴾.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Monotheism suffices as worship, and Paradise suffices as reward."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Remember Me with gratitude; I will remember you with increase." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me upon the surface of the earth; I will remember you in its belly."

Al-Asfa said: "I saw a Bedouin standing on the day of 'Arafah at the place of standing, saying: 'Voices have cried out to You in all kinds of tongues, asking You for their needs. My need from You is that You remember me when I am decayed, if the people of this world forget me.'"

It was also said: "Remember Me with acts of obedience; I will remember you with well-being." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me in solitude and in company; I will remember you in the open and in the assembly." Its clarification is what is related in some books that Allah said: "I am as My servant thinks of Me, so let him think of Me what he will, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; if he remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it. If he draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running; and if he comes to Me with earth-filling sins, I come to him with an earth-filling forgiveness, provided he does not associate anything with Me."

And it has been said: "Remember Me in ease and prosperity, and I will remember you in hardship and affliction." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify [Allah], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾

Salman al-Farisi said: Indeed, when a servant has a supplication in secret, and then calamity befalls him, the angels say: "Your servant has been struck by calamity," and they intercede for him, and Allah rescues him. But if he has no supplication, they say: "Now [there is no one]; so you do not intercede for him." Its evidence is the word of Pharaoh: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with submission and reliance, and I will remember you with the best choice." Its evidence is: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with longing and love, and I will remember you with union and nearness."

And it has been said: "Remember Me with praise and commendation, and I will remember you with reward." And it has been said: "Remember Me with return [to Me in repentance], and I will remember you with the forgiveness of sin." And it has been said: "Remember Me with supplication, and I will remember you with giving." "Remember Me with request, and I will remember you with bestowal." "Remember Me without heedlessness, and I will remember you without delay." "Remember Me with regret, and I will remember you with generosity." "Remember Me with apology, and I will remember you with forgiveness." "Remember Me with desire, and I will remember you with benefit." "Remember Me with disavowal [of your sins], and I will remember you with bounty." "Remember Me with sincerity, and I will remember you with deliverance." "Remember Me with hearts, and I will remember you with the removal of distress." "Remember Me without forgetfulness, and I will remember you with security." "Remember Me with neediness, and I will remember you with power." "Remember Me with humility and seeking forgiveness, and I will remember you with mercy and pardon." "Remember Me with faith, and I will remember you with Paradise." "Remember Me with Islam, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with the heart, and I will remember you with the lifting of anguish." "Remember Me with a remembrance that passes, and I will remember you with a remembrance that remains." "Remember Me with entreaty, and I will remember you with abundance." "Remember Me with the shade [of humility], and I will remember you with pardon for error." "Remember Me with acknowledgment, and I will remember you with the erasure of transgression." "Remember Me with purity of secret, and I will remember you with pure righteousness." "Remember Me with truthfulness, and I will remember you with gentleness." "Remember Me with clarity, and I will remember you with pardon." "Remember Me with glorification, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with magnification [takbir], and I will remember you with purification." "Remember Me with exaltation, and I will remember you with increase." "Remember Me with intimate conversation, and I will remember you with salvation." "Remember Me by abandoning disdain, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me by abandoning error, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me with striving in creation, and I will remember you with the completion of blessing." "Remember Me from where you are, and I will remember you from where I am." ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater.﴾

Al-Rabi' said regarding this verse: Indeed, Allah remembers whoever remembers Him, increases whoever thanks Him, and punishes whoever disbelieves in Him.

Al-Suddi said regarding it: There is no servant who mentions Allah except that Allah mentions him. No believer mentions Him except that He mentions him with mercy, and no disbeliever mentions Him except that He mentions him with punishment.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: It has reached us that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "I have given My servants what, if I had given it to Jibril and Mika'il, I would have been generous to them. I said: 'Remember Me, and I will remember you.' And I said to Musa: 'Tell the wrongdoers not to mention Me, for I remember whoever mentions Me, and My remembrance of them is that I curse them.'"

Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: Indeed I know when my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, remembers me. It was said: "How is that?" He said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾, and when you remember Allah, the Exalted, He remembers you.

﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ [[Marginal note in the manuscript: by giving; whoever obeys Allah has given thanks, and whoever disobeys Him has disbelieved.]] for My favor,

﴿and do not deny Me.﴾

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 2, verses 148–152 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿For every nation there is a direction﴾. That is, for every community of a religion there is a qibla.

﴿to which it turns﴾: facing it and turning towards it. One says *wallaytuhu* and *wallaytu ilayhi* ("I turned it" and "I turned towards it"). When you come towards something you say *wallaytu ilayhi*, and when you turn away from it you say *wallaytu 'anhu*.

The root meaning of *tawliyah* is turning away. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Raja' and Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik recited it as *huwa muwalliha* (﴿He is the one who turns it﴾), meaning: turned towards it.

In the codex of Ubayy it reads: *wa-lika qiblatun huwa muwalliha*, and in the codex of 'Abdullah: *wa-li-kull ja'alna qiblatan huwa muwalliha*.

*wa-huwa al-da'i [......] 'alaykum bi-al-harb... wa-man yamil siwakum fa-innI minhu ghayru mail*

He meant: "whoever inclines towards others than you."

﴿wherever you may be﴾: this refers to the People of the Book.

﴿Allah will bring you all together﴾: on the Day of Resurrection, and He will recompense you for your deeds.

﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾.

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾: *haythu* is a particle indicating place. It has three dialectal forms: with *ya'* and *tha'* (*ḥaythu*), which is the dialect of Quraysh and the reading of the majority; scholars differed over the case of its final vowel. Some said it is indeclinable on a *damma*, like *mundhu* and *qattu*. Others said it is in the accusative of termination, as in His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the command before and after﴾.

*Ḥaythu* with *ya'* and a fatha on the *tha'* is the reading of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. Al-Kisa'i said: it is pronounced with a fatha because the *ya'* is quiescent, and when two quiescent letters come together in one word they move the second to a fatha, since fatha is the lightest vowel, as in *layta* and *kayfa*.

*Ḥawthu* with *waw* and *damma* is the dialect of Ibn 'Umar. It is reported that he was asked where the worshipper should place his hands during prayer, and he said: "Throw them wherever they fall."

﴿So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque. And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord﴾, up to: ﴿And wherever you are, O believers, turn your faces towards it﴾.

﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾: here the *lam* is the lam of purpose (*lam kay*), which entered upon *an*, so the preceding *kasra* was written with it. Some omitted the hamza of *an* for ease. *Ḥujjah* is of the pattern *fu'lah*, from *ḥajj*, meaning "clarification," from which comes *maḥajjah*, the clear and well-travelled path, because it is intended. One says *muḥajjah* for disputation, because each of the two opponents seeks to establish his proof and to refute what is in the hand of his adversary.
