Some of the interpreters said: the meaning of the verse is that the qibla was changed to the Ka'bah, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, for if you pray towards it, they would argue against you saying: "Why did you abandon facing the Ka'bah and turn to something else? Unless you have no qibla!" ﴿except those who wronged﴾: they are the Quraysh and the Jews. As for the Quraysh, they would say: "He only returned to the Ka'bah because he knew it was the qibla of his fathers and that it is the truth; and so he will return to our religion, knowing that it is the truth." As for the Jews, they would say: "He did not turn away from Bayt al-Maqdis while knowing it is the truth, unless he does things by his own opinion and claims that he was commanded to do so." This is the view chosen by al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah al-Dabbi, and it is a sound and accepted view.

Others said: the meaning of the verse is ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the People of the Book will have no argument against you. Their argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions in their prayer towards Bayt al-Maqdis was that they would say: "Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qibla is until we guided them!" and "Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our qibla." These are the arguments with which they would argue against the believers, in a spirit of hostility and deception, to mislead the ignorant polytheists. Then He said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾, and they are the polytheists of Mecca. Their argument was that when the qibla was turned to the Ka'bah they said: "Muhammad has become confused in his religion, so he turned towards our qibla, and he knows that we are more rightly guided than him, that he cannot do without us, and that he will soon return to our religion just as he returned to our qibla." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi, and it is the view preferred by Muhammad ibn Jarir.

On these two views, the exception with *illa* is a valid exception in the manner of your saying: "No one among the people travelled except your brother," which affirms travel for the brother, while it is negated for everyone else among the people. Likewise His saying, ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those who wronged﴾: it negates that anyone has an argument against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions because of their turning to the Ka'bah, ﴿except those who wronged﴾ of the Quraysh, for they have an argument against them for the reason we mentioned.

The meaning of *ḥujjah* in these two views is disputation, argument, and false claim, as in His saying: ﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾, i.e., there is no dispute. And His saying: ﴿Do you argue with us about Allah?﴾ and ﴿that they may argue with you﴾ and ﴿and you argue﴾ and ﴿you disputed﴾: all of these mean argumentation and contention, not evidence and proof. The word *alladhina* is in the genitive position, as if He had said "except to those who wronged." When the preposition *lam* was dropped, *alladhina* took its place. So said al-Kisa'i.

Al-Farra' said: its position is accusative by the exception, and [......] from them was returned to the wording *al-nas* because it is general, even though each one of them differs from the other. Allah knows best.

Some said: it is a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*) from the first sentence, and its meaning is: "unless there will be an argument against you from all the people, except for those who wronged, for they will argue against you in falsehood and dispute with you by injustice." This is like saying to a man: "All the people are your companions except the wrongdoer to you," meaning [......] that he does not praise you because of his enmity towards you. And like saying to a man: "You have no right with me except if you wrong," and "You have no argument except falsehood, and falsehood is not an argument." This is an exception that is not from the speech of al-Hasan.

Like the saying of one who says: "There is no one in the house except the wild animals," as in the saying of al-Nabighah:

*wa-ma bi-al-rab'i min ahad illa wa-ara li-aya ma... amamha wa-nawi ka-al-hawd bi-al-mazlumah al-jald*

And this is the view of al-Farra' and al-Mu'arrikh.

Abu Rawq said: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, meaning the Jews, will have no argument against you. This is because they had known that the Ka'bah is the qibla of Ibrahim, and they had found in the Torah that Muhammad would be turned towards it. So Allah turned him towards it, so that they would have no argument, so that they could not argue that: "This Prophet whom we find in our Book will be turned towards it, but you were not turned!" When the Prophet (ﷺ) was turned, their argument disappeared. Then He said: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, meaning: except that they wrong you and conceal what they knew.

Al-Akhfash said: its meaning is "it is sufficient for those who wronged" (*li-kafa al-ladhina zalamu*): ﴿they have no knowledge of it, they follow only assumption﴾, meaning: rather, they follow assumption. And His saying: ﴿and for no one has he any favour to be repaid, except seeking the countenance of his Lord﴾, meaning: but rather seeking the countenance of your Lord. So it is an independent sentence apart from the first.

Abu 'Ubaydah said, as transmitted by Abu 'Ubayd: "The place of *illa* here is not an exception, because a wrongdoer does not have an argument. Rather, its place is that of the conjunction *waw*, as if He had said: 'Nor those who wronged,' meaning: 'and those who wronged do not have an argument either.'"

Al-Mufaddal recited:

*ma bi-al-madinah dar ghayr wahidah... dar al-khalifah illa dar Marwan*

And he also recited:

*wa-kull akh mufariqah akhuhu... la-'amr abika illa al-farqadan*

Meaning: "the two Farqadan (stars) are also separated." Al-Akhfash recited:

*wa-ara laha dara bi-aghdarah al-Sayyidan... lam yadrus laha rasm*

*illa ramadan hamidan dafa'at 'anhu al-riyah khawalid suham*

That is: "I see for it a dwelling and ashes."

This view is supported by what Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid transmitted from some of them that some recited ﴿to those who wronged﴾ with a lightened *lam*, meaning ﴿with those who wronged﴾.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿so that people will have no argument﴾, meaning the Jews, ﴿against you﴾ concerning the matter of the Ka'bah, since they would not face it, though it is the qibla of Ibrahim. They would say: "You claim you are upon the religion of Ibrahim, yet you do not face his qibla!" ﴿nor those who wronged﴾, meaning the polytheists of Mecca, because they said: "The Ka'bah is the qibla of our grandfather Ibrahim. Why has Muhammad turned away from it, so that he does not pray towards it, but prays towards the qibla of the Jews?"

Qatrub said: the meaning is "except upon those who wronged," so that its reference returns to the *kaf* and *mim* (of *'alaykum*), i.e., "except upon those who wronged, for upon them is the argument." So the preposition was omitted. This is the choice of Abu Mansur al-Azhari.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi relating it from him, and Muhammad ibn Jarir related from some of them that he said: ﴿except those who wronged﴾ here refers to some people among the Arabs who were Jews and Christians, and who used to argue against the Prophet (ﷺ). As for the rest of the Arabs, they had no argument. And the argument of whoever argued was also refuted and false, because you say to one whose argument you want to break: "You have an argument against me, but it is broken; you argue without an argument, and your argument is weak." So the meaning of the verse: ﴿except those among them who wronged﴾, from the People of the Book, for they have against you a flimsy argument.

﴿So do not fear them﴾ regarding your turning towards the Ka'bah, and their backing one another against you in argument and reply. ﴿Rather, fear Me﴾: I am your protector, and I will make you prevail over them with proof and victory.

﴿and fear Me﴾ in abandoning it and opposing it.

﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾: this is coordinated (*'atf*) on His saying ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, but rather: and I complete My favour by guiding you to the qibla of Ibrahim, so that the upright religion (*al-milla al-hanifiyyah*) is completed for you.

'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said: "The completion of the favour is dying upon Islam."

It is also reported from him that he said: "The blessings are six: Islam, the Qur'an, Muhammad, concealment (of faults), well-being, and wealth of what is in the hands of people."

﴿and that you may be guided﴾: *la'alla* has six dialects: *'alla*, *la'alla*, *la'anna*, *'anna*, and *la'a*.

It has six meanings, some of which are obligatory from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and others from people:

It may mean interrogation, as when someone says: "Perhaps you did that?" asking a question.

It may mean supposition, as when someone says: "So-and-so has arrived," and the reply is: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "I suppose and think that."

It may mean affirmation, in the position of *ma akhlaqah* ("how fitting it is"), as in His saying: "The prayer has become obligatory," and the reply: "Perhaps that is so," meaning: "how fitting it is." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alla al-manaya marratan sata'ud... wa-akhir 'ahd al-za'irin jadid*

It may mean hope and wish, as when you say: "Perhaps Allah will grant me wealth," and "Perhaps I will perform Hajj." Al-Farra' recited:

*la'alli fi huda afi wujudi... wa-taqti'i al-tanwaqah wa-ikhtiyali*

*sa-yushik an yatih ila karim... yunalaka bi-al-dhura qabla al-su'al*

It may mean *'asa* ("perhaps"), in which the desired thing may or may not occur, as in His saying: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾, i.e., "perhaps I may reach." Abu Dawud said:

*fa-ablawni baliyatakum la'alli... usalihukum wa-astadriju nawiyya*

Meaning: "my companion." And it may mean *kay* ("in order that") for the consequence, as in His saying: ﴿See how We diversify the verses, that they may understand﴾, i.e., "in order that they may understand," and there are many similar examples. And His saying: ﴿and that you may be guided﴾, i.e., in order that you may be guided from error.

Al-Rabi' said: A Jew disputed with Abu al-'Aliyah and said: "Moses used to pray towards the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "He prayed beside the rock towards the Sacred House." The Jew said: "Between me and you is a righteous mosque, for he carved it from the mountain." Abu al-'Aliyah said: "I have prayed in it, and its qibla is the Sacred House."

He said: Abu al-'Aliyah reported that he passed by the mosque of Dhu al-Qarnayn, whose qibla is the Ka'bah. [See the Tafsir of al-Tabari: 2/48.]

﴿as We sent﴾: the *kaf* here is for comparison, and it requires something to which it refers. The scholars differed about it. Some said: it refers to what precedes it, and the *kaf* of what precedes it is "as," its meaning being: ﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me, and that I may complete My favour upon you, as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾. So the sending of the Messenger becomes a condition for fear, and an addition to the completion of the favour.

It was also said: its meaning is ﴿and that you may be guided, as We sent﴾.

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: Ibrahim made two supplications, saying: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims to You and from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾. That is the first supplication. The second is his saying: ﴿Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves﴾. Allah sent the Messenger, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), and in this verse He promised to answer the second supplication, and to make from his descendants a Muslim nation to Him. So the meaning of the verse: ﴿and that I may complete My favour upon you﴾, by clarifying the laws of your upright religion, and I guide you to the religion of My intimate friend Ibrahim.

﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves﴾: meaning, just as He answered his supplication by sending the Messenger, so He answered his supplication by guiding you to his religion and making you Muslims. This is according to the view of those who connect it to what precedes it, as a response to the first verse, and it is the choice of al-Farra'.

Others said: it is connected to what follows it, which is His saying: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾. Its estimate: ﴿as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves ... so remember Me, I will remember you﴾. So it becomes a part of it with two responses, a preceding and a following one, as you say: "If so-and-so comes to you, then go to him, he will satisfy you." So His saying "then go to him" and "he will satisfy you" are two responses to "if he comes to you." And like your saying: "If you come to me, I will be good to you, I will honour you." This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Kalbi, Muqatil, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan, and it is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

This verse is addressed to the Arabs and the people of Mecca, meaning: ﴿as We sent among you﴾, O assembly of Arabs, ﴿a messenger from yourselves﴾, Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿who recites to you Our verses﴾: meaning the Qur'an.

﴿and purifies you﴾: meaning, they teach you the rulings and the laws of Islam.

﴿So remember Me; I will remember you.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My help." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us﴾, etc.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My forgiveness." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger that you may receive mercy﴾.

Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: "Remember Me by obedience to Me, I will remember you by My reward." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one whose work is good. Those will have gardens of perpetual residence﴾.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"Whoever obeys Allah has remembered Allah, even if his prayer and fasting and recitation of the Qur'an are few."

[6] [Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/258; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/149.]

It was also said: "Remember Me with monotheism and faith; I will remember you with the gardens and the degrees." Its clarification is: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe ... of gardens﴾.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Monotheism suffices as worship, and Paradise suffices as reward."

Ibn Kaysan said: "Remember Me with gratitude; I will remember you with increase." Its clarification is His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me upon the surface of the earth; I will remember you in its belly."

Al-Asfa said: "I saw a Bedouin standing on the day of 'Arafah at the place of standing, saying: 'Voices have cried out to You in all kinds of tongues, asking You for their needs. My need from You is that You remember me when I am decayed, if the people of this world forget me.'"

It was also said: "Remember Me with acts of obedience; I will remember you with well-being." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾.

It was also said: "Remember Me in solitude and in company; I will remember you in the open and in the assembly." Its clarification is what is related in some books that Allah said: "I am as My servant thinks of Me, so let him think of Me what he will, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; if he remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than it. If he draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; if he draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; if he comes to Me walking, I come to him running; and if he comes to Me with earth-filling sins, I come to him with an earth-filling forgiveness, provided he does not associate anything with Me."

And it has been said: "Remember Me in ease and prosperity, and I will remember you in hardship and affliction." Its evidence is His saying: ﴿Had he not been one of those who glorify [Allah], he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾

Salman al-Farisi said: Indeed, when a servant has a supplication in secret, and then calamity befalls him, the angels say: "Your servant has been struck by calamity," and they intercede for him, and Allah rescues him. But if he has no supplication, they say: "Now [there is no one]; so you do not intercede for him." Its evidence is the word of Pharaoh: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with submission and reliance, and I will remember you with the best choice." Its evidence is: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him.﴾

And it has been said: "Remember Me with longing and love, and I will remember you with union and nearness."

And it has been said: "Remember Me with praise and commendation, and I will remember you with reward." And it has been said: "Remember Me with return [to Me in repentance], and I will remember you with the forgiveness of sin." And it has been said: "Remember Me with supplication, and I will remember you with giving." "Remember Me with request, and I will remember you with bestowal." "Remember Me without heedlessness, and I will remember you without delay." "Remember Me with regret, and I will remember you with generosity." "Remember Me with apology, and I will remember you with forgiveness." "Remember Me with desire, and I will remember you with benefit." "Remember Me with disavowal [of your sins], and I will remember you with bounty." "Remember Me with sincerity, and I will remember you with deliverance." "Remember Me with hearts, and I will remember you with the removal of distress." "Remember Me without forgetfulness, and I will remember you with security." "Remember Me with neediness, and I will remember you with power." "Remember Me with humility and seeking forgiveness, and I will remember you with mercy and pardon." "Remember Me with faith, and I will remember you with Paradise." "Remember Me with Islam, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with the heart, and I will remember you with the lifting of anguish." "Remember Me with a remembrance that passes, and I will remember you with a remembrance that remains." "Remember Me with entreaty, and I will remember you with abundance." "Remember Me with the shade [of humility], and I will remember you with pardon for error." "Remember Me with acknowledgment, and I will remember you with the erasure of transgression." "Remember Me with purity of secret, and I will remember you with pure righteousness." "Remember Me with truthfulness, and I will remember you with gentleness." "Remember Me with clarity, and I will remember you with pardon." "Remember Me with glorification, and I will remember you with honor." "Remember Me with magnification [takbir], and I will remember you with purification." "Remember Me with exaltation, and I will remember you with increase." "Remember Me with intimate conversation, and I will remember you with salvation." "Remember Me by abandoning disdain, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me by abandoning error, and I will remember you by preserving fidelity." "Remember Me with striving in creation, and I will remember you with the completion of blessing." "Remember Me from where you are, and I will remember you from where I am." ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater.﴾

Al-Rabi' said regarding this verse: Indeed, Allah remembers whoever remembers Him, increases whoever thanks Him, and punishes whoever disbelieves in Him.

Al-Suddi said regarding it: There is no servant who mentions Allah except that Allah mentions him. No believer mentions Him except that He mentions him with mercy, and no disbeliever mentions Him except that He mentions him with punishment.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: It has reached us that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "I have given My servants what, if I had given it to Jibril and Mika'il, I would have been generous to them. I said: 'Remember Me, and I will remember you.' And I said to Musa: 'Tell the wrongdoers not to mention Me, for I remember whoever mentions Me, and My remembrance of them is that I curse them.'"

Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi said: Indeed I know when my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, remembers me. It was said: "How is that?" He said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾, and when you remember Allah, the Exalted, He remembers you.

﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ [[Marginal note in the manuscript: by giving; whoever obeys Allah has given thanks, and whoever disobeys Him has disbelieved.]] for My favor,

﴿and do not deny Me.﴾

O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient. ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with those who are patient.﴾ (meaning: by aid and support).

﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive.﴾ This was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr from among the Muslims. They were fourteen men: eight from the Ansar and six from the Muhajirun. This was because people used to say, "So-and-so has been killed in the way of Allah; he has died and has lost the bounties and pleasures of this world." So Allah the Exalted revealed, ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead,"﴾ that is, "They are not dead; rather, they are alive."

﴿Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive.﴾ Indeed, they are as such.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the souls of the martyrs are in the bellies of green birds that graze among the fruits of Paradise, drink from its rivers, and at night take shelter in lamps of light suspended beneath the Throne." [7] [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 5/298, and al-Mu'jam al-Kabir of al-Tabarani: 9/183.]]

Al-Hasan said: The martyrs are alive with Allah. Their provision is presented to their souls, so joy and delight reach them, just as the Fire is presented to the souls of the people of Pharaoh morning and evening, so pain reaches them.

Abu Sinan al-Sulami said: The souls of the martyrs are in white domes at the gate of Paradise. In each dome are two spouses. Their provision each day the sun rises is a light and a fish. As for the light, in it is the taste of every fruit in Paradise. As for the fish, in it is the taste of every drink in Paradise.

Qatada said concerning this verse: We used to be told that the souls of the martyrs recognize one another in white birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise, and that their dwellings are the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary (al-Sidrat al-Muntaha). For the one who fights in the way of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, there are three qualities: whoever is killed in the way of Allah becomes living and provided for; whoever is victorious, Allah gives him a great reward; and whoever dies, Allah provides him with a good provision.

On the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The martyr is given six qualities at the first drop of his blood: all his sins are expiated, he sees his seat in Paradise, he is married to the wide-eyed houris, he is secured from the greatest terror and from the punishment of the grave, and he is adorned with the adornment of faith." [8] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/200, and Majma' al-Zawa'id: 5/293.]]

﴿And We will surely test you﴾ O community of Muhammad, ﴿we will surely test you.﴾

﴿with something of fear and hunger﴾ and so on. Ibn Abbas said: "Fear" means fear of the enemy, and "hunger" means famine and drought.

﴿and loss of wealth﴾ means loss and decrease in property, and the death of livestock. ﴿and lives﴾ means death and killing. It was also said: illness. It was also said: old age.

﴿and fruits﴾ means needs (al-hawa'ij), and that fruit does not come forth as it used to. Al-Shafi'i said:

﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear﴾ means the fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿and hunger﴾ means fasting the month of Ramadan. ﴿and loss of wealth﴾ means paying zakat and charity. ﴿and lives﴾ means illnesses. ﴿and fruits﴾ means the death of children, because a man's child is the fruit of his heart. This is evidenced by what

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak narrated from Hammad ibn Salama from Abu Sinan, who said: I buried my son Sinan, and Abu Talha al-Khawlani was sitting at the edge of the grave. When I was about to leave, he took my hand, lifted me up, and said: "Shall I not give you good news, O Abu Sinan?" I said: "Yes." He said: al-Dahhak ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Arzab narrated to us from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When a servant's child dies, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says to the angels, 'Have you taken the child of My servant?' They say, 'Yes.' He says, 'Have you taken the fruit of his heart?' They say, 'Yes.' He says, 'What did My servant say?' They say, 'He praised You and said, "Inna lillah wa inna ilayhi raji'un."' Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says, 'Build for My servant a house in Paradise and name it the House of Praise.'" [9] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 2/243, hadith 1026, and Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/204.]]

﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ in calamities and afflictions. Then He described them, saying: ﴿Who, when a misfortune strikes them, say, "Indeed, we belong to Allah"﴾ as slaves, to be gathered, and as property.

﴿and indeed to Him we will return﴾ in the Hereafter. Those who recited ﴿Inna lillah﴾ with the nun inclined (amal) its vowel. Qutayba inclined both the nun and the lam together, while the others made them emphatic (fakhkhama). Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: ﴿Inna lillah﴾ is our acknowledgment that He owns us, and ﴿wa inna ilayhi raji'un﴾ in the Hereafter is our acknowledgment against ourselves of our perishing.

Ikrima said: The lamp of the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, and he said: ﴿Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.﴾ It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, is that a calamity?" He said: "Yes. Everything that harms the believer is a calamity for him." [10] [[al-Jami' al-Saghir: 2/282, hadith 6323, where it reads "distresses the believer" (sa'a); Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/298, hadith 6639.]]

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: No one has been given in calamity what this community has been given, namely the istirja' (saying "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un"). Had it been given to anyone, it would have been given to Ya'qub (peace be upon him). Do you not hear his words over the loss of Yusuf: ﴿Alas, my grief over Yusuf!﴾ [[Surat Yusuf: 84.]]

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says istirja' at a calamity, Allah will mend his calamity, make its outcome good for him, and give him a righteous successor whom he is pleased with." [11] [[al-'Uhud al-Muhammadiyya: 597, and Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/300, hadith 6650.]]

On the authority of Fatima bint al-Husayn, from her mother, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is afflicted by a calamity and then renews his istirja', even if its time has long passed, Allah writes for him the reward of the day he was afflicted." [12] [[al-Jami' al-Saghir: 2/573, hadith 8459, and Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/264, hadith 6471.]]

﴿Those﴾ meaning the people of this description.

﴿upon them are blessings﴾ Ibn Abbas said: forgiveness. ﴿from their Lord and mercy﴾ and grace.

Ibn Kaysan said: "Blessings" here means praise, mercy and purification. He mentioned "blessings" and "mercy" though their meaning is one, because the two wordings differ, as in the saying of al-Hutay'a:

Ah, how lovely is Hind, and the land where Hind dwells,
and Hind, beyond it, is distance and remoteness.

The plural "blessings" is used because it means mercy upon mercy.

﴿And those are the guided﴾ to the istirja'. It was also said: to Paradise and reward. It was also said: to the truth and what is right.

When Umar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse, he would say: "What an excellent pair of two, and what an excellent addition."

O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with the patient. ﴿Seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, Allah is with those who are patient.﴾ (meaning: by aid and support).

﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive.﴾ This was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr from among the Muslims. They were fourteen men: eight from the Ansar and six from the Muhajirun. Ikrima said: The lamp of the Prophet (ﷺ) went out, and he said: ﴿Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.﴾ It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, is that a calamity?" He said: "Yes. Everything that harms the believer is a calamity for him." [10] [[al-Jami' al-Saghir: 2/282, hadith 6323, where it reads "distresses the believer" (sa'a); Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/298, hadith 6639.]]

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: No one has been given in calamity what this community has been given, namely the istirja' (saying "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un"). Had it been given to anyone, it would have been given to Ya'qub (peace be upon him). Do you not hear his words over the loss of Yusuf: ﴿Alas, my grief over Yusuf!﴾ [[Surat Yusuf: 84.]]

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says istirja' at a calamity, Allah will mend his calamity, make its outcome good for him, and give him a righteous successor whom he is pleased with." [11] [[al-'Uhud al-Muhammadiyya: 597, and Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/300, hadith 6650.]]

On the authority of Fatima bint al-Husayn, from her mother, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is afflicted by a calamity and then renews his istirja', even if its time has long passed, Allah writes for him the reward of the day he was afflicted." [12] [[al-Jami' al-Saghir: 2/573, hadith 8459, and Kanz al-'Ummal: 3/264, hadith 6471.]]

﴿Those﴾ meaning the people of this description.

﴿upon them are blessings﴾ Ibn Abbas said: forgiveness. ﴿from their Lord and mercy﴾ and grace.

Ibn Kaysan said: "Blessings" here means praise, mercy and purification. He mentioned "blessings" and "mercy" though their meaning is one, because the two wordings differ, as in the saying of al-Hutay'a:

Ah, how lovely is Hind, and the land where Hind dwells,
and Hind, beyond it, is distance and remoteness.

The plural "blessings" is used because it means mercy upon mercy.

﴿And those are the guided﴾ to the istirja'. It was also said: to Paradise and reward. It was also said: to the truth and what is right.

When Umar ibn al-Khattab recited this verse, he would say: "What an excellent pair of two, and what an excellent addition."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 158–162:

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God.﴾ Al-Safa is the plural of al-saffa, which is a hard, smooth rock. Imru' al-Qais said:

*She has a rump like the rock of the watercourse, when the bristling of Mudar has exposed it.* [[Majma' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 1/438.]]

It is said: saffa and safa, like hasa and hasa, qata and qata, and nawa and nawa. It is also said that al-Safa is singular, with its dual being Safwan, like asa and asawan, and its plural being asfa', like raja and arja'. And safa and safi, like asa and asi. The rajiz said:

*As if his two sides, from the rough ground, are the perches of birds upon the safi.* [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/59.]]

Al-Marwah is the stone that is soft and small. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

*Until I am, for calamities, a marwah, struck every day upon the rock of the east.*

That is, a soft, small rock. The plural of marwah is marwan, and its plural for the large one is marw, like thamra and thamarat, thamr, hamra and hamarat, and hamra'. Al-A'sha Maymun ibn Qays, describing his she-camel, said:

*You see the earth a passing, light ground, and when it meets the marw, it crumbles.* [[Ibid.: 2/60.]]

God, exalted is He, meant by them the two well-known mountains in Makkah, not the rest of the safa and marwa, and for that reason the definite article (al) was added to them. The symbols of God (sha'a'ir Allah) are the markers of His religion; its singular is sha'ira. Everything that was marked as an offering by which one draws near to God, mighty and majestic, whether supplication, prayer, sacrifice, performance of an obligation, or other such things, is a sha'ira.

Al-Kumayt ibn Zayd said:

*We kill them generation after generation; you see them as symbols of an offering through which one draws near.*

Its root is from al-ash'ar, which means the markers upon a thing.

In a hadith: when 'Umar was wounded during the Hajj, someone said: "Has the Commander of the Faithful bled?" Here, by the symbols, he meant the rites of Hajj which God, mighty and majestic, made as markers of His obedience. Mujahid said: "It means from the report which I have told you about." The root of the word, according to this view, is from sha'artu, meaning "I knew," as if they were signs from God to His servants concerning the matter of al-Safa and al-Marwah.

The sense of the verse: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾, so the mention of circumambulation (tawaf) is omitted and suffices with mentioning the two, that being known to the addressees.

﴿So whoever performs Hajj to the House﴾. The root meaning of hajj in the language is "intention."

The poet said:

*Like a monk who goes on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, a monotheist, with a cloak and a hooded cape.* [[Words unreadable, and this is the apparent reading.]]

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "Whoever frequently turns to something is a hajj (one who makes pilgrimage) to it." Al-Mihmal al-Sa'di said:

*And witness from 'Awf many gatherings, who visit the House of al-Zibriqan the saffron-clad.* [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/61.]]

That is, they frequently go to him for his affection and leadership.

The pilgrim is called hajj because he comes to the House from 'Arafah, then returns to it for the tawaf on the day of sacrifice, then departs from it to Mina, then returns to it for the farewell tawaf. Because of the repetition of returning to it time after time, he is called hajj.

﴿Or performs 'umrah﴾. 'Umrah is from al-i'timar, which is visiting. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*Indeed the son of Ma'mar rose when he visited, far, to a far one, and a steed.*

That is, whoever intends and visits it. Al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah said: ﴿or performs 'umrah﴾ means he settles in Makkah after the tawaf and the sa'y, and does what the one who is in the state of ihram lawfully does.

'Umrah (from 'amara) means to inhabit a place, and 'imarah means to repair and restore it.

From 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Follow up the Hajj with the 'umrah, for following up between them increases one's lifespan and provision and removes sins as the bellows removes the impurity of iron." [13]

﴿Then there is no blame upon him﴾. Al-Jina' is sin, and its root is from janaha, when one deviates from the right course.

It is said: "The night inclined (janah) when its darkness came." And "The ship leaned (janahat) when it inclined toward the earth." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [Qur'an 8:61]. From it comes janah al-tair, the wing of a bird.

﴿that he circumambulates (yattawwafa)﴾, meaning goes around; its root is yatatawwafa, and the taa was assimilated into the ta' (of tawwafa).

Abu Hayyah al-Shami read yatufa with a lightened ta'. They differed concerning the meaning and interpretation of the verse and the occasion of its revelation.

Anas ibn Malik said: "We used to dislike circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah, because they were among the rites of the Quraysh in the Jahiliyyah, so we left it in Islam. Then God revealed this verse."

'Umar ibn Habib said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about this verse, and he said: 'Go to Ibn 'Abbas, for he is the most knowledgeable of those remaining in what was revealed upon Muhammad (ﷺ).' I went to him and asked him, and Ibn 'Abbas said: 'On al-Safa there was an idol in the form of a man called Isaf, and on al-Marwah an idol in the form of a woman called Na'ilah. They mentioned al-Safa for the masculine (Isaf) and mentioned al-Marwah for the feminine (Na'ilah).'"

The People of the Book claimed that the two had committed fornication in the sacred precinct, so God, mighty and majestic, transformed them into two stones and placed them on al-Safa and al-Marwah as a lesson. When the period lengthened, they were worshipped besides God. So when the people of the Jahiliyyah circumambulated between them, they would rub the two idols. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims disliked circumambulating between them because of the two idols, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "In the Jahiliyyah there were devils that played music at night between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and there were gods between them. When Islam appeared, the Muslims said to the Messenger of God: 'Do not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah, for it is polytheism, which we used to practise in the Jahiliyyah.' So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse." [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 28.]]

Qatadah: "Some people from Tihamah used to run between al-Safa and al-Marwah in the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, they felt uneasy about running between them, as they had felt uneasy about it in the Jahiliyyah, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

Qatadah: "A tribe from Tihamah did not run between them, so He informed them that it was the Sunnah of Abraham and Isma'il, peace be upon them." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/65.]]

Al-Zuhri narrated from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'What are al-Safa and al-Marwah?' She said: 'It is the saying of God: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾ — the verse. By God, there is no blame upon anyone for not circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah.'" She said: "What you said is not correct, my nephew. If this verse were as you understand it, there would be no blame upon one who does not circumambulate between them. But it was revealed concerning the Ansar, for before they embraced Islam they used to worship Manat the Tyrant, an idol at al-Mushallal between Makkah and Madinah. Whoever assumed the ihram for her would be reluctant to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah. When they embraced Islam, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked them about that. They said: 'O Messenger of God, we used not to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah because they were two idols. Is there any sin upon us if we circumambulate between them?'"

So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Then 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) established the circumambulation between them. So no one has the right to abandon it."

Al-Zuhri said: "I mentioned that to Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham." He said: "This is knowledge."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "The people had abandoned circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah, except the Hums, who were the Quraysh, Kinanah, Khuza'ah, and 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah. They were called Hums (the strict ones) for their strictness in their religion; al-hamasah means courage and firmness. So the Hums asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about running between al-Safa and al-Marwah: is it among the symbols of God or not? For none circumambulates between them except us. So this verse was revealed."

The scholars differed concerning this verse. Al-Shafi'i and Malik said: circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah is an obligatory pillar (fard). Whoever abandons it must make up for it and repeat it; no expiation (fidyah) or anything else suffices for him except returning to Makkah and circumambulating between them, just as one who abandons the tawaf al-ifadah cannot be excused except by making up that same tawaf.

They said: "They are two obligatory circumambulations: one commanded with the House, and the other between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and their ruling is one."

Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: If the one who abandons the circumambulation between them returns to make it up, that is good; if he does not return, he must offer a sacrifice (dam). They held that the ruling for these circumambulations is the ruling for throwing some of the pebbles, standing at al-Mash'ar, the farewell tawaf, and similar things, for which the one who abandons them owes an expiation by abandoning them, and he is not required to return to make up that very act.

Anas ibn Malik, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and 'Ata' said: circumambulating between them is a voluntary act (tatawwu'); if one performs it he is virtuous, and if one abandons it he is not obligated to anything by abandoning it.

Those who did not make running and circumambulation between them obligatory argued by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and Ibn Sirin: ﴿then there is no blame upon him that he does not circumambulate between them﴾, with the particle "not" (la) affirmed. It is likewise in the codex of 'Abd Allah.

The answer to this: the (la) is an added particle (za'idah silah), like the saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [Qur'an 7:12], and like: ﴿that they do not return﴾ [Qur'an 21:95], and ﴿So I swear not﴾ [Qur'an 75:1–2; 90:1], and the poet said:

*So I do not blame the white women that they did not mock, when they saw the grey-haired, dishevelled man.*

The structure of the written codex is thus; there is no proof in it with the possibility of the speech as we have described, and how much more so since it contradicts the established script of the Shaykh, the Imam, and the codices of Islam.

Then, the evidence that running between them is obligatory, and that whoever abandons it must repeat the Hajj, whether he forgot it or did it deliberately, is by the apparent reports: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did it and commanded it.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated from his father from Jabir who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approached al-Safa in his Hajj, he said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾. Begin with what God began with." So he began with al-Safa, ascended it until he saw the House, then walked until his feet came down into the valley, and then ran." [14]

Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father from 'A'ishah who said: "By my life, whoever does not run between al-Safa and al-Marwah has not performed Hajj; it is obligatory in the Book of God and the Sunnah. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, running has been prescribed for you, so run." [15]

Kulayb said: "Ibn 'Abbas saw some people circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah and said: 'This is what your mother Umm Isma'il bequeathed to you. She set out when her son became thirsty and hungry, and she found al-Safa the nearest mountain to the earth, so she stood upon it, then faced the valley looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. So she descended from the valley, lifted the hem of her garment, and ran like a man in distress until she passed the valley. Then she came to al-Marwah and stood upon it, looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. She did this seven times.'"

Muhammad said: "Musa (peace be upon him) performed Hajj upon a red mountain, wearing two woollen cloaks daubed with tar. He circumambulated the House, then ascended al-Safa and supplicated, then descended to run, while uttering the talbiyah: 'Here I am, O God, here I am.' God, mighty and majestic, said: 'Here I am, My servant, and I am with you.' So Musa fell down prostrate."

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read tatawwa'a with a ta' and a shaddah on the ta' and a jazm on the 'ayn, and likewise the ta' in yatawwa' (meaning "he volunteers"). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, reasoning from the reading of 'Abd Allah: "and whoever volunteers (tatawwa'a) with a ta'."

The rest read tatawwa'a with a ta' and a shaddah on the 'ayn, in the past tense.

Mujahid said: "Whoever volunteers in circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah." He also said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) volunteered, and he was among the prophets."

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ means one who increases in the circumambulation; the obligatory part is in it.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ means he performs 'umrah, for the Hajj is an obligation and the 'umrah is voluntary.

It is said: "Whoever volunteers with Hajj and 'umrah after fulfilling his obligatory pilgrimage."

Al-Hasan and others said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ is meant for the whole religion: whatever act beyond what is obligatory upon him, of circumambulation, prayer, zakah, or any kind of the acts of obedience.

﴿then God is Appreciative﴾, He rewards him for his deed.

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intention of the one who gives thanks, who appreciates the little, gives the much, and forgives the great. The root of shukr (thanks) comes from the saying of the Arabs: "a shakur beast," when its fat appears upon it beyond what it is fed.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of the clear proofs﴾, meaning the stoning (rajm), the prescribed punishments, the rulings, and what is lawful and unlawful.

﴿and the guidance﴾, meaning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description.

﴿after We have made it clear to the people﴾, meaning to the Children of Israel.

﴿in the Book﴾, meaning in the Torah. It was revealed concerning the scholars and chiefs of the Jews who concealed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, God curses them﴾. The root meaning of la'n in the language is "expulsion." God cursed Iblis by expelling him when He said to him: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ [Qur'an 15:34; 38:77].

Al-Shammakh said, mentioning what came to him:

*The sandgrouse were startled by it, and you remained in it, like the wolf standing, like the accursed man.*

And al-Nabighah said:

*So I passed the night as if I were a cursed outcast, driven away by people, or a wounded sick man.*

So the meaning of our saying "God curses him" is: He expelled him and removed him far away. The root of la'nah is what we have mentioned; then it became common until it became a formula.

﴿and those who curse curse them﴾, meaning they ask God to curse them and say: "O God, curse them." The exegetes differed concerning who these cursers are.

Qatadah said: They are the angels.

'Ata': The jinn and mankind.

Al-Hasan: All the servants of God together.

Ibn 'Abbas: Everything except the jinn and mankind.

Al-Dahhak: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, he is asked: "Who is your Lord? And who is your prophet? And what is your religion?" He says: "I do not know." It is said to him: "You did not know," then he is struck with a blow of a hammer, and he cries out a cry which everything hears except the two weighty ones, mankind and jinn. Nothing hears his voice but curses him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾.

Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, a beast comes to him whose eyes are like two copper cauldrons, with an iron club, and it strikes him a blow between his shoulders, and he cries out. No one hears his voice without cursing him, and nothing remains that does not hear his voice except the two weighty ones.

Ibn Mas'ud: It is the man who curses his companion, and the curse rises to the sky, then descends, and does not find its target worthy of it, so it returns to the one who uttered it, and does not find him worthy of it either, so it goes and falls upon the Jews. This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾. Whoever among them repents, the curse is lifted from him, and it was upon those of the Jews who met it.

Mujahid: ﴿those who curse﴾ are the beasts, which curse the sinners of the children of Adam when the year becomes barren and the rain is withheld. They say: "This is because of the sins of the children of Adam."

'Ikrimah: The beasts of the earth and its creeping things, even the beetles and scorpions, say: "We have been withheld from rain because of the sins of the children of Adam." He said of these things ﴿those who curse﴾ and did not say "those who curse" (feminine), because it is the way of the Arabs, when they describe something of the inanimate things, animals, and others with what is a description of humans, of an act or a speech, that they do not take it out of the manner of the children of Adam and their group, as in their saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Qur'an 12:4], and he did not say "prostrating" (feminine). And His saying concerning the idols: ﴿Rather, their chief did it; so ask them, if they can speak﴾ [Qur'an 21:63]; and His saying: ﴿O ant, enter your dwellings﴾ [Qur'an 27:18]; and His saying: ﴿And they will say to their skins: "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ [Qur'an 41:21], and then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except those who repented﴾ from disbelief.

﴿and set right their deeds﴾ between themselves and their Lord.

﴿and make clear﴾ the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, I turn to them in forgiveness﴾, meaning I overlook them and accept their repentance.

﴿And I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾, who returns to the hearts of My servants who turned away from Me, and is Merciful to them after they turn to Me.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾, the "and" here is a circumstantial (wa of hal).

﴿those, upon them is the curse of God and of the angels﴾, meaning and the curse of the angels.

﴿and of mankind, all together﴾. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: it means mankind all together, the believers.

Abu al-'Aliyah: This is on the Day of Resurrection: the disbeliever is made to stand, and God, mighty and majestic, curses him, then the angels curse him, then all mankind curses him.

Al-Suddi: No two believers curse each other, nor two disbelievers, where one says "May God curse the wrongdoer," without that curse falling upon the disbeliever, because he is a wrongdoer; so every creature curses him.

﴿abiding therein﴾, remaining in the curse and the Fire.

﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning the torment will not be eased for them.

﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be given respite or delay.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "'Nor will they be reprieved' means they will not be given an excuse, as in His saying: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted, so they may make excuse﴾ [Qur'an 77:35–36]."

'Umrah (from 'amara) means to inhabit a place, and 'imarah means to repair and restore it.

From 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Follow up the Hajj with the 'umrah, for following up between them increases one's lifespan and provision and removes sins as the bellows removes the impurity of iron." [13]

﴿Then there is no blame upon him﴾. Al-Jina' is sin, and its root is from janaha, when one deviates from the right course.

It is said: "The night inclined (janah) when its darkness came." And "The ship leaned (janahat) when it inclined toward the earth." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [Qur'an 8:61]. From it comes janah al-tair, the wing of a bird.

﴿that he circumambulates (yattawwafa)﴾, meaning goes around; its root is yatatawwafa, and the taa was assimilated into the ta' (of tawwafa).

Abu Hayyah al-Shami read yatufa with a lightened ta'. They differed concerning the meaning and interpretation of the verse and the occasion of its revelation.

Anas ibn Malik said: "We used to dislike circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah, because they were among the rites of the Quraysh in the Jahiliyyah, so we left it in Islam. Then God revealed this verse."

'Umar ibn Habib said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about this verse, and he said: 'Go to Ibn 'Abbas, for he is the most knowledgeable of those remaining in what was revealed upon Muhammad (ﷺ).' I went to him and asked him, and Ibn 'Abbas said: 'On al-Safa there was an idol in the form of a man called Isaf, and on al-Marwah an idol in the form of a woman called Na'ilah. They mentioned al-Safa for the masculine (Isaf) and mentioned al-Marwah for the feminine (Na'ilah).'"

The People of the Book claimed that the two had committed fornication in the sacred precinct, so God, mighty and majestic, transformed them into two stones and placed them on al-Safa and al-Marwah as a lesson. When the period lengthened, they were worshipped besides God. So when the people of the Jahiliyyah circumambulated between them, they would rub the two idols. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims disliked circumambulating between them because of the two idols, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "In the Jahiliyyah there were devils that played music at night between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and there were gods between them. When Islam appeared, the Muslims said to the Messenger of God: 'Do not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah, for it is polytheism, which we used to practise in the Jahiliyyah.' So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse." [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 28.]]

Qatadah: "Some people from Tihamah used to run between al-Safa and al-Marwah in the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, they felt uneasy about running between them, as they had felt uneasy about it in the Jahiliyyah, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

Qatadah: "A tribe from Tihamah did not run between them, so He informed them that it was the Sunnah of Abraham and Isma'il, peace be upon them." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/65.]]

Al-Zuhri narrated from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'What are al-Safa and al-Marwah?' She said: 'It is the saying of God: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾ — the verse. By God, there is no blame upon anyone for not circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah.'" She said: "What you said is not correct, my nephew. If this verse were as you understand it, there would be no blame upon one who does not circumambulate between them. But it was revealed concerning the Ansar, for before they embraced Islam they used to worship Manat the Tyrant, an idol at al-Mushallal between Makkah and Madinah. Whoever assumed the ihram for her would be reluctant to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah. When they embraced Islam, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked them about that. They said: 'O Messenger of God, we used not to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah because they were two idols. Is there any sin upon us if we circumambulate between them?'"

So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Then 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) established the circumambulation between them. So no one has the right to abandon it."

Al-Zuhri said: "I mentioned that to Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham." He said: "This is knowledge."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "The people had abandoned circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah, except the Hums, who were the Quraysh, Kinanah, Khuza'ah, and 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah. They were called Hums (the strict ones) for their strictness in their religion; al-hamasah means courage and firmness. So the Hums asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about running between al-Safa and al-Marwah: is it among the symbols of God or not? For none circumambulates between them except us. So this verse was revealed."

The scholars differed concerning this verse. Al-Shafi'i and Malik said: circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah is an obligatory pillar (fard). Whoever abandons it must make up for it and repeat it; no expiation (fidyah) or anything else suffices for him except returning to Makkah and circumambulating between them, just as one who abandons the tawaf al-ifadah cannot be excused except by making up that same tawaf.

They said: "They are two obligatory circumambulations: one commanded with the House, and the other between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and their ruling is one."

Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: If the one who abandons the circumambulation between them returns to make it up, that is good; if he does not return, he must offer a sacrifice (dam). They held that the ruling for these circumambulations is the ruling for throwing some of the pebbles, standing at al-Mash'ar, the farewell tawaf, and similar things, for which the one who abandons them owes an expiation by abandoning them, and he is not required to return to make up that very act.

Anas ibn Malik, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and 'Ata' said: circumambulating between them is a voluntary act (tatawwu'); if one performs it he is virtuous, and if one abandons it he is not obligated to anything by abandoning it.

Those who did not make running and circumambulation between them obligatory argued by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and Ibn Sirin: ﴿then there is no blame upon him that he does not circumambulate between them﴾, with the particle "not" (la) affirmed. It is likewise in the codex of 'Abd Allah.

The answer to this: the (la) is an added particle (za'idah silah), like the saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [Qur'an 7:12], and like: ﴿that they do not return﴾ [Qur'an 21:95], and ﴿So I swear not﴾ [Qur'an 75:1–2; 90:1], and the poet said:

*So I do not blame the white women that they did not mock, when they saw the grey-haired, dishevelled man.*

The structure of the written codex is thus; there is no proof in it with the possibility of the speech as we have described, and how much more so since it contradicts the established script of the Shaykh, the Imam, and the codices of Islam.

Then, the evidence that running between them is obligatory, and that whoever abandons it must repeat the Hajj, whether he forgot it or did it deliberately, is by the apparent reports: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did it and commanded it.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated from his father from Jabir who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approached al-Safa in his Hajj, he said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾. Begin with what God began with." So he began with al-Safa, ascended it until he saw the House, then walked until his feet came down into the valley, and then ran." [14]

Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father from 'A'ishah who said: "By my life, whoever does not run between al-Safa and al-Marwah has not performed Hajj; it is obligatory in the Book of God and the Sunnah. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, running has been prescribed for you, so run." [15]

Kulayb said: "Ibn 'Abbas saw some people circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah and said: 'This is what your mother Umm Isma'il bequeathed to you. She set out when her son became thirsty and hungry, and she found al-Safa the nearest mountain to the earth, so she stood upon it, then faced the valley looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. So she descended from the valley, lifted the hem of her garment, and ran like a man in distress until she passed the valley. Then she came to al-Marwah and stood upon it, looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. She did this seven times.'"

Muhammad said: "Musa (peace be upon him) performed Hajj upon a red mountain, wearing two woollen cloaks daubed with tar. He circumambulated the House, then ascended al-Safa and supplicated, then descended to run, while uttering the talbiyah: 'Here I am, O God, here I am.' God, mighty and majestic, said: 'Here I am, My servant, and I am with you.' So Musa fell down prostrate."

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read tatawwa'a with a ta' and a shaddah on the ta' and a jazm on the 'ayn, and likewise the ta' in yatawwa' (meaning "he volunteers"). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, reasoning from the reading of 'Abd Allah: "and whoever volunteers (tatawwa'a) with a ta'."

The rest read tatawwa'a with a ta' and a shaddah on the 'ayn, in the past tense.

Mujahid said: "Whoever volunteers in circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah." He also said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) volunteered, and he was among the prophets."

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ means one who increases in the circumambulation; the obligatory part is in it.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ means he performs 'umrah, for the Hajj is an obligation and the 'umrah is voluntary.

It is said: "Whoever volunteers with Hajj and 'umrah after fulfilling his obligatory pilgrimage."

Al-Hasan and others said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ is meant for the whole religion: whatever act beyond what is obligatory upon him, of circumambulation, prayer, zakah, or any kind of the acts of obedience.

﴿then God is Appreciative﴾, He rewards him for his deed.

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intention of the one who gives thanks, who appreciates the little, gives the much, and forgives the great. The root of shukr (thanks) comes from the saying of the Arabs: "a shakur beast," when its fat appears upon it beyond what it is fed.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of the clear proofs﴾, meaning the stoning (rajm), the prescribed punishments, the rulings, and what is lawful and unlawful.

﴿and the guidance﴾, meaning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description.

﴿after We have made it clear to the people﴾, meaning to the Children of Israel.

﴿in the Book﴾, meaning in the Torah. It was revealed concerning the scholars and chiefs of the Jews who concealed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, God curses them﴾. The root meaning of la'n in the language is "expulsion." God cursed Iblis by expelling him when He said to him: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ [Qur'an 15:34; 38:77].

Al-Shammakh said, mentioning what came to him:

*The sandgrouse were startled by it, and you remained in it, like the wolf standing, like the accursed man.*

And al-Nabighah said:

*So I passed the night as if I were a cursed outcast, driven away by people, or a wounded sick man.*

So the meaning of our saying "God curses him" is: He expelled him and removed him far away. The root of la'nah is what we have mentioned; then it became common until it became a formula.

﴿and those who curse curse them﴾, meaning they ask God to curse them and say: "O God, curse them." The exegetes differed concerning who these cursers are.

Qatadah said: They are the angels.

'Ata': The jinn and mankind.

Al-Hasan: All the servants of God together.

Ibn 'Abbas: Everything except the jinn and mankind.

Al-Dahhak: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, he is asked: "Who is your Lord? And who is your prophet? And what is your religion?" He says: "I do not know." It is said to him: "You did not know," then he is struck with a blow of a hammer, and he cries out a cry which everything hears except the two weighty ones, mankind and jinn. Nothing hears his voice but curses him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾.

Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, a beast comes to him whose eyes are like two copper cauldrons, with an iron club, and it strikes him a blow between his shoulders, and he cries out. No one hears his voice without cursing him, and nothing remains that does not hear his voice except the two weighty ones.

Ibn Mas'ud: It is the man who curses his companion, and the curse rises to the sky, then descends, and does not find its target worthy of it, so it returns to the one who uttered it, and does not find him worthy of it either, so it goes and falls upon the Jews. This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾. Whoever among them repents, the curse is lifted from him, and it was upon those of the Jews who met it.

Mujahid: ﴿those who curse﴾ are the beasts, which curse the sinners of the children of Adam when the year becomes barren and the rain is withheld. They say: "This is because of the sins of the children of Adam."

'Ikrimah: The beasts of the earth and its creeping things, even the beetles and scorpions, say: "We have been withheld from rain because of the sins of the children of Adam." He said of these things ﴿those who curse﴾ and did not say "those who curse" (feminine), because it is the way of the Arabs, when they describe something of the inanimate things, animals, and others with what is a description of humans, of an act or a speech, that they do not take it out of the manner of the children of Adam and their group, as in their saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Qur'an 12:4], and he did not say "prostrating" (feminine). And His saying concerning the idols: ﴿Rather, their chief did it; so ask them, if they can speak﴾ [Qur'an 21:63]; and His saying: ﴿O ant, enter your dwellings﴾ [Qur'an 27:18]; and His saying: ﴿And they will say to their skins: "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ [Qur'an 41:21], and then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except those who repented﴾ from disbelief.

﴿and set right their deeds﴾ between themselves and their Lord.

﴿and make clear﴾ the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, I turn to them in forgiveness﴾, meaning I overlook them and accept their repentance.

﴿And I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾, who returns to the hearts of My servants who turned away from Me, and is Merciful to them after they turn to Me.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾, the "and" here is a circumstantial (wa of hal).

﴿those, upon them is the curse of God and of the angels﴾, meaning and the curse of the angels.

﴿and of mankind, all together﴾. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: it means mankind all together, the believers.

Abu al-'Aliyah: This is on the Day of Resurrection: the disbeliever is made to stand, and God, mighty and majestic, curses him, then the angels curse him, then all mankind curses him.

Al-Suddi: No two believers curse each other, nor two disbelievers, where one says "May God curse the wrongdoer," without that curse falling upon the disbeliever, because he is a wrongdoer; so every creature curses him.

﴿abiding therein﴾, remaining in the curse and the Fire.

﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning the torment will not be eased for them.

﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be given respite or delay.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "'Nor will they be reprieved' means they will not be given an excuse, as in His saying: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted, so they may make excuse﴾ [Qur'an 77:35–36]."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 158–162:

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God.﴾ Al-Safa is the plural of al-saffa, which is a hard, smooth rock. Imru' al-Qais said:

*She has a rump like the rock of the watercourse, when the bristling of Mudar has exposed it.* [[Majma' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 1/438.]]

It is said: saffa and safa, like hasa and hasa, qata and qata, and nawa and nawa. It is also said that al-Safa is singular, with its dual being Safwan, like asa and asawan, and its plural being asfa', like raja and arja'. And safa and safi, like asa and asi. The rajiz said:

*As if his two sides, from the rough ground, are the perches of birds upon the safi.* [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/59.]]

Al-Marwah is the stone that is soft and small. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

*Until I am, for calamities, a marwah, struck every day upon the rock of the east.*

That is, a soft, small rock. The plural of marwah is marwan, and its plural for the large one is marw, like thamra and thamarat, thamr, hamra and hamarat, and hamra'. Al-A'sha Maymun ibn Qays, describing his she-camel, said:

*You see the earth a passing, light ground, and when it meets the marw, it crumbles.* [[Ibid.: 2/60.]]

God, exalted is He, meant by them the two well-known mountains in Makkah, not the rest of the safa and marwa, and for that reason the definite article (al) was added to them. The symbols of God (sha'a'ir Allah) are the markers of His religion; its singular is sha'ira. Everything that was marked as an offering by which one draws near to God, mighty and majestic, whether supplication, prayer, sacrifice, performance of an obligation, or other such things, is a sha'ira.

Al-Kumayt ibn Zayd said:

*We kill them generation after generation; you see them as symbols of an offering through which one draws near.*

Its root is from al-ash'ar, which means the markers upon a thing.

In a hadith: when 'Umar was wounded during the Hajj, someone said: "Has the Commander of the Faithful bled?" Here, by the symbols, he meant the rites of Hajj which God, mighty and majestic, made as markers of His obedience. Mujahid said: "It means from the report which I have told you about." The root of the word, according to this view, is from sha'artu, meaning "I knew," as if they were signs from God to His servants concerning the matter of al-Safa and al-Marwah.

The sense of the verse: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾, so the mention of circumambulation (tawaf) is omitted and suffices with mentioning the two, that being known to the addressees.

﴿So whoever performs Hajj to the House﴾. The root meaning of hajj in the language is "intention."

The poet said:

*Like a monk who goes on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, a monotheist, with a cloak and a hooded cape.* [[Words unreadable, and this is the apparent reading.]]

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "Whoever frequently turns to something is a hajj (one who makes pilgrimage) to it." Al-Mihmal al-Sa'di said:

*And witness from 'Awf many gatherings, who visit the House of al-Zibriqan the saffron-clad.* [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/61.]]

That is, they frequently go to him for his affection and leadership.

The pilgrim is called hajj because he comes to the House from 'Arafah, then returns to it for the tawaf on the day of sacrifice, then departs from it to Mina, then returns to it for the farewell tawaf. Because of the repetition of returning to it time after time, he is called hajj.

﴿Or performs 'umrah﴾. 'Umrah is from al-i'timar, which is visiting. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*Indeed the son of Ma'mar rose when he visited, far, to a far one, and a steed.*

That is, whoever intends and visits it. Al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah said: ﴿or performs 'umrah﴾ means he settles in Makkah after the tawaf and the sa'y, and does what the one who is in the state of ihram lawfully does.

'Umrah (from 'amara) means to inhabit a place, and 'imarah means to repair and restore it.

From 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Follow up the Hajj with the 'umrah, for following up between them increases one's lifespan and provision and removes sins as the bellows removes the impurity of iron." [13]

﴿Then there is no blame upon him﴾. Al-Jina' is sin, and its root is from janaha, when one deviates from the right course.

It is said: "The night inclined (janah) when its darkness came." And "The ship leaned (janahat) when it inclined toward the earth." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [Qur'an 8:61]. From it comes janah al-tair, the wing of a bird.

﴿that he circumambulates (yattawwafa)﴾, meaning goes around; its root is yatatawwafa, and the taa was assimilated into the ta' (of tawwafa).

Abu Hayyah al-Shami read yatufa with a lightened ta'. They differed concerning the meaning and interpretation of the verse and the occasion of its revelation.

Anas ibn Malik said: "We used to dislike circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah, because they were among the rites of the Quraysh in the Jahiliyyah, so we left it in Islam. Then God revealed this verse."

'Umar ibn Habib said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about this verse, and he said: 'Go to Ibn 'Abbas, for he is the most knowledgeable of those remaining in what was revealed upon Muhammad (ﷺ).' I went to him and asked him, and Ibn 'Abbas said: 'On al-Safa there was an idol in the form of a man called Isaf, and on al-Marwah an idol in the form of a woman called Na'ilah. When the period lengthened, they were worshipped besides God. So when the people of the Jahiliyyah circumambulated between them, they would rub the two idols. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims disliked circumambulating between them because of the two idols, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "In the Jahiliyyah there were devils that played music at night between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and there were gods between them. When Islam appeared, the Muslims said to the Messenger of God: 'Do not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah, for it is polytheism, which we used to practise in the Jahiliyyah.' So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse." [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 28.]]

Qatadah: "A tribe from Tihamah did not run between them, so He informed them that it was the Sunnah of Abraham and Isma'il, peace be upon them." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/65.]]

By God, there is no blame upon anyone for not circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah.'" She said: "What you said is not correct, my nephew. If this verse were as you understand it, there would be no blame upon one who does not circumambulate between them. But it was revealed concerning the Ansar, for before they embraced Islam they used to worship Manat the Tyrant, an idol at al-Mushallal between Makkah and Madinah. Whoever assumed the ihram for her would be reluctant to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah. When they embraced Islam, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked them about that. So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Then 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) established the circumambulation between them. So no one has the right to abandon it."

Al-Zuhri said: "I mentioned that to Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham." He said: "This is knowledge."

So the Hums asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about running between al-Safa and al-Marwah: is it among the symbols of God or not? For none circumambulates between them except us. So this verse was revealed."
