Whoever abandons it must make up for it and repeat it; no expiation (fidyah) or anything else suffices for him except returning to Makkah and circumambulating between them, just as one who abandons the tawaf al-ifadah cannot be excused except by making up that same tawaf.

They said: "They are two obligatory circumambulations: one commanded with the House, and the other between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and their ruling is one."

Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: If the one who abandons the circumambulation between them returns to make it up, that is good; if he does not return, he must offer a sacrifice (dam). They held that the ruling for these circumambulations is the ruling for throwing some of the pebbles, standing at al-Mash'ar, the farewell tawaf, and similar things, for which the one who abandons them owes an expiation by abandoning them, and he is not required to return to make up that very act.

Anas ibn Malik, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and 'Ata' said: circumambulating between them is a voluntary act (tatawwu'); if one performs it he is virtuous, and if one abandons it he is not obligated to anything by abandoning it.

Those who did not make running and circumambulation between them obligatory argued by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and Ibn Sirin: ﴿then there is no blame upon him that he does not circumambulate between them﴾, with the particle "not" (la) affirmed. It is likewise in the codex of 'Abd Allah.

The answer to this: the (la) is an added particle (za'idah silah), like the saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [Qur'an 7:12], and like: ﴿that they do not return﴾ [Qur'an 21:95], and ﴿So I swear not﴾ [Qur'an 75:1–2; 90:1], and the poet said:

*So I do not blame the white women that they did not mock, when they saw the grey-haired, dishevelled man.*

The structure of the written codex is thus; there is no proof in it with the possibility of the speech as we have described, and how much more so since it contradicts the established script of the Shaykh, the Imam, and the codices of Islam.

Then, the evidence that running between them is obligatory, and that whoever abandons it must repeat the Hajj, whether he forgot it or did it deliberately, is by the apparent reports: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did it and commanded it.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated from his father from Jabir who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approached al-Safa in his Hajj, he said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾. Begin with what God began with." So he began with al-Safa, ascended it until he saw the House, then walked until his feet came down into the valley, and then ran." [14]

Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father from 'A'ishah who said: "By my life, whoever does not run between al-Safa and al-Marwah has not performed Hajj; it is obligatory in the Book of God and the Sunnah. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, running has been prescribed for you, so run." [15]

Kulayb said: "Ibn 'Abbas saw some people circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah and said: 'This is what your mother Umm Isma'il bequeathed to you. She set out when her son became thirsty and hungry, and she found al-Safa the nearest mountain to the earth, so she stood upon it, then faced the valley looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. So she descended from the valley, lifted the hem of her garment, and ran like a man in distress until she passed the valley. Then she came to al-Marwah and stood upon it, looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. She did this seven times.'"

Muhammad said: "Musa (peace be upon him) performed Hajj upon a red mountain, wearing two woollen cloaks daubed with tar. He circumambulated the House, then ascended al-Safa and supplicated, then descended to run, while uttering the talbiyah: 'Here I am, O God, here I am.' God, mighty and majestic, said: 'Here I am, My servant, and I am with you.' So Musa fell down prostrate."

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read tatawwa'a with a ta' and a shaddah on the ta' and a jazm on the 'ayn, and likewise the ta' in yatawwa' (meaning "he volunteers"). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, reasoning from the reading of 'Abd Allah: "and whoever volunteers (tatawwa'a) with a ta'."

The rest read tatawwa'a with a ta' and a shaddah on the 'ayn, in the past tense.

Mujahid said: "Whoever volunteers in circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah." He also said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) volunteered, and he was among the prophets."

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ means one who increases in the circumambulation; the obligatory part is in it.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ means he performs 'umrah, for the Hajj is an obligation and the 'umrah is voluntary.

It is said: "Whoever volunteers with Hajj and 'umrah after fulfilling his obligatory pilgrimage."

Al-Hasan and others said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ is meant for the whole religion: whatever act beyond what is obligatory upon him, of circumambulation, prayer, zakah, or any kind of the acts of obedience.

﴿then God is Appreciative﴾, He rewards him for his deed.

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intention of the one who gives thanks, who appreciates the little, gives the much, and forgives the great. The root of shukr (thanks) comes from the saying of the Arabs: "a shakur beast," when its fat appears upon it beyond what it is fed.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of the clear proofs﴾, meaning the stoning (rajm), the prescribed punishments, the rulings, and what is lawful and unlawful.

﴿and the guidance﴾, meaning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description.

﴿after We have made it clear to the people﴾, meaning to the Children of Israel.

﴿in the Book﴾, meaning in the Torah. It was revealed concerning the scholars and chiefs of the Jews who concealed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, God curses them﴾. The root meaning of la'n in the language is "expulsion." God cursed Iblis by expelling him when He said to him: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ [Qur'an 15:34; 38:77].

Al-Shammakh said, mentioning what came to him:

*The sandgrouse were startled by it, and you remained in it, like the wolf standing, like the accursed man.*

And al-Nabighah said:

*So I passed the night as if I were a cursed outcast, driven away by people, or a wounded sick man.*

So the meaning of our saying "God curses him" is: He expelled him and removed him far away. The root of la'nah is what we have mentioned; then it became common until it became a formula.

﴿and those who curse curse them﴾, meaning they ask God to curse them and say: "O God, curse them." The exegetes differed concerning who these cursers are.

Qatadah said: They are the angels.

'Ata': The jinn and mankind.

Al-Hasan: All the servants of God together.

Ibn 'Abbas: Everything except the jinn and mankind.

Al-Dahhak: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, he is asked: "Who is your Lord? And who is your prophet? And what is your religion?" He says: "I do not know." It is said to him: "You did not know," then he is struck with a blow of a hammer, and he cries out a cry which everything hears except the two weighty ones, mankind and jinn. Nothing hears his voice but curses him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾.

Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, a beast comes to him whose eyes are like two copper cauldrons, with an iron club, and it strikes him a blow between his shoulders, and he cries out. No one hears his voice without cursing him, and nothing remains that does not hear his voice except the two weighty ones.

Ibn Mas'ud: It is the man who curses his companion, and the curse rises to the sky, then descends, and does not find its target worthy of it, so it returns to the one who uttered it, and does not find him worthy of it either, so it goes and falls upon the Jews. This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾. Whoever among them repents, the curse is lifted from him, and it was upon those of the Jews who met it.

Mujahid: ﴿those who curse﴾ are the beasts, which curse the sinners of the children of Adam when the year becomes barren and the rain is withheld. They say: "This is because of the sins of the children of Adam."

'Ikrimah: The beasts of the earth and its creeping things, even the beetles and scorpions, say: "We have been withheld from rain because of the sins of the children of Adam." He said of these things ﴿those who curse﴾ and did not say "those who curse" (feminine), because it is the way of the Arabs, when they describe something of the inanimate things, animals, and others with what is a description of humans, of an act or a speech, that they do not take it out of the manner of the children of Adam and their group, as in their saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Qur'an 12:4], and he did not say "prostrating" (feminine). And His saying concerning the idols: ﴿Rather, their chief did it; so ask them, if they can speak﴾ [Qur'an 21:63]; and His saying: ﴿O ant, enter your dwellings﴾ [Qur'an 27:18]; and His saying: ﴿And they will say to their skins: "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ [Qur'an 41:21], and then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except those who repented﴾ from disbelief.

﴿and set right their deeds﴾ between themselves and their Lord.

﴿and make clear﴾ the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, I turn to them in forgiveness﴾, meaning I overlook them and accept their repentance.

﴿And I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾, who returns to the hearts of My servants who turned away from Me, and is Merciful to them after they turn to Me.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾, the "and" here is a circumstantial (wa of hal).

﴿those, upon them is the curse of God and of the angels﴾, meaning and the curse of the angels.

﴿and of mankind, all together﴾. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: it means mankind all together, the believers.

Abu al-'Aliyah: This is on the Day of Resurrection: the disbeliever is made to stand, and God, mighty and majestic, curses him, then the angels curse him, then all mankind curses him.

Al-Suddi: No two believers curse each other, nor two disbelievers, where one says "May God curse the wrongdoer," without that curse falling upon the disbeliever, because he is a wrongdoer; so every creature curses him.

﴿abiding therein﴾, remaining in the curse and the Fire.

﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning the torment will not be eased for them.

﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be given respite or delay.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "'Nor will they be reprieved' means they will not be given an excuse, as in His saying: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted, so they may make excuse﴾ [Qur'an 77:35–36]."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 158–162:

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God.﴾ Al-Safa is the plural of al-saffa, which is a hard, smooth rock. Imru' al-Qais said:

*She has a rump like the rock of the watercourse, when the bristling of Mudar has exposed it.* [[Majma' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 1/438.]]

It is said: saffa and safa, like hasa and hasa, qata and qata, and nawa and nawa. It is also said that al-Safa is singular, with its dual being Safwan, like asa and asawan, and its plural being asfa', like raja and arja'. And safa and safi, like asa and asi. The rajiz said:

*As if his two sides, from the rough ground, are the perches of birds upon the safi.* [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/59.]]

Al-Marwah is the stone that is soft and small. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

*Until I am, for calamities, a marwah, struck every day upon the rock of the east.*

That is, a soft, small rock. The plural of marwah is marwan, and its plural for the large one is marw, like thamra and thamarat, thamr, hamra and hamarat, and hamra'. Al-A'sha Maymun ibn Qays, describing his she-camel, said:

*You see the earth a passing, light ground, and when it meets the marw, it crumbles.* [[Ibid.: 2/60.]]

God, exalted is He, meant by them the two well-known mountains in Makkah, not the rest of the safa and marwa, and for that reason the definite article (al) was added to them. The symbols of God (sha'a'ir Allah) are the markers of His religion; its singular is sha'ira. Everything that was marked as an offering by which one draws near to God, mighty and majestic, whether supplication, prayer, sacrifice, performance of an obligation, or other such things, is a sha'ira.

Al-Kumayt ibn Zayd said:

*We kill them generation after generation; you see them as symbols of an offering through which one draws near.*

Its root is from al-ash'ar, which means the markers upon a thing.

In a hadith: when 'Umar was wounded during the Hajj, someone said: "Has the Commander of the Faithful bled?" Here, by the symbols, he meant the rites of Hajj which God, mighty and majestic, made as markers of His obedience. Mujahid said: "It means from the report which I have told you about." The root of the word, according to this view, is from sha'artu, meaning "I knew," as if they were signs from God to His servants concerning the matter of al-Safa and al-Marwah.

The sense of the verse: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾, so the mention of circumambulation (tawaf) is omitted and suffices with mentioning the two, that being known to the addressees.

﴿So whoever performs Hajj to the House﴾. The root meaning of hajj in the language is "intention."

The poet said:

*Like a monk who goes on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, a monotheist, with a cloak and a hooded cape.* [[Words unreadable, and this is the apparent reading.]]

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "Whoever frequently turns to something is a hajj (one who makes pilgrimage) to it." Al-Mihmal al-Sa'di said:

*And witness from 'Awf many gatherings, who visit the House of al-Zibriqan the saffron-clad.* [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/61.]]

That is, they frequently go to him for his affection and leadership.

The pilgrim is called hajj because he comes to the House from 'Arafah, then returns to it for the tawaf on the day of sacrifice, then departs from it to Mina, then returns to it for the farewell tawaf. Because of the repetition of returning to it time after time, he is called hajj.

﴿Or performs 'umrah﴾. 'Umrah is from al-i'timar, which is visiting. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*Indeed the son of Ma'mar rose when he visited, far, to a far one, and a steed.*

That is, whoever intends and visits it. Al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah said: ﴿or performs 'umrah﴾ means he settles in Makkah after the tawaf and the sa'y, and does what the one who is in the state of ihram lawfully does.

'Umrah (from 'amara) means to inhabit a place, and 'imarah means to repair and restore it.

From 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Follow up the Hajj with the 'umrah, for following up between them increases one's lifespan and provision and removes sins as the bellows removes the impurity of iron." [13]

﴿Then there is no blame upon him﴾. Al-Jina' is sin, and its root is from janaha, when one deviates from the right course.

It is said: "The night inclined (janah) when its darkness came." And "The ship leaned (janahat) when it inclined toward the earth." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [Qur'an 8:61]. From it comes janah al-tair, the wing of a bird.

﴿that he circumambulates (yattawwafa)﴾, meaning goes around; its root is yatatawwafa, and the taa was assimilated into the ta' (of tawwafa).

Abu Hayyah al-Shami read yatufa with a lightened ta'. They differed concerning the meaning and interpretation of the verse and the occasion of its revelation.

Anas ibn Malik said: "We used to dislike circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah, because they were among the rites of the Quraysh in the Jahiliyyah, so we left it in Islam. Then God revealed this verse."

'Umar ibn Habib said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about this verse, and he said: 'Go to Ibn 'Abbas, for he is the most knowledgeable of those remaining in what was revealed upon Muhammad (ﷺ).' I went to him and asked him, and Ibn 'Abbas said: 'On al-Safa there was an idol in the form of a man called Isaf, and on al-Marwah an idol in the form of a woman called Na'ilah. They mentioned al-Safa for the masculine (Isaf) and mentioned al-Marwah for the feminine (Na'ilah).'"

The People of the Book claimed that the two had committed fornication in the sacred precinct, so God, mighty and majestic, transformed them into two stones and placed them on al-Safa and al-Marwah as a lesson. When the period lengthened, they were worshipped besides God. So when the people of the Jahiliyyah circumambulated between them, they would rub the two idols. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims disliked circumambulating between them because of the two idols, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "In the Jahiliyyah there were devils that played music at night between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and there were gods between them. When Islam appeared, the Muslims said to the Messenger of God: 'Do not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah, for it is polytheism, which we used to practise in the Jahiliyyah.' So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse." [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 28.]]

Qatadah: "Some people from Tihamah used to run between al-Safa and al-Marwah in the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, they felt uneasy about running between them, as they had felt uneasy about it in the Jahiliyyah, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

Qatadah: "A tribe from Tihamah did not run between them, so He informed them that it was the Sunnah of Abraham and Isma'il, peace be upon them." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/65.]]

Al-Zuhri narrated from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'What are al-Safa and al-Marwah?' She said: 'It is the saying of God: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾ — the verse. By God, there is no blame upon anyone for not circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah.'" She said: "What you said is not correct, my nephew. If this verse were as you understand it, there would be no blame upon one who does not circumambulate between them. But it was revealed concerning the Ansar, for before they embraced Islam they used to worship Manat the Tyrant, an idol at al-Mushallal between Makkah and Madinah. Whoever assumed the ihram for her would be reluctant to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah. When they embraced Islam, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked them about that. They said: 'O Messenger of God, we used not to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah because they were two idols. Is there any sin upon us if we circumambulate between them?'"

So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Then 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) established the circumambulation between them. So no one has the right to abandon it."

Al-Zuhri said: "I mentioned that to Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham." He said: "This is knowledge."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "The people had abandoned circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah, except the Hums, who were the Quraysh, Kinanah, Khuza'ah, and 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah. They were called Hums (the strict ones) for their strictness in their religion; al-hamasah means courage and firmness. So the Hums asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about running between al-Safa and al-Marwah: is it among the symbols of God or not? For none circumambulates between them except us. So this verse was revealed."

The scholars differed concerning this verse. Al-Shafi'i and Malik said: circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah is an obligatory pillar (fard). Whoever abandons it must make up for it and repeat it; no expiation (fidyah) or anything else suffices for him except returning to Makkah and circumambulating between them, just as one who abandons the tawaf al-ifadah cannot be excused except by making up that same tawaf.

They said: "They are two obligatory circumambulations: one commanded with the House, and the other between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and their ruling is one."

Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: If the one who abandons the circumambulation between them returns to make it up, that is good; if he does not return, he must offer a sacrifice (dam). They held that the ruling for these circumambulations is the ruling for throwing some of the pebbles, standing at al-Mash'ar, the farewell tawaf, and similar things, for which the one who abandons them owes an expiation by abandoning them, and he is not required to return to make up that very act.

Anas ibn Malik, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and 'Ata' said: circumambulating between them is a voluntary act (tatawwu'); if one performs it he is virtuous, and if one abandons it he is not obligated to anything by abandoning it.

Those who did not make running and circumambulation between them obligatory argued by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and Ibn Sirin: ﴿then there is no blame upon him that he does not circumambulate between them﴾, with the particle "not" (la) affirmed. It is likewise in the codex of 'Abd Allah.

The answer to this: the (la) is an added particle (za'idah silah), like the saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [Qur'an 7:12], and like: ﴿that they do not return﴾ [Qur'an 21:95], and ﴿So I swear not﴾ [Qur'an 75:1–2; 90:1], and the poet said:

*So I do not blame the white women that they did not mock, when they saw the grey-haired, dishevelled man.*

The structure of the written codex is thus; there is no proof in it with the possibility of the speech as we have described, and how much more so since it contradicts the established script of the Shaykh, the Imam, and the codices of Islam.

Then, the evidence that running between them is obligatory, and that whoever abandons it must repeat the Hajj, whether he forgot it or did it deliberately, is by the apparent reports: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did it and commanded it.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated from his father from Jabir who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approached al-Safa in his Hajj, he said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾. Begin with what God began with." So he began with al-Safa, ascended it until he saw the House, then walked until his feet came down into the valley, and then ran." [14]

Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father from 'A'ishah who said: "By my life, whoever does not run between al-Safa and al-Marwah has not performed Hajj; it is obligatory in the Book of God and the Sunnah. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, running has been prescribed for you, so run." [15]

Kulayb said: "Ibn 'Abbas saw some people circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah and said: 'This is what your mother Umm Isma'il bequeathed to you. She set out when her son became thirsty and hungry, and she found al-Safa the nearest mountain to the earth, so she stood upon it, then faced the valley looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. So she descended from the valley, lifted the hem of her garment, and ran like a man in distress until she passed the valley. Then she came to al-Marwah and stood upon it, looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. She did this seven times.'"

Muhammad said: "Musa (peace be upon him) performed Hajj upon a red mountain, wearing two woollen cloaks daubed with tar. He circumambulated the House, then ascended al-Safa and supplicated, then descended to run, while uttering the talbiyah: 'Here I am, O God, here I am.' God, mighty and majestic, said: 'Here I am, My servant, and I am with you.' So Musa fell down prostrate."

Mujahid: ﴿those who curse﴾ are the beasts, which curse the sinners of the children of Adam when the year becomes barren and the rain is withheld. They say: "This is because of the sins of the children of Adam."

'Ikrimah: The beasts of the earth and its creeping things, even the beetles and scorpions, say: "We have been withheld from rain because of the sins of the children of Adam." He said of these things ﴿those who curse﴾ and did not say "those who curse" (feminine), because it is the way of the Arabs, when they describe something of the inanimate things, animals, and others with what is a description of humans, of an act or a speech, that they do not take it out of the manner of the children of Adam and their group, as in their saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Qur'an 12:4], and he did not say "prostrating" (feminine). And His saying concerning the idols: ﴿Rather, their chief did it; so ask them, if they can speak﴾ [Qur'an 21:63]; and His saying: ﴿O ant, enter your dwellings﴾ [Qur'an 27:18]; and His saying: ﴿And they will say to their skins: "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ [Qur'an 41:21], and then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except those who repented﴾ from disbelief.

﴿and set right their deeds﴾ between themselves and their Lord.

﴿and make clear﴾ the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, I turn to them in forgiveness﴾, meaning I overlook them and accept their repentance.

﴿And I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾, who returns to the hearts of My servants who turned away from Me, and is Merciful to them after they turn to Me.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾, the "and" here is a circumstantial (wa of hal).

﴿those, upon them is the curse of God and of the angels﴾, meaning and the curse of the angels.

﴿and of mankind, all together﴾. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: it means mankind all together, the believers.

Abu al-'Aliyah: This is on the Day of Resurrection: the disbeliever is made to stand, and God, mighty and majestic, curses him, then the angels curse him, then all mankind curses him.

Al-Suddi: No two believers curse each other, nor two disbelievers, where one says "May God curse the wrongdoer," without that curse falling upon the disbeliever, because he is a wrongdoer; so every creature curses him.

﴿abiding therein﴾, remaining in the curse and the Fire.

﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning the torment will not be eased for them.

﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be given respite or delay.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "'Nor will they be reprieved' means they will not be given an excuse, as in His saying: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted, so they may make excuse﴾ [Qur'an 77:35–36]."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 158–162:

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God.﴾ Al-Safa is the plural of al-saffa, which is a hard, smooth rock. Imru' al-Qais said:

*She has a rump like the rock of the watercourse, when the bristling of Mudar has exposed it.* [[Majma' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 1/438.]]

It is said: saffa and safa, like hasa and hasa, qata and qata, and nawa and nawa. It is also said that al-Safa is singular, with its dual being Safwan, like asa and asawan, and its plural being asfa', like raja and arja'. And safa and safi, like asa and asi. The rajiz said:

*As if his two sides, from the rough ground, are the perches of birds upon the safi.* [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/59.]]

Al-Marwah is the stone that is soft and small. Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

*Until I am, for calamities, a marwah, struck every day upon the rock of the east.*

That is, a soft, small rock. The plural of marwah is marwan, and its plural for the large one is marw, like thamra and thamarat, thamr, hamra and hamarat, and hamra'. Al-A'sha Maymun ibn Qays, describing his she-camel, said:

*You see the earth a passing, light ground, and when it meets the marw, it crumbles.* [[Ibid.: 2/60.]]

God, exalted is He, meant by them the two well-known mountains in Makkah, not the rest of the safa and marwa, and for that reason the definite article (al) was added to them. The symbols of God (sha'a'ir Allah) are the markers of His religion; its singular is sha'ira. Everything that was marked as an offering by which one draws near to God, mighty and majestic, whether supplication, prayer, sacrifice, performance of an obligation, or other such things, is a sha'ira.

Al-Kumayt ibn Zayd said:

*We kill them generation after generation; you see them as symbols of an offering through which one draws near.*

Its root is from al-ash'ar, which means the markers upon a thing.

In a hadith: when 'Umar was wounded during the Hajj, someone said: "Has the Commander of the Faithful bled?" Here, by the symbols, he meant the rites of Hajj which God, mighty and majestic, made as markers of His obedience. Mujahid said: "It means from the report which I have told you about." The root of the word, according to this view, is from sha'artu, meaning "I knew," as if they were signs from God to His servants concerning the matter of al-Safa and al-Marwah.

The sense of the verse: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾, so the mention of circumambulation (tawaf) is omitted and suffices with mentioning the two, that being known to the addressees.

﴿So whoever performs Hajj to the House﴾. The root meaning of hajj in the language is "intention."

The poet said:

*Like a monk who goes on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, a monotheist, with a cloak and a hooded cape.* [[Words unreadable, and this is the apparent reading.]]

Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "Whoever frequently turns to something is a hajj (one who makes pilgrimage) to it." Al-Mihmal al-Sa'di said:

*And witness from 'Awf many gatherings, who visit the House of al-Zibriqan the saffron-clad.* [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/61.]]

That is, they frequently go to him for his affection and leadership.

The pilgrim is called hajj because he comes to the House from 'Arafah, then returns to it for the tawaf on the day of sacrifice, then departs from it to Mina, then returns to it for the farewell tawaf. Because of the repetition of returning to it time after time, he is called hajj.

﴿Or performs 'umrah﴾. 'Umrah is from al-i'timar, which is visiting. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*Indeed the son of Ma'mar rose when he visited, far, to a far one, and a steed.*

That is, whoever intends and visits it. Al-Mufaddal ibn Salamah said: ﴿or performs 'umrah﴾ means he settles in Makkah after the tawaf and the sa'y, and does what the one who is in the state of ihram lawfully does.

'Umrah (from 'amara) means to inhabit a place, and 'imarah means to repair and restore it.

From 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Follow up the Hajj with the 'umrah, for following up between them increases one's lifespan and provision and removes sins as the bellows removes the impurity of iron." [13]

﴿Then there is no blame upon him﴾. Al-Jina' is sin, and its root is from janaha, when one deviates from the right course.

It is said: "The night inclined (janah) when its darkness came." And "The ship leaned (janahat) when it inclined toward the earth." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [Qur'an 8:61]. From it comes janah al-tair, the wing of a bird.

﴿that he circumambulates (yattawwafa)﴾, meaning goes around; its root is yatatawwafa, and the taa was assimilated into the ta' (of tawwafa).

Abu Hayyah al-Shami read yatufa with a lightened ta'. They differed concerning the meaning and interpretation of the verse and the occasion of its revelation.

Anas ibn Malik said: "We used to dislike circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah, because they were among the rites of the Quraysh in the Jahiliyyah, so we left it in Islam. Then God revealed this verse."

'Umar ibn Habib said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar about this verse, and he said: 'Go to Ibn 'Abbas, for he is the most knowledgeable of those remaining in what was revealed upon Muhammad (ﷺ).' I went to him and asked him, and Ibn 'Abbas said: 'On al-Safa there was an idol in the form of a man called Isaf, and on al-Marwah an idol in the form of a woman called Na'ilah. They mentioned al-Safa for the masculine (Isaf) and mentioned al-Marwah for the feminine (Na'ilah).'"

The People of the Book claimed that the two had committed fornication in the sacred precinct, so God, mighty and majestic, transformed them into two stones and placed them on al-Safa and al-Marwah as a lesson. When the period lengthened, they were worshipped besides God. So when the people of the Jahiliyyah circumambulated between them, they would rub the two idols. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims disliked circumambulating between them because of the two idols, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse.

Al-Suddi narrated from Abu Malik from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "In the Jahiliyyah there were devils that played music at night between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and there were gods between them. When Islam appeared, the Muslims said to the Messenger of God: 'Do not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah, for it is polytheism, which we used to practise in the Jahiliyyah.' So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse." [[Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 28.]]

Qatadah: "Some people from Tihamah used to run between al-Safa and al-Marwah in the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, they felt uneasy about running between them, as they had felt uneasy about it in the Jahiliyyah, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

Qatadah: "A tribe from Tihamah did not run between them, so He informed them that it was the Sunnah of Abraham and Isma'il, peace be upon them." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/65.]]

Al-Zuhri narrated from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr who said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'What are al-Safa and al-Marwah?' She said: 'It is the saying of God: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾ — the verse. By God, there is no blame upon anyone for not circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah.'" She said: "What you said is not correct, my nephew. If this verse were as you understand it, there would be no blame upon one who does not circumambulate between them. But it was revealed concerning the Ansar, for before they embraced Islam they used to worship Manat the Tyrant, an idol at al-Mushallal between Makkah and Madinah. Whoever assumed the ihram for her would be reluctant to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah. When they embraced Islam, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked them about that. They said: 'O Messenger of God, we used not to circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah because they were two idols. Is there any sin upon us if we circumambulate between them?'"

So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. Then 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her) said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) established the circumambulation between them. So no one has the right to abandon it."

Al-Zuhri said: "I mentioned that to Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham." He said: "This is knowledge."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "The people had abandoned circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah, except the Hums, who were the Quraysh, Kinanah, Khuza'ah, and 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah. They were called Hums (the strict ones) for their strictness in their religion; al-hamasah means courage and firmness. So the Hums asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about running between al-Safa and al-Marwah: is it among the symbols of God or not? For none circumambulates between them except us. So this verse was revealed."

The scholars differed concerning this verse. Al-Shafi'i and Malik said: circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah is an obligatory pillar (fard). Whoever abandons it must make up for it and repeat it; no expiation (fidyah) or anything else suffices for him except returning to Makkah and circumambulating between them, just as one who abandons the tawaf al-ifadah cannot be excused except by making up that same tawaf.

They said: "They are two obligatory circumambulations: one commanded with the House, and the other between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and their ruling is one."

Al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad said: If the one who abandons the circumambulation between them returns to make it up, that is good; if he does not return, he must offer a sacrifice (dam). They held that the ruling for these circumambulations is the ruling for throwing some of the pebbles, standing at al-Mash'ar, the farewell tawaf, and similar things, for which the one who abandons them owes an expiation by abandoning them, and he is not required to return to make up that very act.

Anas ibn Malik, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and 'Ata' said: circumambulating between them is a voluntary act (tatawwu'); if one performs it he is virtuous, and if one abandons it he is not obligated to anything by abandoning it.

Those who did not make running and circumambulation between them obligatory argued by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and Ibn Sirin: ﴿then there is no blame upon him that he does not circumambulate between them﴾, with the particle "not" (la) affirmed. It is likewise in the codex of 'Abd Allah.

The answer to this: the (la) is an added particle (za'idah silah), like the saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [Qur'an 7:12], and like: ﴿that they do not return﴾ [Qur'an 21:95], and ﴿So I swear not﴾ [Qur'an 75:1–2; 90:1], and the poet said:

*So I do not blame the white women that they did not mock, when they saw the grey-haired, dishevelled man.*

The structure of the written codex is thus; there is no proof in it with the possibility of the speech as we have described, and how much more so since it contradicts the established script of the Shaykh, the Imam, and the codices of Islam.

Then, the evidence that running between them is obligatory, and that whoever abandons it must repeat the Hajj, whether he forgot it or did it deliberately, is by the apparent reports: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did it and commanded it.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated from his father from Jabir who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) approached al-Safa in his Hajj, he said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾. Begin with what God began with." So he began with al-Safa, ascended it until he saw the House, then walked until his feet came down into the valley, and then ran." [14]

Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father from 'A'ishah who said: "By my life, whoever does not run between al-Safa and al-Marwah has not performed Hajj; it is obligatory in the Book of God and the Sunnah. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of God﴾."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, running has been prescribed for you, so run." [15]

Kulayb said: "Ibn 'Abbas saw some people circumambulating between al-Safa and al-Marwah and said: 'This is what your mother Umm Isma'il bequeathed to you. She set out when her son became thirsty and hungry, and she found al-Safa the nearest mountain to the earth, so she stood upon it, then faced the valley looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. So she descended from the valley, lifted the hem of her garment, and ran like a man in distress until she passed the valley. Then she came to al-Marwah and stood upon it, looking to see if she could see anyone, but she saw no one. She did this seven times.'"

Muhammad said: "Musa (peace be upon him) performed Hajj upon a red mountain, wearing two woollen cloaks daubed with tar. He circumambulated the House, then ascended al-Safa and supplicated, then descended to run, while uttering the talbiyah: 'Here I am, O God, here I am.' God, mighty and majestic, said: 'Here I am, My servant, and I am with you.' So Musa fell down prostrate."

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read tatawwa'a with a ta' and a shaddah on the ta' and a jazm on the 'ayn, and likewise the ta' in yatawwa' (meaning "he volunteers"). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this, reasoning from the reading of 'Abd Allah: "and whoever volunteers (tatawwa'a) with a ta'."

The rest read tatawwa'a with a ta' and a shaddah on the 'ayn, in the past tense.

Mujahid said: "Whoever volunteers in circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwah." He also said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) volunteered, and he was among the prophets."

Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ means one who increases in the circumambulation; the obligatory part is in it.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ means he performs 'umrah, for the Hajj is an obligation and the 'umrah is voluntary.

It is said: "Whoever volunteers with Hajj and 'umrah after fulfilling his obligatory pilgrimage."

Al-Hasan and others said: ﴿and whoever volunteers good﴾ is meant for the whole religion: whatever act beyond what is obligatory upon him, of circumambulation, prayer, zakah, or any kind of the acts of obedience.

﴿then God is Appreciative﴾, He rewards him for his deed.

﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intention of the one who gives thanks, who appreciates the little, gives the much, and forgives the great. The root of shukr (thanks) comes from the saying of the Arabs: "a shakur beast," when its fat appears upon it beyond what it is fed.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of the clear proofs﴾, meaning the stoning (rajm), the prescribed punishments, the rulings, and what is lawful and unlawful.

﴿and the guidance﴾, meaning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description.

﴿after We have made it clear to the people﴾, meaning to the Children of Israel.

﴿in the Book﴾, meaning in the Torah. It was revealed concerning the scholars and chiefs of the Jews who concealed the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, God curses them﴾. The root meaning of la'n in the language is "expulsion." God cursed Iblis by expelling him when He said to him: ﴿So get out of it, for you are accursed﴾ [Qur'an 15:34; 38:77].

Al-Shammakh said, mentioning what came to him:

*The sandgrouse were startled by it, and you remained in it, like the wolf standing, like the accursed man.*

And al-Nabighah said:

*So I passed the night as if I were a cursed outcast, driven away by people, or a wounded sick man.*

So the meaning of our saying "God curses him" is: He expelled him and removed him far away. The root of la'nah is what we have mentioned; then it became common until it became a formula.

﴿and those who curse curse them﴾, meaning they ask God to curse them and say: "O God, curse them." The exegetes differed concerning who these cursers are.

Qatadah said: They are the angels.

'Ata': The jinn and mankind.

Al-Hasan: All the servants of God together.

Ibn 'Abbas: Everything except the jinn and mankind.

Al-Dahhak: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, he is asked: "Who is your Lord? And who is your prophet? And what is your religion?" He says: "I do not know." It is said to him: "You did not know," then he is struck with a blow of a hammer, and he cries out a cry which everything hears except the two weighty ones, mankind and jinn. Nothing hears his voice but curses him. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾.

Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, a beast comes to him whose eyes are like two copper cauldrons, with an iron club, and it strikes him a blow between his shoulders, and he cries out. No one hears his voice without cursing him, and nothing remains that does not hear his voice except the two weighty ones.

Ibn Mas'ud: It is the man who curses his companion, and the curse rises to the sky, then descends, and does not find its target worthy of it, so it returns to the one who uttered it, and does not find him worthy of it either, so it goes and falls upon the Jews. This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿and those who curse curse them﴾. Whoever among them repents, the curse is lifted from him, and it was upon those of the Jews who met it.

Mujahid: ﴿those who curse﴾ are the beasts, which curse the sinners of the children of Adam when the year becomes barren and the rain is withheld. They say: "This is because of the sins of the children of Adam."

'Ikrimah: The beasts of the earth and its creeping things, even the beetles and scorpions, say: "We have been withheld from rain because of the sins of the children of Adam." He said of these things ﴿those who curse﴾ and did not say "those who curse" (feminine), because it is the way of the Arabs, when they describe something of the inanimate things, animals, and others with what is a description of humans, of an act or a speech, that they do not take it out of the manner of the children of Adam and their group, as in their saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Qur'an 12:4], and he did not say "prostrating" (feminine). And His saying concerning the idols: ﴿Rather, their chief did it; so ask them, if they can speak﴾ [Qur'an 21:63]; and His saying: ﴿O ant, enter your dwellings﴾ [Qur'an 27:18]; and His saying: ﴿And they will say to their skins: "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ [Qur'an 41:21], and then He made an exception, saying: ﴿except those who repented﴾ from disbelief.

﴿and set right their deeds﴾ between themselves and their Lord.

﴿and make clear﴾ the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning.

﴿those, I turn to them in forgiveness﴾, meaning I overlook them and accept their repentance.

﴿And I am the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾, who returns to the hearts of My servants who turned away from Me, and is Merciful to them after they turn to Me.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾, the "and" here is a circumstantial (wa of hal).

﴿those, upon them is the curse of God and of the angels﴾, meaning and the curse of the angels.

﴿and of mankind, all together﴾. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: it means mankind all together, the believers.

Abu al-'Aliyah: This is on the Day of Resurrection: the disbeliever is made to stand, and God, mighty and majestic, curses him, then the angels curse him, then all mankind curses him.

Al-Suddi: No two believers curse each other, nor two disbelievers, where one says "May God curse the wrongdoer," without that curse falling upon the disbeliever, because he is a wrongdoer; so every creature curses him.

﴿abiding therein﴾, remaining in the curse and the Fire.

﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, meaning the torment will not be eased for them.

﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be given respite or delay.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "'Nor will they be reprieved' means they will not be given an excuse, as in His saying: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted, so they may make excuse﴾ [Qur'an 77:35–36]."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 163–165:

﴿And your God is one God; there is no god but Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.﴾ Al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas: It was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh, who said: "O Muhammad, describe for us your Lord and give us His lineage." So God Most High revealed Surat al-Ikhlas and this verse.

Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The polytheists had three hundred and sixty idols in the Ka'bah, which they worshipped besides God, falsely and wickedly. So God Most High made clear to them that He is One, and revealed: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no god but Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.﴾

Sa'id, from Abu al-Duha, said: When this verse was revealed, the polytheists marvelled and said: "Muhammad says, 'Your God is one God.' Let him then bring us a sign, if he is among the truthful." So God Most High revealed: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day﴾

"Alternation" (al-ikhtilaf) means their succession in going and coming. It is the reflexive form (ifti'al) from khalafa, yakhlifu, khulufan, meaning that whenever one of the two departs, the other comes in its stead, i.e., after it. Compare His saying: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeed each other﴾ [Surat al-Furqan: 62].

'Ata' and Ibn Kaysan said: He intended the alternation of the night and the day in colour, length and shortness, light and darkness, increase and decrease, one being over the other. "Night" (al-layl) is the plural of layla, like tamra and tamr, nakhla and nakhl; and al-layali is the plural of the plural. "Day" (al-nahar) is singular, and its plural is nahr. The poet said:

Were it not for the two bowls of tharid, we would have perished from hunger:
the tharid of night and the tharid of day.

He mentioned the night before the day because it is the origin, and it precedes. God Most High said: ﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day﴾ [Surat Ya-Sin: 37]. God Most High created the earth in darkness, then created the sun and the moon. This is like His placing the monasteries, churches and prayers before the mosques.

﴿And the ship that runs in the sea﴾: it means the ships; its singular is fulk and its plural is the same. God Most High said: ﴿And indeed Yunus was among the messengers, when he fled to the laden ship﴾ [Surat al-Saffat: 139–140].

He said in the plural: ﴿until when you are in the ships and they sail with them with a good wind﴾ [Surah Yunus: 22]. It may be masculine or feminine. God Most High said: ﴿the laden ship﴾, and He said in the feminine: ﴿the ship that runs in the sea﴾. So the masculine follows the word's form (lafz al-wahid), and the feminine follows the sense of plurality (ma'na al-jam').

﴿with that which benefits mankind﴾: it means riding them and carrying upon them for trade, gain and various kinds of livelihood.

﴿and what God sends down from the sky of water﴾: it means rain.

﴿and with it He revives the earth after its death﴾: after its dryness and barrenness.

﴿and He scattered﴾: spread out and dispersed.

﴿therein of every creature﴾; ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾: that is, He turns them: the northern, the southern, the eastern and the western.

It was also said: "turning them" means once with mercy and once with punishment.

Hamzah, al-A'mash, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read al-rih (the wind) without alif, in the singular. The rest read al-riyah (the winds), in the plural.

Ibn 'Abbas said: al-riyah is for mercy, and al-rih is for punishment.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): when the wind blew, he would say: "O God, make it winds (riyah) and do not make it a wind (rih)."

[Al-Faʾiq fi Gharib al-Hadith of al-Zamakhshari: 2/65; Taj al-'Arus: 2/148.]

And al-rih is masculine and feminine.

Abu al-Barakhtham and Ibn 'Amir read yurawna with a damma on the ya', in the transitive sense; the others read it with a fatha, in the intransitive sense.

﴿that power belongs entirely to God﴾: al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Salam and Ya'qub read innal-quwwata and wa-innallaha with a kasra on the alif in both places, as a resumption (isti'naf). The sentence is complete at ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, with the answer omitted as we have mentioned.

The rest read them with a fatha, in the sense of "that power [belongs to God]" and "that God [is severe in punishment]." It was also said: the meaning is "so that they might see that power belongs to God," that is, they would be certain and would witness it.

'Ata' said: ﴿And if those who did wrong could see﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿when they see the punishment﴾, when Hell is brought forth to them from a distance of five hundred years, to snatch them up as the pigeon picks up a grain, they would know that ﴿power, might, dominion and majesty belong entirely to God﴾, and that ﴿God is severe in punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 166–167:

﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed them﴾. Mujahid recited it with the subject placed before the object: "tuburri'a" with "alladhina" as the agent acting upon "al-ladhina ittaba'u".

The rest recited it in the opposite manner. The ones who were followed (al-mutbu'un) are the tyrants and leaders in shirk and evil, and the followers (al-tabi'un) are the followers, the weak and the lowly. This is what most of the exegetes said.

Al-Suddi said: they are the devils, who disown mankind.

﴿And their bonds are severed﴾: meaning "from them", the preposition "bi" (with) having the sense of "'an" (from).

﴿Al-asbab (the bonds)﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah said: it means the affection and connection that existed between them in the world, or their opposition became enmity.

Al-Rabi' said: it means the positions that they had among the people of the world. Ibn Juraij and al-Kalbi said: it means the lineages and kinship ties, as in His saying: ﴿So there will be no kinship ties between them that Day﴾ [Surah al-Mu'minun: 101].

Al-Suddi said: it means the deeds that they used to do in the world. Its explanation is His saying: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [Surah al-Furqan: 23], and His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah, He will waste their deeds﴾ [Surah Muhammad: 1].

So the people of taqwa are given bonds of firm deeds, by which they take hold and are saved, while the others are given the bonds of their evil deeds, so their deeds are severed from them and they go to the Fire.

Abu Rawq said: they are the covenants that existed between them in the world. The root of "sabab" (bond) is everything by which one reaches something, whether a means, a kinship or an affection. From this it is said: jihad is a "sabab", the road is a "sabab", and the ladder is a "sabab". Zuhayr said:

*"And whoever fears the causes of death, they will overtake him, even if he tries to climb to the sky by a ladder."*

﴿And those who followed said﴾: meaning the followers.

﴿If only we had a return﴾: a return to the world.

﴿So that we might disown them﴾: meaning the ones who were followed.

﴿As they have disowned us﴾ today. The answer to the wish is given by the verb.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning as He showed them the punishment, ﴿Allah will show them﴾. It was also said: so that they would disown one another, Allah shows them ﴿their deeds as regrets (hasarat)﴾, meaning remorse.

﴿Upon them﴾: it was said he meant their righteous deeds which they neglected.

Al-Suddi said: Paradise is raised up for them, so they look at it and at their houses, and they ask, it was said: he meant their deeds, had they obeyed Allah. It is said to them: "Those are your dwellings, had you obeyed Allah." Then it is divided among the believers, who inherit them, and that is when they regret.

Al-Rabi' said: he meant their evil deeds, why they did them, and why they did not do other things that please Allah, the Exalted.

Ibn Kaysan said: they associated idols with Allah, hoping that they would bring them near to Allah. When they were punished for what they had hoped for in reward, they were grieved and regretted. The word "hasarat" is the plural of "hasrah", and every noun of this form that is one instance of an action, with an open first letter and a sukun second letter, has its plural on the pattern "fa'alat", like "thamarah" and "thamarat", and "shahwah" and "shahwat". But when it is an adjective, you make the second letter sukun, like "dakhmah" and "dakhmat", and "ay'alah" and "ay'alat". Likewise, nouns whose first letter is kasra, such as "ni'mah" and "sidrah".

﴿And they will never come out of the Fire﴾.

﴿And they will never come out of the Fire﴾.

O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good. This was revealed concerning Thaqif, Khuza'a, 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'a and Banu Mudlij, who had forbidden for themselves [certain things] of the tilth and livestock: the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham. So He said: "eat of what is in the earth." The particle min (of) here is for partitive sense, since not everything in the earth is possible to eat or lawful to eat. "Lawful" (halal) and "good" (tayyib), meaning pure, are both in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (hal).

It is said they are in the accusative as an object: the meaning being "eat what is lawful and good of what is in the earth."

And do not follow the footsteps (khutuwat) of Satan. Shayba, Nafi', 'Asim, al-A'mash and Hamza read khutwat with the ta' sukun throughout the Qur'an, and this is the most common transmission from Abu 'Amr.

Abu Ja'far, Abu Majlaz, Abu 'Amr in some transmissions, al-Zuhri, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with damma on the kha' and the ta'.

'Ali, 'Amr ibn Maymun and Salam read it with damma on the kha' and the ta', and a hamza after the ta'.

Abu al-Sammak al-'Adawi and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read khatawat with fatha on the kha' and the ta'. Whoever lightened it kept it to its original form and sought lightness, since it is the plural of khatwa (a single step) with a sakin ta'. Whoever put damma on the ta' made it follow the damma of the kha'. Every noun whose singular follows the pattern fa'la and whose plural takes the ta' ending, the commoner and more usual form of its plural is with heaviness and with the vowel of the verb's first radical, as in zulma/zulumat, qurba/qurbat, hujra/hujurat; it is also sometimes lightened.

Whoever put damma on the kha' and the ta' together with the hamza: al-Akhfash said, he intended to take it in the manner of khati'a (error), making it on the pattern of khata' (sin). Abu Hatim said they intended to lengthen the damma into a waw, which then became a hamza; this is common in every damma-ed waw. Whoever put fatha on the kha' and the ta' intended the plural of khatwa, like tamra/tamarat.

Scholars differed on the meaning of "footsteps of Satan." Ali ibn Abi Talha related from Ibn 'Abbas: "the footsteps of Satan" means his deeds. Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak said: his sins. al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: his obedience. 'Ata from Ibn 'Abbas said: his slips and desires. Abu Majlaz said: they are the seeds of disobedience. al-Mawarrij said: his traces. Abu 'Ubayd said: the minor sins. al-Qutaybi and al-Zajjaj said: his paths.

The khatwa is the distance between the two feet, and khatwa (with fatha) is the single act, from the speaker's saying: "I took one step" (khataw-tu khatwa wahida) [Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/105].

Indeed he is to you a manifest enemy: clearly hostile. It is said: one who displays hostility. He has made his enmity to you clear by his refusal to prostrate to your father Adam, peace be upon him, and by his deception of him when he expelled him from Paradise. "Abana" can be intransitive and transitive.

Then He clarified his enmity, saying: He commands you only to evil [al-Baqara 169]: meaning sin. The root of "su'" (evil) is anything that harms its possessor; it is a verbal noun: sa'ahu, yasu'uhu, su'an and masa'a, when it grieves him; and su'ahu shay'un means it grieved him, so he grieved. God the Exalted said: "When they saw it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved were darkened" [al-Mulk 27]. The poet said:

If this age has grieved me,
how often has the age also delighted me.
The matter for me in both is one,
so I endure it, and so I give thanks.

And indecency (al-fahsha'): meaning acts of disobedience, and whatever is ugly of speech and deed. It is a verbal noun like al-ba'sa', al-darra' and al-la'wa'; it may also be an adjective without a verb, like al-adhra' and al-husna'. Mutammim ibn Nuwayra said:

He does not hide under his garments
a character whose manners are chaste and whose sleeves are pure.

The exegetes differed on the meaning of "fahsha'" in this verse.

Baduhan related from Ibn 'Abbas: "fahsha'" is every disobedience which has a prescribed penalty in this world, whether of speech or deed; and "su'" among sins is that which has no prescribed penalty.

Tawus, from him: it is what is unknown in shari'a and sunna.

'Ata, from him: it is miserliness. al-Suddi: it is adultery.

Muqatil claimed that wherever fahsha' is mentioned in the Qur'an it means adultery, except His words "Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency" [al-Baqara 268], where it means withholding zakat.

And that you say about God what you do not know: such as the prohibition of the tilth and livestock.

When it is said to them: "Follow what God has sent down," the exegetes differed about the connection of this verse. Some said: it is a new narrative, and it was revealed concerning the Jews. On this view, the ha' and mim in "lahum" refer to an unmentioned party.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar related from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr or 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ called the Jews to Islam, encouraged them to it, and warned them of God's punishment and vengeance. Nafi' ibn Kharija and Malik ibn 'Awf said to him: "No, we follow what we found our fathers doing," for they were better and more knowledgeable than us. So God revealed this verse.

Others said: rather, this verse is connected to what precedes it, and it was revealed concerning the polytheist Arabs and the disbelieving Quraysh. They differed about it. al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas: "When it is said to them: follow what God has sent down," meaning the disbelieving Quraysh of Banu 'Abd al-Dar. "They say: no, we follow what we found our fathers upon," namely worshipping idols.

God said: "Even though their fathers understood nothing" of tawhid and knowledge of the Merciful, "and were not guided" to the conclusive proof. On this view, the ha' and mim refer back to "those who take rivals besides God" in His words "And among people are those who take rivals besides God" [al-Baqara 165].

Others said: "When it is said to them: follow what God has sent down," regarding the permissibility of what they had forbidden for themselves of the tilth, livestock, sa'iba, wasila, bahira and ham, and all other laws and rulings. "They say: no, we follow what we found our fathers upon," of prohibition and permission, religion and method. On this view, the ha' and mim refer back to "people" in His words: "O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good" [al-Baqara 168]. The shift from address to report is like His words: "until when you are in the ship and they sail with them with a good wind" [Yunus 22]. This is the most preferable of the opinions, because this narrative comes right after "O mankind," so it is more fitting to be a report about them than a report about those who take rivals, given the length of the intervening discourse.

Ali ibn Hamza al-Kisa'i assimilated the lam of hal and bal before eight letters: the ta', as in bal tu'thirun and hal ta'lamu; the tha', as in hal thuwwiba; the sin, as in bal sawwalat lakum; the zay, as in bal zuyyina; the dad, as in bal dallu; the za', as in bal zanantum; the ta', as in bal taba'a Allahu; and the nun, as in bal nahnu, and bal nattabi'u ma alfayna 'alayhi aba'ana. The lam of hal and bal was singled out from the other lams because it is sakin by itself, whereas the other lams are sakin for reasons which, once they cease, their sukun ceases too.

God said: "Even though their fathers..." The waw is the waw of conjunction; it is also said to be the waw of astonishment, with the interrogative alif entering upon it for rebuke and affirmation, which is why it is in the accusative. The meaning is: they follow their fathers even if they were ignorant. The answer to the conditional is omitted because it is known.

His words "who understand nothing" are general in wording but specific in meaning, since they understood the affairs of this world, so the meaning is that they understand nothing of the affairs of religion, "and are not guided."

Then He struck a parable for them, saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: "The likeness of those who disbelieve."

The scholars took two routes concerning this verse and interpreted it in two ways. Some said: He intended by "what hears nothing but a call and a cry" the beasts that do not reason, like camels, sheep, cattle, donkeys and the like. On this view were Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, Qatada, 'Ata, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi, and most exegetes. Then the people of the meanings differed about the sense of this view and the structure of the verse.

Some of them said: the meaning of the verse is "the likeness of you, O Muhammad, and of those who disbelieve in your admonition and your calling to God, the Mighty and Majestic," as said by al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj.

Others said: "the likeness of the preacher of those who disbelieve and their caller," so He omitted that and attributed the likeness to "those who disbelieve," since the context indicates it; this kind of address is called the elided form, and there are many such examples in the Qur'an, like His words "and ask the town" [Yusuf 82]. The poet said:

I thought the bellowing of my she-camel was the cry of a female camel,
though it was not, rather it was your jump at the thrust.

meaning: I thought the bellowing of my she-camel was the bellowing of a female camel. Another said:

I will not be a Muslim as long as I live,
greeting Zayd like the greeting of a prince.

meaning: like my greeting of the prince.

So God the Mighty and Majestic likened the preacher of the disbelievers to the shepherd who calls out to the sheep, that is, shouts and cries to them. It is said: "na'aqa, ya'iqu, na'iqan, na'aqan, and na'qan" when he shouts and rebukes. al-Akhtal said:

So call to your sheep, O Jarir, for you have
only made yourself lost in the wilderness.

Just as these beasts hear the voice but do not understand it, nor benefit from it, nor comprehend what is said to them, so too the disbeliever does not benefit from your admonition, whether you command him to good or rebuke him from evil; he only hears your voice.

al-Hasan said: He says their likeness regarding what they received from their fathers and what you bring them, in that they do not hear it nor understand it, is like the likeness of the shepherd of sheep who calls to them; when they hear the voice they raise their heads and listen to the voice and the call, but understand nothing of it, then return to their pastures, not grasping what is meant for them.

Others said: the meaning of the verse "and the likeness of those who disbelieve" concerns their lack of understanding and their failure to grasp God the Mighty and Majestic and His Messenger, and their poor acceptance of them, is like the likeness of the beasts addressed by the shepherd, which grasp nothing of command and prohibition except the sound; so too the disbeliever, in his poor comprehension and poor reflection on what he is commanded and forbidden. The meaning then is of the one addressed, while the speech is directed at the caller. This is common in Arabic speech, which they do and accept since the meaning is clear to them. They say: "So-and-so fears you like the fear of the lion," meaning "like his fear of the lion." They say: "He presented the basin to the she-camel," when actually it is "he presented the she-camel to the basin." God the Mighty and Majestic said: "Its keys would weigh down a band of strong men" [al-Qasas 76], whereas it is really "the band is weighed down by the keys." The poet said:

I feared so that my fear did not increase
beyond the fear of a wild bull in the thicket of the thorn-tree, reasonable.

meaning: until my fear does not increase beyond the fear of... Another said:

It was an obligation, as you say, just as
adultery is an obligation for stoning.

meaning: just as stoning is an obligation for adultery. al-Farra' recited:

Indeed a lamp is noble in its glory,
by which the eye is adorned when it is kindled.

meaning: adorned by the eye. Its parallels are many.

On this view were Abu 'Ubayda, al-Farra' and a group of scholars.

Others said: the meaning of the verse is: the likeness of the disbelievers in their poor understanding and reasoning is like the likeness of shepherds who speak to dumb animals, which do not understand them. On this interpretation, the verse is not turned into the pronoun form.

Others said: its meaning is: the likeness of those who disbelieve in their calling upon idols, which do not comprehend their call, is like the one who calls his flock, who gains nothing from his calling except fatigue; so the disbeliever gains from calling upon his gods and worshipping idols nothing but toil and trouble, and benefits from them in nothing. This is shown by God's words about idols: "If you call them, they do not hear your call, and if they heard, they would not respond to you" [Fatir 14]. This is a sound interpretation.

As for the other interpretation: some said: the meaning of the verse is: the likeness of the disbelievers in calling upon idols and worshipping images is like the man who shouts in the hollow of the mountains, and a voice called the echo answers him in them, but it does not benefit him. So the interpretation of the verse on this view is: the likeness of the disbelievers in worshipping idols is like the one who calls out to what hears from him nothing but calling and crying.

Then He said: "deaf," meaning they are deaf, and the Arabs say of one who hears but does not act upon what he hears that he is as if deaf. The poet said:

Deaf to what displeases him, hearing well;
dumb about good, so they do not say it;
blind to guidance, so they do not see it.

"So they do not understand."

O you who believe, eat of the good things (tayyibat), meaning the lawful ones,

of what We have provided for you, of the tilth, livestock and all other foods and blessings.

Abu Hurayra related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "God is good and accepts only what is good, and God commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers. He said: 'O messengers, eat of the good things' [al-Mu'minun 51] and He said: 'O you who believe, eat of the good things of what We have provided for you.' Then he mentioned a man who lengthens his journey, dishevelled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky saying: 'O Lord, O Lord,' while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished by the unlawful; so how could he be answered?" [18].

And give thanks to God for His blessing.

If it is Him you worship.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "God the Mighty and Majestic says: I and the jinn and mankind are in a grave matter: I create, and others are worshipped; I provide, and others are thanked" [19].

Then He clarified what He has forbidden to you, saying: "He has forbidden you only carrion (al-maytata), blood, and the flesh of swine" [al-Baqara 173]. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read innama harrama with a light ra' and damma. (Carrion, blood and swine's flesh are in the nominative, as the verb is attributed to them.) Abu Ja'far was related to have read harrama with damma on the ha' and kasra on the ra' with shadda, and the following word in the nominative. This has two possibilities: first, the subject is unnamed; second, what has been forbidden to you, the dead, is the predicate of inna. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah read harrama with fatha on the ha' and the ra' with shadda, and the following word in the nominative, making ma a relative pronoun separate from inna; then inna's noun is in the accusative and what follows is in the nominative as its predicate, as you say: "Inna ma akhadhta malaka" and "Inna ma rakibta dabbataka," i.e., inna alladhi qala Allahu innama sana'u kaydu sahir [Taha 69]. The rest read harrama 'alaykum al-maytata with fatha, placing the verb on the action and treating innama as a single word for emphasis and affirmation.

Abu Ja'far read al-mayyita [and its like] with shadda throughout the Qur'an. The others lightened some and doubled some. Whoever doubled it says the root is mayyut, a verb from death; the ya' was assimilated into the waw and the waw became a doubled ya' because of the kasra, as they did in sayyid, hayyid and sayyib. Whoever did not double it sought lightness; both are dialects, like hayyin and hayn, layyin and layn. The poet said:

He who has died and rested is not a dead one;
rather the dead one is the dead of the living.

So he combined the two dialects.

Abu Mu'adh related from the grammarians and said: al-mayt with lightness is the one from whom the soul has departed, and al-mayyit with doubling is the one who has not yet died but is dying. God the Mighty and Majestic said: "Indeed you are dying and they are dying" [al-Zumar 30]; they did not differ about its doubling, and God knows best. Al-maytata is everything whose slaughter was not achieved and which is of what is slaughtered. Al-dam means flowing blood, indicated by God's words: "or flowing blood" [al-An'am 145], which is restricted.

This verse is specified by the Sunna, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Two dead things and two bloods have been made lawful for us: the two dead things are fish and locusts, and the two bloods are liver and spleen" [20].

As for His words "and the flesh of swine," He meant all its parts and its whole body; He expressed it by the flesh because it is its main part and its substance.

"And what has been dedicated to other than God" means what was slaughtered for idols and tyrants, as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak said. The root of ihlal is raising the voice, and from it comes the ihlal of pilgrimage, which is raising the voice in the talbiya. Ibn Ahmar said:

Half a wilderness, its riders calling out at the Pleiades (al-Farqad) as the pilgrim calling out (ihlal) in the state of ihram calls out.

And another poet said:

Or a pearl from an oyster, whose diver is stirred whenever he sees it glisten (tahill) and prostrate (tasjud).

From the same root comes *ahalla al-sabiyy* and *istihlal al-sabiyy*, which means the infant's crying when it emerges from its mother's womb.

In a hadith: "How can I harm one who has neither spoken, nor cried out (istahalla), nor drunk, nor eaten?"

[21] Likewise, *yatull* (to drip, to be wet with dew). Similarly, *ihlal al-matar*, *istihlal* and *inhilal* (the rain's pouring), which is the sound of its falling upon the ground.

'Umar ibn Qami'ah said:

*Zulm al-bitah lahu inhilal hurayisah,*
*fasafa al-nitaf lahu ba'id al-maqla'*

(Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/116.)

He said *wa ma uhilla bihi* because, when they slaughtered for their idols which they had set up, they raised their voices over it. This practice became so established that it was said: "Every slaughterer, whether he pronounces the name (tasmiyah) or not, whether he raises his voice or not, is one who utters an invocation (muhill)."

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said: *wa ma uhilla bihi li-ghayri Allah* means "that over which other than God's name has been mentioned." Al-Zuhri said: "The *ihlal* for other than God is to say, 'in the name of the Messiah.' This verse is specific to the People of the Book, as in His saying: ﴿The food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾."

Sayyah narrated from 'Uqbah ibn Muslim al-Tujibi and Qays ibn Rafi' al-Ash'ari that they both said: "What is lawful for us is only what is slaughtered for the festivals of the churches, and what is offered to them of bread or meat, for that is only the food of the People of the Book." Sayyah said:

"I said: 'Have you considered the saying of God Most High: ﴿wa ma uhilla bihi li-ghayri Allah﴾?' He said: 'That refers only to the Magians, the worshippers of idols, and the polytheists.'" (Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/117.)

*Fa-man idturra*: 'Asim, Hamzah, Ya'qub and Abu 'Amr read *fa-man idtarra* with a kasrah on the nun, both here and in similar forms such as *an iqtulu* and *aw ikhrujū*, because the jazm (the sukun of the jussive) moves toward a kasrah. The others read with a dammah on the nun, since when they made the final letter of the preceding verb quiescent for the sake of connection (wasl), they transferred its dammah to the nun.

Ibn Muhaysin read *fa-man idtarra* with the *dad* assimilated into the *ta'*, so that it becomes a pure *ta'*. Abu Ja'far read it with a kasrah on the *ta'*, returning it to the *ta'*, and the assimilated *ra'* took a kasrah, because its original form is *idtarrara*, on the pattern of *ifta'ala*, from *al-darurah* (necessity).

The rest read it with a dammah on the *ta'*, according to the original form. Its meaning is: he was pressed, exhausted, and compelled to that.

Mujahid said: "He is forced to it, like a man whom the enemy seizes and forces to eat the flesh of swine or other things forbidden by God."

*Ghayra* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and it was also said to be an exception (istithna'). When you see that *ghayr* cannot take the place of *illa* in that position, then it is a circumstantial qualifier; and when *illa* can take its place, then it is an exception. Measure by this whatever you encounter of this kind.

*Ba'in wa la 'adin.* The original meaning of *al-baghy* in the language is intending corruption. It is said: "*baghā al-jurhu yabghī baghyan*" when a wound progresses toward corruption. From this comes the word *bighā'* for fornication.

God Most High said: ﴿And do not compel your slave-girls to prostitution﴾ [Surah al-Nur: 33]. And a fornicator is called *baghiyy*.

God said: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste (baghiyyan)﴾ [Surah Maryam: 28].

The original meaning of *al-'udwan* is injustice and transgressing the limit. It is said: "*'adā 'alayhi 'adwan wa 'udwanan wa 'adā'an*" when he wronged him.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of His saying: *ghayra baghin wa la 'adin*.

Some of them said: *ghayra baghin* means not one who cuts the road (qati' al-tariq); *wa la 'adin* means one who divides the community (mufarriq li-l-a'immah), who breaks away from the community and rebels against its rulers with his sword. So whoever goes out to sever the ties of kinship, or to terrify the traveler, or to spread corruption in the land, or who runs away from his master, or flees from his creditor, or goes out in disobedience in any way, and is then compelled to eat carrion, it is not lawful for him to eat it; or if he is compelled to drink wine out of thirst, it is not lawful for him to drink it, and he has no concession (rukhsah) nor any honour. But as for one who goes out in obedience and for whom that is permitted, he is granted the concession. This is the view of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi and Yaman, and it is the position of al-Shafi'i. He said: "If we permit it for him, we have helped him in his corruption and wrongdoing, until he repents; he should not be permitted it."

Others said: "This baghy and 'udwan refer back to the eating itself," and this is the view of Abu Hanifah, who permitted the one compelled to eat carrion even if he was disobedient.

Then the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed in detailing this exegesis:

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd said: *ghayra baghin* means eating it without necessity; *wa la 'adin* means one who transgresses, going beyond the lawful to the unlawful, eating it while he is free of need for it.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan: *ghayra baghin* means one who considers it lawful (mustahill lahā); *wa la 'adin* means one who takes provision from it.

Al-Suddi: *ghayra baghin* means eating it out of desire, eating it for pleasure; *wa la 'adin* means eating until he is sated, but he eats only enough as sustenance, the amount that keeps the breath in him.
