He said: 'O messengers, eat of the good things' [al-Mu'minun 51] and He said: 'O you who believe, eat of the good things of what We have provided for you.' Then he mentioned a man who lengthens his journey, dishevelled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky saying: 'O Lord, O Lord,' while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished by the unlawful; so how could he be answered?" [18].

And give thanks to God for His blessing.

If it is Him you worship.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "God the Mighty and Majestic says: I and the jinn and mankind are in a grave matter: I create, and others are worshipped; I provide, and others are thanked" [19].

Then He clarified what He has forbidden to you, saying: "He has forbidden you only carrion (al-maytata), blood, and the flesh of swine" [al-Baqara 173]. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read innama harrama with a light ra' and damma. (Carrion, blood and swine's flesh are in the nominative, as the verb is attributed to them.) Abu Ja'far was related to have read harrama with damma on the ha' and kasra on the ra' with shadda, and the following word in the nominative. This has two possibilities: first, the subject is unnamed; second, what has been forbidden to you, the dead, is the predicate of inna. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah read harrama with fatha on the ha' and the ra' with shadda, and the following word in the nominative, making ma a relative pronoun separate from inna; then inna's noun is in the accusative and what follows is in the nominative as its predicate, as you say: "Inna ma akhadhta malaka" and "Inna ma rakibta dabbataka," i.e., inna alladhi qala Allahu innama sana'u kaydu sahir [Taha 69]. The rest read harrama 'alaykum al-maytata with fatha, placing the verb on the action and treating innama as a single word for emphasis and affirmation.

Abu Ja'far read al-mayyita [and its like] with shadda throughout the Qur'an. The others lightened some and doubled some. Whoever doubled it says the root is mayyut, a verb from death; the ya' was assimilated into the waw and the waw became a doubled ya' because of the kasra, as they did in sayyid, hayyid and sayyib. Whoever did not double it sought lightness; both are dialects, like hayyin and hayn, layyin and layn. The poet said:

He who has died and rested is not a dead one;
rather the dead one is the dead of the living.

So he combined the two dialects.

Abu Mu'adh related from the grammarians and said: al-mayt with lightness is the one from whom the soul has departed, and al-mayyit with doubling is the one who has not yet died but is dying. God the Mighty and Majestic said: "Indeed you are dying and they are dying" [al-Zumar 30]; they did not differ about its doubling, and God knows best. Al-maytata is everything whose slaughter was not achieved and which is of what is slaughtered. Al-dam means flowing blood, indicated by God's words: "or flowing blood" [al-An'am 145], which is restricted.

This verse is specified by the Sunna, as in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Two dead things and two bloods have been made lawful for us: the two dead things are fish and locusts, and the two bloods are liver and spleen" [20].

As for His words "and the flesh of swine," He meant all its parts and its whole body; He expressed it by the flesh because it is its main part and its substance.

"And what has been dedicated to other than God" means what was slaughtered for idols and tyrants, as Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak said. The root of ihlal is raising the voice, and from it comes the ihlal of pilgrimage, which is raising the voice in the talbiya. Ibn Ahmar said:

Half a wilderness, its riders calling out at the Pleiades (al-Farqad) as the pilgrim calling out (ihlal) in the state of ihram calls out.

And another poet said:

Or a pearl from an oyster, whose diver is stirred whenever he sees it glisten (tahill) and prostrate (tasjud).

From the same root comes *ahalla al-sabiyy* and *istihlal al-sabiyy*, which means the infant's crying when it emerges from its mother's womb.

In a hadith: "How can I harm one who has neither spoken, nor cried out (istahalla), nor drunk, nor eaten?"

[21] Likewise, *yatull* (to drip, to be wet with dew). Similarly, *ihlal al-matar*, *istihlal* and *inhilal* (the rain's pouring), which is the sound of its falling upon the ground.

'Umar ibn Qami'ah said:

*Zulm al-bitah lahu inhilal hurayisah,*
*fasafa al-nitaf lahu ba'id al-maqla'*

(Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/116.)

He said *wa ma uhilla bihi* because, when they slaughtered for their idols which they had set up, they raised their voices over it. This practice became so established that it was said: "Every slaughterer, whether he pronounces the name (tasmiyah) or not, whether he raises his voice or not, is one who utters an invocation (muhill)."

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others said: *wa ma uhilla bihi li-ghayri Allah* means "that over which other than God's name has been mentioned." Al-Zuhri said: "The *ihlal* for other than God is to say, 'in the name of the Messiah.' This verse is specific to the People of the Book, as in His saying: ﴿The food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you﴾."

Sayyah narrated from 'Uqbah ibn Muslim al-Tujibi and Qays ibn Rafi' al-Ash'ari that they both said: "What is lawful for us is only what is slaughtered for the festivals of the churches, and what is offered to them of bread or meat, for that is only the food of the People of the Book." Sayyah said:

"I said: 'Have you considered the saying of God Most High: ﴿wa ma uhilla bihi li-ghayri Allah﴾?' He said: 'That refers only to the Magians, the worshippers of idols, and the polytheists.'" (Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/117.)

*Fa-man idturra*: 'Asim, Hamzah, Ya'qub and Abu 'Amr read *fa-man idtarra* with a kasrah on the nun, both here and in similar forms such as *an iqtulu* and *aw ikhrujū*, because the jazm (the sukun of the jussive) moves toward a kasrah. The others read with a dammah on the nun, since when they made the final letter of the preceding verb quiescent for the sake of connection (wasl), they transferred its dammah to the nun.

Ibn Muhaysin read *fa-man idtarra* with the *dad* assimilated into the *ta'*, so that it becomes a pure *ta'*. Abu Ja'far read it with a kasrah on the *ta'*, returning it to the *ta'*, and the assimilated *ra'* took a kasrah, because its original form is *idtarrara*, on the pattern of *ifta'ala*, from *al-darurah* (necessity).

The rest read it with a dammah on the *ta'*, according to the original form. Its meaning is: he was pressed, exhausted, and compelled to that.

Mujahid said: "He is forced to it, like a man whom the enemy seizes and forces to eat the flesh of swine or other things forbidden by God."

*Ghayra* is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and it was also said to be an exception (istithna'). When you see that *ghayr* cannot take the place of *illa* in that position, then it is a circumstantial qualifier; and when *illa* can take its place, then it is an exception. Measure by this whatever you encounter of this kind.

*Ba'in wa la 'adin.* The original meaning of *al-baghy* in the language is intending corruption. It is said: "*baghā al-jurhu yabghī baghyan*" when a wound progresses toward corruption. From this comes the word *bighā'* for fornication.

God Most High said: ﴿And do not compel your slave-girls to prostitution﴾ [Surah al-Nur: 33]. And a fornicator is called *baghiyy*.

God said: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste (baghiyyan)﴾ [Surah Maryam: 28].

The original meaning of *al-'udwan* is injustice and transgressing the limit. It is said: "*'adā 'alayhi 'adwan wa 'udwanan wa 'adā'an*" when he wronged him.

The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of His saying: *ghayra baghin wa la 'adin*.

Some of them said: *ghayra baghin* means not one who cuts the road (qati' al-tariq); *wa la 'adin* means one who divides the community (mufarriq li-l-a'immah), who breaks away from the community and rebels against its rulers with his sword. So whoever goes out to sever the ties of kinship, or to terrify the traveler, or to spread corruption in the land, or who runs away from his master, or flees from his creditor, or goes out in disobedience in any way, and is then compelled to eat carrion, it is not lawful for him to eat it; or if he is compelled to drink wine out of thirst, it is not lawful for him to drink it, and he has no concession (rukhsah) nor any honour. But as for one who goes out in obedience and for whom that is permitted, he is granted the concession. This is the view of Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Kalbi and Yaman, and it is the position of al-Shafi'i. He said: "If we permit it for him, we have helped him in his corruption and wrongdoing, until he repents; he should not be permitted it."

Others said: "This baghy and 'udwan refer back to the eating itself," and this is the view of Abu Hanifah, who permitted the one compelled to eat carrion even if he was disobedient.

Then the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed in detailing this exegesis:

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd said: *ghayra baghin* means eating it without necessity; *wa la 'adin* means one who transgresses, going beyond the lawful to the unlawful, eating it while he is free of need for it.

Muqatil ibn Hayyan: *ghayra baghin* means one who considers it lawful (mustahill lahā); *wa la 'adin* means one who takes provision from it.

Al-Suddi: *ghayra baghin* means eating it out of desire, eating it for pleasure; *wa la 'adin* means eating until he is sated, but he eats only enough as sustenance, the amount that keeps the breath in him.

Shahr ibn Hawshab: *ghayra baghin* means exceeding the measure that is lawful for him; *wa la 'adin* means not falling short of what is lawful for him, so that he leaves it and does not eat it.

Masruq said: "It has reached me that whoever is compelled to eat carrion and does not eat it until he dies, enters the Fire." The jurists differed concerning the amount the one compelled may lawfully eat of carrion.

Some of them said: the amount that keeps his breath in him. This is one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions and the choice of al-Muzani.

The other opinion: he may eat until he is sated. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: he should not exceed three mouthfuls.

Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: *ghayra baghin* means one who does not separate from the community; *wa la 'adin* means one who innovates and opposes the Sunnah. He did not grant the innovator the concession to take what is forbidden in cases of necessity.

*Fa-la ithma 'alayhi* means there is no sin or blame upon him for eating it.

*Inna Allaha ghafur* means forgiving of what he ate of the unlawful in a state of necessity.

*Rahim* means merciful to him in that He granted him this concession.

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book...﴾ (the verse).

Jawbir narrated from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas: "The kings were asked by the Jews before the mission of Muhammad ﷺ about what they found in the Torah. The Jews said: 'We find in the Torah that God, mighty and majestic, will send a prophet after the Messiah, called Muhammad, who will forbid fornication, wine, musical instruments, and the shedding of blood.' When God sent Muhammad ﷺ and he came to Medina, the kings said to the Jews: 'Is this the one you find in your book?' The Jews, out of greed for the kings' wealth, said: 'This is not that prophet ﷺ.' So the kings gave them wealth, and God, Most High, revealed this verse, refuting the Jews."

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas: "It was revealed concerning the chiefs and scholars of the Jews, who used to receive gifts and surplus from their common people, and who hoped that the awaited Prophet would be from among them. When God sent Muhammad ﷺ from among others, they feared the loss of their rule and the end of their leadership. So they set about the description of Muhammad ﷺ, changed it, and then brought it out to their people, saying: 'This is the description of the Prophet who will appear at the end of time, and it does not resemble the description of this prophet who is in Mecca.'

When the common people looked at the altered description, they found it contradicted the description of Muhammad ﷺ, so they did not follow him.

So God, Most High, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book﴾, meaning the description of Muhammad ﷺ and his prophethood.

*Wa yashtarūna bihi*: by the concealed matter.

*Thamanan qalilan*: a small price, a little worldly gain, meaning the foods they used to receive from their common people.

*Ula'ika ma ya'kulūna fi butunihim*: the mention of "belly" here is for emphasis, because a person may say "So-and-so ate my property" when he has ruined and squandered it. It is also said "kalimah min fihi" because he speaks to him by correspondence and writing, and "he handed him from his hand," and similar phrases.

A poet said:

*Nazartu fa-lam tanzur bi-'aynika manzaran*
*illa al-nar*

*Illa al-nar* means: except what leads them into the Fire, namely bribery, unlawful gain, and the price of religion and Islam.

Since its outcome is the Fire, He named it "fire" in the present, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire in their bellies﴾ [Surah al-Nisa': 10], meaning that its outcome leads to the Fire.

And his saying ﷺ about the one who drinks from vessels of gold and silver: "He is only swallowing the fire of Hell into his belly" [Sunan al-Darimi: 2/121, and Sahih al-Bukhari: 6/251]. [22] He informed about the wealth by its outcome.

*Wa la yukallimuhumu Allahu yawm al-qiyamah*: speech that benefits them or gladdens them. This is the view of the people of tafsir. The people of the meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He means that He is angry with them, as one says "So-and-so does not speak to so-and-so," meaning he is angry with him.

*Wa la yuzakkihim*: He will not purify them from the defilement of their sins.

*Wa lahum 'adhab alim*: a painful punishment.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error﴾: that is, they exchanged error.

*Bil-huda wal-'adhaba bil-maghfirah*, *fa-ma asbarahum 'ala al-nar*: they differed concerning *ma*.

Some said: it is the *ma* of wonder (ma al-ta'ajjub), and they differed about its meaning.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: "By God, they have no patience for it; rather, how bold they are in doing the deed that brings them near to the Fire." They said: this is a Yemeni usage.

Al-Farra' said: al-Kisa'i informed me, that the judge of Yemen informed him: two litigants came before him, and an oath became obligatory upon one of them, so he swore it. His opponent said: "How patient you are with God!" meaning: how bold you are against Him.

Al-Mawrij said: "How patient they are in a deed that leads them to the Fire," because those were scholars, and whoever opposes the Prophet ﷺ becomes one of the people of the Fire.

Al-Kisa'i and Qutrub said: its meaning is: how patient they are in the deeds of the people of the Fire, that is, how constant they are in them, just as one says: "How similar your generosity is to Hatim's," meaning to the generosity of Hatim.

Mujahid said: "How knowledgeable they are of the deeds of the people of the Fire." It was also said: "How long they will remain in the Fire!" just as one says: "How patient So-and-so is with beating and imprisonment!"

'Ata', al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Abu Bakr ibn 'Abbas said: *ma* is interrogative, and its meaning is: what has made them patient, and what thing has made them endure the Fire, since they abandoned the truth and followed falsehood?

It was said that this is said in the manner of belittling them.

﴿That is because God sent down the Book with truth﴾. Some of them said: its meaning is: "That punishment is because God sent down the Book with truth." They differed about this, and in that case *dhalika* is in the nominative position. Others said its position is accusative, meaning: We did that to them because God, mighty and majestic, [sent down the Book with truth], or because God sent down the Book with truth; they differed about it and disbelieved in it, so the particle of causation was omitted.

Al-Akhfash said: the predicate of *dhalika* is implied; its meaning is: that is known to them, because God sent down the Book with truth.

Others said: its meaning is: "*dhalika*," that is, their deed which they perform, of disbelief, disagreement, and audacity against God Most High, is because God sent down the Book with truth; and His sending down the Book with truth is His informing about them: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same to them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. God has sealed their hearts﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 6].

﴿Indeed, those who differed concerning the Book﴾: they believed in part and disbelieved in part.

﴿are in extreme dissension﴾: that is, in far-reaching opposition and lengthy error.

Al-Tha'alibi's commentary (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 177–179 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west.﴾ Hamzah and Hafs read *laysa al-birra* with the *ra'* in the accusative (*naṣb*). The rest read it in the nominative (*raf'*). Whoever reads *al-birru* in the nominative makes it the subject of *laysa* (the copula "is not"), and takes its predicate to be in the phrase *an tuwallū*. The meaning is: "Righteousness is not your turning [your faces]." Whoever reads it in the accusative makes *an* and what follows it in the position of the nominative, as the subject of *laysa*. The meaning is: "Your turning your faces is not all of righteousness." This is like His saying ﴿Their argument was only that they said﴾ (45:25), and His saying ﴿so the outcome for both of them was that they were in the Fire﴾ (59:17).

Hārūn reported from ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that they both recited it as: *Laysa al-birru bi-an tuwallū wujūhakum* ("Righteousness is not in your turning your faces").

The exegetes differed concerning this verse:

Some said: Allah meant by this verse the Jews and the Christians. The Jews used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) in the west, and the Christians facing the east. Each group claimed that righteousness lay in that. So Allah informed them that righteousness is other than their religion and their deeds, and He explained what it is in this verse. Those who held this view include Qatadah, al-Rabīʿ, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and ʿAwf al-Aʿrābī.

Others said: The verse refers to the believers. A man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about righteousness, so Allah revealed this verse, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned that man and recited it to him.

Before the obligatory duties (*farāʾiḍ*) were prescribed, a man who testified that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and who prayed toward whatever direction, and died in that state, was granted Paradise. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) migrated, the obligatory duties were revealed, the limits (*ḥudūd*) were set, and the *qiblah* was turned toward the Kaʿbah. Then Allah revealed this verse and said: "Righteousness is not all that you pray and do other than that."

﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah.﴾ The *man* (in the sense of "one who") is the subject, and the *birr* (righteousness) is the predicate, and it is a verb-type phrase, since one does not say "righteousness is Zayd." The scholars differed about how to understand the verse:

Some said: Since *man* stands in the place of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), it is taken to be a hidden noun in the sense of *birr*, as if he said: "But righteousness is the belief in Allah." The Arabs make a noun the predicate of a verb, as in their saying: "The truly righteous one is the one who keeps ties of kinship and gives charity in secret." They mean: keeping ties of kinship and concealing charity. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Salamah held this view. Al-Farrāʾ recited this verse of poetry:

*"By your life, the youths are not those whose beards grow,*
*but the youth is every generous man."*

So he made the growth of the beard the predicate of "youth."

It was also said: The meaning is: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah and is independent of people," like their saying: "Generosity is Ḥātim, bravery is ʿAntarah, poetry is Zuhayr," meaning the generosity of Ḥātim, the bravery of ʿAntarah, and the poetry of Zuhayr. And the Arabs say: "The Banū Fulān—the road tramples them," meaning the people of the road. Allah the Exalted said ﴿and ask the town﴾ (12:82), and said ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾ (31:28). Al-Nābighah al-Jaʿdī said:

*"How can we be connected to one whose majesty is like that of Abu Marḥab?"*

That is, like the majesty of Abū Marḥab. Qaṭrub, al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj also held this view.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: The meaning is: "But the pious (*al-bār*) is one who believes in Allah," like His saying ﴿and the final outcome is for piety (*al-taqwā*)﴾ (20:132), meaning the one who is pious.

It was also said: The meaning of "one of righteousness" is "one who believes in Allah." This was related by al-Zajjāj, like His saying ﴿they have degrees with Allah﴾ (3:163), meaning "possessors of degrees."

Al-Mubarrad said: If I were one of those who read the Qur'an, I would have read *lākinna al-birra man āmana bi-llāh* with the *bāʾ* of *al-birr* vowelled with a *fatḥah*. The Arabs say: "a *barr* man and a *bārr* man," and the plural is *barrah* and *abrār*. *Al-birr* means kindness and beneficence, and *al-birr* also means truthfulness. Here *al-birr* means faith and piety, and this is what is meant in this verse, as indicated by His saying ﴿who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾.

﴿and the angels﴾ all of them.
﴿and the Book﴾ [i.e., the books]. ﴿and the prophets﴾ all of them.

﴿and gives wealth, despite love for it﴾. The exegetes differed about the interpretation of this phrase:

Most of the exegetes said: The pronoun in *ḥubbihi* ("love for it") refers to wealth, meaning: he gives wealth while he is healthy and loves it, and is attached to it. This is supported by the statement of Ibn Masʿūd about this verse, who said: "It is that you bequeath it while you are healthy, desiring life and fearing poverty, and you do not delay, until when the throat rattles you say, 'To so-and-so such-and-such.'" Some transmitted this as a hadith raised to the Prophet.

It was also said: The pronoun refers to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, meaning the love of Allah, glorified is He.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-Faḍl said: "It refers to love of giving." It was also said: The pronoun refers to the giver, meaning the love of the giver.

﴿to relatives, orphans﴾: the people of kinship.

It was related from Umm Rābiḥ bint Ṣalīḥ, from Sulaymān ibn ʿĀmir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Charity to a poor person is one charity, but to one who is a relative it is two, because it is both charity and maintaining kinship."

Al-Zuhrī, from Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from his mother Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The best charity is to a relative who harbors enmity (*al-kāshiḥ*)." *Al-kāshiḥ* is the enemy who conceals his enmity and keeps it hidden in his side (*kashḥ*), that is, his inner self.

Sulaymān ibn Yasār, from Maymūnah, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), said: "I freed a slave-girl of mine, and I entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and told him of her manumission. He said: 'May Allah reward you. But if you had given her to your maternal uncles, it would have been greater for your reward.'"

﴿and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ — the wayfarer (*ibn al-sabīl*) is named as a metaphor (*majāz*). The scholars differed about it. Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāriqī and Mujāhid said: it means the traveler cut off from his family who passes by you.

Qatādah said: It is the guest who alights with a person. He said: "We have mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest.'" [In al-Ṭabarī's Tafsīr (2/132), it reads: "let him say something good or remain silent."] And he used to say: "The right of hospitality is three nights; whatever he offers beyond that is charity."

The traveler and the guest who comes and goes are called *ibn al-sabīl* ("son of the road") because of their constant attachment to the road, just as a man who has been through the ages and nights is called "son of days and nights," and the water-bird is called "son of water" because of its constant attachment to it. Dhū al-Rummah said:

*"I came to them by a rugged path, while the Pleiades were like*
*a "son of water" hovering over the crown of the head."*

﴿and those who ask﴾: those who seek food, those who request.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥusayn, from his mother Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who asks has a right, even if he comes on a horse."

Mālik ibn Anas, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The gift of Allah to the believer is the one who asks at his door."

﴿and in [freeing] slaves﴾: this means the *mukātabūn* (slaves who have contracted to buy their freedom). Most exegetes said this. It was also said: it means ransoming captives; and it was said: it means freeing a soul and unfastening a neck.

﴿and establishes the prayer﴾: the obligatory prayer.
﴿and gives the zakāt﴾: the obligatory alms.

﴿and those who fulfill their covenant when they make it﴾: in their dealings among themselves and with people. When they promise, they fulfill; when they swear oaths, they honor them; when they speak, they tell the truth; and when they are entrusted, they return the trust.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: Whoever gives the covenant of Allah and then breaks it, Allah the Glorified will be his adversary. And whoever gives his pledge to the Prophet (ﷺ) and then betrays it, the Prophet (ﷺ) will be his adversary on the Day of Resurrection.

Regarding the grammatical case (*iʿrāb*) of *al-mūfūna* (those who fulfill), there are two opinions: al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash said it is in apposition (*ʿaṭf*) to the position (*maḥall*) of *man* in His saying ﴿but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾. *Man* is in the position of a plural, and its position is nominative, as if He said: "But the righteous are the believers and those who fulfill [their covenants]."

It was also said: it is nominative as the beginning of a sentence (*mubtadaʾ*), and the predicate is understood to be: "They are those who fulfill."

﴿and the patient﴾. There are four opinions on its accusative case (*naṣb*). Abū ʿUbayd said: it is accusative because the sentence has been lengthened, and it is a feature of Arabic that the case-endings change when the sentence is long.

Al-Kisāʾī said: it is accusative as a coordinate (*nasaq*) to His saying ﴿to relatives﴾, that is, "the patient."

Some said: the meaning is "and I mean the patient."

Khalīl ibn Aḥmad and al-Farrāʾ said: it is accusative for praise (*madḥ*). The Arabs use the accusative for praise and for blame, as though they intend to single out the one praised or blamed, and do not link it to the beginning of the sentence, so they put it in the accusative. For praise, there is His saying ﴿and those who establish the prayer﴾ (4:162). Al-Kisāʾī recited:

*"Every people obeyed the command of their guide,*
*except the Numayr, who obeyed the command of their misguider.*
*And the spearmen, though they have not stabbed anyone,*
*and those who say to the one who has a home, 'Abandon it.'"*

Abū ʿUbayda recited for Ḥuzniq ibn ʿAffān:

*"Let not my people be far away, those who are*
*the poison of the enemies and their sharp sword,*
*who alight in every battle,*
*and are the good ones at the knots of the ropes."*

As for blame, there is His saying ﴿cursed, wherever they are found, they will be seized﴾ (33:61). ʿUrwah ibn al-Ward said:

*"They give us wine, then they suffice us against the enemies of Allah, who lie and deceive."*

﴿in poverty (*al-baʾsāʾ*)﴾: this means hardship and poverty. ﴿and affliction (*al-ḍarrāʾ*)﴾: illness and disability. These two are nouns formed on the pattern *faʿlāʾ*, which has no comparative form (*afʿal*), because they are nouns and not adjectives.

﴿and at the time of battle (*ḥīna al-baʾs*)﴾: the time of fighting.

ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "When the fighting grew fierce, we would seek shelter behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the closest of us to the enemy was the one who fought most fiercely."

﴿Those are the ones who are truthful﴾: in their faith.
﴿and those are the God-conscious﴾.

Al-Qāsim narrated: Abū Dharr was asked about faith, so he recited this verse. The questioner said: "We only asked you about faith, and you tell us about righteousness." He said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about faith, and he recited this verse."

Abū Maysarah said: "He recited this verse, and whoever acts by this verse has completed righteousness."

﴿O you who believe, retaliation (*al-qiṣāṣ*) is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ (2:178). Al-Shaʿbī, al-Kalbī, Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: This verse was revealed concerning two tribes of the Arabs who fought one another in the pre-Islamic period shortly before Islam. Between them there were slain and wounds which some had not yet taken retribution for from others, until Islam came.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: They were the two tribes, al-Aws and al-Khazraj.

Ibn Kaysān said: They were Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr. He said: One of the two tribes had superiority over the other in nobility and honor. They used to marry their women without dowries. So they swore that they would kill, in retaliation for a slave among us, a free man among them; for a woman among us, a man among them; and for a man among us, two men among them. They also made their wounds double the wounds of the others, and they treated them thus in the pre-Islamic period. They brought their matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah the Exalted revealed this verse and commanded them to equality, and they agreed and submitted.

Al-Suddī and a group said: This verse was revealed concerning blood money (*diyāt*). The reason was that the people of two groups among the Arabs fought, one of them Muslim and the other a covenanted group (*muʿāhad*). So Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to reconcile them by making the blood money for women from each of the two groups a retaliation equal to the blood money for women of the other group, and the blood money for men equal to that for men, and for slaves equal to that for slaves. Then He revealed ﴿O you who believe, prescribed for you is retaliation regarding the slain﴾: "was prescribed and decreed upon you concerning the slain." [See al-Ṭabarī's Tafsīr: 2/140.]

*Al-qiṣāṣ* (retaliation) means equality and parity in lives, wounds and blood money. Its root is from *qaṣṣ al-athar*, following a trail: the one who is wronged follows what was done to him and does the same. Then He explained, saying: ﴿the free for the free, the slave for the slave, the female for the female﴾.

Mention of the ruling of the verses:

When two bloods are equal, whether they be free Muslims or Muslim slaves, or free covenanted persons or covenanted slaves, then from each category one is killed: a male if he has killed a male, a female if she has killed a female. The consensus (*ijmāʿ*) holds that a man is killed for a woman, because they are equal in sacredness, inheritance, the penalty for fornication and slander, and other matters, so they must be equal in retaliation. A free man is not killed for a slave, but he owes the slave's value, even if it reaches a third [of the blood-money], because of the difference in rank between them. A Muslim is not killed for an unbeliever. The proof for this is what

al-Shaʿbī narrated from Abū Ḥujayfah, who said: I asked ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, "Do you have anything from the Prophet (ﷺ) apart from the Qur'an?" He said: "No, by the One who split the grain and created the soul. Except that Allah the Mighty and Majestic may grant a servant understanding of His Book, and what is in this sheet." I said: "And what is in the sheet?" He said: "The blood-money (*ʿaql*), the ransom of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for an unbeliever, and a master is not to be killed for his slave, and a father is not to be killed for his son." [The first part is in both sources.] [Kitāb al-Musnad of al-Shāfiʿī: 190; al-Muṣannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzāq: 10/100, no. 18507.]

The evidence for this is what was narrated: a man named Qatādah struck his son with a sword, hitting his leg, and he bled and died. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Were it not that I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, 'A father is not to be retaliated against for his son,' I would have retaliated against you."

﴿But if anything is pardoned for him by his brother﴾: that is, he gives up and forgives him for what is obligatory upon him, which is retaliation.

It was narrated from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) that he killed three men for one in a case of deliberate murder.

This is the view of most exegetes, who said: pardon means accepting the blood-money in a case of deliberate murder. Al-Suddī said: it means that some remainder of his brother's blood-money, or of the compensation for his wound, remains for him.

﴿then there should be a following up in a fair manner﴾: that is, then it is incumbent upon him to follow up.

﴿and payment to him with good conduct﴾: The claimant is commanded to demand in a fair manner, and to pursue the right owed to him from the one bound to him, without demanding an increase or imposing what Allah has not made obligatory for him, or being harsh with him. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever adds a camel to the camels of the blood-money and their obligations, it is from the practice of the Jāhiliyyah."
[Jāmiʿ al-Bayān of al-Ṭabarī: 2/150.]

The ruling of the verse:

Know that the kinds of killing are three: deliberate (*ʿamd*), quasi-deliberate (*shibh al-ʿamd*), and mistaken (*khaṭaʾ*).

Deliberate killing is when one intends to strike with something that usually causes death, such as an iron tool, a large piece of wood, a big stone, or the like, or burning him, drowning him, strangling him with a rope, throwing him from a roof or into a well, and similar things that are intentionally done to kill. For this there is retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*) or blood-money (*diyah*).

The blood-money for a Muslim is a thousand dinars, or twelve thousand dirhams in silver, or one hundred camels, of which forty are pregnant (with their young in their bellies), thirty are three-year-olds (*ḥiqqah*), and thirty are four-year-olds (*jadhaʿah*). The basis for a man is camels; the blood-money for women is half of that.

As for quasi-deliberate killing: it is when one intends to strike with something that usually does not cause death, such as a small pebble, a small stick, a slap, a push, a punch, or a sword-blow struck deliberately, or what is similar to that, and the person dies from it. In this case the blood-money is required and is aggravated (*mughallaẓah*) upon the paternal kin (*ʿāqilah*), as we described for the blood-money of deliberate killing.

As for mistaken killing: it is when one intends one thing and misses, hitting something else. Like a man who shoots at a target or at game, and the arrow misses and falls upon a person and kills him. This is pure mistake, and in it there is a lighter blood-money upon the paternal kin, in sixty-three portions (*akhmās*): twenty bint makhāḍ (she-camel in her second year), twenty bint labūn (in her third year), twenty ibn labūn, twenty khinaq (in her fourth year), and twenty jadhaʿah. Silver or gold is not specified, as the camels mentioned are reduced by the pardon and the blood-money.

﴿a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾: this is because Allah the Exalted prescribed for the people of the Torah, in cases of life and wounds, that they must retaliate, and not take blood-money, and not pardon. And for the people of the Gospel, that they must pardon, and not retaliate, and not take blood-money.

So Allah the Exalted gave this ummah the choice between retaliation, blood-money, and pardon.

As Saʿīd ibn Abī Saʿīd al-Maqburī narrated from Abū Shurayḥ: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Then you, O Khuzāʿah, have killed this slain man from Hudhayl, and I, by Allah, am his payer of blood-money. Whoever kills a person after this, his family have a choice between two options: if they wish, they may retaliate, and if they wish, they may take the blood-money."

﴿Whoever transgresses after that﴾: he wrongs and exceeds the limit.

﴿after that﴾: it was said: after taking the blood-money. Al-Ḥasan said: "In the pre-Islamic period, if a man killed someone he would flee to his people, and his people would come and make peace by paying blood-money, and that is the transgression."

﴿then for him there is a painful punishment﴾: he is killed in this world, and is not pardoned. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will not pardon a man who kills after taking the blood-money from him." And in the Hereafter there is the punishment of the Fire. And this verse is evidence that the killer does not become an unbeliever and does not remain eternally in the Fire, because Allah the Exalted…

He addressed them, saying: "O you who have believed, prescribed for you is qisas (retaliation)." There is no disagreement that qisas applies in cases of deliberate killing, and so the name of faith is not removed from the one who commits this grave sin. In the latter part of the verse He says: ﴿But if he is pardoned by his brother [something]﴾, and so He calls the killer the brother of the one killed. He also says: ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy﴾, and both of these are specific to the believers, not the disbelievers.

It is related that Masruq was asked: "Is there repentance for the killer?" He said: "I will not close a door that Allah has opened."

﴿And for you in qisas is life﴾: that is, survival, because when a person knows that if he kills he will himself be killed, he refrains and restrains himself from killing. Thus there is life in it for the one who intends to kill him, and life for the one who would have been killed. For this reason it is said in the proverb: "Killing reduces killing."

Qatadah said: "How many a man has intended a calamity, and had it not been for fear of qisas he would have committed it. But Allah, exalted is He, restrains His servants from one another." This is the view of most of the exegetes.

Al-Suddi said: "They used to kill one man for a single man, two men, ten, or a hundred. When they limited the killing to one for one, there was life in that." It has also been said: He meant the life in the Hereafter, because whoever is retaliated against in this world will be spared retaliation in the Hereafter, whereas whoever is not retaliated against in this world will be retaliated against in the Hereafter. The "life" then means his safety from retaliation in the Hereafter.

Abu al-Jawza' recited: ﴿And for you in qisas is life﴾ and meant by it the Qur'an, that in it is life for the hearts.

He said: ﴿O people of understanding﴾: that is, O possessors of intellects.

﴿That you may become righteous﴾: that is, that you may avoid killing out of fear of retaliation.

Al-Tha'alibi's commentary (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 177–179 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west.﴾ Hamzah and Hafs read *laysa al-birra* with the *ra'* in the accusative (*naṣb*). The rest read it in the nominative (*raf'*). Whoever reads *al-birru* in the nominative makes it the subject of *laysa* (the copula "is not"), and takes its predicate to be in the phrase *an tuwallū*. The meaning is: "Righteousness is not your turning [your faces]." Whoever reads it in the accusative makes *an* and what follows it in the position of the nominative, as the subject of *laysa*. The meaning is: "Your turning your faces is not all of righteousness." This is like His saying ﴿Their argument was only that they said﴾ (45:25), and His saying ﴿so the outcome for both of them was that they were in the Fire﴾ (59:17).

Hārūn reported from ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that they both recited it as: *Laysa al-birru bi-an tuwallū wujūhakum* ("Righteousness is not in your turning your faces").

The exegetes differed concerning this verse:

Some said: Allah meant by this verse the Jews and the Christians. The Jews used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) in the west, and the Christians facing the east. Each group claimed that righteousness lay in that. So Allah informed them that righteousness is other than their religion and their deeds, and He explained what it is in this verse. Those who held this view include Qatadah, al-Rabīʿ, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and ʿAwf al-Aʿrābī.

Others said: The verse refers to the believers. A man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about righteousness, so Allah revealed this verse, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned that man and recited it to him.

Before the obligatory duties (*farāʾiḍ*) were prescribed, a man who testified that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and who prayed toward whatever direction, and died in that state, was granted Paradise. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) migrated, the obligatory duties were revealed, the limits (*ḥudūd*) were set, and the *qiblah* was turned toward the Kaʿbah. Then Allah revealed this verse and said: "Righteousness is not all that you pray and do other than that."

﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah.﴾ The *man* (in the sense of "one who") is the subject, and the *birr* (righteousness) is the predicate, and it is a verb-type phrase, since one does not say "righteousness is Zayd." The scholars differed about how to understand the verse:

Some said: Since *man* stands in the place of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), it is taken to be a hidden noun in the sense of *birr*, as if he said: "But righteousness is the belief in Allah." The Arabs make a noun the predicate of a verb, as in their saying: "The truly righteous one is the one who keeps ties of kinship and gives charity in secret." They mean: keeping ties of kinship and concealing charity. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Salamah held this view. Al-Farrāʾ recited this verse of poetry:

*"By your life, the youths are not those whose beards grow,*
*but the youth is every generous man."*

So he made the growth of the beard the predicate of "youth."

It was also said: The meaning is: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah and is independent of people," like their saying: "Generosity is Ḥātim, bravery is ʿAntarah, poetry is Zuhayr," meaning the generosity of Ḥātim, the bravery of ʿAntarah, and the poetry of Zuhayr. And the Arabs say: "The Banū Fulān—the road tramples them," meaning the people of the road. Allah the Exalted said ﴿and ask the town﴾ (12:82), and said ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾ (31:28). Al-Nābighah al-Jaʿdī said:

*"How can we be connected to one whose majesty is like that of Abu Marḥab?"*

That is, like the majesty of Abū Marḥab. Qaṭrub, al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj also held this view.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: The meaning is: "But the pious (*al-bār*) is one who believes in Allah," like His saying ﴿and the final outcome is for piety (*al-taqwā*)﴾ (20:132), meaning the one who is pious.

It was also said: The meaning of "one of righteousness" is "one who believes in Allah." This was related by al-Zajjāj, like His saying ﴿they have degrees with Allah﴾ (3:163), meaning "possessors of degrees."

Al-Mubarrad said: If I were one of those who read the Qur'an, I would have read *lākinna al-birra man āmana bi-llāh* with the *bāʾ* of *al-birr* vowelled with a *fatḥah*. The Arabs say: "a *barr* man and a *bārr* man," and the plural is *barrah* and *abrār*. *Al-birr* means kindness and beneficence, and *al-birr* also means truthfulness. Here *al-birr* means faith and piety, and this is what is meant in this verse, as indicated by His saying ﴿who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾.

﴿and the angels﴾ all of them.
﴿and the Book﴾ [i.e., the books]. ﴿and the prophets﴾ all of them.

﴿and gives wealth, despite love for it﴾. The exegetes differed about the interpretation of this phrase:

Most of the exegetes said: The pronoun in *ḥubbihi* ("love for it") refers to wealth, meaning: he gives wealth while he is healthy and loves it, and is attached to it. This is supported by the statement of Ibn Masʿūd about this verse, who said: "It is that you bequeath it while you are healthy, desiring life and fearing poverty, and you do not delay, until when the throat rattles you say, 'To so-and-so such-and-such.'" Some transmitted this as a hadith raised to the Prophet.

It was also said: The pronoun refers to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, meaning the love of Allah, glorified is He.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-Faḍl said: "It refers to love of giving." It was also said: The pronoun refers to the giver, meaning the love of the giver.

﴿to relatives, orphans﴾: the people of kinship.

It was related from Umm Rābiḥ bint Ṣalīḥ, from Sulaymān ibn ʿĀmir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Charity to a poor person is one charity, but to one who is a relative it is two, because it is both charity and maintaining kinship."

Al-Zuhrī, from Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from his mother Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The best charity is to a relative who harbors enmity (*al-kāshiḥ*)." *Al-kāshiḥ* is the enemy who conceals his enmity and keeps it hidden in his side (*kashḥ*), that is, his inner self.

Sulaymān ibn Yasār, from Maymūnah, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), said: "I freed a slave-girl of mine, and I entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and told him of her manumission. He said: 'May Allah reward you. But if you had given her to your maternal uncles, it would have been greater for your reward.'"

﴿and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ — the wayfarer (*ibn al-sabīl*) is named as a metaphor (*majāz*). The scholars differed about it. Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāriqī and Mujāhid said: it means the traveler cut off from his family who passes by you.

Qatādah said: It is the guest who alights with a person. He said: "We have mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest.'" [In al-Ṭabarī's Tafsīr (2/132), it reads: "let him say something good or remain silent."] And he used to say: "The right of hospitality is three nights; whatever he offers beyond that is charity."

The traveler and the guest who comes and goes are called *ibn al-sabīl* ("son of the road") because of their constant attachment to the road, just as a man who has been through the ages and nights is called "son of days and nights," and the water-bird is called "son of water" because of its constant attachment to it. Dhū al-Rummah said:

*"I came to them by a rugged path, while the Pleiades were like*
*a "son of water" hovering over the crown of the head."*

﴿and those who ask﴾: those who seek food, those who request.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥusayn, from his mother Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who asks has a right, even if he comes on a horse."

Mālik ibn Anas, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The gift of Allah to the believer is the one who asks at his door."

﴿and in [freeing] slaves﴾: this means the *mukātabūn* (slaves who have contracted to buy their freedom). Most exegetes said this. It was also said: it means ransoming captives; and it was said: it means freeing a soul and unfastening a neck.

﴿and establishes the prayer﴾: the obligatory prayer.
﴿and gives the zakāt﴾: the obligatory alms.

﴿and those who fulfill their covenant when they make it﴾: in their dealings among themselves and with people. When they promise, they fulfill; when they swear oaths, they honor them; when they speak, they tell the truth; and when they are entrusted, they return the trust.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: Whoever gives the covenant of Allah and then breaks it, Allah the Glorified will be his adversary. And whoever gives his pledge to the Prophet (ﷺ) and then betrays it, the Prophet (ﷺ) will be his adversary on the Day of Resurrection.

Regarding the grammatical case (*iʿrāb*) of *al-mūfūna* (those who fulfill), there are two opinions: al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash said it is in apposition (*ʿaṭf*) to the position (*maḥall*) of *man* in His saying ﴿but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾. *Man* is in the position of a plural, and its position is nominative, as if He said: "But the righteous are the believers and those who fulfill [their covenants]."

It was also said: it is nominative as the beginning of a sentence (*mubtadaʾ*), and the predicate is understood to be: "They are those who fulfill."

﴿and the patient﴾. There are four opinions on its accusative case (*naṣb*). Abū ʿUbayd said: it is accusative because the sentence has been lengthened, and it is a feature of Arabic that the case-endings change when the sentence is long.

Al-Kisāʾī said: it is accusative as a coordinate (*nasaq*) to His saying ﴿to relatives﴾, that is, "the patient."

Some said: the meaning is "and I mean the patient."

Khalīl ibn Aḥmad and al-Farrāʾ said: it is accusative for praise (*madḥ*). The Arabs use the accusative for praise and for blame, as though they intend to single out the one praised or blamed, and do not link it to the beginning of the sentence, so they put it in the accusative. For praise, there is His saying ﴿and those who establish the prayer﴾ (4:162). Al-Kisāʾī recited:

*"Every people obeyed the command of their guide,*
*except the Numayr, who obeyed the command of their misguider.*
*And the spearmen, though they have not stabbed anyone,*
*and those who say to the one who has a home, 'Abandon it.'"*

Abū ʿUbayda recited for Ḥuzniq ibn ʿAffān:

*"Let not my people be far away, those who are*
*the poison of the enemies and their sharp sword,*
*who alight in every battle,*
*and are the good ones at the knots of the ropes."*

As for blame, there is His saying ﴿cursed, wherever they are found, they will be seized﴾ (33:61). ʿUrwah ibn al-Ward said:

*"They give us wine, then they suffice us against the enemies of Allah, who lie and deceive."*

﴿in poverty (*al-baʾsāʾ*)﴾: this means hardship and poverty. ﴿and affliction (*al-ḍarrāʾ*)﴾: illness and disability. These two are nouns formed on the pattern *faʿlāʾ*, which has no comparative form (*afʿal*), because they are nouns and not adjectives.

﴿and at the time of battle (*ḥīna al-baʾs*)﴾: the time of fighting.

ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "When the fighting grew fierce, we would seek shelter behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the closest of us to the enemy was the one who fought most fiercely."

﴿Those are the ones who are truthful﴾: in their faith.
﴿and those are the God-conscious﴾.

Al-Qāsim narrated: Abū Dharr was asked about faith, so he recited this verse. The questioner said: "We only asked you about faith, and you tell us about righteousness." He said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about faith, and he recited this verse."

Abū Maysarah said: "He recited this verse, and whoever acts by this verse has completed righteousness."

﴿O you who believe, retaliation (*al-qiṣāṣ*) is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ (2:178). Al-Shaʿbī, al-Kalbī, Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: This verse was revealed concerning two tribes of the Arabs who fought one another in the pre-Islamic period shortly before Islam. Between them there were slain and wounds which some had not yet taken retribution for from others, until Islam came.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: They were the two tribes, al-Aws and al-Khazraj.

Ibn Kaysān said: They were Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr. He said: One of the two tribes had superiority over the other in nobility and honor. They used to marry their women without dowries. So they swore that they would kill, in retaliation for a slave among us, a free man among them; for a woman among us, a man among them; and for a man among us, two men among them. They also made their wounds double the wounds of the others, and they treated them thus in the pre-Islamic period. They brought their matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah the Exalted revealed this verse and commanded them to equality, and they agreed and submitted.

Al-Suddī and a group said: This verse was revealed concerning blood money (*diyāt*). The reason was that the people of two groups among the Arabs fought, one of them Muslim and the other a covenanted group (*muʿāhad*). So Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to reconcile them by making the blood money for women from each of the two groups a retaliation equal to the blood money for women of the other group, and the blood money for men equal to that for men, and for slaves equal to that for slaves. Then He revealed ﴿O you who believe, prescribed for you is retaliation regarding the slain﴾: "was prescribed and decreed upon you concerning the slain." [See al-Ṭabarī's Tafsīr: 2/140.]

*Al-qiṣāṣ* (retaliation) means equality and parity in lives, wounds and blood money. Its root is from *qaṣṣ al-athar*, following a trail: the one who is wronged follows what was done to him and does the same. Then He explained, saying: ﴿the free for the free, the slave for the slave, the female for the female﴾.

Mention of the ruling of the verses:

When two bloods are equal, whether they be free Muslims or Muslim slaves, or free covenanted persons or covenanted slaves, then from each category one is killed: a male if he has killed a male, a female if she has killed a female. The consensus (*ijmāʿ*) holds that a man is killed for a woman, because they are equal in sacredness, inheritance, the penalty for fornication and slander, and other matters, so they must be equal in retaliation. A free man is not killed for a slave, but he owes the slave's value, even if it reaches a third [of the blood-money], because of the difference in rank between them. A Muslim is not killed for an unbeliever. The proof for this is what

al-Shaʿbī narrated from Abū Ḥujayfah, who said: I asked ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, "Do you have anything from the Prophet (ﷺ) apart from the Qur'an?" He said: "No, by the One who split the grain and created the soul. Except that Allah the Mighty and Majestic may grant a servant understanding of His Book, and what is in this sheet." I said: "And what is in the sheet?" He said: "The blood-money (*ʿaql*), the ransom of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for an unbeliever, and a master is not to be killed for his slave, and a father is not to be killed for his son." [The first part is in both sources.] [Kitāb al-Musnad of al-Shāfiʿī: 190; al-Muṣannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzāq: 10/100, no. 18507.]

The evidence for this is what was narrated: a man named Qatādah struck his son with a sword, hitting his leg, and he bled and died. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Were it not that I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, 'A father is not to be retaliated against for his son,' I would have retaliated against you."

﴿But if anything is pardoned for him by his brother﴾: that is, he gives up and forgives him for what is obligatory upon him, which is retaliation.

It was narrated from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) that he killed three men for one in a case of deliberate murder.

This is the view of most exegetes, who said: pardon means accepting the blood-money in a case of deliberate murder. Al-Suddī said: it means that some remainder of his brother's blood-money, or of the compensation for his wound, remains for him.

﴿then there should be a following up in a fair manner﴾: that is, then it is incumbent upon him to follow up.

﴿and payment to him with good conduct﴾: The claimant is commanded to demand in a fair manner, and to pursue the right owed to him from the one bound to him, without demanding an increase or imposing what Allah has not made obligatory for him, or being harsh with him. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever adds a camel to the camels of the blood-money and their obligations, it is from the practice of the Jāhiliyyah."
[Jāmiʿ al-Bayān of al-Ṭabarī: 2/150.]

The ruling of the verse:

Know that the kinds of killing are three: deliberate (*ʿamd*), quasi-deliberate (*shibh al-ʿamd*), and mistaken (*khaṭaʾ*).

Deliberate killing is when one intends to strike with something that usually causes death, such as an iron tool, a large piece of wood, a big stone, or the like, or burning him, drowning him, strangling him with a rope, throwing him from a roof or into a well, and similar things that are intentionally done to kill. For this there is retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*) or blood-money (*diyah*).

The blood-money for a Muslim is a thousand dinars, or twelve thousand dirhams in silver, or one hundred camels, of which forty are pregnant (with their young in their bellies), thirty are three-year-olds (*ḥiqqah*), and thirty are four-year-olds (*jadhaʿah*). The basis for a man is camels; the blood-money for women is half of that.

As for quasi-deliberate killing: it is when one intends to strike with something that usually does not cause death, such as a small pebble, a small stick, a slap, a push, a punch, or a sword-blow struck deliberately, or what is similar to that, and the person dies from it. In this case the blood-money is required and is aggravated (*mughallaẓah*) upon the paternal kin (*ʿāqilah*), as we described for the blood-money of deliberate killing.

As for mistaken killing: it is when one intends one thing and misses, hitting something else. Like a man who shoots at a target or at game, and the arrow misses and falls upon a person and kills him. This is pure mistake, and in it there is a lighter blood-money upon the paternal kin, in sixty-three portions (*akhmās*): twenty bint makhāḍ (she-camel in her second year), twenty bint labūn (in her third year), twenty ibn labūn, twenty khinaq (in her fourth year), and twenty jadhaʿah. Silver or gold is not specified, as the camels mentioned are reduced by the pardon and the blood-money.

﴿a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾: this is because Allah the Exalted prescribed for the people of the Torah, in cases of life and wounds, that they must retaliate, and not take blood-money, and not pardon. And for the people of the Gospel, that they must pardon, and not retaliate, and not take blood-money.

So Allah the Exalted gave this ummah the choice between retaliation, blood-money, and pardon.

As Saʿīd ibn Abī Saʿīd al-Maqburī narrated from Abū Shurayḥ: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Then you, O Khuzāʿah, have killed this slain man from Hudhayl, and I, by Allah, am his payer of blood-money. Whoever kills a person after this, his family have a choice between two options: if they wish, they may retaliate, and if they wish, they may take the blood-money."

﴿Whoever transgresses after that﴾: he wrongs and exceeds the limit.

﴿after that﴾: it was said: after taking the blood-money. Al-Ḥasan said: "In the pre-Islamic period, if a man killed someone he would flee to his people, and his people would come and make peace by paying blood-money, and that is the transgression."

﴿then for him there is a painful punishment﴾: he is killed in this world, and is not pardoned. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I will not pardon a man who kills after taking the blood-money from him." And in the Hereafter there is the punishment of the Fire. And this verse is evidence that the killer does not become an unbeliever and does not remain eternally in the Fire, because Allah the Exalted…

He addressed them, saying: "O you who have believed, prescribed for you is qisas (retaliation)." There is no disagreement that qisas applies in cases of deliberate killing, and so the name of faith is not removed from the one who commits this grave sin. In the latter part of the verse He says: ﴿But if he is pardoned by his brother [something]﴾, and so He calls the killer the brother of the one killed. He also says: ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy﴾, and both of these are specific to the believers, not the disbelievers.

It is related that Masruq was asked: "Is there repentance for the killer?" He said: "I will not close a door that Allah has opened."

﴿And for you in qisas is life﴾: that is, survival, because when a person knows that if he kills he will himself be killed, he refrains and restrains himself from killing. Thus there is life in it for the one who intends to kill him, and life for the one who would have been killed. For this reason it is said in the proverb: "Killing reduces killing."

Qatadah said: "How many a man has intended a calamity, and had it not been for fear of qisas he would have committed it. But Allah, exalted is He, restrains His servants from one another." This is the view of most of the exegetes.

Al-Suddi said: "They used to kill one man for a single man, two men, ten, or a hundred. When they limited the killing to one for one, there was life in that." It has also been said: He meant the life in the Hereafter, because whoever is retaliated against in this world will be spared retaliation in the Hereafter, whereas whoever is not retaliated against in this world will be retaliated against in the Hereafter. The "life" then means his safety from retaliation in the Hereafter.

Abu al-Jawza' recited: ﴿And for you in qisas is life﴾ and meant by it the Qur'an, that in it is life for the hearts.

He said: ﴿O people of understanding﴾: that is, O possessors of intellects.

﴿That you may become righteous﴾: that is, that you may avoid killing out of fear of retaliation.

Al-Tha'alibi's commentary (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 177–179 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west.﴾ Hamzah and Hafs read *laysa al-birra* with the *ra'* in the accusative (*naṣb*). The rest read it in the nominative (*raf'*). Whoever reads *al-birru* in the nominative makes it the subject of *laysa* (the copula "is not"), and takes its predicate to be in the phrase *an tuwallū*. The meaning is: "Righteousness is not your turning [your faces]." Whoever reads it in the accusative makes *an* and what follows it in the position of the nominative, as the subject of *laysa*. The meaning is: "Your turning your faces is not all of righteousness." This is like His saying ﴿Their argument was only that they said﴾ (45:25), and His saying ﴿so the outcome for both of them was that they were in the Fire﴾ (59:17).

Hārūn reported from ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that they both recited it as: *Laysa al-birru bi-an tuwallū wujūhakum* ("Righteousness is not in your turning your faces").

The exegetes differed concerning this verse:

Some said: Allah meant by this verse the Jews and the Christians. The Jews used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) in the west, and the Christians facing the east. Each group claimed that righteousness lay in that. So Allah informed them that righteousness is other than their religion and their deeds, and He explained what it is in this verse. Those who held this view include Qatadah, al-Rabīʿ, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān and ʿAwf al-Aʿrābī.

Others said: The verse refers to the believers. A man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about righteousness, so Allah revealed this verse, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned that man and recited it to him.

Before the obligatory duties (*farāʾiḍ*) were prescribed, a man who testified that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger, and who prayed toward whatever direction, and died in that state, was granted Paradise. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) migrated, the obligatory duties were revealed, the limits (*ḥudūd*) were set, and the *qiblah* was turned toward the Kaʿbah. Then Allah revealed this verse and said: "Righteousness is not all that you pray and do other than that."

﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah.﴾ The *man* (in the sense of "one who") is the subject, and the *birr* (righteousness) is the predicate, and it is a verb-type phrase, since one does not say "righteousness is Zayd." The scholars differed about how to understand the verse:

Some said: Since *man* stands in the place of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), it is taken to be a hidden noun in the sense of *birr*, as if he said: "But righteousness is the belief in Allah." The Arabs make a noun the predicate of a verb, as in their saying: "The truly righteous one is the one who keeps ties of kinship and gives charity in secret." They mean: keeping ties of kinship and concealing charity. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Salamah held this view. Al-Farrāʾ recited this verse of poetry:

*"By your life, the youths are not those whose beards grow,*
*but the youth is every generous man."*

So he made the growth of the beard the predicate of "youth."

It was also said: The meaning is: "But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah and is independent of people," like their saying: "Generosity is Ḥātim, bravery is ʿAntarah, poetry is Zuhayr," meaning the generosity of Ḥātim, the bravery of ʿAntarah, and the poetry of Zuhayr. And the Arabs say: "The Banū Fulān—the road tramples them," meaning the people of the road. Allah the Exalted said ﴿and ask the town﴾ (12:82), and said ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾ (31:28). Al-Nābighah al-Jaʿdī said:

*"How can we be connected to one whose majesty is like that of Abu Marḥab?"*

That is, like the majesty of Abū Marḥab. Qaṭrub, al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj also held this view.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: The meaning is: "But the pious (*al-bār*) is one who believes in Allah," like His saying ﴿and the final outcome is for piety (*al-taqwā*)﴾ (20:132), meaning the one who is pious.

It was also said: The meaning of "one of righteousness" is "one who believes in Allah." This was related by al-Zajjāj, like His saying ﴿they have degrees with Allah﴾ (3:163), meaning "possessors of degrees."

Al-Mubarrad said: If I were one of those who read the Qur'an, I would have read *lākinna al-birra man āmana bi-llāh* with the *bāʾ* of *al-birr* vowelled with a *fatḥah*. The Arabs say: "a *barr* man and a *bārr* man," and the plural is *barrah* and *abrār*. *Al-birr* means kindness and beneficence, and *al-birr* also means truthfulness. Here *al-birr* means faith and piety, and this is what is meant in this verse, as indicated by His saying ﴿who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾.

﴿and the angels﴾ all of them.
﴿and the Book﴾ [i.e., the books]. ﴿and the prophets﴾ all of them.

﴿and gives wealth, despite love for it﴾. The exegetes differed about the interpretation of this phrase:

Most of the exegetes said: The pronoun in *ḥubbihi* ("love for it") refers to wealth, meaning: he gives wealth while he is healthy and loves it, and is attached to it. This is supported by the statement of Ibn Masʿūd about this verse, who said: "It is that you bequeath it while you are healthy, desiring life and fearing poverty, and you do not delay, until when the throat rattles you say, 'To so-and-so such-and-such.'" Some transmitted this as a hadith raised to the Prophet.

It was also said: The pronoun refers to Allah the Mighty and Majestic, meaning the love of Allah, glorified is He.

Al-Ḥusayn ibn Abī al-Faḍl said: "It refers to love of giving." It was also said: The pronoun refers to the giver, meaning the love of the giver.

﴿to relatives, orphans﴾: the people of kinship.

It was related from Umm Rābiḥ bint Ṣalīḥ, from Sulaymān ibn ʿĀmir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Charity to a poor person is one charity, but to one who is a relative it is two, because it is both charity and maintaining kinship."

Al-Zuhrī, from Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from his mother Umm Kulthūm bint ʿUqbah ibn Abī Muʿayṭ, said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The best charity is to a relative who harbors enmity (*al-kāshiḥ*)." *Al-kāshiḥ* is the enemy who conceals his enmity and keeps it hidden in his side (*kashḥ*), that is, his inner self.

Sulaymān ibn Yasār, from Maymūnah, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), said: "I freed a slave-girl of mine, and I entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and told him of her manumission. He said: 'May Allah reward you. But if you had given her to your maternal uncles, it would have been greater for your reward.'"

﴿and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ — the wayfarer (*ibn al-sabīl*) is named as a metaphor (*majāz*). The scholars differed about it. Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāriqī and Mujāhid said: it means the traveler cut off from his family who passes by you.

Qatādah said: It is the guest who alights with a person. He said: "We have mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest.'" [In al-Ṭabarī's Tafsīr (2/132), it reads: "let him say something good or remain silent."] And he used to say: "The right of hospitality is three nights; whatever he offers beyond that is charity."

The traveler and the guest who comes and goes are called *ibn al-sabīl* ("son of the road") because of their constant attachment to the road, just as a man who has been through the ages and nights is called "son of days and nights," and the water-bird is called "son of water" because of its constant attachment to it. Dhū al-Rummah said:

*"I came to them by a rugged path, while the Pleiades were like*
*a "son of water" hovering over the crown of the head."*

﴿and those who ask﴾: those who seek food, those who request.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥusayn, from his mother Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥusayn, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who asks has a right, even if he comes on a horse."

Mālik ibn Anas, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The gift of Allah to the believer is the one who asks at his door."

﴿and in [freeing] slaves﴾: this means the *mukātabūn* (slaves who have contracted to buy their freedom). Most exegetes said this. It was also said: it means ransoming captives; and it was said: it means freeing a soul and unfastening a neck.

﴿and establishes the prayer﴾: the obligatory prayer.
﴿and gives the zakāt﴾: the obligatory alms.

﴿and those who fulfill their covenant when they make it﴾: in their dealings among themselves and with people. When they promise, they fulfill; when they swear oaths, they honor them; when they speak, they tell the truth; and when they are entrusted, they return the trust.

Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: Whoever gives the covenant of Allah and then breaks it, Allah the Glorified will be his adversary. And whoever gives his pledge to the Prophet (ﷺ) and then betrays it, the Prophet (ﷺ) will be his adversary on the Day of Resurrection.

Regarding the grammatical case (*iʿrāb*) of *al-mūfūna* (those who fulfill), there are two opinions: al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash said it is in apposition (*ʿaṭf*) to the position (*maḥall*) of *man* in His saying ﴿but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾. *Man* is in the position of a plural, and its position is nominative, as if He said: "But the righteous are the believers and those who fulfill [their covenants]."

It was also said: it is nominative as the beginning of a sentence (*mubtadaʾ*), and the predicate is understood to be: "They are those who fulfill."

﴿and the patient﴾. There are four opinions on its accusative case (*naṣb*). Abū ʿUbayd said: it is accusative because the sentence has been lengthened, and it is a feature of Arabic that the case-endings change when the sentence is long.

Al-Kisāʾī said: it is accusative as a coordinate (*nasaq*) to His saying ﴿to relatives﴾, that is, "the patient."

Some said: the meaning is "and I mean the patient."

Khalīl ibn Aḥmad and al-Farrāʾ said: it is accusative for praise (*madḥ*). The Arabs use the accusative for praise and for blame, as though they intend to single out the one praised or blamed, and do not link it to the beginning of the sentence, so they put it in the accusative. For praise, there is His saying ﴿and those who establish the prayer﴾ (4:162). Al-Kisāʾī recited:

*"Every people obeyed the command of their guide,*
*except the Numayr, who obeyed the command of their misguider.*
*And the spearmen, though they have not stabbed anyone,*
*and those who say to the one who has a home, 'Abandon it.'"*

Abū ʿUbayda recited for Ḥuzniq ibn ʿAffān:

*"Let not my people be far away, those who are*
*the poison of the enemies and their sharp sword,*
*who alight in every battle,*
*and are the good ones at the knots of the ropes."*

As for blame, there is His saying ﴿cursed, wherever they are found, they will be seized﴾ (33:61). ʿUrwah ibn al-Ward said:

*"They give us wine, then they suffice us against the enemies of Allah, who lie and deceive."*

﴿in poverty (*al-baʾsāʾ*)﴾: this means hardship and poverty. ﴿and affliction (*al-ḍarrāʾ*)﴾: illness and disability. These two are nouns formed on the pattern *faʿlāʾ*, which has no comparative form (*afʿal*), because they are nouns and not adjectives.

﴿and at the time of battle (*ḥīna al-baʾs*)﴾: the time of fighting.

ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "When the fighting grew fierce, we would seek shelter behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the closest of us to the enemy was the one who fought most fiercely."

﴿Those are the ones who are truthful﴾: in their faith.
﴿and those are the God-conscious﴾.

Al-Qāsim narrated: Abū Dharr was asked about faith, so he recited this verse. The questioner said: "We only asked you about faith, and you tell us about righteousness." He said: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him about faith, and he recited this verse."

Abū Maysarah said: "He recited this verse, and whoever acts by this verse has completed righteousness."

﴿O you who believe, retaliation (*al-qiṣāṣ*) is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾ (2:178). Al-Shaʿbī, al-Kalbī, Qatādah, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: This verse was revealed concerning two tribes of the Arabs who fought one another in the pre-Islamic period shortly before Islam. Between them there were slain and wounds which some had not yet taken retribution for from others, until Islam came.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: They were the two tribes, al-Aws and al-Khazraj.

Ibn Kaysān said: They were Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr. He said: One of the two tribes had superiority over the other in nobility and honor. They used to marry their women without dowries. So they swore that they would kill, in retaliation for a slave among us, a free man among them; for a woman among us, a man among them; and for a man among us, two men among them. They also made their wounds double the wounds of the others, and they treated them thus in the pre-Islamic period. They brought their matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah the Exalted revealed this verse and commanded them to equality, and they agreed and submitted.

Al-Suddī and a group said: This verse was revealed concerning blood money (*diyāt*). The reason was that the people of two groups among the Arabs fought, one of them Muslim and the other a covenanted group (*muʿāhad*). So Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to reconcile them by making the blood money for women from each of the two groups a retaliation equal to the blood money for women of the other group, and the blood money for men equal to that for men, and for slaves equal to that for slaves. Then He revealed ﴿O you who believe, prescribed for you is retaliation regarding the slain﴾: "was prescribed and decreed upon you concerning the slain." [See al-Ṭabarī's Tafsīr: 2/140.]

*Al-qiṣāṣ* (retaliation) means equality and parity in lives, wounds and blood money. Its root is from *qaṣṣ al-athar*, following a trail: the one who is wronged follows what was done to him and does the same. Then He explained, saying: ﴿the free for the free, the slave for the slave, the female for the female﴾.

Mention of the ruling of the verses:

When two bloods are equal, whether they be free Muslims or Muslim slaves, or free covenanted persons or covenanted slaves, then from each category one is killed: a male if he has killed a male, a female if she has killed a female. The consensus (*ijmāʿ*) holds that a man is killed for a woman, because they are equal in sacredness, inheritance, the penalty for fornication and slander, and other matters, so they must be equal in retaliation. A free man is not killed for a slave, but he owes the slave's value, even if it reaches a third [of the blood-money], because of the difference in rank between them. A Muslim is not killed for an unbeliever. The proof for this is what

al-Shaʿbī narrated from Abū Ḥujayfah, who said: I asked ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, "Do you have anything from the Prophet (ﷺ) apart from the Qur'an?" He said: "No, by the One who split the grain and created the soul. Except that Allah the Mighty and Majestic may grant a servant understanding of His Book, and what is in this sheet." I said: "And what is in the sheet?" He said: "The blood-money (*ʿaql*), the ransom of captives, and that a Muslim is not to be killed for an unbeliever, and a master is not to be killed for his slave, and a father is not to be killed for his son." [The first part is in both sources.] [Kitāb al-Musnad of al-Shāfiʿī: 190; al-Muṣannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzāq: 10/100, no. 18507.]

The evidence for this is what was narrated: a man named Qatādah struck his son with a sword, hitting his leg, and he bled and died. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Were it not that I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, 'A father is not to be retaliated against for his son,' I would have retaliated against you."

﴿But if anything is pardoned for him by his brother﴾: that is, he gives up and forgives him for what is obligatory upon him, which is retaliation.

It was narrated from ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) that he killed three men for one in a case of deliberate murder.

This is the view of most exegetes, who said: pardon means accepting the blood-money in a case of deliberate murder. Al-Suddī said: it means that some remainder of his brother's blood-money, or of the compensation for his wound, remains for him.

﴿then there should be a following up in a fair manner﴾: that is, then it is incumbent upon him to follow up.

﴿and payment to him with good conduct﴾: The claimant is commanded to demand in a fair manner, and to pursue the right owed to him from the one bound to him, without demanding an increase or imposing what Allah has not made obligatory for him, or being harsh with him. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever adds a camel to the camels of the blood-money and their obligations, it is from the practice of the Jāhiliyyah."
[Jāmiʿ al-Bayān of al-Ṭabarī: 2/150.]

The ruling of the verse:

Know that the kinds of killing are three: deliberate (*ʿamd*), quasi-deliberate (*shibh al-ʿamd*), and mistaken (*khaṭaʾ*).

Deliberate killing is when one intends to strike with something that usually causes death, such as an iron tool, a large piece of wood, a big stone, or the like, or burning him, drowning him, strangling him with a rope, throwing him from a roof or into a well, and similar things that are intentionally done to kill. For this there is retaliation (*qiṣāṣ*) or blood-money (*diyah*).

The blood-money for a Muslim is a thousand dinars, or twelve thousand dirhams in silver, or one hundred camels, of which forty are pregnant (with their young in their bellies), thirty are three-year-olds (*ḥiqqah*), and thirty are four-year-olds (*jadhaʿah*).
