He said: "If you wish, fast; and if you wish, break your fast." [48] [Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/531, no. 1662; Sunan al-Nasa'i: 4/186.]

And from 'Urwah ibn Abi Qurrah, from Hamzah ibn 'Amr, that he said: "O Messenger of God, I find in myself strength to fast while travelling; is there any sin upon me?" He said: "It is a concession from God, the Mighty and Majestic; whoever takes it, it is good, and whoever wishes to fast, there is no sin upon him." [49] [al-Majmu' of al-Nawawi: 6/264; Sahih Muslim: 3/145.]

As for his saying (ﷺ): "It is not righteousness to fast while travelling," the complete report indicates its interpretation, which is what Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by a man in the shade of a tree who was being sprinkled with water, and he said: "What is wrong with this companion of yours?" They said: "O Messenger of God, he is fasting." He said: "It is not righteousness that you fast while travelling; rather, take the concession of God which He has granted you and accept it." Likewise is the interpretation of his saying (ﷺ): "The fasting one during travel is like the one breaking the fast while resident." [50] [Sunan al-Nasa'i: 4/176; Sahih Ibn Khuzaymah: 3/259.]

It is supported by the report of Mujahid from Ibn 'Umar: that he passed by a man pouring water on his face while fasting, and he said: "Break your fast, woe to you; for I see that if you die in this state you will enter the Fire."

What gathers these reports and supports what we have said is what Ayyub narrated from 'Urwah and Salim: that they were with 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, who was then governor of Medina. They discussed fasting while travelling. Salim said: "Ibn 'Umar did not fast while travelling." 'Urwah said: "'A'ishah used to fast while travelling." Salim said: "I only narrate from Ibn 'Umar." 'Urwah said: "I only narrate from 'A'ishah." Their voices rose, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "O God, forgive..." — [and he said]: "If it is easy, fast; and if it is difficult, break your fast."

Then they differed regarding which is preferable among them. Some said: fasting is better; this is the view of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Anas, Ibrahim and Mujahid.

It is reported that Anas ibn Malik ordered a servant of his to fast while travelling, and it was said to him concerning this verse; he said: "It was revealed while we were then travelling hungry and dismounting without being satisfied; so whoever breaks the fast does so by concession, and whoever fasts, fasting is better."

Others said: breaking the fast is preferable, because of what Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated from his father, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to Makkah in the year of the Conquest in Ramadan and fasted until he reached Kura' al-Ghamim; the people fasted too. It reached him that the people found fasting hard, so he called for a cup of water and drank after the 'asr prayer while the people watched; some people broke their fast and some continued fasting. It reached him that the people had fasted, and he said: "Those are the disobedient." [51] [Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 2/106; Sunan al-Nasa'i: 4/177.]

'Asim al-Ahwal narrated from [Buraid] al-'Ijli, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ); some of us were fasting and some were not. We alighted on a hot day and made shades; the fasting ones collapsed, while the ones breaking their fast stood up and watered the riding animals. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Today the ones breaking their fast have taken the reward." [52] [al-Majmu' of al-Nawawi: 6/264; Sahih al-Bukhari: 3/224.]

Shu'bah narrated from Mu'alla, from Yusuf ibn al-Hakam, who said: I asked Ibn 'Umar about fasting while travelling. He said: "What do you think if you gave charity to a man and he returned it to you; would you not be angry?" He said: "Yes." He said: "It is a charity from God, the Mighty and Majestic, which He has given to you." The distances for which breaking the fast is permitted are sixteen farsakhs or more.

﴿God desires for you ease﴾ — when He granted concession in journeys to the sick and the traveller.

﴿And He does not desire for you hardship﴾ — Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read al-'usr and al-yusr with heavy vowels throughout the Qur'an. The rest read them with light vowels, and both are good dialects. There is no proof for the Qadariyyah in this verse, because it is built upon the beginning of the discussion concerning the obligation of fasting; it is specific in its rulings to the people of Islam.

﴿And that you may complete the period﴾ — Abu Bakr and Ruways read it with a shaddah on the mim. The rest read it without a shaddah, and this is the preferred reading, because of His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 3]. The waw in His saying ﴿wa-litukmilu﴾ is the waw of coordination (wa al-nasq), and the lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay); its sense is: "and He desires that you complete the period."

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: God did that so that it would be easy for you, and that you might complete the period.

'Ata' said: that you might complete the number of days of the month.

The rest of the exegetes said: that you may complete the period of what you broke the fast of during your illness and your travel, when you have recovered and are resident, and make it up.

﴿And that you may magnify God﴾ — that you may glorify God.

﴿For that He has guided you﴾ — to His religion, and has granted you success, and provided you with the month of Ramadan, lightened for you, and singled you out with it above the rest of the peoples of other religions.

Most scholars said: it means the takbir on the night of the 'Id al-Fitr. Al-Shafi'i said: it was reported from Ibn al-Musayyab and 'Urwah ibn Salamah that they used to say the takbir on the night of the 'Id al-Fitr and would recite the takbir aloud. He said: and he compared [......] [a word not legible in the manuscript] to its sacrifice.

Ibn 'Abbas and Zayd ibn Aslam said: in this verse it is an obligation upon the Muslims, when the crescent of Shawwal is seen, to say the takbir until the imam comes out on the road and in the mosque; when the imam arrives, they cease, and do not say the takbir except after his takbir. The preferred form of the takbir is three times in succession.

﴿And that you may be thankful﴾ — for His blessings.

﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ — the exegetes differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and his companions when they had relations with their wives during the nights of Ramadan; their story will come later, God willing.

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih, from him [Ibn 'Abbas], who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "How does our Lord hear our supplication, when you claim that between us and the heaven is a distance of five hundred years, and the thickness of each heaven is likewise?" Then this verse was revealed.

Al-Hasan said: the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) asked the Messenger of God: "Where is our Lord?" So God revealed this verse.

Qatadah and 'Ata' said: when His saying was revealed: ﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will answer you﴾, they said: "O Messenger of God, how should we call upon our Lord, and when should we call upon Him?" So God revealed this verse.

Al-Dahhak said: some of the Companions asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Is our Lord near so that we may whisper to Him, or far?" So he asked his Lord, and God revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you, O Muhammad, concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 183–187 (part 3 of 4):

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: there is an ellipsis here, as if it were: "He knows what they do, and whether they are near to Him in knowledge."

The people of allusion (ahl al-isharah) said: the removal of the intermediary is a manifestation of power.

﴿I respond to the prayer of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾; ﴿so let them respond to Me﴾, meaning: let them obey Me. It is said that ajaba and istajaba have the same meaning.

Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi said:

"A caller called out, 'O you who answer to generosity,' but no one answered him at that moment."

Abu Raja' al-Khurasani said: it means "let them call on Me to respond." In the language, it means obedience and giving what is asked. It is said: "The sky answered with rain, and the earth answered with plants," as if the earth asked the sky for rain and it gave, and the sky asked the earth and it gave.

Zuhayr said:

"A rain-cloud from the high ones, whose rain-bearing clouds answered [...] (an illegible word; the likely reading is what we have set down)."

He means: its mountains gathered the rain-bearing clouds when it asked for rain, and they gave it that.

Response from God is giving, and response from the servant is obedience.

﴿And let them believe in Me, that they may be guided﴾, meaning: so that they may be rightly guided. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿I respond to the prayer of the supplicant﴾ and His saying ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾, when many people supplicate and are not answered? We say: the scholars differed regarding the meaning and interpretation of the two verses.

Some of them said: the meaning of "supplication" here is obedience, and the meaning of "response" is reward, as if He said: "I will respond to the prayer of the supplicant with reward if he obeys Me."

Others said: the meaning of the two verses is specific, although their wording is general. Their implied sense is: I respond to the prayer of the supplicant if I wish; I respond to the prayer of the supplicant when it accords with the decree; I respond to the prayer of the supplicant when he does not ask for something impossible; I respond to the prayer of the supplicant when the response is good for him. What supports this is what

Abu al-Mutawakkil narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim calls upon God, Mighty and Majestic, with a supplication that contains no severing of ties of kinship and no sin, except that God gives him one of three things: either his supplication is hastened for him, or it is stored up for him in the Hereafter, or He averts from him an evil equal to it." They said: "O Messenger of God, then we will increase (our supplications)." He said: "God is more abundant (in giving)." [53] [54]

Others said: it is general, and the verse contains nothing more than the answering of the supplication; as for granting the desired end and fulfilling the need, that is not mentioned in the verse. A master may respond to his servant, and a father to his son, yet not give him his request. So the response is certain without doubt upon the occurrence of supplication, because His saying "I respond" and "it is responded to" is a report, and a report cannot be contested, for if it were abrogated the one reporting would be a liar, and God is exalted above that. The evidence for this interpretation is what

Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever has a door opened to him in supplication, the doors of response will be opened to him. God revealed to Dawud (ﷺ): Tell the wrongdoers not to call upon Me, for I have made it binding upon Myself to respond to whoever calls upon Me, and if I respond to the wrongdoers I will curse them." [55]

It was also said: God responds to the supplication of the believer immediately, but He delays granting his desire so that He may hear his voice. What supports this is what

Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a servant supplicates God while He loves him, and He says: 'O Jibril, fulfil the need of this servant of Mine, but delay it, for I love to keep hearing his voice.' And indeed a servant supplicates God while He hates him, and He says to Jibril: 'Fulfil the need of My servant, though his sincerity is lacking, and hasten it, for I dislike to hear his voice.'"

We have also been told [on the authority of Yahya, the sacrificed one of God] that he said: I asked the Lord of Might in a dream, "O Lord, how often do I call upon You and You do not respond to me?" He said: "O Yahya, I love to hear your voice." [56]

Some said: supplication has etiquettes and conditions which are the causes of response and the attainment of one's wish. Whoever observes them and perfects them is among the people of response, and whoever neglects them and falls short in them [is among those ... ] (illegible words) in supplication.

It is related that Ibrahim ibn Adham was asked: "Why is it that we call upon God and He does not respond to us?" He said: "Because you have known God but have not obeyed Him; you have known the Messenger but have not followed his sunnah; you have known the Qur'an but have not acted upon what is in it; you have eaten the blessings of God but have not rendered their thanks; you have known Paradise but have not sought it; you have known the Fire but have not fled from it; you have known Satan but have not fought him, and have agreed with him; you have known death but have not prepared for it; you have buried the dead but have not taken heed from them; you have left your own faults and occupied yourselves with the faults of people."

On His saying ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in unto your wives on the night of the fast﴾, the verse:

The exegetes said: At the beginning of the matter, when a man broke his fast, eating, drinking and intercourse were lawful for him until the late evening prayer ('isha') or until he slept before it. But if he prayed the late evening prayer or slept before praying and had not broken his fast, eating and drinking were forbidden to him, and this remained so until the same time the following year. [1]

Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) had intercourse with his wife after he had prayed the late evening prayer. When he had washed himself, he began to weep and blame himself, and he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, I seek pardon from God and from you for this sin of mine. I returned to my wife after I had prayed the late evening prayer, and I smelled a pleasant scent, and my soul adorned it for me, so I had intercourse with my wife. Do you find for me any concession?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You were not worthy of this, O 'Umar." Then men stood up and confessed what they had done after the late evening prayer. So there was revealed concerning 'Umar and his companions: ﴿It is made lawful for you﴾, that is, permitted and allowed for you, ﴿on the night of the fast﴾, in the night of the fast, ﴿intercourse (al-rafath)﴾.

Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read: "al-Rufuth" ﴿to your wives﴾. Rafath and rufuth are euphemisms for intercourse. Ibn 'Abbas said: God, the Living, the Generous, employs euphemism; so whatever God mentions in the Qur'an of touching, contact, consummation, entering, or rafath, He means by it intercourse.

The poet said:

"We spent that time among delights, and every pleasure was other than rafath."

Al-Qutaybi said: al-rafath is speaking openly of what ought to be expressed euphemistically, such as mention of marriage; its root meaning is obscenity and foul speech. Al-'Ajjaj said:

"And many a flock of pilgrims restrained from idle talk and from speaking of rafath."

Al-Zajjaj said: al-rafath is a comprehensive word for everything men desire from women.

The poet said:

"And she adorns with pleasant speech in narration, while they are shy of the rafath of men."

﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾: they are a dwelling for you, and you are a dwelling for them. This was said by most of the exegetes. Its parallel is His saying ﴿And We made the night a garment﴾ [78:10], meaning a dwelling, and its evidence is His saying ﴿And made of it its mate, that he might find rest with her﴾ [7:189].

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: al-libas is the undergarment that is next to the body among garments. Each of the spouses is therefore called a garment, because they are naked when sleeping, come together under one garment, and each one's body is joined to the body of the other, until each becomes to the other like the garment next to the body.

The poet of Banu Ja'dah said:

"When the bedfellow bends her neck, she bends, and she is a garment."

He alluded by garment to their coming together naked in one bed. What confirms this interpretation is the statement of al-Rabi' ibn Anas on this verse: "They are a quilt for you, and you are a quilt for them."

Some said: whatever covers a thing and conceals it is called libas. It is permissible that each of them is a covering for the other, protecting from what is unlawful, and also a covering in what passes between them of intercourse from the eyes of people. What supports this is the statement of Abu Zayd on His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾: he said, "for copulation."

Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: a woman is called your garment, your bedding, and your wrapper. A man said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab:

"Would that you conveyed to Abu Hafs a message: may I be ransomed for you by a brother trusted, my wrapper."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: that is, my wives.

﴿God knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾: you were betraying and wronging yourselves after the late evening prayer during the nights of fasting.

﴿So He turned to you﴾: He pardoned you.

﴿And pardoned you﴾: He erased your sins.

﴿Now﴾: this word combines two times, past and future.

﴿Lie with them﴾: have intercourse with them lawfully. Intercourse was called "contact" (mubasharah) because each of the two touches the skin of the other.

﴿And seek what God has prescribed for you﴾: that is, do it. The common reading, which is sound, is "wa-ibtaghu." Ibtaghu means to seek, as one says: yabghi al-shay' yabghihi bughyah and bughan, and ibtaghahu yabtaghihi ibtighaa' — to seek it. ﴿What God has prescribed for you﴾: what God has decreed for you. It was said: it is written in the Preserved Tablet.

Most of the exegetes said: this means offspring. Mujahid said: seek offspring; if this one does not give birth, then that one.

Ibn Zayd said: seek what God has made lawful for you of intercourse.

Qatadah said: seek the concession that has been prescribed for you.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾ means the Night of Power. Abu al-Jawza' narrated the same from Ibn 'Abbas. The sayings most consistent with the apparent meaning of the verse are the view of those who interpreted it as offspring, because it follows His saying ﴿so now lie with them﴾, which is a command of permission and recommendation, like His saying (ﷺ): "Marry, so that you may multiply, for I will boast of you before the nations on the Day of Resurrection, even of the miscarried child." [57] [58]

The people of the outward meaning (ahl al-zahir) said: it is a command of obligation and necessity. What supports this is what

Ziyad ibn Maymun narrated from Anas ibn Malik: a woman called al-Hawla', a perfumer from the people of Madinah, came to 'A'ishah and said: "O Mother of the Believers, my husband, so-and-so, I adorn myself for him every night and perfume myself, as if I were a bride brought in to him. When he retires to his bed, I enter upon him under his quilt, seeking thereby the pleasure of God, Mighty and Majestic, but he turns his face away from me; I see that he has come to hate me." She said: "Sit until the Prophet (ﷺ) enters." While they were thus, the Prophet (ﷺ) entered and said: "What is this scent I smell? Has al-Hawla' come to you? Have you bought anything from her?" 'A'ishah said: "No, by God, O Messenger of God." Al-Hawla' related her story. He said to her: "Go and listen to him and obey him." She said: "I will do so, O Messenger of God. But what is my reward?" He said: "No woman raises anything in her husband's house and places it in a place, seeking reform, except that God records for her a good deed, erases a bad deed, and raises her a degree. No woman conceives from her husband, except that she has the reward of one who stands in prayer and fasts by day and fights in the way of God. No woman goes into labour except that for each pang she has the reward of freeing a soul, and for each suckling the reward of freeing a neck. When she weans her child, a caller from heaven calls to her: 'O woman, you have been relieved of the work of the past; begin afresh in what remains.'" [58]

'A'ishah said: "God has given women much good; so what about you, O men?" The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed, then said: "No man takes the hand of his wife, seeking to be intimate with her, except that he is clothed with light and has a good deed. If he embraces her, he has ten good deeds; if he kisses her, he has twenty; and if he approaches her, it is better for him than the world and what is in it. When he rises to wash, no water passes over any part of his body except that a sin is erased from him, and he is given, by his washing, something better than the world and what is in it. God, Mighty and Majestic, boasts to the angels, saying: 'Look at My servant who rose on a cold night to wash from impurity, certain that I am his Lord; I call you to witness that I have forgiven him.'" [59] [Not found in the sources.]

﴿Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾: it was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar, and his name is disputed. Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: Abu Sirmah al-Bara' Qays ibn Sirmah. 'Ikrimah and al-Suddi said: Abu Qays ibn Sirmah. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: Sirmah ibn Iyas. Al-Kalbi said: Abu Qays Sirmah ibn Anas ibn Abi Sirmah ibn Malik ibn 'Adi al-Najjar. That was because he spent his day working on his land while fasting. When evening came he returned to his family with dates and said: "Serve the food." His wife wanted to feed him a hot evening meal, and began preparing a hot porridge for him. In the early period of fasting, whoever prayed the late evening prayer or slept became forbidden to eat, drink, and have intercourse. When she had finished his food, she found that he had fallen asleep, and he was exhausted. She woke him, but he disliked disobeying God and His Messenger, and refused to eat. He woke up fasting and weary, and before midday he fainted. When he recovered, he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When the Messenger of God saw him, he said: "O Abu Qays, what is wrong with you? You have become wretched." He said: "I spent yesterday among the palm trees and I spent the whole day carrying loads of earth until evening. I came, and my wife wanted to feed me something hot, but she delayed for me, so I slept. They woke me, but the food and drink had already been forbidden to me. So I spent the night hungry, and the fast has exhausted me." The Messenger of God was saddened by this, and God revealed: ﴿Eat and drink﴾, that is, in the nights of fasting, ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾, that is, the brightness of day and its light from the darkness and gloom of night. So said the exegetes. The poet said:

"The white thread at the time of dawn has broken forth, and the black thread is the color of the night, gathered."

It was called so by way of comparison to a thread, because of the beginning of light and darkness and their extension.

Abu Dawud said:

"When the morning shone upon us at daybreak, and a thread of dawn appeared and shone."

There is a textual report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) explaining this verse.

Makhlad narrated from 'Amir, from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) taught me prayer and fasting. He said: "Pray so-and-so, and fast so-and-so. When the sun sets, eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, and fast thirty days until you see the new moon before that." He said: "I took two threads, one white and one black, and I kept looking at them, but they did not become distinct to me." I mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Messenger of God laughed until his molars showed, and said: "O son of Hatim, that is only the whiteness of day from the blackness of night." [61]

Abu Hazim narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: This verse was revealed: ﴿Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾, and he did not say "from the dawn." Men who wanted to fast would place a white thread and a black thread on their feet and would not cease eating and drinking until they became distinct to them. So God revealed ﴿from the dawn﴾, and they knew that what was meant was the night and the day.

Fajr is the splitting of the column of dawn and the beginning of its light. It is a verbal noun from your saying: fajara al-ma' yafjuru fajran, when water gushes out and flows. Its likeness is the splitting of light from the darkness of dawn, as water of a pool when it splits and flows out. There are two dawns. One rises in the sky, elongated like the tail of a wolf, and does not spread; this does not make prayer permissible or make food forbidden for the fasting person, and it is the false dawn. The second is the one that spreads, takes hold of the horizon; this is the true dawn, which makes prayer permissible and makes food forbidden for the fasting person, and it is what is meant by this verse.

From Samurah ibn Jundab, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let not the call of Bilal, nor the elongated dawn, keep you from suhur; rather, it is the dawn that spreads across the horizon." [62]

Then he mentioned the time of breaking the fast, saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until nightfall﴾.

Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and he was fasting. When the sun set, he said to a man: "Get down and prepare the drink for me." The man said: "O Messenger of God, has it become evening?" He said: "Get down and prepare it for me." The man said: "If only it were evening!" He said: "Get down and prepare it for me." The man said: "O Messenger of God, there is still daylight for us." Then for the third time he said: "Get down and prepare it for me." So the man got down and prepared it for him. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the night approaches from here and the day withdraws from here, and the sun has set, then the fasting person has broken his fast." [63]

In some wordings: "whether he has eaten or not."

﴿And do not have intercourse with them while you are devoted to worship in the mosques﴾. Mujahid used to read it in the mosque. The root of 'ukuf and i'tikaf is staying and dwelling.

[1] See al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/177.

[2] Note: the bracketed numerals in the source refer to the original footnotes and hadith references, which are preserved above.

He said: "I stayed (ʿakaftu) in the place when I remained in it." God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿They came upon a people devoting themselves to idols they had﴾ [Qur'an 7:138], meaning: who remain in devotion (yuqimūn).

Al-Farazdaq, describing cooking pots, said:
"He sees around them supplicants, as if they were
upon an idol in the high place, a devoted circle."

And al-Tirimmah said:
"The daughters of the night stayed around me, devoted,
like weeping women devoted, a fallen one among them."

Another said: "She confronted her, while the darkness had gathered, a phantom whose guidance the passion led to it."

Iʿtikaf (retreat in the mosque) is confining oneself in the mosque for the worship of God, the Exalted.

The scholars differed over the meaning of the "touching" (mubashara) from which the one in seclusion is forbidden.

One group said: it refers specifically to sexual intercourse; the meaning is: do not have intercourse with them while you are in seclusion in the mosques, for intercourse invalidates the seclusion. This was the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAtaʾ, al-Dahhak and al-Rabiʿ.

Qatada, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: this verse was revealed concerning a group of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ who used to seclude themselves in the mosque. When one of them felt a need for his wife, he would go out to her, have intercourse with her, then bathe and return to the mosque. So they were forbidden to have intercourse, by night or by day, until they finished their seclusion.

Abu Zayd said: "touching" includes intercourse and what is other than intercourse, such as caressing, kissing and all kinds of enjoyment. Intercourse invalidates the seclusion by consensus, while touching other than intercourse is of two kinds. One kind is intended for sensual pleasure with the woman; this is disliked, and according to most jurists it does not invalidate the seclusion, though Malik ibn Anas said it does invalidate it.

Ibn Jurayj said: "I said to ʿAtaʾ, 'Does mubashara mean intercourse?' He said, 'Intercourse itself.' I said, 'What about kissing in the mosque, and touching?' He said, 'As for what is forbidden, it is intercourse, and I dislike every such thing in the mosque.'" [Source cited: al-Sabiq, 2/247.]

The second kind is touching not intended for sensual pleasure with the woman; this is permissible, as reported in the hadith from ʿAʾisha, may God be pleased with her, that the Messenger of God ﷺ would put his head out to her from the mosque and she would comb his hair while he was in seclusion.

Farqad al-Sajni, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas: The Messenger of God ﷺ said concerning the one in seclusion: "He is in seclusion from sins, and there is recorded for him the reward of all good deeds, as one who performs all good deeds." [64] [Sources: Ibn Qudama, al-Mughni, 3/118; Sunan Ibn Majah, 1/567, no. 1781.]

From ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Whoever secludes himself ten days in Ramadan is credited with two pilgrimages and two ʿumras." [65] [Sources: al-Jami al-Saghir, 2/575, no. 8479; Kanz al-ʿUmmal, 8/530, no. 34006.]

﴿These are the limits of God⦆ — the rulings we have mentioned concerning fasting and seclusion.

al-Suddi said: the conditions of God.
Shahr ibn Hawshab said: the obligations of God.
al-Dahhak said: the disobedience of God.
al-Mufaddal ibn Salama said: the limit (hadd) is the boundary at which a person stops and which is described for him until he is distinguished from other described things; a limit separates two things, and a limit is the end of a thing.

al-Khalil said: the limit is that which gathers and prevents.
al-Zajjaj said: the limits are what God, exalted, has forbidden from transgressing.

I say: the root meaning of hadd in the language is prevention, and from it the doorkeeper is called haddad.
al-Aʿsha said:
"We rose while our rooster had not crowed,
toward a jar near its guardian."
meaning its owner, who guards it and keeps it from others.

al-Nabigha said:
"Except Solomon, when the King said to him: 'Stand in the wilderness and set a boundary against the ravens.'"
From it come the boundaries of the land. A house is what prevents another from entering it. Iron is called hadid because it resists being worked. It is said that a woman "mourns" (haddat) for her husband when she restrains herself from adornment. So the limits of God are what is prohibited within them, or what is forbidden from transgressing them and exceeding them to others.

﴿So do not approach them⦆ — do not go near them. One says: qaraba al-shay' aqrabuhu and qarubtu minhu (with u-vowel on the r) when one draws near to it.

﴿Thus God makes clear His signs to the people, that they may be wary⦆ — so that they might guard against them, and thus be saved from wrath and punishment.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 183–187 (part 1 of 4):

"O you who have believed" (Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū). Al-Hasan said: When you hear God Most High say "O you who have believed," lend it your full attention, for it is either about a matter you are commanded to do or a prohibition from which you are forbidden.

Ja'far al-Sadiq (may God be pleased with him) said: The pleasure of the "yā" in the address removes the weariness and hardship of worship.

"Prescribed" (kutiba): obligatory, made binding.

"Fasting" (al-ṣiyām) is the verbal noun of your saying "ṣumtu ṣiyāman" (I fasted), just as you say "qumtu qiyāman" (I stood). The root meaning of ṣawm and ṣiyām in the language is restraint (al-imsāk). It is said "ṣāmat al-rīḥ" when the wind became still and stopped blowing, and "ṣāmat al-khayl" when horses stood still and stopped running. Al-Nābigha said:

Horses standing still and horses not standing still, beneath the dust, and horses chewing on their bits.

He also said "ṣāma al-nahār" when the day became balanced (at its midpoint), and "qāma qā'im al-ẓahīrah" (the sun stood at midday), because when the sun rises to the middle of the sky it halts and stops its swift movement. Imru' al-Qays said:

So leave this aside and drive away your worry with a sigh, a camel that plods on when the day stands still and grows hot.

And the rajaz poet said:

Until, when the day stood still and became balanced, and the saliva of the sun flowed and it descended.

It is also said of a man who keeps silent and refrains from speech: he "ṣāma."

God Most High said: "Indeed I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast" (Qur'an 19:26), meaning silence.

So fasting is abstaining from the usual food, drink and intercourse.

"As it was prescribed for those before you" (kamā kutiba ʿalā alladhīna min qablikum): from the prophets and the nations, the first of whom was Adam (peace be upon him). This is what ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Hārūn ibn ʿAntarah narrated from his father, from his grandfather, from ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him), who said: I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) one day at midday while he was in al-Ḥijr. I greeted him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) returned my greeting and then said: "O ʿAlī, this is Jibrīl; he conveys his greetings to you." I said: "And upon you and upon him be peace, O Messenger of God. Why?" He said: "Come close to me." I drew near to him, and he said: "O ʿAlī, Jibrīl says to you: Fast three days of every month, and there will be written for you on the first day ten thousand [years of reward], on the second day thirty thousand [years], and on the third day one hundred thousand [years]."

I said: "O Messenger of God, is this reward for me specifically, or for the people in general?" He said: "O ʿAlī, God will give you this reward, and to whoever does works like yours after you." I said: "O Messenger of God, what are they?" He said: "The white days: the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth" (Sharḥ al-Azhār lil-Imām Aḥmad al-Murtaḍā; Ghunyat al-Ṭālibīn) [37].

ʿAntarah said: I asked ʿAlī (may God be pleased with him): Why were these days called "the white days"? He said: When Adam (peace be upon him) was brought down from the Garden to the earth, the sun scorched him, and his body turned black. Then on the third day he fasted, and Jibrīl came to him and said: "O Adam, would you like your body to become white?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then fast the thirteenth, fourteenth and fifteenth of the month." Adam (peace be upon him) fasted the first day, and a third of his body became white; then he fasted the second day, and two-thirds of his body became white; then he fasted the third day, and his whole body became white. Thus they were named the white days.

The exegetes said: God prescribed upon His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) and upon the believers the fast of ʿĀshūrāʾ and three days of every month, when he came to Madina; they used to fast these until the fast of the month of Ramadan was revealed, a month and some days before the Battle of Badr.

Al-Ḥasan and a group of scholars said: By "those before you" he meant the Christians; our fasting was likened to theirs because of their agreement in the timing and the measure. God had prescribed the fast of Ramadan upon the Christians, and it became difficult for them, for it might fall in intense heat or intense cold, and it would harm them in their journeys and their livelihoods. The opinion of their scholars and leaders converged on making their fast in a season of the year between winter and summer, so they made it in spring and added ten days as an expiation for what they had done, so it became forty. Then a king of theirs had a mouth ailment, and God made it binding upon him that if he recovered from his illness he would add a week to his fast. He recovered and a week was added. Then that king died and another king succeeded them, who said: "Complete it to fifty days," and they completed it fifty days. Mujāhid said: a plague struck them and they said: "Add to your fasting," so they added ten before and ten after.

Abū Umayya al-Ṭanāfisī narrated from al-Shaʿbī, who said: If you fast the whole year and break the fast on the day that is doubtful, which is said to be from Shaʿbān and said to be from Ramaḍān, that would be (sufficient). That is because the Christians were obligated to fast Ramadan just as it was obligated upon us, but they shifted it to a season; for they used to fast it in the heat of summer, and they counted thirty days. Then a generation came after them who took confidence in themselves and fasted a day before the thirty and a day after them. The next generation continued to follow the practice of the generation before, until they reached fifty days. This is the meaning of His words, Mighty and Majestic: "as it was prescribed for those before you" (Tafsir al-Ṭabarī, 2/175).

"So that you may be God-fearing" (laʿallakum tattaqūn): that you may refrain from eating, drinking and intercourse.

"For a specified number of days" (ayyāman maʿdūdāt): meaning the month of Ramadan, thirty days or twenty-nine days, because of what Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ narrated: he heard Ibn ʿUmar relate from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "We are an unlettered nation; we do not calculate or write. The month is like this, and like this, and like this," and he folded his thumb at the third, "and the month is like this, and like this, and like this" — a full thirty (Sunan al-Kubrā of al-Nasāʾī, 2/74) [38].

"Ayyāman" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning "during days." It is said it is in the accusative as an explanation. It is said it is the predicate of an unnamed subject, and it is said it is by supposing a verb: "fast specified days."

"Whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number (of other days)": that is, whoever breaks the fast, then the same number. This is like His words: "Whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head, then a ransom" (Qur'an 2:196), meaning: whoever shaves or trims (his hair), then a ransom. And "fa-ʿiddah" means: then upon him is a number, and therefore it is in the nominative.

Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla read "fa-ʿiddatan" in the accusative, meaning: then let him fast a number.

"Of other days" (min ayyāmin ukhar): other than the days of his illness or journey. "ʿIddah" means the count. "Ukhar" is in a position of genitive but is not declined, so it is accusative, because it is diverted from its original form: its basis would be "awākhir" and "ukhayrāt," but when it was shifted to the form fuʿal, it was not inflected, like ʿUmar and Zufar.

"And upon those who are able to do it" (wa-ʿalā alladhīna yuṭīqūnahu): Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾisha, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Rabāḥ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid read "yuṭṭayqūnahu" with a damma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ with lightened pronunciation, and with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and intensified pronunciation, meaning: they bear it and carry it (yulfūnahu wa-yaḥmilūnahu).

It is reported from Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah also: "yaṭṭayqūnahu" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and a shadda on the ṭāʾ, meaning "yataṭawwaqūnahu," that is, they burden themselves with it.

Ibn al-Anbārī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "yaṭṭayyaqūnahu" with a fatḥa on the first yāʾ, a shadda on the ṭāʾ and a shadda on the second yāʾ, both vowelled with fatḥa, meaning "yuṭīqūnahu." It is said: "ṭāqa," "aṭāqa" and "aṭyaqa" have one meaning.

"A ransom: the feeding of a poor man" (fidyatun ṭaʿāmu miskīn). The people of Madina and Syria read "fidyatu ṭaʿāmi masākīn," in the plural, with the feeding attributed to the ransom, although it is singular, because the two wordings differ, like His words, "and the grain of the harvest" (Qur'an 50:9), and their saying "al-masjid al-jāmiʿ" and "bayʿ al-awwal" and similar. This is the reading of Abū ʿAmr and Mujāhid. Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd narrated from ʿAbdullāh, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, that he read it "ṭaʿāmu masākīn" in the plural. Marwān ibn Muʿāwiya al-Fazārī narrated from ʿUthmān ibn al-Aswad, from Mujāhid, that he read it so: "masākīn."

The rest read "fidyatan" in the accusative, "ṭaʿāmu" in the nominative, "miskīnin" in the genitive, in the singular. This is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās.

It was narrated by Ibn Abī Najīḥ from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār from Ibn ʿAbbās that he read it "ṭaʿāmu miskīnin," in the singular. Whoever reads in the singular, its meaning is: for each day, the feeding of one poor man; whoever reads in the plural refers it to all. This is the preference of Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim.

"Whoever volunteers good" (faman tatawwaʿa khayran): ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar, Yaḥyā ibn Thābit, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "yataṭawwaʿa" with the yāʾ, shadda on the ṭāʾ and jazm on the ʿayn, in the sense of "yataṭawwaʿ." The others read "taṭawwaʿa" with the tāʾ, a fatḥa on the ʿayn and lightened ṭāʾ, as a past verb.

The scholars differed about the interpretation and ruling of this verse:

A group said: This was the first thing when fasting was prescribed, for when God Most High revealed the obligation of fasting the month of Ramadan upon His Messenger (ﷺ) and commanded his companions to do so, it was hard on them, for they were a people not accustomed to fasting. So God gave them the choice between fasting and feeding. Whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished broke the fast and paid the ransom with food. Then God abrogated that by His words: "Whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it" (Qur'an 2:185), and the firm command regarding the obligation of fasting was revealed. Upon this view were Muʿādh ibn Jabal, Anas ibn Mālik, Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAlqamah, ʿAmr ibn Murrah, al-Shaʿbī, al-Zuhrī, Ibrāhīm, ʿUbaydah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and one of the narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Others said: Rather, it is specific to the aged old man and the aged old woman, and to those who are able to fast but for whom it is difficult; a concession was granted to them: if they wish to break the fast while able, they feed one poor man for each day. Then that was abrogated by His words, "Whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it," and the concession remained for those who are unable. This is the view of Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, and the narration of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Al-Ḥasan said: This concerns the sick person: when the name of illness applied to him, even if he is able to fast, he has the choice: if he wishes he fasts, and if he wishes he breaks the fast and feeds, until that is abrogated. According to these opinions, the verse is abrogated, and this is the view of the majority of the jurist-exegetes.

Another group said: This verse was not abrogated, nor any part of it. Rather its interpretation is: "and upon those who are able to do it" in their youth, in their health and strength; then if they became unable to fast, a ransom of feeding a poor man, because the people had been granted a concession to break the fast while they were capable of fasting. They said: this is an expression of their initial state, and they regarded the verse as muḥkam (not abrogated). This is the view of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and al-Suddī, and one of the two narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās. What led those who hold these opinions to the reading of "yuṭīqūnahu" is: from "al-iṭāqah," which is the correct reading upon which the common people of the Qur'an and the codices of the regions agree. As for those who read "yaṭawwaqūnahu," they interpreted it as referring to the aged old man, the aged old woman, and the sick person whose recovery is not hoped for: they are burdened with fasting and cannot bear it, so they may break the fast and feed a poor man for each day they break it.

They said: The verse is muḥkam, not abrogated, and the ransom (fidyah) is the recompense and substitute, from your saying: "fadaytu hādhā bi-hādhā," meaning I protected this with that and gave it as a substitute for it. It is said "fadaytu fidyatan," just as one says "mashaytu mashyatan." "Faman tatawwaʿa khayran": whoever adds to one poor man and feeds two or more. This was said by Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs and al-Suddī.

Some of them said: "whoever adds to the obligatory measure of feeding" — the food is increased. This was related by Ibn Jurayj and Khuṭayf from Mujāhid. Ibn Shihāb said: He means, whoever fasts along with the ransom and combines fasting and feeding, that is better for him.

"And that you fast is better for you" (fa-huwa khayrun lahu wa-an tasūmū): the "an" is a connecting particle; it means: fasting is better for you than breaking the fast and the ransom, "if you knew" (in kuntum taʿlamūn).

Section on the ruling of the verse

Know that there is no concession for any believing adult to break the fast of Ramadan except in four cases:

The first: he is liable for both making up the fast and expiation (kaffārah).
The second: he is liable for making up the fast without expiation.
The third: he is liable for expiation without making up the fast.
The fourth: he is liable for neither making up nor expiation.

As for the one liable for both making up and expiation: whoever neglects making up Ramadan until another Ramadan arrives. And the pregnant woman and the nursing woman, if they fear for their children, break the fast and are liable for both making up and expiation; if they fear for themselves, they are like the sick person, and their ruling is his ruling. This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar and Mujāhid, and the position of al-Shāfiʿī.

Some said: For the pregnant and nursing woman who fear for themselves and their child, they are liable for expiation and not making up. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

Others said: They are liable for making up and not expiation. This is the view of Ibrāhīm, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, the position of the people of Iraq, Mālik and al-Awzāʿī.

As for the one liable for making up without expiation: the sick person, the traveler, the menstruating woman and the woman in postnatal bleeding are liable for making up without expiation.

Anas said: I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while he was taking his midday meal, and he said: "Sit down." I said: "I am fasting." He said: "Sit, and I will tell you: God has lifted from the traveler the fast and half of the prayer" (Mawāhib al-Jalīl lil-Raʿīnī, 2/6; Talkhīṣ al-Ḥabīr, 6/426) [39].

As for the one liable for expiation without making up: the decrepit old man, the aged old woman, the one with a permanent illness whose recovery is not hoped for, and the one with the thirst-disease (ʿaṭāsh) who fears death; they are liable for expiation and not making up. This is the view of the majority of jurists.

It is narrated from Rabīʿah ibn Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and Khālid ibn al-Dorīk that they said regarding the old man and old woman: if they are able, they fast; otherwise there is no expiation for them, and nothing is upon them if they break the fast.

Mālik said: I do not regard that as obligatory for them, but I would like them to do it.

As for the one liable for neither making up nor expiation: the insane person.

The scholars differed about the measure of feeding in the expiation for fasting. Some said: the obligatory measure is half a ṣāʿ for each day he breaks the fast; this is the view of the people of Iraq.

Others among them said: half a ṣāʿ of wheat, or a ṣāʿ of dates, raisins, or other grains.

Some jurists said: what the one breaking the fast normally subsists on for the day he broke it.

Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah (may God be pleased with him) said: he feeds for each day a mudd of the staple food and a mudd of condiment.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: he gives one poor man his evening meal when he breaks the fast and his pre-dawn meal when he eats it before dawn.

Some said: he feeds one poor man a mudd for each day. This is the view of Ibn Hurayrah, ʿAṭāʾ, Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, al-Layth ibn Saʿd, Mālik ibn Anas, al-Shāfiʿī, and the majority of the jurists of the Ḥijāz. And success is from God.

Then He explained the days of fasting, saying:

"The month of Ramadan" (shahru Ramaḍāna): the common readers read it in the nominative, meaning: "there has come to you the month of Ramadan."

Al-Farrāʾ said: "That is the month of Ramadan" (dhālikum shahru Ramaḍān).

Al-Akhfash: "It is the month of Ramadan" (huwa shahru Ramaḍān).

Al-Kisāʾī: "The month of Ramadan has been prescribed for you" (kutiba ʿalaykum shahru Ramaḍān). It is also said: it is an inceptive and what follows is its predicate.

Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and Shahr ibn Ḥawshab read "shahra Ramaḍāna" in the accusative, meaning "fast the month of Ramadan," as said by al-Mubarrij.

Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: fasting has been prescribed for you during the month of Ramadan.

Abū ʿUbayda: it is in the accusative as an incitement (ighrāʾ).

Abū ʿAmr read it assimilated, "shahra Ramaḍān," according to his method of assimilating every two letters that meet and are of one kind and one point of articulation, or of close points of articulation, seeking lightness.

The month was called "shahr" for its fame (shuhrah).

Al-Farrāʾ said: it is derived from "al-shuhrah," which is whiteness; from it one says: "shahartu al-sayf" when I unsheathed the sword, and "shahra al-hilāl" when the crescent appeared.

They differed about the meaning of "Ramaḍān." Some said: Ramaḍān is one of the names of God, so one says "shahr Ramaḍān" as one says "shahr Allāh."

Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq narrated from his forefathers (may God be pleased with them) from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The month of Ramadan is the month of God" [40].

What also indicates this is what Hushaym narrated from Ābān, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not say 'Ramaḍān'; attribute it as God Most High attributed it in the Qur'an, saying: 'The month of Ramaḍān'" [41] (Tafsir al-Qurṭubī, 2/291).

It is narrated from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: Abū ʿAmr said: It was only named Ramaḍān because deeds of goodness were scorched in it (ramaḍat fīhi al-fiʿāl min al-khayr).

Others said: because stones would be scorched in it from the heat, and "ramaḍāʾ" is stones heated by the sun.

It was said: it was named so because it scorches sins, that is, burns them.

It was said: because hearts absorb in it the heat of admonition, wisdom and reflection on the matter of the Hereafter, as sand and stones absorb the heat of the sun.

Al-Khalīl said: it derives from "al-ramaḍ," which is rain that comes in autumn; this month was named Ramaḍān because it washes bodies from impurities, washing them thoroughly, and purifies hearts with purification.

"In which the Qur'an was revealed" (alladhī unzila fīhi al-Qur'ān): Hushaym narrated from Dāwūd, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās; and al-Suddī narrated from Muḥammad ibn Abī al-Mujālid, from Muqsim, from Ibn ʿAbbās: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah al-Aswad asked him, saying: There has arisen doubt regarding His words, "The month of Ramaḍān in which the Qur'an was revealed" (Qur'an 2:185), and His words, "We revealed it on the Night of Power" (Qur'an 97:1), and His words, "We revealed it on a blessed night" (Qur'an 44:3), whereas it was revealed in the other months as well.

God said: "And a Qur'an We have divided, that you may recite it to the people gradually" (Qur'an 17:106), and they said: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" (Qur'an 25:32).

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 183–187 (part 2 of 4):

He said: The Qur'an was sent down all at once from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) on the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr) in the month of Ramadan. It was placed in the House of Honour (Bayt al-'Izzah) in the lowest heaven (sama' al-dunya). Then Jibril (peace be upon him) brought it down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) in installments, piece by piece, over twenty years. This is His saying: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [Surah al-Waqi'ah: 75].

Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: I said to al-Sha'bi: "The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down — was it not revealed to him throughout the rest of the year?" He said: "Yes, but Jibril used to review with Muhammad (ﷺ) in Ramadan what God had sent down; He decrees what He wills, establishes what He wills, and causes him to forget what He wills."

Shihab ibn Tariq narrated from Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the third night of Ramadan, the Torah of Musa on the sixth night of Ramadan, the Gospel of Isa on the thirteenth night of Ramadan, the Psalms of Dawud on the eighteenth night of Ramadan, and the Furqan (the Criterion) was sent down upon Muhammad on the twenty-fourth night, after six nights had passed." Then he described the Qur'an, saying:

﴿A guidance for mankind from error﴾ — it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (qat'), because "the Qur'an" is definite and "guidance" is indefinite.

﴿And clear proofs (bayyinat)﴾ — of the lawful and the unlawful, the prescribed limits and the rulings.

﴿Of the guidance and the Criterion (al-Furqan)﴾ — the distinction between truth and falsehood.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab narrated from Salman, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) addressed us on the last day of Sha'ban, saying: "O people, a great month has come over you, a blessed month, a month in which there is a night better than a thousand months (Surah al-Qadr). God has made its fasting an obligation and its night prayer a voluntary act. Whoever draws near to God in it with one of the good qualities is like one who performed an obligation in another month, and whoever performs an obligation in it is like one who performed seventy obligations in another month. It is the month of patience, and the reward of patience is Paradise; the month of consolation; and the month in which the provision of the believer is increased. Its beginning is mercy, its middle is forgiveness, and its end is freedom from the Fire. Whoever gives iftar to a fasting person, it will be forgiveness for his sins and freedom of his neck from the Fire, and he will have a reward like his, without his reward being diminished in any way." They said: "O Messenger of God, not all of us have the means to give iftar to a fasting person." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God gives this reward to one who gives iftar to a fasting person even with a sip of milk, a date, or a mouthful of water. Whoever feeds a fasting person to satiety, God will give him to drink from my Pool a drink after which he will never thirst until he enters Paradise. He is like one who freed a slave. Whoever lightens the burden of his servant in it, God will forgive him and free him from the Fire. So increase in four qualities in it: two by which you please your Lord, and two of which you have no independence from. As for the two by which you please your Lord: the testimony that there is no god but God, and seeking His forgiveness. As for those you cannot do without: you ask God, the Mighty and Majestic, for Paradise, and you seek refuge with Him from the Fire." [42] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 8/477, no. 33714; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/184.]

And from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the gates of heaven and the gates of Paradise are opened on the first night of Ramadan, and they are not closed until its last night. No servant prays on one of its nights except that God, the Mighty and Majestic, records for him one thousand seven hundred good deeds for every prostration, and builds for him a house in Paradise of red ruby with seventy thousand doors, each door having two leaves of gold inlaid with red ruby. When he fasts the first day of Ramadan, God forgives him every sin up to the last day of Ramadan, and it is an expiation for the like of it. For every day he fasts he has a palace in Paradise with a thousand golden doors, and seventy thousand angels seek forgiveness for him from morning until he is hidden by the veil. For every prostration he makes, by night or by day, he has a tree in whose shade a rider could travel for a hundred years without crossing it." [43] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 8/471, no. 23706; al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/186.]

Muhammad ibn Yunus al-Harithi narrated from Qatadah, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the first night of Ramadan comes, the Majestic, whose majesty is exalted, calls out to Ridwan, the keeper of the Gardens, and he says: 'At Your service, and at Your bidding.' He says: 'Renew My Garden and adorn it with the community of Ahmad, and do not close it upon them until their month ends.' Then He calls out to Malik, the keeper of the Fire: 'O Malik!' He says: 'At Your service, my Lord, and at Your bidding.' He says: 'Close the gates of Hellfire against the fasting ones of the community of Ahmad, and do not open them upon them until their month ends.' Then He calls out to Jibril, who says: 'At Your service, my Lord, and at Your bidding.' He says: 'Descend to the earth and chain the rebellious devils so that they do not spoil their fasting and their breaking of the fast.' God has, every day of Ramadan at the rising of the sun and at the time of breaking the fast, freed servants and maidservants from the Fire. And He has in every heaven a caller calling among them; an angel whose station is beneath the Throne of the Lord of the Worlds, and whose feet are in the lowest depths of the seventh earth; one wing in the east, adorned with coral, pearls and jewels, and one wing in the west, adorned with coral, pearls and jewels, calling out: 'Is there a penitent who will be accepted? Is there a supplicant who will be answered? Is there a wronged one whom God will help? Is there a seeker of forgiveness who will be forgiven? Is there a petitioner who will be given his request?'" He said: "The Lord, may His remembrance be exalted, calls out to the whole month: 'My servants and My maidservants, rejoice and be patient [and persist]; soon the burdens will be lifted from you, and you will reach My mercy and My honour.' When the Night of Decree comes, Jibril descends in a kabkabah [a Kabkabah: a group of a thing] of angels, sending blessings [and greetings] upon every servant standing or sitting who remembers God, the Mighty and Majestic." [44] [See Zad al-Masir: 8/287.]

Ibrahim ibn Hudayyah narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If God permitted the heavens and the earth to speak, they would give glad tidings to whoever fasts Ramadan: Paradise." [45]

Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umar narrated from Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The sleep of the fasting person is worship, his silence is glorification, his supplication is answered, and his deeds are multiplied." [46] [al-Jami' al-Saghir: 2/678, with the addition: "and his sin is forgiven"; likewise in al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/180.]

﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ — the common readers recite the lam with a jazm (sukun), while al-Hasan and al-A'raj recite it with a kasra, and it is the imperative lam (lam al-amr), whose original form is kasra when it stands alone. When it is joined to something, there are two possibilities: jazm and kasra. It is joined with three letters: the fa' as in His saying ﴿li-ya'budu rabba hadha al-bayt﴾ [Surah Quraysh: 3], the waw as in His saying ﴿wa-liyuwfu nudhurahum wa-liyattawwafu﴾ [Surah al-Hajj: 29], and thumma as in His saying ﴿thumma liyaqdu tafathahum﴾ [Surah al-Hajj: 29].

The scholars differed regarding the meaning and ruling of this verse:

Some of them said: its meaning is: whoever witnesses it while sane, adult, resident, healthy and legally responsible, let him fast it. This was said by Abu Hanifah and his companions. Another group said: its meaning is: when the month of Ramadan comes upon him while he is residing in his home, let him fast the whole month.

Hence, if he travels after it begins, or remains without moving, [the ruling is the same]. This was said by al-Nakha'i and al-Suddi.

Qatadah said: Ali (may God be pleased with him) used to say: if Ramadan reaches him while he is resident and then he travels, he must fast.

Muhammad ibn Sirin said: I asked 'Ubaydah al-Salmani about a man whom Ramadan reaches and then he travels. He said: "If you witnessed its beginning, fast its end; do you not see that He says: ﴿whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾?" They said: "It is recommended for him not to travel if Ramadan reaches him while he is resident, until he completes the month." It is narrated on this matter from Ibrahim ibn Talhah that he came to 'A'ishah (may God be pleased with her) to greet her. She said: "Where are you going?" He said: "I intend 'umrah." She said: "Did you sit until Ramadan came upon you and then you went out during it?" He said: "My burden has gone out." She said: "Sit until you break your fast, then go out. If Ramadan had reached me while I was on part of the road, I would have stayed for it."

Others said: the meaning of the verse ﴿whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ is what he witnessed of it while present; if he travels, he has the choice to break the fast if he wishes. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and the general body of interpreters, and it is the most correct of the opinions. It is supported by what al-Zuhri narrated from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out in the year of the Conquest fasting in Ramadan, until when he reached al-Qantarah he called for water and drank.

And from al-Sha'bi: that he travelled in Ramadan and broke his fast at the gate of the bridge.

Then he mentioned, saying: ﴿And whoever is sick﴾ — the scholars differed regarding the condition under which God permits breaking the fast. Some said: it is any illness that is called illness. Tarif ibn Tammam al-'Utaridi said: I entered upon Muhammad ibn Sirin one day in Ramadan while he was eating, and when he finished he said: "This finger of mine has been hurt."

Others said: any illness in which the more likely outcome, if its sufferer is commanded to fast, is an increase in his ailment to an unbearable degree; this is the choice of al-Shafi'i.

Al-Hasan and Ibrahim said: if the sick person cannot pray standing, he breaks his fast. The principle is that if fasting is not possible for him and it exhausts him, he breaks it; but if fasting does not exhaust him, then he is in the category of the healthy person who is able to fast.

﴿Or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ — the scholars differed concerning the fasting of the traveller.

Some said: breaking the fast during travel is an obligatory resolve (azimah), not a concession (rukhsah); so whoever fasts during travel must make up the fast if he resides. This is the view of 'Amr Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and al-Dahhak, and they argued by what Umm al-Darda' narrated from Ka'b ibn 'Asim, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "It is not righteousness to fast while travelling."

[47] [Kitab al-Umm of al-Shafi'i: 2/112; Musnad al-Humaydi: 2/381.]

Al-Zuhri narrated from Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, from his father, who said: "The one who fasts while travelling is like the one who breaks the fast while resident."

Others said: breaking the fast during travel is a concession from God, the Mighty and Majestic, and the obligation is fasting; so whoever fasts, his obligation is fulfilled, and whoever breaks the fast, he has taken God's concession, and there is no making-up for one who fasted and then resided. This is the sound view, and it is the position of the general body of jurists. It is supported by what 'Asim ibn al-Ahwal narrated from Abu Nadrah, from Jabir, who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey; some of us were fasting and some were not, and none of us would blame another.

Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated from Hisham, from his father, from 'A'ishah: that Hamzah ibn 'Amr said: "O Messenger of God, I used to be accustomed to fasting; shall I fast while travelling?" He said: "If you wish, fast; and if you wish, break your fast." [48] [Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/531, no. 1662; Sunan al-Nasa'i: 4/186.]

And from 'Urwah ibn Abi Qurrah, from Hamzah ibn 'Amr, that he said: "O Messenger of God, I find in myself strength to fast while travelling; is there any sin upon me?" He said: "It is a concession from God, the Mighty and Majestic; whoever takes it, it is good, and whoever wishes to fast, there is no sin upon him." [49] [al-Majmu' of al-Nawawi: 6/264; Sahih Muslim: 3/145.]

As for his saying (ﷺ): "It is not righteousness to fast while travelling," the complete report indicates its interpretation, which is what Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by a man in the shade of a tree who was being sprinkled with water, and he said: "What is wrong with this companion of yours?" They said: "O Messenger of God, he is fasting." He said: "It is not righteousness that you fast while travelling; rather, take the concession of God which He has granted you and accept it." Likewise is the interpretation of his saying (ﷺ): "The fasting one during travel is like the one breaking the fast while resident." [50] [Sunan al-Nasa'i: 4/176; Sahih Ibn Khuzaymah: 3/259.]

It is supported by the report of Mujahid from Ibn 'Umar: that he passed by a man pouring water on his face while fasting, and he said: "Break your fast, woe to you; for I see that if you die in this state you will enter the Fire."

What gathers these reports and supports what we have said is what Ayyub narrated from 'Urwah and Salim: that they were with 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, who was then governor of Medina. They discussed fasting while travelling. Salim said: "Ibn 'Umar did not fast while travelling." 'Urwah said: "'A'ishah used to fast while travelling." Salim said: "I only narrate from Ibn 'Umar." 'Urwah said: "I only narrate from 'A'ishah." Their voices rose, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: "O God, forgive..." — [and he said]: "If it is easy, fast; and if it is difficult, break your fast."

Then they differed regarding which is preferable among them. Some said: fasting is better; this is the view of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Anas, Ibrahim and Mujahid.

It is reported that Anas ibn Malik ordered a servant of his to fast while travelling, and it was said to him concerning this verse; he said: "It was revealed while we were then travelling hungry and dismounting without being satisfied; so whoever breaks the fast does so by concession, and whoever fasts, fasting is better."

Others said: breaking the fast is preferable, because of what Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated from his father, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to Makkah in the year of the Conquest in Ramadan and fasted until he reached Kura' al-Ghamim; the people fasted too. It reached him that the people found fasting hard, so he called for a cup of water and drank after the 'asr prayer while the people watched; some people broke their fast and some continued fasting. It reached him that the people had fasted, and he said: "Those are the disobedient." [51] [Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 2/106; Sunan al-Nasa'i: 4/177.]

'Asim al-Ahwal narrated from [Buraid] al-'Ijli, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: We were with the Messenger of God (ﷺ); some of us were fasting and some were not. We alighted on a hot day and made shades; the fasting ones collapsed, while the ones breaking their fast stood up and watered the riding animals. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Today the ones breaking their fast have taken the reward." [52] [al-Majmu' of al-Nawawi: 6/264; Sahih al-Bukhari: 3/224.]

Shu'bah narrated from Mu'alla, from Yusuf ibn al-Hakam, who said: I asked Ibn 'Umar about fasting while travelling. He said: "What do you think if you gave charity to a man and he returned it to you; would you not be angry?" He said: "Yes." He said: "It is a charity from God, the Mighty and Majestic, which He has given to you." The distances for which breaking the fast is permitted are sixteen farsakhs or more.

﴿God desires for you ease﴾ — when He granted concession in journeys to the sick and the traveller.

﴿And He does not desire for you hardship﴾ — Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read al-'usr and al-yusr with heavy vowels throughout the Qur'an. The rest read them with light vowels, and both are good dialects. There is no proof for the Qadariyyah in this verse, because it is built upon the beginning of the discussion concerning the obligation of fasting; it is specific in its rulings to the people of Islam.

﴿And that you may complete the period﴾ — Abu Bakr and Ruways read it with a shaddah on the mim. The rest read it without a shaddah, and this is the preferred reading, because of His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 3]. The waw in His saying ﴿wa-litukmilu﴾ is the waw of coordination (wa al-nasq), and the lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay); its sense is: "and He desires that you complete the period."

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is: God did that so that it would be easy for you, and that you might complete the period.

'Ata' said: that you might complete the number of days of the month.

The rest of the exegetes said: that you may complete the period of what you broke the fast of during your illness and your travel, when you have recovered and are resident, and make it up.

﴿And that you may magnify God﴾ — that you may glorify God.

﴿For that He has guided you﴾ — to His religion, and has granted you success, and provided you with the month of Ramadan, lightened for you, and singled you out with it above the rest of the peoples of other religions.

Most scholars said: it means the takbir on the night of the 'Id al-Fitr. Al-Shafi'i said: it was reported from Ibn al-Musayyab and 'Urwah ibn Salamah that they used to say the takbir on the night of the 'Id al-Fitr and would recite the takbir aloud. He said: and he compared [......] [a word not legible in the manuscript] to its sacrifice.

Ibn 'Abbas and Zayd ibn Aslam said: in this verse it is an obligation upon the Muslims, when the crescent of Shawwal is seen, to say the takbir until the imam comes out on the road and in the mosque; when the imam arrives, they cease, and do not say the takbir except after his takbir. The preferred form of the takbir is three times in succession.

﴿And that you may be thankful﴾ — for His blessings.

﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ — the exegetes differed concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and his companions when they had relations with their wives during the nights of Ramadan; their story will come later, God willing.

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih, from him [Ibn 'Abbas], who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "How does our Lord hear our supplication, when you claim that between us and the heaven is a distance of five hundred years, and the thickness of each heaven is likewise?" Then this verse was revealed.

Al-Hasan said: the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) asked the Messenger of God: "Where is our Lord?" So God revealed this verse.

Qatadah and 'Ata' said: when His saying was revealed: ﴿And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will answer you﴾, they said: "O Messenger of God, how should we call upon our Lord, and when should we call upon Him?" So God revealed this verse.

Al-Dahhak said: some of the Companions asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Is our Lord near so that we may whisper to Him, or far?" So he asked his Lord, and God revealed: ﴿And when My servants ask you, O Muhammad, concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 183–187 (part 3 of 4):

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: there is an ellipsis here, as if it were: "He knows what they do, and whether they are near to Him in knowledge."

The people of allusion (ahl al-isharah) said: the removal of the intermediary is a manifestation of power.

﴿I respond to the prayer of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾; ﴿so let them respond to Me﴾, meaning: let them obey Me. It is said that ajaba and istajaba have the same meaning.

Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi said:

"A caller called out, 'O you who answer to generosity,' but no one answered him at that moment."

Abu Raja' al-Khurasani said: it means "let them call on Me to respond." In the language, it means obedience and giving what is asked. It is said: "The sky answered with rain, and the earth answered with plants," as if the earth asked the sky for rain and it gave, and the sky asked the earth and it gave.

Zuhayr said:

"A rain-cloud from the high ones, whose rain-bearing clouds answered [...] (an illegible word; the likely reading is what we have set down)."

He means: its mountains gathered the rain-bearing clouds when it asked for rain, and they gave it that.

Response from God is giving, and response from the servant is obedience.

﴿And let them believe in Me, that they may be guided﴾, meaning: so that they may be rightly guided. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿I respond to the prayer of the supplicant﴾ and His saying ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾, when many people supplicate and are not answered? We say: the scholars differed regarding the meaning and interpretation of the two verses.

Some of them said: the meaning of "supplication" here is obedience, and the meaning of "response" is reward, as if He said: "I will respond to the prayer of the supplicant with reward if he obeys Me."

Others said: the meaning of the two verses is specific, although their wording is general. Their implied sense is: I respond to the prayer of the supplicant if I wish; I respond to the prayer of the supplicant when it accords with the decree; I respond to the prayer of the supplicant when he does not ask for something impossible; I respond to the prayer of the supplicant when the response is good for him. What supports this is what

Abu al-Mutawakkil narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No Muslim calls upon God, Mighty and Majestic, with a supplication that contains no severing of ties of kinship and no sin, except that God gives him one of three things: either his supplication is hastened for him, or it is stored up for him in the Hereafter, or He averts from him an evil equal to it." They said: "O Messenger of God, then we will increase (our supplications)." He said: "God is more abundant (in giving)." [53] [54]

Others said: it is general, and the verse contains nothing more than the answering of the supplication; as for granting the desired end and fulfilling the need, that is not mentioned in the verse. A master may respond to his servant, and a father to his son, yet not give him his request. So the response is certain without doubt upon the occurrence of supplication, because His saying "I respond" and "it is responded to" is a report, and a report cannot be contested, for if it were abrogated the one reporting would be a liar, and God is exalted above that. The evidence for this interpretation is what

Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever has a door opened to him in supplication, the doors of response will be opened to him. God revealed to Dawud (ﷺ): Tell the wrongdoers not to call upon Me, for I have made it binding upon Myself to respond to whoever calls upon Me, and if I respond to the wrongdoers I will curse them." [55]

It was also said: God responds to the supplication of the believer immediately, but He delays granting his desire so that He may hear his voice. What supports this is what

Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, a servant supplicates God while He loves him, and He says: 'O Jibril, fulfil the need of this servant of Mine, but delay it, for I love to keep hearing his voice.' And indeed a servant supplicates God while He hates him, and He says to Jibril: 'Fulfil the need of My servant, though his sincerity is lacking, and hasten it, for I dislike to hear his voice.'"

We have also been told [on the authority of Yahya, the sacrificed one of God] that he said: I asked the Lord of Might in a dream, "O Lord, how often do I call upon You and You do not respond to me?" He said: "O Yahya, I love to hear your voice." [56]

Some said: supplication has etiquettes and conditions which are the causes of response and the attainment of one's wish. Whoever observes them and perfects them is among the people of response, and whoever neglects them and falls short in them [is among those ... ] (illegible words) in supplication.

It is related that Ibrahim ibn Adham was asked: "Why is it that we call upon God and He does not respond to us?" He said: "Because you have known God but have not obeyed Him; you have known the Messenger but have not followed his sunnah; you have known the Qur'an but have not acted upon what is in it; you have eaten the blessings of God but have not rendered their thanks; you have known Paradise but have not sought it; you have known the Fire but have not fled from it; you have known Satan but have not fought him, and have agreed with him; you have known death but have not prepared for it; you have buried the dead but have not taken heed from them; you have left your own faults and occupied yourselves with the faults of people."

On His saying ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in unto your wives on the night of the fast﴾, the verse:

The exegetes said: At the beginning of the matter, when a man broke his fast, eating, drinking and intercourse were lawful for him until the late evening prayer ('isha') or until he slept before it. But if he prayed the late evening prayer or slept before praying and had not broken his fast, eating and drinking were forbidden to him, and this remained so until the same time the following year. [1]

Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) had intercourse with his wife after he had prayed the late evening prayer. When he had washed himself, he began to weep and blame himself, and he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, I seek pardon from God and from you for this sin of mine. I returned to my wife after I had prayed the late evening prayer, and I smelled a pleasant scent, and my soul adorned it for me, so I had intercourse with my wife. Do you find for me any concession?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You were not worthy of this, O 'Umar." Then men stood up and confessed what they had done after the late evening prayer. So there was revealed concerning 'Umar and his companions: ﴿It is made lawful for you﴾, that is, permitted and allowed for you, ﴿on the night of the fast﴾, in the night of the fast, ﴿intercourse (al-rafath)﴾.

Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read: "al-Rufuth" ﴿to your wives﴾. Rafath and rufuth are euphemisms for intercourse. Ibn 'Abbas said: God, the Living, the Generous, employs euphemism; so whatever God mentions in the Qur'an of touching, contact, consummation, entering, or rafath, He means by it intercourse.

The poet said:

"We spent that time among delights, and every pleasure was other than rafath."

Al-Qutaybi said: al-rafath is speaking openly of what ought to be expressed euphemistically, such as mention of marriage; its root meaning is obscenity and foul speech. Al-'Ajjaj said:
