The second is that it separated the feminine noun from the verb, so the masculine was applied, as in the saying of the poet:

"Indeed, a man whom one of you (women) deceives,
after me and after you, in this world, is deluded."

[Zad al-Masir: 1/305; Lisan al-Arab: 5/11.]

﴿And they mock those who believe﴾ because of their poverty.

It is narrated from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever humiliates a believing man or woman, or belittles him for his poverty and lack of means, Allah will expose him on the Day of Resurrection and then disgrace him. And whoever slanders a believing man or woman, or says about him what is not in him, Allah will station him on a hill of fire until he comes out of what he said about him. Indeed the believer is greater in the sight of Allah and more honoured by Him than a near angel. There is nothing more beloved to Allah than a believing man or woman who repents. Indeed the believer [man] is recognised in the heaven just as a man recognises his family and children." [109] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/29.]]

And from Ibrahim ibn Adham, who said: 'Abbad ibn Kathir ibn Qays narrated to us, who said: A man wearing a fine garment came and sat with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then a man wearing [lamar] [[as in the manuscript.]] came and sat with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He (the first man) gathered his garments around himself. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is it all this disgust at your Muslim brother? Were you afraid that something of his poverty would befall you, or of your wealth, something would befall him?" He said to the Prophet: "I apologise to Allah and to His Messenger. Indeed the soul commands evil, and Satan plots against me. I bear witness, O Messenger of Allah, that half of my wealth is his." The man said: "I do not want that." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "And why?" He said: "Lest my heart be corrupted as his heart was corrupted." [110]

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Do not belittle anyone among the Muslims, for the least of the Muslims is great in the sight of Allah." Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: "Evil is the people among whom, if a believer becomes wealthy, they envy him, and if he becomes poor among them, they humiliate him."

﴿And those who are mindful of Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

It is narrated from Abu Dhar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "O Abu Dhar, raise your eyes to the most exalted man you see in the mosque." I looked and saw a man sitting, wearing a fine garment, so I said: "This one." He said: "O Abu Dhar, raise your eyes to the lowliest man you see in the mosque." I looked and saw a weak man wearing worn-out clothes, so I said: "This one." The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, this one, in the sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, is better than the filling of the earth with the likes of that one." [111] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/170.]]

﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means abundantly, without loss and without [hindaz] [[as in the manuscript.]], because whatever is subject to reckoning is little.

Al-Dahhak said: it means without consequence. He provides for him in this world and does not call him to account or punish him in the Hereafter.

It has been said that this refers back to Allah, and on this view it allows two meanings. The first is that He is not obligated, and He is not held to account regarding what He provides, and it is not said to Him: "Why did You give this and withhold that? Why did You give this more than that?" because He has no partner in what He possesses, and no equal disputing with Him.

The other meaning is that He does not fear the exhaustion of His treasuries, so as to need to account for what goes out of them, when accounting is done by the giver in order to reach the appropriate measure of giving, so as not to exceed in giving to the point of harming Himself. He has no need of reckoning, because He is the Knowing, the Rich, who does not fear the exhaustion of His treasuries, for they are between the "kaf" and the "nun" (i.e., His command "Be" and it is).

﴿Mankind was one community﴾, the verse. Al-Hasan and 'Ata' said: mankind, from the time of the death of Adam until the sending of Nuh (peace be upon him), was one community upon one religion, which was disbelief. They were all disbelievers, like the beasts. ﴿So Allah sent Nuh and Ibrahim and others of the prophets﴾.

Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: mankind, from the time of Adam until the sending of Nuh, was one community, and there were ten centuries between Adam and Nuh, all upon one law of truth and guidance. Then they differed in the time of Nuh, ﴿so Allah sent to them Nuh﴾, who was the first prophet sent, ﴿then He sent after him the prophets﴾.

Al-Kalbi and al-Waqidi said: the people of Nuh's ark were all believers, then they differed after the death of Nuh.

﴿So Allah sent the prophets﴾. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: mankind in the time of Ibrahim was one community, all disbelievers, and Ibrahim's offspring were in jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). ﴿So Allah sent to them Ibrahim and other prophets﴾.

Al-Rabi' narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ubayy, who said: mankind, when they were presented to Adam and were brought out from his loins and acknowledged servitude, were one community, all Muslims, and they had never been one community other than on that day. Then they differed after Adam, so Allah sent the messengers and revealed the books. Likewise, in the recitation of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah ibn Ishaq: ﴿So they differed, and Allah sent the prophets﴾.

Muhammad ibn Yasar and Mujahid said: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ means Adam alone, who was named "the one" because he bears the offspring and is the father of mankind. Then Allah created Hawwa' (Eve) and spread from the two of them mankind, who spread and multiplied. They were all Muslims until Qabil killed Habil. Then they differed at that time, so Allah sent [prophets] at that time.

Al-Tha'labi said: I saw in some tafsirs: mankind was one community in [Paradise], with no commander over them and no prohibition, ﴿so Allah sent the prophets﴾. Their total was one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and the messengers among them were three hundred and thirteen, and those mentioned by name in the Qur'an are twenty-eight prophets.

﴿Bearers of good tidings﴾ of reward to those who believe and obey, ﴿and warners﴾ who warn of punishment to those who disbelieve and disobey.

Musa ibn 'Ubayd narrated from Muhammad ibn Thabit, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Send blessings upon the prophets and messengers of Allah, for Allah sent them just as He sent me." [112] [[Fadl al-Salat 'ala al-Nabi by al-Jahdhami: 48; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/523.]]

﴿And He sent down with them the Book﴾, that is, the books; He sent down with them the Book ﴿with truth﴾, with justice and truthfulness, ﴿to judge between the people﴾. The common reading is with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the kaf (*liyahkuma*, "that it may judge"), and it occurs in the Qur'an in four places: here, in Al 'Imran, and two places in al-Nur.

Abu Ja'far al-Qari' and 'Asim al-Jahdari read all of them with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the kaf (*liyuhkama*, "that it may be judged"), because the Book is the judge in reality; it is what judges. The common reading has two explanations. One is that it is figurative speech, as in His saying: ﴿This is Our Book, which speaks against you with truth﴾. The other is that its meaning is: that each prophet should judge by his book, and when he judges by the Book, it is as if the Book judges.

﴿Concerning that over which they differed﴾, ﴿and none differed over it﴾, that is, over the Book, ﴿except those who were given it﴾, that is, received it, and they are the Jews and Christians, ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾, meaning the rulings of the Torah and the Gospel.

Al-Farra' said: their differing has two meanings. One is that some of them disbelieved in the book of others, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾ [[Surah al-Nisa': 150.]] the verse [ ... ] [[unreadable word.]] and some of them declared others to be disbelievers. The other is their distortion and alteration of the Book of Allah the Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ [[Surah al-Nisa': 46.]].

It has been said: this verse refers back to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his book. The People of the Book differed concerning it after clear proofs had come to them, namely the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) in their books, ﴿out of insolent envy among themselves﴾, out of injustice and jealousy. ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed﴾, as in His saying: "Who guided us to this" and His saying: "They return to what they had said of truth, by His permission," by His knowledge and His will concerning them.

Ibn Zayd said concerning this verse: They differed about the prayer. Some pray facing the east, some face the west, and some face Bayt al-Maqdis, so Allah guided us to the Ka'bah. They differed about fasting: some fast part of a day, and some fast part of a night, so Allah guided us to the month of Ramadan. They differed about Friday: the Jews took Saturday and the Christians took Sunday, so Allah guided us to it. They differed about Ibrahim: the Jews said he was a Jew, and the Christians said he was a Christian, so Allah guided us to the truth in that. They differed about 'Isa: the Jews made him a son, and the Christians made him a lord, so Allah guided us to the truth regarding him. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/361.]]

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾.

﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while the example of those who passed away before you has not yet come to you?﴾, the verse. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: this verse was revealed concerning the Battle of the Trench, when the Muslims were afflicted with what befell them of hardship and difficulty [and heat and cold] and narrowness of living and various kinds of harm, as He said: ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud, and its parallel is in Al 'Imran: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾.

And it was said: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions said to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How long will you kill yourselves and not possess your wealth? If Muhammad were a prophet, he would not have been subjected to captivity and killing." So they said: "Undoubtedly, whoever among us is killed enters Paradise." So they said: "How long will you wish for yourselves falsehood [and you have heard] this verse."

'Ata' said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Madinah, the hardship intensified upon them, because they had left without wealth, so their lands and wealth were in the hands of the polytheists. So they preferred the pleasure of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and the pleasure of His Messenger (ﷺ). The Jews openly showed enmity to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a group of the wealthy secretly concealed hypocrisy. So Allah revealed, to comfort their hearts: ﴿Or did you think...﴾

"Am" here is an inceptive particle with no interrogation. The alif and mim are a connective; its meaning is "a'hasibtum" (did you think), as al-Farra' said.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "bal hasibtum" (rather, did you think), as in the saying of the poet:

"She appeared like the horn of the sun in the brightness of the forenoon,
and her form, or are you more graceful in the eye?"

[Lisan al-Arab: 14/54.]

That is, "bal anta" (rather, you). Everything in the Qur'an of this kind follows this path and this interpretation. The meaning of the verse is: did you suppose, while the Messenger (was among you), that you would enter Paradise, ﴿and the example has not yet come to you﴾, meaning "and it has not come to you," and its substance is like His exalted saying: ﴿And others from among them who have not yet joined them﴾. And al-Nabighah said:

"The time of departure has drawn near, but our riding beasts
have not yet stood by our saddles, as if it had already come."

[Lisan al-Arab: 3/346, "afad"; likewise in al-Mughni: 1/171.]

That is, "lam tazal" (they have not yet stood).

﴿The example of those who passed away before you﴾, who passed on, from the prophets and believers [and their way] [[as in the manuscript.]].

Then He mentioned what befell them, saying: ﴿Hardship touched them﴾, meaning poverty, harm, adversity and affliction, ﴿and adversity﴾, meaning illness and disease, ﴿and they were shaken﴾, that is, they were moved by various kinds of trials and calamities, and frightened, ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ Those trials were such that they were slow to receive provision. Allah said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾.

The reciters differed over His exalted saying ﴿yaqula al-Rasul﴾ (until the Messenger says). Mujahid read it with a fatha and a damma [on the lam]; al-A'raj: "yaqulu" with a raf'; and the others read it with a nasb. The one who reads with a nasb does so according to the apparent sense of the speech, because "hatta" (until) puts the following verb in the subjunctive. The one who reads with a raf' does so because its meaning is "hatta qala al-Rasul" (until the Messenger said). When the verb that follows "hatta" has the meaning of the past but the form of the present, you have the choice of raf' or nasb. The raf' is because "hatta" does not govern a past verb, and the nasb is by implying "an" (the light "an") according to the Basrans, and by "al-sarf" (the conversion) according to the Kufans. [Like your saying:] "We travelled until we enter Makkah" with raf', meaning "until we entered it." If it has the meaning of the future, then only the nasb is used.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Between Makkah and al-Ta'if there are found seventy [prophets] dead, whose cause of death was hunger and toil. Wahb also said: I read in a book of a man [among the Disciples]: "When the path of affliction leads you, then be content, for it has led you on the path of the prophets and the righteous. And when the path of ease leads you, then weep for yourself, [for it has] diverted you from their path."

[Shu'bah, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah], from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, from his father, that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which people are most severely tested?" He said: "The prophets, then the most excellent of people, then those next in excellence. A man is tested according to the measure of his religion. If his religion is firm, his trial is intensified, and if there is softness in his religion, then it is according to that measure. Affliction does not cease to befall the servant until He leaves him walking on the earth with no sin upon him." [113] [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/174.]]

And from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Dhahl, who said: The minister of 'Isa (peace be upon him), a rider, was one day seized by a predator which devoured him. 'Isa said: "O Lord! My minister in Your religion, and my helper against the Children of Israel, and my successor, You have set Your dog upon him, and it devoured him." He said: "Yes. He had an exalted station with Me. I did not find his deeds reached it, so I tested him with that to bring him to that station."

﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, the verse.

It was revealed concerning 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was an elderly man with wealth. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, with what should I give charity, and to whom should I give charity?" So Allah (ﷺ) revealed: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾.

There are two possibilities in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "dha" in the phrase "madha": one is that "madha" means "ayy shay'" (what thing), and it is [governed by] His saying "yunfiqun" (they spend), and its implied sense is: "They ask you what thing they should spend." The other is that it is in the nominative case with "ma" (what), and the meaning is: "They ask you, what is it that they spend?" ﴿Say: whatever you spend of good﴾, that is, wealth, ﴿is for parents and relatives and orphans and the needy and the traveller﴾, ﴿and whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾, Knowing of it with knowledge of the teachings of the religion. This was before the zakat was obligated, and then the zakat abrogated (naskh) this verse.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 211–215:

Ask the Children of Israel (*Sal Bani Isra'il*), meaning: ask, O Muhammad, the Jews of Madinah, how many clear signs (*ayah bayyinah*), that is, manifest proofs, such as the staff in the hand, the white hand, the splitting of the sea and others, We gave to their fathers and forebears.

﴿And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah﴾, meaning changes the Book of Allah, ﴿after it has come to him, then indeed Allah is severe in punishment. The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve﴾, the verse. Some said: this verse was revealed concerning the polytheists of the Arabs, Abu Jahl and his companions, who enjoyed the comforts that were brought to them in this world of wealth and forgot the Day of Return, ﴿and they mock﴾ the believers who turn away from the world and devote themselves to obedience and worship, saying: "If Muhammad were a prophet, our nobles would have followed him, but only the poor followed him, such as Abu 'Ammarah, Suhayb, 'Ammar, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Bilal, Khabbab and their like." This is the meaning of the narration of al-Kalbi from Ibn 'Abbas.

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, who enjoyed comfort in this world and mocked the weak believers and the poor emigrants, saying: "Look at these people whom Muhammad claims he will prevail through."

'Ata' said: it was revealed concerning the leaders of the Jews and their delegations from the Banu Qurayzah, al-Nadir and al-Qaynuqa', who mocked the poor emigrants, so Allah promised them that He would give them the wealth of the Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir without fighting, the easiest and most facile thing. [Allah] said: ﴿Where are those who disbelieve in the life of this world?﴾ This is according to the view of Mujahid.

(Zayyana) is read with a fatha on the zay and the ya', on the meaning that Allah made it attractive. The verb was made masculine for two reasons. The first is that the feminine marking of "al-hayah" (life) is not real, since the meaning of life, enduring, and living is one. The second is that it separated the feminine noun from the verb, so the masculine was applied, as in the saying of the poet:

"Indeed, a man whom one of you (women) deceives,
after me and after you, in this world, is deluded."

[Zad al-Masir: 1/305; Lisan al-Arab: 5/11.]

﴿And they mock those who believe﴾ because of their poverty.

It is narrated from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever humiliates a believing man or woman, or belittles him for his poverty and lack of means, Allah will expose him on the Day of Resurrection and then disgrace him. Indeed the believer [man] is recognised in the heaven just as a man recognises his family and children." [109] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/29.]]

It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud, and its parallel is in Al 'Imran: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾.

And it was said: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions said to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How long will you kill yourselves and not possess your wealth? If Muhammad were a prophet, he would not have been subjected to captivity and killing." So they said: "Undoubtedly, whoever among us is killed enters Paradise." So they said: "How long will you wish for yourselves falsehood [and you have heard] this verse."

'Ata' said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Madinah, the hardship intensified upon them, because they had left without wealth, so their lands and wealth were in the hands of the polytheists. So they preferred the pleasure of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and the pleasure of His Messenger (ﷺ). The Jews openly showed enmity to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a group of the wealthy secretly concealed hypocrisy. So Allah revealed, to comfort their hearts: ﴿Or did you think...﴾

"Am" here is an inceptive particle with no interrogation. The alif and mim are a connective; its meaning is "a'hasibtum" (did you think), as al-Farra' said.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "bal hasibtum" (rather, did you think), as in the saying of the poet:

"She appeared like the horn of the sun in the brightness of the forenoon,
and her form, or are you more graceful in the eye?"

[Lisan al-Arab: 14/54.]

That is, "bal anta" (rather, you). Everything in the Qur'an of this kind follows this path and this interpretation. The meaning of the verse is: did you suppose, while the Messenger (was among you), that you would enter Paradise, ﴿and the example has not yet come to you﴾, meaning "and it has not come to you," and its substance is like His exalted saying: ﴿And others from among them who have not yet joined them﴾. And al-Nabighah said:

"The time of departure has drawn near, but our riding beasts
have not yet stood by our saddles, as if it had already come."

[Lisan al-Arab: 3/346, "afad"; likewise in al-Mughni: 1/171.]

That is, "lam tazal" (they have not yet stood).

﴿The example of those who passed away before you﴾, who passed on, from the prophets and believers [and their way] [[as in the manuscript.]].

Then He mentioned what befell them, saying: ﴿Hardship touched them﴾, meaning poverty, harm, adversity and affliction, ﴿and adversity﴾, meaning illness and disease, ﴿and they were shaken﴾, that is, they were moved by various kinds of trials and calamities, and frightened, ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ Those trials were such that they were slow to receive provision. Allah said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾.

The reciters differed over His exalted saying ﴿yaqula al-Rasul﴾ (until the Messenger says). Mujahid read it with a fatha and a damma [on the lam]; al-A'raj: "yaqulu" with a raf'; and the others read it with a nasb. The one who reads with a nasb does so according to the apparent sense of the speech, because "hatta" (until) puts the following verb in the subjunctive. The one who reads with a raf' does so because its meaning is "hatta qala al-Rasul" (until the Messenger said). When the verb that follows "hatta" has the meaning of the past but the form of the present, you have the choice of raf' or nasb. The raf' is because "hatta" does not govern a past verb, and the nasb is by implying "an" (the light "an") according to the Basrans, and by "al-sarf" (the conversion) according to the Kufans. [Like your saying:] "We travelled until we enter Makkah" with raf', meaning "until we entered it." If it has the meaning of the future, then only the nasb is used.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Between Makkah and al-Ta'if there are found seventy [prophets] dead, whose cause of death was hunger and toil. Wahb also said: I read in a book of a man [among the Disciples]: "When the path of affliction leads you, then be content, for it has led you on the path of the prophets and the righteous. And when the path of ease leads you, then weep for yourself, [for it has] diverted you from their path."

[Shu'bah, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah], from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, from his father, that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which people are most severely tested?" He said: "The prophets, then the most excellent of people, then those next in excellence. A man is tested according to the measure of his religion. If his religion is firm, his trial is intensified, and if there is softness in his religion, then it is according to that measure. Affliction does not cease to befall the servant until He leaves him walking on the earth with no sin upon him." [113] [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/174.]]

And from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Dhahl, who said: The minister of 'Isa (peace be upon him), a rider, was one day seized by a predator which devoured him. 'Isa said: "O Lord! My minister in Your religion, and my helper against the Children of Israel, and my successor, You have set Your dog upon him, and it devoured him." He said: "Yes. He had an exalted station with Me. I did not find his deeds reached it, so I tested him with that to bring him to that station."

﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, the verse.

It was revealed concerning 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was an elderly man with wealth. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, with what should I give charity, and to whom should I give charity?" So Allah (ﷺ) revealed: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾.

There are two possibilities in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "dha" in the phrase "madha": one is that "madha" means "ayy shay'" (what thing), and it is [governed by] His saying "yunfiqun" (they spend), and its implied sense is: "They ask you what thing they should spend." The other is that it is in the nominative case with "ma" (what), and the meaning is: "They ask you, what is it that they spend?" ﴿Say: whatever you spend of good﴾, that is, wealth, ﴿is for parents and relatives and orphans and the needy and the traveller﴾, ﴿and whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾, Knowing of it with knowledge of the teachings of the religion. This was before the zakat was obligated, and then the zakat abrogated (naskh) this verse.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 211–215:

Ask the Children of Israel (*Sal Bani Isra'il*), meaning: ask, O Muhammad, the Jews of Madinah, how many clear signs (*ayah bayyinah*), that is, manifest proofs, such as the staff in the hand, the white hand, the splitting of the sea and others, We gave to their fathers and forebears.

﴿And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah﴾, meaning changes the Book of Allah, ﴿after it has come to him, then indeed Allah is severe in punishment. The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve﴾, the verse. Some said: this verse was revealed concerning the polytheists of the Arabs, Abu Jahl and his companions, who enjoyed the comforts that were brought to them in this world of wealth and forgot the Day of Return, ﴿and they mock﴾ the believers who turn away from the world and devote themselves to obedience and worship, saying: "If Muhammad were a prophet, our nobles would have followed him, but only the poor followed him, such as Abu 'Ammarah, Suhayb, 'Ammar, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Bilal, Khabbab and their like." This is the meaning of the narration of al-Kalbi from Ibn 'Abbas.

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, who enjoyed comfort in this world and mocked the weak believers and the poor emigrants, saying: "Look at these people whom Muhammad claims he will prevail through."

'Ata' said: it was revealed concerning the leaders of the Jews and their delegations from the Banu Qurayzah, al-Nadir and al-Qaynuqa', who mocked the poor emigrants, so Allah promised them that He would give them the wealth of the Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir without fighting, the easiest and most facile thing. [Allah] said: ﴿Where are those who disbelieve in the life of this world?﴾ This is according to the view of Mujahid.

(Zayyana) is read with a fatha on the zay and the ya', on the meaning that Allah made it attractive. The verb was made masculine for two reasons. The first is that the feminine marking of "al-hayah" (life) is not real, since the meaning of life, enduring, and living is one. The second is that it separated the feminine noun from the verb, so the masculine was applied, as in the saying of the poet:

"Indeed, a man whom one of you (women) deceives,
after me and after you, in this world, is deluded."

[Zad al-Masir: 1/305; Lisan al-Arab: 5/11.]

﴿And they mock those who believe﴾ because of their poverty.

It is narrated from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever humiliates a believing man or woman, or belittles him for his poverty and lack of means, Allah will expose him on the Day of Resurrection and then disgrace him. And whoever slanders a believing man or woman, or says about him what is not in him, Allah will station him on a hill of fire until he comes out of what he said about him. Indeed the believer is greater in the sight of Allah and more honoured by Him than a near angel. There is nothing more beloved to Allah than a believing man or woman who repents. Indeed the believer [man] is recognised in the heaven just as a man recognises his family and children." [109] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/29.]]

And from Ibrahim ibn Adham, who said: 'Abbad ibn Kathir ibn Qays narrated to us, who said: A man wearing a fine garment came and sat with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then a man wearing [lamar] [[as in the manuscript.]] came and sat with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He (the first man) gathered his garments around himself. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is it all this disgust at your Muslim brother? Were you afraid that something of his poverty would befall you, or of your wealth, something would befall him?" He said to the Prophet: "I apologise to Allah and to His Messenger. Indeed the soul commands evil, and Satan plots against me. I bear witness, O Messenger of Allah, that half of my wealth is his." The man said: "I do not want that." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "And why?" He said: "Lest my heart be corrupted as his heart was corrupted." [110]

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Do not belittle anyone among the Muslims, for the least of the Muslims is great in the sight of Allah." Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: "Evil is the people among whom, if a believer becomes wealthy, they envy him, and if he becomes poor among them, they humiliate him."

﴿And those who are mindful of Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

It is narrated from Abu Dhar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "O Abu Dhar, raise your eyes to the most exalted man you see in the mosque." I looked and saw a man sitting, wearing a fine garment, so I said: "This one." He said: "O Abu Dhar, raise your eyes to the lowliest man you see in the mosque." I looked and saw a weak man wearing worn-out clothes, so I said: "This one." The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, this one, in the sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, is better than the filling of the earth with the likes of that one." [111] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/170.]]

﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means abundantly, without loss and without [hindaz] [[as in the manuscript.]], because whatever is subject to reckoning is little.

Al-Dahhak said: it means without consequence. He provides for him in this world and does not call him to account or punish him in the Hereafter.

It has been said that this refers back to Allah, and on this view it allows two meanings. The first is that He is not obligated, and He is not held to account regarding what He provides, and it is not said to Him: "Why did You give this and withhold that? Why did You give this more than that?" because He has no partner in what He possesses, and no equal disputing with Him.

The other meaning is that He does not fear the exhaustion of His treasuries, so as to need to account for what goes out of them, when accounting is done by the giver in order to reach the appropriate measure of giving, so as not to exceed in giving to the point of harming Himself. He has no need of reckoning, because He is the Knowing, the Rich, who does not fear the exhaustion of His treasuries, for they are between the "kaf" and the "nun" (i.e., His command "Be" and it is).

﴿Mankind was one community﴾, the verse. Al-Hasan and 'Ata' said: mankind, from the time of the death of Adam until the sending of Nuh (peace be upon him), was one community upon one religion, which was disbelief. They were all disbelievers, like the beasts. ﴿So Allah sent Nuh and Ibrahim and others of the prophets﴾.

Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: mankind, from the time of Adam until the sending of Nuh, was one community, and there were ten centuries between Adam and Nuh, all upon one law of truth and guidance. Then they differed in the time of Nuh, ﴿so Allah sent to them Nuh﴾, who was the first prophet sent, ﴿then He sent after him the prophets﴾.

Al-Kalbi and al-Waqidi said: the people of Nuh's ark were all believers, then they differed after the death of Nuh.

﴿So Allah sent the prophets﴾. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: mankind in the time of Ibrahim was one community, all disbelievers, and Ibrahim's offspring were in jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). ﴿So Allah sent to them Ibrahim and other prophets﴾.

Al-Rabi' narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ubayy, who said: mankind, when they were presented to Adam and were brought out from his loins and acknowledged servitude, were one community, all Muslims, and they had never been one community other than on that day. Then they differed after Adam, so Allah sent the messengers and revealed the books. Likewise, in the recitation of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah ibn Ishaq: ﴿So they differed, and Allah sent the prophets﴾.

Muhammad ibn Yasar and Mujahid said: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ means Adam alone, who was named "the one" because he bears the offspring and is the father of mankind. Then Allah created Hawwa' (Eve) and spread from the two of them mankind, who spread and multiplied. They were all Muslims until Qabil killed Habil. Then they differed at that time, so Allah sent [prophets] at that time.

Al-Tha'labi said: I saw in some tafsirs: mankind was one community in [Paradise], with no commander over them and no prohibition, ﴿so Allah sent the prophets﴾. Their total was one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and the messengers among them were three hundred and thirteen, and those mentioned by name in the Qur'an are twenty-eight prophets.

﴿Bearers of good tidings﴾ of reward to those who believe and obey, ﴿and warners﴾ who warn of punishment to those who disbelieve and disobey.

Musa ibn 'Ubayd narrated from Muhammad ibn Thabit, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Send blessings upon the prophets and messengers of Allah, for Allah sent them just as He sent me." [112] [[Fadl al-Salat 'ala al-Nabi by al-Jahdhami: 48; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/523.]]

﴿And He sent down with them the Book﴾, that is, the books; He sent down with them the Book ﴿with truth﴾, with justice and truthfulness, ﴿to judge between the people﴾. The common reading is with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the kaf (*liyahkuma*, "that it may judge"), and it occurs in the Qur'an in four places: here, in Al 'Imran, and two places in al-Nur.

Abu Ja'far al-Qari' and 'Asim al-Jahdari read all of them with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the kaf (*liyuhkama*, "that it may be judged"), because the Book is the judge in reality; it is what judges. The common reading has two explanations. One is that it is figurative speech, as in His saying: ﴿This is Our Book, which speaks against you with truth﴾. The other is that its meaning is: that each prophet should judge by his book, and when he judges by the Book, it is as if the Book judges.

﴿Concerning that over which they differed﴾, ﴿and none differed over it﴾, that is, over the Book, ﴿except those who were given it﴾, that is, received it, and they are the Jews and Christians, ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾, meaning the rulings of the Torah and the Gospel.

Al-Farra' said: their differing has two meanings. One is that some of them disbelieved in the book of others, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾ [[Surah al-Nisa': 150.]] the verse [ ... ] [[unreadable word.]] and some of them declared others to be disbelievers. The other is their distortion and alteration of the Book of Allah the Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ [[Surah al-Nisa': 46.]].

It has been said: this verse refers back to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his book. The People of the Book differed concerning it after clear proofs had come to them, namely the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) in their books, ﴿out of insolent envy among themselves﴾, out of injustice and jealousy. ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed﴾, as in His saying: "Who guided us to this" and His saying: "They return to what they had said of truth, by His permission," by His knowledge and His will concerning them.

Ibn Zayd said concerning this verse: They differed about the prayer. Some pray facing the east, some face the west, and some face Bayt al-Maqdis, so Allah guided us to the Ka'bah. They differed about fasting: some fast part of a day, and some fast part of a night, so Allah guided us to the month of Ramadan. They differed about Friday: the Jews took Saturday and the Christians took Sunday, so Allah guided us to it. They differed about Ibrahim: the Jews said he was a Jew, and the Christians said he was a Christian, so Allah guided us to the truth in that. They differed about 'Isa: the Jews made him a son, and the Christians made him a lord, so Allah guided us to the truth regarding him. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/361.]]

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾.

﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while the example of those who passed away before you has not yet come to you?﴾, the verse. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: this verse was revealed concerning the Battle of the Trench, when the Muslims were afflicted with what befell them of hardship and difficulty [and heat and cold] and narrowness of living and various kinds of harm, as He said: ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud, and its parallel is in Al 'Imran: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾.

And it was said: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions said to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How long will you kill yourselves and not possess your wealth? And al-Nabighah said:

"The time of departure has drawn near, but our riding beasts
have not yet stood by our saddles, as if it had already come."

[Lisan al-Arab: 3/346, "afad"; likewise in al-Mughni: 1/171.]

That is, "lam tazal" (they have not yet stood).

Then He mentioned what befell them, saying: ﴿Hardship touched them﴾, meaning poverty, harm, adversity and affliction, ﴿and adversity﴾, meaning illness and disease, ﴿and they were shaken﴾, that is, they were moved by various kinds of trials and calamities, and frightened, ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ Those trials were such that they were slow to receive provision. Then a man wearing [lamar] [[as in the manuscript.]] came and sat with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He (the first man) gathered his garments around himself. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is it all this disgust at your Muslim brother? Were you afraid that something of his poverty would befall you, or of your wealth, something would befall him?" He said to the Prophet: "I apologise to Allah and to His Messenger. Indeed the soul commands evil, and Satan plots against me. I bear witness, O Messenger of Allah, that half of my wealth is his." The man said: "I do not want that." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "And why?" He said: "Lest my heart be corrupted as his heart was corrupted." [110]

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Do not belittle anyone among the Muslims, for the least of the Muslims is great in the sight of Allah." Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: "Evil is the people among whom, if a believer becomes wealthy, they envy him, and if he becomes poor among them, they humiliate him."

﴿And those who are mindful of Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

It is narrated from Abu Dhar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "O Abu Dhar, raise your eyes to the most exalted man you see in the mosque." I looked and saw a man sitting, wearing a fine garment, so I said: "This one." He said: "O Abu Dhar, raise your eyes to the lowliest man you see in the mosque." I looked and saw a weak man wearing worn-out clothes, so I said: "This one." The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, this one, in the sight of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, is better than the filling of the earth with the likes of that one." [111] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/170.]]

﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means abundantly, without loss and without [hindaz] [[as in the manuscript.]], because whatever is subject to reckoning is little.

Al-Dahhak said: it means without consequence. He provides for him in this world and does not call him to account or punish him in the Hereafter.

It has been said that this refers back to Allah, and on this view it allows two meanings. The first is that He is not obligated, and He is not held to account regarding what He provides, and it is not said to Him: "Why did You give this and withhold that? Why did You give this more than that?" because He has no partner in what He possesses, and no equal disputing with Him.

The other meaning is that He does not fear the exhaustion of His treasuries, so as to need to account for what goes out of them, when accounting is done by the giver in order to reach the appropriate measure of giving, so as not to exceed in giving to the point of harming Himself. He has no need of reckoning, because He is the Knowing, the Rich, who does not fear the exhaustion of His treasuries, for they are between the "kaf" and the "nun" (i.e., His command "Be" and it is).

﴿Mankind was one community﴾, the verse. Al-Hasan and 'Ata' said: mankind, from the time of the death of Adam until the sending of Nuh (peace be upon him), was one community upon one religion, which was disbelief. They were all disbelievers, like the beasts. ﴿So Allah sent Nuh and Ibrahim and others of the prophets﴾.

Qatadah and 'Ikrimah said: mankind, from the time of Adam until the sending of Nuh, was one community, and there were ten centuries between Adam and Nuh, all upon one law of truth and guidance. Then they differed in the time of Nuh, ﴿so Allah sent to them Nuh﴾, who was the first prophet sent, ﴿then He sent after him the prophets﴾.

Al-Kalbi and al-Waqidi said: the people of Nuh's ark were all believers, then they differed after the death of Nuh.

﴿So Allah sent the prophets﴾. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: mankind in the time of Ibrahim was one community, all disbelievers, and Ibrahim's offspring were in jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). ﴿So Allah sent to them Ibrahim and other prophets﴾.

Al-Rabi' narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ubayy, who said: mankind, when they were presented to Adam and were brought out from his loins and acknowledged servitude, were one community, all Muslims, and they had never been one community other than on that day. Then they differed after Adam, so Allah sent the messengers and revealed the books. Likewise, in the recitation of Ubayy and 'Abd Allah ibn Ishaq: ﴿So they differed, and Allah sent the prophets﴾.

Muhammad ibn Yasar and Mujahid said: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ means Adam alone, who was named "the one" because he bears the offspring and is the father of mankind. Then Allah created Hawwa' (Eve) and spread from the two of them mankind, who spread and multiplied. They were all Muslims until Qabil killed Habil. Then they differed at that time, so Allah sent [prophets] at that time.

Al-Tha'labi said: I saw in some tafsirs: mankind was one community in [Paradise], with no commander over them and no prohibition, ﴿so Allah sent the prophets﴾. Their total was one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and the messengers among them were three hundred and thirteen, and those mentioned by name in the Qur'an are twenty-eight prophets.

﴿Bearers of good tidings﴾ of reward to those who believe and obey, ﴿and warners﴾ who warn of punishment to those who disbelieve and disobey.

Musa ibn 'Ubayd narrated from Muhammad ibn Thabit, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Send blessings upon the prophets and messengers of Allah, for Allah sent them just as He sent me." [112] [[Fadl al-Salat 'ala al-Nabi by al-Jahdhami: 48; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 3/523.]]

﴿And He sent down with them the Book﴾, that is, the books; He sent down with them the Book ﴿with truth﴾, with justice and truthfulness, ﴿to judge between the people﴾. The common reading is with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the kaf (*liyahkuma*, "that it may judge"), and it occurs in the Qur'an in four places: here, in Al 'Imran, and two places in al-Nur.

Abu Ja'far al-Qari' and 'Asim al-Jahdari read all of them with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the kaf (*liyuhkama*, "that it may be judged"), because the Book is the judge in reality; it is what judges. The common reading has two explanations. One is that it is figurative speech, as in His saying: ﴿This is Our Book, which speaks against you with truth﴾. The other is that its meaning is: that each prophet should judge by his book, and when he judges by the Book, it is as if the Book judges.

﴿Concerning that over which they differed﴾, ﴿and none differed over it﴾, that is, over the Book, ﴿except those who were given it﴾, that is, received it, and they are the Jews and Christians, ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾, meaning the rulings of the Torah and the Gospel.

Al-Farra' said: their differing has two meanings. One is that some of them disbelieved in the book of others, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers﴾ [[Surah al-Nisa': 150.]] the verse [ ... ] [[unreadable word.]] and some of them declared others to be disbelievers. The other is their distortion and alteration of the Book of Allah the Exalted, as in His saying: ﴿They distort words from their places﴾ [[Surah al-Nisa': 46.]].

It has been said: this verse refers back to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his book. The People of the Book differed concerning it after clear proofs had come to them, namely the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) in their books, ﴿out of insolent envy among themselves﴾, out of injustice and jealousy. ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed﴾, as in His saying: "Who guided us to this" and His saying: "They return to what they had said of truth, by His permission," by His knowledge and His will concerning them.

Ibn Zayd said concerning this verse: They differed about the prayer. Some pray facing the east, some face the west, and some face Bayt al-Maqdis, so Allah guided us to the Ka'bah. They differed about fasting: some fast part of a day, and some fast part of a night, so Allah guided us to the month of Ramadan. They differed about Friday: the Jews took Saturday and the Christians took Sunday, so Allah guided us to it. They differed about Ibrahim: the Jews said he was a Jew, and the Christians said he was a Christian, so Allah guided us to the truth in that. They differed about 'Isa: the Jews made him a son, and the Christians made him a lord, so Allah guided us to the truth regarding him. [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/361.]]

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾.

﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while the example of those who passed away before you has not yet come to you?﴾, the verse. Qatadah and al-Suddi said: this verse was revealed concerning the Battle of the Trench, when the Muslims were afflicted with what befell them of hardship and difficulty [and heat and cold] and narrowness of living and various kinds of harm, as He said: ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud, and its parallel is in Al 'Imran: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove﴾.

And it was said: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions said to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How long will you kill yourselves and not possess your wealth? If Muhammad were a prophet, he would not have been subjected to captivity and killing." So they said: "Undoubtedly, whoever among us is killed enters Paradise." So they said: "How long will you wish for yourselves falsehood [and you have heard] this verse."

'Ata' said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Madinah, the hardship intensified upon them, because they had left without wealth, so their lands and wealth were in the hands of the polytheists. So they preferred the pleasure of Allah the Mighty and Majestic and the pleasure of His Messenger (ﷺ). The Jews openly showed enmity to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a group of the wealthy secretly concealed hypocrisy. So Allah revealed, to comfort their hearts: ﴿Or did you think...﴾

"Am" here is an inceptive particle with no interrogation. The alif and mim are a connective; its meaning is "a'hasibtum" (did you think), as al-Farra' said.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "bal hasibtum" (rather, did you think), as in the saying of the poet:

"She appeared like the horn of the sun in the brightness of the forenoon,
and her form, or are you more graceful in the eye?"

[Lisan al-Arab: 14/54.]

That is, "bal anta" (rather, you). Everything in the Qur'an of this kind follows this path and this interpretation. The meaning of the verse is: did you suppose, while the Messenger (was among you), that you would enter Paradise, ﴿and the example has not yet come to you﴾, meaning "and it has not come to you," and its substance is like His exalted saying: ﴿And others from among them who have not yet joined them﴾. And al-Nabighah said:

"The time of departure has drawn near, but our riding beasts
have not yet stood by our saddles, as if it had already come."

[Lisan al-Arab: 3/346, "afad"; likewise in al-Mughni: 1/171.]

That is, "lam tazal" (they have not yet stood).

﴿The example of those who passed away before you﴾, who passed on, from the prophets and believers [and their way] [[as in the manuscript.]].

Then He mentioned what befell them, saying: ﴿Hardship touched them﴾, meaning poverty, harm, adversity and affliction, ﴿and adversity﴾, meaning illness and disease, ﴿and they were shaken﴾, that is, they were moved by various kinds of trials and calamities, and frightened, ﴿until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: "When is the help of Allah?"﴾ Those trials were such that they were slow to receive provision. Allah said: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾.

The reciters differed over His exalted saying ﴿yaqula al-Rasul﴾ (until the Messenger says). Mujahid read it with a fatha and a damma [on the lam]; al-A'raj: "yaqulu" with a raf'; and the others read it with a nasb. The one who reads with a nasb does so according to the apparent sense of the speech, because "hatta" (until) puts the following verb in the subjunctive. The one who reads with a raf' does so because its meaning is "hatta qala al-Rasul" (until the Messenger said). When the verb that follows "hatta" has the meaning of the past but the form of the present, you have the choice of raf' or nasb. The raf' is because "hatta" does not govern a past verb, and the nasb is by implying "an" (the light "an") according to the Basrans, and by "al-sarf" (the conversion) according to the Kufans. [Like your saying:] "We travelled until we enter Makkah" with raf', meaning "until we entered it." If it has the meaning of the future, then only the nasb is used.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Between Makkah and al-Ta'if there are found seventy [prophets] dead, whose cause of death was hunger and toil. Wahb also said: I read in a book of a man [among the Disciples]: "When the path of affliction leads you, then be content, for it has led you on the path of the prophets and the righteous. And when the path of ease leads you, then weep for yourself, [for it has] diverted you from their path."

[Shu'bah, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah], from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, from his father, that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which people are most severely tested?" He said: "The prophets, then the most excellent of people, then those next in excellence. A man is tested according to the measure of his religion. If his religion is firm, his trial is intensified, and if there is softness in his religion, then it is according to that measure. Affliction does not cease to befall the servant until He leaves him walking on the earth with no sin upon him." [113] [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/174.]]

And from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Dhahl, who said: The minister of 'Isa (peace be upon him), a rider, was one day seized by a predator which devoured him. 'Isa said: "O Lord! My minister in Your religion, and my helper against the Children of Israel, and my successor, You have set Your dog upon him, and it devoured him." He said: "Yes. He had an exalted station with Me. I did not find his deeds reached it, so I tested him with that to bring him to that station."

﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, the verse.

It was revealed concerning 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was an elderly man with wealth. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, with what should I give charity, and to whom should I give charity?" So Allah (ﷺ) revealed: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾.

There are two possibilities in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "dha" in the phrase "madha": one is that "madha" means "ayy shay'" (what thing), and it is [governed by] His saying "yunfiqun" (they spend), and its implied sense is: "They ask you what thing they should spend." The other is that it is in the nominative case with "ma" (what), and the meaning is: "They ask you, what is it that they spend?" ﴿Say: whatever you spend of good﴾, that is, wealth, ﴿is for parents and relatives and orphans and the needy and the traveller﴾, ﴿and whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾, Knowing of it with knowledge of the teachings of the religion. This was before the zakat was obligated, and then the zakat abrogated (naskh) this verse.

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 216–218:**

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you.﴾ It was made obligatory (fard) upon you: fighting. The scholars differed concerning the ruling of this verse. Some of them said: it refers specifically to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and not to others. Ibn Jurayj said: I said to ʿAtaʾ, regarding His words, ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you﴾: "Is raiding (ghazw) obligatory upon the people because of it, or was it prescribed upon those people at that time?" Others applied the verse to its apparent meaning and said: raiding is an obligatory duty upon all Muslims until the Hour arrives.

Ibn Abi Unaysah narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three things are from the root of faith: refraining from one who says, 'There is no god but Allah,' so long as he does not commit a sin against it, and do not expel him from Islam by any deed; and jihad continues since Allah sent me until the last of my nation fights the Dajjal; it is not nullified by the tyranny of a tyrant nor the justice of a just ruler; and belief in the divine decrees." [114] [[Sunan Abi Dawud: 1/569, no. 253. After the word "Dajjal" it reads: "It is not nullified by the tyranny of a tyrant nor the justice of a just ruler." Similarly in al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi: 9/156.]]

Abu Salih narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies without having raided, and without having resolved in his soul to raid, dies upon a branch of hypocrisy." [115] [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/245, and Sahih Muslim: 6/94.]]

Others said: it is an obligation of sufficiency (fard kifayah): if some of the people undertake it, the obligation is lifted from the rest.

From Ahmad ibn Anmar: returning the greeting and blessing the one who sneezes. This is the sound, well-known view upon which the majority agree.

Al-Zuhri and al-Awzaʿi said: Allah prescribed jihad upon the people, whether they go out to fight or remain seated. Whoever goes out to fight, it is good and excellent; whoever remains seated is free. If he is sought for help, he assists; if he is called to march forth, he marches; and if he is not needed, he remains seated. Then what is obligatory is only to give wealth (to the expedition) by ʿAtaʾ; otherwise, no. Whoever wills may go out to fight, and whoever wills may not go out. The soundness of this view is shown by the words of Allah Most High: ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit back by a degree; yet to each Allah has promised the best reward﴾ [Q 4:95]. Had those who remain seated been neglecting an obligatory duty, they would have deserved the worst outcome, not the best. And Allah knows best.

﴿And it is hateful to you﴾: burdensome upon you. The readers agreed on pronouncing the letter kaf here with a damma (kurhun), except Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who read it as ﴿kurhun﴾ with a fatha (karhun). Both are two dialects with one meaning, like al-ghusl and al-ghusl, al-duʿf and al-duʿf, al-rahb and al-rahb. Most lexicographers said: al-kurh with a damma means hardship, and with a fatha means exertion. Some said: al-kurh with a fatha is the verbal noun (masdar), and with a damma is the noun (ism).

The people of meanings (ahl al-maʿani) said: this aversion arises from the natural disinclination of the soul toward it, because of the expense it entails upon wealth, the hardship upon the self, and the danger upon life; or because they openly showed aversion, or they disliked the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

ʿIkrimah said: this verse abrogated (nasakhat) the verse ﴿They say: "We hear and we obey"﴾ [Q 2:285]. He meant that they disliked it, then they came to love it; and so they said, "We hear and we obey." Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿It may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾, because in raiding there is one of the two excellent outcomes: either victory and spoils, or martyrdom and Paradise. ﴿And it may be that you love a thing while it is bad for you﴾, meaning remaining behind from raiding, ﴿for in it is humiliation and lowliness, deprivation of spoils and reward﴾. ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbas said: I was riding behind the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "O Ibn ʿAbbas, be content with Allah's decree, even if it opposes your desire, for it is recorded in the Book of Allah." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, where?" I had read the Qur'an. He said: "In two places." ﴿It may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing while it is bad for you﴾. [116] [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/470.]]

ʿAsim ibn ʿAli al-Masʿudi said: al-Hasan said: Do not dislike the calamities that befall you, nor the afflictions that arise, for often a matter you dislike contains your deliverance, and often a matter you hope for contains your destruction. Abu Saʿid al-Darir recited:

*How many a matter you fear draws you to what you approve,*
*its beloved hidden within it, and its hated thing made apparent.* [[Tarikh Madinat Dimashq: 42. It mentions that this is attributed to the Commander of the Faithful ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him.]]

[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/39.]

Muhammad ibn ʿArafah recited for ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Muʿtazz:

*Do not dislike the disliked thing when it descends upon you,*
*for the events of fate are ever varied.*

*How many a blessing you cannot fully thank,*
*within the course of events Allah has hidden it.*

ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hatim narrated from his father, who said: al-Mutawakkil sent a messenger to Muhammad ibn al-Layth, who had remained at his home for a period. When the messenger came to him, he [hesitated] and then mounted out of fear without his spirit. A man passed by him while he was saying:

*How many times did hardships surround you,*
*yet Allah chose for you while you disliked it.*

When he entered upon al-Mutawakkil, he appointed him governor of Egypt, granted him one hundred thousand, and everything he needed of equipment, mounts, and servants.

Al-Tha'labi said: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad recited to me, who said: Abu Saʿid Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Rumayh recited to me, who said: Muhammad ibn al-Farhan recited to me:

*How many a joy is folded for you within the folds of calamities,*
*and a harm has come from where you expected misfortunes.*

He said: Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi recited to us, who said: Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Wadddahi recited to us:

*Often a youth chooses, while he dislikes the good,*
*then joy comes from where the hardships come.*

﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it.﴾ The verse.

The exegetes said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh, who was the son of the Prophet's (ﷺ) paternal aunt, in Jumada al-Akhirah, two months before the battle of Badr, sixteen months after his arrival in Medina. With him he sent eight men of the Emigrants: Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas al-Zuhri, ʿUkkashah ibn Mihsan al-Asadi, ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwan al-Sulami, Abu Hudhayfah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Suhayl ibn Bayda, ʿAmir ibn Rabiʿah, Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah, and Khalid ibn Bukayr. He wrote for ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh, appointing him commander, a letter, and said: "Set out in the name of Allah, and do not look at the letter until you have traveled two days. When you have descended two stations, open the letter and read it to your companions, then proceed as I have commanded you. Do not compel any of your companions to march with you." ʿAbd Allah traveled two days, then halted, opened the letter, and in it was:

"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. To proceed: set out in the blessing of Allah with those who follow you from your companions, until you descend at the valley of Nakhlah, and keep watch there for the caravan of Quraysh, that perhaps you may bring us news of it."

When ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh read it, he said: "Hearing and obedience." Then he said this to his companions, and said: "He has forbidden me to compel any of you. Whoever desires martyrdom, let him set out; and whoever dislikes that, let him return, for I am proceeding in obedience to the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

He proceeded, and his companions proceeded with him; none of them stayed behind. When they reached a mine above al-Furaʿ called Najwan, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas and ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwan lost a camel of theirs which they had been riding in turns. They asked permission to stay behind to search for their camel, and he permitted them, so they stayed behind to search for it. ʿAbd Allah proceeded with the rest until they descended at the valley of Nakhlah, between Mecca and al-Taʾif. While they were there, a caravan of Quraysh passed by them carrying raisins, leather, and merchandise of the merchants of al-Taʾif, among them ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami, al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, and Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Makhzumiyyun. When they saw the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they feared them. ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh said: "The people are alarmed by you. Shave the head of one of you, and let him approach them; when they see him shaven, they will feel safe, and they will say, 'These are the people of ʿUmrah.'" So they shaved the head of ʿUkkashah, then he overlooked them and they said, "These are the people of ʿUmrah; there is no harm upon you," and they gave them safety.

That was on the last day of Jumada al-Akhirah, but they thought it was from Jumada, while it was from Rajab. The people consulted among themselves and said: "If you leave them this night, they will enter the Sanctuary, and they will be protected from you. So resolve your matter to engage the people." Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah [[In Tarikh al-Madinah: al-Tamimi.]] al-Sahmi shot ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami with an arrow and killed him. He was the first slain from the polytheists. They took al-Hakam and ʿUthman [[al-Hakam ibn Kaysan and ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah.]] as captives; they were the first two captives in Islam. The other two escaped and eluded them. The believers drove off the caravan and the two captives until they came before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina.

Quraysh said: "Muhammad has made lawful the sacred month, a month in which the fearful is secure and people are alarmed for their livelihood. He has shed blood in it, and taken captives in it." They reproached the Muslims who were in Mecca with this, and said:

"O assembly of the apostates, you have made lawful the sacred month, and fought in it!"

The Jews took an omen from this and said: "Waqid" means the war has been kindled (waqadat al-harb); "ʿAmr" means the war has been prolonged (ʿamarat al-harb); and "al-Hadrami" means the war has come present (hadarat al-harb).

When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said to Ibn Jahsh and his companions: "I did not command you to fight in the sacred month." He refused to take anything from that, and he returned the caravan and the two captives. This weighed heavily upon the companions of the expedition, and they thought they had been ruined; they were bewildered and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we killed Ibn al-Hadrami, then we entered the evening, and we looked at the crescent of Rajab, and we do not know whether we entered the evening in Rajab or in Jumada." The people disputed this, and Allah Most High revealed this verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the caravan and separated from it the fifth; it was the first fifth in Islam. He divided the rest among the companions of the expedition; it was the first spoil in Islam. The people of Mecca sent to ransom their captives, but he said: "Rather, we will hold them until Saʿd and ʿUtbah arrive; if they do not arrive, we will kill them." When they arrived, he ransomed them.

As for al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, he embraced Islam and remained with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina, and was killed as a martyr on the day of Bi'r Maʿunah. As for ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah, he returned to Mecca and died there as a disbeliever. As for Nawfal, he struck the belly of his horse on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) to enter the trench against the Muslims, so he fell into the trench with his horse, and both were smashed. Allah killed him, and the polytheists refrained from his corpse for a ransom. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Take him, for his corpse is foul and his blood-money is foul." [117] [[Asbab Nuzul al-Ayat: 44.]]

This is the occasion of revelation of His words, ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾, meaning, out of eagerness. It was named so because fighting in it is forbidden due to its great sanctity, and so it was called in the Jahiliyyah. He wrote for ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh, appointing him commander, a letter, and said: "Set out in the name of Allah, and do not look at the letter until you have traveled two days. When you have descended two stations, open the letter and read it to your companions, then proceed as I have commanded you. Do not compel any of your companions to march with you." ʿAbd Allah traveled two days, then halted, opened the letter, and in it was:

When ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh read it, he said: "Hearing and obedience." Then he said this to his companions, and said: "He has forbidden me to compel any of you. He proceeded, and his companions proceeded with him; none of them stayed behind. They asked permission to stay behind to search for their camel, and he permitted them, so they stayed behind to search for it. ʿAbd Allah proceeded with the rest until they descended at the valley of Nakhlah, between Mecca and al-Taʾif. While they were there, a caravan of Quraysh passed by them carrying raisins, leather, and merchandise of the merchants of al-Taʾif, among them ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami, al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, and Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Makhzumiyyun. When they saw the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they feared them. ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh said: "The people are alarmed by you. Shave the head of one of you, and let him approach them; when they see him shaven, they will feel safe, and they will say, 'These are the people of ʿUmrah.'" So they shaved the head of ʿUkkashah, then he overlooked them and they said, "These are the people of ʿUmrah; there is no harm upon you," and they gave them safety.

That was on the last day of Jumada al-Akhirah, but they thought it was from Jumada, while it was from Rajab. The people consulted among themselves and said: "If you leave them this night, they will enter the Sanctuary, and they will be protected from you. So resolve your matter to engage the people." Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah [[In Tarikh al-Madinah: al-Tamimi.]] al-Sahmi shot ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami with an arrow and killed him. He was the first slain from the polytheists. They took al-Hakam and ʿUthman [[al-Hakam ibn Kaysan and ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah.]] as captives; they were the first two captives in Islam. The other two escaped and eluded them. The believers drove off the caravan and the two captives until they came before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina.

Quraysh said: "Muhammad has made lawful the sacred month, a month in which the fearful is secure and people are alarmed for their livelihood. He has shed blood in it, and taken captives in it." They reproached the Muslims who were in Mecca with this, and said:

"O assembly of the apostates, you have made lawful the sacred month, and fought in it!"

The Jews took an omen from this and said: "Waqid" means the war has been kindled (waqadat al-harb); "ʿAmr" means the war has been prolonged (ʿamarat al-harb); and "al-Hadrami" means the war has come present (hadarat al-harb).

When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said to Ibn Jahsh and his companions: "I did not command you to fight in the sacred month." He refused to take anything from that, and he returned the caravan and the two captives. This weighed heavily upon the companions of the expedition, and they thought they had been ruined; they were bewildered and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we killed Ibn al-Hadrami, then we entered the evening, and we looked at the crescent of Rajab, and we do not know whether we entered the evening in Rajab or in Jumada." He divided the rest among the companions of the expedition; it was the first spoil in Islam. The people of Mecca sent to ransom their captives, but he said: "Rather, we will hold them until Saʿd and ʿUtbah arrive; if they do not arrive, we will kill them." When they arrived, he ransomed them.

As for ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah, he returned to Mecca and died there as a disbeliever. Allah killed him, and the polytheists refrained from his corpse for a ransom. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Take him, for his corpse is foul and his blood-money is foul." With him he sent eight men of the Emigrants: Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas al-Zuhri, ʿUkkashah ibn Mihsan al-Asadi, ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwan al-Sulami, Abu Hudhayfah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah, Suhayl ibn Bayda, ʿAmir ibn Rabiʿah, Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah, and Khalid ibn Bukayr. He wrote for ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh, appointing him commander, a letter, and said: "Set out in the name of Allah, and do not look at the letter until you have traveled two days. When you have descended two stations, open the letter and read it to your companions, then proceed as I have commanded you. Do not compel any of your companions to march with you." ʿAbd Allah traveled two days, then halted, opened the letter, and in it was:

"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. To proceed: set out in the blessing of Allah with those who follow you from your companions, until you descend at the valley of Nakhlah, and keep watch there for the caravan of Quraysh, that perhaps you may bring us news of it."

When ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh read it, he said: "Hearing and obedience." Then he said this to his companions, and said: "He has forbidden me to compel any of you. Whoever desires martyrdom, let him set out; and whoever dislikes that, let him return, for I am proceeding in obedience to the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

He proceeded, and his companions proceeded with him; none of them stayed behind. When they reached a mine above al-Furaʿ called Najwan, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas and ʿUtbah ibn Ghazwan lost a camel of theirs which they had been riding in turns. They asked permission to stay behind to search for their camel, and he permitted them, so they stayed behind to search for it. ʿAbd Allah proceeded with the rest until they descended at the valley of Nakhlah, between Mecca and al-Taʾif. While they were there, a caravan of Quraysh passed by them carrying raisins, leather, and merchandise of the merchants of al-Taʾif, among them ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami, al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughirah, and Nawfal ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Makhzumiyyun. When they saw the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they feared them. ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh said: "The people are alarmed by you. Shave the head of one of you, and let him approach them; when they see him shaven, they will feel safe, and they will say, 'These are the people of ʿUmrah.'" So they shaved the head of ʿUkkashah, then he overlooked them and they said, "These are the people of ʿUmrah; there is no harm upon you," and they gave them safety.

That was on the last day of Jumada al-Akhirah, but they thought it was from Jumada, while it was from Rajab. The people consulted among themselves and said: "If you leave them this night, they will enter the Sanctuary, and they will be protected from you. So resolve your matter to engage the people." Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah [[In Tarikh al-Madinah: al-Tamimi.]] al-Sahmi shot ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami with an arrow and killed him. He was the first slain from the polytheists. They took al-Hakam and ʿUthman [[al-Hakam ibn Kaysan and ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah.]] as captives; they were the first two captives in Islam. The other two escaped and eluded them. The believers drove off the caravan and the two captives until they came before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina.

Quraysh said: "Muhammad has made lawful the sacred month, a month in which the fearful is secure and people are alarmed for their livelihood. He has shed blood in it, and taken captives in it." They reproached the Muslims who were in Mecca with this, and said:

"O assembly of the apostates, you have made lawful the sacred month, and fought in it!"

The Jews took an omen from this and said: "Waqid" means the war has been kindled (waqadat al-harb); "ʿAmr" means the war has been prolonged (ʿamarat al-harb); and "al-Hadrami" means the war has come present (hadarat al-harb).

When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said to Ibn Jahsh and his companions: "I did not command you to fight in the sacred month." He refused to take anything from that, and he returned the caravan and the two captives. This weighed heavily upon the companions of the expedition, and they thought they had been ruined; they were bewildered and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we killed Ibn al-Hadrami, then we entered the evening, and we looked at the crescent of Rajab, and we do not know whether we entered the evening in Rajab or in Jumada." The people disputed this, and Allah Most High revealed this verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the caravan and separated from it the fifth; it was the first fifth in Islam. He divided the rest among the companions of the expedition; it was the first spoil in Islam. The people of Mecca sent to ransom their captives, but he said: "Rather, we will hold them until Saʿd and ʿUtbah arrive; if they do not arrive, we will kill them." When they arrived, he ransomed them.

As for al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, he embraced Islam and remained with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina, and was killed as a martyr on the day of Bi'r Maʿunah. As for ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah, he returned to Mecca and died there as a disbeliever. As for Nawfal, he struck the belly of his horse on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab) to enter the trench against the Muslims, so he fell into the trench with his horse, and both were smashed. Allah killed him, and the polytheists refrained from his corpse for a ransom. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Take him, for his corpse is foul and his blood-money is foul." [117] [[Asbab Nuzul al-Ayat: 44.]]

This is the occasion of revelation of His words, ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾, meaning, out of eagerness. It was named so because fighting in it is forbidden due to its great sanctity, and so it was called in the Jahiliyyah. They would remove the spear-heads and separate the arrow-shafts (?), because they used to remove the spear-heads and arrowheads upon the entry of Rajab, out of restraint from fighting in it. It was also called al-Asamm (the deaf), because the clash of weapons is not heard in it, and deafness was attributed to it, as it is said: "a sleeping night" and "a concealed secret."

This is indicated by what:

ʿAtaʾ narrated from ʿAʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Rajab is the month of Allah, and it is called al-Asamm. The people of the Jahiliyyah, when Rajab entered, would disable their weapons and put them down, and people would be safe, and the road would be secure, so that none feared another until it ended." [118] [[Kanz al-ʿUmmal: 12/311, no. 35167.]]

﴿About fighting in it﴾: in the genitive (khafḍ) by repetition of "ʿan" (about), its meaning being: "and about fighting in it." Likewise it is in the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas. ﴿Say, O Muhammad: fighting in it is a great matter﴾ (kabir), great, then [speech omitted] then fighting. ﴿And hindering from the way of Allah﴾: preventing from the path of Allah, as a subject beginning a sentence, and its predicate is ﴿greater﴾ (akbar). This was when they prevented the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the House. ﴿And disbelief in Him﴾, meaning in Allah; ﴿and in the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning and in the mosque; ﴿and expelling its people from it is greater﴾, meaning the people of the mosque, and it is greater in burden and punishment ﴿with Allah. And persecution﴾, meaning polytheism, ﴿is greater than killing﴾, meaning the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami. When this verse was revealed, ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh wrote to the believers of Mecca: "If the polytheists reproach you for fighting in the sacred month, then reproach them in turn with disbelief, and with the expulsion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Mecca, and with preventing them from the House."

Then He said: ﴿And they will not cease﴾, meaning the polytheists of Quraysh, and it is an intransitive verb with no object, like "ʿasā" (it may be), ﴿fighting you﴾, O assembly of believers, ﴿until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. And whoever of you apostatizes from his religion and dies while a disbeliever, those—their deeds are nullified﴾, meaning their good deeds are voided, ﴿in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ The root of ḥabaṭ is from ḥibāṭ, which is a corruption affecting livestock in their bellies from eating ḥibāṭ [[a kind of herbage]], which is that the belly swells and it dies. Then the crescent was called ḥabaṭ. Al-Hasan read ﴿ḥabiṭat﴾ with a fatha on the ba' throughout the Qur'an, and yaḥbaṭu with a kasra on the ba'. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾
