The companions of the expedition said: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be blamed for our sacred month? And do we hope that this journey of ours will be counted as a raid?" So Allah Most High revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who emigrated﴾, who left their clans, dwellings, and wealth, ﴿and struggled in the cause of Allah﴾ against the polytheists in support of the religion, ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, in obedience to Allah, so He made it jihad: ﴿those hope for the mercy of Allah, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 219–221 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling.﴾
It was revealed concerning ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), Muʿadh ibn Jabal, and a group of the Ansar who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling concerning wine and gambling, for they take away the intellect and deprive one of wealth." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse. The summary of the matter is that the prohibition of wine, according to the statements of the exegetes and the scholars of hadith, varies, and some of these statements agree with one another. It is that Allah revealed four verses concerning wine. The first, revealed in Mecca, was: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes you take from them an intoxicant (sakar)﴾, which is that which intoxicates. The Muslims used to drink it, and it was lawful for them at that time. Then, concerning the question of ʿUmar and Muʿadh, came: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾ When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed your Lord has ordained in advance the prohibition of wine." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/495.]] So some people abandoned it, due to His saying: ﴿in them is great sin﴾, and they said: "We have no need for anything that contains great sin." [119] Due to His saying: ﴿and benefits for people﴾, they continued to enjoy its benefits and avoid its sins, until ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf prepared a meal and invited some of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and wine was served before them. They drank and became intoxicated. When the time of the Maghrib prayer arrived, they put one of them forward to lead them in prayer, and he recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship...﴾ until the end of the surah, dropping the "not" (lā). So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying.﴾
Thus the intoxicant was prohibited during the times of prayer. ʿUmar said: "Indeed Allah has come close in forbidding the drinking of wine, and I do not see it except that He will prohibit it entirely." When it was revealed, [Allah prohibited it], some people abandoned it and said: "There is no good in a thing that comes between us and the prayer."
Some people continued to drink it in their houses, abstaining during the times of prayer and drinking it at other times, until a man [[Ibn Hajar mentioned that he was Abu Bakr. See Fath al-Bari: 10/31, ed. al-Maʿrifa, Beirut; also in al-Isabah: 4/22; and see Majmaʿ al-Zawaid: 5/51.]] among the Muslims drank it and began to lament over the dead of Badr, saying:
"Greet with peace Umm Bakr... and is there for you, after your kinsmen, any peace?
Leave me to drink wine in the morning, for I... would that death were far from the tents.
And the Banu al-Mughirah wished to ransom him with a thousand men or cattle.
As if I see the well of Badr... filled with bowls of the finest wood, crowned with fat humps.
As if I see the well of Badr... with the young men and the noble garments."
When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he went out hastily, dragging his cloak, until he reached him and raised something that was in his hand to strike him. When the man saw him, he said: "I seek refuge in Allah from the anger of Allah and the anger of His Messenger. By Allah, I will never eat it again." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/493.]]

And concerning Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, there is what was narrated: al-Zuhri related from ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, from his father, from his grandfather (peace be upon them), who said: "I had a she-camel (shārif) from my share of the spoils, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave me a portion of the fifth. I had arranged with a goldsmith to travel with me so that we could bring idhkhir (a fragrant plant) which I wished to sell, and with its price I would be assisted in the marriage to Fatimah and her wedding feast." [[Addition from Asbab al-Nuzul.]]
He said: "I brought my she-camel to the wall of a man from the Ansar, and I went to gather ropes, sacks and saddles. When I returned, her belly had been split open and her humps had been cut off (ijtabba: cut)." He said: "I could not hold back my tears, and I said: 'Who did this to my she-camel?' They said: 'Your uncle Hamzah did it, and he is in the house with them drinking. They have a singing girl, and they were merry.' She sang:
'Ah, O Hamz, of the high-hilled, with the camels kneeling in the courtyard,
He thrust the knife into their necks and reddened them with blood,
And fed from their slices a roasted meat, sizzling over the heat of the fire,
So prepare from their finest parts a broth for your drinking, from a pot or otherwise.
So you, O Abu ʿAmarah, are the one to be called upon to remove harm and affliction from us.'
Then he rose to your two she-camels and killed them." [ʿAli said:] "So I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in the house of Umm Salamah, with his freedman Zayd. He said: 'What brings you, may my father and mother be ransom for you, O ʿAli?' I said: 'What did my uncle do to my two she-camels?' and I told him the news. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, put on his sandals and cloak, and walked on, and I and Zayd followed him. He greeted and asked permission and entered the house, and said: 'O Hamzah, what moved you to do what you did to the two she-camels of your nephew?' He raised his head and began looking at the hands and shins of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He then fixed his gaze on him and said: 'Are you not, and your fathers, slaves of my father?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) backed away and said: 'Your sheep and camels are owed to me,' and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made him pay compensation for them." [[Asbab al-Nuzul, with variation: 139–140.]]

When morning came, Hamzah went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) apologising. He said: "Enough, O uncle, for you asked Allah and He pardoned you."

They also said: ʿUtban ibn Malik prepared a meal and invited men from among the Muslims, among them Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, and he had roasted the head of a camel for them. They ate and drank wine until it overcame them. Then they boasted before ʿUtban, traced their lineages and recited poetry to one another. Saʿd recited a qasidah containing satire of the Ansar and pride for his own people. A man from the Ansar rose, took the jawbone of the camel, and struck Saʿd on the head, wounding him. Saʿd went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained to him about the Ansari. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Allah, make clear to us Your judgment on wine with a complete clarification." So Allah revealed the prohibition of wine in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling... until ﴿so will you not desist?﴾﴾, and that was a few days after the Battle of the Confederates. ʿUmar said: "We have desisted, O Lord." [[Iʿanat al-Talibin: 4/174.]]

Anas said: "It was prohibited, and there was no livelihood more beloved to the Arabs than it on the day it was prohibited to them, and nothing was heavier upon them than its prohibition." He said: "We took the jars out to the road and poured out what was in them. Some of them broke their jars, and some washed them with water and clay. The alleys of Medina, after that time, whenever it rained, showed the color of wine by it and its scent spread."

As for the nature of wine (mahiyyat al-khamr), the jurists differed concerning it. Some of them said: it is specific to what is pressed from the grape and the date palm, which ferments by its own nature without the action of fire; anything other than that is not wine. This is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf and most of the people of opinion. Then they differed concerning what is cooked, and they said: every must that is boiled until two-thirds of it is gone is lawful, though it is disliked. If it is boiled until two-thirds is gone and one-third remains, it is lawful, permissible to drink and to sell, except that its intoxicating part is forbidden. They argued for this with what
Abu Kathir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wine is from these two trees: the date palm and the grapevine." [[al-Musannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzaq: 9/234, no. 7053.]] [120]

They differed concerning what is cooked with apricot [......] [[Illegible words.]] Nabatah narrated from Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wrote to some of his governors that the provision of the Muslims is the ṭilāʾ (boiled must) of which two-thirds have gone and one-third remains. [[Sunan al-Nasa'i: 8/328–329.]]

And from Ibn Sirin, that ʿAbd Allah ibn Suwayd al-Khatmi said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wrote to us: "To proceed: boil your drink until the portion of Satan is gone from it, for he has two parts and you have one." [[al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Nasa'i: 3/241.]]

And from Anas ibn Sirin, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: Satan disputed with Noah (peace be upon him) over a vine stalk. The one said: "This is mine," and the other said: "This is mine," and they agreed that Noah would have one third of it and Satan two thirds. [[Tarikh Dimashq: 62/259.]]

Ibn Abi ... and Abi from Dawud, who said: I asked Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab what was the rubb that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) made lawful. He said: that which is boiled until two-thirds is gone and one-third remains.

And from Qays ibn Abi ... narrated from Musa al-Umawi that he used to drink ṭilāʾ (what is boiled from must until it thickens, likened to the tar with which camels' mange is smeared) of which two-thirds had gone and one-third remained.

And from Yahya ibn Saʿid from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who said: when ṭilāʾ is boiled down to a third, there is no harm; and al-Musawwar said the same.

Al-Tha'alibi said: What I hold is that these reports refer to a third that is not intoxicating. This is shown by what Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Tufayl al-Jazari, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz wrote to us: "Do not drink ṭilāʾ until two-thirds of it have gone and one-third remains; every intoxicant is forbidden." Another group said: when must is boiled even slightly so that it becomes ṭilāʾ; this is the view of Ismaʿil ibn ʿUlayyah and a group of the people of Iraq.

It is narrated from ʿIsa ibn Ibrahim that he does not prohibit any of the nabidh (fermented drinks), neither the fresh (nayy) nor the cooked, except one drink, which is strong fresh grape juice that has not been mixed with water or altered, but only wine.

They also argued with what
Ibn al-Ahwas narrated from Simak, from al-Qasim ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Burdah ibn Sahl, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Drink in vessels, but do not get intoxicated." [121] Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sudi said: the hadith is munkar; Abu al-Ahwas Sallam ibn Sulaym erred in it, and we know of no one among the companions of Simak on whom reliance was placed; and Simak himself was not strong, and he would accept suggestion (talqin). [[See: Sunan al-Nasa'i: 3/232.]]

Ahmad said: It was said that Abu al-Ahwas was confused in this hadith; Shurayk differed from him in its chain and wording. Shurayk narrated it from Simak ibn Harb, from Abu Buraydah, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the diyya, the hantam, the naqir and the muzaffat. They also relied on what was traced to Simak from Qurasafah, a woman among them, from ʿAʾishah, who said: Drink, but do not get intoxicated.
Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, the Imam, said: this is not established, and we do not know who Qurasafah is. [[See al-Muhalla of Ibn Hazm: 7/486.]] The well-known report from ʿAʾishah is what Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated from ʿAbd Allah, from Qudamah al-ʿAmiri, that Jasrah bint Dujajah al-ʿAmiriyyah related to us, saying: I heard ʿAʾishah being asked by Ayyash about nabidh. They said: "We steep wine in the morning and drink it in the evening, and steep it in the evening and drink it in the morning." She said: "I do not make lawful any intoxicant, even if it is bread." They said: she said it three times. [[Sunan al-Nasa'i: 8/320–321.]]

They also argued with what Hushaym narrated from Ibn Shubrumah, who said: a trustworthy person related to me from ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: wine was forbidden in its entirety, its little and its much, and every intoxicant from every drink.

This is closer to the truth, for Sufyan narrated from Abu al-Juwayriyah al-Jarmi, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about al-baadhaq, and he said: whatever intoxicates is forbidden. And Shuʿbah narrated from Salamah ibn Kumayl, who said: I heard Abu al-Hakam relate that Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever is pleased to forbid what Allah and His Messenger forbade, let him forbid nabidh.

They also argued with what they traced to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Nafiʿ, who said: I saw Ibn ʿUmar... I saw a man come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a cup containing nabidh, while he was at the Corner (of the Kaʿbah). He handed him the cup, and he raised it to his mouth and found it strong, so he returned it to its owner. A man from the people said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it forbidden?" He said: "Bring the man to me." He was brought, and he took the cup from him, then called them both, poured it into it, raised it to his mouth and poured again, then called them again, poured into it, and said: "As for when these vessels have been used among you, break their sides with water."

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman said: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Rafiʿ is well known, but he related it to us, contrary to what Wahb ibn Harun narrated from Muhammad ibn ʿAmr, from Abu Salamah, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is forbidden, and every intoxicant is khamr." [122] [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/29.]]

Ibn Sirin narrated from Ibn ʿUmar: "The intoxicant, its little and its much, is forbidden." And Abu ʿAwanah narrated from Zayd ibn ʿUmar, who said: I asked Ibn ʿUmar about drinks, and he said: avoid everything in which there is an intoxicant.

They also argued with what they traced to Yahya ibn Yaman, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mikhlad ibn Saʿid, from Ibn Masʿud, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) became thirsty around the Kaʿbah, asked for drink, and was brought nabidh from the watering place (al-siqayah). He smelled it, frowned, and said: "Bring me a bucket of Zamzam water." He poured it over it, then drank. A man said: "Is it forbidden, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "No." [[Sunan al-Nasa'i: 8/325.]]

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman said: This report is weak, for Yahya ibn Yaman transmitted it alone apart from the companions of Sufyan, and Yahya ibn Yaman's narrations are not relied upon because of his many errors and poor memory.

And from Zayd ibn Waqid, from Khalid ibn al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Hurayrah say: I knew that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to fast on some of the days on which he fasted, so I sought out his breaking of the fast with nabidh that I had made in a gourd. When evening came I brought it to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I knew you were fasting on this day, so I prepared this nabidh for your iftar." He said: "Come close to me, O Abu Hurayrah." I lifted it to him, and it was hissing, and he said: "Take this and strike it against the wall, for this is the drink of one who does not believe in Allah and the Last Day." [[Sunan Abi Dawud: 2/192; al-Sunan al-Kubra: 3/237.]]

They also argued with what they traced to Sufyan, from Yahya ibn Saʿid, who said: I heard Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab say: Thaqif brought wine to ʿUmar, and he asked for it; when he brought it near his mouth he disliked it, so he mixed it with water and said: "Do thus." They also argued with what they traced to Abu Rafiʿ, that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "If you fear from nabidh its strength, then break it (with water)." [[Ibid.]]

They also argued with what one of our companions, ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, said: the meaning of "break it with water" is before it becomes strong. The evidence for this interpretation is what Ibn Shihab (who is Sufyan ibn Yazid) narrated, that ʿUmar came out to them and said: "I found the smell of drink on so-and-so, and he claimed he drank ṭilāʾ. I will question what they drink; if it is intoxicating, I will flog him," and ʿUmar gave him the full prescribed flogging.

Ibrahim narrated from Ibn Sirin, who said: he considers it a must (ʿasir) from the one who prepares it as ṭilāʾ, and does not consider it wine. Abu Saʿid said: ṭilāʾ is that which has been boiled until two-thirds are gone and one-third remains; it was so named because it resembles the tar of camels in its thickness and blackness. [[al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi: 8/295.]]

ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras said:
"It is wine, called ṭilāʾ, as the wolf is called Abu Jaʿdah." [[Ibid.]]

Al-Tha'alibi said: The ṭilāʾ for which concession was given is in fact the rubb, for when it is boiled down to a third, its intoxication and its evil are gone and its devil has departed.

They also argued with what Hushaym narrated from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim, that a thick melon drink was brought to him, and he would taste it and wash it with what was intoxicating.

And from Mughirah, from Abu Maʿshar, from Ibrahim, who said: there is no harm in melon nabidh.

From Abu Usamah, who said: I heard Ibn al-Mubarak say: I have not found a concession regarding intoxicants authentically from anyone except Ibrahim.

Hammad ibn Salamah, from ʿUmar, from Anas, who said: Umm Salamah had a cup, and she said: "I gave the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) every kind of drink: water, honey, milk and nabidh."

And from Ibn Shubrumah, who said: Talhah ibn Musarrif said to the people of Kufa concerning nabidh: "In it the young grow and the old age." He said: al-Miqdad and al-Zubayr used to give milk mixed with honey to drink. It was said to Talhah: "Shall we not give them nabidh?" He said: "I dislike that a Muslim should become intoxicated in my Sunnah."

And from Sufyan, who said: Talhah's statement was mentioned to Abu Ishaq regarding nabidh, and Ibn Ishaq said: "I gave it to the companions of ʿAli and the companions of ʿAbd Allah in al-Khawafi before Talhah was born." And from Ibn Shubrumah, who said: "May Allah have mercy on Ibrahim: he was strict with people regarding nabidh and he also granted concession in it."

They also argued with what they traced to ʿAbd Allah ibn Buraydah, from his father, that while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was traveling, he came upon a people and heard a clamor from them. He said: "What is this sound?" They said: "O Prophet of Allah, they have a drink they are drinking." The Prophet sent to them and called them and said: "What do you make nabidh in?" They said: "We make nabidh in the naqir and the dubba'; we have no other vessels." He said: "Do not drink except what you have sealed." He remained so for as long as Allah willed, then returned to them and found that a plague had struck them and they had become pale. He said: "What is wrong with you? I see you have perished." They said: "O Prophet of Allah, our land is unhealthy, and you forbade us except what we have sealed." He said: "Drink, and every intoxicant is forbidden." [[al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi: 3/226, no. 5165.]]

They said: By this he meant the khamr that produces intoxication, because nabadh is that which brings elation and vigor, and these are only obtained from an intoxicating drink.

Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to have nabidh made for him in [a jar of ʿAfar] [[So in the manuscript.]].

Al-Tha'labi said: It is possible that these reports and similar ones have two meanings. The first is that they came before the prohibition of wine (khamr, intoxicating drink). The second, which is closer to the correct view, is that by *nabidh* (a steeped drink, made by soaking dates or raisins in water) they meant water in which dates or raisins had been soaked until it took on their sweetness and strength, before it fermented and became intoxicating. What indicates this is what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would have *nabidh* prepared for him, and he would drink it that day, the next day, and the day after.

Al-A'mash narrated from Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would have raisin *nabidh* steeped for him at night, placed in a water-skin, and he would drink it that day, the next day, and the day after. When it reached the last of the vessels, he would give it to be drunk or drink it himself, and if any of it remained in the morning, he would pour it out.

And from 'Abdullah ibn al-Daylami, from his father Fayruz, who said: I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are people of vineyards, and Allah has revealed the prohibition of wine, so what should we do?" He said: "Make it into raisins." I said: "And what should we do with the raisins?" He said: "Soak them for your midday meal and drink them for your evening meal, and soak them for your evening meal and drink them for your midday meal." I said: "Shall we not delay it until it becomes strong?" He said: "Do not put it in baskets; put it in waterskins, for if it is delayed it becomes wine."

And from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that he would have *nabidh* steeped for him in a raisin waterskin in the morning and drink it at night, and would have it steeped in the evening and drink it in the morning. He would wash the waterskins and would not put in them any *nardi* (a kind of date-based drink) or anything else. Nafi' said: "We used to drink it like honey."

And from Bassam, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far about *nabidh*, and he said: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn would have it steeped for him at night and drink it in the morning, and have it steeped in the morning and drink it at night.

And from 'Abdullah, who said: I heard Sufyan, when he was asked about *nabidh*, say: "I steep it in the evening and drink it in the morning."

These reports indicate that it was the steeping of raisins and dates before it fermented.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Thawr, and most of the people of hadith said: *khamr* is every intoxicating drink, whether it is the juice of grapes or not. Whether it is cooked or raw, every intoxicating drink is forbidden, whether little or much, and the one who drinks it is liable to the *hadd* (the prescribed legal punishment), except that one who consumes a cooked drink [after two-thirds of it has evaporated], for he is not subject to the *hadd*, and his testimony is not rejected. The linguistic proof for this school is that *khamr* originally means "covering." Anything that covers something, whether a tree, a stone, or other things, is called *khamr*. It is said: "So-and-so covered (kharrama) the people's ... " and from it comes *khimar* (a woman's head-cover) and *khumrat al-sajjadah* (the cover of a prayer mat). *Khamr* was named so because it covers the intellect. What indicates this is what al-Sha'bi narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: 'Umar gave a sermon and said: "The prohibition of *khamr* has been revealed, and it is made from five things: grapes, dates, wheat, barley, and honey. *Khamr* is that which covers the intellect."

Anas ibn Malik said: "It was named *khamr* because they used to leave it in jars until it fermented (takhtamir) and changed."

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "*Khamr* was named so only because it is left until its clear part is settled and its sediment has sunk."

Anas said: "*Khamr* was prohibited, and most of their *khamr* at that time was *fadikh*." He said: "In Medina they did not make *khamr*, and they did not have enough grapes to make it. We only heard of *khamr* in the lands of non-Arabs. We used to drink *fadikh* made from dates and unripe dates. *Fadikh* is what is crushed from dates and unripe dates without being touched by fire."

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "It is not *fadikh* but *fadukh*."

Their evidence from the Sunnah is what Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is *khamr*, and every *khamr* is intoxicating and forbidden." [123] [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/29.]]

Salim ibn 'Abdullah narrated from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is *khamr*, and whatever intoxicates in large quantity, its small quantity is also forbidden." [124] [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/91.]]

From Abu 'Uthman 'Amr ibn Salim al-Ansari, from al-Qasim, from 'A'ishah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "If the *gharq* of it intoxicates, then a handful of it is forbidden." *Gharq* is a vessel that holds sixteen *ratl* (a unit of weight).

And from Abu al-Ghusn, known as Hujja, who said: Hisham ibn 'Urwah said to me: "Do you drink *nabidh*?" I said: "Yes, by Allah, I drink it." He said: "My father narrated to me from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Every intoxicant is forbidden, both its beginning and its end.'" [125] [[Tadhkirat al-Huffaz by al-Dhahabi: 3/1000.]]

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said: "Indeed, from dates there is *khamr*, indeed from grapes there is *khamr*, indeed from raisins there is *khamr*, indeed from honey there is *khamr*, indeed from wheat there is *khamr*, indeed from barley there is *khamr*, indeed from millet there is *khamr*, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [126]

From Ibn Sirin, who said: A man came to Ibn 'Umar and said: "Our family steeps a drink for us in the evening, and when we wake in the morning we drink it." He said: "I forbid you from an intoxicant, whether little or much, and worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic. I forbid you from an intoxicant, whether little or much, and worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Do you know that the people of Khaybar steep a drink for themselves, which they call such-and-such, and that your father steeped a drink from such-and-such, which they call such-and-such, and it is *khamr*?" He went on counting four drinks for him, the last of which was honey. [[Al-Musannaf by Ibn Abi Shaybah: 5/474.]]

From 'Ikrimah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon some of his wives when they had steeped grape juice for themselves in a jug, so he poured it out and broke the jug.

'Ubadah ibn al-Samit narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my nation will make *khamr* lawful under a name they give it." [127] [[Al-Durr al-Manthur: 324, with variations.]]

And it is narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "As for *khamr*, it was not forbidden because of its name; it was forbidden because of what is in it. Every drink whose end result is *khamr* is forbidden." [128] [[Sunan al-Daraqutni: 4/171.]]

It is related that a man from the wise men of the Arabs was asked: "Why do you not drink *nabidh*?" He said: "Allah granted me my intellect sound, so how could I bring into it what spoils it?" [[From the book Dhamm al-Sukr by Ibn Abi al-Dunya: 77, where the text reads: "By Allah, I do not accept my intellect being sound..."]]

*Al-Maysir* (gambling) means *al-qimar*. Ibn 'Abbas said: In the Jahiliyyah, a man would gamble with another man over his family and his wealth. Whichever of them won against his companion would take away his wealth and his family. So Allah, Exalted, revealed this verse.

*Al-maysir* is on the pattern *maf'il* from the saying of the speaker: "*yasura hadha al-shay'*" when it became obligatory, so he says *yayassaru yasran* and *maysiran*. *Al-yasir* is the one who shoots with arrows, whether that is obligatory or permitted or otherwise. Then gambling was called *maysir*, and the gambler was called *yasir* and *yasar*. Al-Nabighah said:

"Or a gambler whose arrows have taken away his fortune, a bereaved one whom his friend has left sad, with a broken heart."

Another poet said:

"So I spent the night as if I were a bereaved gambler, turning over the arrows after they had been drawn out."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/475.]]

Muqatil said: It was called *maysir* because they would say: "*Yasar huwa lana*" ("it is easy for us"), and the price of the camel. The origin of *yasar* is in the camel, for the wealthy Arabs would buy a camel, slaughter it, and divide it into portions.

They differed about the number of portions. Abu 'Amr said: ten. Al-Asma'i said: it is twenty. Then they would place on it ten arrows. It is said that with them are the *azlam* (divining arrows), and seven of them have shares: *al-fadh* (the single one), which has one share; *al-tawam* (the twin), which has two; *al-raqib*, which has three; *al-jals*, which has four; *al-nafis*, which has five; *al-musil*, which has six; and *al-mughalla*, which has seven. Three of them have no shares: *al-nasij*, *al-safaniz*, and *al-wagh*.

Then they would put the arrows in a bag called *al-rabab*. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"And it is as if they were a *rabab*, and he is like a *yasar* that spills over the arrows and splits them."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 14/90; al-Sihah: 1/132.]]

They would place the *rabab* in the hand of a man among them who was trusted, called *al-mujil* and *al-mufid*. He would shake it and draw out an arrow bearing the name of one of them. Whoever's arrow came out would take his share in accordance with what was drawn. If one of the three without shares came out, they would disagree about it, and each one of them would be obliged to pay the full price of the camel.

Some of them said: he takes nothing and pays nothing, and that arrow is void, so it is drawn again a second time. These are the gamblers (*al-yasiriyyun*) and the players (*al-iyasar*). Then they would give that camel to the poor and would not eat any of it. They took pride in this and would blame whoever among them did not do so, calling him *al-barim*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah said:

"Nor a *barim* to whose wedding the women bring gifts, when the rattling skin is shaking in the cold of winter."

[[Kitab al-'Ayn by al-Farahidi: 1/65.]]

So the origin of this gambling was what the Arabs used to do, and Allah, Exalted, in this verse forbade all kinds of gambling.

Layth narrated from Tawus, Mujahid, and 'Ata', who said: Everything in which there is gambling is *maysir*, even the children's games with knucklebones and dice.

From Abu al-Ahwas, from 'Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of these two marked knucklebones, for they are from the gambling of the non-Arabs." [129] [[Al-Adab al-Mufrad by al-Bukhari: 271.]]

And from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, that 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) said about backgammon (*nard*) and chess (*shatranj*): "They are from *maysir*."

And from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, who said: Everything that diverts from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer is *maysir*.

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both there is great sin and great harm, and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾ The great sin includes quarrelling, abusing, speaking obscenity and falsehood, loss of the intellect, prevention from the prayer, and taking the property of others without right.

The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read *kathir* with the letter *tha'*, and the rest read it with *ba'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose the reading with *ba'* because of Allah's saying: ﴿and their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ and His saying: ﴿a great sin (huban kabiran)﴾.

"And benefits for people" means what they used to gain from wine through trade and pleasure when drinking them. Al-A'sha says:

"For us, from its sobriety comes bad temper and sorrow, and remembrance of worries whose after-effects do not leave."

"And during the evening there is joy of soul and pleasure, and abundant wealth, the cost of its drinking bouts."

[[Jami' al-Bayan by al-Tabari: 2/489.]]

The benefit of gambling is what is won from gambling and what the poor benefit from.

﴿But their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾ The exegetes said: The sin of wine is that a man drinks and becomes intoxicated, and so harms people. The sin of gambling is that a man gambles, withholds what is due, and oppresses.

Al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: The benefits were before the prohibition, and the sin is after the prohibition.

﴿They ask you what they should spend.﴾ That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged them to give charity and encouraged them to do so without any obligation. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what should we spend? And to whom should we give charity?" So Allah, Exalted, revealed: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, meaning, what thing they should spend, and it is an interrogative. ﴿Say: The surplus.﴾

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu 'Amr read *al-'afwu* with *damma* (nominative), and Muhammad ibn al-Sadi chose it in the sense: "What they spend is the surplus," evidenced by Allah's saying: ﴿And when it is said to them: What has your Lord revealed? They say: Fables of the ancients.﴾ [[Surat al-An'am: 25.]] The others read it with *fatha* (accusative), and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose it: "Say: They spend the surplus." [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/61.]]

They differed about the meaning of *al-'afw*. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Qatadah, 'Ata', al-Sudi, and Ibn Abi Layla said: it is what remains of wealth after dependents are provided for; this is the narration of Muqsim from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Hasan said: It is that you do not strain your wealth in spending and then sit down begging from people.

Al-Walibi said, from Ibn 'Abbas: It is what is not clearly visible in your wealth.

Mujahid said: It is charity that is from the richness of a rich man.

'Amr ibn Dinar and 'Ata' said: It is the middle course of spending, neither extravagance nor stinginess.

Al-Dahhak said: It is what one can bear.

Al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas, said: Whatever they bring you of something small or great, accept it from them.

Tawus and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: We heard [Bishr] say: "*Al-'afw* is the ease of everything."

Al-Rabi' said: *Al-'afw* is the good; he says: the best of your wealth is what you spend.

All of these are close in meaning. The meaning of *al-'afw* in the language is surplus and abundance. Allah said: ﴿until they multiplied (hatta 'afaw)﴾, meaning they increased. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let the beards grow (a'fu al-lihā)." A poet said:

"But we, the sword bites among us, with fat-laden, abundant thighs."

That is, with many fats. *Al-'afw* is what a person gives or takes easily without hardship, from the saying of the Arabs: "'afa," meaning he obtained it easily without compulsion. A similar report to this verse is what Abu Hurayrah narrated: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have some good." He said: "Spend it on yourself." He said: "I have another." He said: "Spend it on your family." He said: "I have another." He said: "Spend it on your children." He said: "I have another." He said: "Spend it on your parents." He said: "I have another." He said: "Spend it on your relatives." He said: "I have another." He said: "You know best."

Mahmud ibn Sahl narrated from 'Amir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a gold nugget that he had extracted from one of the mines, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, take it from me as charity, for by Allah, I have nothing else to own." He turned away from him. Then he came from his right side and said the same, and he turned away. Then he came from his left side and said the same, and he turned away. Then he said the same again, and [the Prophet] said in anger: "Give it here." He took it from him and threw it at him with a throw that would have wounded or injured him. Then he said: "Does one of you bring everything he owns to give in charity and then sit begging from people? The best charity is that given from a state of richness. Let one of you begin with those he supports."

Al-Kalbi said: After the revelation of this verse, when a man had wealth in gold, silver, crops, or livestock, he would look at what would suffice himself and his dependents for a year, and keep it, and give the rest in charity. If he was one who worked with his hands, he would keep what sufficed himself and his dependents for that day, and give the rest in charity. Then the obligatory *zakat* was revealed, and it abrogated (*nasakhat*) this verse, and every charity they had been commanded before the revelation of *zakat* was abrogated.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "thus" in the singular while addressing a group, because the group means a tribe, as if he said: "O tribe, Allah makes clear to you." It is also permissible that it be addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), because his address includes the address to his nation, as in His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾.

Al-Mufadhdhal ibn Salamah said: The meaning of the verse, ﴿thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾ concerning spending, ﴿so that you may reflect﴾ on this world and the Hereafter, so you retain from your wealth what is good for your livelihood in this world, and spend the rest on what benefits you in the Hereafter.

Most exegetes said: Its meaning is: Allah makes clear to you the signs concerning the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, ﴿so that you may reflect﴾ on the passing and ending of this world, so you may renounce it, and on the coming and departure of the Hereafter, so you may desire it.

﴿They ask you about orphans.﴾ Al-Dahhak, al-Sudi, and Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of 'Atiyyah, said: The Arabs in the Jahiliyyah would greatly honor the status of an orphan and be severe about his affairs, to the point that they would not eat with him, would not ride his animal, would not employ his servant, and would avoid mixing their property with his, considering it inauspicious. When Islam came, they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about this, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse.

Qatadah, al-Rabi', and Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, said: When the verse ﴿and do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner until he reaches maturity﴾ was revealed concerning the affairs of orphans, and His saying ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾, they withdrew from the property of orphans, separated their food from the orphan's food, and avoided mixing with them in everything, to the point that food would be prepared for an orphan and some of it would be left over, and they would leave it and not eat it until it spoiled. This became very hard on them, and they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and this verse was revealed: ﴿They ask you about orphans.﴾

﴿Say: Setting things right for them is best.﴾ Tawus read: "Say: Setting things right for them is better," meaning setting right their property without a wage, and without compensation for them, is better and greater in reward.

﴿And if you mix with them﴾, by partnering with them in their property, and mixing your property with theirs in your expenses, food, housing, servants, and animals, so that you receive from their property as compensation for your work in their affairs, and you repay them for what you take from their property, ﴿then they are your brothers﴾, meaning they are your brothers. Abu Mijlaz read: "*fa-ikhwanukum nasiba*," meaning: so mix with your brothers, or "so your brothers mix with you." Brothers help one another and keep one another in view. It is said: "*ba'ada 'ala wajh al-islah wa al-rida*" ("he did it in the manner of reform and contentment"). 'A'ishah said: "I dislike that the property of an orphan be with me as an ill-gotten thing until I mix his food with mine and his drink with mine."

Then He said: ﴿And Allah knows the one who corrupts from the one who sets right﴾. So fear Allah regarding the property of orphans, and do not make your mixing with them a means to corrupting their property and consuming it without right. ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have burdened you﴾, meaning He would have constricted you and made you sinful for your wrongdoing toward them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "And if Allah had willed, He would have made what you took from the property of orphans a destruction."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 219–221 (part 3 of 3):

The root of ʿanat (ʿanat: hardship, distress) is hardship and difficulty. It is said: "ʿaqabahu ʿanūt," meaning it is a steep, arduous climb. Al-Zajjaj said: the root of ʿanat is that a camel's leg suffers a break after having been set, so that it cannot walk. Al-Qutami said:

"They did not deal kindly with anyone who sought their ʿanat (hardship), nor did they spoil the good they had done."
[Amali al-Murtada: 3/104.]

﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾ — the verse was revealed concerning ʿAmmar ibn Abi Marthad al-Ghanawi.

Muqatil said: he is Abu Marthad al-Ghanawi, whose name was Ayman.

ʿAta' said: he is Abu Marthad ʿAmmar ibn al-Husayn, who was a brave and strong man. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent him to Makkah to secretly bring out some Muslims from it. When he arrived there, a polytheistic woman called ʿAnaq, who had been his lover in the Jahiliyyah, heard of him, came to him and said: "O Marthad, will you not be alone with me?" He said to her: "Woe to you, ʿAnaq! Islam has come between us and that." She said: "Then would you marry me?" He said: "Yes, but I must return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and seek his permission, and then I will marry you." She said: "Are you being stubborn with me?" Then she called for help against him, and they beat him severely, then let him go. When he had finished his task in Makkah and returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he informed him of what had happened to him, of the matter of ʿAnaq, and of what he had suffered because of her, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it lawful for me to marry her?" Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾, meaning: do not marry them until they believe.
[Zad al-Masir of Ibn al-Jawzi: 1/221.]

Al-Mufaddal said: the original meaning of nikah (nikah: marriage) is intercourse; then its use widened until the contract itself was called nikah, just as ʿudhrah (ʿudhrah: courtyard of a house, so named because refuse was thrown into courtyards) originally meant the courtyard of a house because people threw refuse there, and the sacrifice for a child is called ʿaqiqah (ʿaqiqah: the sacrifice made for a newborn), whose original meaning is the hair born to the child, and this is the reason for their slaughtering it at its shaving. There are many similar examples. Thus Allah forbade marrying polytheistic women, both the contract and sexual relations. Then He made an exception for the free women of the People of the Book, saying: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾.

Then He said: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist, even though she may please you with her beauty and wealth﴾. It was revealed concerning Khansa', who was a black woman belonging to Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman. He said: "O Khansa', you have been mentioned in the highest assembly despite your blackness and ugliness," and Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed your mention in His Book. Hudhayfah then freed her and married her.

Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah, who had a black slave-woman; he became angry with her and harmed her. Then he went to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of this. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "And what is it, O Abu ʿAbd Allah?" He said: "She testifies that there is no god but Allah and that you are His Messenger, fasts in Ramadan, performs ablution well and prays." He (ﷺ) said: "She is a believer [mu'minah]." ʿAbd Allah said: "By Him who sent you with truth, I will free her and marry her." He did so, but some Muslims criticised him, saying: "Will you marry a slave-woman?" and they offered him a free polytheist woman, for they used to be eager to marry polytheistic women in hope of their conversion. Then Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.
[Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 1/265.]

Then He said: ﴿And do not marry [give in marriage] polytheistic men until they believe. And a believing slave is better than a polytheist, even though he may please you with his wealth and good condition.﴾

It is narrated from Marwan ibn Muhammad, who said: I asked Malik ibn Anas about marrying a slave, and he said: ﴿And a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾.

﴿Those invite to the Fire﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿to the Fire﴾, i.e., to the state that necessitates the Fire. ﴿But Allah invites to Paradise and forgiveness by His permission, and He makes clear His signs﴾, i.e., His commands and prohibitions, ﴿to the people, that they may be mindful﴾, i.e., that they may take heed.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 219–221 (part 1 of 3):

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling.﴾
It was revealed concerning ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), Muʿadh ibn Jabal, and a group of the Ansar who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling concerning wine and gambling, for they take away the intellect and deprive one of wealth." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse. The summary of the matter is that the prohibition of wine, according to the statements of the exegetes and the scholars of hadith, varies, and some of these statements agree with one another. It is that Allah revealed four verses concerning wine. The first, revealed in Mecca, was: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes you take from them an intoxicant (sakar)﴾, which is that which intoxicates. The Muslims used to drink it, and it was lawful for them at that time. Then, concerning the question of ʿUmar and Muʿadh, came: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾ When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed your Lord has ordained in advance the prohibition of wine." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/495.]] So some people abandoned it, due to His saying: ﴿in them is great sin﴾, and they said: "We have no need for anything that contains great sin." [119] Due to His saying: ﴿and benefits for people﴾, they continued to enjoy its benefits and avoid its sins, until ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf prepared a meal and invited some of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and wine was served before them. They drank and became intoxicated. When the time of the Maghrib prayer arrived, they put one of them forward to lead them in prayer, and he recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship...﴾ until the end of the surah, dropping the "not" (lā). So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying.﴾
Thus the intoxicant was prohibited during the times of prayer. ʿUmar said: "Indeed Allah has come close in forbidding the drinking of wine, and I do not see it except that He will prohibit it entirely." When it was revealed, [Allah prohibited it], some people abandoned it and said: "There is no good in a thing that comes between us and the prayer."
Some people continued to drink it in their houses, abstaining during the times of prayer and drinking it at other times, until a man [[Ibn Hajar mentioned that he was Abu Bakr. See Fath al-Bari: 10/31, ed. al-Maʿrifa, Beirut; also in al-Isabah: 4/22; and see Majmaʿ al-Zawaid: 5/51.]] among the Muslims drank it and began to lament over the dead of Badr, saying:
"Greet with peace Umm Bakr... and is there for you, after your kinsmen, any peace?
Leave me to drink wine in the morning, for I... would that death were far from the tents.
And the Banu al-Mughirah wished to ransom him with a thousand men or cattle.
As if I see the well of Badr... filled with bowls of the finest wood, crowned with fat humps.
As if I see the well of Badr... with the young men and the noble garments."
When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he went out hastily, dragging his cloak, until he reached him and raised something that was in his hand to strike him. When the man saw him, he said: "I seek refuge in Allah from the anger of Allah and the anger of His Messenger. By Allah, I will never eat it again." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/493.]]

And concerning Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, there is what was narrated: al-Zuhri related from ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, from his father, from his grandfather (peace be upon them), who said: "I had a she-camel (shārif) from my share of the spoils, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave me a portion of the fifth. I had arranged with a goldsmith to travel with me so that we could bring idhkhir (a fragrant plant) which I wished to sell, and with its price I would be assisted in the marriage to Fatimah and her wedding feast." [[Addition from Asbab al-Nuzul.]]
He said: "I brought my she-camel to the wall of a man from the Ansar, and I went to gather ropes, sacks and saddles. When I returned, her belly had been split open and her humps had been cut off (ijtabba: cut)." He said: "I could not hold back my tears, and I said: 'Who did this to my she-camel?' They said: 'Your uncle Hamzah did it, and he is in the house with them drinking. They have a singing girl, and they were merry.' She sang:
'Ah, O Hamz, of the high-hilled, with the camels kneeling in the courtyard,
He thrust the knife into their necks and reddened them with blood,
And fed from their slices a roasted meat, sizzling over the heat of the fire,
So prepare from their finest parts a broth for your drinking, from a pot or otherwise.
So you, O Abu ʿAmarah, are the one to be called upon to remove harm and affliction from us.'
Then he rose to your two she-camels and killed them." [ʿAli said:] "So I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was in the house of Umm Salamah, with his freedman Zayd. He said: 'What brings you, may my father and mother be ransom for you, O ʿAli?' I said: 'What did my uncle do to my two she-camels?' and I told him the news. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, put on his sandals and cloak, and walked on, and I and Zayd followed him. He greeted and asked permission and entered the house, and said: 'O Hamzah, what moved you to do what you did to the two she-camels of your nephew?' He raised his head and began looking at the hands and shins of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He then fixed his gaze on him and said: 'Are you not, and your fathers, slaves of my father?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) backed away and said: 'Your sheep and camels are owed to me,' and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made him pay compensation for them." [[Asbab al-Nuzul, with variation: 139–140.]]

When morning came, Hamzah went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) apologising. He said: "Enough, O uncle, for you asked Allah and He pardoned you."

They also said: ʿUtban ibn Malik prepared a meal and invited men from among the Muslims, among them Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, and he had roasted the head of a camel for them. They ate and drank wine until it overcame them. Then they boasted before ʿUtban, traced their lineages and recited poetry to one another. Saʿd recited a qasidah containing satire of the Ansar and pride for his own people. A man from the Ansar rose, took the jawbone of the camel, and struck Saʿd on the head, wounding him. Saʿd went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained to him about the Ansari. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Allah, make clear to us Your judgment on wine with a complete clarification." So Allah revealed the prohibition of wine in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling... until ﴿so will you not desist?﴾﴾, and that was a few days after the Battle of the Confederates. ʿUmar said: "We have desisted, O Lord." [[Iʿanat al-Talibin: 4/174.]]

Anas said: "It was prohibited, and there was no livelihood more beloved to the Arabs than it on the day it was prohibited to them, and nothing was heavier upon them than its prohibition." He said: "We took the jars out to the road and poured out what was in them. Some of them broke their jars, and some washed them with water and clay. The alleys of Medina, after that time, whenever it rained, showed the color of wine by it and its scent spread."

As for the nature of wine (mahiyyat al-khamr), the jurists differed concerning it. Some of them said: it is specific to what is pressed from the grape and the date palm, which ferments by its own nature without the action of fire; anything other than that is not wine. This is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf and most of the people of opinion. Then they differed concerning what is cooked, and they said: every must that is boiled until two-thirds of it is gone is lawful, though it is disliked. If it is boiled until two-thirds is gone and one-third remains, it is lawful, permissible to drink and to sell, except that its intoxicating part is forbidden. They argued for this with what
Abu Kathir narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wine is from these two trees: the date palm and the grapevine." [[al-Musannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzaq: 9/234, no. 7053.]] [120]

They differed concerning what is cooked with apricot [......] [[Illegible words.]] Nabatah narrated from Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wrote to some of his governors that the provision of the Muslims is the ṭilāʾ (boiled must) of which two-thirds have gone and one-third remains. [[Sunan al-Nasa'i: 8/328–329.]]

And from Ibn Sirin, that ʿAbd Allah ibn Suwayd al-Khatmi said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wrote to us: "To proceed: boil your drink until the portion of Satan is gone from it, for he has two parts and you have one." [[al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Nasa'i: 3/241.]]

And from Anas ibn Sirin, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: Satan disputed with Noah (peace be upon him) over a vine stalk. The one said: "This is mine," and the other said: "This is mine," and they agreed that Noah would have one third of it and Satan two thirds. [[Tarikh Dimashq: 62/259.]]

Ibn Abi ... and Abi from Dawud, who said: I asked Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab what was the rubb that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) made lawful. He said: that which is boiled until two-thirds is gone and one-third remains.

And from Qays ibn Abi ... narrated from Musa al-Umawi that he used to drink ṭilāʾ (what is boiled from must until it thickens, likened to the tar with which camels' mange is smeared) of which two-thirds had gone and one-third remained.

And from Yahya ibn Saʿid from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who said: when ṭilāʾ is boiled down to a third, there is no harm; and al-Musawwar said the same.

Al-Tha'alibi said: What I hold is that these reports refer to a third that is not intoxicating. This is shown by what Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn al-Tufayl al-Jazari, who said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz wrote to us: "Do not drink ṭilāʾ until two-thirds of it have gone and one-third remains; every intoxicant is forbidden." Another group said: when must is boiled even slightly so that it becomes ṭilāʾ; this is the view of Ismaʿil ibn ʿUlayyah and a group of the people of Iraq.

It is narrated from ʿIsa ibn Ibrahim that he does not prohibit any of the nabidh (fermented drinks), neither the fresh (nayy) nor the cooked, except one drink, which is strong fresh grape juice that has not been mixed with water or altered, but only wine.

They also argued with what
Ibn al-Ahwas narrated from Simak, from al-Qasim ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Burdah ibn Sahl, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Drink in vessels, but do not get intoxicated." [121] Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sudi said: the hadith is munkar; Abu al-Ahwas Sallam ibn Sulaym erred in it, and we know of no one among the companions of Simak on whom reliance was placed; and Simak himself was not strong, and he would accept suggestion (talqin). [[See: Sunan al-Nasa'i: 3/232.]]

Ahmad said: It was said that Abu al-Ahwas was confused in this hadith; Shurayk differed from him in its chain and wording. Shurayk narrated it from Simak ibn Harb, from Abu Buraydah, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the diyya, the hantam, the naqir and the muzaffat. They also relied on what was traced to Simak from Qurasafah, a woman among them, from ʿAʾishah, who said: Drink, but do not get intoxicated.
Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, the Imam, said: this is not established, and we do not know who Qurasafah is. [[See al-Muhalla of Ibn Hazm: 7/486.]] The well-known report from ʿAʾishah is what Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated from ʿAbd Allah, from Qudamah al-ʿAmiri, that Jasrah bint Dujajah al-ʿAmiriyyah related to us, saying: I heard ʿAʾishah being asked by Ayyash about nabidh. They said: "We steep wine in the morning and drink it in the evening, and steep it in the evening and drink it in the morning." She said: "I do not make lawful any intoxicant, even if it is bread." They said: she said it three times. [[Sunan al-Nasa'i: 8/320–321.]]

They also argued with what Hushaym narrated from Ibn Shubrumah, who said: a trustworthy person related to me from ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: wine was forbidden in its entirety, its little and its much, and every intoxicant from every drink.

This is closer to the truth, for Sufyan narrated from Abu al-Juwayriyah al-Jarmi, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about al-baadhaq, and he said: whatever intoxicates is forbidden. And Shuʿbah narrated from Salamah ibn Kumayl, who said: I heard Abu al-Hakam relate that Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever is pleased to forbid what Allah and His Messenger forbade, let him forbid nabidh.

They also argued with what they traced to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Nafiʿ, who said: I saw Ibn ʿUmar... I saw a man come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a cup containing nabidh, while he was at the Corner (of the Kaʿbah). He handed him the cup, and he raised it to his mouth and found it strong, so he returned it to its owner. A man from the people said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it forbidden?" He said: "Bring the man to me." He was brought, and he took the cup from him, then called them both, poured it into it, raised it to his mouth and poured again, then called them again, poured into it, and said: "As for when these vessels have been used among you, break their sides with water."

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman said: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Rafiʿ is well known, but he related it to us, contrary to what Wahb ibn Harun narrated from Muhammad ibn ʿAmr, from Abu Salamah, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is forbidden, and every intoxicant is khamr." [122] [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/29.]]

Ibn Sirin narrated from Ibn ʿUmar: "The intoxicant, its little and its much, is forbidden." And Abu ʿAwanah narrated from Zayd ibn ʿUmar, who said: I asked Ibn ʿUmar about drinks, and he said: avoid everything in which there is an intoxicant.

They also argued with what they traced to Yahya ibn Yaman, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mikhlad ibn Saʿid, from Ibn Masʿud, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) became thirsty around the Kaʿbah, asked for drink, and was brought nabidh from the watering place (al-siqayah). He smelled it, frowned, and said: "Bring me a bucket of Zamzam water." He poured it over it, then drank. A man said: "Is it forbidden, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "No." [[Sunan al-Nasa'i: 8/325.]]

Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman said: This report is weak, for Yahya ibn Yaman transmitted it alone apart from the companions of Sufyan, and Yahya ibn Yaman's narrations are not relied upon because of his many errors and poor memory.

And from Zayd ibn Waqid, from Khalid ibn al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Hurayrah say: I knew that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to fast on some of the days on which he fasted, so I sought out his breaking of the fast with nabidh that I had made in a gourd. When evening came I brought it to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I knew you were fasting on this day, so I prepared this nabidh for your iftar." He said: "Come close to me, O Abu Hurayrah." I lifted it to him, and it was hissing, and he said: "Take this and strike it against the wall, for this is the drink of one who does not believe in Allah and the Last Day." [[Sunan Abi Dawud: 2/192; al-Sunan al-Kubra: 3/237.]]

They also argued with what they traced to Sufyan, from Yahya ibn Saʿid, who said: I heard Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab say: Thaqif brought wine to ʿUmar, and he asked for it; when he brought it near his mouth he disliked it, so he mixed it with water and said: "Do thus." They also argued with what they traced to Abu Rafiʿ, that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "If you fear from nabidh its strength, then break it (with water)." [[Ibid.]]

They also argued with what one of our companions, ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, said: the meaning of "break it with water" is before it becomes strong. The evidence for this interpretation is what Ibn Shihab (who is Sufyan ibn Yazid) narrated, that ʿUmar came out to them and said: "I found the smell of drink on so-and-so, and he claimed he drank ṭilāʾ. I will question what they drink; if it is intoxicating, I will flog him," and ʿUmar gave him the full prescribed flogging.

Ibrahim narrated from Ibn Sirin, who said: he considers it a must (ʿasir) from the one who prepares it as ṭilāʾ, and does not consider it wine. Abu Saʿid said: ṭilāʾ is that which has been boiled until two-thirds are gone and one-third remains; it was so named because it resembles the tar of camels in its thickness and blackness. [[al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi: 8/295.]]

ʿUbayd ibn al-Abras said:
"It is wine, called ṭilāʾ, as the wolf is called Abu Jaʿdah." [[Ibid.]]

Al-Tha'alibi said: The ṭilāʾ for which concession was given is in fact the rubb, for when it is boiled down to a third, its intoxication and its evil are gone and its devil has departed.

They also argued with what Hushaym narrated from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim, that a thick melon drink was brought to him, and he would taste it and wash it with what was intoxicating.

And from Mughirah, from Abu Maʿshar, from Ibrahim, who said: there is no harm in melon nabidh.

From Abu Usamah, who said: I heard Ibn al-Mubarak say: I have not found a concession regarding intoxicants authentically from anyone except Ibrahim.

Hammad ibn Salamah, from ʿUmar, from Anas, who said: Umm Salamah had a cup, and she said: "I gave the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) every kind of drink: water, honey, milk and nabidh."

And from Ibn Shubrumah, who said: Talhah ibn Musarrif said to the people of Kufa concerning nabidh: "In it the young grow and the old age." He said: al-Miqdad and al-Zubayr used to give milk mixed with honey to drink. It was said to Talhah: "Shall we not give them nabidh?" He said: "I dislike that a Muslim should become intoxicated in my Sunnah."

And from Sufyan, who said: Talhah's statement was mentioned to Abu Ishaq regarding nabidh, and Ibn Ishaq said: "I gave it to the companions of ʿAli and the companions of ʿAbd Allah in al-Khawafi before Talhah was born." And from Ibn Shubrumah, who said: "May Allah have mercy on Ibrahim: he was strict with people regarding nabidh and he also granted concession in it."

They also argued with what they traced to ʿAbd Allah ibn Buraydah, from his father, that while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was traveling, he came upon a people and heard a clamor from them. He said: "What is this sound?" They said: "O Prophet of Allah, they have a drink they are drinking." The Prophet sent to them and called them and said: "What do you make nabidh in?" They said: "We make nabidh in the naqir and the dubba'; we have no other vessels." He said: "Do not drink except what you have sealed." He remained so for as long as Allah willed, then returned to them and found that a plague had struck them and they had become pale. He said: "What is wrong with you? I see you have perished." They said: "O Prophet of Allah, our land is unhealthy, and you forbade us except what we have sealed." He said: "Drink, and every intoxicant is forbidden." [[al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi: 3/226, no. 5165.]]

They said: By this he meant the khamr that produces intoxication, because nabadh is that which brings elation and vigor, and these are only obtained from an intoxicating drink.

Abu al-Zubayr narrated from Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to have nabidh made for him in [a jar of ʿAfar] [[So in the manuscript.]].

Al-Tha'labi said: It is possible that these reports and similar ones have two meanings. The first is that they came before the prohibition of wine (khamr, intoxicating drink). The second, which is closer to the correct view, is that by *nabidh* (a steeped drink, made by soaking dates or raisins in water) they meant water in which dates or raisins had been soaked until it took on their sweetness and strength, before it fermented and became intoxicating. What indicates this is what has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would have *nabidh* prepared for him, and he would drink it that day, the next day, and the day after.

Al-A'mash narrated from Yahya ibn Abi 'Amr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would have raisin *nabidh* steeped for him at night, placed in a water-skin, and he would drink it that day, the next day, and the day after. When it reached the last of the vessels, he would give it to be drunk or drink it himself, and if any of it remained in the morning, he would pour it out.

And from 'Abdullah ibn al-Daylami, from his father Fayruz, who said: I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we are people of vineyards, and Allah has revealed the prohibition of wine, so what should we do?" He said: "Make it into raisins." I said: "And what should we do with the raisins?" He said: "Soak them for your midday meal and drink them for your evening meal, and soak them for your evening meal and drink them for your midday meal." I said: "Shall we not delay it until it becomes strong?" He said: "Do not put it in baskets; put it in waterskins, for if it is delayed it becomes wine."

And from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that he would have *nabidh* steeped for him in a raisin waterskin in the morning and drink it at night, and would have it steeped in the evening and drink it in the morning. He would wash the waterskins and would not put in them any *nardi* (a kind of date-based drink) or anything else. Nafi' said: "We used to drink it like honey."

And from Bassam, who said: I asked Abu Ja'far about *nabidh*, and he said: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn would have it steeped for him at night and drink it in the morning, and have it steeped in the morning and drink it at night.

And from 'Abdullah, who said: I heard Sufyan, when he was asked about *nabidh*, say: "I steep it in the evening and drink it in the morning."

These reports indicate that it was the steeping of raisins and dates before it fermented.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Abu Thawr, and most of the people of hadith said: *khamr* is every intoxicating drink, whether it is the juice of grapes or not. Whether it is cooked or raw, every intoxicating drink is forbidden, whether little or much, and the one who drinks it is liable to the *hadd* (the prescribed legal punishment), except that one who consumes a cooked drink [after two-thirds of it has evaporated], for he is not subject to the *hadd*, and his testimony is not rejected. The linguistic proof for this school is that *khamr* originally means "covering." Anything that covers something, whether a tree, a stone, or other things, is called *khamr*. It is said: "So-and-so covered (kharrama) the people's ... " and from it comes *khimar* (a woman's head-cover) and *khumrat al-sajjadah* (the cover of a prayer mat). *Khamr* was named so because it covers the intellect. What indicates this is what al-Sha'bi narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: 'Umar gave a sermon and said: "The prohibition of *khamr* has been revealed, and it is made from five things: grapes, dates, wheat, barley, and honey. *Khamr* is that which covers the intellect."

Anas ibn Malik said: "It was named *khamr* because they used to leave it in jars until it fermented (takhtamir) and changed."

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "*Khamr* was named so only because it is left until its clear part is settled and its sediment has sunk."

Anas said: "*Khamr* was prohibited, and most of their *khamr* at that time was *fadikh*." He said: "In Medina they did not make *khamr*, and they did not have enough grapes to make it. We only heard of *khamr* in the lands of non-Arabs. We used to drink *fadikh* made from dates and unripe dates. *Fadikh* is what is crushed from dates and unripe dates without being touched by fire."

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Umar that he said: "It is not *fadikh* but *fadukh*."

Their evidence from the Sunnah is what Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is *khamr*, and every *khamr* is intoxicating and forbidden." [123] [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/29.]]

Salim ibn 'Abdullah narrated from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every intoxicant is *khamr*, and whatever intoxicates in large quantity, its small quantity is also forbidden." [124] [[Musnad Ahmad: 2/91.]]

From Abu 'Uthman 'Amr ibn Salim al-Ansari, from al-Qasim, from 'A'ishah, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "If the *gharq* of it intoxicates, then a handful of it is forbidden." *Gharq* is a vessel that holds sixteen *ratl* (a unit of weight).

And from Abu al-Ghusn, known as Hujja, who said: Hisham ibn 'Urwah said to me: "Do you drink *nabidh*?" I said: "Yes, by Allah, I drink it." He said: "My father narrated to me from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Every intoxicant is forbidden, both its beginning and its end.'" [125] [[Tadhkirat al-Huffaz by al-Dhahabi: 3/1000.]]

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also said: "Indeed, from dates there is *khamr*, indeed from grapes there is *khamr*, indeed from raisins there is *khamr*, indeed from honey there is *khamr*, indeed from wheat there is *khamr*, indeed from barley there is *khamr*, indeed from millet there is *khamr*, and I forbid you from every intoxicant." [126]

From Ibn Sirin, who said: A man came to Ibn 'Umar and said: "Our family steeps a drink for us in the evening, and when we wake in the morning we drink it." He said: "I forbid you from an intoxicant, whether little or much, and worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic. I forbid you from an intoxicant, whether little or much, and worship Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Do you know that the people of Khaybar steep a drink for themselves, which they call such-and-such, and that your father steeped a drink from such-and-such, which they call such-and-such, and it is *khamr*?" He went on counting four drinks for him, the last of which was honey. [[Al-Musannaf by Ibn Abi Shaybah: 5/474.]]

From 'Ikrimah, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon some of his wives when they had steeped grape juice for themselves in a jug, so he poured it out and broke the jug.

'Ubadah ibn al-Samit narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my nation will make *khamr* lawful under a name they give it." [127] [[Al-Durr al-Manthur: 324, with variations.]]

And it is narrated from him (ﷺ) that he said: "As for *khamr*, it was not forbidden because of its name; it was forbidden because of what is in it. Every drink whose end result is *khamr* is forbidden." [128] [[Sunan al-Daraqutni: 4/171.]]

It is related that a man from the wise men of the Arabs was asked: "Why do you not drink *nabidh*?" He said: "Allah granted me my intellect sound, so how could I bring into it what spoils it?" [[From the book Dhamm al-Sukr by Ibn Abi al-Dunya: 77, where the text reads: "By Allah, I do not accept my intellect being sound..."]]

*Al-Maysir* (gambling) means *al-qimar*. Ibn 'Abbas said: In the Jahiliyyah, a man would gamble with another man over his family and his wealth. Whichever of them won against his companion would take away his wealth and his family. So Allah, Exalted, revealed this verse.

*Al-maysir* is on the pattern *maf'il* from the saying of the speaker: "*yasura hadha al-shay'*" when it became obligatory, so he says *yayassaru yasran* and *maysiran*. *Al-yasir* is the one who shoots with arrows, whether that is obligatory or permitted or otherwise. Then gambling was called *maysir*, and the gambler was called *yasir* and *yasar*. Al-Nabighah said:

"Or a gambler whose arrows have taken away his fortune, a bereaved one whom his friend has left sad, with a broken heart."

Another poet said:

"So I spent the night as if I were a bereaved gambler, turning over the arrows after they had been drawn out."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/475.]]

Muqatil said: It was called *maysir* because they would say: "*Yasar huwa lana*" ("it is easy for us"), and the price of the camel. The origin of *yasar* is in the camel, for the wealthy Arabs would buy a camel, slaughter it, and divide it into portions.

They differed about the number of portions. Abu 'Amr said: ten. Al-Asma'i said: it is twenty. Then they would place on it ten arrows. It is said that with them are the *azlam* (divining arrows), and seven of them have shares: *al-fadh* (the single one), which has one share; *al-tawam* (the twin), which has two; *al-raqib*, which has three; *al-jals*, which has four; *al-nafis*, which has five; *al-musil*, which has six; and *al-mughalla*, which has seven. Three of them have no shares: *al-nasij*, *al-safaniz*, and *al-wagh*.

Then they would put the arrows in a bag called *al-rabab*. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"And it is as if they were a *rabab*, and he is like a *yasar* that spills over the arrows and splits them."

[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 14/90; al-Sihah: 1/132.]]

They would place the *rabab* in the hand of a man among them who was trusted, called *al-mujil* and *al-mufid*. He would shake it and draw out an arrow bearing the name of one of them. Whoever's arrow came out would take his share in accordance with what was drawn. If one of the three without shares came out, they would disagree about it, and each one of them would be obliged to pay the full price of the camel.

Some of them said: he takes nothing and pays nothing, and that arrow is void, so it is drawn again a second time. These are the gamblers (*al-yasiriyyun*) and the players (*al-iyasar*). Then they would give that camel to the poor and would not eat any of it. They took pride in this and would blame whoever among them did not do so, calling him *al-barim*. Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah said:

"Nor a *barim* to whose wedding the women bring gifts, when the rattling skin is shaking in the cold of winter."

[[Kitab al-'Ayn by al-Farahidi: 1/65.]]

So the origin of this gambling was what the Arabs used to do, and Allah, Exalted, in this verse forbade all kinds of gambling.

Layth narrated from Tawus, Mujahid, and 'Ata', who said: Everything in which there is gambling is *maysir*, even the children's games with knucklebones and dice.

From Abu al-Ahwas, from 'Abdullah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of these two marked knucklebones, for they are from the gambling of the non-Arabs." [129] [[Al-Adab al-Mufrad by al-Bukhari: 271.]]

And from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, that 'Ali (may Allah honor his face) said about backgammon (*nard*) and chess (*shatranj*): "They are from *maysir*."

And from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, who said: Everything that diverts from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer is *maysir*.

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both there is great sin and great harm, and some benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾ The great sin includes quarrelling, abusing, speaking obscenity and falsehood, loss of the intellect, prevention from the prayer, and taking the property of others without right.

The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read *kathir* with the letter *tha'*, and the rest read it with *ba'*. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose the reading with *ba'* because of Allah's saying: ﴿and their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ and His saying: ﴿a great sin (huban kabiran)﴾.

"And benefits for people" means what they used to gain from wine through trade and pleasure when drinking them. Al-A'sha says:

"For us, from its sobriety comes bad temper and sorrow, and remembrance of worries whose after-effects do not leave."

"And during the evening there is joy of soul and pleasure, and abundant wealth, the cost of its drinking bouts."

[[Jami' al-Bayan by al-Tabari: 2/489.]]

The benefit of gambling is what is won from gambling and what the poor benefit from.

﴿But their sin is greater than their benefit.﴾ The exegetes said: The sin of wine is that a man drinks and becomes intoxicated, and so harms people. The sin of gambling is that a man gambles, withholds what is due, and oppresses.

Al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' said: The benefits were before the prohibition, and the sin is after the prohibition.

﴿They ask you what they should spend.﴾ That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged them to give charity and encouraged them to do so without any obligation. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what should we spend? And to whom should we give charity?" So Allah, Exalted, revealed: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, meaning, what thing they should spend, and it is an interrogative. ﴿Say: The surplus.﴾

Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Abu 'Amr read *al-'afwu* with *damma* (nominative), and Muhammad ibn al-Sadi chose it in the sense: "What they spend is the surplus," evidenced by Allah's saying: ﴿And when it is said to them: What has your Lord revealed? They say: Fables of the ancients.﴾ [[Surat al-An'am: 25.]] The others read it with *fatha* (accusative), and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose it: "Say: They spend the surplus." [[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/61.]]

They differed about the meaning of *al-'afw*. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Qatadah, 'Ata', al-Sudi, and Ibn Abi Layla said: it is what remains of wealth after dependents are provided for; this is the narration of Muqsim from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Hasan said: It is that you do not strain your wealth in spending and then sit down begging from people.

Al-Walibi said, from Ibn 'Abbas: It is what is not clearly visible in your wealth.

Mujahid said: It is charity that is from the richness of a rich man.

'Amr ibn Dinar and 'Ata' said: It is the middle course of spending, neither extravagance nor stinginess.

Al-Dahhak said: It is what one can bear.

Al-'Awfi, from Ibn 'Abbas, said: Whatever they bring you of something small or great, accept it from them.

Tawus and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: We heard [Bishr] say: "*Al-'afw* is the ease of everything."

Al-Rabi' said: *Al-'afw* is the good; he says: the best of your wealth is what you spend.

All of these are close in meaning. The meaning of *al-'afw* in the language is surplus and abundance. Allah said: ﴿until they multiplied (hatta 'afaw)﴾, meaning they increased. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let the beards grow (a'fu al-lihā)." A poet said:

"But we, the sword bites among us, with fat-laden, abundant thighs."
