[148] [[Musnad Ahmad: 6/34, 37, 226; and Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 2/626.]] The word 'usayla (sweetness) is a name for intercourse. Its root is from 'asal (honey); it is used as a comparison for the pleasure that a person obtains in that state, and from it one says:

"'asalaha ya'salaha 'asalan" when he has had intercourse with her.

She remained as long as God willed her to remain, then she returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My husband had indeed touched me." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "You lied in your first statement, so we will not believe you in the last." [149] She remained until the Prophet (ﷺ) passed away, then she came to Abu Bakr and said: "O Successor of the Messenger of Allah, may I return to my first husband? For my second husband has touched me and divorced me." Abu Bakr said: "You saw the Messenger of Allah when you came to him, and he said to you what he said, so do not return to him." When Abu Bakr passed away, she came to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) and said to him the same as she had said to Abu Bakr. 'Umar said: "If you return to him, I will stone you, for Allah the Exalted has indeed revealed: 'And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband.'"

And if her second husband divorces her or dies leaving her after he has had intercourse with her, "there is no blame upon them both" (meaning upon the divorced woman and the first husband) "that they return to one another" in a new marriage; thus the marriage is mentioned with the wording of returning to one another. "If they think" (zanna), meaning they know; and it has been said: "they hope." They said: It is not permissible that it means knowledge, because no one knows what will occur except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "That they keep within the limits of Allah" means what Allah has made clear of the right of each of them over the other. The position of "an" in His saying "that they return to one another" is accusative by the removal of the preposition, i.e. "in that they return"; and in His saying "that they keep" it is accusative by the governing of the verb of thinking (zanna) upon it.

Mujahid said: its meaning is, "if they know that their marriage is not based on deceit (dalsa)," and by deceit he meant halala (the arrangement of a marriage to make a woman lawful to a former husband). This is the view of Sufyan, al-Awza'i, Malik, Abu 'Ubayda, Ahmad and Ishaq. They said concerning a man who divorces his wife three times and she then marries another man in order to make her lawful to her first husband: the marriage is invalid. Al-Shafi'i used to say: if he marries her in order to make her lawful, the marriage is valid so long as that condition is not stipulated in the marriage contract, such as saying: "I marry you so that I may have intercourse with you, so that you become lawful to your first husband." If this is stipulated, the marriage is void. And whatever condition is made before the contract of marriage does not invalidate the marriage.

Nafi' said: A man came to Ibn 'Umar and said: "A man divorced his wife three times, and then a brother of his, without any consultation, married her in order to make her lawful to the first." He said: "No, unless it is a marriage of desire. We used to count this as fornication (sifah) in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "May Allah curse the muhallil (the one who makes lawful) and the muhallal lahu (the one for whom she is made lawful)." [150] [[Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/622.]]

'Uqba ibn 'Amir said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I inform you of the borrowed ram?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "It is the muhallil and the muhallal lahu." [151] [[Kanz al-'Ummal: 9/706, no. 28066.]]

Qabisa ibn Jabir al-Asadi said: I heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab delivering a sermon while on the pulpit: "By Allah, I will not be brought a muhallil or a muhallal lahu except that I stone her."

"These are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear for a people who know." (Al-Mufaddal and Aban narrated from 'Asim with the letter nun, "We make clear.")

"And when you divorce women and they reach their term..." This was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar called Thabit ibn Yasar. He divorced his wife until her waiting period was about to end, with only two or three days remaining, and she was about to be separated from him. He took her back, then divorced her again, and he did this to her until nine months had passed for her, harming her by doing so. Divorce at that time was not limited (to three), and when a man wished to harm his wife, he would divorce her, then leave her until she had the third menstruation, then take her back and divorce her again; so prolonging it over her is the harm. Thus Allah the Exalted revealed: "And when you divorce women and they reach their term," meaning, their affair is about to conclude by the completion of the waiting period. He did not intend "when their waiting period has ended," because once the waiting period has ended the husband no longer has the right to retain her. So "reach" here means reaching in the sense of approaching. His later saying "they reach their term" in "then do not prevent them" refers to reaching in the sense of completion and conclusion. The word "reach" encompasses both meanings, as one says: "He reached the city" when he arrives at its boundary, and when he enters it.

"Then retain them in kindness" means take them back, "with kindness." Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "with kindness" means with witnesses for the return and a contract for it, apart from the return by intercourse. "Or release them with kindness" means leave them until their waiting period ends, and they will be more in control of themselves.

"And do not retain them to harm them, to transgress against them" by prolonging the waiting period, "and whoever does that, he has wronged himself," harming his soul by opposing the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Murra al-Tayyib, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Cursed is whoever harms a Muslim or deceives him." [152] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 3/223.]]

"And do not take the signs of Allah in jest." Al-Hasan, from Abu al-Darda', said: A man in the Jahiliyya would divorce and say: "I divorced only in jest," then he would take her back and manumit (a slave), then say the same thing and take her back and marry, and say the same again. So Allah the Exalted revealed: "And do not take the signs of Allah in jest," meaning: the limits of Allah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it and said: "Whoever divorces, or frees, or marries, and claims he was joking, his jest is earnest."

And there is a report: "Five things, their earnest is earnest and their jest is earnest: divorce, manumission, marriage, return (to a wife), and vow."

On the authority of Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry with the Ash'aris and said: "One of you says to his wife: 'I have divorced you, I have taken you back'; this is not the divorce of the Muslims. Divorce women at the time of their purity (qubl tamthihā)" [[In the tafsir of al-Tabari and al-Durr al-Manthur (1/286): "their waiting period" ('iddatuha).]] [[With variation in Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/650, no. 2017; al-Sunan al-Kubra: 7/322; and its full text in Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/655.]]

Al-Kalbi said: "And do not take the signs of Allah in jest," meaning His saying: "Then retention in kindness or release with good treatment."

"And remember the favour of Allah upon you," by faith; "and what He sent down to you of the Book," meaning the Qur'an, "and the wisdom," meaning the admonitions of the Qur'an, its limits and rulings.

"He admonishes you thereby. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Knowing of everything." "And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them..." the verse.

It was revealed concerning Jumayla bint Yasar, sister of Ma'qil ibn Yasar al-Muzani. She was married to Abu al-Badah' 'Asim ibn 'Adi ibn 'Ajlan, who divorced her with a single pronouncement, then left her until her waiting period ended. Then he came to propose to her and wished to take her back, and he was a man of truth, and the woman desired to return to him. Her brother Ma'qil prevented her and said to her: "If you return to him, I will never speak to you again." He said to her husband: "I gave you my noble sister as a bed and preferred you over my people, and you divorced her, then did not take her back until her waiting period ended, and now you come to propose to her. By Allah, I will never marry her to you." He became fiercely protective, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Ma'qil and recited it to him. He said: "I believe in Allah and the Last Day," and so he married her to him and expiated his oath.

This is according to the view of most of the exegetes.

Al-Suddi said: This verse was revealed concerning Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari. He had a paternal cousin whose husband divorced her with a single pronouncement, and her waiting period ended, then he wished to take her back. Jabir came and said: "You divorced my cousin, and now you want to marry her again." The woman wished for her husband, so Allah revealed: "And when you divorce women and they reach their term," meaning their waiting period ended. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ajal is the end of a period and the outcome of affairs. Labid said:

"Boast to him by piety, for God is the outcome (al-ajal)."

meaning the outcome of affairs.

"Do not prevent them": do not hinder them. Al-'adl is preventing from marriage. Al-Akhfash recited:

"We have restrained with spears a tongue, and among you there is no restrainer of its sanctity."

And he recited:

"Be generous to me, for my poems are yours, noble women who have been prevented from marriage."

The root of 'adl is constriction and hardship. It is said: the woman and the sheep were restrained when their offspring became entangled in their bellies, so that exit was constricted for it; and the hen was restrained when the eggs became entangled within her; and the crowd restrained the open space when it became cramped for them due to their multitude. It is said: "dha 'idal" when its treatment is constricted and cannot be endured. It is said: "'adala al-amr" when the matter becomes severe and constricted.

'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The people of Kufa have become difficult (u'dila): they do not accept any governor, and no governor accepts them. Aws ibn Hajar said:

"Your brother who is constant in covenant is not one who blames you if he turns away, nor one who pleases you when he approaches;
rather he is the distant one when you are secure, and your companion is the nearest when the matter becomes grave."

[[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 2/661.]]

Tawus said: Verily, cases of 'adl (difficult judgments) came to us which none but Ibn 'Abbas could resolve. Every difficult matter among the Arabs is mu'dal (problematic). From this is the saying of al-Shafi'i:

"When difficult matters have passed from me, I have uncovered their realities by reflection."

"That they marry their former husbands with a new marriage when they agree among themselves in kindness," through a lawful contract and a permissible dower. The structure of the verse: "Do not prevent them from marrying their husbands with kindness when they agree among themselves." In this verse is evidence for the view of those who say: there is no marriage except with a guardian (wali), because He addressed the guardians regarding marriage; and if the woman had the right to contract her own marriage, there would be no prevention, and God's prohibition to the guardians against preventing would have no meaning. This is supported by what

Abu Burda narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no marriage except with a guardian." [153] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/394.]]

"That is admonished by it whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day." He said this in the singular, though the address is to the guardians, because the original form of addressing a plural is "dhalikum," but this became common until they thought the kaf was part of the word itself and not the pronoun of address, so they said "dhalika." When they said this, the kaf became singular, fixed in the accusative in both verses, applicable to the plural, masculine and feminine.

It has also been said: here the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), which is why it is singular, then He returned to addressing the believers, saying: "That is purer for you (azka lakum) and more pure (atharu) for your hearts" from doubt, because if there is a bond of love in the heart of each of them, one cannot be secure that it will not exceed what Allah has made lawful to them, and one cannot be secure from their guardians lest it come to their hearts about them that they might be innocent of that and so sin.

"And Allah knows" the state of each of them toward the other, "and you do not know."

In this verse is evidence for the view of those who say: there is no marriage except with a guardian (wali), because He addressed the guardians regarding marriage; and if the woman had the right to contract her own marriage, there would be no prevention, and God's prohibition to the guardians against preventing would have no meaning. This is supported by what

Abu Burda narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no marriage except with a guardian." [153] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/394.]]

"That is admonished by it whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day." He said this in the singular, though the address is to the guardians, because the original form of addressing a plural is "dhalikum," but this became common until they thought the kaf was part of the word itself and not the pronoun of address, so they said "dhalika." When they said this, the kaf became singular, fixed in the accusative in both verses, applicable to the plural, masculine and feminine.

It has also been said: here the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), which is why it is singular, then He returned to addressing the believers, saying: "That is purer for you (azka lakum) and more pure (atharu) for your hearts" from doubt, because if there is a bond of love in the heart of each of them, one cannot be secure that it will not exceed what Allah has made lawful to them, and one cannot be secure from their guardians lest it come to their hearts about them that they might be innocent of that and so sin.

"And Allah knows" the state of each of them toward the other, "and you do not know."

Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 230–232:

Then if he divorces her (meaning, a third time), she is not lawful to him after that (meaning, after the third pronouncement of divorce), and "after" is in the accusative as a terminal limit, "until she marries another husband" (zawjan ghayrahu), i.e. other than the one who divorced her, so that he has intercourse with her. The word nikah (marriage) encompasses both the contract and the sexual intercourse together.

This verse was revealed concerning Tamima, and it has been said: 'A'isha bint 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Atik al-Qurazi. She was married to Rifa'a ibn Wahb ibn 'Atik al-Qurazi, who was her cousin, and he divorced her three times. Then she married 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr, and with him was nothing but like the fringe of a garment. She said: He divorced me before he had touched me, so shall I return to my first husband, my cousin? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) smiled and said: "Do you want to return to Rifa'a? No, not until you taste his honey (sweetness) and he tastes yours."

He said: Abu Bakr was sitting with the Prophet (ﷺ), and Khalid ibn Sa'id ibn al-'As was sitting at the door of the chamber, and Khalid began calling out: "O Abu Bakr, will you not restrain this woman from what she is saying in the presence of the Messenger of Allah?" [148] [[Musnad Ahmad: 6/34, 37, 226; and Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 2/626.]] The word 'usayla (sweetness) is a name for intercourse. Its root is from 'asal (honey); it is used as a comparison for the pleasure that a person obtains in that state, and from it one says:

"'asalaha ya'salaha 'asalan" when he has had intercourse with her.

She remained as long as God willed her to remain, then she returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My husband had indeed touched me." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "You lied in your first statement, so we will not believe you in the last." [149] She remained until the Prophet (ﷺ) passed away, then she came to Abu Bakr and said: "O Successor of the Messenger of Allah, may I return to my first husband? For my second husband has touched me and divorced me." Abu Bakr said: "You saw the Messenger of Allah when you came to him, and he said to you what he said, so do not return to him." When Abu Bakr passed away, she came to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) and said to him the same as she had said to Abu Bakr. 'Umar said: "If you return to him, I will stone you, for Allah the Exalted has indeed revealed: 'And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband.'"

And if her second husband divorces her or dies leaving her after he has had intercourse with her, "there is no blame upon them both" (meaning upon the divorced woman and the first husband) "that they return to one another" in a new marriage; thus the marriage is mentioned with the wording of returning to one another. "If they think" (zanna), meaning they know; and it has been said: "they hope." They said: It is not permissible that it means knowledge, because no one knows what will occur except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. "That they keep within the limits of Allah" means what Allah has made clear of the right of each of them over the other. The position of "an" in His saying "that they return to one another" is accusative by the removal of the preposition, i.e. "in that they return"; and in His saying "that they keep" it is accusative by the governing of the verb of thinking (zanna) upon it.

Mujahid said: its meaning is, "if they know that their marriage is not based on deceit (dalsa)," and by deceit he meant halala (the arrangement of a marriage to make a woman lawful to a former husband). This is the view of Sufyan, al-Awza'i, Malik, Abu 'Ubayda, Ahmad and Ishaq. They said concerning a man who divorces his wife three times and she then marries another man in order to make her lawful to her first husband: the marriage is invalid. Al-Shafi'i used to say: if he marries her in order to make her lawful, the marriage is valid so long as that condition is not stipulated in the marriage contract, such as saying: "I marry you so that I may have intercourse with you, so that you become lawful to your first husband." If this is stipulated, the marriage is void. And whatever condition is made before the contract of marriage does not invalidate the marriage.

Nafi' said: A man came to Ibn 'Umar and said: "A man divorced his wife three times, and then a brother of his, without any consultation, married her in order to make her lawful to the first." He said: "No, unless it is a marriage of desire. We used to count this as fornication (sifah) in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "May Allah curse the muhallil (the one who makes lawful) and the muhallal lahu (the one for whom she is made lawful)." [150] [[Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/622.]]

'Uqba ibn 'Amir said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Shall I inform you of the borrowed ram?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "It is the muhallil and the muhallal lahu." [151] [[Kanz al-'Ummal: 9/706, no. 28066.]]

Qabisa ibn Jabir al-Asadi said: I heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab delivering a sermon while on the pulpit: "By Allah, I will not be brought a muhallil or a muhallal lahu except that I stone her."

"These are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear for a people who know." (Al-Mufaddal and Aban narrated from 'Asim with the letter nun, "We make clear.")

"And when you divorce women and they reach their term..." This was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar called Thabit ibn Yasar. He divorced his wife until her waiting period was about to end, with only two or three days remaining, and she was about to be separated from him. He took her back, then divorced her again, and he did this to her until nine months had passed for her, harming her by doing so. Divorce at that time was not limited (to three), and when a man wished to harm his wife, he would divorce her, then leave her until she had the third menstruation, then take her back and divorce her again; so prolonging it over her is the harm. Thus Allah the Exalted revealed: "And when you divorce women and they reach their term," meaning, their affair is about to conclude by the completion of the waiting period. He did not intend "when their waiting period has ended," because once the waiting period has ended the husband no longer has the right to retain her. So "reach" here means reaching in the sense of approaching. His later saying "they reach their term" in "then do not prevent them" refers to reaching in the sense of completion and conclusion. The word "reach" encompasses both meanings, as one says: "He reached the city" when he arrives at its boundary, and when he enters it.

"Then retain them in kindness" means take them back, "with kindness." Muhammad ibn Jarir said: "with kindness" means with witnesses for the return and a contract for it, apart from the return by intercourse. "Or release them with kindness" means leave them until their waiting period ends, and they will be more in control of themselves.

"And do not retain them to harm them, to transgress against them" by prolonging the waiting period, "and whoever does that, he has wronged himself," harming his soul by opposing the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic.

Murra al-Tayyib, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Cursed is whoever harms a Muslim or deceives him." [152] [[Sunan al-Tirmidhi: 3/223.]]

"And do not take the signs of Allah in jest." Al-Hasan, from Abu al-Darda', said: A man in the Jahiliyya would divorce and say: "I divorced only in jest," then he would take her back and manumit (a slave), then say the same thing and take her back and marry, and say the same again. So Allah the Exalted revealed: "And do not take the signs of Allah in jest," meaning: the limits of Allah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited it and said: "Whoever divorces, or frees, or marries, and claims he was joking, his jest is earnest."

And there is a report: "Five things, their earnest is earnest and their jest is earnest: divorce, manumission, marriage, return (to a wife), and vow."

On the authority of Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry with the Ash'aris and said: "One of you says to his wife: 'I have divorced you, I have taken you back'; this is not the divorce of the Muslims. Divorce women at the time of their purity (qubl tamthihā)" [[In the tafsir of al-Tabari and al-Durr al-Manthur (1/286): "their waiting period" ('iddatuha).]] [[With variation in Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/650, no. 2017; al-Sunan al-Kubra: 7/322; and its full text in Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/655.]]

Al-Kalbi said: "And do not take the signs of Allah in jest," meaning His saying: "Then retention in kindness or release with good treatment."

"And remember the favour of Allah upon you," by faith; "and what He sent down to you of the Book," meaning the Qur'an, "and the wisdom," meaning the admonitions of the Qur'an, its limits and rulings.

"He admonishes you thereby. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Knowing of everything." "And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them..." the verse.

It was revealed concerning Jumayla bint Yasar, sister of Ma'qil ibn Yasar al-Muzani. She was married to Abu al-Badah' 'Asim ibn 'Adi ibn 'Ajlan, who divorced her with a single pronouncement, then left her until her waiting period ended. Then he came to propose to her and wished to take her back, and he was a man of truth, and the woman desired to return to him. Her brother Ma'qil prevented her and said to her: "If you return to him, I will never speak to you again." He said to her husband: "I gave you my noble sister as a bed and preferred you over my people, and you divorced her, then did not take her back until her waiting period ended, and now you come to propose to her. By Allah, I will never marry her to you." He became fiercely protective, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Ma'qil and recited it to him. He said: "I believe in Allah and the Last Day," and so he married her to him and expiated his oath.

This is according to the view of most of the exegetes.

Al-Suddi said: This verse was revealed concerning Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ansari. He had a paternal cousin whose husband divorced her with a single pronouncement, and her waiting period ended, then he wished to take her back. Jabir came and said: "You divorced my cousin, and now you want to marry her again." The woman wished for her husband, so Allah revealed: "And when you divorce women and they reach their term," meaning their waiting period ended. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ajal is the end of a period and the outcome of affairs. Labid said:

"Boast to him by piety, for God is the outcome (al-ajal)."

meaning the outcome of affairs.

"Do not prevent them": do not hinder them. Al-'adl is preventing from marriage. Al-Akhfash recited:

"We have restrained with spears a tongue, and among you there is no restrainer of its sanctity."

And he recited:

"Be generous to me, for my poems are yours, noble women who have been prevented from marriage."

The root of 'adl is constriction and hardship. It is said: the woman and the sheep were restrained when their offspring became entangled in their bellies, so that exit was constricted for it; and the hen was restrained when the eggs became entangled within her; and the crowd restrained the open space when it became cramped for them due to their multitude. It is said: "dha 'idal" when its treatment is constricted and cannot be endured. It is said: "'adala al-amr" when the matter becomes severe and constricted.

'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The people of Kufa have become difficult (u'dila): they do not accept any governor, and no governor accepts them. Aws ibn Hajar said:

"Your brother who is constant in covenant is not one who blames you if he turns away, nor one who pleases you when he approaches;
rather he is the distant one when you are secure, and your companion is the nearest when the matter becomes grave."

[[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 2/661.]]

Tawus said: Verily, cases of 'adl (difficult judgments) came to us which none but Ibn 'Abbas could resolve. Every difficult matter among the Arabs is mu'dal (problematic). From this is the saying of al-Shafi'i:

"When difficult matters have passed from me, I have uncovered their realities by reflection."

"That they marry their former husbands with a new marriage when they agree among themselves in kindness," through a lawful contract and a permissible dower. The structure of the verse: "Do not prevent them from marrying their husbands with kindness when they agree among themselves." In this verse is evidence for the view of those who say: there is no marriage except with a guardian (wali), because He addressed the guardians regarding marriage; and if the woman had the right to contract her own marriage, there would be no prevention, and God's prohibition to the guardians against preventing would have no meaning. This is supported by what

Abu Burda narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no marriage except with a guardian." [153] [[Musnad Ahmad: 4/394.]]

"That is admonished by it whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day." He said this in the singular, though the address is to the guardians, because the original form of addressing a plural is "dhalikum," but this became common until they thought the kaf was part of the word itself and not the pronoun of address, so they said "dhalika." When they said this, the kaf became singular, fixed in the accusative in both verses, applicable to the plural, masculine and feminine.

It has also been said: here the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), which is why it is singular, then He returned to addressing the believers, saying: "That is purer for you (azka lakum) and more pure (atharu) for your hearts" from doubt, because if there is a bond of love in the heart of each of them, one cannot be secure that it will not exceed what Allah has made lawful to them, and one cannot be secure from their guardians lest it come to their hearts about them that they might be innocent of that and so sin.

"And Allah knows" the state of each of them toward the other, "and you do not know."

﴿And the mothers, divorced women who have children by their divorcing husbands, whether they bore them before or after the divorce, shall nurse their children.﴾ This means that they have more right to nursing them than others. It is a recommendation (amr istihbab), not a binding command (amr ijab), that nursing be their obligation, because He, glorified and exalted, said in Surat al-Talaq: ﴿And if they nurse for you, give them their wages﴾ [[Surat al-Talaq: 6.]].

Then He specified the limit of nursing, saying: ﴿two full years﴾. That is, two years. The root is from the saying "hala al-shay'" (the thing changed) when it moved and altered. ﴿Full﴾ is for emphasis, like His saying ﴿That is ten, complete﴾. The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He only said "full two years" because the Arabs say, "So-and-so stayed in the place of such-and-such for two years or two months," while he stayed a year and part of another, and they say:

"Today is two days since I have not seen him," while they mean a day and part of another. From this is His saying: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [Q 2:203]. It is known that one hastens or delays within a day and a half. There are many like this. So God made clear that the two years are full, twenty-four months from the day of birth until weaning.

The scholars differed over whether this limit applies to every infant or only to some. ʿIkrima reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: if she gives birth after six months, she nurses him for two full years, twenty-four months; if she bore him after seven months, she nurses him twenty-three months; if she bore him after nine months, she nurses him twenty-one months. All of that totals thirty months, as God said: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [Q 46:15].

Others said: it is a limit for every infant at a given time, and it must not be less than two years nor more, unless they wish to extend it. If the father wants to wean him before two years and the mother does not agree, he has no right to do so. If the mother says, "I will wean him before two years," and the father says, "No," then she has no right to wean him until both agree. If they both agree before two years, they may wean him; if they disagree, they may not wean him before two years. This is His saying: ﴿by mutual consent between them﴾ [Q 2:233]. This is also the view of Ibn Jurayj, al-Thawri, and a report of al-Walibi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Others said: the verse refers to nursing that falls within the two years, because nursing after the two years does not establish prohibition. This is the view of ʿAli, ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAlqama, al-Shaʿbi, and al-Zuhri. There is a hadith: "There is no nursing (that creates kinship) after two years, and only that which makes flesh grow and bones strong creates prohibition."

Qatada and al-Rabiʿ said: God, mighty and majestic, made it obligatory upon mothers to nurse their children for two full years, then He revealed a concession and relief after that, saying: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ [Q 2:233]. That is, this is the end of nursing; there is no fixed period below that, but it depends on the child's welfare and what sustains him.

Abu Rajaʾ read ﴿li-man arada an yutimma al-riḍāʿa﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ. al-Khalil and al-Farraʾ said: they are two dialects (lughatan), like al-wikala and al-wikala, and al-dalala.

Mujahid and Ibn Muhsin read ﴿al-riḍʿa﴾ (with the sukun), which is a single nursing, like "the single time." ʿIkrima, Humayd, and ʿAwn al-ʿUqayli read ﴿an tatimma al-riḍāʿa﴾ with an open tāʾ and the raising of "al-riḍāʿa," making the verb refer to her. Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿yukmil al-riḍāʿa﴾.

﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs﴾, that is, the father, ﴿is their provision﴾: their food and sustenance, ﴿and their clothing﴾: their garments. Talha, from Musarrif, read ﴿kuswatuhunna﴾ with a ḍamma on the kāf. Both are dialects, like ʾuswa and ʾiswa, and rushwa and rushwa. ﴿According to what is customary﴾: God knew the differences in the conditions of His creatures in wealth and poverty, so He said ﴿according to what is customary﴾, that is, according to one's ability. He made nursing the mother's responsibility and maintenance the father's. ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾. Taklif (imposition) means obligation. The poet said:

"He imposes on me the livelihood of the family of Fahr,
and who is there for me besides delicacies and mustard?" [[al-Sihah by al-Jawhari: 1/164; Lisan al-Arab: 1/531, where it reads "the livelihood of the family of Zayd." The verse is by Jarir.]]

Wus (capacity) is what a person can bear, so that he is able to manage it without it being straitened for him. It is a noun like juhd (effort) and wajd (sorrow). It was said: wus means strength. The word ﴿nafs﴾ (soul) is raised as the subject of the passive verb, since it stands in the place of the agent, and ﴿wus﴾ is in the accusative as the object of the passive verb, since it was placed in the position of the object. Its parallel is in Surat al-Talaq.

﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child﴾. Ibn Muhsin, Ibn Kathir, Shibl, Abu ʿAmr, Salam, Yaʿqub, and Qutayba read it with a raised rāʾ, doubled. Abu Hatim permitted this as a declarative statement (khabar), following the preceding ﴿no soul is burdened﴾. The original is ﴿fa-la yuḍārir﴾, and the rāʾ was assimilated into the rāʾ. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim, Hamza, al-Kinani, and Khalaf read ﴿la tuḍārru﴾ with a doubled and fatḥa-ended rāʾ. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this as a prohibition (nahy). The original is ﴿la tuḍārir﴾; it was assimilated, and its vowel was moved to the lightest vowel, which is the fatḥa. This is supported by ʿUmar's reading ﴿la tuḍārir﴾ with the doubling made explicit. Al-Hasan read ﴿la tuḍārri﴾ with an assimilated, kasra-ended rāʾ, because when it was assimilated it became sākin, and when it is jazm it moves to the kasra. Abban reported from ʿAsim: ﴿la tuḍārir﴾ with a clear, kasra-ended rāʾ, the verb referring to her. Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿la tuḍārru﴾ with a jazm on the rāʾ and its lightening, by elision, seeking lightness.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child﴾, meaning the child is taken from her and given to another after she agreed to nurse him and he has become accustomed to her. ﴿Nor a father through his child﴾, meaning she does not hand the child over to his father after he has become familiar with her, harming him by this.

It was also said: its meaning is, ﴿No mother shall be harmed﴾, so that he compels her to nurse when he accepts (the child) from another woman and she dislikes nursing him, because it is not obligatory upon her. ﴿Nor a father through his child﴾, so that he is made to give the mother more than what is due to her for him, if the child will nurse only from her. These two views are based on the passive verb, in the sense that it is done to her and to the father; the words "mother" and "father" are the two objects. The root word is originally yuḍārr with a fatḥa on the first rāʾ. It is possible that the verb is for both of them (active), and it is possible that tuḍārr is in the manner of a verb whose agent is not named. The meaning is: the mother should not harm the father by refusing to nurse her child in order to trouble the father, nor should the father harm the mother by preventing her from nursing him and taking him from her. On this view, the original is yuḍārir with a kasra on the first rāʾ. On these views, harm returns to both parents, each harming the other because of the child.

It is permissible that the harm returns to the child, meaning neither of them should harm the child: the mother should not refrain from nursing him until he dies, nor should the father stop supporting her, or take him from his mother, so that the child is harmed. The yāʾ is a superfluous letter (ziyada). The meaning is: the mother should not harm her child, nor the father harm his child. All these sayings are transmitted from the exegetes.

﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾. The people of legal opinions (ahl al-fatawa) differed about it: which heir is meant, and who the heir is? One group said: it is the heir of the child. The meaning: upon the heir of the child, who, if the child died and had a maternal uncle, would inherit from him, is the same obligation that was upon his father during his life.

Then they differed about which heir among his heirs. Some said: it is his ʿasaba (agnatic kin), whoever they are among men, not women, such as the grandfather, brother, son of a brother, paternal uncle, son of a paternal uncle, and similar. This is the view of ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him), al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Mujahid, ʿAta', and the school of Sufyan. He said: if the child's share is not enough to support him, the ʿasaba who inherit from him are compelled to have him nursed.

Ibn Sirin said: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtba was approached about nursing an orphan child, and his guardian refused, so he made the nursing paid from his property. He said to the heir: "If he had no property, we would have made his nursing paid from your property. Do you not see that God, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾?" al-Dahhak said: if the child's father dies and the child has wealth, his nursing is paid from the wealth; if he has no wealth, it is taken from the ʿasaba; if the ʿasaba have no wealth, his mother is compelled to nurse him.

Others said: it is anyone who is a mahram relative (dhu rahim mahram) among the heirs of the child, men and women alike. This is the view of Qatada, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Ibn Abi Layla, and the school of Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. They said: each heir is compelled to support him according to the share of his inheritance, whether they are ʿasaba or others.

Others said: it is the one who is a mahram relative among the heirs of the child, and whoever is not a mahram, such as a paternal cousin, a patron (mawla), or the like, is not among those whom God meant by ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾, even if they are among the ʿasaba; they are not compelled to support him. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad. He said: no one is compelled to support the child except a mahram relative.

Others said: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾ means the child himself, who is the heir of his deceased father. Thus, if he has property, the cost of his nursing is paid from his property; if he has no property, his mother is compelled to nurse him. Only the parents are compelled to support a child. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafiʿi.

It was said: it is the surviving one of the child's two parents after the death of the other. Upon him is the like of that, meaning the like of what was upon the father of the wages of nursing, maintenance, and clothing. This was said by most scholars. al-Shaʿbi and al-Zuhri said:

﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾ means that no one should harm (the other).

﴿If both of them wish﴾, that is, the two parents, ﴿weaning﴾: to wean before the two years. The root meaning of fisal is cutting, ﴿by mutual consent from both of them﴾: together, and in agreement, ﴿and consultation﴾, which is the extraction of opinion. Its root is from "sharrat al-dabba" and "shawwartuha" when one draws out what is within her, and this knowledge is called al-mushawar (consultation).

﴿There is no blame upon them﴾. ﴿And if you wish, O fathers, to have your children nursed by wet-nurses other than their mothers﴾, when the mothers are unwilling to nurse them, or because of a problem with them, or the cessation of their milk, or they desire marriage, or you fear loss for your children, ﴿there is no blame upon you if you hand over to their mothers what you give them, according to what is customary.﴾ It was also said: hand over the wages of the wet-nurses to them.

It was said: when you hand over the arrangement of nursing by mutual agreement, without harm. This is His saying: ﴿And what you give, according to what is customary. And fear God, and know that God is seeing of what you do.﴾

﴿And those of you who die and leave wives﴾: that is, who receive their due and die. The root of tawaffa is taking a thing in full (wafiyan). ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God honor his face, read ﴿yatawaffawna﴾ with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, meaning they receive their lifespans and provisions in full. Tawaffa and istawfa have the same meaning. ﴿And leave behind wives, who shall wait, keeping themselves (from marriage) for four months and ten days.﴾

If it is asked: where is the predicate for His saying ﴿And those of you who die﴾? It is said: it is omitted, because the intent was not to state a predicate about them. This is permissible in a noun that is mentioned, with the completion of its predicate in another noun. The first is mentioned and the second is given as the predicate, so the meaning is: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives, who wait for four months and ten days﴾. It is like the words of the poet:

"The sons of Asad, that the son of Qays and his killing
without blood-wit, the abode of humiliation has settled in them." [[Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 2/693.]]

Here he omitted "the son of Qays" though he had begun by mentioning him, and gave the predicate about his killing, that it was humiliation. He also recited:

"Perhaps the wind has inclined me once
toward the son of Abi Dhabban, that he may regret." [[Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 2/693.]]

Here he said "perhaps" (laʿalli), then said "that he may regret" (yatanaddam), because the meaning in it is "perhaps," according to al-Farraʾ.

al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives, their wives shall wait, keeping themselves.﴾

al-Akhfash said: its predicate is in His saying ﴿yatarabbasna﴾, that is, they wait after them.

Qutrub said: the meaning is: it is befitting for them to wait, that is, to remain and be confined, keeping themselves, observing the ʿidda (waiting period) for their husbands, abstaining from perfume and adornment, from marriage and from moving away from the dwelling in which they lived during their husbands' lives, for four months and ten days. But if they are pregnant, they wait until they deliver their pregnancy. When they give birth, their ʿidda ends.

al-Zuhri narrated from ʿUrwa, from ʿAisha, that she used to give the ruling to a woman whose husband had died, until her ʿidda was complete, that she should not wear dyed clothing, but should wear white, and not wear black, and not adorn herself, nor wear jewelry, nor apply kohl with antimony (ithmid) or with kohl containing perfume, even if her eye was in pain. Rather, she should adorn herself with patience, and with whatever kohl appears to her other than antimony, that which has no perfume.

Nafiʿ narrated from Zaynab bint Umm Salama that a woman from Quraysh came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "My daughter's husband has died, and her eye has become sore, so that I fear for her eye, and she wants kohl." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Some of you used to wear the worst of their garments, sit in the lowliest of their houses, and remain a full year in her house. When the year was complete, she would come out, and she would throw a piece of dung behind her. Is it not [enough] four months and ten days?" [[In the sources: she throws a piece of dung, or she threw a piece of dung behind her. al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan: 2/696; al-Sunan al-Kubra: 6/206, with variations.]]

Nafiʿ narrated from Safiyya bint ʿAbd al-Rahman, from Hafsa bint ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in God and the Last Day to mourn over a dead person for more than three days, except over a husband, for she mourns over him four months and ten days." [[Sahih al-Bukhari: 2/79.]]

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: the wisdom in this period is that in it the spirit is breathed into the child. He said ﴿ten﴾ in the feminine form because he meant nights, since when the Arabs complete a count of nights and days, they give precedence to the nights, so they say, "We fasted ten," and fasting is only in the day. The poet said:

"She circled three times between a day and a night,
and the reproach would be that she be hosted and protected."

That is, one who fears a disgracer. This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas: "four months and ten nights." al-Mubarrad said: ten was made feminine because he meant the periods (al-mudad).

﴿Then when they have reached their term﴾, that is, the completion of the ʿidda, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, addressing the guardians, ﴿concerning what they do with themselves﴾, of good conduct in that the guardians should arrange it for them, ﴿according to what is customary.﴾ ﴿And God is Aware of what you do.﴾

﴿And the mothers, divorced women who have children by their divorcing husbands, whether they bore them before or after the divorce, shall nurse their children.﴾ This means that they have more right to nursing them than others. It is a recommendation (amr istihbab), not a binding command (amr ijab), that nursing be their obligation, because He, glorified and exalted, said in Surat al-Talaq: ﴿And if they nurse for you, give them their wages﴾ [[Surat al-Talaq: 6.]].

Then He specified the limit of nursing, saying: ﴿two full years﴾. That is, two years. The root is from the saying "hala al-shay'" (the thing changed) when it moved and altered. ﴿Full﴾ is for emphasis, like His saying ﴿That is ten, complete﴾. The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: He only said "full two years" because the Arabs say, "So-and-so stayed in the place of such-and-such for two years or two months," while he stayed a year and part of another, and they say:

"Today is two days since I have not seen him," while they mean a day and part of another. From this is His saying: ﴿Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [Q 2:203]. It is known that one hastens or delays within a day and a half. There are many like this. So God made clear that the two years are full, twenty-four months from the day of birth until weaning.

The scholars differed over whether this limit applies to every infant or only to some. ʿIkrima reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: if she gives birth after six months, she nurses him for two full years, twenty-four months; if she bore him after seven months, she nurses him twenty-three months; if she bore him after nine months, she nurses him twenty-one months. All of that totals thirty months, as God said: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [Q 46:15].

Others said: it is a limit for every infant at a given time, and it must not be less than two years nor more, unless they wish to extend it. If the father wants to wean him before two years and the mother does not agree, he has no right to do so. If the mother says, "I will wean him before two years," and the father says, "No," then she has no right to wean him until both agree. If they both agree before two years, they may wean him; if they disagree, they may not wean him before two years. This is His saying: ﴿by mutual consent between them﴾ [Q 2:233]. This is also the view of Ibn Jurayj, al-Thawri, and a report of al-Walibi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Others said: the verse refers to nursing that falls within the two years, because nursing after the two years does not establish prohibition. This is the view of ʿAli, ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAlqama, al-Shaʿbi, and al-Zuhri. There is a hadith: "There is no nursing (that creates kinship) after two years, and only that which makes flesh grow and bones strong creates prohibition."

Qatada and al-Rabiʿ said: God, mighty and majestic, made it obligatory upon mothers to nurse their children for two full years, then He revealed a concession and relief after that, saying: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ [Q 2:233]. That is, this is the end of nursing; there is no fixed period below that, but it depends on the child's welfare and what sustains him.

Abu Rajaʾ read ﴿li-man arada an yutimma al-riḍāʿa﴾ with a kasra on the rāʾ. al-Khalil and al-Farraʾ said: they are two dialects (lughatan), like al-wikala and al-wikala, and al-dalala.

Mujahid and Ibn Muhsin read ﴿al-riḍʿa﴾ (with the sukun), which is a single nursing, like "the single time." ʿIkrima, Humayd, and ʿAwn al-ʿUqayli read ﴿an tatimma al-riḍāʿa﴾ with an open tāʾ and the raising of "al-riḍāʿa," making the verb refer to her. Ibn ʿAbbas read ﴿yukmil al-riḍāʿa﴾.

﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs﴾, that is, the father, ﴿is their provision﴾: their food and sustenance, ﴿and their clothing﴾: their garments. Talha, from Musarrif, read ﴿kuswatuhunna﴾ with a ḍamma on the kāf. Both are dialects, like ʾuswa and ʾiswa, and rushwa and rushwa. ﴿According to what is customary﴾: God knew the differences in the conditions of His creatures in wealth and poverty, so He said ﴿according to what is customary﴾, that is, according to one's ability. He made nursing the mother's responsibility and maintenance the father's. ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾. Taklif (imposition) means obligation. The poet said:

"He imposes on me the livelihood of the family of Fahr,
and who is there for me besides delicacies and mustard?" [[al-Sihah by al-Jawhari: 1/164; Lisan al-Arab: 1/531, where it reads "the livelihood of the family of Zayd." The verse is by Jarir.]]

Wus (capacity) is what a person can bear, so that he is able to manage it without it being straitened for him. It is a noun like juhd (effort) and wajd (sorrow). It was said: wus means strength. The word ﴿nafs﴾ (soul) is raised as the subject of the passive verb, since it stands in the place of the agent, and ﴿wus﴾ is in the accusative as the object of the passive verb, since it was placed in the position of the object. Its parallel is in Surat al-Talaq.

﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child﴾. Ibn Muhsin, Ibn Kathir, Shibl, Abu ʿAmr, Salam, Yaʿqub, and Qutayba read it with a raised rāʾ, doubled. Abu Hatim permitted this as a declarative statement (khabar), following the preceding ﴿no soul is burdened﴾. The original is ﴿fa-la yuḍārir﴾, and the rāʾ was assimilated into the rāʾ. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim, Hamza, al-Kinani, and Khalaf read ﴿la tuḍārru﴾ with a doubled and fatḥa-ended rāʾ. Abu ʿUbayd preferred this as a prohibition (nahy). The original is ﴿la tuḍārir﴾; it was assimilated, and its vowel was moved to the lightest vowel, which is the fatḥa. This is supported by ʿUmar's reading ﴿la tuḍārir﴾ with the doubling made explicit. Al-Hasan read ﴿la tuḍārri﴾ with an assimilated, kasra-ended rāʾ, because when it was assimilated it became sākin, and when it is jazm it moves to the kasra. Abban reported from ʿAsim: ﴿la tuḍārir﴾ with a clear, kasra-ended rāʾ, the verb referring to her. Abu Jaʿfar read ﴿la tuḍārru﴾ with a jazm on the rāʾ and its lightening, by elision, seeking lightness.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child﴾, meaning the child is taken from her and given to another after she agreed to nurse him and he has become accustomed to her. ﴿Nor a father through his child﴾, meaning she does not hand the child over to his father after he has become familiar with her, harming him by this.

It was also said: its meaning is, ﴿No mother shall be harmed﴾, so that he compels her to nurse when he accepts (the child) from another woman and she dislikes nursing him, because it is not obligatory upon her. ﴿Nor a father through his child﴾, so that he is made to give the mother more than what is due to her for him, if the child will nurse only from her. These two views are based on the passive verb, in the sense that it is done to her and to the father; the words "mother" and "father" are the two objects. The root word is originally yuḍārr with a fatḥa on the first rāʾ. It is possible that the verb is for both of them (active), and it is possible that tuḍārr is in the manner of a verb whose agent is not named. The meaning is: the mother should not harm the father by refusing to nurse her child in order to trouble the father, nor should the father harm the mother by preventing her from nursing him and taking him from her. On this view, the original is yuḍārir with a kasra on the first rāʾ. On these views, harm returns to both parents, each harming the other because of the child.

It is permissible that the harm returns to the child, meaning neither of them should harm the child: the mother should not refrain from nursing him until he dies, nor should the father stop supporting her, or take him from his mother, so that the child is harmed. The yāʾ is a superfluous letter (ziyada). The meaning is: the mother should not harm her child, nor the father harm his child. All these sayings are transmitted from the exegetes.

﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾. The people of legal opinions (ahl al-fatawa) differed about it: which heir is meant, and who the heir is? One group said: it is the heir of the child. The meaning: upon the heir of the child, who, if the child died and had a maternal uncle, would inherit from him, is the same obligation that was upon his father during his life.

Then they differed about which heir among his heirs. Some said: it is his ʿasaba (agnatic kin), whoever they are among men, not women, such as the grandfather, brother, son of a brother, paternal uncle, son of a paternal uncle, and similar. This is the view of ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him), al-Zuhri, al-Hasan, Mujahid, ʿAta', and the school of Sufyan. He said: if the child's share is not enough to support him, the ʿasaba who inherit from him are compelled to have him nursed.

Ibn Sirin said: ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtba was approached about nursing an orphan child, and his guardian refused, so he made the nursing paid from his property. He said to the heir: "If he had no property, we would have made his nursing paid from your property. Do you not see that God, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾?" al-Dahhak said: if the child's father dies and the child has wealth, his nursing is paid from the wealth; if he has no wealth, it is taken from the ʿasaba; if the ʿasaba have no wealth, his mother is compelled to nurse him.

Others said: it is anyone who is a mahram relative (dhu rahim mahram) among the heirs of the child, men and women alike. This is the view of Qatada, al-Hasan ibn Salih, Ibn Abi Layla, and the school of Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr. They said: each heir is compelled to support him according to the share of his inheritance, whether they are ʿasaba or others.

Others said: it is the one who is a mahram relative among the heirs of the child, and whoever is not a mahram, such as a paternal cousin, a patron (mawla), or the like, is not among those whom God meant by ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾, even if they are among the ʿasaba; they are not compelled to support him. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad. He said: no one is compelled to support the child except a mahram relative.

Others said: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾ means the child himself, who is the heir of his deceased father. Thus, if he has property, the cost of his nursing is paid from his property; if he has no property, his mother is compelled to nurse him. Only the parents are compelled to support a child. This is the view of Malik and al-Shafiʿi.

It was said: it is the surviving one of the child's two parents after the death of the other. Upon him is the like of that, meaning the like of what was upon the father of the wages of nursing, maintenance, and clothing. This was said by most scholars. al-Shaʿbi and al-Zuhri said:

﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾ means that no one should harm (the other).

﴿If both of them wish﴾, that is, the two parents, ﴿weaning﴾: to wean before the two years. The root meaning of fisal is cutting, ﴿by mutual consent from both of them﴾: together, and in agreement, ﴿and consultation﴾, which is the extraction of opinion. Its root is from "sharrat al-dabba" and "shawwartuha" when one draws out what is within her, and this knowledge is called al-mushawar (consultation).

﴿There is no blame upon them﴾. ﴿And if you wish, O fathers, to have your children nursed by wet-nurses other than their mothers﴾, when the mothers are unwilling to nurse them, or because of a problem with them, or the cessation of their milk, or they desire marriage, or you fear loss for your children, ﴿there is no blame upon you if you hand over to their mothers what you give them, according to what is customary.﴾ It was also said: hand over the wages of the wet-nurses to them.

It was said: when you hand over the arrangement of nursing by mutual agreement, without harm. This is His saying: ﴿And what you give, according to what is customary. And fear God, and know that God is seeing of what you do.﴾

﴿And those of you who die and leave wives﴾: that is, who receive their due and die. The root of tawaffa is taking a thing in full (wafiyan). ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may God honor his face, read ﴿yatawaffawna﴾ with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, meaning they receive their lifespans and provisions in full. Tawaffa and istawfa have the same meaning. ﴿And leave behind wives, who shall wait, keeping themselves (from marriage) for four months and ten days.﴾

If it is asked: where is the predicate for His saying ﴿And those of you who die﴾? It is said: it is omitted, because the intent was not to state a predicate about them. This is permissible in a noun that is mentioned, with the completion of its predicate in another noun. The first is mentioned and the second is given as the predicate, so the meaning is: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives, who wait for four months and ten days﴾. It is like the words of the poet:

"The sons of Asad, that the son of Qays and his killing
without blood-wit, the abode of humiliation has settled in them." [[Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 2/693.]]

Here he omitted "the son of Qays" though he had begun by mentioning him, and gave the predicate about his killing, that it was humiliation. He also recited:

"Perhaps the wind has inclined me once
toward the son of Abi Dhabban, that he may regret." [[Jami al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 2/693.]]

Here he said "perhaps" (laʿalli), then said "that he may regret" (yatanaddam), because the meaning in it is "perhaps," according to al-Farraʾ.

al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives, their wives shall wait, keeping themselves.﴾

al-Akhfash said: its predicate is in His saying ﴿yatarabbasna﴾, that is, they wait after them.

Qutrub said: the meaning is: it is befitting for them to wait, that is, to remain and be confined, keeping themselves, observing the ʿidda (waiting period) for their husbands, abstaining from perfume and adornment, from marriage and from moving away from the dwelling in which they lived during their husbands' lives, for four months and ten days. But if they are pregnant, they wait until they deliver their pregnancy. When they give birth, their ʿidda ends.

al-Zuhri narrated from ʿUrwa, from ʿAisha, that she used to give the ruling to a woman whose husband had died, until her ʿidda was complete, that she should not wear dyed clothing, but should wear white, and not wear black, and not adorn herself, nor wear jewelry, nor apply kohl with antimony (ithmid) or with kohl containing perfume, even if her eye was in pain. Rather, she should adorn herself with patience, and with whatever kohl appears to her other than antimony, that which has no perfume.

Nafiʿ narrated from Zaynab bint Umm Salama that a woman from Quraysh came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "My daughter's husband has died, and her eye has become sore, so that I fear for her eye, and she wants kohl." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Some of you used to wear the worst of their garments, sit in the lowliest of their houses, and remain a full year in her house. When the year was complete, she would come out, and she would throw a piece of dung behind her. Is it not [enough] four months and ten days?" [[In the sources: she throws a piece of dung, or she threw a piece of dung behind her. al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan: 2/696; al-Sunan al-Kubra: 6/206, with variations.]]

Nafiʿ narrated from Safiyya bint ʿAbd al-Rahman, from Hafsa bint ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in God and the Last Day to mourn over a dead person for more than three days, except over a husband, for she mourns over him four months and ten days." [[Sahih al-Bukhari: 2/79.]]

Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: the wisdom in this period is that in it the spirit is breathed into the child. He said ﴿ten﴾ in the feminine form because he meant nights, since when the Arabs complete a count of nights and days, they give precedence to the nights, so they say, "We fasted ten," and fasting is only in the day. The poet said:

"She circled three times between a day and a night,
and the reproach would be that she be hosted and protected."

That is, one who fears a disgracer. This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas: "four months and ten nights." al-Mubarrad said: ten was made feminine because he meant the periods (al-mudad).

﴿Then when they have reached their term﴾, that is, the completion of the ʿidda, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, addressing the guardians, ﴿concerning what they do with themselves﴾, of good conduct in that the guardians should arrange it for them, ﴿according to what is customary.﴾ ﴿And God is Aware of what you do.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 235–237 (part 1 of 2):

"And there is no blame upon you, O men, for what you hint at of proposing to the women in waiting (ʿiddah), and the root of taʿrīd (hinting, allusion) is to suggest something indirectly." The poet said:
"As one who writes Hebrew script with his right hand, in Taymāʾ, ink-marked, then lines up the rows [of writing]."
[[al-Ṣiḥāḥ by al-Jawhari: 3/1087; the verse was recited by al-Aṣmaʿi and attributed to al-Shammākh.]]

Taʿrīd in speech is that indirect allusion of speech by which the listener understands the meaning without explicit statement. Its root is from ʿarḍ al-shay', meaning its side; it is said: "He struck with it the side of the wall," as if he circles around it without making it manifest. The taʿrīd of proposal mentioned in this verse, according to what has come in the tafsir, is that he says to her while she is in her ʿiddah:
"Indeed you are beautiful, indeed you are righteous, indeed you are beneficial, indeed I have resolved to marry, indeed I am desirous of you, indeed I am eager for you, and perhaps Allah will bring good to you, and if Allah brings us together in what is lawful, I would be pleased, and if I marry you I will give you and treat you well," and similar speech, without saying to her: "Marry me."

Ibrahim said: "There is no harm in his sending her a gift and attending to her affairs during her ʿiddah, if she is one of his concerns."

Ibn ʿAwf related from Muhammad, from ʿUbaydah, concerning this verse, that he said: "He says to her guardian, 'Let no one precede me to her.'" Mujahid said: "A man said to a woman at the funeral of her husband: 'Do not precede me with yourself.' She said: 'You have already preceded me.'"

Ibn al-Mubarak related from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sulayman, from his maternal aunt, that Sukayna bint Handhala said: "Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn ʿAli entered upon me while I was in my ʿiddah and said: 'O daughter of Handhala, you know my kinship to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the right of my grandfather over me and his precedence in Islam.' She said: 'May Allah forgive you, Abu Jaʿfar! Do you propose to me during my ʿiddah while you are taken as a source of knowledge?' He said: 'Or did I actually do that? I only sought your favour by my kinship to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and my standing. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon Umm Salama, who had been married to her cousin Abu Salama, and when her husband died, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ continued mentioning to her his station with Allah while he was leaning on his hand, until the mat left its mark on his hand from the intensity of his leaning on it. That was not a proposal.'"
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/705.]]

Ibn Yazid said concerning this verse: "My father used to say: Everything that falls short of resolving the bond of marriage is zina." Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "And there is no blame upon you for what you hint at of proposing to women," and khitbah (proposal) is a request for marriage, the verbal noun of your saying: "The man proposed to the woman, khatabahā khiṭbatan and khuṭbā."

Some people said: it is on the pattern of jilsah (sitting), qiʿdah (sitting), and rukbah (riding), and the meaning of their saying "So-and-so proposed to so-and-so" is: he asked her for a proposal regarding what was in her mind, that is, her needs and her affair, from their saying "What is your khaṭb?" i.e., your need and your affair. Allah said: "What is your affair, O Samiri?" [Q 20:95]

Al-Akhfash said: al-khuṭbah is mention, and al-khuṭbah is the gathering, so the meaning is: "in what you hint at, of those among whom you propose to women, in their presence." "Or you conceal within yourselves," i.e., you keep secret and hide in your souls, regarding their proposal and their marriage. It is said: "kanantu al-shay' and akannantuhu" are two dialects. Thaʿlab said: "akannat al-shay'" means I concealed it in my soul, and "kannatuhu" means I covered it. Al-Suddi said: it is that he enters and makes himself known to them as he wishes, without speaking anything.

"Allah knows that you will mention them in your hearts." Al-Hasan said: meaning the proposal. "But do not promise them secretly" [or: "do not make a pledge with them"] — some of them said: it is zina. A man would enter upon a woman for the sake of suspicion, while hinting at marriage, and say to her: "Leave me; when you complete your ʿiddah I will reveal my marriage to you." So Allah, exalted, forbade that. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibrahim, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ibn Abi Mujliz, al-Dahhak, al-Rabiʿ and ʿAtaʾ, and it is the narration of ʿAtiyya from Ibn ʿAbbas. What proves it is the saying of al-Aʿsha:

"Do not approach a neighbour's woman, for her secret is forbidden to you, [so marry her or remain forever]."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 2/625.]]

And al-Hutay'a said:
"He forbids the secret of their neighbour to them, and their neighbour eats the nose of the dishes."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 2/625.]]

Mujahid said: it is the man's saying to the woman: "Do not let yourself escape me, for I will marry you." Al-Shaʿbi and al-Suddi said: he does not take her pledge that she will not marry anyone else. ʿIkrima said: he does not propose to her during her ʿiddah. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he does not bargain with her for such and such amount of wealth on condition that she does not marry anyone else. All these interpretations are close in meaning, and the "secret" in these sayings is marriage. Imru' al-Qays said:

"Did not Bisasa claim today that I have grown old, and that those like me cannot do well with the secret?"
[[Gharib al-Hadith: 1/238; Lisan al-ʿArab: 15/259.]]

Al-Aʿsha said:
"They did not seek her secret for wealth, and they did not leave her for her asceticism."
[[al-Ṣiḥāḥ by al-Jawhari: 2/481.]]

That is, her marriage. Al-Kalbi said: "But do not promise them secretly" means: do not describe yourselves to them by frequent intercourse, so that he says to her, "I will come to you four or five times," and similar things. According to this view, the "secret" is intercourse itself. Al-Farazdaq said:

"Withholding the secrets except from their own people, and failing what the jealous, wasted lover supposed."
[[al-Ṣiḥāḥ by al-Jawhari: 4/1383.]]

He means that they are chaste in their hands from intercourse except with their husbands. Ru'ba said:

"He abstained from their secrets after the dusk, and did not place her between a rubbing and a passion."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 4/358.]]

He means he refrained from having relations with her after he had been bound to that.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "But do not promise them secretly" means: do not marry them secretly, then keep her until she is released, and then reveal it. The root of sirr is what you conceal in yourself, and marriage, adultery and intercourse are called sirr only because they occur between a man and a woman in secrecy. It is also said that the private part is called sirr because it is not made apparent. Thaʿlab related from Ibn al-Aʿrabi:

"When she saw my secret changed and bent, from beyond [its] desire, her secret when it turned away."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 4/358; attributed to al-Afwah al-Awdi, where it reads: "When she saw my secret change and turn, from beyond the desire of its ... when it turned away."]]

Then He excepted, saying: "Except that you say a fair word." It was said: a good promise. Mujahid said: it is allusion without explicit declaration or disclosure. The "an" [in "an taqūlū"] is in the place of an accusative, as a substitute for "secret." ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: all of this is abrogated by His saying: "And do not resolve the bond of marriage," meaning do not validate the bond of marriage. Ibn al-Zajjaj said: "Do not resolve upon the bond of marriage," as it is said: "He struck the hand of purity and blessing." ʿAntara said:

"I have spent nights hungry, and its shade covered me, until I attain by it the generous feast."
[[Lisan al-ʿArab: 11/419; where it reads "generous food."]]

That is, and its shade was over me.

"Until the Book reaches its term" — until the ʿiddah ends. He called it "Book" because it is an obligation from Allah, exalted, like His saying: "Fasting is prescribed for you."

"And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him," i.e., fear Allah. "And know that Allah is Forgiving, Forbearing," who does not hasten to punishment. The Arabs say: "Place the howdah upon the most patient of the camels."

"There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them, [or] fixed for them an obligation," the verse.

It was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar who married a woman from the Banu Hanifa, did not name a dowry for her, then divorced her before touching her. Allah revealed this verse, and when it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "Provide for her, even if it is with your cap." So this is His saying: "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them," i.e., have not had intercourse with them.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "tamāssūhunna" with an alif, in the form of mufā'alah, because the body of each of them touches the body of the other, so both touch one another; its proof is His saying: "before they touch one another." The rest read "tamassūhunna" without alif, because the coming together is only from the action of the man; its proof is His saying: "No human has touched me."

"Or fix for them an obligation" — i.e., establish for them a dowry. It is said: "The ruler assigned for so-and-so," meaning he recorded for him a charity in the register. If it is asked: what is the reason for negating blame regarding one who divorces, and would there be blame on the man if he divorced after consummation, so that it is removed from him before consummation? It is answered:

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "What is the matter with people who play with the limits of Allah, saying: 'I have divorced you, I have taken you back'?"
[[Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/650, no. 2017.]]

And he ﷺ said: "Do not divorce your wives except because of suspicion, for Allah does not love those who taste [much] or the women who taste [much]."
[[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 4/335.]]

And he peace be upon him said: "The most detested of lawful things to Allah is divorce."
[[Sunan Ibn Majah: 1/650, no. 2018.]]

And he peace be upon him said: "Indeed Allah detests every frequent divorcer who tastes [many]."
[[al-Musannaf of Ibn Abi Shayba: 4/172, with variation.]]

When the Messenger said this, they thought they would sin by doing so, so Allah, exalted, informed them that there is no blame in divorcing women when it is done in the commendable manner, since separation is sometimes better than retention. It was also said: the meaning of His saying "There is no blame upon you" is that there is no way for the women against you if you divorce them, while you have not touched them and you have not fixed for them an obligation of dowry or maintenance.

It was also said: the meaning is "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them," at whatever time you wish, since there is no prescribed sunnah in their divorce. So a man may divorce them when he has not touched them, whether she is menstruating or pure, and at any time he likes. This is not the case for one who has been consummated with, because it is not permitted for her husband to divorce her if she is one of those with menstrual cycles, except in a ʿiddah, clearly, in a purity during which he has not had intercourse with her. If he divorces her while she is menstruating, or past the age [of menstruation], the divorce takes effect.

"And provide for them," i.e., furnish them and give them from your wealth what they may enjoy. Al-mutʿah and al-matāʿ are what one is provided with as provision. "According to the wealthy" (al-mūsiʿ), i.e., the rich, "his measure" (qadaruhu), "and according to the straitened" (al-muqtir), the poor, "his measure," i.e., his capacity and his ability. Abu Jaʿfar, Hafs, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Ibn Dhakwan read the dāl in both with a fatḥah, and Abu ʿUbayda chose it, saying: because of its grandeur in both. The others read the dāl in both with a sukūn, and Abu Hatim chose it. Both are dialects; he said: the Qur'an was recited with both. The confirmation of the fatḥah is His saying: "So the valleys flowed according to their measure" [Q 13:17], and the confirmation of the sukūn is His saying: "They did not measure Allah with His true measure" [Q 6:91]. The Arabs say: "al-qaḍāʾ and al-qadar." Abu Yazid al-Ansari said: "al-qaḍāʾ and al-qadr" with a sukūn on the dāl. The poet, al-Farazdaq, said:

"My sand was not poured into the iron of Mujashi', along with the decree, except for a need of mine that I wanted."

Some said: qadar (with fatḥah) is the verbal noun, and qadr (with sukūn) is the noun. "Matāʿan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, i.e., "provide for them a provision." It may be accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, because matāʿ is indefinite and qadr is definite. "According to what is fair" (bil-maʿrūf), i.e., what Allah has commanded you, without injustice or procrastination. "Ḥaqqan" is in the accusative by way of reporting, its meaning: "I inform you of it as a truth." It was also said that it is in the accusative as a qualifier.

Ruling of the verse

The commentators said: it was said that this concerns a man who marries a woman and does not name a dowry for her, then divorces her before touching her; she has the mutʿah and no fixed dowry, by consensus of the scholars. They differed regarding the provision for a divorced woman in other than this case. Some said: every divorced woman has a provision, whoever she is and in whatever manner the divorce occurred. The provision is obligatory, to be paid from the divorcer's wealth as all other debts obligatory upon him are paid, whether he consummated with her or not, whether a dowry was fixed or not, provided the divorce came from him. As for when the separation comes from her, she has neither provision nor dowry. This is the view of al-Hasan, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu al-ʿAliya and Muhammad ibn Jarir, who said: because of His saying:

"And for divorced women is provision according to what is fair, a duty upon the righteous." So He made the provision obligatory for all divorced women and did not distinguish. The meaning of the verse on this view is: "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them, whether you have fixed for them an obligation or not," because every wife is either one for whom a dowry is named or one for whom none is named. From what they transmitted of His saying "or fix for them an obligation," we know that what is meant by "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women" is those for whom an obligation has been fixed, and those for whom none was fixed, for there is no sense in saying: "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them or fixed for them an obligation," and then saying: "And provide for them," meaning all of them.

Others said: the provision is obligatory for every divorced woman except the one for whom an obligation was fixed when she is divorced before consummation; for her there is no provision, but she has half of the named dowry. This is the view of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, Nafiʿ, ʿAtaʾ and Mujahid, and the school of al-Shafiʿi. The meaning of the verse on this view is: "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them and have not fixed for them an obligation." The alif is extra, like His saying "or they increase" [Q 37:147] and similar. Then He commanded provision for them.

It is also possible that His saying "And provide for them" refers to divorced women for whom no obligation was fixed before touching, and not to those for whom it was fixed. Then His following saying "And if you divorce them before you touch them" is specific to that. The beginning of the verse follows the apparent generality for those for whom an obligation was fixed and those for whom none was fixed, while in "And provide for them" it is specific to those for whom none was fixed, in accordance with the following verse.

Al-Zuhri said: there are two kinds of provision, one of which the ruler adjudicates and the other he does not adjudicate, but it is binding upon him between himself and Allah. As for the one the ruler adjudicates, it is for one who divorced before a dowry was fixed and before consummation; he is compelled to pay the provision, which is His saying: "a duty upon the doers of good." The provision that is binding between him and Allah, which the ruler does not adjudicate, is for one who divorces after consummation and after a dowry was fixed, which is His saying: "a duty upon the righteous."

Others said: none of that is obligatory; rather, provision is a kindness, and the command to it is a command of recommendation and encouragement, not a command of obligation and requirement. This is the view of Abu Hanifa. Ibn Sirin related that a man divorced a woman after consummation, and she brought a case against him before Shurayh regarding the provision. Shurayh said: "It is not the case that you must be among the doers of good, nor that you must be among the righteous," and he did not compel him to it.

They differed regarding the amount and extent of the provision.
