They went out and encamped, then they became cowardly, disliked death, and made excuses, saying to their king: "The land to which we go has plague, so we will not go there until the plague ends from it." God sent death upon them. When they saw that death had multiplied among them, they went out from their homes fleeing from death. When the king saw that, he said: "O God, Lord of Ya'qub and God of Musa, You see the disobedience of Your servants. Show them a sign in themselves so that they know they cannot flee from You." When they went out, God said to them: "Die," as a punishment, and they all died, and their animals died as the death of one man. Eight days passed over them until they swelled and their bodies became bloated. People came out to them but were unable to bury them, so they built an enclosure around them to keep off the beasts and left them there.

They differed regarding the number of them. 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: They were three thousand. Ibn 'Abbas and Wahb said: four thousand. Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: eight thousand. Abu Rawq said: ten thousand. Abu Malik said: thirty thousand. al-Waqidi said: a little over two hundred thousand. Ibn Jurayj said: forty thousand. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: seventy thousand. al-Dahhak said: they were a great number. The most correct of the sayings is the one who said: they exceeded ten thousand, because God said ﴿and they were thousands﴾, and what is less than ten is not called thousands; rather it is said: three thousand and above up to ten thousand. Among the plurals, "alf" (thousands) is the plural of the great number, and its plural of the small number is "alaf," like yawm and ayyam, waqt and awqat, and alf on the pattern of af'al.

[It was said:] They were three thousand. [Wakisa] [The manuscript reads thus.] al-Yaman was a non-Arab from the Banu al-Fidaham.

They said: A period passed, and their bodies had decayed, their bones were stripped, and their joints had come apart. A prophet called Hizqil ibn Buri Tharim, one of the successors of the Children of Israel after Musa (peace be upon him), passed by them. The one entrusted with the affairs of the Children of Israel after Musa (peace be upon him) was Yusha' ibn Nun, then Kalib ibn Yufuna, then Hizqil, who was called Ibn al-'Ajuz (son of the old woman), because his mother was an old woman who asked God for a child when she had grown old and barren, and God granted her him, which is why he was called Ibn al-'Ajuz. [Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/322.]

al-Hasan and Muqatil said: He was Dhu al-Kifl, because he took responsibility for seventy prophets and saved them from being killed, and said to them: "Go, for if I am killed it is better than that you all be killed." When the Jews came and asked Hizqil about the seventy prophets, he said: "They have gone, and I do not know where they are." God protected Dhu al-Kifl from the Jews. When Hizqil passed by those dead, he stopped over them and began to reflect upon them, marveling at them. God revealed to him: "O Hizqil, do you wish that I show you a sign, that I show you how I give life to the dead?" He said: "Yes." So God gave them life. This is the saying of al-Suddi and a group of exegetes.

Hilal ibn Yasaf and a group of scholars said: Rather, Hizqil supplicated his Lord that they be revived. He said: "O Lord, if You willed, You would revive these, and they would populate Your lands and worship You." God said: "Would you like Me to do that?" He said: "Yes," so He revived them.

'Ata', Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: Rather, they were the people of Hizqil, whom God revived after eight days, for when that befell them, Hizqil went out seeking them, found them dead, and wept, saying: "O Lord, I was among a people who praised You, glorified You, sanctified You, declared Your oneness and magnified You, and now I am left alone with no people." God revealed to him: "I have made their life to be in your hand." Hizqil said: "Live, by God's command," and they lived.

And he said: Affliction and hardship of the times befell them. They complained of what had befallen them and said: "We have not remained long; would that we had died and found rest from what we are in." God revealed to Hizqil: "Your people have cried out from the affliction and claim that they wish they had died and rested. But what rest is there in death? Do they think that I am unable to resurrect them after death? Go to the cemetery of such-and-such, for there are dead people there." He came to them, and God said: "O Hizqil, arise and call to them." Their bodies and bones had been scattered. Hizqil called out: "O bones, God commands you to be clothed with flesh," and they were all clothed with flesh; then after the flesh, skin, blood, sinews and veins, and they became bodies. Then he called out: "O spirits, God commands you to return to your bodies," and they all stood up, wearing the garments in which they had died, and they uttered one takbir together.

Al-Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir related from Mujahid that when they were revived they said: "Glory be to You, our Lord, and praise be to You; there is no god but You." They returned to their people after God revived them, had offspring and lived for a long time, knowing that they had been dead; the pallor of death was upon their faces, and they did not wear a garment but it became greasy like a shroud, until they died at their appointed times that had been decreed for them. [In full, with variation, in Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/322-323.]

Ibn 'Abbas said: Indeed, that scent is still found today in that tribe of the Jews. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/798.]

Qatada said: God despised them for their fleeing from death, so He caused them to die, then raised them to complete their remaining appointed terms, and had their terms not come, they would not have been raised after their death. [The same source.] That is His saying ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes﴾ — "Have you not considered" means: Have you not been informed, have you not known through My informing you. It is a seeing of the heart, not of the eye, so the confirmation of God's reports, the Mighty and Majestic, becomes like seeing them with one's own eyes.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: It is an expression of wonder and magnification, saying: Have you seen the like of them? Just as you say: "Have you not seen what so-and-so is doing?" Every "alam tara" (have you not seen) in the Qur'an, where the Prophet (ﷺ) did not witness it, has this meaning. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read all of them as ﴿alam tara﴾ with the rā' sukun, which is a dialect of a tribe of the Arabs: when they dropped the yā' for the jussive, they imagined the rā' to be the end of the word and so made it sakin. al-Farra' recited:

Sulayma said: "Travel for us a little,"

﴿to those who left their homes﴾ — wa-hum (and they) is the waw of circumstance; ﴿alluf﴾ is the plural of alf (thousand). Ibn Zayd said: "Their hearts are united," making it the plural of alf, like jalis and julus, qa'id and qu'ud. ﴿for fear of death﴾, i.e., out of fear of death. ﴿God said to them: "Die"﴾ is a command of transformation, like His saying ﴿Be apes, despised﴾.

﴿Then He gave them life after their death. Indeed God is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks.﴾ Then He urged them to jihad, saying: ﴿And fight in the way of God﴾ — obedience to God, against the enemies of God — ﴿and know that God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ Most exegetes said: This is addressed to those who were revived. al-Dahhak said: They were commanded to fight in the way of God, but they went out from their homes fleeing from jihad, so God caused them to die, then revived them, then commanded them to return to jihad. Some of them said: This address is for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan...﴾

Sufyan said: When the verse ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times the like thereof﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My Lord, increase my community." Then ﴿Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan﴾ was revealed, and he said: "Increase my community," and then ﴿Only those who are patient will be given their reward without reckoning﴾ was revealed. [177]

The scholars differed about the meaning of this loan. al-Akhfash said: His saying "yuqridu" (lends) is not because God has need, but the Arabs say: "You have with me a loan of goodness and a loan of evil," for an event that will come, in which there is its joy or its harm.

al-Zajjaj said: "Qard" (loan) in the language means good trial and bad trial. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

Do not mix the wicked with the good,
And strip off your garments from them and escape naked.
Every man will surely be repaid his loan,
Good or evil, or in debt, in the measure he owed.

[The first verse is in Tarikh al-Tabari: 3/454, the second in Lisan al-'Arab: 7/216.] And al-Kisa'i recited:

Loans are repaid with their likes:
Good with good, and evil with evil.

[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/239.]

He also said: It is what you have sent forward of righteous or evil deed.

Ibn Kaysan said: The loan is that you give something so that its like returns to you and is repaid. God likened the deeds of believers for God, in hope of His reward, to a loan, because they only give what they spend seeking what is with God, the Mighty and Majestic, of abundant reward. So "qard" is the name of everything a person gives in order to be repaid for it. Labid said:

When you are repaid a loan, repay it in kind,
For a young man is only repaid as he has done.

[Lisan al-'Arab: 7/217.]

Some scholars of meanings said: In the verse there is ellipsis and implication; its meaning is: Who is it that will lend to the servants of God a loan, like His saying ﴿Indeed those who harm God and His Messenger﴾, and His saying ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾. He here attributed it to Himself for magnification and to incline the heart, as in the hadith: God, the Exalted, says to His servant: "I asked you for food but you did not feed Me; I asked you for drink but you did not give Me drink; I asked you for clothing but you did not clothe Me." The servant says: "My Lord, how is that?" He says: "Such-and-such a hungry man passed by you, and such-and-such a naked man, and you did not show kindness to him with your bounty; so today I will withhold from you My bounty as you withheld it from him."

The people of allusion (ahl al-isharah) said: God commanded charity in the wording of a loan, to show His love for His believing servants, for one only borrows from the beloved. That is why Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: "I marvel at one who keeps wealth while the Lord of the Throne borrows from him." Some said: This is a kindness from God in consolation and lending to His servants.

Abu al-Qasim, on the authority of Abu Umama, said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I saw written on the gate of Paradise: charity is rewarded tenfold, and the loan eighteen-fold. I said: O Jibril, why is the loan greater in reward? He said: Because the one who asks for a loan comes to you only in need, whereas charity may fall into the hands of those who do not deserve it." [178] [Kanz al-'Ummal: 6/211, no. 15382.]

Abu Salama, on the authority of Abu Hurayra and Ibn 'Abbas, both said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever lends to his Muslim brother, for him there are good deeds for every dirham equal to the weight of Uhud, Thabir and Mount Sinai." [179] [Bughyat al-Ba-hith: 77.]

So the meaning of the verse: "Who is it" (man) is an interrogative whose position is nominative as the subject, and "alladhi" (who) is its predicate; "yuqridu Allah" (lends God) means spends in obedience to God. The root of qard is cutting, from which comes "the mouse cuts the cloth" (qarada al-fa'r al-thawb), and poetry is called "qarid" because it cuts it from speech, and debt is called "qard" because it cuts it from one's wealth.

﴿a goodly loan﴾. 'Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Waqidi said: i.e., seeking reward, his soul content with it. Ibn al-Mubarak said: It is that the wealth is from what is lawful. 'Umar ibn 'Uthman al-Sadafi said: It is that one does not reproach for it nor cause harm. Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah said: It is that one does not expect a return for one's loan.

﴿and He will multiply it for him﴾ — yudā'if-hu, increase it for him. The readers differed about it. 'Asim, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Hatim read ﴿fa-yudā'ifahu﴾ with the nasb and alif. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read with tashdid, nasb and alif. Ibn Kathir and Abu Ja'far read with tashdid and raf'. The others read with alif and takhfif and raf' of the fa'. Whoever reads with raf' makes it a conjunction to His saying "yuqridu"; it is said: "fa-huwa yudā'ifuhu" (so He multiplies it). Whoever reads with nasb makes it an answer to the interrogative with the fa', and it is said: by the implied "an" (that). Tashdid and takhfif are two dialects. The evidence for tashdid is His saying ﴿manifold increase﴾, because tashdid is for multiplicity.

al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: This multiplication is known only to God, like His saying ﴿and gives from Him a great reward﴾. Abu Hurayra said: This is about the expense for jihad. He said: We used to reckon—while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was among us—that a man's expense on himself, his companions and his mount was two thousand thousand.

﴿And God withholds﴾ — i.e., He withholds provision from whom He wills, and restricts and constricts it for him. Its evidence is His saying ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾, i.e., they hold them back from spending in the way of God. ﴿And He expands﴾ — i.e., He widens provision for whom He wills. Its parallel is His saying ﴿Had God expanded provision for His servants...﴾ The origin of this is the withholding of the hand at stinginess and its extending at giving.

It was also said: It is giving life and causing death; whoever He causes to die, He has withheld him, and whoever He extends his life, He has expanded for him. It was also said: ﴿God withholds﴾ the charity, and ﴿expands﴾ by replacement. al-Yazidi related from 'Amr that he said: with the ṣād in some narrations. From some of them, as if he said: this is about hearts: when God commanded them to give charity, He informed them that they could not do so except by His enabling. ﴿And God withholds and expands﴾, i.e., He grips hearts and withdraws them so that they do not expand toward good, and expands some of them so that they send forward good for themselves.

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ — i.e., to God you return, and He will reward you for your deeds. Qatada said: The pronoun refers to the dust, a metaphor for something unmentioned, i.e., from dust He created them and to it they return.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Umama and Zayd ibn Aslam — some of their narrations entering into one another — that they said: When the verse ﴿Who is it that will lend God a goodly loan﴾ was revealed, Abu al-Dahdah said: "May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of God! Indeed God asks for a loan, while He is free of need of loans." He said: "Yes, He wishes to admit you into Paradise." He said: "If I lend my Lord a loan, will He guarantee me Paradise?" He said: "Yes, whoever gives charity, for him is its like in Paradise." He said: "And is my wife Umm al-Dahdah with me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And are the children of Abu al-Dahdah with me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Give me your hand," and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave him his hand. He said: "I have two orchards, one in the lower part and the other in the upper part, and by God I own nothing other than them, and I make them a loan to God, the Mighty and Majestic." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Make one of them for God, the Mighty and Majestic, and the other a livelihood for you and your dependents." He said: "I call you to witness, O Messenger of God, that I have made the other for God, the Exalted," and it was a garden in which there were six hundred palm trees. He said: "God will reward you with Paradise for it."

Abu al-Dahdah set out until he came to Umm al-Dahdah, who was with her children in the garden, moving among the palm trees, and he began to recite:

My Lord guided me to the paths of right guidance,
To the way of goodness and rectitude.
My loan from the orchard is for me in the valley;
It has gone forward as a loan to the Hereafter.
I lent it to God, trusting,
Willingly, without reproach or reversal,
Only hoping for multiplication in the return;
So depart with the soul and the children.
Piety, without doubt, is the best provision
A man sends forward to the Hereafter.

Umm al-Dahdah said: "May your sale profit; may God bless you in what you have bought." Then Abu al-Dahdah began to recite:

Like you, one who gives counsel is most useful;
Indeed you have the lot when the truth is clear.
God has provided for my dependents and granted them,
With the black date and the ripe red date.
The servant strives, and for him is what he has earned,
Through the nights, and upon him is what he has committed.

Then Umm al-Dahdah turned to her children, taking out what was in their mouths and shaking out what was in their sleeves, until she reached the other orchard. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "How many a lush date cluster and a spacious house in Paradise belong to Abu al-Dahdah." [180] [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/238; see the variation there.]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 246:

﴿Have you not considered the chiefs (al-mala') of the Children of Israel...﴾ Al-mala' means the notables and chiefs of a people, and their most eminent members. The original sense of al-mala' is a group of people. It has no singular from its own root, like al-ibl (camels), al-khayl (horses) and al-jaysh (army), but its plural is amla'. The poet said:

[Wasat] [[As it stands in the manuscript; we have not found it.]] al-amla' wa-iftataha al-du'a' ... la'alla Allah yakshifu dha al-bala'

﴿after Moses﴾ meaning: after the death of Moses. ﴿when they said to a prophet of theirs...﴾ They differed concerning who that prophet was. Qatadah said: He is Yushu' ibn Nun ibn Afraim ibn Yusuf ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim. Al-Suddi said: His name was Shim'un. He was named Shim'un because his mother asked Allah to grant her a boy, and Allah answered her prayer, so she bore a boy and named him Shim'un, saying: "Allah has heard my prayer" (sami'a Allahu du'a'i), the sin becoming a shin in the Hebrew language. He is Shim'un ibn Safiyyah ibn Alqamah ibn Abi Ya'sif ibn Qarun ibn Nasahr ibn Fahith ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub.

The rest of the exegetes said: He is Ishmuwil, which in Arabic is Isma'il ibn Nali ibn Alqamah ibn Hazim ibn al-Har ibn Arsawf ibn Alqamah ibn Fahith ibn Amusa ibn Arzaya. Muqatil said: He is from the descendants of Harun (peace be upon him). Mujahid said: He is Ismawil ibn Halfana, and he did not trace his lineage beyond this.

Wahb, Ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi and others said: The cause of their fighting against him was that when Musa (peace be upon him) died, he left behind among the Children of Israel Yusha', who upheld the Torah among them and the command of Allah until Allah took him. Then he left Kalib among them, who did likewise until Allah took him. Then he left Hizqil in the same manner, and then Allah took Hizqil. Wrongdoing grew among the Children of Israel and they forgot the covenant of Allah, until they worshipped idols. So Allah sent to them Ilyas as a prophet, and he began calling them to Allah. The prophets among the Children of Israel after Musa were sent to them only to renew what they had forgotten of the Torah.

Then after Ilyas came al-Yasa', and there was among them what Allah willed. Then Allah took him to Himself, and bad successors came after them, and their sins grew great. An enemy appeared against them called al-Balthana, and they were the people of Jalut. They lived along the coast of the Roman Sea, from Egypt to Palestine, and they were the Amalekites. They prevailed over the Children of Israel, overcame them in much of their land, took their offspring captive, enslaved forty and four hundred of their sons, imposed the jizyah upon them, and seized their Torah. The Children of Israel suffered from them affliction and hardship, and they had no prophet to manage their affairs. They used to ask that Allah send them a prophet with whom they might fight.

The tribe of prophethood had been destroyed, and nothing remained of them but a pregnant woman. They seized her and imprisoned her in a house of worship, fearing she would give birth to a girl and she would swap her for a boy, because of the Children of Israel's eagerness for her offspring. The woman began to call upon Allah, may He be exalted and glorified, to grant her a boy. She bore a boy and named him Ishmuwil, saying: "Allah has heard my prayer." The boy grew up, and she gave him over to study the Torah in Bayt al-Maqdis. A scholar of theirs took charge of him and adopted him. When the boy reached the age at which Allah would send him as a prophet, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him while the boy was sleeping beside the shaykh, who did not entrust him to anyone. He called him in the voice of the shaykh: "O Ishmuwil!" The boy rose in alarm to the shaykh and said: "O father, you called me." The shaykh disliked to say "No," lest the boy be frightened, so he said: "My son, go back and sleep." The boy returned and slept. Then he called him a second time, and the boy came again and said: "You called me." He said: "Go back and sleep. If I call you a third time, do not answer me." When it was the third time, Jibril (peace be upon him) appeared to him and said: "Go to your people and convey to them the message of your Lord, for Allah has sent you among them as a prophet." When he came to them, they denied him and said: "You have hastened the prophethood and the time has not yet come for you."

They said: "If you are truthful, send us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah." This was the sign of his prophethood. The order of the Children of Israel's affairs depended on gathering around kings, and obedience to kings went together with obedience to their prophets. The king was the one who led the armies, and the prophet arranged his affairs for him and advised him, guiding him and bringing him news from his Lord, may He be exalted and glorified.

Wahb said: Allah sent Ishmuwil as a prophet, and they remained for forty years in the best of conditions. Then came what came of the affair of Jalut and the Amalekites, and they said to Ishmuwil: "Send us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read it as yuqatilu with the letter ya', making the verb refer to the king, and it is jussive as an answer to the imperative. When they said this to him, he said to them: ﴿Would you perhaps, if fighting were prescribed for you, not fight?﴾ The phrase "hal 'asaytum" is an interrogative [from you], meaning: "Perhaps you." Nafi' and al-Hasan read 'asaytum with a kasrah on the sin throughout the Qur'an, and this is a dialect form; the rest read it with a fathah, which is the eloquent standard form. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman said: If 'asaytum were permissible, it would be read "'asa rabbukum in kutiba" (perhaps your Lord, if it is prescribed). ﴿...that you will not fight﴾, meaning: that you will not keep what you say, and will not fight with him.

They said: ﴿And what is it with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah?﴾ If it is asked: what is the reason for the presence of "an" in this place, when the Arabs do not say "mālaka an lā taf'al" but say "mālaka lā taf'al"? It is answered: the presence and the omission of "an" are both sound and eloquent dialects. As for its presence, it is like His words: ﴿What is the matter with you that you are not among those who prostrate?﴾ As for its omission, it is like His words: ﴿And what is the matter with you that you do not believe in Allah?﴾

Al-Kisa'i said: The meaning is: "wa-ma lana fi an la nuqatil" (and what is it for us regarding not fighting), "ma lana wa-an la nuqatil", the wa having been dropped, as transmitted by Muhammad ibn Jarir. ﴿And we have been expelled from our homes and our children﴾ Ubayd ibn Humayd read "qad akhraja-na" with a fathah on the hamzah and the jim, meaning the enemy.

The meaning of the speech: "And we have been expelled from our homes and our children," the apparent sense being general and its inner sense specific, for those who said to their prophet "Send us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah" were in their homes and their lands; only those of them who were removed from their dwellings by capture and subjugation were expelled.

The meaning of the verse: they answered, saying: "We only held back from jihad when we were prevented in our lands, and our enemy did not trample us nor prevail over us. But now that this has reached us, there is no escape from jihad, so we will obey our Lord in the raid and protect our women and children."

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away﴾, meaning they turned away from jihad and neglected the command of Allah, may He be exalted and glorified. ﴿except a few of them﴾ There is an omission in the speech, its meaning being: So Allah sent them a king, and fighting was prescribed for them. ﴿But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them﴾, and they are the ones who crossed the river, and we will mention them in their place.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 247–248:

Their prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent Talut (Saul) to you as king," etc. The occasion of this, as mentioned by the exegetes, was that Ushmuwil (Samuel), peace be upon him, asked Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to send them a king. He was brought a staff and a horn in which was the oil of holiness (dahn al-quds). It was said to him: "Your companion who will be king is as tall as this staff." And it was said to him: "Look at the horn containing the oil; when a man enters upon you and the oil in the horn bubbles up (nashsha), he is the king of the Children of Israel. Anoint his head with it and make him king over them." They measured themselves against the staff, but they were not like it.

Talut, whose name was Shadil ibn Qays ibn Abyal ibn Darar ibn Yahrub ibn Ufayh ibn Ays ibn Binyamin ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was a tanner who worked in leather. This was related by Wahb [Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/815.].

'Ikrimah and al-Suddi said: He was a water-carrier who watered (people) from the Nile with a donkey of his, and his donkey strayed, so he went out searching for it. It was also said: he was a kharbandah (a seller of cheap goods/ a cloth-maker).

Wahb said: Rather, the she-asses of Talut's father strayed, so he sent him and a servant of his to search for them. They passed by the house of Ushmuwil, and the servant said to Talut: "If we entered upon this prophet and asked him about the matter of the she-asses, that he might guide us and pray for us for good concerning them." Talut said, "Yes," so they entered upon him. While they were with him, mentioning to him the matter of the she-asses, the oil in the horn bubbled up. Ushmuwil stood up and measured Talut with the staff, and he was of its height. He said to Talut, "Bring your head near," and he brought it near, and he anointed it with the oil of holiness. Then he said to him: "You are the king of the Children of Israel whom Allah, exalted, commanded me to make king over them." Talut said, "Me?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Did you not know that my tribe is the lowest of the tribes of the Children of Israel?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Did you not know that my house is the lowest of the houses of the Children of Israel?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then what is the sign?" He said, "The sign is that you will return and your father will have found his she-asses," and it was so. Then he said to the Children of Israel: "Indeed, Allah, exalted, has sent Talut to you as king." Mujahid said: as commander over the army.

They said, "Anna (how?/from where?) shall he have kingship over us, when we have more right to kingship than he?" They only said this because among the Children of Israel there were two tribes: the tribe of prophethood and the tribe of kingship. The tribe of prophethood was the tribe of Lawi ibn Ya'qub, from which were Musa and Harun; the tribe of kingship was the tribe of Yahuda ibn Ya'qub, from which were Dawud and Sulayman. Talut was neither of the tribe of prophethood nor of the tribe of kingship; he was only of the tribe of Ibn Yamin ibn Ya'qub. They had committed a great sin: they used to have intercourse with women on the road openly in daylight. So Allah became angry with them and removed kingship and prophethood from them. When their prophet said, "Indeed, Allah has sent Talut to you as king," they denied it because he was of that tribe, and they said, "How shall he have kingship over us, when we have more right to kingship than he?" Moreover, he is poor, "and he has not been given abundance of wealth" (i.e., he was not given a large amount of wealth). He said, "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you" (i.e., selected him), "and has increased him in breadth" (fadilah, i.e., virtue) "and abundance of knowledge"—and that is because he was the most knowledgeable of the Children of Israel in his time. It is mentioned that revelation came to him when he was given the kingship. Al-Kalbi said: "and breadth in knowledge" of warfare, "and in physique," meaning in height; he surpassed the people by his head and shoulders. He was named Talut only because of his height, and so he was like the staff by which he was measured. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying, exalted: "and He has increased you in creation with breadth" (Q 7:69), meaning height of stature. Ibn Kaysan said: "in beauty"; Talut was the most handsome man among the Children of Israel and the most knowledgeable of them.

"And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills"—meaning: do not deny the kingship of Talut despite his being from outside the household of kingship, for kingship is not by inheritance; it is in the hand of Allah, who gives it to whom He wills [Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/820.]. "And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing." So they said to him: "What is the sign of that?" And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the ark (tabut) will come to you," etc.

The story of the ark and its description, as mentioned by the people of exegesis and the narrators of reports: Allah, exalted, sent down an ark upon Adam, in which were the images of the prophets from his descendants, and in it were houses equal in number to all the prophets; the last of the houses was the house of Muhammad (ﷺ). His image, adorned above the images of all the prophets, was of red ruby, standing and praying; on his right was the elderly, obedient man, with written on his forehead: "This is the first of his community to follow him, Abu Bakr." On his left was al-Faruq, with written on his forehead: "A horn of iron; the blame of no blamer shall take him in (the cause of) Allah." Behind him was Dhu'l-Nurayn, holding his waistband, with written on his brow: "a righteous one among the righteous." In front of him was Ali ibn Abi Talib, drawing his sword upon his shoulder, with written on his forehead: "This is his brother and cousin, supported with victory from Allah." Around him were his paternal uncles, the caliphs, the nuqaba' (chiefs), and the green constellation, and they are the helpers of Allah and the helpers of His Messenger; the light of the hooves of their animals on the Day of Resurrection will be like the light of the sun in the abode of this world.

The ark was about three cubits by two cubits, made of shimshar wood (the wood from which combs are made), overlaid with gold. It was with Adam, peace be upon him, until he died; then with Shith; then Adam's descendants inherited it until it reached Ibrahim. When he died, it was with Isma'il, because he was the eldest of his sons. When Isma'il died, it was with his son Qaydhar, and the sons of Ishaq disputed with him, saying: "Prophethood has been removed from you, so there remains for you only this one light; give us the ark." Qaydhar would refuse them, saying, "It is the bequest of my father, and I will not give it to anyone in the worlds."

He said: One day he went to open that ark, and it was difficult for him to open it. A caller called out to him from heaven: "Patience, O Qaydhar, you have no way to open this ark, for it is the bequest of a prophet, and none opens it except a prophet. Hand it over to your cousin Ya'qub Isra'il, the Allah (servant of Allah)."

So Qaydhar carried the ark on his neck and set out for the land of Canaan, where Ya'qub was. When he drew near to him, the ark gave a sound (sarra), which Ya'qub heard. He said to his sons: "I swear by Allah, Qaydhar has brought you the ark; so stand up toward him." Ya'qub and all his sons stood up to him. When Ya'qub looked at Qaydhar, he wept and said: "O Qaydhar, why do I see your color changed and your strength weak? Has an enemy overtaken you, or have you committed a sin that troubles you?" He said: "No enemy has overtaken me, nor have I committed a sin, but the light of Muhammad (ﷺ) was transferred from my loins, and for that my color has changed and my strength has weakened."

He said: "Is it from the daughters of Ishaq?" He said: "No, it is from the Arabic Jurhumite (women), and she is al-Ghadirah." Ya'qub said: "Bakh bakh! Give her the good news of Muhammad. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would not have stored him except in pure Arab women. O Qaydhar, I will give you good news." He said: "What is it?" He said: "Know that al-Ghadirah bore you a boy last night." Qaydhar said: "How do you know this, O my cousin, when you are in the land of Sham and she is in the land of Jurhum?" Ya'qub said: "I knew it because I saw the gates of heaven opened, and I saw a light like the extended moon between heaven and earth, and I saw the angels descending from heaven with blessings and mercy, so I knew that this was on account of Muhammad (ﷺ)."

So Qaydhar handed the ark over to Ya'qub and returned to his family, and he found that she had borne a boy, and he named him [Hamd], and in him was the light of Muhammad, peace be upon him.

They said: The ark remained among the Children of Israel until it reached Musa; Musa would place in it the Torah and some of his belongings. It remained with him until he died. Then the prophets of the Children of Israel passed it along until the time of Ushmuwil; it reached Ushmuwil when the matter of the ark with what was in it was complete, and in it was what Allah mentioned.

"In it is tranquility (sakinah) from your Lord." They differed regarding what the sakinah is.

'Ali, peace be upon him, said: The sakinah is a swift, fluttering wind with two heads and a face like a human face.

Mujahid: it has a head like a cat's head, a tail like a cat's tail, and two wings. Ibn Ishaq from Wahb from some scholars of the Children of Israel: the sakinah is a dead cat, which, when it cried out in the ark with the cry of a cat, they were certain of victory and conquest would come to them [Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/327.].

Al-Suddi from Abu Malik from Ibn 'Abbas: it is a basin of gold from Paradise in which the hearts of the prophets were washed. Bakkar ibn 'Abd Allah from Wahb ibn Munabbih: a spirit from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, which speaks; whenever they disagreed about something, it spoke and informed them with a clarification of what they wanted.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: it is what you know of the signs, by which you are calmed. Qatadah and al-Kalbi: it is fa'ilah from the sukun (tranquility), meaning calm from your Lord; and wherever the ark was, they were at peace with it and calmed by it. Al-Rabi': mercy from your Lord.

"And a remnant (baqiyyah)," which is the remainder, fa'iliyyah from baqa' (remaining), and the ha' in it is for emphasis, "of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun have left behind," meaning Musa and Harun themselves. Jamil said:

Buthaynah of the women's family, and indeed they (women) veil themselves
for the lesser (one), not the union of the absent.

That is, of the women. Al (family) also means the person, and its origin is ahl (people); the ha' was replaced with a hamza. When they diminutivize al they say uhayl, returning it to its origin.

The exegetes said: In it were Musa's staff and the fragments of the tablets, that is, their pieces; for when Musa threw down the tablets, they broke, so he picked up some of them and gathered what remained and placed it in the ark. In it were also two tablets of the Torah, a qafiz of the manna that used to descend upon them, Musa's sandals, Harun's turban, and his staff. And they said:

It was with the Children of Israel, and whenever they disagreed about something, it spoke and judged between them; when they came to battle, they put it before them and sought victory over their enemy by it. When they disobeyed and became corrupt, Allah set the 'Amalaqah over them, and they overcame them, took the ark, and plundered it.

The cause of that was that 'Ili, who had raised Ushmuwil, had two young sons, and 'Ili was the best of them and the custodian of their offering. His sons did nothing in the offering that was not in it: in the meat-hook used for the offering, which they used to take it with, there were hooks (kalalib), and whatever was on it was for the priest who took it; so his sons made hooks.

The women used to pray in the sanctuary, and they began to pursue them as well. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Ushmuwil: "Go to 'Ili and tell him: love of children has prevented you from restraining your two sons from altering My offering and My sanctuary and from disobeying Me. I will surely remove the priesthood from you and your descendants, and I will destroy him and them."

Ushmuwil informed 'Ili of that, and he was greatly alarmed. An enemy from among those around them marched against them, so he ordered his two sons to take the people out and fight that enemy. They went out, and they took the ark out with them. When they prepared for battle, 'Ili kept awaiting the news: "What have they done?" A man came to him while he was sitting on his chair and told him that the people had been defeated and that his two sons had been killed. He said: "What became of the ark?" He said: "The enemy has taken it." He gasped, fell on his back from his chair, and died. The affairs of the Children of Israel became confused and disordered, and they scattered until Allah sent Talut as king. They asked for a sign, and "their prophet said to them: Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the ark will come to you" [Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/822.].

The story of the coming of the ark: those who had captured the ark brought it to a village of the villages of Palestine called Azdud, and placed it in the house of an idol of theirs, putting it beneath the greatest idol. In the morning, the idol was beneath it; they took it and put it on top, and they fastened the idol's feet to the ark. In the morning, the idol's two hands and two feet had been cut off, and it lay beneath the ark. All their idols were overturned. They removed it from the idol's house and placed it in a district of their city, and the people of that district were seized by a pain in their necks until most of them perished.

Some of them said to others: "Did I not tell you that the God of the Children of Israel cannot be withstood by anything? Take it out of your city." They took it to another village, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent upon the people of that village mice, which bit a man so that he woke up dead, having had the contents of his belly eaten through his anus. They took it out from there into the desert and buried it in a latrine of theirs, and everyone who relieved himself there was afflicted with fistula and colic. They remained in that state and were bewildered. A woman who was among them, one of the captives of the Children of Israel, of the descendants of the prophets, said to them: "You will keep seeing what you dislike as long as this ark is among you; so remove it from yourselves." [In al-Tabari there is a continuation here, so refer to it: 2/823.] They brought a cart as the woman indicated, loaded the ark onto it, then tied it to two bulls and struck their flanks, and the two bulls set off walking, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, appointed four angels to drive them. Nothing touched the ark on the ground without becoming sanctified. They came until they stopped at the land of the Children of Israel; the two bulls broke with their horns and tore apart their harness, and they placed the ark in a field of harvest belonging to the Children of Israel, and the two bulls returned to their land. The Children of Israel did not lose anything except the ark, so they exclaimed "Allahu akbar" and praised Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and they rallied together behind Talut. That is His saying: "carried by the angels," meaning driven by them [Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/824.].

Ibn 'Abbas said: The angels brought the ark, carrying it between heaven and earth while they looked at it, until they placed it before Talut.

Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and al-A'mash read (yahmiluhu al-malaikatu) with the ya' (masculine form).

Qatadah said: Rather, the ark was in the wilderness of Tih; Musa had placed it with Yusha' ibn Nun, and it remained there. Then the angels carried it until they placed it in the house of Talut, and they acknowledged his kingship. Ibn Zayd said: "unwilling."

"Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers." Ibn 'Abbas said: Indeed, the ark and the staff of Musa are in al-Jizah al-Tabariyyah, and they will come out before the Day of Resurrection.

So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Ushmuwil: "Go to 'Ili and tell him: love of children has prevented you from restraining your two sons from altering My offering and My sanctuary and from disobeying Me. I will surely remove the priesthood from you and your descendants, and I will destroy him and them."

Ushmuwil informed 'Ili of that, and he was greatly alarmed. An enemy from among those around them marched against them, so he ordered his two sons to take the people out and fight that enemy. They went out, and they took the ark out with them. When they prepared for battle, 'Ili kept awaiting the news: "What have they done?" A man came to him while he was sitting on his chair and told him that the people had been defeated and that his two sons had been killed. He said: "What became of the ark?" He said: "The enemy has taken it." He gasped, fell on his back from his chair, and died. The affairs of the Children of Israel became confused and disordered, and they scattered until Allah sent Talut as king. They asked for a sign, and "their prophet said to them: Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the ark will come to you" [Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/822.].

The story of the coming of the ark: those who had captured the ark brought it to a village of the villages of Palestine called Azdud, and placed it in the house of an idol of theirs, putting it beneath the greatest idol. In the morning, the idol was beneath it; they took it and put it on top, and they fastened the idol's feet to the ark. In the morning, the idol's two hands and two feet had been cut off, and it lay beneath the ark. All their idols were overturned. They removed it from the idol's house and placed it in a district of their city, and the people of that district were seized by a pain in their necks until most of them perished.

Some of them said to others: "Did I not tell you that the God of the Children of Israel cannot be withstood by anything? Take it out of your city." They took it to another village, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent upon the people of that village mice, which bit a man so that he woke up dead, having had the contents of his belly eaten through his anus. They took it out from there into the desert and buried it in a latrine of theirs, and everyone who relieved himself there was afflicted with fistula and colic. They remained in that state and were bewildered. A woman who was among them, one of the captives of the Children of Israel, of the descendants of the prophets, said to them: "You will keep seeing what you dislike as long as this ark is among you; so remove it from yourselves." [In al-Tabari there is a continuation here, so refer to it: 2/823.] They brought a cart as the woman indicated, loaded the ark onto it, then tied it to two bulls and struck their flanks, and the two bulls set off walking, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, appointed four angels to drive them. Nothing touched the ark on the ground without becoming sanctified. They came until they stopped at the land of the Children of Israel; the two bulls broke with their horns and tore apart their harness, and they placed the ark in a field of harvest belonging to the Children of Israel, and the two bulls returned to their land. The Children of Israel did not lose anything except the ark, so they exclaimed "Allahu akbar" and praised Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and they rallied together behind Talut. That is His saying: "carried by the angels," meaning driven by them [Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/824.].

Ibn 'Abbas said: The angels brought the ark, carrying it between heaven and earth while they looked at it, until they placed it before Talut.

Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and al-A'mash read (yahmiluhu al-malaikatu) with the ya' (masculine form).

Qatadah said: Rather, the ark was in the wilderness of Tih; Musa had placed it with Yusha' ibn Nun, and it remained there. Then the angels carried it until they placed it in the house of Talut, and they acknowledged his kingship. Ibn Zayd said: "unwilling."

"Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers." Ibn 'Abbas said: Indeed, the ark and the staff of Musa are in al-Jizah al-Tabariyyah, and they will come out before the Day of Resurrection.

The commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 249–252 (part 1 of 2):

When Talut set out with the troops (﴿فَلَمَّا فَصَلَ طالُوتُ بِالْجُنُودِ﴾), meaning he departed with them and moved off. The root of *fasl* is cutting off, so the meaning of His words *fasala* is that he cut off from a settled place, leaving it and moving on to another, like the words of God Most High: ﴿وَلَمَّا فَصَلَتِ الْعِيرُ﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 94].

So Talut went out from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) with the troops, who at that time numbered seventy thousand fighters. It is also said they numbered eighty thousand. No one stayed behind except an elderly man because of his old age, a sick man because of his illness, a blind man because of his blindness, or someone excused for his excuse [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/250; Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/834].

This was because, when they saw the *tabut* (ark), they said: "The ark has come to us, and it is the light about which there is no doubt," so they hastened to jihad.

Talut said: "I have no need of all that I see. No man should go out with me who has built a building he has not finished, nor a merchant occupied with his trade, nor a man who is in debt, nor a man who has married a woman he has not yet consummated with. I want only the young, vigorous, and unoccupied man."

Eighty thousand gathered who met this condition. It was in intense heat, and they complained of the scarcity of water between them and their enemy, and said: "Water will not carry us, so ask God Most High to make a river flow for us."

So Talut said: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ مُبْتَلِيكُمْ﴾ ("Indeed God will test you"), meaning He will examine you to see your obedience, ﴿وَهُوَ أَعْلَمُ﴾ ("and He knows best"). ﴿بِنَهَرٍ﴾ ("by a river"): the common readers recite it with a fatha on the ha' (*bi-nahar*), while Hamid and Ibn Muhsin recite *bi-nahrin* with a sukun on the ha'. Both are dialectal variants, like *shi'r* and *shi'r*, *sakhr* and *sakhr*, *samagh* and *samagh*, *sam'* and *sam'*, *fahm* and *fahm*.

Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: it is the river of Palestine. Qatada and al-Rabi' said: it is a sweet river between the Jordan and Palestine.

﴿فَمَنْ شَرِبَ مِنْهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي﴾ ("Whoever drinks from it is not of me"), meaning he is not of the people of my religion and obedience. ﴿وَمَنْ لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ﴾ ("and whoever does not taste it," meaning does not drink it) ﴿فَإِنَّهُ مِنِّي﴾ ("indeed he is of me"). This is like His words: ﴿لَيْسَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ جُناحٌ فِيما طَعِمُوا﴾ ("There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten") [Surah al-Ma'idah: 93]. Then He made an exception, saying: ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اغْتَرَفَ غُرْفَةً بِيَدِهِ﴾ ("except one who takes a handful with his hand").

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Sulayman al-Taymi, Ibn Abi al-Jawza', Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Abu Mukhrima, Abu Amr and Ayyub recited *ghurfatan* with a fatha on the ghayn. The rest recited it with a damma, and this is the recitation of Uthman. Both are dialectal forms.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubayda said: *al-ghurfa* with a damma is what is held in the palm of the hand when one scoops water.

*Al-ghurfa* (with a fatha) is the act of scooping (*al-ightirafa*); so the damma form is a noun and the fatha form is a verbal noun.

Abu Hatim said: *al-ghurfa* with a damma is a handful, or a scoopful, and *al-ghurfa* (with a fatha) is a single time of scooping, whether little or much.

﴿فَشَرِبُوا مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْهُمْ﴾ ("So they drank from it, except a few of them"). *Qalilan* is in the accusative as an exception. Ibn Mas'ud recited *qalilun* in the nominative, like the words of the poet:

*"Every brother who is parted from his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads;*
*And every companion who is joined with another, though he is miserly with them, will be separated."* [Lisan al-Arab: 15/432]

They differed about the few who did not drink. Al-Suddi said they were four thousand. Others said they were three hundred and some, and this is the correct view. The evidence for it is the report of al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to us on the day of Badr: "Today you are on the number of the companions of Talut when they crossed the river, and no one came with him except a believer." [Kanz al-Ummal: 10/400, no. 29955; Jami' al-Bayan: 2/839, with variation]. He said: "On that day we were three hundred and some men."

They said: whoever scooped a handful, as God commanded, his heart was strengthened, his faith was sound, and he crossed the river safely; that single handful sufficed him for drinking, for his load, and for his animals. But those who drank and disobeyed God's command had their lips blackened, thirst overcame them, they did not quench their thirst, they remained on the bank of the river, shrank from meeting the enemy, and did not witness the victory.

﴿فَلَمَّا جاوَزَهُ﴾ ("So when he crossed it"), meaning the river, ﴿هُوَ﴾ ("he," meaning Talut) ﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَهُ﴾ ("and those who believed with him"), meaning the few, ﴿قالُوا﴾ ("they said"): those who drank and disobeyed God's command, who were people of doubt and hypocrisy, ﴿لا طاقَةَ لَنَا الْيَوْمَ بِجالُوتَ وَجُنُودِهِ﴾ ("We have no power today against Jalut and his troops"). They turned away from Talut and did not witness the fighting with Jalut.

﴿قالَ الَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ﴾ ("Said those who think"), meaning those who are certain and know, ﴿أَنَّهُمْ مُلاقُوا اللَّهِ﴾ ("that they will meet God"), and they are the ones who stood firm with Talut: ﴿كَمْ﴾ ("how many") — Ubayy recited *ka'in* (meaning "how many a") — ﴿مِنْ فِئَةٍ﴾ ("a group"), meaning a company. It is a collective noun with no singular of its own from the same form; its plural is *fi'at* and *fi'un* in the nominative, and *fi'in* in the accusative and genitive. ﴿قَلِيلَةٍ غَلَبَتْ فِئَةً كَثِيرَةً بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("a small group has overcome a large group by God's permission"). ﴿وَاللَّهُ مَعَ الصَّابِرِينَ﴾ ("And God is with the patient"), meaning their helper and supporter.

Al-Zajjaj said: a group is called *fi'a* only because it is from *fa'autu ra'sahu* (I split his head) with the stick, and *fa'at* (I split) when I cut it, as if it were a piece cut off.

﴿وَلَمَّا بَرَزُوا﴾ ("And when they came out"), meaning Talut and his believing troops, ﴿لِجالُوتَ وَجُنُودِهِ﴾ ("to Jalut and his troops"), the polytheists. *Baraza* means they came out onto *al-barāz* of the earth, which is the open ground that is exposed and level. ﴿قالُوا﴾ ("they said"), and they are the people of insight and obedience: ﴿رَبَّنا أَفْرِغْ﴾ ("Our Lord, pour out"), meaning send down and pour, ﴿عَلَيْنا صَبْراً﴾ ("upon us patience"), as a bucket is emptied; ﴿وَثَبِّتْ أَقْدامَنا﴾ ("and make firm our feet"), and strengthen our hearts; ﴿وَانْصُرْنا عَلَى الْقَوْمِ الْكافِرِينَ﴾ ("and help us against the disbelieving people"). In the verse there is an implied meaning, and its sense is: so God sent down upon them patience and victory. ﴿فَهَزَمُوهُمْ بِإِذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("So they routed them by God's permission"), ﴿وَقَتَلَ داوُدُ جالُوتَ﴾ ("and Dawud killed Jalut").

**Description of how Dawud killed Jalut**

The exegetes said, in similar wording and agreeing in meaning: Abu Dawud crossed the river with Talut too, along with his thirteen sons, and Dawud was the youngest of them. One day he came to them and said: "O father, I never throw my sling at anything without knocking it down." He said: "Rejoice, for God has placed your provision in your sling." Then he came to him another time and said: "O father, I went into the mountains and found a lion lying down; I mounted it and took hold of its ears, and it did not trouble me." He said: "Rejoice, my son, for this is a good thing God has given you."

Then he came to him another day and said: "O father, I walk among the mountains and glorify God, and no mountain remains without glorifying God along with me." He said: "Rejoice, my son, for this is a good thing God has given you."

They said: Jalut sent to Talut: "Send out to me someone who will fight me. If he kills me, the kingdom is yours; if I kill him, the kingdom is mine over you." This weighed heavily on Talut, and he proclaimed in his army: "Whoever kills Jalut, I will marry him to my daughter and share my kingdom with him." The people feared Jalut, and no one answered him.

Talut asked their prophet Ishmuil to supplicate God. He supplicated God Mighty and Majestic about this, and a horn of oil and an iron cauldron were brought. It was said: "The one who will kill Jalut is the one upon whose head this horn is placed, and the oil will boil until it anoints his head, without flowing onto his face, and it will be on his head like a crown, and he will enter this cauldron and fill it, without shifting in it." Talut called the Children of Israel and tested them, but none of them suited it.

God Most High revealed to their prophet that among the sons of Ayshā there is one through whom God will kill Jalut. Talut summoned Ayshā and said: "Present your sons to me." He brought out twelve men, like pillars. He began presenting them to the horn, but saw nothing, and said to one of them: "Pray for them." Each time he said, "Return," and it was repeated to him. God revealed to him: "We do not take men by their forms, but we take them by the soundness of their hearts." He said to Ayshā: "Do you have any son other than these?" He said: "No."

The prophet (peace be upon him) said: "O Lord, he claims he has no son other than these." God said: "He lies." The prophet said: "My Lord has called you a liar." He said: "God has spoken the truth, O Prophet of God. I have a young son called Dawud. I was ashamed for people to see him because of his short stature and lowliness, so I left him tending the sheep in such-and-such a valley." Dawud (peace be upon him) was a short man, slight, with a yellow complexion, blue eyes, and a reddish... *amʿad* (a man with a slight stoop or a reddish tinge in his hair).

Talut summoned him. It is also said: rather, Talut went out to him and found the valley had flooded between him and the pen to which he brings the flock. He found him carrying two sheep at a time, which the flood carried across without his wading through the water with them. When the prophet (peace be upon him) saw him, he said: "This is the one, without doubt. This one has mercy on animals, so he is more merciful to people." He summoned him and placed the horn on his head, and it overflowed [Jami' al-Bayan: 2/851; Tarikh al-Tabari: 1/337].

Talut said to him: "Would you like to kill Jalut, and I will marry you to my daughter, and place your ring in my kingdom?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Have you noticed in yourself anything by which you are strong enough to kill him?" He said: "Yes. I graze, and a lion, a panther, or a wolf comes and takes a sheep. I stand up to it, open its jaws from it, and tear them apart to the back of its neck."

So Talut sent him back to his army. Dawud passed by a stone, which called out: "O Dawud, carry me, for I am the stone of Harun, with which such-and-such a king was killed." So he carried it in his wallet. Then he passed by another stone, which called out: "O Dawud, carry me, for I am the stone of Musa, with which such-and-such a king was killed." So he carried it in his wallet. Then he passed by another stone, which said: "Carry me, for I am your stone with which you will kill Jalut, and God has hidden me for you." So he placed it in his wallet.

When the two sides lined up for battle, Jalut came out and asked for single combat. Dawud volunteered, and Talut gave him a horse, armor, and weapons. He put on the weapons and mounted the horse, went a short distance, then turned back and returned to the king. Those around him said: "The boy has become a coward." So he came and stood before the king, who said: "What is your matter?" He said: "If God does not help me, the weapons will not avail me anything. Leave me to fight as I wish." He said: "Yes." So Dawud took his wallet, slung it over his shoulder, took his sling, and set off toward Jalut. Jalut was one of the strongest and most powerful men, and he used to rout armies single-handedly. He had a helmet made of three hundred pieces of iron. When he looked at Dawud, fear was cast into his heart, and he said: "You come out to me?" He said: "Yes."

Jalut was on a dappled horse, fully armed. He said: "Did you come to me with a sling and a stone, as one approaches dogs?" He said: "Yes, for you are worse than a dog." He said: "Indeed I will divide your flesh among the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky." Dawud said: "Rather, may God divide your flesh." Then Dawud said: "In the name of the God of Ibrahim," and he took out a stone; then he took out another and said: "In the name of the God of Ishaq," and placed it in his sling; then he took out a third and said: "In the name of the God of Ya'qub," and placed it in his sling, and they became one stone. He whirled the sling and hurled it at him. God sent the wind until the stone struck the front of the helmet, penetrated his brain, and came out through the back of his neck, and it killed thirty men behind him. God routed the army, and Jalut fell dead. Dawud dragged him until he threw him before Talut.

The Muslims rejoiced greatly, and they returned to the city safe and victorious, while the people spoke of Dawud. Dawud came to Talut and said: "Fulfill for me what you promised, and give me my wife." He said to him: "Do you want the king's daughter without a dowry?" Dawud said: "You did not stipulate a dowry for me, and I have nothing." He said: "I will not burden you except with what you can bear. You are a man of war, and in our mountains there are enemies of ours, the uncircumcised (*ghulf*). If you kill two hundred of them and bring me their foreskins, I will marry you to my daughter." So he went to them, and every time he killed a man, he threaded his foreskin on a string, until he had threaded all their foreskins. He brought them to Talut, threw them before him, and said: "Give my wife to me." So he married him to his daughter and placed his ring in his kingdom.

The people inclined toward Dawud and loved him and spoke of him often. Talut resented this and envied him, and he intended to kill him. A man called Dhu al-Mughnayn informed Talut's daughter about this, and she said to Dawud: "You will certainly be killed tonight." He said: "And who will kill me?" She said: "My father." He said: "Have you been certain of it?" She said: "Someone who does not lie told me, and you will not escape tonight until you see the truth of it." He said: "If he intends that, I cannot go out. But bring me a skin of wine." She brought it to him, and he placed it on his bed, on the couch, and covered it, and he went under the couch.

Talut entered at midnight and intended to kill Dawud. He said to her: "Where is your husband?" She said: "He is asleep on the couch." So he struck it with a sword, and the wine flowed. When he smelled the scent of the drink, he said: "May God have mercy on Dawud; how much wine he drinks!" and he went out. When he woke in the morning, he realized he had not accomplished anything, and said: "If a man whom I have sought to harm like this should not leave me until he takes his revenge on me..." He reinforced his chamberlains and guards and closed his doors against him.

Then Dawud came to him one night, when the eyes had grown still and God blinded the guards. The doors were opened for him, and he entered upon him while he was asleep on his bed. He placed an arrow by his head, an arrow by his feet, an arrow on his right, and an arrow on his left, and then went out. When Talut woke, he saw the arrows and recognized them, and said: "May God have mercy on Dawud; he is better than me. I had the upper hand over him, and I intended to kill him, but he had the upper hand over me and refrained from me. Had he wished, he would have placed this arrow in my throat. I am not one to feel safe from him."

When the next encounter came, he came to him a second time. God blinded the chamberlains, so he entered upon him while he was asleep, took Talut's ewer with which he used to perform ablution, his cup from which he used to drink, cut some hairs from his beard and some threads from the hem of his garments, and then left and fled and hid.

When Talut woke and saw this, he set spies upon Dawud and sought him with the utmost pursuit, but he could not find him. Then Talut rode out one day and found Dawud walking in the desert. Talut said: "Today I will kill Dawud; I am riding and he is on foot." Dawud, when frightened, could not be overtaken, so Talut spurred after him. Dawud ran and entered a cave, and God revealed to the spider, and it spun a web over him.

When Talut reached the cave and looked at the spider's web, he said: "If he had entered here, he would have torn the spider's web." So he left it and went on. Dawud went off and came to the mountain with the ascetics, and he worshipped there.

The scholars and the devout criticized Talut concerning Dawud. So Talut would not let anyone forbid him from killing Dawud without killing that person, and he incited the killing of scholars. He could not find any scholar in the Children of Israel whom he was able to kill without killing him, and he could not fight an army without routing it. Until he brought a woman who knew the Greatest Name of God, and he ordered a tyrant to kill her. The tyrant took pity on her and said: "Perhaps we will need a scholar," so he left her. Then repentance entered Talut's heart, and he regretted what he had done and began to weep until he took pity on him.

Every night he would go out to the graves and weep and call out: "I call upon God any servant who knows I have a repentance to inform me of it!"

When he kept insisting upon them, a voice called out to him from the graves: "O Talut, are you not content that you killed us, that you must also harm us now that we are dead?" He wept and grieved even more. The tyrant took pity on him and spoke to him, saying: "What is wrong with you, O King?"

He said: "Do you know of any scholar on earth whom I could ask whether there is any repentance for me?"

The tyrant said: "Do you know what your likeness is? Your likeness is that of a king who alighted in a village at evening. A rooster crowed, and he took it as an omen and said: 'Do not leave a rooster in the village without slaughtering it.' When he wanted to sleep, he said to his companions: 'When the rooster crows, wake us so that we may travel by night.'" They said: "Have you left a rooster whose voice we can hear?" "But have you left a scholar on earth?" So Talut grieved and wept even more.

When the tyrant saw this, he said: "Tell me, if I show you a scholar, perhaps you will kill him." He said: "No." So the tyrant made a firm covenant with him and informed him that the woman who knows is with him. Talut said: "Take me to her, so I may ask her whether there is any repentance for me."

It was only that family who knew that Name: when their men had perished, their women knew it.

When Talut reached the door, the tyrant said: "O King, if she sees you she will be terrified." So he left him behind him and entered upon her and said: "Are you not the one most indebted to me, since I saved you from death and sheltered you with me?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Then I have a need of you: this is Talut, who asks whether there is any repentance for him." She swooned from fear. He said: "He does not intend to kill you, but he asks you whether there is any repentance for him." She said: "By God, I do not know of any repentance for Talut, but do you know the place of a prophet's grave?"

So he took her to the grave of Ishmuil. She prayed and made supplication, then called out to the one in the grave, and Ishmuil came out of the grave and shook the dust from his head. When he saw the three of them—the woman, Talut, and the tyrant—he said: "What is the matter with you? Has the Resurrection come?" They said: "No, but Talut asks you whether there is any repentance for him."

Ishmuil said: "O Talut, what have you done since I left?" He said: "I have left no evil undone, and I have come seeking repentance."

He said: "How many children do you have?" He said: "Ten men."

He said: "I know of no repentance for you except that you renounce your kingdom and go out with your sons in the way of God. Then you should send your son forward, so that they are killed before your eyes, and then you should fight until you are killed, the last of them." Then Ishmuil returned to the grave and fell dead.

Talut returned, more grieved than ever, out of fear that his son would not follow him. He had wept until the lashes of his eyes fell out and his body wasted away. His sons came in to him, and he said to them: "Tell me, if I were thrown into the fire, would you ransom me?" They said: "Yes, we would ransom you with whatever we could." He said: "Then it is the fire, if you do not do what I tell you." They said: "Then present it to us." So he told them the story. They said: "And will you indeed be killed?" He said: "Yes."

They said: "Then we have no good in life, for our souls are content with what you have asked." So he equipped himself with his wealth and his children. He sent forward his sons, and they were ten; they fought until they were killed before him. Then he charged forward after them until he too was killed. His killer came to the Prophet Dawud, peace be upon him, to give him good news, and said: "I have killed your enemy."

He said: "You are not the one who will live after him," and he struck off his neck. The Children of Israel brought Dawud and gave him the treasuries of Talut, and they made him king over themselves.

The rule of Talut, from its beginning until he was killed in the battle along with his son, lasted forty years.

Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: Dawud's rule after Jalut lasted sixty-nine years.

The Children of Israel did not unite under one king except under Dawud. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom﴾. He is Dawud son of Ayshah son of Sawil son of Nagir son of Salmun son of Yakhshun son of Ammi-Ya Rabb son of Ram son of Hasrun son of Faris son of Yahud son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom﴾, meaning prophethood.

﴿And taught him of what He willed﴾. Al-Kalbi and others said: this means the craft of making coats of mail, and the sense is: in secret. He used to make them and sell them until he gathered wealth from that, and he would not eat except from the work of his hands. Its evidence is His words: ﴿And We taught him the craft of making coats of mail for you﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya: 80.]]. It was also said: the speech of birds, and the speech of bees and ants. It was also said: the Psalms (al-Zabur). It was also said: a beautiful voice and melodies. Allah did not give any of His creatures a voice like his. When he recited the Psalms, wild beasts would draw near until they could be taken by their necks, birds would shade him while listening attentively, flowing water would become still, and the wind would calm. Musical instruments, lutes, and cymbals were only made in imitation of his voice.

Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah, glorified is He, gave him a chain attached to the Milky Way and the sphere, its top at the sanctuary (mihrab) of Dawud, peace be upon him. Its strength was the strength of iron, its color was the color of fire, its links were round, set with jewels and adorned with moist pearl rods. No event occurred in the air without the chain ringing, so Dawud knew of that event. Whoever was afflicted with a disability and touched it would be healed. The sign of his people's entry into the religion was that they would touch it with their hands and then wipe their palms over their chests. After Dawud they would take their disputes to it until it was lifted up. They would come to it, and whoever transgressed against his companion and denied him a right would come to the chain. If he was truthful and right, he would extend his hand to the chain and reach it; if he was a liar and an oppressor, he would not reach it. It remained so until deceit and treachery appeared among them.

It has reached us that one of their kings deposited a precious jewel with a man. When he demanded it back, the man denied it, and they went to the chain for judgment. The one who held the jewel knew that his hand would not reach the chain, so he went to his staff, hollowed it out, placed the jewel inside it, and leaned on it until they came to the chain.

The owner of the jewel said: "Return my deposit to me."

His companion said: "I know of no deposit of yours with me. If you are truthful, then take hold of the chain." So he reached for it with his hand. It was said to the denier as well: "Stand up, you too, and take hold of it." He said to the owner of the jewel: "Take my staff, this one, and keep it safe until I reach the chain." So he took it, while the man did not know that his jewel was in it. The man said: "O Allah, if You know that this deposit which he claims from me has reached him, then bring the chain near." He extended his hand and took hold of it. The people marveled and doubted it, and in the morning Allah had lifted the chain.

﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others﴾. Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi' and Ya'qub and Ayyub read (difa' Allah) with an alif here and in Surah al-Hajj, and Abu Hatim chose this reading. The others read without an alif in both places, and Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, saying: because no one can overpower Allah, and He alone is the Repeller. Abu Hatim said: a form of fi'al may come from a single agent, like the Arabs' saying: "May Allah give you good repayment for the defense (ahsan Allahu 'anka al-difa')," "May Allah grant you well-being (a'afaka Allah)," "May Allah requite him (a'aqabahu Allah)," and "He handed over something (nawala shay'an)."

Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: Had Allah not repelled by means of the armies, expeditions, and frontier guards of the Muslims, the polytheists would have prevailed over the earth, killing the believers and ruining the lands and the mosques.

The rest of the exegetes said: Had Allah not repelled, by means of believers and the righteous, the disbelievers and the wicked, ﴿the earth would have been corrupted﴾, meaning its people would have been destroyed.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah repels punishment through the one who prays on behalf of the one who does not pray, through the one who gives zakat on behalf of the one who does not, through the one who fasts on behalf of the one who does not fast, through the one who performs Hajj on behalf of the one who does not perform Hajj, and through the one who fights in jihad on behalf of the one who does not fight in jihad. Even if they all united in abandoning these things, Allah would not give them respite for the blink of an eye." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse [182] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/260.]].

Malik ibn Ubayd reported from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for servants of Allah who bow in prayer, infants who are nursing, and animals grazing, the punishment would have been poured upon you in a torrent, and then you would be crushed to pieces." [[Al-Sunan al-Kubra: 3/345; al-Mu'jam al-Kabir: 22/310, where it reads: "thumma rudda radda" (then he was crushed to pieces); and in al-Aahad wa al-Mathani of al-Dahhak (2/210): "thumma rassa rassa," with a sad.]]

Al-Tha'labi said, and recited his own verses:
Were it not for servants of God who bow in prayer,
and orphaned infants who are nursing,
and neglected ones grazing in the wilderness,
the most painful punishment would be poured upon you.
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/260.]]

Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir reported from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, glorified is He, improves the son, the son's son, the people of his household, and the households around him through the righteousness of a man [[In the source: the Muslim.]], and they will remain in Allah's protection as long as he is among them." [183] [[Jami' al-Bayan: 2/855.]]

Qatada said: Allah tests the believer through the disbeliever, and He grants well-being to the disbeliever through the believer.

[ ... ] [[Illegible in the manuscript.]]

...ibn Abd al-Rahman reported from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah repels affliction from a hundred members of a household of his neighbors through a righteous Muslim." [184] [[Kanz al-Ummal: 9/5, no. 24654.]] Then Ibn Umar recited: ﴿And had Allah not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾.

﴿But Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you in truth﴾, meaning the speech of Allah.

﴿And indeed, you are among the messengers.﴾

The commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 249–252 (part 1 of 2):

When Talut set out with the troops (﴿فَلَمَّا فَصَلَ طالُوتُ بِالْجُنُودِ﴾), meaning he departed with them and moved off. The root of *fasl* is cutting off, so the meaning of His words *fasala* is that he cut off from a settled place, leaving it and moving on to another, like the words of God Most High: ﴿وَلَمَّا فَصَلَتِ الْعِيرُ﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 94].

So Talut went out from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) with the troops, who at that time numbered seventy thousand fighters. It is also said they numbered eighty thousand. No one stayed behind except an elderly man because of his old age, a sick man because of his illness, a blind man because of his blindness, or someone excused for his excuse [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/250; Tafsir al-Tabari: 2/834].

This was because, when they saw the *tabut* (ark), they said: "The ark has come to us, and it is the light about which there is no doubt," so they hastened to jihad.

Talut said: "I have no need of all that I see. No man should go out with me who has built a building he has not finished, nor a merchant occupied with his trade, nor a man who is in debt, nor a man who has married a woman he has not yet consummated with. I want only the young, vigorous, and unoccupied man."

Eighty thousand gathered who met this condition. It was in intense heat, and they complained of the scarcity of water between them and their enemy, and said: "Water will not carry us, so ask God Most High to make a river flow for us."

So Talut said: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ مُبْتَلِيكُمْ﴾ ("Indeed God will test you"), meaning He will examine you to see your obedience, ﴿وَهُوَ أَعْلَمُ﴾ ("and He knows best"). ﴿بِنَهَرٍ﴾ ("by a river"): the common readers recite it with a fatha on the ha' (*bi-nahar*), while Hamid and Ibn Muhsin recite *bi-nahrin* with a sukun on the ha'. Both are dialectal variants, like *shi'r* and *shi'r*, *sakhr* and *sakhr*, *samagh* and *samagh*, *sam'* and *sam'*, *fahm* and *fahm*.

Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi said: it is the river of Palestine. Qatada and al-Rabi' said: it is a sweet river between the Jordan and Palestine.

﴿فَمَنْ شَرِبَ مِنْهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي﴾ ("Whoever drinks from it is not of me"), meaning he is not of the people of my religion and obedience. ﴿وَمَنْ لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ﴾ ("and whoever does not taste it," meaning does not drink it) ﴿فَإِنَّهُ مِنِّي﴾ ("indeed he is of me"). This is like His words: ﴿لَيْسَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحاتِ جُناحٌ فِيما طَعِمُوا﴾ ("There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten") [Surah al-Ma'idah: 93]. Then He made an exception, saying: ﴿إِلَّا مَنِ اغْتَرَفَ غُرْفَةً بِيَدِهِ﴾ ("except one who takes a handful with his hand").

Ibn Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Sulayman al-Taymi, Ibn Abi al-Jawza', Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', Abu Mukhrima, Abu Amr and Ayyub recited *ghurfatan* with a fatha on the ghayn. The rest recited it with a damma, and this is the recitation of Uthman. Both are dialectal forms.

Al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubayda said: *al-ghurfa* with a damma is what is held in the palm of the hand when one scoops water.

*Al-ghurfa* (with a fatha) is the act of scooping (*al-ightirafa*); so the damma form is a noun and the fatha form is a verbal noun.

Abu Hatim said: *al-ghurfa* with a damma is a handful, or a scoopful, and *al-ghurfa* (with a fatha) is a single time of scooping, whether little or much.

﴿فَشَرِبُوا مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِنْهُمْ﴾ ("So they drank from it, except a few of them"). *Qalilan* is in the accusative as an exception. Ibn Mas'ud recited *qalilun* in the nominative, like the words of the poet:

*"Every brother who is parted from his brother, by the life of your father, except the two Farqads;*
*And every companion who is joined with another, though he is miserly with them, will be separated."* [Lisan al-Arab: 15/432]

They differed about the few who did not drink. Al-Suddi said they were four thousand. Others said they were three hundred and some, and this is the correct view. The evidence for it is the report of al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to us on the day of Badr: "Today you are on the number of the companions of Talut when they crossed the river, and no one came with him except a believer." [Kanz al-Ummal: 10/400, no. 29955; Jami' al-Bayan: 2/839, with variation]. He said: "On that day we were three hundred and some men."

They said: whoever scooped a handful, as God commanded, his heart was strengthened, his faith was sound, and he crossed the river safely; that single handful sufficed him for drinking, for his load, and for his animals.
