[Another said: "Ta Ha."] The people advanced and delayed. Then Ali (peace be upon him) said:
"Where are you, O Companions of Muhammad, from the Verse of the Throne?"
They said to him: "Inform us, O Abu al-Hasan, what did you hear the Prophet (ﷺ) say?" Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said:
The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Ali, the master of the prophets is Adam, the master of the Arabs is Muhammad, without boasting; the master of the Persians is Salman, the master of the Romans is Suhayb, the master of the Abyssinians is Bilal, the master of mountains is Mount Sinai (al-Tur), the master of trees is the lote tree (al-sidr), the master of months is the sacred months, the master of days is Friday, the master of speech is the Qur'an, the master of the Qur'an is al-Baqara, and the master of al-Baqara is the Verse of the Throne.
O Ali, indeed in it are fifty words, and in each word are fifty blessings" [[Mustadrak al-Wasa'il: 4/336.]].

Umar ibn Abi al-Miqdam said: I heard Abu Ja'far al-Baqir say: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne once, a thousand disliked things of the world and a thousand disliked things of the Hereafter are averted from him. The least disliked thing of the world is poverty, and the least disliked thing of the Hereafter is the punishment of the grave."

The words of Allah, Allah (Allahu), are in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and their predicate is in "there is no god but Him" (la ilaha illa Huwa).
It was also said: it is in the nominative as an affirmation and confirmation, like His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "Muhammad is only a messenger" [[Surat Al 'Imran: 144.]].

Al-Hayy is the one who possesses life, and it is the attribute by which the one described is alive, distinct from inanimate objects and the dead. It is on the pattern fa'il (fa'l) like al-hadhar and al-tama', so the yā' is made quiescent and assimilated.

Al-Qayyum is fay'ul from al-qiyam (standing), and it has three dialects: al-qiyam, which is the reading of Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash; al-qayyim, which is the reading of Alqama; and al-Qayyum, which is the reading of the rest. All are dialects with one meaning. The original forms are qayyum, qiwam and qayyum, as one says: ma fi al-dar diyyur, diyyar and dayr. Al-Qayyum: the one who is intensively standing over His creation.

Mujahid said: al-Qayyum is the one standing over everything. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the one who is not seen. Al-Dahhak: the everlasting. Abu Rawq: the one who is not governed. Al-Rabi': the custodian of everything, who preserves and provides for it. Al-Kalbi: the one standing over every soul for what it has earned. Abu Ubayd: the one who does not cease.

Ahiyya said:
"He did not create the heavens, the stars, and the sun with the moon, its measure set,
the Guardian, the Self-Subsisting; and the gathering, Paradise, and Hellfire, only for a matter of great significance."

Qatada narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to supplicate: "O Living, O Self-Subsisting." Ibn Abbas used to say: The greatest of the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is al-Hayy al-Qayyum, and He is ever the source of good.

This is indicated by what al-Qasim narrated from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the Greatest Name of Allah is in three suras of the Qur'an: al-Baqara, Al 'Imran, and Ta Ha" [[al-Mustadrak: 1/505-506.]].

Some of them said: I looked into these three suras and found in them a name that is not in anything else of the Qur'an:
In the Verse of the Throne: Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.
In Al 'Imran: Alif Lam Mim. Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting [[Surat Al 'Imran: 2.]].
In Ta Ha: "And faces will be humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting" [[Surat Ta Ha: 111.]].

Neither sleep nor slumber overtakes Him. The exegetes said:
Al-sina (sinah) is drowsiness, which is light sleep. It is a breeze that comes from the direction of the head, gentle, and it covers the eye. A man is wasnan when he is between sleeping and waking; it is said: wasana yasinu wasanan and sinatan, so he is wasnan.

Ibn al-Raqqa' said:
"A drowsy man whom sleep has overtaken, its drowsiness settled [[Raqana al-nawm fi 'aynayhi: it mixed with his eyes; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/272.]] in his eye, though he is not asleep."

Nor sleep. Sleep is the deep slumber that removes strength and reason. Allah, Exalted, negated sleep from Himself because it is a defect, and defects are not permissible for Him; because it is a change, and changes of states are not permissible for Him; because it is subjugation, and Allah is the Subduer who is not subdued; because it is for rest, and no fatigue reaches Him so that He would rest; and because it is the brother of death.

Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir narrated from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Do the people of Paradise sleep?"
He said: "No. Sleep is the brother of death, and the people of Paradise do not die" [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/34, with slight variation.]]. And because if reason slept or became heedless, His dominion and His management would be disrupted.

Abu Ubayda narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us and spoke five [[In all sources: four.]] words: "Indeed Allah does not sleep, nor is it fitting for Him to sleep, but He lowers the scale and raises it. The deed of the night is lifted up to Him before the deed of the day, and the deed of the day before the deed of the night. His veil is light; if He were to uncover it, the glories of His face would burn away whatever His sight reaches of His creation" [[al-Mu'jam al-Awsat: 2/142, with variation.]].

Ikrima narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) relate on the pulpit about Musa (peace be upon him) that he said:
"It occurred to Musa: does Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sleep? So Allah sent to him an angel [who kept him awake [[Arraqahu: al-arq is wakefulness; i.e., kept him awake.]] three times, then] gave him two flasks, one in each hand, and commanded him to guard them. He began to sleep, and his hands nearly met, and one of them restrained the other, until he slept his sleep and his hands convulsed, and the two flasks broke."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/13.]]
He said: Allah, Exalted, set forth an example that if Allah, glorified be He, were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would not remain firm.

To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, in dominion and in creation. Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission, that is, by His command. The people of allusion said: In this verse there is an attraction by which He draws the hearts of His servants to Himself, in this world and the next; so glory be to the One to whom there is no means.

The verse: He knows what is before them and what is behind them. Mujahid, Ata', al-Hakam and al-Suddi said: "what is before them" is the matter of this world, and "what is behind them" is the matter of the Hereafter.
Al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: "what is before them" means the Hereafter, because they will come upon it, and "what is behind them" means this world, because they will leave it behind. Ibn Juraij: "what is before them" means what was before the creation of the angels, and "what is behind them" means what will be after their creation.
It was also said: "He knows what is before them" means what they have done of good and evil, and "what is behind them" means what is before them of what they have done.

And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge, that is, the knowledge of Allah, except what He wills to teach them and make them aware of. His Kursi (Footstool) has encompassed the heavens and the earth, that is, it filled and surrounded them. The scholars differed concerning the Kursi. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: it is His knowledge, and from this the sheet on which written knowledge is kept is called kurrasa.
And from it is the saying of the rajiz describing a hunter:
"Until, when he came to him, he was crouched."
That is: knowledge.
Scholars are called al-karasi.
The poet said:
"Around them are fair-faced ones and a company, scholars (karasi) in the times of repentance."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/277.]]
Some of them said: His authority, His dominion and His power.
The Arabs call the origin of everything the kursi. It is said: so-and-so is noble in kursi, meaning in origin.
Al-Ajjaj said:
"The Holy One, the Lord of the Holy, has known that Abu al-Abbas is the first in soul, in the noble mine of kingship, the kursi."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/17; Lisan al-Arab: 6/169.]]
Al-Tha'labi said: I saw in some tafsirs "kursiyyuhu" as "his secret." And they recited on it:
"What is with me in your affair is a kursi I conceal, and is there with the kursi of the knowledge of the unseen any created being?"
[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/158.]]
Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari claimed that the Kursi is the term (ajal), meaning His term encompassed the heavens and the earth.
Abu Musa and al-Suddi and others said: it is the Kursi itself, and it is pearl, and the seven heavens within the Kursi are nothing but seven dirhams thrown into a shield.
[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/16.]]
Ali and Muqatil said: every span of the Kursi is as long as the seven heavens and the seven earths, and it is before the Throne. Four angels carry the Kursi, each angel having four faces, their feet on the rock beneath the lowest seventh earth, a distance of five hundred years: one in the form of the master of the children of Adam, Adam (peace be upon him), who asks for the Adamites' provision and rain from year to year, and on whose face there is grief since the worship of the calf apart from Allah; one in the form of the master of livestock, the bull, who asks for the livestock's provision from year to year, and on whose face there is grief since the worship of the calf apart from Allah; one in the form of the master of beasts, the lion, who asks provision for the beasts from year to year; and one in the form of the master of birds, the eagle, who asks Allah provision for the birds from year to year.

Abu Idris al-Khawlani narrated from Abu Dharr, who said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, which verse was sent down to you that is greatest?"
He said: "The Verse of the Throne."
Then he said: "O Abu Dharr, the seven heavens with the Kursi are nothing but a ring [of iron] [[Addition from al-Tabari.]] thrown in a desert wasteland, and the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of the wasteland over the ring" [[Sahih Ibn Hibban: 2/77; Kanz al-Ummal: 16/132, no. 44158.]].

In some reports it is said that between the bearers of the Throne and the bearers of the Kursi are seventy veils of darkness and seventy veils of light, the thickness of each veil being a five-hundred-year journey; were it not so, the bearers of the Kursi would be burned by the light of the bearers of the Throne.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: The Kursi is the Throne itself. Abu Sa'id Abd al-Malik, the Ustadh, related from Abu Uthman al-Zahid, from some of the earlier scholars, that the Kursi is the name of an angel whom He attributed to Himself as a specification and an honour, and by it He alerted His servants to His greatness and power.
He said: If a creature of Mine encompasses the heavens and the earth [wasi'a] [[Illegible in the manuscript; what we have written is apparently correct.]], how then would you measure My power and know My greatness. And Allah knows best.

And it does not burden Him (wa la ya'uduhu): that is, it does not weigh Him down, nor exhaust Him, nor cause Him difficulty.
Al-Khansa' said:
"The bearer of burdens, with loads, they know; when some of what they carried weighs men down."
It was also said: ya'uduhu means that it makes him fall from its weight.
The poet said:
"To me, and what the enemies of ours bewitched, at the donkey the mind (aql) makes her fall."

Its preservation (hifzuhuma) is the preservation of the heavens and the earth. And He is the Most High (al-Ali), exalted above His creation in management, strength and power, not by distance, place or direction. The Mighty (al-Azim), so nothing is greater than Him.

The exegetes said: The reason for the revelation of this verse is that the unbelievers used to worship idols and say: "These are our intercessors with Allah," so Allah, Exalted, revealed this verse.

There is no compulsion in religion, the verse...
Mujahid said: This verse was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar called Abu al-Husayn, who had two sons. Traders from Syria came to Medina carrying olive oil. When they wanted to return to Syria, the two sons of Abu al-Husayn came to them and invited them to Christianity, so they became Christians and went out to Syria. Abu al-Husayn informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of that, and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Seek them out." So Allah, Exalted, revealed: "There is no compulsion in religion." He (ﷺ) said: "May Allah remove them far away; they are the first to have disbelieved." Abu al-Husayn was resentful toward the Prophet (ﷺ) because he had not sent anyone to pursue them, so Allah, Exalted, revealed: "But no, by your Lord, they do not believe until they make you judge in what is in dispute between them" [[Surat al-Nisa': 65.]], the verse.
He said: This was before the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to fight the People of the Book. Then his saying "There is no compulsion in religion" was abrogated (nasakha), and he was commanded to fight the People of the Book in Surat Bara'a.

And so Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Zayd said that it is abrogated (mansukha, "abrogated") by the verse of the sword, while the rest said that it is muhkama (definitive, not abrogated).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. He said: A woman from the Ansar used to be one whose children did not survive, so she would vow that if a child survived for her she would make him a Jew. Then Islam came, and among them [the children] were from them. When Banu al-Nadir were expelled, there were among them some people from the Ansar. The Ansar said: "O Messenger of Allah, they are our sons and our brothers." So he (ﷺ) remained silent about them, and ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ was revealed, the verse.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Your companions have been given a choice. If they choose you, then they are of you; and if they choose them, then make them go with them."

He said: The distinction between the Ansar and the Jews was the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir; whoever joined them, they chose them, and whoever stayed, chose Islam.

The exegetes said: A man from the Ansar, from Banu Salim, had two sons who had become Christians before the Prophet (ﷺ) was sent. Then they came to Madinah with a group of Christians carrying food. Their father came to them and clung to them and said: "I will not leave you until you become Muslims." But they refused to become Muslims, so they brought their dispute to the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: "O Messenger of Allah, will part of me enter the Fire while I am watching?" So Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, the verse, and he released them [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/22, and Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 53.]].

Ibn Abi [Hatim] narrated from Mujahid, who said: Some people were nursed among the Jews, of Qurayzah and al-Nadir. When the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir, their women from the Aws, who had been nursed among them, said: "We will certainly go with them, and we will be struck by what strikes them." Their families prevented them and wanted to compel them to Islam, so this verse was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾.

Qatada, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', Abu Rawq and al-Waqidi said: The meaning of ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾ is after the Arabs had become Muslim, when they accepted the jizya (poll tax on non-Muslim subjects). That is because the Arabs were an unlettered people; they had neither religion nor scripture. So nothing was accepted from them except Islam or the sword, and they were compelled to Islam, and the jizya was not accepted from them. When they had become Muslim, and no one among the Arabs remained except that he had entered Islam willingly or by compulsion, Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. So He commanded that the People of the Book, the Magians and the Sabians be fought until they become Muslim or agree to pay the jizya. Whoever among them agreed to the jizya, it was accepted from him, he was left alone, and he was not compelled to Islam.

Muqatil said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would not accept the jizya except from the People of the Book. When the Arabs became Muslim, willingly or by compulsion, the kharaj (tribute) was accepted from non-People of the Book. So the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to al-Mundhir ibn Sawi and the people of Hajar, calling them to Islam:

"Whoever bears witness to our testimony, prays our prayer, faces our qibla, eats our slaughtered animals, and follows our religion, that is the Muslim, who has the protection of Allah and the protection of His Messenger. If you become Muslim, you will have what we have and you will have what is upon us. And whoever refuses Islam, upon him is the jizya."

Al-Mundhir wrote to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I read your letter to the people of Hajar. Some of them became Muslim and some refused. As for the Jews and the Magians, they acknowledged the jizya and disliked Islam, so the Prophet (ﷺ) accepted the jizya from them." The hypocrites of the people of Madinah said: "Muhammad claims that he was only commanded to take the jizya from the People of the Book; so what about the Magians of Hajar? He has rejected that for our fathers and brothers, until he killed them." This grieved the Muslims, so they mentioned that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, meaning after the Arabs became Muslim.

Shurayk narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Hilal, from Wasaq, who said: I was a slave of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), and I was a Christian. He used to say: "O Wasaq, become Muslim, for if you became Muslim I would appoint you over some of the affairs of the Muslims, since it is not right that one who is not of their religion should govern their affairs." I refused him, so he said: "There is no compulsion in religion." When he died, he freed me.

Ibn Abi Najih said: I heard Mujahid say to a Christian slave of his: "O Jarir, become Muslim." Then he said: "So it used to be said: [Or do they not compel?]" [[al-Musannaf of 'Abd al-Razzaq: 10/316, no. 19221, and Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/24, and in both: "It used to be said to them."]].

Al-Zajjaj and others said: It is from the usage of the Arabs: "I made the man hateful (akrahtu al-rajul)" when I attributed to him hatred, just as it is said: "I called him a disbeliever (akfartuhu), made him a sinner (afsaqtuhu), and made him a wrongdoer (az-lamtuhu)" when I attributed these to him.

Al-Kumayt said:
"A group has called me a disbeliever for love of you,
and a group said: 'He is a wrongdoer and a sinner.'" [[al-Tibyan: 3/283, and Khizanat al-Adab: 236.]]

The meaning of the verse: Do not say of one who entered Islam after the war that he entered it under compulsion, and do not attribute to compulsion the entry of one into Islam. What points to this is His words: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾ [[Surat al-Nisa': 94.]].

﴿The right course has become clear from error﴾: faith became clear from disbelief, guidance from misguidance, and truth from falsehood.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has been guided aright" [[Kitab al-Musnad of al-Shafi'i: 68.]].

And from Muqatil ibn Hassan, who said: Al-Dahhak claimed that when people entered Islam willingly or by compulsion, and none of the enemies of the Prophet of Allah among the polytheist Arabs remained except that they entered Islam willingly or by compulsion, and the religion was completed, this was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from error﴾. Whoever wishes, let him become Muslim; and whoever wishes, let him give the jizya.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-A'raj read ar-rashad with a fatha on the ra' and the shin, and they are two dialects, like al-hazan and al-hazan, and al-bakhl and al-bakhl.

'Isa ibn 'Umar read ar-rushud with two dammas.

The rest read it with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the shin, and they are two dialects, like ar-ru'b and ar-ru'b, and as-suht and as-suht.

﴿So whoever disbelieves in the Taghut﴾: meaning the Satan, said by Ibn 'Amr [sic], Ibn 'Abbas, Muqatil and al-Kalbi.

It was also said: it is the idol. It was said: it is the soothsayer. It was said: it is everything worshipped besides Allah.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: al-taghut is everything that covers a person. It is on the pattern of fa'ut from at-tughyan, the ta' being added to it in place of the radical letter of the verb, as in his words: "hanut" and "tabut".

The people of allusion (ahl al-isharah) said: the taghut of every person is his own self, its evidence being His words: ﴿Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil﴾ [[Surat Yusuf: 53.]], the verse.

﴿And believes in Allah﴾: It is narrated from Sa'id, who said: Faith is affirmation, and affirmation is that the servant act upon what he affirms from the Qur'an.

And from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Allah the Exalted informed that faith is the firmest handhold, and no deed is accepted without it. And from Ibn 'Abbas also, who said: Allah the Exalted informed that faith is: there is no god but Allah.

﴿Has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾: he held fast and clung to it. ﴿The most trustworthy handhold﴾: the firm protection, the wisdom. ﴿For it there is no breaking﴾. ﴿And Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾.

﴿Allah is the ally of those who believe﴾: that is, their helper and supporter. It was said: their lover. It was said: the one who manages their affairs, who does not leave them to other than Him. It is said: "I took charge of the affair of so-and-so" and "I appointed him to it, a guardianship (wilayah)" with the waw kasra. It was said: He is more fitting and more entitled to them, because He nurtures them. Al-Hasan said: He is the guardian of their guidance.

﴿He brings them out of darkness into light﴾: that is, from disbelief and misguidance into faith and guidance. Likewise they were in the knowledge of Allah the Mighty and Majestic before He created them, and when He created them, His knowledge took effect in them, so they believed.

Al-Waqidi said: everything in the Qur'an concerning darkness and light means disbelief and faith, except the one in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [[Surat al-An'am: 1.]], for that means night and day.

Ibn 'Abbas said: These are people who disbelieved in 'Isa (peace be upon him), then believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), so He brought them [out of disbelief] in 'Isa into their faith in the Chosen One and all the prophets (peace be upon them). Others said: it is general to all believers. Ibn 'Ata' said: this verse [suffices them from] their attributes, by an attribute, so they become standing with the truth, for the truth, with the truth.

Al-Wasiti: He brings them out of the darknesses of their souls into their virtues, such as contentment, truthfulness, reliance, knowledge and love.

Abu 'Uthman: He brings them out of seeing actions into seeing favours and bounties. It was said: He brings them out of the darknesses of loneliness and separation into the light of union and nearness.

﴿And those who disbelieve, their allies are the taghut﴾: thus the common readers recited it. Al-Hasan read al-tawaghit in the plural.

Abu Hatim said: The Arabs make taghut singular and plural, masculine and feminine.

Allah the Exalted said concerning the singular and masculine: ﴿They desire to go to judgment before the taghut, though they were commanded to reject it﴾ [[Surat al-Nisa': 60.]].

And He said concerning the feminine: ﴿And those who avoid the taghut from worshipping it﴾ [[Surat al-Zumar: 17.]]. And He said concerning the plural:

﴿They bring them out from the light into the darknesses﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas said: By the taghut he means the Satan.

Muqatil said: He means Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and the rest of the heads of misguidance. ﴿They bring them out﴾: they call them, ﴿from the light into the darknesses﴾. Its evidence is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We had already sent Musa with Our signs, [saying], "Bring your people out from darknesses into light"﴾ [[Surat Ibrahim: 5.]], meaning: call them.

If it is asked: what is the sense of His words ﴿They bring them out from the light into the darknesses﴾, when they are disbelievers who were never in light at all? How can they bring them out of what they never entered?

The answer is what Muqatil and Qatada said: They are the Jews, who were believers in Muhammad (ﷺ) before he was sent. When he was sent, they disbelieved in him and denied what they had found in their scriptures about his description, attributes and prophethood. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿But when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [[Surat al-Baqarah: 89.]]. So that is their departure from the light, meaning by their faith in Muhammad before the sending. By the darknesses is meant their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ) after the sending. Entering and exiting are to Allah the Mighty and Majestic alone, not to anyone else, except by way of the sacred law and figurative usage. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And say, "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance and cause me to exit a sound exit"﴾ [[Surat al-Isra': 80.]]. The people of meanings applied this to generality over all disbelievers.

They said: Preventing them from entering it is a bringing out. This is as a man says to his father: "You expelled me from your wealth," when it was never in it. Allah the Exalted said, reporting about Yusuf: ﴿Indeed, I have left the religion of a people who do not believe in Allah﴾ [[Surat Yusuf: 37.]], though he had never been upon their religion until he left it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾ [[Surat al-Nahl: 70.]], though it was never in it.

Imru' al-Qays said:
"They eat the substitute; the bloodshed has returned... 
the voices said to him: 'O, you there, be still'" [[Thus in the manuscript.]]

Another said:
"I obeyed the self in its desires until
it made me again a servant, a slave of a slave."
[[Lisan al-Arab: 9/246.]]

But he had never been a slave.

Al-Ghanawi said:
"For if the days were once kind to me,
then sins have returned to them." [[Tarikh Dimashq: 63/172, and the witness is that they had no sins before that.]]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 258–259 (part 1 of 2):

Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord? That is, he disputed and debated with him. The root of the word is *ḥujjah* (proof, argument). He was Nimrod son of Kan'an, son of Sakhariyb, son of Kush, son of Sam, son of Noah. He was the first to place a crown on his head, he became tyrannical on earth, and he claimed lordship. ﴿that Allah had given him the kingdom﴾, that is, because Allah had given him the kingdom, so he became arrogant. The position of *an* (that) is in the accusative, the preposition (*ḥarf al-ṣifah*, the particle governing the sense) having been dropped.

Al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Ayyami narrated from Mujahid, who said: Two believers and two disbelievers ruled the earth. The two believers were Sulayman son of Dawud and Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and the two disbelievers were Nimrod and Bukht Nasr.

The scholars differed about the time of this debate. Muqatil said: When Abraham broke the idols, Nimrod imprisoned him, then brought him out to burn him in the fire. Nimrod said to him: "Who is your Lord whom you call us to?"

He said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾

Others said: This happened after he was thrown into the fire.

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar ibn Zayd ibn Aslam that the first tyrant on earth was Nimrod ibn Kan'an, and people used to go out and obtain food from him.

He said: Abraham, peace be upon him, went out to obtain food. Whenever people passed by him, he would say: "Who is your lord?" They said: "You." Until Abraham passed by him, and he said: "Who is your lord?" He said: ﴿He who gives life and causes death,﴾ as Allah the Exalted mentioned.

He said: So he sent him away without food. Abraham, peace be upon him, returned to his family and passed by a red sand dune, and said: "Should I not take some of this and bring it to my family, so that their hearts are at ease when I enter upon them?" So he took some of it and brought it to his family, and set down his provisions and slept. His wife got up to his provisions and opened them, and behold, it was the finest food anyone had seen. So she prepared some of it for him and brought it near to him, and they had been without food.

He said: "Where is this from?"

She said: "From the food you brought." He knew that Allah had provided for him, so he praised Allah.

He said: Then Allah sent an angel to the tyrant, saying: "Believe in Me and I will leave you in your kingdom." Nimrod said: "Is there any lord other than me?!" The angel came to him a second time and said the same to him, but he refused. Then he came a third time and he refused and said: "I do not know the one you speak of. Does your lord have armies?"

He said: "Yes."

He said: "Let him fight me, if he is a king, for kings fight one another."

The angel said to him: "Yes, if you wish." He said: "I wish."

He said: "Gather your army for three days, until the armies of my Lord come to you."

He said: So the tyrant gathered his armies.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed to the keepers of the gnats: "Open a gate of gnats from them." They opened a gate of gnats. When the third day dawned, Nimrod looked at the sun and said: "What is wrong with it that it does not rise?" He thought that it had been delayed. The angel said: "The armies of my Lord have come between it and you."

He said: So the gnats surrounded them, ate their flesh and drank their blood, so that nothing remained of the people and animals but bones, while Nimrod remained as he was, untouched by anything.

The angel said to him: "Do you believe now?"

He said: "No."

So Allah the Mighty and Majestic commanded a gnat, which stung his lower lip and drank and grew large. Then it stung his upper lip, drank and grew large. Then it entered his nostril and reached his brain and ate from his brain until it became like a mouse. He remained for four hundred years being struck on the head with hammers. The most merciful people to him were those who would gather his hand and strike his head with it. So Allah punished him for four hundred years, just as he had ruled for four hundred years.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿When Abraham said: My Lord is He who gives life and causes death,﴾ this is the answer to an earlier question that is not mentioned; its implied meaning is: he said to him: "Who is your lord?" Abraham said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾

Al-A'mash, Hamzah and 'Isa recited *rabbi* (with the *yā'* sukūn), and the rest recited it with a fatḥah because of the *alif* and *lām* following.

﴿Nimrod said: I give life and cause death.﴾

The people of Madinah recited *anā* (I) with a long vowel throughout the Qur'an, and this is the dialect of a people who treat pausal forms as the basic forms.

Al-Kisa'i recited:
"I am the sword of the ten, so know me,
Ḥumayd, who has grown the hump (of his camel)..."

Another said:
"I am the servant of Allah, [my right hand] 'Umar,
the best of Quraysh of those who passed and those who remain,
except the Messenger of Allah and the noble elder."

The original form of *anā* is that the *nūn* should carry a fatḥah, but they sought to make it pausal, so they wrote an *alif* with the intention of stopping, and it became *anā*.

Most Arabs, in pause, say *anā-h* (anāh).

Most of the exegetes said: Nimrod summoned two men, killed one and spared the other, so he called sparing the one from being killed "giving life," as in His saying: ﴿And whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:32], meaning he did not kill it.

As for al-Suddi, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿I give life and cause death,﴾ he said: He took four men and put them in a house, where they were given neither food nor drink, until they approached death. Then he fed two of them and gave them drink, and left two, and they died. Abraham then moved to another argument, not from inability, for he could have said: "Then bring to life the one you have caused to die, if you are truthful." Rather, to make the proof clear, he said: ﴿Abraham said: Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west.﴾ ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded,﴾ that is, he was bewildered, stupefied, and his argument was cut off.

It is said: "a man *mabhūt*," that is, stupefied.

The poet said:
"Indeed, its (the lion's) roar came suddenly,
so I was struck dumb, until I could hardly walk."

Muhammad ibn al-Sumay' al-Yamani recited *fa-bahata* with a fatḥah on the *bā'* and the *hā'*, meaning Abraham confounded him. Its confirmation is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Rather it will come upon them suddenly, and it will stun them﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:40], that is, it will astonish them.

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ to the proof.

﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾ This is coordinated with the meaning of the first verse; its implied meaning is: "Have you seen one like the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, or have you seen one like the one who passed by a town?"

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: the *kāf* (like) is an extra (ṣilah) element; it is as if he said: "Have you not considered the one who..." or "the one..."

They differed about who this passer-by was. Qatadah, al-Rabi', 'Ikrimah, Najiyah ibn Ka'b, Sulayman ibn Buraydah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Salim al-Khawwas said: he was 'Uzayr ibn Sharhiya.

Wahb ibn Munabbih and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: he was Armiya ibn Khalfiya, who was of the tribe of Harun ibn 'Imran, and he was al-Khidr.

Mujahid said: he was a disbelieving man who doubted the resurrection.

They differed about the town over which he passed. Wahb, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: it was Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). al-Dahhak said: it was the holy land. Ibn Zayd said: it was the land in which Allah destroyed those who left their homes in their thousands, fearing death.

al-Kalbi said: it was the monastery of Sa'daba'ad. al-Suddi said: it was Salmabad. It was also said: the monastery of Harafil; and it was said: the town of the grapes, which is two farsakhs from Bayt al-Maqdis.

﴿And it was in ruins﴾ fallen down. It is said: *khawā al-bayt yakhwā khawan* (the house collapsed) when it falls, and *khawā al-bayt* with a fatḥah, *khawā'* (with long vowel), when it becomes empty.

﴿Upon its roofs﴾ its ceilings and its buildings. Its singular is *'arsh*, and its plural in the paucal is *a'rush*. Every building is an *'arsh*. It is said: *'arsha fulān*, when he builds, so he *ya'rishu* and *ya'rushu* *'arshan*. Allah said: ﴿and what they built (ya'rishūn)﴾ [al-A'raf 7:137], that is, what they built.

The meaning of the verse is: the ceilings fell, and then the walls fell upon them.

It was also said: *'alā* means *ma'a* (with), that is: "in ruins along with their roofs."

The poet said:
"As if the polished columns in its (the valley's) heights
and towers over which were the cloudy ones..."
that is, with them.

Its parallels are in surah al-Kahf and al-Hajj.

﴿He said: How will Allah give life to this after its death?﴾ The cause of this, as Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, was that Allah the Exalted said to Armiya, peace be upon him, when He sent him as a prophet to the Children of Israel: "O Armiya, before I created you I chose you; before I formed you in your mother's womb I sanctified you; before you reached the age of striving I appointed you a prophet; and for a great matter I loved you." So Allah sent Armiya to Nashi'ah ibn Amus, the king of the Children of Israel, to guide him and bring him news from Allah the Exalted. The Children of Israel's sins grew great; they committed transgressions and considered the forbidden lawful. So Allah the Exalted revealed to Armiya: "Remind your people of My blessings, make them aware of their misdeeds, and call them to Me."

Armiya said: "I am weak; if You do not strengthen me, I am incapable; if You do not help me..."

Allah the Exalted said: "I will inspire you." So Armiya stood among them and did not know what to say, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic inspired him at that moment with an eloquent, lengthy sermon in which he explained to them the reward of obedience and the punishment of disobedience.

At its end he said: "I am Allah, by My might, I will surely bring upon them a trial in which the forbearing will be bewildered, and I will set over them a cruel tyrant whom I will clothe in awe and from whose heart I will remove mercy, followed by a multitude like the darkness of a black night."

Allah the Exalted revealed to Armiya: "I will destroy the Children of Israel through Yafith and Yafith, the people of Babylon, who are descendants of Yafith son of Noah." When Armiya heard that, he cried out, wept, tore his garments and threw ashes on his head. When Allah heard Armiya's supplication and his weeping, He called to him: "O Armiya, is what I revealed to you hard on you?"

He said: "Yes, my Lord. Let me die before I see among the Children of Israel what does not please me."

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: "By My might, I will not destroy the Children of Israel until the matter in that regard comes from you." Armiya was delighted by this and his soul was content, and he said: "By He who sent Moses with the truth, I will not accept the destruction of the Children of Israel." Then he went to the king and informed him of this. He was a righteous king. He rejoiced and was glad and said: "If our Lord punishes us, it is for our many sins; and if He pardons us, it is by His mercy."

Then they remained for three years after the revelation, increasing only in disobedience and persistence in evil. This was when their destruction drew near. The revelation ceased, and the king called them to repentance, but they did not do so. So Allah gave power over them to Bukht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), who set out with six hundred thousand banners, intending the people of Bayt al-Maqdis. When he set out on his march, news reached the king, and he said to Armiya: "Where is what you claimed Allah revealed to you?"

Armiya said: ﴿Indeed Allah does not break the promise,﴾ and "I am certain of Him."

When the appointed time drew near and Allah determined to destroy them, Allah sent to Armiya an angel who had taken the form of a man from the Children of Israel.

He said: "O prophet of Allah, I seek your help regarding the people of my kin. I have kept ties with their relations and I have not done to them except for a while, and they increase in hostility toward me despite my honoring them. So give me a ruling about them."

He said to him: "Be good in what is between you and Allah, keep ties with them, and receive good news."

The angel departed, stayed a few days, then came to him in the form of that man, and sat before him. Armiya said to him: "Have their characters not yet been revealed to you?"

He said: "O prophet of Allah, by He who sent you with the truth, I know of no kindness that anyone shows to his kin that I have not offered them first and more."

The prophet said: "Return to your family, be good to them, and ask Allah, who sets right the righteous servants, to set them right." The angel rose, stayed a few days, and by then Bukht Nasr and his armies had encamped around Bayt al-Maqdis, more numerous than locusts. The Children of Israel were terrified and it weighed heavily on them.

The angel said to Armiya: "O prophet of Allah, where is what Allah promised you?"

He said: "I am certain of my Lord."

Then the angel came to Armiya, who was sitting on the wall of Bayt al-Maqdis. He laughed and rejoiced at the victory of his Lord that He had promised, sat before him and said: "I am the one who informed you about my family twice."

The prophet said: "Has the time not come for them to awaken from what they are in?"

The angel said: "O prophet of Allah, whatever I used to suffer from them before today I would endure, but today I have seen them in an action that does not please Allah the Mighty and Majestic."

The prophet said: "What action did you see them doing?"

He said: "A great action of Allah's wrath. So I became angry for Allah and for you, and I came to inform you, and I ask you by Allah who sent you with the truth to supplicate against them that He destroy them."

Armiya said: "O Master of the heavens and the earth, if they are upon truth and righteousness, then spare them; and if they are upon Your wrath and an action You do not approve, then destroy them."

When the word came out of Armiya's mouth, Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent a thunderbolt from the sky upon Bayt al-Maqdis; the place of the offering caught fire, and seven of its gates sank into the earth.

When Armiya saw that, he cried out, tore his garments, threw ashes on his head, and said: "O Master of the heavens and the earth, where is Your promise that You made to me?" It was called out to him: "They were struck by what struck them only because of your ruling and your supplication." The prophet was certain that it was his ruling that he had given, and that he was the messenger of his Lord.

Armiya flew off until he mixed with the wild beasts. Bukht Nasr and his armies entered Bayt al-Maqdis, trampled al-Sham, slaughtered the Children of Israel until he annihilated them, and destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis. Then he ordered his armies that each man fill his shield with earth and hurl it into Bayt al-Maqdis, so they hurled earth into it until they filled it. Then he ordered them to gather everyone who was in the regions of Bayt al-Maqdis, so every young and old person from the Children of Israel was gathered before him. He chose one hundred thousand boys from them and divided them among the kings who were with him, so that each man received four youths. Bukht Nasr divided the remaining Children of Israel into three groups: one third he left in al-Sham, one third he took captive, and one third he killed. This was the first calamity that Allah sent upon the Children of Israel because of their wrongdoing.

When Bukht Nasr turned back from them, returning to Babylon with the captives of the Children of Israel, Armiya came on his donkey, with a jar of grape juice and a basket of figs, until he reached Iliya. When he stopped there and saw its ruin, he said: ﴿How will Allah give life to this after its death?!﴾ Those who said that this passer-by was 'Uzayr said: When Bukht Nasr destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis and brought the captives of the Children of Israel to the land of Babylon, among them were 'Uzayr, who was one of the scholars of the Children of Israel, Daniel, and seven thousand people from the family of Dawud.

When 'Uzayr escaped from Babylon, he set out on a donkey until he came down at the monastery of Harqal (Heraclius) on the bank of the Tigris. He went around the town but saw no one in it, and he learned of its condition. He ate some fruit and pressed some grapes, drank from them, put the surplus fruit in a basket and the surplus juice in a skin. When he saw the ruin of the town and the destruction of its people, he said: ﴿How will Allah give life to this after its death?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:259]. He did not doubt the resurrection, but said it in wonder.

Returning to the account of Wahb: He said: Armiya tied his donkey with a new rope, and Allah cast sleep upon him. When he slept, Allah took his soul for a hundred years and caused his donkey to die. His juice and his figs were with him, and Allah blinded the eyes from him so that no one saw him, and that was in the forenoon. Allah prevented the predators and the birds from his flesh. When seventy years had passed since his death, Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent an angel to a great king of the Children of Israel called [Yuswak], saying: "Allah the Mighty and Majestic commands you to mobilize your people to rebuild Bayt al-Maqdis and Iliya and its land, until it returns to being more flourishing than it ever was." The king appointed one thousand commanders, with three hundred thousand workers under each commander, and they began rebuilding it. Allah the Exalted destroyed Bukht Nasr with a gnat that entered his brain [...] [unreadable in the manuscript]. Allah the Exalted gathered those of the Children of Israel who remained and had not died in Babylon, and returned them all to Bayt al-Maqdis and its environs. They rebuilt it for thirty years and multiplied until they became as they had been at their finest. When the hundred years had passed, Allah the Exalted restored his eyes and the rest of his body, which was dead. Then He restored his body while he watched. Then he looked at his donkey, and behold, its bones were scattered, white and shining. He heard a voice from the sky: "O white bones, Allah commands you to come together." Some of them came together and joined to one another.

Then it was called out: "Allah commands you to clothe yourselves with flesh and skin." So it was. Then it was called out: "Allah commands you to live." It stood, by the permission of Allah, and the donkey brayed.

Allah gave Armiya long life, and he is the one who is seen in the wilderness. This is the meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him,﴾ that is, He gave him life. [Lengthy version in Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/47–50 and his History: 1/392 with variations.]

﴿He said: How long have you remained?﴾ a question about the amount of the number. Ibn Muhays, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *labiththa* and *labithtum* with assimilation (idgham) throughout the Qur'an. The rest recited with clear pronunciation (izhar).

As for the one who assimilates, the sound does not border it in articulation, and in the similarity in whispering (hams); and as for the one who makes it clear, [because of its clarity] [clarity is due to the difference in articulation between the *thā'* and the *tā'*; see Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/292] in the Mushaf. Both are unusual but eloquent. Its meaning is: how long did you stay and remain here? It is said: *labitha yalbathu labthan* and *labāthan* (to remain).

[See Majma' al-Bahrayn: 4/103.]

He said, "I have remained a day." That is because God caused him to die at the forenoon and revived him a hundred years later, at the end of the day, before the sun set. So he said, "I have remained a day," as he thought the sun had set. Then he turned and saw some remnant of the sun, so he said, "Or part of a day," meaning "Rather, part of a day," because his words "part of a day" are a retraction of his words "I have remained a day," like the verse ﴿or they would increase [them]﴾ [[Surah al-Saffat: 147.]].

He said, "Nay, you have remained a hundred years. But look at your food and your drink ﴿which has not spoiled﴾." The food means the figs, and the drink means the juice. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ (lam yatasannah) with the ha' omitted in continuous recitation (wasl), and likewise in His words ﴿fa-bi-hudahumu iqtadih﴾ [[Surah al-An'am: 90.]]. The rest read it with the ha' both in continuous recitation and in pause (waqf). Abu Hatim reported from Talhah that it is read لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ with the ta' assimilated into the sin, and he claimed that it is so in the codex of Ubayy. Its meaning is: the years have not changed it.

Whoever drops the ha' in continuous recitation regards the ha' as a superfluous (silah) addition and says: its original form is lam yatasannay; the ya' is elided by the jussive and a ha' is substituted for it in pause. This is according to the view of those who consider the ha' in sanah (year) to be superfluous.

He said: its root is yasnawhu, its plural is sanawat, and the verb from it is sanaytu, musanah, and tasannaytu, tasannyan, except that the waw is returned to the remaining form, tafa''ul and tafa'ul, as in their saying al-tada'i and al-tadani, because ya' is lighter than waw.

Abu 'Amr said: it is from al-tasannun with two nuns, meaning change, as in His words ﴿of black mud, moulded﴾ [[Surah al-Hijr: 26.]], i.e., changed. Then one of the two nuns was compensated for, as in the poet's words:

"Why, when you heard, did you not search for it, / and the judgment was not touched by conjecture (al-tazanni)?"

He meant bi-l-ta'ayyun (by certainty).

Al-'Ajjaj said:

"He escaped like the falcon when the falcon swoops,"

meaning tafaddad (was silvered/pierced).

The Arabs say: nata'la, when they go out to gather a soft plant called al-maq'a.

God Almighty said: ﴿And he has failed who covered it up﴾ [[Surah al-Shams: 10.]], meaning dassasaha (buried it).

Whoever affirms the ha' in both states regards it as an original ha' of the verb's final radical. On this basis is the view of those who make sanah into sanhiyyah, its diminutive sunayhiyyah, and the verb from it al-musanahah.

The poet said:

"It is not a sanha' nor a rajabiyyah, / but 'arayaa in the years of calamities."

[[Lisan al-'Arab: 1/412. al-'ariyyah: a palm tree its owner gives as a gift; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/293.]]

If it is asked: he speaks of two things, then says لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ and not "did not change" in the dual, the answer is: the change refers to the nearer of the two expressions, which is the years, and he suffices with mention of one of the two mentioned items over the other because it is in the place of what is perishable, as in the poet's words:

[An eagle we pursued, whose hunting-trace was... and a khartu'ah except upon the spear of Falaj.] [[Thus in the manuscript.]]

He did not say "two spears of Falaj." The evidence for this interpretation is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Look at your food, and this your drink, it has not changed."

﴿And look at your donkey﴾ and ﴿that We may make you a sign for the people﴾. Most scholars said: in the verse there is inversion and reordering, i.e., "And look at your food and your drink, it has not changed, and that We may make you a sign for the people, and look at your donkey." It is possible that the meaning is: "So look at your food and your drink, it has not changed, and look at your donkey."

﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh.﴾

As for the explanation of the verse and its readings: Kharijah, al-A'raj, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ḥimārika and al-ḥimār with imalah (inclination); the rest with tafkhim (emphatic pronunciation). As for His words ﴿how We raise them﴾:

Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read nunshizuha with a zay, with the nun vowelled by a damma and the shin by a kasra.

Abu al-'Aliyah reported from Zayd ibn Thabit that he said: it is only a ra' which he read as a zay, i.e., he put a dot on it. Likewise Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah reported from Ibn 'Abbas with a zay, and Abu 'Ubaydah chose it.

The raising (inshaz) of a thing means lifting it, moving it and disturbing it. He said: "I made it rise, so it rose," i.e., I lifted it and it was lifted. From it comes the rising (nushuz) of a wife against her husband, and the rising (nushuz) of a boy, i.e., he rose up. So the meaning of the verse: how We lift them from the earth, then return them to their places in the body and assemble some of them upon others.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: "We bring them out." Al-Kisa'i said: "We cause them to grow and magnify them."

Qatadah, 'Ata', Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Ayyub read nunshiruha with a ra', damma on the nun and kasra on the shin, and Abu Hatim chose it. Its meaning: We give it life.

He said: "Allah revived the dead with inshar, and he (the dead) rises by nushur." God Almighty said: ﴿Then when He wills, He will resurrect him﴾ [[Surah 'Abasa: ...]]... He said: ﴿They rise up﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 21.]], and He said: ﴿Nay, they did not expect a resurrection﴾ [[Surah al-Furqan: 40.]], and He said: ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾ [[Surah Fatir: 9.]], and ﴿and to Him is the resurrection﴾ [[Surah al-Mulk: 15.]]. Harithah ibn Badr al-Ghudani said:

"So He revived its dead and distributed justice among them, / and its minds returned to it after they had been scattered."

Al-A'sha said, using it intransitively:

"Until people say, from what they saw: / 'How strange, the dead one raised up!'"

[[Lisan al-'Arab: 5/206.]]

Al-Hasan and al-Mufaddal read nunshiruha with a ra', the nun with a fatha and the shin with a damma.

Al-Farra' said: he went to the meaning of spreading and folding.

Some of them said: it is also from giving life, it is said: "Allah revived (anshara) the dead and raised him (nasharahu)" when He gave him life. Abu Hatim said: this is not well known.

Al-Nakha'i read it with a zay, the nun with a fatha and the shin with a damma.

Abu Hatim said: that is an error. Others said: it is said nashazahu [wa-nashatahu] and anshazahu with the same meaning.

﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾, i.e., We clothe them and conceal them with it, as we conceal the body with a garment. They differed about the meaning of the verse. Some said: it refers to the bones of his donkey, because God caused his donkey to die, then revived it as a complete creature while he was watching. Al-Suddi said: God revived 'Uzayr, then said, "Look at your donkey, it has perished and its bones have decayed." So God sent a wind which brought the bones of the donkey from every plain and mountain; the birds and beasts had carried them away, and they gathered and were joined one to another while he watched, until it became a donkey of bones with no flesh or blood. Then He clothed the bones with flesh and blood, and it became a donkey without a spirit. Then an angel came walking until he took hold of the donkey's nostril and blew into it, and the donkey stood up and brayed by God's leave.

The meaning of the verse on this view: "Look at the flesh of your donkey and at its bones, how We raise them," and when the ha' was dropped from the bones, the alif was substituted... And on this view most exegetes agree.

Others said: it refers to the bones of this man himself, for God did not cause his donkey to die; rather God revived his eyes and his head, while the rest of his body was dead. Then He said to him, "Look at your donkey," and he looked and saw his donkey standing upright, in the state it was in on the day he tied it, alive, not having eaten or drunk for a hundred years, and he looked at the halter on its neck, new and unchanged.

The estimate of the verse on this view: "Look at your donkey, and look at your bones, how We raise them." This is the view of al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾: We did this so that We might make you [a sign]. If you wish, you may take the waw as emphatic and superfluous, as in the poet al-Aswad ibn Ja'far's words:

"Then when that, there is no forgetting it, / and time brings good after corruption."

i.e., "then when that."

The meaning of the verse: We did this to you so that We might make you a sign for the people, i.e., an example and evidence of resurrection after death, as most exegetes said.

Al-Dahhak and others said: this verse [means] that he returned to his village a young man, while his children and grandchildren were old men and old women, and he had black hair and beard.

Qatadah reported from Ka'b, and from al-Hasan, Muqatil and Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Abd Allah ibn Isma'il al-Suddi from his father from Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, they said: When God revived 'Uzayr after he had made him die for a hundred years, he rode his donkey until he came to his quarter, and the people did not recognize him, and he did not recognize the people or his dwelling. He went on, in some confusion, until he came to his house, and there was a blind, paralysed old woman who was a hundred and twenty years old; she had been a slave-girl of theirs. She had left them, and 'Uzayr had left her when she was twenty years old; she had known him and cared for him. When old age and infirmity afflicted her, 'Uzayr said to her: "O woman, is this the house of 'Uzayr?"

She said: "Yes, this is the house of 'Uzayr," and she wept and said: "I have not seen anyone from such-and-such years mention 'Uzayr, and the people have forgotten him." He said: "I am 'Uzayr."

She said: "Glory be to God! 'Uzayr has been missing from us for a hundred years and we have not heard any mention of him."

He said: "I am 'Uzayr. God Almighty caused me to die for a hundred years, then raised me."

She said: "'Uzayr was one whose supplication was answered; he would pray for the sick and the afflicted for health and cure. So pray to God that He return my sight to me, so that I may see you; if you are 'Uzayr, I shall recognize you." He prayed to his Lord and wiped his hand over her eyes, and they opened; he took her hand and said: "Rise, by God's leave." Then God Almighty loosed her legs, and she stood up sound, by God's leave, as if she had been released from a fetter. She looked and said: "I bear witness that you are 'Uzayr." She went to the quarter of the Children of Israel, who were in their clubs and assemblies, and the son of 'Uzayr, a shaikh of a hundred and eighteen years, and his sons' sons were old men in the assembly. She called out: "This is 'Uzayr, he has come to you." They denied her.

She said: "I am so-and-so, your freedwoman. He prayed to his Lord, Almighty and Majestic, and He returned my sight to me and loosed my legs, and he claims that God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him."

He said: the people rose and came to him. His son said: "My father had a dark mole like the crescent between his shoulders." He uncovered his shoulders, and there he was: 'Uzayr.

Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: 'Uzayr returned to his village after Bukhtnassar had burned the Torah, and God had not made a covenant with creation (concerning it). 'Uzayr wept over the Torah, and an angel came to him with a vessel containing water and gave him to drink from that vessel, and the Torah was formed in his breast. He returned to the Children of Israel, and God had taught him the Torah and sent him as a prophet.

He said: "I am 'Uzayr," but they did not believe him.

He said: "Our fathers told us that 'Uzayr died in the land of Babylon."

He said: "I am 'Uzayr, whom God sent to you to renew your Torah for you."

They said: "Dictate it to us, if you are truthful." So he dictated it to them from memory [[See Tarikh Dimashq: 40/322, and al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/332.]].

A man among them said: "My father told me that my grandfather buried the Torah on the day we were taken captive, in a jar in a vineyard of my father's. If you show me my grandfather's vineyard, I will bring it out to you." They showed him, and he brought it out for them. They compared it with what 'Uzayr had dictated, and they did not differ in a single letter. No one had recited the Torah from memory since it was sent down except 'Uzayr, until this day.

They said: "God has put the Torah in the heart of no man after it was abrogated and gone, except that he is his son." Then they said: "'Uzayr is the son of God." We shall mention this story in detail in Surat al-Tawbah, God willing.

﴿So when it became clear to him, by direct observation, he said: I know that God is capable of all things.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Raja', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read قالَ اِعْلَمْ (qala i'lam) with a connected hamzah and a jussive, as a command, meaning: God said to him, "Know!" This is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah and al-A'mash: "Say: know." The rest read قالَ أَعْلَمُ (qala a'lamu), in the indicative, coordinated with the report about 'Uzayr that he said when he saw that: "I know that God is capable of all things."

From al-Mun'im ibn Idris, from his father, from Wahb, who said: There is no dog or donkey in Paradise except the dog of the People of the Cave and the donkey of Jeremiah, whom God caused to die for a hundred years.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 258–259 (part 1 of 2):

Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord? That is, he disputed and debated with him. The root of the word is *ḥujjah* (proof, argument). He was Nimrod son of Kan'an, son of Sakhariyb, son of Kush, son of Sam, son of Noah. He was the first to place a crown on his head, he became tyrannical on earth, and he claimed lordship. ﴿that Allah had given him the kingdom﴾, that is, because Allah had given him the kingdom, so he became arrogant. The position of *an* (that) is in the accusative, the preposition (*ḥarf al-ṣifah*, the particle governing the sense) having been dropped.

Al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Ayyami narrated from Mujahid, who said: Two believers and two disbelievers ruled the earth. The two believers were Sulayman son of Dawud and Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and the two disbelievers were Nimrod and Bukht Nasr.

The scholars differed about the time of this debate. Muqatil said: When Abraham broke the idols, Nimrod imprisoned him, then brought him out to burn him in the fire. Nimrod said to him: "Who is your Lord whom you call us to?"

He said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾

Others said: This happened after he was thrown into the fire.

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar ibn Zayd ibn Aslam that the first tyrant on earth was Nimrod ibn Kan'an, and people used to go out and obtain food from him.

He said: Abraham, peace be upon him, went out to obtain food. Whenever people passed by him, he would say: "Who is your lord?" They said: "You." Until Abraham passed by him, and he said: "Who is your lord?" He said: ﴿He who gives life and causes death,﴾ as Allah the Exalted mentioned.

He said: So he sent him away without food. Abraham, peace be upon him, returned to his family and passed by a red sand dune, and said: "Should I not take some of this and bring it to my family, so that their hearts are at ease when I enter upon them?" So he took some of it and brought it to his family, and set down his provisions and slept. His wife got up to his provisions and opened them, and behold, it was the finest food anyone had seen. So she prepared some of it for him and brought it near to him, and they had been without food.

He said: "Where is this from?"

She said: "From the food you brought." He knew that Allah had provided for him, so he praised Allah.

He said: Then Allah sent an angel to the tyrant, saying: "Believe in Me and I will leave you in your kingdom." Nimrod said: "Is there any lord other than me?!" The angel came to him a second time and said the same to him, but he refused. Then he came a third time and he refused and said: "I do not know the one you speak of. Does your lord have armies?"

He said: "Yes."

He said: "Let him fight me, if he is a king, for kings fight one another."

The angel said to him: "Yes, if you wish." He said: "I wish."

He said: "Gather your army for three days, until the armies of my Lord come to you."

He said: So the tyrant gathered his armies.

Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed to the keepers of the gnats: "Open a gate of gnats from them." They opened a gate of gnats. When the third day dawned, Nimrod looked at the sun and said: "What is wrong with it that it does not rise?" He thought that it had been delayed. The angel said: "The armies of my Lord have come between it and you."

He said: So the gnats surrounded them, ate their flesh and drank their blood, so that nothing remained of the people and animals but bones, while Nimrod remained as he was, untouched by anything.

The angel said to him: "Do you believe now?"

He said: "No."

So Allah the Mighty and Majestic commanded a gnat, which stung his lower lip and drank and grew large. Then it stung his upper lip, drank and grew large. Then it entered his nostril and reached his brain and ate from his brain until it became like a mouse. He remained for four hundred years being struck on the head with hammers. The most merciful people to him were those who would gather his hand and strike his head with it. So Allah punished him for four hundred years, just as he had ruled for four hundred years.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿When Abraham said: My Lord is He who gives life and causes death,﴾ this is the answer to an earlier question that is not mentioned; its implied meaning is: he said to him: "Who is your lord?" Abraham said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾

Al-A'mash, Hamzah and 'Isa recited *rabbi* (with the *yā'* sukūn), and the rest recited it with a fatḥah because of the *alif* and *lām* following.

﴿Nimrod said: I give life and cause death.﴾

The people of Madinah recited *anā* (I) with a long vowel throughout the Qur'an, and this is the dialect of a people who treat pausal forms as the basic forms.

Al-Kisa'i recited:
"I am the sword of the ten, so know me,
Ḥumayd, who has grown the hump (of his camel)..."

Another said:
"I am the servant of Allah, [my right hand] 'Umar,
the best of Quraysh of those who passed and those who remain,
except the Messenger of Allah and the noble elder."

The original form of *anā* is that the *nūn* should carry a fatḥah, but they sought to make it pausal, so they wrote an *alif* with the intention of stopping, and it became *anā*.

Most Arabs, in pause, say *anā-h* (anāh).

Most of the exegetes said: Nimrod summoned two men, killed one and spared the other, so he called sparing the one from being killed "giving life," as in His saying: ﴿And whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all mankind﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:32], meaning he did not kill it.

As for al-Suddi, regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿I give life and cause death,﴾ he said: He took four men and put them in a house, where they were given neither food nor drink, until they approached death. Then he fed two of them and gave them drink, and left two, and they died. Abraham then moved to another argument, not from inability, for he could have said: "Then bring to life the one you have caused to die, if you are truthful." Rather, to make the proof clear, he said: ﴿Abraham said: Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west.﴾ ﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded,﴾ that is, he was bewildered, stupefied, and his argument was cut off.

It is said: "a man *mabhūt*," that is, stupefied.

The poet said:
"Indeed, its (the lion's) roar came suddenly,
so I was struck dumb, until I could hardly walk."

Muhammad ibn al-Sumay' al-Yamani recited *fa-bahata* with a fatḥah on the *bā'* and the *hā'*, meaning Abraham confounded him. Its confirmation is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Rather it will come upon them suddenly, and it will stun them﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:40], that is, it will astonish them.

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ to the proof.

﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾ This is coordinated with the meaning of the first verse; its implied meaning is: "Have you seen one like the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, or have you seen one like the one who passed by a town?"

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: the *kāf* (like) is an extra (ṣilah) element; it is as if he said: "Have you not considered the one who..." or "the one..."

They differed about who this passer-by was. Qatadah, al-Rabi', 'Ikrimah, Najiyah ibn Ka'b, Sulayman ibn Buraydah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Salim al-Khawwas said: he was 'Uzayr ibn Sharhiya.

Wahb ibn Munabbih and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: he was Armiya ibn Khalfiya, who was of the tribe of Harun ibn 'Imran, and he was al-Khidr.

Mujahid said: he was a disbelieving man who doubted the resurrection.

They differed about the town over which he passed. Wahb, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: it was Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). al-Dahhak said: it was the holy land. Ibn Zayd said: it was the land in which Allah destroyed those who left their homes in their thousands, fearing death.

al-Kalbi said: it was the monastery of Sa'daba'ad. al-Suddi said: it was Salmabad. It was also said: the monastery of Harafil; and it was said: the town of the grapes, which is two farsakhs from Bayt al-Maqdis.

﴿And it was in ruins﴾ fallen down. It is said: *khawā al-bayt yakhwā khawan* (the house collapsed) when it falls, and *khawā al-bayt* with a fatḥah, *khawā'* (with long vowel), when it becomes empty.

﴿Upon its roofs﴾ its ceilings and its buildings. Its singular is *'arsh*, and its plural in the paucal is *a'rush*. Every building is an *'arsh*. It is said: *'arsha fulān*, when he builds, so he *ya'rishu* and *ya'rushu* *'arshan*. Allah said: ﴿and what they built (ya'rishūn)﴾ [al-A'raf 7:137], that is, what they built.

The meaning of the verse is: the ceilings fell, and then the walls fell upon them.

It was also said: *'alā* means *ma'a* (with), that is: "in ruins along with their roofs."

The poet said:
"As if the polished columns in its (the valley's) heights
and towers over which were the cloudy ones..."
that is, with them.

Its parallels are in surah al-Kahf and al-Hajj.

﴿He said: How will Allah give life to this after its death?﴾ The cause of this, as Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, was that Allah the Exalted said to Armiya, peace be upon him, when He sent him as a prophet to the Children of Israel: "O Armiya, before I created you I chose you; before I formed you in your mother's womb I sanctified you; before you reached the age of striving I appointed you a prophet; and for a great matter I loved you." So Allah sent Armiya to Nashi'ah ibn Amus, the king of the Children of Israel, to guide him and bring him news from Allah the Exalted. The Children of Israel's sins grew great; they committed transgressions and considered the forbidden lawful. So Allah the Exalted revealed to Armiya: "Remind your people of My blessings, make them aware of their misdeeds, and call them to Me."

Armiya said: "I am weak; if You do not strengthen me, I am incapable; if You do not help me..."

Allah the Exalted said: "I will inspire you." So Armiya stood among them and did not know what to say, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic inspired him at that moment with an eloquent, lengthy sermon in which he explained to them the reward of obedience and the punishment of disobedience.

At its end he said: "I am Allah, by My might, I will surely bring upon them a trial in which the forbearing will be bewildered, and I will set over them a cruel tyrant whom I will clothe in awe and from whose heart I will remove mercy, followed by a multitude like the darkness of a black night."

Allah the Exalted revealed to Armiya: "I will destroy the Children of Israel through Yafith and Yafith, the people of Babylon, who are descendants of Yafith son of Noah." When Armiya heard that, he cried out, wept, tore his garments and threw ashes on his head. When Allah heard Armiya's supplication and his weeping, He called to him: "O Armiya, is what I revealed to you hard on you?"

He said: "Yes, my Lord. Let me die before I see among the Children of Israel what does not please me."

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: "By My might, I will not destroy the Children of Israel until the matter in that regard comes from you." Armiya was delighted by this and his soul was content, and he said: "By He who sent Moses with the truth, I will not accept the destruction of the Children of Israel." Then he went to the king and informed him of this. He was a righteous king. He rejoiced and was glad and said: "If our Lord punishes us, it is for our many sins; and if He pardons us, it is by His mercy."

Then they remained for three years after the revelation, increasing only in disobedience and persistence in evil. This was when their destruction drew near. The revelation ceased, and the king called them to repentance, but they did not do so. So Allah gave power over them to Bukht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), who set out with six hundred thousand banners, intending the people of Bayt al-Maqdis. When he set out on his march, news reached the king, and he said to Armiya: "Where is what you claimed Allah revealed to you?"

Armiya said: ﴿Indeed Allah does not break the promise,﴾ and "I am certain of Him."

When the appointed time drew near and Allah determined to destroy them, Allah sent to Armiya an angel who had taken the form of a man from the Children of Israel.

He said: "O prophet of Allah, I seek your help regarding the people of my kin. I have kept ties with their relations and I have not done to them except for a while, and they increase in hostility toward me despite my honoring them. So give me a ruling about them."

He said to him: "Be good in what is between you and Allah, keep ties with them, and receive good news."

The angel departed, stayed a few days, then came to him in the form of that man, and sat before him. Armiya said to him: "Have their characters not yet been revealed to you?"

He said: "O prophet of Allah, by He who sent you with the truth, I know of no kindness that anyone shows to his kin that I have not offered them first and more."

The prophet said: "Return to your family, be good to them, and ask Allah, who sets right the righteous servants, to set them right." The angel rose, stayed a few days, and by then Bukht Nasr and his armies had encamped around Bayt al-Maqdis, more numerous than locusts. The Children of Israel were terrified and it weighed heavily on them.

The angel said to Armiya: "O prophet of Allah, where is what Allah promised you?"

He said: "I am certain of my Lord."

Then the angel came to Armiya, who was sitting on the wall of Bayt al-Maqdis. He laughed and rejoiced at the victory of his Lord that He had promised, sat before him and said: "I am the one who informed you about my family twice."

The prophet said: "Has the time not come for them to awaken from what they are in?"

The angel said: "O prophet of Allah, whatever I used to suffer from them before today I would endure, but today I have seen them in an action that does not please Allah the Mighty and Majestic."

The prophet said: "What action did you see them doing?"

He said: "A great action of Allah's wrath. So I became angry for Allah and for you, and I came to inform you, and I ask you by Allah who sent you with the truth to supplicate against them that He destroy them."

Armiya said: "O Master of the heavens and the earth, if they are upon truth and righteousness, then spare them; and if they are upon Your wrath and an action You do not approve, then destroy them."

When the word came out of Armiya's mouth, Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent a thunderbolt from the sky upon Bayt al-Maqdis; the place of the offering caught fire, and seven of its gates sank into the earth.

When Armiya saw that, he cried out, tore his garments, threw ashes on his head, and said: "O Master of the heavens and the earth, where is Your promise that You made to me?" It was called out to him: "They were struck by what struck them only because of your ruling and your supplication." The prophet was certain that it was his ruling that he had given, and that he was the messenger of his Lord.

Armiya flew off until he mixed with the wild beasts. Bukht Nasr and his armies entered Bayt al-Maqdis, trampled al-Sham, slaughtered the Children of Israel until he annihilated them, and destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis. Then he ordered his armies that each man fill his shield with earth and hurl it into Bayt al-Maqdis, so they hurled earth into it until they filled it. Then he ordered them to gather everyone who was in the regions of Bayt al-Maqdis, so every young and old person from the Children of Israel was gathered before him. He chose one hundred thousand boys from them and divided them among the kings who were with him, so that each man received four youths. Bukht Nasr divided the remaining Children of Israel into three groups: one third he left in al-Sham, one third he took captive, and one third he killed. This was the first calamity that Allah sent upon the Children of Israel because of their wrongdoing.

When Bukht Nasr turned back from them, returning to Babylon with the captives of the Children of Israel, Armiya came on his donkey, with a jar of grape juice and a basket of figs, until he reached Iliya. When he stopped there and saw its ruin, he said: ﴿How will Allah give life to this after its death?!﴾ Those who said that this passer-by was 'Uzayr said: When Bukht Nasr destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis and brought the captives of the Children of Israel to the land of Babylon, among them were 'Uzayr, who was one of the scholars of the Children of Israel, Daniel, and seven thousand people from the family of Dawud.

When 'Uzayr escaped from Babylon, he set out on a donkey until he came down at the monastery of Harqal (Heraclius) on the bank of the Tigris. He went around the town but saw no one in it, and he learned of its condition. He ate some fruit and pressed some grapes, drank from them, put the surplus fruit in a basket and the surplus juice in a skin. When he saw the ruin of the town and the destruction of its people, he said: ﴿How will Allah give life to this after its death?﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:259]. He did not doubt the resurrection, but said it in wonder.

Returning to the account of Wahb: He said: Armiya tied his donkey with a new rope, and Allah cast sleep upon him. When he slept, Allah took his soul for a hundred years and caused his donkey to die. His juice and his figs were with him, and Allah blinded the eyes from him so that no one saw him, and that was in the forenoon. Allah prevented the predators and the birds from his flesh. When seventy years had passed since his death, Allah the Mighty and Majestic sent an angel to a great king of the Children of Israel called [Yuswak], saying: "Allah the Mighty and Majestic commands you to mobilize your people to rebuild Bayt al-Maqdis and Iliya and its land, until it returns to being more flourishing than it ever was." The king appointed one thousand commanders, with three hundred thousand workers under each commander, and they began rebuilding it. Allah the Exalted destroyed Bukht Nasr with a gnat that entered his brain [...] [unreadable in the manuscript]. Allah the Exalted gathered those of the Children of Israel who remained and had not died in Babylon, and returned them all to Bayt al-Maqdis and its environs. They rebuilt it for thirty years and multiplied until they became as they had been at their finest. When the hundred years had passed, Allah the Exalted restored his eyes and the rest of his body, which was dead. Then He restored his body while he watched. Then he looked at his donkey, and behold, its bones were scattered, white and shining. He heard a voice from the sky: "O white bones, Allah commands you to come together." Some of them came together and joined to one another.

Then it was called out: "Allah commands you to clothe yourselves with flesh and skin." So it was. Then it was called out: "Allah commands you to live." It stood, by the permission of Allah, and the donkey brayed.

Allah gave Armiya long life, and he is the one who is seen in the wilderness.
