This is the meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him,﴾ that is, He gave him life. [Lengthy version in Tafsir al-Tabari: 3/47–50 and his History: 1/392 with variations.]

﴿He said: How long have you remained?﴾ a question about the amount of the number. Ibn Muhays, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *labiththa* and *labithtum* with assimilation (idgham) throughout the Qur'an. The rest recited with clear pronunciation (izhar).

As for the one who assimilates, the sound does not border it in articulation, and in the similarity in whispering (hams); and as for the one who makes it clear, [because of its clarity] [clarity is due to the difference in articulation between the *thā'* and the *tā'*; see Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/292] in the Mushaf. Both are unusual but eloquent. Its meaning is: how long did you stay and remain here? It is said: *labitha yalbathu labthan* and *labāthan* (to remain).

[See Majma' al-Bahrayn: 4/103.]

He said, "I have remained a day." That is because God caused him to die at the forenoon and revived him a hundred years later, at the end of the day, before the sun set. So he said, "I have remained a day," as he thought the sun had set. Then he turned and saw some remnant of the sun, so he said, "Or part of a day," meaning "Rather, part of a day," because his words "part of a day" are a retraction of his words "I have remained a day," like the verse ﴿or they would increase [them]﴾ [[Surah al-Saffat: 147.]].

He said, "Nay, you have remained a hundred years. But look at your food and your drink ﴿which has not spoiled﴾." The food means the figs, and the drink means the juice. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ (lam yatasannah) with the ha' omitted in continuous recitation (wasl), and likewise in His words ﴿fa-bi-hudahumu iqtadih﴾ [[Surah al-An'am: 90.]]. The rest read it with the ha' both in continuous recitation and in pause (waqf). Abu Hatim reported from Talhah that it is read لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ with the ta' assimilated into the sin, and he claimed that it is so in the codex of Ubayy. Its meaning is: the years have not changed it.

Whoever drops the ha' in continuous recitation regards the ha' as a superfluous (silah) addition and says: its original form is lam yatasannay; the ya' is elided by the jussive and a ha' is substituted for it in pause. This is according to the view of those who consider the ha' in sanah (year) to be superfluous.

He said: its root is yasnawhu, its plural is sanawat, and the verb from it is sanaytu, musanah, and tasannaytu, tasannyan, except that the waw is returned to the remaining form, tafa''ul and tafa'ul, as in their saying al-tada'i and al-tadani, because ya' is lighter than waw.

Abu 'Amr said: it is from al-tasannun with two nuns, meaning change, as in His words ﴿of black mud, moulded﴾ [[Surah al-Hijr: 26.]], i.e., changed. Then one of the two nuns was compensated for, as in the poet's words:

"Why, when you heard, did you not search for it, / and the judgment was not touched by conjecture (al-tazanni)?"

He meant bi-l-ta'ayyun (by certainty).

Al-'Ajjaj said:

"He escaped like the falcon when the falcon swoops,"

meaning tafaddad (was silvered/pierced).

The Arabs say: nata'la, when they go out to gather a soft plant called al-maq'a.

God Almighty said: ﴿And he has failed who covered it up﴾ [[Surah al-Shams: 10.]], meaning dassasaha (buried it).

Whoever affirms the ha' in both states regards it as an original ha' of the verb's final radical. On this basis is the view of those who make sanah into sanhiyyah, its diminutive sunayhiyyah, and the verb from it al-musanahah.

The poet said:

"It is not a sanha' nor a rajabiyyah, / but 'arayaa in the years of calamities."

[[Lisan al-'Arab: 1/412. al-'ariyyah: a palm tree its owner gives as a gift; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/293.]]

If it is asked: he speaks of two things, then says لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ and not "did not change" in the dual, the answer is: the change refers to the nearer of the two expressions, which is the years, and he suffices with mention of one of the two mentioned items over the other because it is in the place of what is perishable, as in the poet's words:

[An eagle we pursued, whose hunting-trace was... and a khartu'ah except upon the spear of Falaj.] [[Thus in the manuscript.]]

He did not say "two spears of Falaj." The evidence for this interpretation is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "Look at your food, and this your drink, it has not changed."

﴿And look at your donkey﴾ and ﴿that We may make you a sign for the people﴾. Most scholars said: in the verse there is inversion and reordering, i.e., "And look at your food and your drink, it has not changed, and that We may make you a sign for the people, and look at your donkey." It is possible that the meaning is: "So look at your food and your drink, it has not changed, and look at your donkey."

﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh.﴾

As for the explanation of the verse and its readings: Kharijah, al-A'raj, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ḥimārika and al-ḥimār with imalah (inclination); the rest with tafkhim (emphatic pronunciation). As for His words ﴿how We raise them﴾:

Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read nunshizuha with a zay, with the nun vowelled by a damma and the shin by a kasra.

Abu al-'Aliyah reported from Zayd ibn Thabit that he said: it is only a ra' which he read as a zay, i.e., he put a dot on it. Likewise Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah reported from Ibn 'Abbas with a zay, and Abu 'Ubaydah chose it.

The raising (inshaz) of a thing means lifting it, moving it and disturbing it. He said: "I made it rise, so it rose," i.e., I lifted it and it was lifted. From it comes the rising (nushuz) of a wife against her husband, and the rising (nushuz) of a boy, i.e., he rose up. So the meaning of the verse: how We lift them from the earth, then return them to their places in the body and assemble some of them upon others.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: "We bring them out." Al-Kisa'i said: "We cause them to grow and magnify them."

Qatadah, 'Ata', Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Ayyub read nunshiruha with a ra', damma on the nun and kasra on the shin, and Abu Hatim chose it. Its meaning: We give it life.

He said: "Allah revived the dead with inshar, and he (the dead) rises by nushur." God Almighty said: ﴿Then when He wills, He will resurrect him﴾ [[Surah 'Abasa: ...]]... He said: ﴿They rise up﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 21.]], and He said: ﴿Nay, they did not expect a resurrection﴾ [[Surah al-Furqan: 40.]], and He said: ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾ [[Surah Fatir: 9.]], and ﴿and to Him is the resurrection﴾ [[Surah al-Mulk: 15.]]. Harithah ibn Badr al-Ghudani said:

"So He revived its dead and distributed justice among them, / and its minds returned to it after they had been scattered."

Al-A'sha said, using it intransitively:

"Until people say, from what they saw: / 'How strange, the dead one raised up!'"

[[Lisan al-'Arab: 5/206.]]

Al-Hasan and al-Mufaddal read nunshiruha with a ra', the nun with a fatha and the shin with a damma.

Al-Farra' said: he went to the meaning of spreading and folding.

Some of them said: it is also from giving life, it is said: "Allah revived (anshara) the dead and raised him (nasharahu)" when He gave him life. Abu Hatim said: this is not well known.

Al-Nakha'i read it with a zay, the nun with a fatha and the shin with a damma.

Abu Hatim said: that is an error. Others said: it is said nashazahu [wa-nashatahu] and anshazahu with the same meaning.

﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾, i.e., We clothe them and conceal them with it, as we conceal the body with a garment. They differed about the meaning of the verse. Some said: it refers to the bones of his donkey, because God caused his donkey to die, then revived it as a complete creature while he was watching. Al-Suddi said: God revived 'Uzayr, then said, "Look at your donkey, it has perished and its bones have decayed." So God sent a wind which brought the bones of the donkey from every plain and mountain; the birds and beasts had carried them away, and they gathered and were joined one to another while he watched, until it became a donkey of bones with no flesh or blood. Then He clothed the bones with flesh and blood, and it became a donkey without a spirit. Then an angel came walking until he took hold of the donkey's nostril and blew into it, and the donkey stood up and brayed by God's leave.

The meaning of the verse on this view: "Look at the flesh of your donkey and at its bones, how We raise them," and when the ha' was dropped from the bones, the alif was substituted... And on this view most exegetes agree.

Others said: it refers to the bones of this man himself, for God did not cause his donkey to die; rather God revived his eyes and his head, while the rest of his body was dead. Then He said to him, "Look at your donkey," and he looked and saw his donkey standing upright, in the state it was in on the day he tied it, alive, not having eaten or drunk for a hundred years, and he looked at the halter on its neck, new and unchanged.

The estimate of the verse on this view: "Look at your donkey, and look at your bones, how We raise them." This is the view of al-Dahhak, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾: We did this so that We might make you [a sign]. If you wish, you may take the waw as emphatic and superfluous, as in the poet al-Aswad ibn Ja'far's words:

"Then when that, there is no forgetting it, / and time brings good after corruption."

i.e., "then when that."

The meaning of the verse: We did this to you so that We might make you a sign for the people, i.e., an example and evidence of resurrection after death, as most exegetes said.

Al-Dahhak and others said: this verse [means] that he returned to his village a young man, while his children and grandchildren were old men and old women, and he had black hair and beard.

Qatadah reported from Ka'b, and from al-Hasan, Muqatil and Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Abd Allah ibn Isma'il al-Suddi from his father from Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, they said: When God revived 'Uzayr after he had made him die for a hundred years, he rode his donkey until he came to his quarter, and the people did not recognize him, and he did not recognize the people or his dwelling. He went on, in some confusion, until he came to his house, and there was a blind, paralysed old woman who was a hundred and twenty years old; she had been a slave-girl of theirs. She had left them, and 'Uzayr had left her when she was twenty years old; she had known him and cared for him. When old age and infirmity afflicted her, 'Uzayr said to her: "O woman, is this the house of 'Uzayr?"

She said: "Yes, this is the house of 'Uzayr," and she wept and said: "I have not seen anyone from such-and-such years mention 'Uzayr, and the people have forgotten him." He said: "I am 'Uzayr."

She said: "Glory be to God! 'Uzayr has been missing from us for a hundred years and we have not heard any mention of him."

He said: "I am 'Uzayr. God Almighty caused me to die for a hundred years, then raised me."

She said: "'Uzayr was one whose supplication was answered; he would pray for the sick and the afflicted for health and cure. So pray to God that He return my sight to me, so that I may see you; if you are 'Uzayr, I shall recognize you." He prayed to his Lord and wiped his hand over her eyes, and they opened; he took her hand and said: "Rise, by God's leave." Then God Almighty loosed her legs, and she stood up sound, by God's leave, as if she had been released from a fetter. She looked and said: "I bear witness that you are 'Uzayr." She went to the quarter of the Children of Israel, who were in their clubs and assemblies, and the son of 'Uzayr, a shaikh of a hundred and eighteen years, and his sons' sons were old men in the assembly. She called out: "This is 'Uzayr, he has come to you." They denied her.

She said: "I am so-and-so, your freedwoman. He prayed to his Lord, Almighty and Majestic, and He returned my sight to me and loosed my legs, and he claims that God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him."

He said: the people rose and came to him. His son said: "My father had a dark mole like the crescent between his shoulders." He uncovered his shoulders, and there he was: 'Uzayr.

Qatadah, Muqatil, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: 'Uzayr returned to his village after Bukhtnassar had burned the Torah, and God had not made a covenant with creation (concerning it). 'Uzayr wept over the Torah, and an angel came to him with a vessel containing water and gave him to drink from that vessel, and the Torah was formed in his breast. He returned to the Children of Israel, and God had taught him the Torah and sent him as a prophet.

He said: "I am 'Uzayr," but they did not believe him.

He said: "Our fathers told us that 'Uzayr died in the land of Babylon."

He said: "I am 'Uzayr, whom God sent to you to renew your Torah for you."

They said: "Dictate it to us, if you are truthful." So he dictated it to them from memory [[See Tarikh Dimashq: 40/322, and al-Durr al-Manthur: 1/332.]].

A man among them said: "My father told me that my grandfather buried the Torah on the day we were taken captive, in a jar in a vineyard of my father's. If you show me my grandfather's vineyard, I will bring it out to you." They showed him, and he brought it out for them. They compared it with what 'Uzayr had dictated, and they did not differ in a single letter. No one had recited the Torah from memory since it was sent down except 'Uzayr, until this day.

They said: "God has put the Torah in the heart of no man after it was abrogated and gone, except that he is his son." Then they said: "'Uzayr is the son of God." We shall mention this story in detail in Surat al-Tawbah, God willing.

﴿So when it became clear to him, by direct observation, he said: I know that God is capable of all things.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Raja', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read قالَ اِعْلَمْ (qala i'lam) with a connected hamzah and a jussive, as a command, meaning: God said to him, "Know!" This is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah and al-A'mash: "Say: know." The rest read قالَ أَعْلَمُ (qala a'lamu), in the indicative, coordinated with the report about 'Uzayr that he said when he saw that: "I know that God is capable of all things."

From al-Mun'im ibn Idris, from his father, from Wahb, who said: There is no dog or donkey in Paradise except the dog of the People of the Cave and the donkey of Jeremiah, whom God caused to die for a hundred years.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 260:

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." ...﴾ If it is asked: what was the reason for Abraham's request to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, that He show him how He gives life to the dead, and what is the purpose of that? And was Abraham doubtful about the giving of life to the dead, such that he said: ﴿but [it is] so that my heart may be at ease﴾?

The answer to this has several aspects. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jurayj said:

The reason for that question was that Abraham passed by a dead animal. Ibn Jurayj said: it was the carcass of a donkey on the seashore. 'Ata' said: the Lake of Tiberias. They said: he saw it, and it had been shared out by [the beasts of] the land and the sea. Whenever the sea rose, the fish and the sea creatures came and ate from it, so what fell from it went into the water; and whenever the sea receded, the predatory beasts came and ate from it, so what fell from it turned to dust; and when the beasts had gone, the birds came and ate from it, so what fell was carried away by the wind into the air. When Abraham, peace be upon him, saw this, he was amazed and said: "O Lord, You know that You will gather these together from the bellies of these beasts, the crops of these birds and the bodies of the land creatures. So show me how You give them life, that I may witness it and increase in certainty." Then his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, rebuked him, saying: ﴿Do you not believe?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, O Lord, I know and I believe, but a report is not like seeing﴾. That is His saying: ﴿but [it is] so that my heart may be at ease﴾, that is, that my heart may be settled through witnessing and observation.

According to this view, Abraham, peace be upon him, wished that knowledge of certainty should become the eye of certainty, just as a person knows a thing and is certain of it, but loves to see it, without any doubt in it on his part, just as the believers love to see the Prophet ﷺ, and to see Paradise, and to see God, Exalted, while believing in that and with no doubt remaining about it.

Ibn Zayd said: Abraham passed by a dead fish, half of it on the land and half in the sea. What was in the sea was eaten by the sea creatures, and what was on the land was eaten by the land creatures. The wicked Iblis said to him: "When will God gather this from the bellies of these?"

So he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ He said: ﴿Do you not believe?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, but [it is] so that my heart may be at ease﴾, by the removal of Iblis's whisper from him, and so that Satan may become defeated and humiliated.

Some of them said: When Abraham, peace be upon him, argued against Nimrod and said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death.﴾ Nimrod said: ﴿I give life and cause death.﴾ So he killed the man and released the other. Abraham said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, gives life by directing Himself to a dead body and giving it life and placing the spirit in it."

Nimrod said to him: "You have witnessed this?" He could not say, "Yes, I saw it," so he moved on to another argument, saying: "God, Mighty and Majestic, brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." Then he asked his Lord, saying: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ He said: ﴿Do you not believe?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, but [it is] so that my heart may be at ease﴾, so that when someone says to me, "Have you witnessed it?" I can say, "Yes, I have witnessed it," and I need not turn to any other argument, and so that Nimrod may know that giving life is as You do it, not as he does. This is the meaning of the statement of Muhammad ibn Ishaq from Ibn Yasarah.

It is related in a report that Nimrod said to Abraham, peace be upon him: "You claim that your Lord gives life to the dead and you call me to worship Him. Ask your Lord to give life to the dead, if He is able; otherwise I will kill you."

Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ He said: ﴿Do you not believe?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, but [it is] so that my heart may be at ease﴾, by the strength of my argument and my deliverance from being killed, for the enemy of God threatened me with death unless I bring a dead man to life for him.

Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said: When God took Abraham as a friend (khalil), the Angel of Death asked permission to give Abraham the good news of this. He was permitted, so he came to Abraham, who was not in the house. He entered his house, and Abraham, peace be upon him, was the most jealous of people: when he went out he would lock his door. When [the Angel of Death] entered, he found a man in his house, so he sprang at him to seize him, and said: "Who permitted you to enter my house?"

The Angel of Death said: "The Lord of this house permitted me." Abraham said: "You have spoken the truth," and he recognised that he was the Angel of Death.

He said: "Who are you?" He said: "The Angel of Death. I have come to give you the good news that God, Mighty and Majestic, has taken you as a friend." So he praised God, Exalted, and said to him: "What is the sign of that?"

He said: "That God answers your supplication and gives life to the dead at your request." Then the Angel of Death departed.

Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ He said: ﴿Do you not believe?﴾

He said: ﴿Yes, but [it is] so that my heart may be at ease﴾, by my knowledge that You answer me when I call upon You and give me when I ask You.

And You have taken me as a friend.

Muhammad ibn Muslim from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Abu 'Ubaydah from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said:

"May God have mercy on Abraham. We are more entitled to doubt than he was, when he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾ He said: ﴿Do you not believe?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes, but [it is] so that my heart may be at ease﴾." Then he recited to the end of the verse.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah said: I heard Abu Ibrahim al-Muzani say: The meaning of his saying ﷺ, "We are more entitled to doubt than Abraham," is only that Abraham doubted whether God, Mighty and Majestic, would respond to what he asked or not.

'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Nasrabadhi being asked about this verse, and he said: The Friend yearned for the work of his Friend and did not accuse Him. That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Do you not believe?﴾ That is, "You are a believer," bearing witness to his faith, like the saying of Jarir:

"Are you not the best of those who have mounted mounts, and the most generous of the peoples in the bellies of the pots?"

That is, "You are indeed that."

﴿He said: "Yes, but [it is] so that my heart may be at ease"﴾, that is, that my heart may be settled by an increase in certainty and proof, and the reality of friendship and the answering of supplication.

God, Exalted, said to Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿So take four birds﴾, of differing species and natures, so that the demonstration of power would be more complete. He singled out birds from among all animals for the distinctive quality of flight. They differed about which birds they were.

Ibn 'Abbas said: he took a peacock, a vulture, a crow and a rooster.

Mujahid, 'Ata' ibn Yasar, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd said: they were a crow, a rooster, a peacock and a dove.

Sa'id ibn Ayyub from Sa'id ibn al-Harith al-Ghurab from Abu Hurayrah al-Sinani: they were the peacock, the rooster, the crow and the dove.

'Ata' al-Khurasani said: God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to His Prophet that he should bring four birds: a green duck, a black crow, a white dove and a red rooster.

﴿Then make them incline toward you﴾: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honour his face, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan al-Basri, 'Ikrimah, al-A'raj, Shaybah, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Ayyub read it with a damma on the sād, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose it: "ḍummahunna ilayka" (gather them and incline them toward you).

It is said: "ṣarttu al-shay' aṣūruhu" when I inclined it.

Imru' al-Qays said:

"And a slender, inclining one, who nearly makes her lean, and a rump like a sandhill weighed down by its bulges."

And al-Tirimmah said:

"Chaste of hems, or love that inclines them, and love is a bewilderment for lovers."

That is, love inclines them.

It is said: "a man ṣa'war" when his neck is inclined.

It is said: "innī ilaykum la-aṣwar," that is, I am longing and inclined.

A woman is "ṣawrā'", and the plural is "ṣuwar," like "'awdā'" and "'ud."

A poet said:

"God knows that we, in our glancing back on the day of parting toward our neighbours, are inclined."

'Ata', 'Atiyyah, Ibn Zayd and al-Mu'arrikh said: its meaning is: gather them and join them together. It is said: "ṣāra yaṣūru ṣawran" when he gathered. From this comes the saying: [I am inclined toward you].

A poet said:

"There came a plentiful milk-camel herd, pure, its young ones gathered by a black, dark-coloured one."

That is, with the gathering of a milk-camel herd, and the milk-camel is the best of wealth; "dahs" is the colour of sand-dunes; "ṣafāyā" means abundant, admired [milk-camels].

Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is: cut them up and make small pieces.

Ibn al-Himyar said it:

"When I pulled the rope, its strands creaked against the ends of the pieces of wood, strong, its loops."

"Then the cords brought me near until I reached them, with a leap, and my climbing nearly cut them into pieces."

Ru'bah said:

"We made the judgement of it, and the judge became weary," that is, we cut the judgement of it.

ʿAlqamah, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Talhah, Qatadah, Abu Ja'far, Yahya ibn Ri'ab, al-A'mash, Hamzah and Khalaf read: ﴿fa-ṣirhunna﴾ with a kasra on the sād, and its meaning is: cut them up and separate them. It is said: "ṣāra yaṣīru ṣayran" when he cut, and "infaṣara al-shay'" when a thing was cut off.

Al-Khansa' said:

"Had the one who was struck by Mudar met [the calamity], the mountains would have been split apart from it, and they were cut."

That is, cut up, split, and levelled.

Abu Suhayl Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ath al-Talaqani recited in the book of 'Aza'im:

"A youth whom I saw became a dog ... [...] for two hours, became a gazelle."

Al-Farra' said: it is inverted from "ṣirtu aṣrī ṣayran," when I cut, the initial letter being moved forward, as it is said "'awatha" and "'atha", meaning he cut them. Then it was inverted and it became "ṣāra." A poet said:

"They say that Syria kills its people; so for me, since I did not come to it with eternity, [my fathers] went abroad. Would that they had averted from them death if they did not go, and my grandfathers."

Some of them said: its meaning is "amilhunna" (incline them), and this is the dialect of Hudhayl and Sulaym. Al-Kisa'i recited:

"And a branch that inclines the neck, and thick growth like it upon the cheek, like the heavy clusters of grapes."

That is, the neck is inclined by its abundance.

From Ibn 'Abbas there are two reports: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ with the sād open, the rā' shadda and kasra, from al-tasriyah, which is gathering, and from it al-muṣarrāh (the milk-stored animal).

The second: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ with a damma on the sād and a fatha on the rā' and shadda, from al-ṣurrah, which has the meaning of gathering and binding as well. Whoever interprets it as cutting and separating, there is inversion and displacement in the sentence, its sense being: "take four birds to you, then cut them." Whoever explains it with damma has an implied element, meaning: "incline them to you, then cut them," and he omitted it, being content with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿then place upon every mountain a portion of them﴾, because it indicates it. This is like saying: "Take this garment and place upon every spear you have a piece of it," meaning cut it and place on every spear a piece.

﴿Then place upon every mountain of them﴾: its wording is general and its meaning specific, because four birds do not reach all the mountains, nor could Abraham, peace be upon him, reach that. This is like the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and she was given of everything﴾ and like His saying: ﴿destroying everything﴾.

﴿a portion﴾: 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal, read juz'an (with a heavy hamza) wherever it occurs. Abu Ja'far read juzzan with a shadda on the zay. The rest read it with a hamza and light pronunciation. These are dialects with the meaning: share and part.

The exegetes said: God, Exalted, commanded Abraham, peace be upon him, to slaughter those birds with their feathers, cut them up, separate their parts, and mix their feathers, blood and flesh together with one another. Abraham did so, and then He commanded him to place their parts upon the mountains.

They differed about the number of parts and mountains. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Abi Ishaq said: he was commanded to make each bird four parts, then to go to four mountains and place upon each mountain a quarter of each bird, then call them: "Come, by God's permission." This is a parable God, Mighty and Majestic, struck for Abraham and showed him, meaning: as these birds were raised from these four mountains, so will I raise people on the Day of Resurrection from the quarters and regions of the earth.

Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi said: he divided them into seven parts and placed them upon seven mountains. He did so and held their heads with himself, then called them: "Come, by God's command, glorified is He." So every drop of a bird's blood flew to another drop, every feather flew to another feather, every bone went to another, every piece went to another, and Abraham was looking until every body met the others in the sky without a head. Then they came to me, and whenever a bird came it inclined its head; if its head was near it drew close, and if it was not its head it held back, until every bird met its head.

That is His saying: ﴿Then call them, and they will come to you running.﴾ It is a verbal noun, meaning they will come running; it is said that it is in the accusative by removal of the particle of description, meaning "with running." They differed about the meaning of "sa'y" (running). Some said it means hastening and running; others said walking on their feet, like His saying in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿And there came a man from the farthest part of the city, running﴾, and its parallel in Surat al-Jumu'ah: ﴿then hasten to the remembrance of God﴾, that is, proceed.

The wisdom in walking rather than flying is that it is more conclusive as proof and further from suspicion, for had they flown, someone might have imagined that they were other birds, or that their legs were not sound. And God knows best.

Others said it means flying. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: I asked al-Khalil ibn Ahmad about His saying ﴿they will come to you running﴾: is it said of a bird that when it flies it "runs"? He said: No. I said: Then what is the meaning of ﴿they will come to you running﴾? He said: its meaning is: they will come to you while you are running, running.

Al-Tha'labi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib say: I heard my father say: I heard Abu al-Hasan al-Aqta', who was a sage, say: it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Every verse has an outer and an inner meaning, and every letter has a limit and a point of ascent."

The apparent meaning of the verse is what the people of exegesis have mentioned. Its inner meaning: Abraham, peace be upon him, was commanded to slaughter four things within himself with a knife of resignation, just as in the outer sense the four birds were slaughtered with an iron knife. The vulture is a symbol of long life and term; the peacock is the adornment and splendour of the world; the crow is greed; and the rooster is desire.

God, Exalted, said: ﴿And know that God is Mighty and Wise.﴾

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 261–264:

مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أَمْوالَهُمْ الآية فيها إضمار واختصار تقديرها: مثل صدقات الذين ينفقون أموالهم، فإن شئت قلت: مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أَمْوالَهُمْ.

Translation: "The parable of those who spend their wealth" — the verse contains an ellipsis and abbreviation; its implied sense is: "the parable of the charity of those who spend their wealth." If you wish, you may say: "The parable of those who spend their wealth."

﴿In the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains.﴾

Abu 'Amr, Abu [Ghaziyya], Hamza and al-Kisa'i assimilated (idgham) the *ta'* and *sin* in *anbatat sab'a sanabil* (أَنْبَتَتْ سَبْعَ سَنابِلَ), which is the plural of *sunbula* (ear of grain). The rest pronounced them distinctly (izhar). As for the one who assimilates, it is because the *ta'* and the *sin* are both *hamzated* — do you not see that they are interchangeable?

Abu 'Amr recited:

"May Allah curse the sons of the *si'lat* ... 'Amr ibn Maymun, the vilest of men."
[[al-si'lat: the most wicked of the ghouls (ghul), and a repulsive woman is likened to it. The verse is in Lisan al-'Arab 2/101, where, as in the rest of the lexicons, it reads: 'Amr ibn Yarbu'.]]

He meant *li'am al-nas* (لئام الناس, "the vile people") and changed the *sin* into *ta'*. As for the one who pronounces them distinctly, it is because they are two separate words, which is the original form and the widespread usage.

﴿In every ear a hundred grains.﴾ Abu Ja'far and al-A'mash read it as "five hundred and a hundred" (خمس مائة ومائة), where it is used for lightness (istikhfaf).
[[Thus in the manuscript.]]

The rest read it with the *mad* (مِائَةُ).

If you ask: "Have you seen an ear containing a hundred grains, or has that reached you?" It is said: "We do not deny it, nor is it impossible. If it exists, then it is so; otherwise, it is possible that its meaning is: 'like a grain that grew seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains,' as God, glory be to Him, made that within it. It may also mean that when it is sown, it produces a hundred grains, so what arises from the seed that came from it of the hundred grains is equivalent to it, because it came from it." Likewise is what al-Dahhak said: "Every ear produced a hundred grains."

﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ between seven hundred and seven hundred-fold, up to what Allah, mighty and majestic, wills, which none knows but Allah.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ — (He is) rich enough for those multiples, and All-Knowing of whoever spends.

Al-Dahhak said regarding this verse: Whoever brings forth a dirham seeking the good pleasure of Allah, he will have in this world, for every dirham, seven hundred dirhams as a swift replacement, and will meet a thousand dirhams on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Kalbi said regarding His words ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾: it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (رضي الله عنه) and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. As for 'Abd al-Rahman, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with four thousand dirhams as charity and said: "I had eight thousand; I kept four thousand for myself and my dependents, and four thousand I lent to my Lord, mighty and majestic."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "May Allah bless you in what you kept and in what you gave." As for 'Uthman, he said: "Upon me is the equipping of one who has no equipment for the expedition of Tabuk," so he equipped the Muslims with a thousand camels with their saddle-cloths and pack-saddles, and gave in charity the well of Rumah, a well in the outskirts of Madinah which had been his, to the Muslims. So this verse was revealed concerning both of them.
[[Well of Rumah in the 'Aqiq of Madinah; see Mu'jam al-Buldan 1/300.]]

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura said: 'Uthman (رضي الله عنه) came with a thousand dinars in the army of hardship (jaysh al-'usra) and poured them into the lap of the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) put his hand into them and kiss them, saying: 'What harm does Ibn 'Affan do after today by what he does.'"

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) raising his hands, supplicating for 'Uthman (رضي الله عنه): 'O Lord, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan — be pleased with him, so be You pleased with him.' He continued to supplicate with his hands raised until dawn broke, and then Allah, exalted, revealed concerning him: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾, i.e., in the obedience of Allah."

﴿Then they do not follow what they have spent with reminders (mann) and injury (adhan)﴾ — mann is that one bestows his gift upon another and counts his favors upon him, thereby spoiling them; he continues the reminder (al-mannah) to the favor.

It is said: "One performs a *manna*, *mannan* and *maniyyah* when he bestows and gives." Allah, exalted, said: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold﴾ [Sad 38:39], i.e., give; then this became so common that the mention of the favor and reckoning it became a reminder (mannah).
[[Surah Sad: 39.]]

﴿And there is no injury to them; their reward is with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ — through making the gift apparent and mentioning it to one who does not deserve to be informed of it, and similar speech that causes harm.

Sufyan and al-Mufaddal said regarding His words ﴿reminders and injury﴾: it is that one says, "I gave you, yet you did not thank me."

Al-Dahhak said: "That a man does not spend his wealth is better than that he spends it and then follows it with reminder and injury."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "My father used to say: 'When you give a man something and you think your greeting weighs heavily upon him, withhold your greeting from him.'"

Ibn Zayd said: "Is there anything better than greeting?"

He said: A woman said to my father: "O Abu Usama, direct me to a man who will truly go out in the way of Allah, for they only go out to eat fruits. I have a quiver and arrows in it." He said: "May Allah not bless you in your quiver or in your arrows, for you have harmed them before you gave them."

So Allah forbade His servants from reminding of a favor, and reserved it as an attribute of Himself, because the reminder of servants is reproach and spoiling, while the reminder of Allah, mighty and majestic, is bounty, favor and admonition. Mu'adh ibn al-Muthanna al-'Anbari recited, from his father Mahmud ibn al-Warraq:

"Most beautiful of every beauty, at every time and season,
a favor nurtured, free of reminders."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/311.]]

Al-Tha'alabi said: Abu 'Ali Zahir ibn Ahmad al-Sarakhsi said: Abu Dhar al-Qurtubi recited to us:

"Your kindness has not been perfected in the sight of my ruler, when it burdened him with honor.
Indeed, of righteousness, do not deny it: the honoring of one who displays your honoring.
Reminding the benefactor is a deficiency, so do not spoil your favor with reminders.
Honor in generosity, and the miserliness of a youth is a humiliation I loved to make known to you."

He said: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim recited to me, who said: Muhammad ibn Tahir recited to me, who said: Abu 'Ali al-Basri recited to me:

"A companion from whom I received a favor delayed his repayment to me, so he became hostile to me.
When he was certain that fate had made war against me, he showed regret for what he had done for me."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/311; in it: asdaytu instead of qaddamtu, and asda instead of a'ta.]]

Another said:

"You spoiled with reminders the good you had done;
the noble, when he gives, is not a reminder-giver."

﴿Kind speech (qawlun ma'ruf)﴾ — that is good words and a gracious reply to the questioner. It was said: [ ... ] [[Illegible in the manuscript, perhaps: (overlooking), as in Zad al-Masir 1/276.]] good.

Al-Kalbi said: it is a righteous supplication, invoking for his brother in his absence. Al-Dahhak said: a word in reconciling between people. ﴿And forgiveness﴾ — that is, forgiveness from Him toward him, because He knows his need and poverty. This was said by Muhammad ibn Jarir. Al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak said: He overlooks his wrong. He said: He overlooks it if he is insolent toward him when refusing him. Allah, exalted, knows that the poor man, when he is turned away without a gift, is grieved by it, which leads to foul speech or the display of complaint, and He knows what befalls the one who withholds. So He urged him to pardon and forgive, and clarified that this is better for him than a charity he gives which is followed by ﴿injury﴾, i.e., reminder and reproach of the beggar for asking, or complaint from him, or fault-finding, or speech that harms him.

﴿And Allah is Free of need﴾ from the charity of servants; had He willed, He would have enriched all creation, but He gave to the rich so He might see how they give thanks, and He left the poor so He might see how they endure patiently. This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Allah has favored some of you over others in provision﴾ [al-Nahl 16:71], through obligation, charity and kindness. [[Illegible in the manuscript.]]

﴿Forbearing﴾, for He did not hasten against one who reminds and injures with his charity.

It is reported from 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulaymani, client of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the beggar asks, do not cut off his request until he finishes it, then respond to him with dignity and gentleness, or with a little giving, or with a gracious refusal; for there may come to you one who is neither a human nor a jinn, watching how you act regarding what Allah, mighty and majestic, has entrusted to you."
[190] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/309.]]

It is reported from Bishr ibn al-Harith, who said: I saw the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (عليه السلام) in a dream, and I said:

"O Commander of the Faithful, say something that Allah, mighty and majestic, may benefit me by."

He said: "How beautiful is the kindness of the rich toward the poor, desiring the reward of Allah; and more beautiful than it is the dignity of the poor toward the rich, trusting in Allah, mighty and majestic."

I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, add more." He turned away saying:

"You were dead, then you became alive,
and soon you will become dead.
So pitch a tent in the abode of perishing,
and build a tent in the abode of everlasting."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/310; Tarikh Baghdad: 9/432.]]

﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ — that is, do not cancel the rewards of your charities and the reward of your spending by reminding the beggar.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "By reminding Allah, exalted, and injury to its recipient."

Then He struck a parable for that, saying: ﴿Like one who spends his wealth﴾ — that is, like the nullification of one who spends his wealth ﴿to be seen by people﴾ — showing off and ostentation, so that they see his spending and say that he is generous, benevolent, righteous, ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. This is for the hypocrites, because the disbeliever openly declares his disbelief and is not a show-off. ﴿So his parable﴾, i.e., the parable of this hypocritical show-off, ﴿is like a smooth rock (safwan)﴾ — bare stone without anything on it.

The poet said:

"Why do I see you as if I had sown pebbles
in a barren year, while the face of the earth is a smooth rock?
For my crop, the month of Aban, I shall harvest it,
just as there is a time for sowing, there is an Aban."

It is both singular and plural. Whoever takes it as plural says its singular is *safwana*, like *tamra* and *tamr*, *nakhla* and *nakhl*. Whoever takes it as singular says its plural is *safy* and *safa*.

The poet said: "The perching of birds upon the *safy*."

Al-Zar'i said: "Safwan" with the *fa'* vowelled with a fatha, and its plural is *safwan*, like *karwan* and *karwan*, *warshan* and *warshan*.

﴿Upon it is dust, and a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare (saldan)﴾ — *wabil* is the heavy rain, great in its drops; *saldan* is the hard, smooth stone upon which there is nothing.

Tabbata Sharran said:

"I am not a bucket-rope of a wind and cold ... nor a hard, smooth rock, detached from goodness."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92; al-Sihah 1/100.]]

It is, of the earth, that which does not grow, and of heads, that which has no hair upon it.

Ru'ba said:

"When the bald-patched, tanned ones saw me, bright of the forehead's hard, bald patch."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92; Kitab al-'Ayn 3/391.]]

He means the bald (al-ajlah).

This is a parable which Allah, exalted, struck for the spending of the hypocrite, the show-off, and the believer who reminds with his charity and injures. That is: people see in outward appearance that these have deeds, as dust is seen upon this *safwan*; but when the Day of Resurrection comes, it all dissolves and perishes, because it was not for Allah, mighty and majestic — as if it had never been, just as the heavy rain removed the dust that was upon the *safwan*.

﴿Leaving it bare (saldan)﴾ — smooth, with nothing upon it. ﴿They have no power over anything﴾ — over the reward of anything ﴿of what they have earned﴾, i.e., done in the world, because they did not do it for Allah, exalted, seeking what is with Him, but did it for the show and praise of people; so that became the greater part of their deeds.
[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92.]]

﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. Its parallel is His saying, exalted, describing the deeds of the disbelievers: ﴿The parable of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim 14:18]. And His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a valley﴾ [al-Nur 24:39], to the end of the verse.

From 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call, and the people of the gathering will hear: 'Where are those who worshipped people? Stand up and take your rewards from those for whom you acted, for I do not accept any deed mixed with anything of this world.'"
[191] [[Kanz al-'Ummal 3/485, no. 7542.]]

Translation: "The parable of those who spend their wealth" — the verse contains an ellipsis and abbreviation; its implied sense is: "the parable of the charity of those who spend their wealth." If you wish, you may say: "The parable of those who spend their wealth."

Abu 'Amr recited:

"May Allah curse the sons of the *si'lat* ... 'Amr ibn Maymun, the vilest of men."

[[Thus in the manuscript.]]

The rest read it with the *mad* (مِائَةُ).

If you ask: "Have you seen an ear containing a hundred grains, or has that reached you?" It is said: "We do not deny it, nor is it impossible. If it exists, then it is so; otherwise, it is possible that its meaning is: 'like a grain that grew seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains,' as God, glory be to Him, made that within it. It may also mean that when it is sown, it produces a hundred grains, so what arises from the seed that came from it of the hundred grains is equivalent to it, because it came from it." Likewise is what al-Dahhak said: "Every ear produced a hundred grains."

﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ between seven hundred and seven hundred-fold, up to what Allah, mighty and majestic, wills, which none knows but Allah.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ — (He is) rich enough for those multiples, and All-Knowing of whoever spends.

Al-Dahhak said regarding this verse: Whoever brings forth a dirham seeking the good pleasure of Allah, he will have in this world, for every dirham, seven hundred dirhams as a swift replacement, and will meet a thousand dirhams on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Kalbi said regarding His words ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾: it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (رضي الله عنه) and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. As for 'Abd al-Rahman, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with four thousand dirhams as charity and said: "I had eight thousand; I kept four thousand for myself and my dependents, and four thousand I lent to my Lord, mighty and majestic."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "May Allah bless you in what you kept and in what you gave." As for 'Uthman, he said: "Upon me is the equipping of one who has no equipment for the expedition of Tabuk," so he equipped the Muslims with a thousand camels with their saddle-cloths and pack-saddles, and gave in charity the well of Rumah, a well in the outskirts of Madinah which had been his, to the Muslims. So this verse was revealed concerning both of them.
[[Well of Rumah in the 'Aqiq of Madinah; see Mu'jam al-Buldan 1/300.]]

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura said: 'Uthman (رضي الله عنه) came with a thousand dinars in the army of hardship (jaysh al-'usra) and poured them into the lap of the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) put his hand into them and kiss them, saying: 'What harm does Ibn 'Affan do after today by what he does.'"

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) raising his hands, supplicating for 'Uthman (رضي الله عنه): 'O Lord, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan — be pleased with him, so be You pleased with him.' He continued to supplicate with his hands raised until dawn broke, and then Allah, exalted, revealed concerning him: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾, i.e., in the obedience of Allah."

﴿Then they do not follow what they have spent with reminders (mann) and injury (adhan)﴾ — mann is that one bestows his gift upon another and counts his favors upon him, thereby spoiling them; he continues the reminder (al-mannah) to the favor.

It is said: "One performs a *manna*, *mannan* and *maniyyah* when he bestows and gives." Allah, exalted, said: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold﴾ [Sad 38:39], i.e., give; then this became so common that the mention of the favor and reckoning it became a reminder (mannah).
[[Surah Sad: 39.]]

﴿And there is no injury to them; their reward is with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ — through making the gift apparent and mentioning it to one who does not deserve to be informed of it, and similar speech that causes harm.

Sufyan and al-Mufaddal said regarding His words ﴿reminders and injury﴾: it is that one says, "I gave you, yet you did not thank me."

Al-Dahhak said: "That a man does not spend his wealth is better than that he spends it and then follows it with reminder and injury."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "My father used to say: 'When you give a man something and you think your greeting weighs heavily upon him, withhold your greeting from him.'"

Ibn Zayd said: "Is there anything better than greeting?"

He said: A woman said to my father: "O Abu Usama, direct me to a man who will truly go out in the way of Allah, for they only go out to eat fruits. I have a quiver and arrows in it." He said: "May Allah not bless you in your quiver or in your arrows, for you have harmed them before you gave them."

So Allah forbade His servants from reminding of a favor, and reserved it as an attribute of Himself, because the reminder of servants is reproach and spoiling, while the reminder of Allah, mighty and majestic, is bounty, favor and admonition. Mu'adh ibn al-Muthanna al-'Anbari recited, from his father Mahmud ibn al-Warraq:

"Most beautiful of every beauty, at every time and season,
a favor nurtured, free of reminders."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/311.]]

Al-Tha'alabi said: Abu 'Ali Zahir ibn Ahmad al-Sarakhsi said: Abu Dhar al-Qurtubi recited to us:

"Your kindness has not been perfected in the sight of my ruler, when it burdened him with honor.
Indeed, of righteousness, do not deny it: the honoring of one who displays your honoring.
Reminding the benefactor is a deficiency, so do not spoil your favor with reminders.
Honor in generosity, and the miserliness of a youth is a humiliation I loved to make known to you."

He said: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim recited to me, who said: Muhammad ibn Tahir recited to me, who said: Abu 'Ali al-Basri recited to me:

"A companion from whom I received a favor delayed his repayment to me, so he became hostile to me.
When he was certain that fate had made war against me, he showed regret for what he had done for me."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/311; in it: asdaytu instead of qaddamtu, and asda instead of a'ta.]]

Another said:

"You spoiled with reminders the good you had done;
the noble, when he gives, is not a reminder-giver."

﴿Kind speech (qawlun ma'ruf)﴾ — that is good words and a gracious reply to the questioner. It was said: [ ... ] [[Illegible in the manuscript, perhaps: (overlooking), as in Zad al-Masir 1/276.]] good.

Al-Kalbi said: it is a righteous supplication, invoking for his brother in his absence. Al-Dahhak said: a word in reconciling between people. ﴿And forgiveness﴾ — that is, forgiveness from Him toward him, because He knows his need and poverty. This was said by Muhammad ibn Jarir. ﴿And Allah is Free of need﴾ from the charity of servants; had He willed, He would have enriched all creation, but He gave to the rich so He might see how they give thanks, and He left the poor so He might see how they endure patiently. ﴿Forbearing﴾, for He did not hasten against one who reminds and injures with his charity.

It is reported from 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulaymani, client of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the beggar asks, do not cut off his request until he finishes it, then respond to him with dignity and gentleness, or with a little giving, or with a gracious refusal; for there may come to you one who is neither a human nor a jinn, watching how you act regarding what Allah, mighty and majestic, has entrusted to you."
[190] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/309.]]

It is reported from Bishr ibn al-Harith, who said: I saw the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (عليه السلام) in a dream, and I said:

"O Commander of the Faithful, say something that Allah, mighty and majestic, may benefit me by."

He said: "How beautiful is the kindness of the rich toward the poor, desiring the reward of Allah; and more beautiful than it is the dignity of the poor toward the rich, trusting in Allah, mighty and majestic."

I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, add more." He turned away saying:

"You were dead, then you became alive,
and soon you will become dead.
So pitch a tent in the abode of perishing,
and build a tent in the abode of everlasting."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/310; Tarikh Baghdad: 9/432.]]

﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ — that is, do not cancel the rewards of your charities and the reward of your spending by reminding the beggar.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "By reminding Allah, exalted, and injury to its recipient."

Then He struck a parable for that, saying: ﴿Like one who spends his wealth﴾ — that is, like the nullification of one who spends his wealth ﴿to be seen by people﴾ — showing off and ostentation, so that they see his spending and say that he is generous, benevolent, righteous, ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. This is for the hypocrites, because the disbeliever openly declares his disbelief and is not a show-off. ﴿So his parable﴾, i.e., the parable of this hypocritical show-off, ﴿is like a smooth rock (safwan)﴾ — bare stone without anything on it.

The poet said:

"Why do I see you as if I had sown pebbles

For my crop, the month of Aban, I shall harvest it,

It is both singular and plural. Whoever takes it as plural says its singular is *safwana*, like *tamra* and *tamr*, *nakhla* and *nakhl*. Whoever takes it as singular says its plural is *safy* and *safa*.

The poet said: "The perching of birds upon the *safy*."

Al-Zar'i said: "Safwan" with the *fa'* vowelled with a fatha, and its plural is *safwan*, like *karwan* and *karwan*, *warshan* and *warshan*.

﴿Upon it is dust, and a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare (saldan)﴾ — *wabil* is the heavy rain, great in its drops; *saldan* is the hard, smooth stone upon which there is nothing.

Tabbata Sharran said:

"I am not a bucket-rope of a wind and cold ... nor a hard, smooth rock, detached from goodness."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92; al-Sihah 1/100.]]

It is, of the earth, that which does not grow, and of heads, that which has no hair upon it.

Ru'ba said:

"When the bald-patched, tanned ones saw me, bright of the forehead's hard, bald patch."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92; Kitab al-'Ayn 3/391.]]

He means the bald (al-ajlah).

That is: people see in outward appearance that these have deeds, as dust is seen upon this *safwan*; but when the Day of Resurrection comes, it all dissolves and perishes, because it was not for Allah, mighty and majestic — as if it had never been, just as the heavy rain removed the dust that was upon the *safwan*.

﴿Leaving it bare (saldan)﴾ — smooth, with nothing upon it. ﴿They have no power over anything﴾ — over the reward of anything ﴿of what they have earned﴾, i.e., done in the world, because they did not do it for Allah, exalted, seeking what is with Him, but did it for the show and praise of people; so that became the greater part of their deeds.
[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92.]]

﴿And Allah is Free of need﴾ from the charity of servants; had He willed, He would have enriched all creation, but He gave to the rich so He might see how they give thanks, and He left the poor so He might see how they endure patiently. This is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Allah has favored some of you over others in provision﴾ [al-Nahl 16:71], through obligation, charity and kindness. [[Illegible in the manuscript.]]

﴿Forbearing﴾, for He did not hasten against one who reminds and injures with his charity.

It is reported from 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulaymani, client of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (رضي الله عنه), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the beggar asks, do not cut off his request until he finishes it, then respond to him with dignity and gentleness, or with a little giving, or with a gracious refusal; for there may come to you one who is neither a human nor a jinn, watching how you act regarding what Allah, mighty and majestic, has entrusted to you."
[190] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/309.]]

It is reported from Bishr ibn al-Harith, who said: I saw the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (عليه السلام) in a dream, and I said:

"O Commander of the Faithful, say something that Allah, mighty and majestic, may benefit me by."

He said: "How beautiful is the kindness of the rich toward the poor, desiring the reward of Allah; and more beautiful than it is the dignity of the poor toward the rich, trusting in Allah, mighty and majestic."

I said: "O Commander of the Faithful, add more." He turned away saying:

"You were dead, then you became alive,
and soon you will become dead.
So pitch a tent in the abode of perishing,
and build a tent in the abode of everlasting."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/310; Tarikh Baghdad: 9/432.]]

﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ — that is, do not cancel the rewards of your charities and the reward of your spending by reminding the beggar.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "By reminding Allah, exalted, and injury to its recipient."

Then He struck a parable for that, saying: ﴿Like one who spends his wealth﴾ — that is, like the nullification of one who spends his wealth ﴿to be seen by people﴾ — showing off and ostentation, so that they see his spending and say that he is generous, benevolent, righteous, ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. This is for the hypocrites, because the disbeliever openly declares his disbelief and is not a show-off. ﴿So his parable﴾, i.e., the parable of this hypocritical show-off, ﴿is like a smooth rock (safwan)﴾ — bare stone without anything on it.

The poet said:

"Why do I see you as if I had sown pebbles
in a barren year, while the face of the earth is a smooth rock?
For my crop, the month of Aban, I shall harvest it,
just as there is a time for sowing, there is an Aban."

It is both singular and plural. Whoever takes it as plural says its singular is *safwana*, like *tamra* and *tamr*, *nakhla* and *nakhl*. Whoever takes it as singular says its plural is *safy* and *safa*.

The poet said: "The perching of birds upon the *safy*."

Al-Zar'i said: "Safwan" with the *fa'* vowelled with a fatha, and its plural is *safwan*, like *karwan* and *karwan*, *warshan* and *warshan*.

﴿Upon it is dust, and a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare (saldan)﴾ — *wabil* is the heavy rain, great in its drops; *saldan* is the hard, smooth stone upon which there is nothing.

Tabbata Sharran said:

"I am not a bucket-rope of a wind and cold ... nor a hard, smooth rock, detached from goodness."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92; al-Sihah 1/100.]]

It is, of the earth, that which does not grow, and of heads, that which has no hair upon it.

Ru'ba said:

"When the bald-patched, tanned ones saw me, bright of the forehead's hard, bald patch."
[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92; Kitab al-'Ayn 3/391.]]

He means the bald (al-ajlah).

That is: people see in outward appearance that these have deeds, as dust is seen upon this *safwan*; but when the Day of Resurrection comes, it all dissolves and perishes, because it was not for Allah, mighty and majestic — as if it had never been, just as the heavy rain removed the dust that was upon the *safwan*.

[[Tafsir al-Tabari 3/92.]]

﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾. Its parallel is His saying, exalted, describing the deeds of the disbelievers: ﴿The parable of those who disbelieve in their Lord: their deeds are like ashes upon which the wind blows violently on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim 14:18]. And His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a valley﴾ [al-Nur 24:39], to the end of the verse.

[191] [[Kanz al-'Ummal 3/485, no. 7542.]]

He said: 'My Friend, Abu al-Qasim, narrated to me,' then he choked and wept; he said: 'My Friend, Abu al-Qasim, narrated to me,' then he choked and wept; he said: 'My Friend, Abu al-Qasim, narrated to me'." Then the man hurried and said: "I am a stranger, not from the people of this town, and I wished that you would narrate to me from the Prophet (ﷺ) — each time the tears choke you. Tell me what you wished to narrate."

He said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'On the Day of Resurrection a man will be brought who had been given wealth, and it will be said: How did you act with what We had entrusted to you?'

He will say: 'I spent and gave.' It will be said: 'You wished that it be said: So-and-so is generous; and it has been said. So what benefit did it bring you?'

Then a brave man will be brought, and it will be said to him: 'Did I not make your heart brave?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said: 'How did you act?' He will say: 'I fought until my life was spent.' It will be said to him: 'You wished that it be said: So-and-so is brave; and it has been said. So what benefit did it bring you?'

Then a man who had been given knowledge will be brought, and it will be said to him: 'Did I not entrust you with knowledge?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said: 'How did you act?' He will say: 'I learned and taught.' It will be said: 'You wished that it be said: So-and-so is a scholar; and it has been said. So what benefit did it bring you?'

Then he said: 'Take them away to the Fire.'"

مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أَمْوالَهُمْ الآية فيها إضمار واختصار تقديرها: مثل صدقات الذين ينفقون أموالهم، فإن شئت قلت: مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أَمْوالَهُمْ.

﴿In the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains.﴾

Abu 'Amr, Abu [Ghaziyya], Hamza and al-Kisa'i assimilated (idgham) the *ta'* and *sin* in *anbatat sab'a sanabil* (أَنْبَتَتْ سَبْعَ سَنابِلَ), which is the plural of *sunbula* (ear of grain). The rest pronounced them distinctly (izhar). As for the one who assimilates, it is because the *ta'* and the *sin* are both *hamzated* — do you not see that they are interchangeable?

Abu 'Amr recited:

"May Allah curse the sons of the *si'lat* ... 'Amr ibn Maymun, the vilest of men."
[[al-si'lat: the most wicked of the ghouls (ghul), and a repulsive woman is likened to it. The verse is in Lisan al-'Arab 2/101, where, as in the rest of the lexicons, it reads: 'Amr ibn Yarbu'.]]

He meant *li'am al-nas* (لئام الناس, "the vile people") and changed the *sin* into *ta'*. As for the one who pronounces them distinctly, it is because they are two separate words, which is the original form and the widespread usage.

﴿In every ear a hundred grains.﴾ Abu Ja'far and al-A'mash read it as "five hundred and a hundred" (خمس مائة ومائة), where it is used for lightness (istikhfaf).
[[Thus in the manuscript.]]

The rest read it with the *mad* (مِائَةُ).

If you ask: "Have you seen an ear containing a hundred grains, or has that reached you?" It is said: "We do not deny it, nor is it impossible. If it exists, then it is so; otherwise, it is possible that its meaning is: 'like a grain that grew seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains,' as God, glory be to Him, made that within it. It may also mean that when it is sown, it produces a hundred grains, so what arises from the seed that came from it of the hundred grains is equivalent to it, because it came from it." Likewise is what al-Dahhak said: "Every ear produced a hundred grains."

﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾ between seven hundred and seven hundred-fold, up to what Allah, mighty and majestic, wills, which none knows but Allah.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ — (He is) rich enough for those multiples, and All-Knowing of whoever spends.

Al-Dahhak said regarding this verse: Whoever brings forth a dirham seeking the good pleasure of Allah, he will have in this world, for every dirham, seven hundred dirhams as a swift replacement, and will meet a thousand dirhams on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Kalbi said regarding His words ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾: it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (رضي الله عنه) and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. As for 'Abd al-Rahman, he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with four thousand dirhams as charity and said: "I had eight thousand; I kept four thousand for myself and my dependents, and four thousand I lent to my Lord, mighty and majestic."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "May Allah bless you in what you kept and in what you gave." As for 'Uthman, he said: "Upon me is the equipping of one who has no equipment for the expedition of Tabuk," so he equipped the Muslims with a thousand camels with their saddle-cloths and pack-saddles, and gave in charity the well of Rumah, a well in the outskirts of Madinah which had been his, to the Muslims. So this verse was revealed concerning both of them.
[[Well of Rumah in the 'Aqiq of Madinah; see Mu'jam al-Buldan 1/300.]]

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samura said: 'Uthman (رضي الله عنه) came with a thousand dinars in the army of hardship (jaysh al-'usra) and poured them into the lap of the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) put his hand into them and kiss them, saying: 'What harm does Ibn 'Affan do after today by what he does.'"

﴿Then they do not follow what they have spent with reminders (mann) and injury (adhan)﴾ — mann is that one bestows his gift upon another and counts his favors upon him, thereby spoiling them; he continues the reminder (al-mannah) to the favor.

It is said: "One performs a *manna*, *mannan* and *maniyyah* when he bestows and gives." Allah, exalted, said: ﴿This is Our gift, so bestow or withhold﴾ [Sad 38:39], i.e., give; then this became so common that the mention of the favor and reckoning it became a reminder (mannah).
