It is supported by His saying in Al 'Imran: [﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it﴾] [[Surah Al 'Imran: 29.]] — concerning allegiance to the disbelievers — and it is supported by what precedes it.

Others said: this verse is general. Then they differed about the aspect of its generality. Some of them said: it is abrogated.

The narration was transmitted with different wordings.

He said: When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and some of the Ansar came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and knelt, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, no verse has ever been revealed that weighed more heavily upon us than this verse. We do not like that any of us should have the world and all that is in it, and we are held to account for what we speak to ourselves about. We are destroyed, by Allah!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "So it was revealed." They said: "We are destroyed, and we have been burdened with deeds we cannot bear."

He said: "Perhaps you are saying as the Children of Israel said to Moses, peace be upon him: 'We hear and we disobey' (sami'na wa 'asayna). Rather, say: 'We hear and we obey' (sami'na wa atha'na)."

It weighed heavily on them, so they remained in this state for a year. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent relief and ease with His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. So this verse abrogated what came before it.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has overlooked for my community what they speak to themselves about, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it."

This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, 'A'ishah, and Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata'. Among the Successors and those who followed them: Muhammad ibn Sirin, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, Qatadah, al-Kalbi and Shaybah.

Sa'id ibn Marjanah said: "While we were sitting with 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, he recited this verse: ﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾. Ibn 'Umar said: 'If Allah takes us to account for it, we will certainly be destroyed.' Then he wept until he could be heard." Ibn Marjanah said: "I mentioned that to Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: 'May Allah forgive Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. The Muslims experienced from it, when it was revealed, what he experienced. So Allah revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. And whisperings were something beyond the Muslims' ability to bear, so the matter came down to speech and action, and that verse was abrogated.'"

Others said: this verse is muhkam (definitive) and not abrogated, because abrogation (naskh) and reports are not permitted except in a report that contains a command, a prohibition, or a condition. Then they differed about its interpretation. A group of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has affirmed earning (kasb) for the heart, and said: ﴿for what your hearts have earned﴾. Every doer is held to account for his earning and recompensed for his deed. [So do not suppose] that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will leave a servant on the Day of Resurrection without informing him of anything he secretly or openly did, whether a movement of his limbs or a [whisper] in his heart, and then He will forgive whom He wills and punish whom He wills for what He wills.

The meaning of the verse: "If you show what is in yourselves of [sins] and act upon it, that is, if you intend it in yourselves and then conceal it, He will inform you of it and call you to account for it, then forgive whom He wills and punish whom He wills."

This is the meaning of the statements of al-Hasan, al-Rabi', Qays ibn Abi Hazim, and the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. It is supported by His saying: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned﴾.

Others said: the meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, calls His creatures to account for all that they have shown of their deeds and concealed, and punishes them for it. However, His punishment of them for what they concealed without doing it is by what befalls them in this world of calamities, misfortunes and matters over which they grieve and suffer. This is the view of 'A'ishah.

It is narrated that she was asked about this verse and she said: "No one has asked me about it except that I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'O 'A'ishah, this is Allah's reproach of the servant for what afflicts him of fever and misfortune, even a thorn or a loss of goods, which he places in his pocket and then loses, and is distressed over it, then finds it in his pocket. Until the believer comes out of his sins as red gold comes out of the purse.'"

His saying supports this: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [[Surah al-Nisa': 123.]], meaning in this world.

Mujahid said, in the narration of Mansur and Ibn Abi Jurayj: "﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves or conceal it﴾, meaning of certainty and doubt."

Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: "﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾, meaning Islam, ﴿or conceal it﴾, meaning faith."

Others said: "﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾, meaning what is in your hearts of what you know and have resolved upon, ﴿or conceal it﴾, so that you do not reveal it while you are determined and resolved upon it, ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾. As for what you speak to yourselves about that you have not resolved upon, Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity and does not hold you to account for it. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿Allah does not hold you to account for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He holds you to account for what your hearts have earned﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 225.]]."

It is narrated from 'Abd ibn al-Mubarak that he said: "I said to Sufyan: 'Is a servant held accountable for a mere intention?' He said: 'If it is a firm resolve, he is held accountable for it.'" It is narrated from 'Amr ibn Jarir that he said: "I went out when I was young for a matter I had resolved upon, and I passed by Abu Talib the storyteller while people were gathered around him. The first thing he said was: 'O you who resolve upon sin, know that the Creator of resolve is watching your resolve.' He said: 'I fell unconscious, by Allah, and I did not come to except in repentance.'"

It is narrated from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid that he said: "The Children of Israel were struck by famine, and a man passed by a heap of sand and said: 'I wish this sand were flour for me, so I could feed the Children of Israel with it.' He was rewarded according to his intention."

It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, that he said: "A man used to go around the scholars saying: 'Who will guide me to a deed by which I may continue always to be doing something for Allah, Mighty and Majestic? For I love that no hour of night or day should pass over me without my being engaged in it.' He was told: 'You have found what you need, so do good as much as you can. When you slacken or leave it, then resolve upon doing it, for indeed one who resolves upon a good deed is like one who does it.'" This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The intention of the believer is better than his deed," because deeds come to an end but intentions do not come to an end.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali said: "The meaning of the verse: ﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾, of the outward deeds, ﴿or conceal it﴾, of the inward states, ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾: the worshipper for his actions and the knower for his states."

Others said: "Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: [On the Day] when secrets are tested and hidden thoughts are brought out, and My scribes wrote down of your deeds only what appeared of them, while I am aware of your secrets which they did not know and did not record. So I will inform you of that and call you to account for it, so that you know that not even the weight of an atom of your deeds escapes Me, and then I forgive whom I will and punish whom I will."

As for the believers, He informs them of it and forgives them and does not hold them to account for it, displaying His grace. As for the disbelievers, He informs them of it and punishes them for it, displaying His justice.

So the meaning of the verse: ﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾ so that you act upon it, ﴿or conceal it﴾ of what you have harboured, kept secret and intended, ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾, informing you and making you aware of it, so He forgives the believers and punishes the disbelievers. This is the meaning of the statements of al-Dahhak and al-Rabi', and the narrations of al-'Awfi and al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It is supported by His saying: ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾.

He did not say "will hold you to account" (yu'akhidhukum), and reckoning (muhasabah) is not the same as punishment ('iqab). Reckoning is established, while punishment is dropped. Among what supports this is the hadith of private consultation (najwa), which is what

Qatadah narrated from Safwan ibn Muhriz, who said: "While we were circumambulating the House with 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, a man approached him and said: 'O Ibn 'Umar, what did you hear from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about private consultation (najwa)?' He said: 'I heard the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The believer draws near to his Lord until He places His hand (kanaf) upon him, and He makes him confess his sins, saying: 'Did you commit such-and-such?' He says: 'My Lord, I know.' Then He makes him stand before his sins, one sin at a time, and Allah says: 'I covered them for you in the world, and today I forgive them for you.' No angel brought near and no prophet sent has been shown this." As for the disbelievers and hypocrites, they are called out before the heads of the witnesses: ﴿These are they who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾."

Al-A'mash, from Ma'rur ibn Suwayd, from Abu Dharr, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and it will be said: 'Present to him the minor sins.' They will be presented to him, and it will be said: 'You did such-and-such on such-and-such a day.' He will admit and not deny, while the major sins are concealed from him, and he is fearful of them. Then it will be said: 'Give him in place of every evil deed a good deed.' He will say: 'I have sins that I do not see here.'"

He said: Abu Dharr said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) laugh until his molars showed."

Al-Husayn ibn Muslim said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will call the believers to account on the Day of Resurrection with kindness and grace, and the disbelievers with proof and justice."

﴿Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Hasan, 'Asim and Ya'qub read both verbs in the nominative (raf'), and Abu Hatim preferred this. Ibn 'Abbas read both in the accusative (nasb), and the rest read both in the jussive (jazm). The jussive is on the conjunction (nasaq), the nominative is on the beginning of a sentence, meaning "so He forgives," and the accusative is on the shift (sarf), and it was said: by implying the light "an" (an al-khafifah).

Tawus narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "﴿Then He forgives whom He wills﴾, the great sin, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾ for the minor sin." It is like His saying: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 23.]].

﴿And Allah is over all things competent.﴾

﴿The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord﴾. The verse.

Talhah ibn Musarrif narrated from Murrah, from 'Abd Allah, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), and he was given the five prayers, and the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and forgiveness for whoever of his community does not associate anything with Allah, except the grave sins (al-muqhimat)." [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/387. Al-muqhimat are the great sins that cast their doers into the Fire.]]

It is narrated from 'Alqamah ibn Qays, from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amr, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down two verses from the treasures of the Throne, which the Merciful, Mighty and Majestic, wrote two thousand years before He created the creation. Whoever recites them after the late evening prayer twice, they suffice him in place of the night prayer: ﴿The Messenger has believed...﴾ to the end of the surah."

Abu Qilabah narrated from Abu al-Ash'ath al-Hamdani, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, wrote a book two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, in which He revealed two verses and concluded Surat al-Baqarah with them. They are not recited in a house for three nights, and a devil approaches it."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever recites the two verses at the end of Surat al-Baqarah in a night, they will suffice him."

Musa ibn Hudhayfah narrated from Ibn al-Munkadir, who said: "He related to us a hadith which he traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'At the end of Surat al-Baqarah are verses which are both Qur'an and supplication, and which please the Most Merciful.'"

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/231.]]

It is also reported in a hadith that it was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The house of Thabit ibn Uways ibn Shammas glows tonight like lamps." He said: "Perhaps he is reciting Surat al-Baqarah." Thabit was asked, and he said: "I recited Surat al-Baqarah."

﴿The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord,﴾

It was said: This verse was revealed when what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, threatened to call them to account for, regarding what their souls concealed, weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Perhaps you are saying 'We hear and we disobey' as the Children of Israel said?" They said: "Rather, we say 'We hear and we obey.'" Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed praise of them and information about them: ﴿The Messenger has believed﴾, that is, he affirmed ﴿in what was revealed to him from his Lord.﴾

Qatadah said: When ﴿The Messenger has believed﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And it is right that he should believe."

﴿And the believers.﴾

In the reading of 'Ali and 'Abd Allah: "And the believers believed; each believed in Allah..."

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 283–286 (part 2 of 2)**

He made the verb singular according to the wording of *kull* (each). The meaning is: each one of them believed. Had he said *āmanū* (they believed), it would also have been permitted, because *kull* can be used in both the singular and the plural. As an example of the singular, the verse says: ﴿Each one knows its prayer and its glorification﴾ [24:41]. As an example of the plural, it says: ﴿Each one of them will come back to Us﴾ [21:93], and ﴿Each one of them will come to Him humbled﴾ [27:88].

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Yahya, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *wa-kitabihi* (and His Book) in the singular, with *alif*. The rest read *wa-kutubihi* (and His Books) in the plural, which is the apparent reading, as in the verse ﴿and His angels and His messengers﴾.

The singular has two possible explanations. The first is that they meant the Qur'an specifically. The second is that they meant all the Books. The Arabs say: "milk has increased" and "dirhams and dinars have increased in people's hands," meaning the *albān* (kinds of milk) and the *darāhim* and *danānīr* (coins). Evidence for this is the verse ﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and as warners, and sent down with them the Book﴾ [2:213].

*wa-rusulihi*: the plural of *rasūl* (messenger).

Al-Hasan and Ibn Salama read the *sīn* with a sukun (*wa-rusulihi* with the vowel omitted) because of the number of vowels. Al-'Abbas reported from Ibn 'Amr, and it was also narrated from Nafi', that they read *wa-kutubihi wa-rusulihi* with the vowels shortened. The rest pronounce them with the full vowels, in accordance with the original form.

﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾, believing in some and disbelieving in others, as the Jews and Christians did. In the codex of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) the reading is *lā nufarriqanna* (we shall not make any distinction).

Jarir ibn 'Abdullah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read *lā yufarriqu* with a *yā'* (they make no distinction), meaning "none of them [the believers] makes any distinction." On this reading the sentence may be a report about the Messenger.

The rest read it with *nūn* (*lā nufarriqu*), with an implied "saying" (*qawl*) before it, the meaning being: "and they say, 'We make no distinction.'" This is like the verse ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate, saying, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [13:23], and like the verse ﴿As for those whose faces turn black, [it will be said:] "Did you disbelieve?"﴾ [3:106], meaning: "it will be said to them, 'Did you disbelieve?'" Also His words ﴿If only you could see when the guilty bow their heads before their Lord, [saying:] "Our Lord, we have seen and heard"﴾ [32:12], meaning: "they say, 'Our Lord.'" And the verse ﴿Those who take protectors besides Him [say]: "We only worship them"﴾ [39:3], meaning: "they say, 'We only worship them.'"

*Bayna* (between) governs two or more things. He said *bayna aḥadin* (between anyone) rather than *ā'ḥād* (individuals), because *ā'ḥād* can refer to one or to many. God says: ﴿Not one of you could withhold Us from him﴾ [69:47].

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Booty was not made lawful for anyone with black heads before you" [Tabari, 10/59, where the wording is "before you" (min qablikum)].

Ru'ba said:
"What has become of the people, [who] have been pounded and crushed, / they fear no one, [since] they have been driven away."

﴿And they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾: their saying *we hear and we obey* is in contrast to the saying of the Jews.

Hakim ibn Jabir reported that when the verse ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ was revealed, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "God, the Mighty and Majestic, has favoured you and your community. Ask, and you will be given." So the Messenger of God asked, and He said: ﴿Your forgiveness﴾.

*Ghufrānaka* (Your forgiveness) is in the accusative as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, from the verb *ghafara*), meaning "we ask You to forgive," like our saying *subḥānaka* (glory be to You), meaning "we glorify You."

It was also said that the meaning is: "we ask You for forgiveness."

﴿Our Lord, and to You is the final return.﴾

﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.﴾ The apparent meaning of the verse is the granting of needs. It contains an implied request and need, as if they had said to Him: "Burden us beyond our capacity," and God answered: "God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity."

*Al-wus'* (capacity) is the name for what a person can bear and what is within his power, and what is difficult for him. It was also said: what is difficult for him and what strains him.

Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla al-Shami read *lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wasi'ahā* with a *wāw* vowelled with a fatha and *sīn* with a kasra, as a verb, meaning: "except that His command would be within its capacity," or he meant "except what it has the capacity for," with the word *mā* ("what") omitted.

The scholars differed about its interpretation. Ibn 'Ata', al-Suddi and most of the commentators said it refers to the inner speech of the soul (*ḥadīth al-nafs*). When God revealed ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾ [2:284], the believers came, [in general], and said: "O Messenger of God, this is [too much]. We are to repent for the deeds of the limbs, but how can we repent for whispering and how can we refrain from the inner speech of the soul?" So God revealed: ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾, meaning its power, and the inner speech of the soul was something they could not bear.

Ibn 'Abbas said in another report: [...] (unreadable in the manuscript). The believers in particular: God made the matter of their religion easy for them. He did not burden them except with what they were able to bear. He said: ﴿God intends ease for you﴾ [2:185], and He said: ﴿He has not placed upon you any difficulty in religion﴾ [22:78], and He said: ﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾ [64:16].

Al-Tha'alibi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi say: I heard Abu 'Abdullah Muhammad ibn Nafi' al-Sijzi say in Herat: I heard Abu Yazid Hatim ibn Mahbub al-Shami say: I heard 'Abd al-Jabbar ibn al-'Ala' al-'Attar say: Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna was asked about the words of God, ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾.

He said: "[It means] except its ease, not its hardship. He does not burden it with its strength, for if He burdened it with its strength, the effort would reach its utmost limit."

Al-Tha'alibi said: This is a good statement, because *al-wus'* is less than *al-ṭāqa* (strength). Some of the theologians said: it means "except what is within its capacity and lawful for it," as one says: "Can this matter be within your capacity?" meaning: "Is this lawful for you from God?" God makes clear that what He has imposed on His servants is within their capacity for them. And God knows best.

﴿It has what it earned﴾: that is, the soul has what it did of good and righteous deeds; it has its reward and recompense. ﴿And against it is what it has earned﴾: that is, of evil, by evil deeds, the burden of them is upon it.

﴿Our Lord, do not take us to account﴾: do not punish us.

The scholars of meaning (*ahl al-ma'ānī*) said: It came in the form of *mufā'ala* (the pattern of reciprocity), though the action is one, because the wrongdoer has plotted and found a way to it, and it is as if he has helped the one who punishes him for his sin and takes him to account for it, so he shares in the taking to account.

﴿If we forget or make a mistake﴾: some of them took this to be forgetting, which is heedlessness.

Al-Kalbi said: When the Children of Israel forgot something of what they had been commanded, or made a mistake, punishment was hastened upon them, and some food or drink was forbidden to them in proportion to that sin. So God commanded His Prophet and the believers to ask Him not to take them to account for this.

Others said it is forgetting in the sense of abandoning and neglecting. God says: ﴿They forgot God, so He caused them to forget themselves﴾ [59:19]. The first explanation is better.

﴿Or make a mistake﴾: some took this to mean intention and deliberation. It is said: "So-and-so erred (*khati'a*)" when he deliberately commits a fault, [in the sense of *yakhta'u khata'an* and *khaṭa'an*].

God says: ﴿Indeed, their killing them was a great sin﴾ [17:31]. And Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt recited:
"Your servants commit faults, and You are the Lord, / the fates and the decrees will suffice you."

Others took it to mean error, which is ignorance and heedlessness, and this is more correct, because a sin committed deliberately is not pardoned, but rather it is subject to God's will, so long as it is not disbelief.

'Ata' said: ﴿If we forget or make a mistake﴾, meaning: if we are ignorant or commit it deliberately.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿If we forget﴾ something of what You have made obligatory upon us, ﴿or make a mistake﴾ regarding something You have forbidden us.

Al-Zuhri said: 'Umar heard a man say: "O God, forgive me my errors." He said: "Errors are forgiven, but say: 'O God, forgive me my deliberate faults.'"

Al-Nabati said: Ibn Fanjawayh told us: 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Shanba told us: 'Abdullah ibn al-Mussafa al-Sukkari told us: Muhammad ibn al-Musalla al-Muhammadi told us: al-Walid told us: Malik told us, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The error and forgetting of my community have been lifted, and what they were compelled to do."

﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (*iṣr*)﴾: some said it means a covenant, a contract and a pact which we cannot bear or maintain, so that You punish us for falling short in it, ﴿as You laid it upon those before us﴾, meaning the Jews, who did not keep it, so You destroyed and punished them. This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi', Muqatil, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi, Ibn Jurayj and al-Farra', and it is the report of 'Atiyya and 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas. The evidence for it is the verse ﴿And you took upon that My covenant (*iṣrī*)﴾ [3:81], meaning My covenant.

Others said: *al-iṣr* means a heavy weight. That is: do not make it difficult for us, do not make it severe, and do not make the burden heavy upon us as You made it heavy upon those before us from the Jews. God obligated them to fifty prayers, commanded them to give the profit of their wealth in zakat, and whoever had a garment touched by impurity had to cut it off, and whoever committed a sin found in the morning that his sin was written on his door, and other such burdens and fetters that were upon them. This is the meaning of the words of 'Uthman ibn 'Ata', Malik ibn Anas, Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mu'arrikh, al-Qutaybi and Ibn al-Anbari. The evidence for it is His words: ﴿and He removes from them their burden and the fetters that were upon them﴾ [7:157].

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: do not place upon us a sin for which there is no repentance or expiation. And *al-iṣr* refers to the binding, the contract and the rulings, and the thing by which things are bound is called *al-iṣr*. One says: "between him and so-and-so is a bond (*iṣra*) of kinship," and "he does not bind me" (*mā ta'aṣṣarnī*), meaning: "he does not bind me to himself by covenant or kinship."

He said: Abu al-Qasim al-Sadusi recited to me, who said: al-Sami' ibn Muhammad al-Hashimi recited to me, who said: Abu al-Hasan al-'Absi recited to us, who said: al-'Abbas ibn Muhammad al-Duri al-Shafi'i recited to us:
"If there is no blessing from a man to me, / nor between us a bond,
[and I have no] profit in his friendship, / nor any gain in this world or the next,
and I have spent my life at his door, / then that is indeed a losing bargain."

﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾, meaning: do not impose upon us actions beyond our power. This is the view of Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Some said: it is the inner speech of the soul and whispering. It is reported from Abu Thawban, from his father, from Makhul, concerning the words of God ﴿and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾, that he said: [...] (gap in the manuscript).

It is also reported from Abu al-Qasim, from Malik al-Shami, that Abu Idris al-Khawlani used to come to his companions and say: "O God, protect me [...] (gap in the manuscript) to Hell."

Sufyan al-Thawri, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, concerning the words of God ﴿and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾, said: "It is hardship."

It is also reported from Abu al-Qasim 'Abdullah ibn Yahya ibn 'Ubayd, who said: I heard Abu al-Qasim 'Abdullah ibn Ahmad say: I heard Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab [say concerning] ﴿and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾: "It means love (*'ishq*)." Khabbab said: I attended the gathering of Dhu al-Nun al-Misri in his tent. He spoke that day about love for God, and eleven people died in the gathering. He cried out, "Do not let anyone who wants more go out," and [then] said: "O Abu al-Qays, you have mentioned love for God, so mention love for created beings." Dhu al-Nun sighed a deep sigh, put his hand to his face, stood up straight and said to him:

"Their hearts were created, their eyes were made to shed tears; they have become accustomed to sleeplessness and parted from sleep. Their nights are long, their sleep short, their sorrows are not to be counted, and their worries are not to be bound. Their affairs are difficult, their tears abundant, their eyes weeping, their eyelids wounded."

Their companions, family and neighbours [turned against] them. Yahya said: "If the punishment were left in my hand on the Day of Resurrection, I would not punish lovers, because their sins are compelled, not chosen."

Ibn Jurayj said: it is the transformation into apes and swine. Some said: it is the gloating of enemies. 'Abd al-Mun'im ibn Idris reported from his father, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: It was said to Ayyub (peace be upon him): "What was the hardest thing for you during the length of your trial?" He said: "The gloating of enemies." Ibn al-A'rabi recited:
"All calamities may pass over a young man, / and become easy, except the gloating of envious people.
Indeed, calamities pass their days, / but the gloating of enemies is lying in wait."

It was also said: it is separation and parting, we seek refuge in God from it. It was said: cutting off the limbs is easier than cutting off union. Al-Nazzam said: If parting had a form, it would not [harm] sins, it would crush the mountains, and it would scorch the ghada tree, less than [...] (unreadable word). And if God, glory be to Him, punished the people of the Fire with separation, they would find rest in [the heat of the punishment].

﴿And pardon us﴾: that is, overlook and forgive our shortcomings and sins. ﴿And forgive us﴾: cover our sins, pass over them, and do not punish us. ﴿And have mercy on us﴾: for we cannot reach obedience to You, nor abandon disobedience to You, except by Your mercy. It was also said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ from transformation, ﴿and forgive us﴾ for the evil deeds, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ from slander. It was also said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ for actions, ﴿and forgive us﴾ for words, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ for contracts and guarantees. It was also said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ for minor sins, ﴿and forgive us﴾ for major sins, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ by making our scale heavy despite our poverty. It was also said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ in the agonies of death, ﴿and forgive us﴾ in the darkness of the grave, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ in the darkness of the grave.

﴿You are our Protector﴾: that is, our helper, our guardian, our patron, and the one who is in charge of us. ﴿So help us against the disbelieving people.﴾

'Ata', from Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words of God ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ up to ﴿and to You is the final return﴾, said: "I have forgiven you." ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. It has what it earned, and against it is what it has earned. Our Lord, do not take us to account if we forget or make a mistake.﴾ He said: "I will not take you to account." ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden﴾. He said: "I will not lay it upon you." ﴿And do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾. He said: "I will not burden you." ﴿And pardon us, and forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so help us against the disbelieving people.﴾ He said: "I have pardoned you, forgiven you, shown mercy to you and helped you against the disbelieving people."

Sufyan reported from Abu Ishaq, from a man, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, that when he finished reciting al-Baqara he would say: "Amin."

Followed by the sura of Al 'Imran.

﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾ And may God bless Muhammad, the best of the first and the last, and his pure and good family, all of them, and grant them peace.

Masruq said: "Indeed, the treasure of the poor man is the sura of al-Baqara and Al 'Imran, which he recites in the last part of the night."

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "Whoever recites al-Baqara and Al 'Imran on Friday night will have a light between [the wonderful] 'Ajibaa and [the strange] Gharibaa." 'Ajiba is the seventh earth and Gharība is the Throne.

Masruq said: "Whoever recites the sura of al-Baqara on a night will be crowned with it."

In a hadith: "The sura in which al-Baqara is mentioned is the tent-pole (*fusṭāṭ*) of the Qur'an."

**Question:** If it is asked: Is it permissible for God to burden anyone with what he cannot bear?

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said to him: If you mean what is not within his power, that is impossible. If you mean what is heavy for him, then God may do of that what He wills, because what He imposed on the Children of Israel, such as killing themselves, was heavy for them.

This is like your saying: "I cannot bear the speech of so-and-so," which does not mean that it is not within your power, but that it is heavy upon you.

If it is asked: Is it permissible for the Just One to burden beyond capacity?

It is said: He has informed us of His vastness, His mercy and His kindness toward His creation, just as He negated injustice from Himself, even though injustice cannot be imagined from Him in any way. Some people said: If He burdened beyond capacity, it would be His right, because creation is His creation and command is His command, but He informed us that He does not do it. And that is enough.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verse 283–286 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah and Mujahid read kitaban (a written document), and they said: "Sometimes a scribe may be found but not the ink or the page." They also said: "There was no tribe among the Arabs without a scribe among them, but they were unable to obtain the pen and inkwell."

Al-Dahhak read kuttaban, the plural of katib (scribe). The rest read katiban in the singular, which is more fitting with the Mushaf.

﴿fa-rihanun maqbudah﴾ (then pledges taken in hand). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read furuhun with a ḍammah on the rā’ and the hā’. 'Ikrimah, al-Minhal and 'Abd al-Warith read furuhn with a ḍammah on the rā’ and a sukun on the hā’. The rest read farihanun, which is the plural of rahn (pledge). This pattern is like fa'l and fi'al (as in ḥabl and ḥibāl, kabsh and kibāsh, and ka'b and ka''ab).

Al-Rahn is the plural of al-rihān, a plural of a plural, as stated by al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i. Others, including Abu 'Ubaydah, said it is the plural of rahn. They said: "We have found no fa'l pattern pluralised as fu'ul except eight words: khalq and khulq, saqf and suqf, qalb and qulub, [wadd and wudd in the sense of fortune, tha and thuth, ward and ward,] nasr and nusur, and rahn and ruhun."

Al-Akhtal and 'Amr ibn Abi 'Awf said: [ ... ] [[A word that cannot be read.]]
"...until the eagles and the vultures leave it behind."

Al-Farra' recited:
"Until, when the throats of the gullets are moistened, he swoops down upon a vertebra at the end of the neck."

Abu 'Amr said: "We read (furuhun) so that it is distinguished from rihan al-khayl (horse-races)." He cited Qu'nab ibn Umm al-Sahib:
"Su'ad has departed, and 'Adan has become remote from her, and the pledge of your heart has been locked up with her."
That is, love for her.

Both the light and heavy forms of rahn are dialectal variants, like kutub and kutub, and rusul and rusul.

The meaning of the verse: ﴿And if you are on a journey and cannot find a scribe﴾ now for writing, then take pledges from those to whom you owe debts, so that they serve as security for your wealth. They agreed that a pledge is valid only with possession (qabḍ). Mujahid said: "A pledge is only permitted on a journey when there is no scribe." Others permitted it in all circumstances.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pledged his armour to a Jew.

﴿And if one of you trusts another﴾. Madani reading. In the reading of Ubayy: fa-in amina, meaning: if the debtor is trustworthy in the eyes of the creditor, and so he does not take a pledge from him because of his trust and good opinion of him, ﴿let him who has been entrusted discharge his trust﴾. Iftaʿala from amanah (trust), which is trust; its hamzah was written as a waw because of the ḍammah preceding it. ﴿his trust﴾, ﴿and let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾ in discharging the right.

Then he returned to addressing the witnesses, saying: ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾ when you are called to establish it. Al-Sulami read wa-la yaktumu with the yā’ (third person), and similarly ya'malun.

Then he mentioned the warning against concealing testimony, saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And whoever conceals it, indeed his heart is sinful﴾. Fajir qalbuhu (his heart is wicked). This is a subject and predicate construction. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ayla read fa-innahu athimun qalbuhu, on the pattern af'ala, meaning he made his heart sinful.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾, regarding the clarifying of testimony and its concealment.

Makhul narrated from Abu Burdah, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Whoever conceals testimony when he is called to it is like one who gave false testimony."

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. The verse. The scholars differed concerning this verse. Some said: it is specific. Then they differed about the aspect of its specificity. Some of them said: it was revealed concerning the concealment of testimony and its establishment, meaning: ﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾, O witnesses, of concealing testimony, ﴿or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, 'Ikrimah, the narration of Mujahid and Muqsim from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is supported by His saying before it: ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾.

Others said: this verse was revealed concerning those among the believers who befriend the disbelievers. Meaning: ﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾ of allegiance to the disbelievers, or conceal it, Allah will call you to account. This is the view of Muqatil and al-Waqidi. It is supported by His saying in Al 'Imran: [﴿Say: Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it﴾] [[Surah Al 'Imran: 29.]] — concerning allegiance to the disbelievers — and it is supported by what precedes it.

Others said: this verse is general. Then they differed about the aspect of its generality. Some of them said: it is abrogated.

The narration was transmitted with different wordings.

He said: When this verse was revealed, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Mu'adh ibn Jabal and some of the Ansar came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and knelt, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, no verse has ever been revealed that weighed more heavily upon us than this verse. We do not like that any of us should have the world and all that is in it, and we are held to account for what we speak to ourselves about. We are destroyed, by Allah!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "So it was revealed." They said: "We are destroyed, and we have been burdened with deeds we cannot bear."

He said: "Perhaps you are saying as the Children of Israel said to Moses, peace be upon him: 'We hear and we disobey' (sami'na wa 'asayna). Rather, say: 'We hear and we obey' (sami'na wa atha'na)."

It weighed heavily on them, so they remained in this state for a year. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent relief and ease with His saying: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. So this verse abrogated what came before it.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has overlooked for my community what they speak to themselves about, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it."

This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, 'A'ishah, and Ibn 'Abbas through the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata'. Among the Successors and those who followed them: Muhammad ibn Sirin, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Musa ibn 'Ubaydah, Qatadah, al-Kalbi and Shaybah.

Sa'id ibn Marjanah said: "While we were sitting with 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, he recited this verse: ﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾. Ibn 'Umar said: 'If Allah takes us to account for it, we will certainly be destroyed.' Then he wept until he could be heard." Ibn Marjanah said: "I mentioned that to Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: 'May Allah forgive Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. The Muslims experienced from it, when it was revealed, what he experienced. So Allah revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾. And whisperings were something beyond the Muslims' ability to bear, so the matter came down to speech and action, and that verse was abrogated.'"

Others said: this verse is muhkam (definitive) and not abrogated, because abrogation (naskh) and reports are not permitted except in a report that contains a command, a prohibition, or a condition. Then they differed about its interpretation. A group of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has affirmed earning (kasb) for the heart, and said: ﴿for what your hearts have earned﴾. Every doer is held to account for his earning and recompensed for his deed. [So do not suppose] that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will leave a servant on the Day of Resurrection without informing him of anything he secretly or openly did, whether a movement of his limbs or a [whisper] in his heart, and then He will forgive whom He wills and punish whom He wills for what He wills.

The meaning of the verse: "If you show what is in yourselves of [sins] and act upon it, that is, if you intend it in yourselves and then conceal it, He will inform you of it and call you to account for it, then forgive whom He wills and punish whom He wills."

This is the meaning of the statements of al-Hasan, al-Rabi', Qays ibn Abi Hazim, and the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. It is supported by His saying: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned﴾.

Others said: the meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, calls His creatures to account for all that they have shown of their deeds and concealed, and punishes them for it. However, His punishment of them for what they concealed without doing it is by what befalls them in this world of calamities, misfortunes and matters over which they grieve and suffer. This is the view of 'A'ishah.

It is narrated that she was asked about this verse and she said: "No one has asked me about it except that I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'O 'A'ishah, this is Allah's reproach of the servant for what afflicts him of fever and misfortune, even a thorn or a loss of goods, which he places in his pocket and then loses, and is distressed over it, then finds it in his pocket. Until the believer comes out of his sins as red gold comes out of the purse.'"

His saying supports this: ﴿Whoever does evil will be recompensed for it﴾ [[Surah al-Nisa': 123.]], meaning in this world.

Mujahid said, in the narration of Mansur and Ibn Abi Jurayj: "﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves or conceal it﴾, meaning of certainty and doubt."

Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: "﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾, meaning Islam, ﴿or conceal it﴾, meaning faith."

Others said: "﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾, meaning what is in your hearts of what you know and have resolved upon, ﴿or conceal it﴾, so that you do not reveal it while you are determined and resolved upon it, ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾. As for what you speak to yourselves about that you have not resolved upon, Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity and does not hold you to account for it. The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿Allah does not hold you to account for what is unintentional in your oaths, but He holds you to account for what your hearts have earned﴾ [[Surah al-Baqarah: 225.]]."

It is narrated from 'Abd ibn al-Mubarak that he said: "I said to Sufyan: 'Is a servant held accountable for a mere intention?' He said: 'If it is a firm resolve, he is held accountable for it.'" It is narrated from 'Amr ibn Jarir that he said: "I went out when I was young for a matter I had resolved upon, and I passed by Abu Talib the storyteller while people were gathered around him. The first thing he said was: 'O you who resolve upon sin, know that the Creator of resolve is watching your resolve.' He said: 'I fell unconscious, by Allah, and I did not come to except in repentance.'"

It is narrated from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid that he said: "The Children of Israel were struck by famine, and a man passed by a heap of sand and said: 'I wish this sand were flour for me, so I could feed the Children of Israel with it.' He was rewarded according to his intention."

It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, that he said: "A man used to go around the scholars saying: 'Who will guide me to a deed by which I may continue always to be doing something for Allah, Mighty and Majestic? For I love that no hour of night or day should pass over me without my being engaged in it.' He was told: 'You have found what you need, so do good as much as you can. When you slacken or leave it, then resolve upon doing it, for indeed one who resolves upon a good deed is like one who does it.'" This is what is meant by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The intention of the believer is better than his deed," because deeds come to an end but intentions do not come to an end.

Muhammad ibn 'Ali said: "The meaning of the verse: ﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾, of the outward deeds, ﴿or conceal it﴾, of the inward states, ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾: the worshipper for his actions and the knower for his states."

Others said: "Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: [On the Day] when secrets are tested and hidden thoughts are brought out, and My scribes wrote down of your deeds only what appeared of them, while I am aware of your secrets which they did not know and did not record. So I will inform you of that and call you to account for it, so that you know that not even the weight of an atom of your deeds escapes Me, and then I forgive whom I will and punish whom I will."

As for the believers, He informs them of it and forgives them and does not hold them to account for it, displaying His grace. As for the disbelievers, He informs them of it and punishes them for it, displaying His justice.

So the meaning of the verse: ﴿And if you reveal what is in yourselves﴾ so that you act upon it, ﴿or conceal it﴾ of what you have harboured, kept secret and intended, ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾, informing you and making you aware of it, so He forgives the believers and punishes the disbelievers. This is the meaning of the statements of al-Dahhak and al-Rabi', and the narrations of al-'Awfi and al-Walibi from Ibn 'Abbas. It is supported by His saying: ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾.

He did not say "will hold you to account" (yu'akhidhukum), and reckoning (muhasabah) is not the same as punishment ('iqab). Reckoning is established, while punishment is dropped. Among what supports this is the hadith of private consultation (najwa), which is what

Qatadah narrated from Safwan ibn Muhriz, who said: "While we were circumambulating the House with 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, a man approached him and said: 'O Ibn 'Umar, what did you hear from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about private consultation (najwa)?' He said: 'I heard the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The believer draws near to his Lord until He places His hand (kanaf) upon him, and He makes him confess his sins, saying: 'Did you commit such-and-such?' He says: 'My Lord, I know.' Then He makes him stand before his sins, one sin at a time, and Allah says: 'I covered them for you in the world, and today I forgive them for you.' No angel brought near and no prophet sent has been shown this." As for the disbelievers and hypocrites, they are called out before the heads of the witnesses: ﴿These are they who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾."

Al-A'mash, from Ma'rur ibn Suwayd, from Abu Dharr, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and it will be said: 'Present to him the minor sins.' They will be presented to him, and it will be said: 'You did such-and-such on such-and-such a day.' He will admit and not deny, while the major sins are concealed from him, and he is fearful of them. Then it will be said: 'Give him in place of every evil deed a good deed.' He will say: 'I have sins that I do not see here.'"

He said: Abu Dharr said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) laugh until his molars showed."

Al-Husayn ibn Muslim said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will call the believers to account on the Day of Resurrection with kindness and grace, and the disbelievers with proof and justice."

﴿Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Muhaysin, al-Hasan, 'Asim and Ya'qub read both verbs in the nominative (raf'), and Abu Hatim preferred this. Ibn 'Abbas read both in the accusative (nasb), and the rest read both in the jussive (jazm). The jussive is on the conjunction (nasaq), the nominative is on the beginning of a sentence, meaning "so He forgives," and the accusative is on the shift (sarf), and it was said: by implying the light "an" (an al-khafifah).

Tawus narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "﴿Then He forgives whom He wills﴾, the great sin, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾ for the minor sin." It is like His saying: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [[Surah al-Anbiya': 23.]].

﴿And Allah is over all things competent.﴾

﴿The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord﴾. The verse.

Talhah ibn Musarrif narrated from Murrah, from 'Abd Allah, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he reached the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), and he was given the five prayers, and the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and forgiveness for whoever of his community does not associate anything with Allah, except the grave sins (al-muqhimat)." [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/387. Al-muqhimat are the great sins that cast their doers into the Fire.]]

It is narrated from 'Alqamah ibn Qays, from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amr, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down two verses from the treasures of the Throne, which the Merciful, Mighty and Majestic, wrote two thousand years before He created the creation. Whoever recites them after the late evening prayer twice, they suffice him in place of the night prayer: ﴿The Messenger has believed...﴾ to the end of the surah."

Abu Qilabah narrated from Abu al-Ash'ath al-Hamdani, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, wrote a book two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, in which He revealed two verses and concluded Surat al-Baqarah with them. They are not recited in a house for three nights, and a devil approaches it."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever recites the two verses at the end of Surat al-Baqarah in a night, they will suffice him."

Musa ibn Hudhayfah narrated from Ibn al-Munkadir, who said: "He related to us a hadith which he traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'At the end of Surat al-Baqarah are verses which are both Qur'an and supplication, and which please the Most Merciful.'"

[[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/231.]]

It is also reported in a hadith that it was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The house of Thabit ibn Uways ibn Shammas glows tonight like lamps." He said: "Perhaps he is reciting Surat al-Baqarah." Thabit was asked, and he said: "I recited Surat al-Baqarah."

﴿The Messenger has believed in what was revealed to him from his Lord,﴾

It was said: This verse was revealed when what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, threatened to call them to account for, regarding what their souls concealed, weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "Perhaps you are saying 'We hear and we disobey' as the Children of Israel said?" They said: "Rather, we say 'We hear and we obey.'" Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed praise of them and information about them: ﴿The Messenger has believed﴾, that is, he affirmed ﴿in what was revealed to him from his Lord.﴾

Qatadah said: When ﴿The Messenger has believed﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And it is right that he should believe."

﴿And the believers.﴾

In the reading of 'Ali and 'Abd Allah: "And the believers believed; each believed in Allah..."

**Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 2, verses 283–286 (part 2 of 2)**

He made the verb singular according to the wording of *kull* (each). The meaning is: each one of them believed. Had he said *āmanū* (they believed), it would also have been permitted, because *kull* can be used in both the singular and the plural. As an example of the singular, the verse says: ﴿Each one knows its prayer and its glorification﴾ [24:41]. As an example of the plural, it says: ﴿Each one of them will come back to Us﴾ [21:93], and ﴿Each one of them will come to Him humbled﴾ [27:88].

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Yahya, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read *wa-kitabihi* (and His Book) in the singular, with *alif*. The rest read *wa-kutubihi* (and His Books) in the plural, which is the apparent reading, as in the verse ﴿and His angels and His messengers﴾.

The singular has two possible explanations. The first is that they meant the Qur'an specifically. The second is that they meant all the Books. The Arabs say: "milk has increased" and "dirhams and dinars have increased in people's hands," meaning the *albān* (kinds of milk) and the *darāhim* and *danānīr* (coins). Evidence for this is the verse ﴿So God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and as warners, and sent down with them the Book﴾ [2:213].

*wa-rusulihi*: the plural of *rasūl* (messenger).

Al-Hasan and Ibn Salama read the *sīn* with a sukun (*wa-rusulihi* with the vowel omitted) because of the number of vowels. Al-'Abbas reported from Ibn 'Amr, and it was also narrated from Nafi', that they read *wa-kutubihi wa-rusulihi* with the vowels shortened. The rest pronounce them with the full vowels, in accordance with the original form.

﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾, believing in some and disbelieving in others, as the Jews and Christians did. In the codex of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) the reading is *lā nufarriqanna* (we shall not make any distinction).

Jarir ibn 'Abdullah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read *lā yufarriqu* with a *yā'* (they make no distinction), meaning "none of them [the believers] makes any distinction." On this reading the sentence may be a report about the Messenger.

The rest read it with *nūn* (*lā nufarriqu*), with an implied "saying" (*qawl*) before it, the meaning being: "and they say, 'We make no distinction.'" This is like the verse ﴿and the angels will enter upon them from every gate, saying, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [13:23], and like the verse ﴿As for those whose faces turn black, [it will be said:] "Did you disbelieve?"﴾ [3:106], meaning: "it will be said to them, 'Did you disbelieve?'" Also His words ﴿If only you could see when the guilty bow their heads before their Lord, [saying:] "Our Lord, we have seen and heard"﴾ [32:12], meaning: "they say, 'Our Lord.'" And the verse ﴿Those who take protectors besides Him [say]: "We only worship them"﴾ [39:3], meaning: "they say, 'We only worship them.'"

*Bayna* (between) governs two or more things. He said *bayna aḥadin* (between anyone) rather than *ā'ḥād* (individuals), because *ā'ḥād* can refer to one or to many. God says: ﴿Not one of you could withhold Us from him﴾ [69:47].

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Booty was not made lawful for anyone with black heads before you" [Tabari, 10/59, where the wording is "before you" (min qablikum)].

Ru'ba said:
"What has become of the people, [who] have been pounded and crushed, / they fear no one, [since] they have been driven away."

﴿And they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾: their saying *we hear and we obey* is in contrast to the saying of the Jews.

Hakim ibn Jabir reported that when the verse ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ was revealed, Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "God, the Mighty and Majestic, has favoured you and your community. Ask, and you will be given." So the Messenger of God asked, and He said: ﴿Your forgiveness﴾.

*Ghufrānaka* (Your forgiveness) is in the accusative as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun, from the verb *ghafara*), meaning "we ask You to forgive," like our saying *subḥānaka* (glory be to You), meaning "we glorify You."

It was also said that the meaning is: "we ask You for forgiveness."

﴿Our Lord, and to You is the final return.﴾

﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.﴾ The apparent meaning of the verse is the granting of needs. It contains an implied request and need, as if they had said to Him: "Burden us beyond our capacity," and God answered: "God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity."

*Al-wus'* (capacity) is the name for what a person can bear and what is within his power, and what is difficult for him. It was also said: what is difficult for him and what strains him.

Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla al-Shami read *lā yukallifu Allāhu nafsan illā wasi'ahā* with a *wāw* vowelled with a fatha and *sīn* with a kasra, as a verb, meaning: "except that His command would be within its capacity," or he meant "except what it has the capacity for," with the word *mā* ("what") omitted.

The scholars differed about its interpretation. Ibn 'Ata', al-Suddi and most of the commentators said it refers to the inner speech of the soul (*ḥadīth al-nafs*). When God revealed ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it﴾ [2:284], the believers came, [in general], and said: "O Messenger of God, this is [too much]. We are to repent for the deeds of the limbs, but how can we repent for whispering and how can we refrain from the inner speech of the soul?" So God revealed: ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾, meaning its power, and the inner speech of the soul was something they could not bear.

Ibn 'Abbas said in another report: [...] (unreadable in the manuscript). The believers in particular: God made the matter of their religion easy for them. He did not burden them except with what they were able to bear. He said: ﴿God intends ease for you﴾ [2:185], and He said: ﴿He has not placed upon you any difficulty in religion﴾ [22:78], and He said: ﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾ [64:16].

Al-Tha'alibi said: I heard Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi say: I heard Abu 'Abdullah Muhammad ibn Nafi' al-Sijzi say in Herat: I heard Abu Yazid Hatim ibn Mahbub al-Shami say: I heard 'Abd al-Jabbar ibn al-'Ala' al-'Attar say: Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna was asked about the words of God, ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity﴾.

He said: "[It means] except its ease, not its hardship. He does not burden it with its strength, for if He burdened it with its strength, the effort would reach its utmost limit."

Al-Tha'alibi said: This is a good statement, because *al-wus'* is less than *al-ṭāqa* (strength). Some of the theologians said: it means "except what is within its capacity and lawful for it," as one says: "Can this matter be within your capacity?" meaning: "Is this lawful for you from God?" God makes clear that what He has imposed on His servants is within their capacity for them. And God knows best.

﴿It has what it earned﴾: that is, the soul has what it did of good and righteous deeds; it has its reward and recompense. ﴿And against it is what it has earned﴾: that is, of evil, by evil deeds, the burden of them is upon it.

﴿Our Lord, do not take us to account﴾: do not punish us.

The scholars of meaning (*ahl al-ma'ānī*) said: It came in the form of *mufā'ala* (the pattern of reciprocity), though the action is one, because the wrongdoer has plotted and found a way to it, and it is as if he has helped the one who punishes him for his sin and takes him to account for it, so he shares in the taking to account.

﴿If we forget or make a mistake﴾: some of them took this to be forgetting, which is heedlessness.

Al-Kalbi said: When the Children of Israel forgot something of what they had been commanded, or made a mistake, punishment was hastened upon them, and some food or drink was forbidden to them in proportion to that sin. So God commanded His Prophet and the believers to ask Him not to take them to account for this.

Others said it is forgetting in the sense of abandoning and neglecting. God says: ﴿They forgot God, so He caused them to forget themselves﴾ [59:19]. The first explanation is better.

﴿Or make a mistake﴾: some took this to mean intention and deliberation. It is said: "So-and-so erred (*khati'a*)" when he deliberately commits a fault, [in the sense of *yakhta'u khata'an* and *khaṭa'an*].

God says: ﴿Indeed, their killing them was a great sin﴾ [17:31]. And Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt recited:
"Your servants commit faults, and You are the Lord, / the fates and the decrees will suffice you."

Others took it to mean error, which is ignorance and heedlessness, and this is more correct, because a sin committed deliberately is not pardoned, but rather it is subject to God's will, so long as it is not disbelief.

'Ata' said: ﴿If we forget or make a mistake﴾, meaning: if we are ignorant or commit it deliberately.

Ibn Zayd said: ﴿If we forget﴾ something of what You have made obligatory upon us, ﴿or make a mistake﴾ regarding something You have forbidden us.

Al-Zuhri said: 'Umar heard a man say: "O God, forgive me my errors." He said: "Errors are forgiven, but say: 'O God, forgive me my deliberate faults.'"

Al-Nabati said: Ibn Fanjawayh told us: 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Shanba told us: 'Abdullah ibn al-Mussafa al-Sukkari told us: Muhammad ibn al-Musalla al-Muhammadi told us: al-Walid told us: Malik told us, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The error and forgetting of my community have been lifted, and what they were compelled to do."

﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (*iṣr*)﴾: some said it means a covenant, a contract and a pact which we cannot bear or maintain, so that You punish us for falling short in it, ﴿as You laid it upon those before us﴾, meaning the Jews, who did not keep it, so You destroyed and punished them. This is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata', Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi', Muqatil, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi, Ibn Jurayj and al-Farra', and it is the report of 'Atiyya and 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas. The evidence for it is the verse ﴿And you took upon that My covenant (*iṣrī*)﴾ [3:81], meaning My covenant.

Others said: *al-iṣr* means a heavy weight. That is: do not make it difficult for us, do not make it severe, and do not make the burden heavy upon us as You made it heavy upon those before us from the Jews. God obligated them to fifty prayers, commanded them to give the profit of their wealth in zakat, and whoever had a garment touched by impurity had to cut it off, and whoever committed a sin found in the morning that his sin was written on his door, and other such burdens and fetters that were upon them. This is the meaning of the words of 'Uthman ibn 'Ata', Malik ibn Anas, Abu 'Ubayda, al-Mu'arrikh, al-Qutaybi and Ibn al-Anbari. The evidence for it is His words: ﴿and He removes from them their burden and the fetters that were upon them﴾ [7:157].

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: do not place upon us a sin for which there is no repentance or expiation. And *al-iṣr* refers to the binding, the contract and the rulings, and the thing by which things are bound is called *al-iṣr*. One says: "between him and so-and-so is a bond (*iṣra*) of kinship," and "he does not bind me" (*mā ta'aṣṣarnī*), meaning: "he does not bind me to himself by covenant or kinship."

He said: Abu al-Qasim al-Sadusi recited to me, who said: al-Sami' ibn Muhammad al-Hashimi recited to me, who said: Abu al-Hasan al-'Absi recited to us, who said: al-'Abbas ibn Muhammad al-Duri al-Shafi'i recited to us:
"If there is no blessing from a man to me, / nor between us a bond,
[and I have no] profit in his friendship, / nor any gain in this world or the next,
and I have spent my life at his door, / then that is indeed a losing bargain."

﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾, meaning: do not impose upon us actions beyond our power. This is the view of Qatada, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Some said: it is the inner speech of the soul and whispering. It is reported from Abu Thawban, from his father, from Makhul, concerning the words of God ﴿and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾, that he said: [...] (gap in the manuscript).

It is also reported from Abu al-Qasim, from Malik al-Shami, that Abu Idris al-Khawlani used to come to his companions and say: "O God, protect me [...] (gap in the manuscript) to Hell."

Sufyan al-Thawri, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, concerning the words of God ﴿and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾, said: "It is hardship."

It is also reported from Abu al-Qasim 'Abdullah ibn Yahya ibn 'Ubayd, who said: I heard Abu al-Qasim 'Abdullah ibn Ahmad say: I heard Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab [say concerning] ﴿and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾: "It means love (*'ishq*)." Khabbab said: I attended the gathering of Dhu al-Nun al-Misri in his tent. He spoke that day about love for God, and eleven people died in the gathering. He cried out, "Do not let anyone who wants more go out," and [then] said: "O Abu al-Qays, you have mentioned love for God, so mention love for created beings." Dhu al-Nun sighed a deep sigh, put his hand to his face, stood up straight and said to him:

"Their hearts were created, their eyes were made to shed tears; they have become accustomed to sleeplessness and parted from sleep. Their nights are long, their sleep short, their sorrows are not to be counted, and their worries are not to be bound. Their affairs are difficult, their tears abundant, their eyes weeping, their eyelids wounded."

Their companions, family and neighbours [turned against] them. Yahya said: "If the punishment were left in my hand on the Day of Resurrection, I would not punish lovers, because their sins are compelled, not chosen."

Ibn Jurayj said: it is the transformation into apes and swine. Some said: it is the gloating of enemies. 'Abd al-Mun'im ibn Idris reported from his father, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: It was said to Ayyub (peace be upon him): "What was the hardest thing for you during the length of your trial?" He said: "The gloating of enemies." Ibn al-A'rabi recited:
"All calamities may pass over a young man, / and become easy, except the gloating of envious people.
Indeed, calamities pass their days, / but the gloating of enemies is lying in wait."

It was also said: it is separation and parting, we seek refuge in God from it. It was said: cutting off the limbs is easier than cutting off union. Al-Nazzam said: If parting had a form, it would not [harm] sins, it would crush the mountains, and it would scorch the ghada tree, less than [...] (unreadable word). And if God, glory be to Him, punished the people of the Fire with separation, they would find rest in [the heat of the punishment].

﴿And pardon us﴾: that is, overlook and forgive our shortcomings and sins. ﴿And forgive us﴾: cover our sins, pass over them, and do not punish us. ﴿And have mercy on us﴾: for we cannot reach obedience to You, nor abandon disobedience to You, except by Your mercy. It was also said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ from transformation, ﴿and forgive us﴾ for the evil deeds, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ from slander. It was also said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ for actions, ﴿and forgive us﴾ for words, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ for contracts and guarantees. It was also said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ for minor sins, ﴿and forgive us﴾ for major sins, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ by making our scale heavy despite our poverty. It was also said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ in the agonies of death, ﴿and forgive us﴾ in the darkness of the grave, ﴿and have mercy on us﴾ in the darkness of the grave.

﴿You are our Protector﴾: that is, our helper, our guardian, our patron, and the one who is in charge of us. ﴿So help us against the disbelieving people.﴾

'Ata', from Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning the words of God ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ up to ﴿and to You is the final return﴾, said: "I have forgiven you." ﴿God does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. It has what it earned, and against it is what it has earned. Our Lord, do not take us to account if we forget or make a mistake.﴾ He said: "I will not take you to account." ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden﴾. He said: "I will not lay it upon you." ﴿And do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾. He said: "I will not burden you." ﴿And pardon us, and forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so help us against the disbelieving people.﴾ He said: "I have pardoned you, forgiven you, shown mercy to you and helped you against the disbelieving people."

Sufyan reported from Abu Ishaq, from a man, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, that when he finished reciting al-Baqara he would say: "Amin."

Followed by the sura of Al 'Imran.

﴿And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.﴾ And may God bless Muhammad, the best of the first and the last, and his pure and good family, all of them, and grant them peace.

Masruq said: "Indeed, the treasure of the poor man is the sura of al-Baqara and Al 'Imran, which he recites in the last part of the night."

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "Whoever recites al-Baqara and Al 'Imran on Friday night will have a light between [the wonderful] 'Ajibaa and [the strange] Gharibaa." 'Ajiba is the seventh earth and Gharība is the Throne.

Masruq said: "Whoever recites the sura of al-Baqara on a night will be crowned with it."

In a hadith: "The sura in which al-Baqara is mentioned is the tent-pole (*fusṭāṭ*) of the Qur'an."

**Question:** If it is asked: Is it permissible for God to burden anyone with what he cannot bear?

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said to him: If you mean what is not within his power, that is impossible. If you mean what is heavy for him, then God may do of that what He wills, because what He imposed on the Children of Israel, such as killing themselves, was heavy for them.

This is like your saying: "I cannot bear the speech of so-and-so," which does not mean that it is not within your power, but that it is heavy upon you.

If it is asked: Is it permissible for the Just One to burden beyond capacity?

It is said: He has informed us of His vastness, His mercy and His kindness toward His creation, just as He negated injustice from Himself, even though injustice cannot be imagined from Him in any way. Some people said: If He burdened beyond capacity, it would be His right, because creation is His creation and command is His command, but He informed us that He does not do it. And that is enough.
